title: Seeing Fast and Slow: Learning the Flow of Time in Videos
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the fundamental limitation of current video models in reasoning about temporal speed by developing methods to perceive and manipulate the flow of time in videos. The authors introduce two key self-supervised training signals for learning playback speed without explicit labels: cross-modal supervision from audio pitch shifts that accompany speed changes, and temporal equivariance constraints enforcing that speed estimates scale proportionally when videos are resampled. Using these techniques, the authors build speed-change detectors and playback-speed estimators, which they then apply to curate a large-scale slow-motion dataset (SloMo-44K) from online videos—the largest generic slow-motion collection to date.

Leveraging this dataset, the authors develop models for two generation tasks: speed-conditioned video generation, which synthesizes events at user-specified temporal speeds, and extreme temporal super-resolution, which converts low-frame-rate, motion-blurred videos into high-frame-rate clear sequences. Both are achieved by finetuning existing video generation architectures with LoRA adapters and speed-conditioning modules.

The speed-change detector achieves 92.4% accuracy, substantially outperforming Gemini 2.5 (59.5%). The playback-speed estimator approaches human-level performance. For temporal super-resolution, the model achieves an 80.3% human-preference win rate over the base model, rising to over 90% on real-world inputs. This work establishes temporal speed as a controllable dimension in video learning, with implications for video forensics, generation, and building world models with richer temporal understanding.
original_abstract: How can we tell whether a video has been sped up or slowed down? How can we generate videos at different speeds? Although videos have been central to modern computer vision research, little attention has been paid to perceiving and controlling the passage of time. In this paper, we study time as a learnable visual concept and develop models for reasoning about and manipulating the flow of time in videos. We first exploit the multimodal cues and temporal structure naturally present in videos to learn, in a self-supervised manner, to detect speed changes and estimate playback speed. We then show that these learned temporal reasoning models enable us to curate the largest slow-motion video dataset to date from noisy in-the-wild sources. Such slow-motion footage, typically filmed by high-speed cameras, contains substantially richer temporal detail than standard videos. Using this data, we further develop models capable of temporal control, including speed-conditioned video generation, which produces motion at specified playback speed, and temporal super-resolution, which tranforms low-FPS, blurry videos into high-FPS sequences with fine-grained temporal details. Our findings highlight time as a manipulable, perceptual dimension in video learning, opening doors to temporally controllable video generation, temporal forensics detection, and potentially richer world-models that understand how events unfold over time.

title: Temporal Taskification in Streaming Continual Learning: A Source of Evaluation Instability
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how the temporal segmentation of continuous data streams into discrete tasks—termed "temporal taskification"—introduces evaluation instability in streaming continual learning (CL). The authors argue that partitioning a stream into tasks is not a neutral preprocessing step but a structural component of the benchmark that can alter experimental conclusions.

The authors formalize temporal taskification and develop a pre-training diagnostic framework comprising plasticity and stability profiles, a profile distance metric between taskifications, and Boundary-Profile Sensitivity (BPS) to assess the structural robustness of different temporal splits without training any CL model. They use the Wasserstein distance to quantify distributional differences between induced tasks and evaluate their framework on the CESNET-Timeseries24 network traffic dataset using four CL methods (continual finetuning, Experience Replay, Elastic Weight Consolidation, and Learning without Forgetting) across 9-day, 30-day, and 44-day taskifications.

Results demonstrate that different taskifications of the same stream produce substantially different CL outcomes in forecasting error, forgetting, and backward transfer across all methods. Shorter windows induce noisier task distributions, higher boundary sensitivity, and lower structural robustness. The profile distance metric successfully captures these structural differences, and BPS reliably identifies fragile taskifications, even under shifted boundary alignments.

These findings highlight that CL benchmark conclusions are not taskification-invariant, urging the community to treat temporal segmentation as an explicit experimental variable rather than an assumed given, with implications for benchmark design and evaluation reliability.
original_abstract: Streaming Continual Learning (CL) typically converts a continuous stream into a sequence of discrete tasks through temporal partitioning. We argue that this temporal taskification step is not a neutral preprocessing choice, but a structural component of evaluation: different valid splits of the same stream can induce different CL regimes and therefore different benchmark conclusions. To study this effect, we introduce a taskification-level framework based on plasticity and stability profiles, a profile distance between taskifications, and Boundary-Profile Sensitivity (BPS), which diagnoses how strongly small boundary perturbations alter the induced regime before any CL model is trained. We evaluate continual finetuning, Experience Replay, Elastic Weight Consolidation, and Learning without Forgetting on network traffic forecasting with CESNET-Timeseries24, keeping the stream, model, and training budget fixed while varying only the temporal taskification. Across 9-, 30-, and 44-day splits, we observe substantial changes in forecasting error, forgetting, and backward transfer, showing that taskification alone can materially affect CL evaluation. We further find that shorter taskifications induce noisier distribution-level patterns, larger structural distances, and higher BPS, indicating greater sensitivity to boundary perturbations. These results show that benchmark conclusions in streaming CL depend not only on the learner and the data stream, but also on how that stream is taskified, motivating temporal taskification as a first-class evaluation variable.

title: Evaluation of Automatic Speech Recognition Using Generative Large Language Models
generated_summary:
This paper systematically evaluates decoder-based large language models (LLMs) for automatic speech recognition (ASR) evaluation, addressing the well-known limitations of traditional metrics like Word Error Rate. The authors investigate three complementary approaches using the HATS dataset, which contains human annotations of speech recognition errors.

First, they employ the "LLM as judge" paradigm, prompting generative LLMs to select the better transcription hypothesis between two candidates. The best-performing models, GPT-4.1 and Qwen3.5-35B, achieve 94% and 92% agreement with human annotators respectively, surpassing both traditional metrics (WER, CER) and sophisticated encoder-based semantic metrics like SemDist with CamemBERT-large. Notably, open-access models rival proprietary ones. Second, the authors evaluate LLM embeddings for computing semantic distance metrics, comparing multiple pooling strategies across various model families. They find that mean pooling generally outperforms last-token representations, that model size is not a determining factor, and that embedding-specific fine-tuning yields the best results. Third, they demonstrate that LLMs can qualitatively classify transcription errors into meaningful categories (identical, useful, bad, incomprehensible) that align consistently with continuous similarity scores derived from human perception data.

These findings suggest that LLMs offer a promising, interpretable alternative for ASR evaluation that better aligns with human perception than conventional metrics, with implications for both automatic annotation and next-generation evaluation frameworks.
original_abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is traditionally evaluated using Word Error Rate (WER), a metric that is insensitive to meaning. Embedding-based semantic metrics are better correlated with human perception, but decoder-based Large Language Models (LLMs) remain underexplored for this task. This paper evaluates their relevance through three approaches: (1) selecting the best hypothesis between two candidates, (2) computing semantic distance using generative embeddings, and (3) qualitative classification of errors. On the HATS dataset, the best LLMs achieve 92--94\% agreement with human annotators for hypothesis selection, compared to 63\% for WER, also outperforming semantic metrics. Embeddings from decoder-based LLMs show performance comparable to encoder models. Finally, LLMs offer a promising direction for interpretable and semantic ASR evaluation.

title: Fine-Tuning Regimes Define Distinct Continual Learning Problems
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how the choice of fine-tuning regime—specifically, which layers remain trainable—affects comparative conclusions in continual learning (CL). The authors argue that trainable depth is not merely an implementation detail but a consequential evaluation variable that can alter the relative ranking of CL methods.

The study formalizes fine-tuning regimes as constrained optimization over fixed parameter subspaces, showing that restricting trainable coordinates changes the feasible update directions for both task-fitting and knowledge-preservation signals. The authors systematically evaluate four standard CL methods (online EWC, LwF, SI, and GEM) across five trainable depth configurations, five benchmark datasets, and eleven task orderings per dataset, using a ResNet-18 backbone.

Key results demonstrate that method rankings are frequently unstable across regimes, with mean Kendall's τ correlation between regime-specific rankings ranging from 0.42 to 0.72 depending on the dataset. The strongest disagreements occur between the most restrictive and most permissive regimes. Additionally, more permissive regimes produce larger gradient magnitudes and greater forgetting, with an increasingly tight coupling between these two quantities as trainable depth grows.

These findings carry significant implications for CL evaluation practices: reporting results under a single fine-tuning setup risks drawing regime-specific conclusions that may not generalize. The authors advocate for treating the adaptation regime as an explicit experimental factor alongside algorithm choice and task order in CL benchmarks.
original_abstract: Continual learning (CL) studies how models acquire tasks sequentially while retaining previously learned knowledge. Despite substantial progress in benchmarking CL methods, comparative evaluations typically keep the fine-tuning regime fixed. In this paper, we argue that the fine-tuning regime, defined by the trainable parameter subspace, is itself a key evaluation variable. We formalize adaptation regimes as projected optimization over fixed trainable subspaces, showing that changing the trainable depth alters the effective update signal through which both current task fitting and knowledge preservation operate. This analysis motivates the hypothesis that method comparisons need not be invariant across regimes. We test this hypothesis in task incremental CL, five trainable depth regimes, and four standard methods: online EWC, LwF, SI, and GEM. Across five benchmark datasets, namely MNIST, Fashion MNIST, KMNIST, QMNIST, and CIFAR-100, and across 11 task orders per dataset, we find that the relative ranking of methods is not consistently preserved across regimes. We further show that deeper adaptation regimes are associated with larger update magnitudes, higher forgetting, and a stronger relationship between the two. These results show that comparative conclusions in CL can depend strongly on the chosen fine-tuning regime, motivating regime-aware evaluation protocols that treat trainable depth as an explicit experimental factor.

title: Seeing Without Eyes: 4D Human-Scene Understanding from Wearable IMUs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a framework for vision-free 4D perception that reconstructs detailed human motion, generates textual activity descriptions, and recovers 3D scene layouts purely from sparse inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals collected by everyday wearable devices such as earbuds, smartwatches, and smartphones. The main contribution lies in repurposing large language models as spatiotemporal reasoners for cross-modal structural reasoning, enabling joint inference across motion, language, and scene modalities from as few as three IMU sensors.

The methodology involves novel tokenization schemes for IMU signals, human motions, and scene layouts, projecting all modalities into a unified embedding space processed by a Phi-1.5 language model backbone. A per-window pose normalization strategy improves motion reconstruction quality, and a two-stage training process—first pretraining on large-scale IMU-to-motion-text data, then finetuning on scarce human-scene interaction datasets—addresses data scarcity. The model formulates prediction as sequential next-token generation with teacher forcing.

Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in motion estimation and strong results in text captioning and scene layout prediction. Critically, the unified joint reasoning framework significantly outperforms modular pipelines that cascade specialized state-of-the-art models, reducing error propagation through shared cross-modal representations. The work also demonstrates a re-localization application where the model recovers absolute position within known environments.

This research establishes that ubiquitous wearable sensors can support rich, privacy-preserving 4D understanding of human activities and environments, offering a scalable alternative to vision-based perception for embodied AI applications.
original_abstract: Understanding human activities and their surrounding environments typically relies on visual perception, yet cameras pose persistent challenges in privacy, safety, energy efficiency, and scalability. We explore an alternative: 4D perception without vision. Its goal is to reconstruct human motion and 3D scene layouts purely from everyday wearable sensors. For this we introduce IMU-to-4D, a framework that repurposes large language models for non-visual spatiotemporal understanding of human-scene dynamics. IMU-to-4D uses data from a few inertial sensors from earbuds, watches, or smartphones and predicts detailed 4D human motion together with coarse scene structure. Experiments across diverse human-scene datasets show that IMU-to-4D yields more coherent and temporally stable results than SoTA cascaded pipelines, suggesting wearable motion sensors alone can support rich 4D understanding.

title: Long-Horizon Manipulation via Trace-Conditioned VLA Planning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a hierarchical framework for long-horizon robotic manipulation that decouples high-level task management from low-level motor control. The main contribution is a modular system where a vision-language model (VLM) serves as a task manager that predicts remaining subtasks and generates visual traces—2D spatial trajectories indicating where the robot should move next—which condition a separate vision-language-action (VLA) executor for short-horizon control.

The methodology centers on receding-horizon task management: the manager is invoked repeatedly, conditioning only on the current observation and a compact textual memory summarizing completed steps. It predicts both remaining subtask sequences and corresponding visual traces, which are rendered onto observations as spatial prompts for the executor. This design enables implicit progress tracking, replanning, and failure recovery without hand-crafted heuristics. Training data is constructed by segmenting demonstration videos into atomic primitives and extracting end-effector trajectories, with additional failure-recovery augmentation.

Evaluations span embodied reasoning benchmarks (RoboVQA, EgoPlan-Bench2, EmbodiedBench), simulation environments (LIBERO, VLABench), and real-world Franka robot experiments. The framework consistently outperforms monolithic VLA baselines and comparable models across all settings, showing particular strength in out-of-distribution generalization with novel objects and instructions.

The significance lies in demonstrating that separating planning from execution creates a scalable, modular architecture where managers and executors can be independently improved or swapped, offering a practical pathway toward robust long-horizon robotic manipulation.
original_abstract: Long-horizon manipulation remains challenging for vision-language-action (VLA) policies: real tasks are multi-step, progress-dependent, and brittle to compounding execution errors. We present LoHo-Manip, a modular framework that scales short-horizon VLA execution to long-horizon instruction following via a dedicated task-management VLM. The manager is decoupled from the executor and is invoked in a receding-horizon manner: given the current observation, it predicts a progress-aware remaining plan that combines (i) a subtask sequence with an explicit done + remaining split as lightweight language memory, and (ii) a visual trace -- a compact 2D keypoint trajectory prompt specifying where to go and what to approach next. The executor VLA is adapted to condition on the rendered trace, thereby turning long-horizon decision-making into repeated local control by following the trace. Crucially, predicting the remaining plan at each step yields an implicit closed loop: failed steps persist in subsequent outputs, and traces update accordingly, enabling automatic continuation and replanning without hand-crafted recovery logic or brittle visual-history buffers. Extensive experiments spanning embodied planning, long-horizon reasoning, trajectory prediction, and end-to-end manipulation in simulation and on a real Franka robot demonstrate strong gains in long-horizon success, robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization. Project page: https://www.liuisabella.com/LoHoManip

title: Characterizing Streaming Decidability of CSPs via Non-Redundancy
generated_summary:
This paper provides a complete characterization of the single-pass streaming complexity of deciding satisfiability for finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), showing it is governed by a structural parameter called non-redundancy. The non-redundancy of a constraint language measures the size of the largest instance over n variables in which every constraint is non-redundant—meaning its removal strictly increases the set of satisfying assignments.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds. The deterministic upper bound follows from a simple greedy algorithm that maintains an equivalent non-redundant sub-instance throughout the stream, requiring space proportional to the non-redundancy times a logarithmic factor. The lower bound is proved via reduction from the Index communication problem, leveraging a novel technical contribution: a binary relation on assignments, where one assignment implies another if every instance satisfied by the first is also satisfied by the second. The authors prove this relation is an equivalence relation for general finite-domain CSPs and for positive Boolean CSPs restricted to non-constant assignments, enabling a unified reduction framework. The characterization extends to positive Boolean CSPs that are non-constant-satisfiable, though counterexamples demonstrate it does not generalize to positive CSPs over larger domains.

The results have several significant implications: they separate streaming satisfiability from exact streaming optimization (governed by multilinear degree), establish that lower bounds for satisfiability transfer to any finite-factor approximation of Min-CSP, and yield quadratic streaming lower bounds for problems like graph q-coloring. This work unifies non-redundancy's role across sparsification, kernelization, and streaming complexity.
original_abstract: We study the single-pass streaming complexity of deciding satisfiability of Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs). A CSP is specified by a constraint language $Γ$, that is, a finite set of $k$-ary relations over the domain $[q] = \{0, \dots, q-1\}$. An instance of $\mathsf{CSP}(Γ)$ consists of $m$ constraints over $n$ variables $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ taking values in $[q]$. Each constraint $C_i$ is of the form $\{R_i,(x_{i_1} + λ_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_k} + λ_{i_k})\}$, where $R_i \in Γ$ and $λ_{i_1}, \ldots, λ_{i_k} \in [q]$ are constants; it is satisfied if and only if $(x_{i_1} + λ_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_k} + λ_{i_k}) \in R_i$, where addition is modulo $q$. In the streaming model, constraints arrive one by one, and the goal is to determine, using minimum memory, whether there exists an assignment satisfying all constraints. For $k$-SAT, Vu (TCS 2024) proves an optimal $Ω(n^k)$ space lower bound, while for general CSPs, Chou, Golovnev, Sudan, and Velusamy (JACM 2024) establish an $Ω(n)$ lower bound; a complete characterization has remained open. We close this gap by showing that the single-pass streaming space complexity of $\mathsf{CSP}(Γ)$ is precisely governed by its non-redundancy, a structural parameter introduced by Bessiere, Carbonnel, and Katsirelos (AAAI 2020). The non-redundancy $\mathsf{NRD}_n(Γ)$ is the maximum number of constraints over $n$ variables such that every constraint $C$ is non-redundant, i.e., there exists an assignment satisfying all constraints except $C$. We prove that the single-pass streaming complexity of $\mathsf{CSP}(Γ)$ is characterized, up to a logarithmic factor, by $\mathsf{NRD}_n(Γ)$.

title: The Sample Complexity of Multicalibration
generated_summary:
This paper resolves the minimax sample complexity of multicalibration—a fairness-motivated strengthening of calibration requiring predictions to be calibrated simultaneously across multiple subpopulations—up to polylogarithmic factors. The main contribution is establishing that the optimal sample complexity for mean Expected Calibration Error (ECE) multicalibration is Θ̃(ε⁻³), and more generally Θ̃(ε⁻³/ᵖ) for weighted Lₚ multicalibration metrics with p ∈ [1,2], separating multicalibration from plain marginal calibration, which requires only Θ(ε⁻²) samples.

The lower bound construction uses a carefully designed hard instance featuring monotone "staircase" regression functions parameterized by binary codes satisfying packing properties, paired with a polylogarithmically-sized group family built via dyadic decompositions and low-correlation codes that can approximate all sign threshold functions. The proof proceeds by showing that any multicalibrated learner must achieve low prediction error on this instance, which in turn forces exact recovery of the hidden parameter, and then applying Fano's inequality to establish the sample lower bound. The matching upper bounds follow from online-to-batch reductions applied to recent online multicalibration algorithms.

The results extend beyond means to a general class of "regular" elicitable properties including expectiles and bounded-density quantiles. Notably, the lower bounds hold even against randomized predictors, closing the gap left by prior work that only addressed deterministic predictors. The matching of batch and online minimax exponents for mean-ECE multicalibration contrasts sharply with marginal calibration, where these settings differ.
original_abstract: We study the minimax sample complexity of multicalibration in the batch setting. A learner observes $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution and must output a (possibly randomized) predictor whose population multicalibration error, measured by Expected Calibration Error (ECE), is at most $\varepsilon$ with respect to a given family of groups. For every fixed $κ> 0$, in the regime $|G|\le \varepsilon^{-κ}$, we prove that $\widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-3})$ samples are necessary and sufficient, up to polylogarithmic factors. The lower bound holds even for randomized predictors, and the upper bound is realized by a randomized predictor obtained via an online-to-batch reduction. This separates the sample complexity of multicalibration from that of marginal calibration, which scales as $\widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and shows that mean-ECE multicalibration is as difficult in the batch setting as it is in the online setting, in contrast to marginal calibration which is strictly more difficult in the online setting. In contrast we observe that for $κ= 0$, the sample complexity of multicalibration remains $\widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-2})$ exhibiting a sharp threshold phenomenon. More generally, we establish matching upper and lower bounds, up to polylogarithmic factors, for a weighted $L_p$ multicalibration metric for all $1 \le p \le 2$, with optimal exponent $3/p$. We also extend the lower-bound template to a regular class of elicitable properties, and combine it with the online upper bounds of Hu et al. (2025) to obtain matching bounds for calibrating properties including expectiles and bounded-density quantiles.

title: Context Unrolling in Omni Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a multimodal foundation model built upon BAGEL that supports any-to-any multimodal learning across text, images, video, and 3D geometry. The central contribution is the concept of **Context Unrolling**, an emergent capability in native multimodal models where the model reasons across heterogeneous modal projections—each representing a partial view of shared world knowledge—to recover a more complete multimodal understanding before producing outputs. Prediction quality improves as the model integrates information from a broader set of modalities.

The methodology expands training beyond image-text pairs to incorporate video, 3D geometry, depth maps, camera transformations, and hidden visual representations. The model employs a mixture-of-experts architecture with 3B active parameters and introduces reasoning-oriented multimodal content during training, including long-form structured descriptions with spatial grounding and geometric constraints, alongside a hidden reasoning space for latent multimodal reasoning.

Key results demonstrate competitive or superior performance across diverse benchmarks: the model matches leading vision-language models like Qwen3-VL and InternVL3.5 on understanding tasks, outperforms strong generators on GenEval2, achieves state-of-the-art camera pose estimation on RealEstate10K, and shows strong zero-shot monocular depth estimation comparable to specialist models—all within a single unified architecture.

The significance lies in demonstrating that unified multimodal pretraining naturally encourages cross-modal reasoning, establishing that structured reasoning across modality-specific projections substantially improves inference quality, positioning native multimodal models as foundational reasoning systems.
original_abstract: We present Omni, a unified multimodal model natively trained on diverse modalities, including text, images, videos, 3D geometry, and hidden representations. We find that such training enables Context Unrolling, where the model explicitly reasons across multiple modal representations before producing predictions. This process enables the model to aggregate complementary information across heterogeneous modalities, facilitating a more faithful approximation of the shared multimodal knowledge manifold and improving downstream reasoning fidelity. As a result, Omni achieves strong performance on both multimodal generation and understanding benchmarks, while demonstrating advanced multimodal reasoning capabilities, including in-context generation of text, image, video, and 3D geometry.

title: CrossCommitVuln-Bench: A Dataset of Multi-Commit Python Vulnerabilities Invisible to Per-Commit Static Analysis
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CrossCommitVuln-Bench, a manually annotated dataset of 15 real-world Python CVEs that are introduced through multiple commits rather than a single change. The authors challenge the fundamental assumption underlying static application security testing (SAST) tools—that vulnerabilities are introduced in isolated commits—by demonstrating that dangerous code patterns can emerge only when contributions from separate commits interact, making them structurally invisible to per-commit analysis.

The dataset captures "cross-commit chains" where one commit introduces a taint source (e.g., a user-controlled parameter) and another introduces a sink (e.g., a dangerous operation), with neither commit appearing malicious in isolation. The authors develop an annotation schema documenting contributing commits, chain rationale, per-commit SAST results, and explanations for why each commit evades individual detection. They establish baseline evaluations using Semgrep and Bandit in both per-commit and cumulative scanning modes, finding a Cross-Commit Detection Rate (CCDR) of zero—neither tool detects any of the vulnerabilities when analyzing commits individually.

The paper also presents a proof-of-concept evaluation using POSTURA, a graph-based cross-commit analysis system maintaining persistent state via a Neo4j threat graph, which detected 60% of a subset of the dataset's CVEs. The dataset and accompanying evaluation scripts are designed to serve as a benchmark for developing cross-commit detection tools, training commit-sequence anomaly models, and motivating CI/CD systems that maintain persistent security state across commits.
original_abstract: We present CrossCommitVuln-Bench, a curated benchmark of 15 real-world Python vulnerabilities (CVEs) in which the exploitable condition was introduced across multiple commits - each individually benign to per-commit static analysis - but collectively critical. We manually annotate each CVE with its contributing commit chain, a structured rationale for why each commit evades per-commit analysis, and baseline evaluations using Semgrep and Bandit in both per-commit and cumulative scanning modes. Our central finding: the per-commit detection rate (CCDR) is 13% across all 15 vulnerabilities - 87% of chains are invisible to per-commit SAST. Critically, both per-commit detections are qualitatively poor: one occurs on commits framed as security fixes (where developers suppress the alert), and the other detects only the minor hardcoded-key component while completely missing the primary vulnerability (200+ unprotected API endpoints). Even in cumulative mode (full codebase present), the detection rate is only 27%, confirming that snapshot-based SAST tools often miss vulnerabilities whose introduction spans multiple commits. The dataset, annotation schema, evaluation scripts, and reproducible baselines are released under open-source licenses to support research on cross-commit vulnerability detection.

title: MathDuels: Evaluating LLMs as Problem Posers and Solvers
generated_summary:
MathDuels introduces a self-play benchmark protocol for evaluating large language models in dual roles as both mathematical problem authors and solvers, addressing the rapid saturation of static benchmarks. Inspired by historical mathematical duels, the framework requires each participating model to generate problems designed to challenge opponents while also solving problems authored by other models.

The methodology involves a three-step prompted generation pipeline with adversarial difficulty amplification. Each of 19 frontier models authors 30 problems across six mathematical domains, and every non-author model attempts each problem. Answers are verified through symbolic checking, and ill-posed problems are filtered out. A Rasch model jointly estimates solver abilities and problem difficulties, producing composite ratings that capture both competencies.

Key findings reveal that authoring and solving capabilities are partially decoupled: the strongest solver (GPT-5.4-high) is not the top-ranked model overall, as Gemini-3.1-Pro-high achieves the highest composite rating through superior problem authoring, generating problems with the lowest average solve rate (62.9%). Critically, when stronger models enter the arena, they author problems that defeat previously dominant solvers at 3.4 times the rate of other participants, demonstrating that benchmark difficulty co-evolves with participant strength.

MathDuels offers a domain-agnostic evaluation paradigm that resists saturation by design, exposing capability dimensions invisible to solve-only benchmarks and providing a sustainable framework for tracking mathematical reasoning progress across models.
original_abstract: As frontier language models attain near-ceiling performance on static mathematical benchmarks, existing evaluations are increasingly unable to differentiate model capabilities, largely because they cast models solely as solvers of fixed problem sets. We introduce MathDuels, a self-play benchmark in which models occupy dual roles: each authors math problems under adversarial prompting and solves problems authored by every other participant. Problems are produced through a three-stage generation pipeline (meta-prompting, problem generation, and difficulty amplification), and validated by an independent verifier that excludes ill-posed questions. A Rasch model (Rasch, 1993) jointly estimates solver abilities and problem difficulties; author quality is derived from the difficulties of each model's authored problems. Experiments across 19 frontier models reveal that authoring and solving capabilities are partially decoupled, and that dual-role evaluation reveals capability separations invisible in single-role benchmarks. As newer models enter the arena, they produce problems that defeat previously dominant solvers, so the benchmark's difficulty co-evolves with participant strength rather than saturating at a fixed ceiling. We host a public leaderboard that updates as new models are released.

title: Vista4D: Video Reshooting with 4D Point Clouds
generated_summary:
Vista4D presents a video reshooting framework that synthesizes dynamic scenes from novel camera trajectories and viewpoints, combining 4D point cloud reconstruction with video diffusion model priors. The main contribution is a temporally-persistent 4D point cloud representation where static pixels remain visible across all frames through segmentation and 4D reconstruction, enabling explicit preservation of source video content and robust camera control even when target viewpoints have minimal overlap with the source.

The methodology involves two key innovations: first, grounding video generation in a 4D point cloud where static elements persist temporally, rather than using per-frame 3D point clouds; second, augmenting training with dynamic multiview video pairs containing realistic depth estimation artifacts from non-frontal views, making the model robust to imperfect real-world reconstruction. The source video is conditioned via in-context frame concatenation alongside point cloud renders processed by a finetuned video diffusion model.

Extensive evaluations demonstrate Vista4D's superiority over state-of-the-art baselines across camera control accuracy, 3D consistency, novel-view synthesis quality, and video fidelity. A user study with 42 participants shows strong preference for Vista4D across all evaluation dimensions. The framework further generalizes to applications including dynamic scene expansion through joint reconstruction of additional scene captures, 4D scene recomposition via direct point cloud editing, and long-video inference using the persistent 4D representation as explicit memory across generation chunks.
original_abstract: We present Vista4D, a robust and flexible video reshooting framework that grounds the input video and target cameras in a 4D point cloud. Specifically, given an input video, our method re-synthesizes the scene with the same dynamics from a different camera trajectory and viewpoint. Existing video reshooting methods often struggle with depth estimation artifacts of real-world dynamic videos, while also failing to preserve content appearance and failing to maintain precise camera control for challenging new trajectories. We build a 4D-grounded point cloud representation with static pixel segmentation and 4D reconstruction to explicitly preserve seen content and provide rich camera signals, and we train with reconstructed multiview dynamic data for robustness against point cloud artifacts during real-world inference. Our results demonstrate improved 4D consistency, camera control, and visual quality compared to state-of-the-art baselines under a variety of videos and camera paths. Moreover, our method generalizes to real-world applications such as dynamic scene expansion and 4D scene recomposition. See our project page for results, code, and models: https://eyeline-labs.github.io/Vista4D

title: VistaBot: View-Robust Robot Manipulation via Spatiotemporal-Aware View Synthesis
generated_summary:
VistaBot introduces a novel framework for view-robust robotic manipulation that combines feed-forward geometric models with video diffusion models, enabling policies trained from a single camera viewpoint to generalize to arbitrary unseen viewpoints without requiring camera calibration or pose information.

The framework comprises three components: (1) 4D geometry estimation, which fine-tunes a feed-forward model to predict depth and relative camera poses, lifting 2D observations into 3D point clouds that are reprojected to the training viewpoint; (2) spatiotemporal latent feature extraction, which uses a conditional video diffusion model with spatial viewpoint interpolation and a temporal memory module to generate consistent latent representations from reprojected views; and (3) closed-loop action learning, where the policy operates directly on diffusion latent features rather than decoded images, improving efficiency and leveraging the model's inherent geometric and object-level understanding.

The authors also introduce the View Generalization Score (VGS), a metric quantifying policy robustness under viewpoint variation. Extensive experiments across eight simulated RLBench tasks and four real-world tasks demonstrate that VistaBot improves VGS by 2.79× over ACT and 2.63× over π₀, while producing high-quality novel view synthesis that outperforms reconstruction-based and generation-based baselines.

VistaBot's significance lies in removing a critical deployment bottleneck—viewpoint sensitivity—from end-to-end manipulation policies, enabling scalable real-world deployment without costly multi-camera setups or demonstration recollection.
original_abstract: Recently, end-to-end robotic manipulation models have gained significant attention for their generalizability and scalability. However, they often suffer from limited robustness to camera viewpoint changes when training with a fixed camera. In this paper, we propose VistaBot, a novel framework that integrates feed-forward geometric models with video diffusion models to achieve view-robust closed-loop manipulation without requiring camera calibration at test time. Our approach consists of three key components: 4D geometry estimation, view synthesis latent extraction, and latent action learning. VistaBot is integrated into both action-chunking (ACT) and diffusion-based ($π_0$) policies and evaluated across simulation and real-world tasks. We further introduce the View Generalization Score (VGS) as a new metric for comprehensive evaluation of cross-view generalization. title: When Prompts Override Vision: Prompt-Induced Hallucinations in LVLMs

original_abstract: Despite impressive progress in capabilities of large vision-language models (LVLMs), these systems remain vulnerable to hallucinations, i.e., outputs that are not grounded in the visual input. Prior work has attributed hallucinations in LVLMs to factors such as limitations of the vision backbone or the dominance of the language component, yet the relative importance of these factors remains unclear. To resolve this ambiguity, We propose HalluScope, a benchmark to better understand the extent to which different factors induce hallucinations. Our analysis indicates that hallucinations largely stem from excessive reliance on textual priors and background knowledge, especially information introduced through textual instructions. To mitigate hallucinations induced by textual instruction priors, we propose HalluVL-DPO, a framework for fine-tuning off-the-shelf LVLMs towards more visually grounded responses. HalluVL-DPO leverages preference optimization using a curated training dataset that we construct, guiding the model to prefer grounded responses over hallucinated ones. title: From Research Question to Scientific Workflow: Leveraging Agentic AI for Science Automation

A deferred generation strategy—regenerating the DAG after measuring actual data volumes—reduces data transfer by up to 92% and eliminates over-parallelization for small genomic regions. The complete pipeline executes queries with LLM overhead below 15 seconds and costs under $0.001 per query.

original_abstract: Scientific workflow systems automate execution -- scheduling, fault tolerance, resource management -- but not the semantic translation that precedes it. Scientists still manually convert research questions into workflow specifications, a task requiring both domain knowledge and infrastructure expertise. We propose an agentic architecture that closes this gap through three layers: an LLM interprets natural language into structured intents (semantic layer); validated generators produce reproducible workflow DAGs (deterministic layer); and domain experts author ``Skills'': markdown documents encoding vocabulary mappings, parameter constraints, and optimization strategies (knowledge layer). This decomposition confines LLM non-determinism to intent extraction: identical intents always yield identical workflows. We implement and evaluate the architecture on the 1000 Genomes population genetics workflow and Hyperflow WMS running on Kubernetes. In an ablation study on 150 queries, Skills raise full-match intent accuracy from 44% to 83%; skill-driven deferred workflow generation reduces data transfer by 92\%; and the end-to-end pipeline completes queries on Kubernetes with LLM overhead below 15 seconds and cost under $0.001 per query.

title: Directional Confusions Reveal Divergent Inductive Biases Through Rate-Distortion Geometry in Human and Machine Vision
generated_summary:

The methodology employs a rate-distortion (RD) framework, treating each system as an information channel and characterizing generalization behavior through efficiency, slope, and curvature signatures of the inferred RD frontier. Mechanistic simulations with controlled asymmetry generators validate the theoretical predictions.

Key results reveal a fundamental dissociation: humans exhibit broad but weak directional asymmetries distributed across many class pairs, while ANNs produce sparse but strong "sink-like" collapses concentrating errors into dominant categories. This dissociation persists across 15 modern architectures including Vision Transformers. Crucially, the organization of asymmetry—not just its magnitude—predicts RD efficiency beyond what accuracy alone captures, with broad-weak and sink-like regimes producing opposite effects on information-error trade-offs. Robustness training reduces aggregate asymmetry toward human levels but fails to recover the human-like breadth-strength profile.

These findings demonstrate that matching human accuracy or even aggregate asymmetry is insufficient for achieving human-like robustness, suggesting that redistributing error structure toward broader, weaker directional patterns represents a more meaningful alignment target.
original_abstract: Humans and modern vision models can reach similar classification accuracy while making systematically different kinds of mistakes - differing not in how often they err, but in who gets mistaken for whom, and in which direction. We show that these directional confusions reveal distinct inductive biases that are invisible to accuracy alone. Using matched human and deep vision model responses on a natural-image categorization task under 12 perturbation types, we quantify asymmetry in confusion matrices and link it to generalization geometry through a Rate-Distortion (RD) framework, summarized by three geometric signatures (slope (beta), curvature (kappa)) and efficiency (AUC). We find that humans exhibit broad but weak asymmetries, whereas deep vision models show sparser, stronger directional collapses. Robustness training reduces global asymmetry but fails to recover the human-like breadth-strength profile of graded similarity. Mechanistic simulations further show that different asymmetry organizations shift the RD frontier in opposite directions, even when matched for performance. Together, these results position directional confusions and RD geometry as compact, interpretable signatures of inductive bias under distribution shift.

title: Low-Rank Adaptation Redux for Large Models
generated_summary:

The discussion covers how structured parameterizations beyond the standard Burer-Monteiro factorization, including SVD-based, Kronecker, and tensor decompositions, can enhance LoRA's expressiveness and efficiency. Beyond standard fine-tuning, the survey maps LoRA's expanding role across the full foundation-model lifecycle, including pre-training, post-training, and deployment serving, as well as applications in diffusion models and multi-modal systems. The authors argue that the relationship between SP and LoRA is bidirectional: SP provides rigorous analytical tools to improve and justify adaptation methods, while the unprecedented scale of modern models introduces challenges that push classical SP boundaries. The survey concludes by identifying open research directions where cross-fertilization between these disciplines can yield more principled and efficient approaches for large-scale model adaptation.
original_abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as the de facto standard for parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of foundation models, enabling the adaptation of billion-parameter networks with minimal computational and memory overhead. Despite its empirical success and rapid proliferation of variants, it remains elusive which architectural choices, optimization techniques, and deployment constraints should guide practical method selection. This overview revisits LoRA through the lens of signal processing (SP), bridging modern adapter designs with classical low-rank modeling tools and inverse problems, as well as highlighting how SP principles can inform principled advances of fine-tuning approaches. Rather than providing a comprehensive enumeration and empirical comparisons of LoRA variants, emphasis is placed on the technical mechanisms underpinning these approaches to justify their effectiveness. These advances are categorized into three complementary axes: architectural design, efficient optimization, and pertinent applications. The first axis builds on singular value decomposition (SVD)-based factorization, rank-augmentation constructions, and cross-layer tensorization, while the second axis deals with initialization, alternating solvers, gauge-invariant optimization, and parameterization-aware methods. Beyond fine-tuning, emerging applications of LoRA are accounted across the entire lifecycle of large models, ranging from pre- and post-training to serving/deployment. Finally, open research directions are outlined at the confluence of SP and deep learning to catalyze a bidirectional frontier: classical SP tools provide a principled vocabulary for designing principled PEFT methods, while the unique challenges facing modern deep learning, especially the overwhelming scale and prohibitive overhead, also offer new research lines benefiting the SP community in return.

title: UniGenDet: A Unified Generative-Discriminative Framework for Co-Evolutionary Image Generation and Generated Image Detection
generated_summary:
UniGenDet introduces the first unified generative-discriminative framework for co-evolutionary image generation and AI-generated image detection, addressing the fundamental limitation that these two tasks have traditionally been optimized in isolation. The core insight, inspired by Feynman's principle that creation and understanding are intrinsically linked, is that generation and detection can mutually enhance each other through closed-loop training.

The framework employs a two-stage training paradigm built upon the BAGEL multimodal model. The first stage, Generation-Detection Unified Fine-tuning (GDUF), jointly trains detection and generation using a Symbiotic Multi-modal Self-Attention module that transfers generative distributional knowledge to improve detection accuracy and interpretability. The second stage, Detector-Informed Generative Alignment (DIGA), uses the trained detector as a frozen authenticity teacher, aligning the generator's internal features with real image representations to reduce detectable artifacts.

UniGenDet achieves 98.0% detection accuracy on the FakeClue dataset, surpassing the best open-source model by 40.2%, and demonstrates strong cross-dataset generalization with 98.6% accuracy on DMImage and 98.1% on ARForensics. For generation, it achieves an FID of 17.5, significantly improving over the baseline BAGEL model's 22.9, confirming that detection feedback enhances visual realism.

This work establishes a new paradigm for addressing the escalating arms race between generative AI and content authentication, demonstrating that bidirectional co-optimization yields superior performance in both tasks compared to isolated approaches.
original_abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in both image generation and generated image detection. Despite their rapid, yet largely independent, development, these two fields have evolved distinct architectural paradigms: the former predominantly relies on generative networks, while the latter favors discriminative frameworks. A recent trend in both domains is the use of adversarial information to enhance performance, revealing potential for synergy. However, the significant architectural divergence between them presents considerable challenges. Departing from previous approaches, we propose UniGenDet: a Unified generative-discriminative framework for co-evolutionary image Generation and generated image Detection. To bridge the task gap, we design a symbiotic multimodal self-attention mechanism and a unified fine-tuning algorithm. This synergy allows the generation task to improve the interpretability of authenticity identification, while authenticity criteria guide the creation of higher-fidelity images. Furthermore, we introduce a detector-informed generative alignment mechanism to facilitate seamless information exchange. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance. Code: \href{https://github.com/Zhangyr2022/UniGenDet}{https://github.com/Zhangyr2022/UniGenDet}.

title: A Scale-Adaptive Framework for Joint Spatiotemporal Super-Resolution with Diffusion Models
generated_summary:
This paper presents a scale-adaptive framework for joint spatiotemporal super-resolution of precipitation data using diffusion models. The main contribution is a versatile architecture capable of performing video super-resolution at arbitrary spatial and temporal granularities with minimal retuning, requiring only three hyperparameters to be adjusted across different super-resolution factor pairs.

The methodology employs a two-stage architecture: a deterministic U-Net with factorized spatiotemporal attention predicts a mean high-resolution sequence, followed by a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model that generates stochastic residuals capturing fine-scale uncertainty. An optional mass-conservation transform ensures physical consistency by preserving aggregated precipitation totals. Scale adaptivity is achieved by tuning three hyperparameters—input sequence length, noise schedule maximum, and mass-conservation function—for each pair of spatial and temporal super-resolution factors.

Key results demonstrate that the model significantly outperforms baselines across most evaluation metrics, particularly for capturing climatic extremes and high-frequency spatial variations, often by a factor of ten. The optimal hyperparameters exhibit interpretable scaling behavior: larger super-resolution factors require greater noise schedules to promote scenario diversity and slower-growing mass-conservation functions for better calibration.

The framework's significance lies in enabling probabilistic downscaling of climate data at multiple resolutions using a consistent architectural design, though future work aims toward a fully foundational model sharing weights across resolution factors and handling imperfect real-world inputs.
original_abstract: Deep-learning video super-resolution has progressed rapidly, but climate applications typically super-resolve (increase resolution) either space or time, and joint spatiotemporal models are often designed for a single pair of super-resolution (SR) factors (upscaling spatial and temporal ratio between the low-resolution sequence and the high-resolution sequence), limiting transfer across spatial resolutions and temporal cadences (frame rates). We present a scale-adaptive framework that reuses the same architecture across factors by decomposing spatiotemporal SR into a deterministic prediction of the conditional mean, with attention, and a residual conditional diffusion model, with an optional mass-conservation (same precipitation amount in inputs and outputs) transform to preserve aggregated totals. Assuming that larger SR factors primarily increase underdetermination (hence required context and residual uncertainty) rather than changing the conditional-mean structure, scale adaptivity is achieved by retuning three factor-dependent hyperparameters before retraining: the diffusion noise schedule amplitude beta (larger for larger factors to increase diversity), the temporal context length L (set to maintain comparable attention horizons across cadences) and optionally a third, the mass-conservation function f (tapered to limit the amplification of extremes for large factors). Demonstrated on reanalysis precipitation over France (Comephore), the same architecture spans super-resolution factors from 1 to 25 in space and 1 to 6 in time, yielding a reusable architecture and tuning recipe for joint spatiotemporal super-resolution across scales.

title: GiVA: Gradient-Informed Bases for Vector-Based Adaptation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces GiVA (Gradient-Informed Bases for Vector-Based Adaptation), a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models that addresses a key limitation of existing vector-based adaptation approaches. While methods like VeRA and OSoRA are extremely parameter-efficient—training only scaling vectors applied to frozen basis matrices—they require substantially higher ranks than LoRA to achieve comparable performance, resulting in longer training times.

GiVA's core contribution is constructing the frozen basis matrices using information from the first-step full fine-tuning gradient of the downstream task. Specifically, the bases are chosen to minimize the difference between GiVA's first-step update and the full fine-tuning first-step update. Through theoretical analysis, the authors show that the optimal solution involves computing the right singular vectors of the first-step gradient corresponding to the largest singular values. The authors also explore three alternative strategies for initializing the second basis matrix, finding similar performance across approaches.

Extensive experiments across natural language understanding (GLUE), natural language generation (mathematical reasoning, code generation), and image classification tasks demonstrate that GiVA consistently outperforms or matches existing vector-based methods and LoRA while operating at significantly lower ranks—approximately eight times lower than prior vector-based approaches. This rank reduction translates to training times comparable to LoRA while preserving the extreme parameter efficiency characteristic of vector-based methods, making GiVA particularly suitable for resource-constrained deployment scenarios such as federated learning and multi-device fine-tuning.
original_abstract: As model sizes continue to grow, parameter-efficient fine-tuning has emerged as a powerful alternative to full fine-tuning. While LoRA is widely adopted among these methods, recent research has explored vector-based adaptation methods due to their extreme parameter efficiency. However, these methods typically require substantially higher ranks than LoRA to match its performance, leading to increased training costs. This work introduces GiVA, a gradient-based initialization strategy for vector-based adaptation. It achieves training times comparable to LoRA and maintains the extreme parameter efficiency of vector-based adaptation. We evaluate GiVA across diverse benchmarks, including natural language understanding, natural language generation, and image classification. Experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms or achieves performance competitive with existing vector-based adaptation methods and LoRA while reducing rank requirements by a factor of eight ($8\times$).

title: Mapping the Political Discourse in the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies: A Multi-Faceted Computational Approach
generated_summary:

The framework addresses three complementary dimensions: *how* speeches are constructed (stylometric analysis), *what* themes organize debate (contextual topic modeling using BERTopic), and *who* speaks in discursively similar ways (semantic clustering using state-of-the-art document embeddings).

The methodology combines diachronic stylometric and linguistic feature analysis, BERTopic-based thematic modeling aggregated into six macro-themes via LLM-assisted classification, and HDBSCAN clustering of deputy-level semantic fingerprints generated from Mistral-based embeddings. The pipeline is applied to a corpus of 354,719 speeches from 1,582 deputies across 11 major political parties.

Key findings reveal a long-term trend toward shorter, simpler, and more action-oriented speeches, consistent with the mediatization of political communication. Thematic analysis shows a highly reactive legislative agenda that shifts abruptly in response to national crises such as the 2016 presidential impeachment and the COVID-19 pandemic. Semantic clustering identifies 49 distinct discursive groups—far exceeding the number of parties—demonstrating that party affiliation incompletely predicts political speech. Clusters reveal cross-party alignments driven by regional identity and gender, with female deputies forming ideologically heterogeneous but discursively cohesive groups.

The work offers a scalable, replicable methodology for studying legislative discourse that complements traditional roll-call analyses, with implications for comparative legislative studies worldwide.
original_abstract: Analyses of legislative behavior often rely on voting records, overlooking the rich semantic and rhetorical content of political speech. In this paper, we ask three complementary questions about parliamentary discourse: how things are said, what is being said, and who is speaking in discursively similar ways. To answer these questions, we introduce a scalable and generalizable computational framework that combines diachronic stylometric analysis, contextual topic modeling, and semantic clustering of deputies' speeches. We apply this framework to a large-scale case study of the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies, using a corpus of over 450,000 speeches from 2003 to 2025. Our results show a long-term stylistic shift toward shorter and more direct speeches, a legislative agenda that reorients sharply in response to national crises, and a granular map of discursive alignments in which regional and gender identities often prove more salient than formal party affiliation. More broadly, this work offers a robust methodology for analyzing parliamentary discourse as a multidimensional phenomenon that complements traditional vote-based approaches.

title: Nemobot Games: Crafting Strategic AI Gaming Agents for Interactive Learning with Large Language Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Nemobot Games, an AI game programming framework that integrates large language models (LLMs) with Claude Shannon's foundational taxonomy of game-playing machines. The framework extends Shannon's four categories—dictionary-based, mathematically rigorous, heuristic-driven, and learning machines—by leveraging modern LLM capabilities such as reasoning, decision generation, and neuralized memoization to create adaptive game-playing agents.

The methodology centers on Nemobot, an interactive platform where users program and deploy strategic game agents through a chatbot interface. The framework employs collaborative prompt engineering through crowdsourcing, enabling multiple human players to contribute gameplay data that iteratively refines AI strategies. LLM functions serve as modular, inspectable components within a structured programming environment, bridging the gap between static algorithmic approaches and dynamic, language-model-driven gameplay. Games including tic-tac-toe, Nim, and Mancala serve as testbeds spanning Shannon's taxonomy.

Key results demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in both AI development and education. In crowdsourced experiments with 98 students, the Nim game agent mastered optimal strategy by round 43, significantly faster than single-player training scenarios. The platform was successfully evaluated in remote learning environments for gamified AI education.

The significance of this work lies in operationalizing Shannon's vision of self-programming machines through a modern LLM-based paradigm, providing both a research framework for investigating classical game-playing approaches enhanced by LLMs and an educational tool that makes foundational AI concepts accessible through interactive gameplay.
original_abstract: This paper introduces a new paradigm for AI game programming, leveraging large language models (LLMs) to extend and operationalize Claude Shannon's taxonomy of game-playing machines. Central to this paradigm is Nemobot, an interactive agentic engineering environment that enables users to create, customize, and deploy LLM-powered game agents while actively engaging with AI-driven strategies. The LLM-based chatbot, integrated within Nemobot, demonstrates its capabilities across four distinct classes of games. For dictionary-based games, it compresses state-action mappings into efficient, generalized models for rapid adaptability. In rigorously solvable games, it employs mathematical reasoning to compute optimal strategies and generates human-readable explanations for its decisions. For heuristic-based games, it synthesizes strategies by combining insights from classical minimax algorithms (see, e.g., shannon1950chess) with crowd-sourced data. Finally, in learning-based games, it utilizes reinforcement learning with human feedback and self-critique to iteratively refine strategies through trial-and-error and imitation learning. Nemobot amplifies this framework by offering a programmable environment where users can experiment with tool-augmented generation and fine-tuning of strategic game agents. From strategic games to role-playing games, Nemobot demonstrates how AI agents can achieve a form of self-programming by integrating crowdsourced learning and human creativity to iteratively refine their own logic. This represents a step toward the long-term goal of self-programming AI.

title: Task-Driven Co-Design of Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems
generated_summary:

Drawing on monotone co-design theory, the authors introduce implementation-agnostic abstractions for robots, fleets, planners, executors, and evaluators, each formulated as interconnected monotone design problems with explicit functionality-resource interfaces. These modular components are composed into a system-level optimization that computes Pareto-optimal designs satisfying specified task profiles while minimizing resources such as cost, energy, and mission time. The authors advocate a "phase-diagram" perspective, partitioning task and environment parameters into regimes where qualitatively different system architectures are optimal.

Four case studies on coverage and probabilistic target-detection missions demonstrate the framework's capabilities. Results show that joint co-design improves hypervolume by up to 15% over sequential optimization baselines that fix either the planner or robot designs. The studies reveal that heterogeneous fleets can simultaneously reduce cost and completion time compared to homogeneous alternatives, though homogeneous ground fleets may dominate in energy efficiency. Under task uncertainty, the framework identifies Pareto-optimal designs that would not emerge from single-task optimization, exposing non-obvious interactions between planner structure, fleet heterogeneity, and task metrics.

The framework's modularity enables integration of new robot catalogs, planners, and task metrics without structural changes, providing a principled foundation for systematic exploration of multi-agent system design spaces.
original_abstract: Designing multi-agent robotic systems requires reasoning across tightly coupled decisions spanning heterogeneous domains, including robot design, fleet composition, and planning. Much effort has been devoted to isolated improvements in these domains, whereas system-level co-design considering trade-offs and task requirements remains underexplored. In this work, we present a formal and compositional framework for the task-driven co-design of heterogeneous multi-robot systems. Building on a monotone co-design theory, we introduce general abstractions of robots, fleets, planners, executors, and evaluators as interconnected design problems with well-defined interfaces that are agnostic to both implementations and tasks. This structure enables efficient joint optimization of robot design, fleet composition, and planning under task-specific performance constraints. A series of case studies demonstrates the capabilities of the framework. Various component models can be seamlessly incorporated, including new robot types, task profiles, and probabilistic sensing objectives, while non-obvious design alternatives are systematically uncovered with optimality guarantees. The results highlight the flexibility, scalability, and interpretability of the proposed approach, and illustrate how formal co-design enables principled reasoning about complex heterogeneous multi-robot systems.

title: Revealing Geography-Driven Signals in Zone-Level Claim Frequency Models: An Empirical Study using Environmental and Visual Predictors
generated_summary:
This study investigates whether geographic information constructed from alternative data sources can improve Motor Third-Party Liability (MTPL) claim frequency prediction at the zone level when only limited location identifiers (postcodes or coordinates) are available. Using the publicly available Belgian beMTPL97 dataset, the authors construct environmental features from OpenStreetMap and CORINE Land Cover data characterizing the built environment (road density, intersections, amenities) at multiple spatial scales, and extract visual features from 1995 historical orthoimagery using ResNet18 and Nomic vision-transformer embeddings.

The methodology employs Poisson regression through GLMs (with and without Elastic Net regularization), XGBoost, and convolutional neural networks, evaluated via a rigorous six-fold out-of-sample procedure with nested cross-validation. Environmental features are computed at 0.5–5 km radii around postcode centroids, and imagery is extracted at multiple spatial scales.

Key results show that combining geographic coordinates with 5 km-radius environmental features in a regularized GLM yields the strongest improvements—reducing mean test RMSE by 19.02% and cross-fold variability by 74.77% relative to the baseline. CNN-based image models do not outperform simpler tabular specifications, though pretrained Nomic vision-transformer embeddings improve predictions when explicit environmental features are unavailable. Spatial scale selection significantly affects performance across all model families.

This work is the first to systematically evaluate constructed environmental and visual geographic information for MTPL claim frequency modeling, demonstrating that interpretable, openly sourced geographic features can meaningfully enhance actuarial risk assessment.
original_abstract: Geographic context is often consider relevant to motor insurance risk, yet public actuarial datasets provide limited location identifiers, constraining how this information can be incorporated and evaluated in claim-frequency models. This study examines how geographic information from alternative data sources can be incorporated into actuarial models for Motor Third Party Liability (MTPL) claim prediction under such constraints. Using the BeMTPL97 dataset, we adopt a zone-level modeling framework and evaluate predictive performance on unseen postcodes. Geographic information is introduced through two channels: environmental indicators from OpenStreetMap and CORINE Land Cover, and orthoimagery released by the Belgian National Geographic Institute for academic use. We evaluate the predictive contribution of coordinates, environmental features, and image embeddings across three baseline models: generalized linear models (GLMs), regularized GLMs, and gradient-boosted trees, while raw imagery is modeled using convolutional neural networks. Our results show that augmenting actuarial variables with constructed geographic information improves accuracy. Across experiments, both linear and tree-based models benefit most from combining coordinates with environmental features extracted at 5 km scale, while smaller neighborhoods also improve baseline specifications. Generally, image embeddings do not improve performance when environmental features are available; however, when such features are absent, pretrained vision-transformer embeddings enhance accuracy and stability for regularized GLMs. Our results show that the predictive value of geographic information in zone-level MTPL frequency models depends less on model complexity than on how geography is represented, and illustrate that geographic context can be incorporated despite limited individual-level spatial information.

title: A Multi-Stage Warm-Start Deep Learning Framework for Unit Commitment
generated_summary:
This paper presents a multi-stage deep learning framework for solving the unit commitment (UC) problem over a 72-hour planning horizon, combining transformer-based neural networks with post-processing heuristics and MILP solver warm-starting. The main contribution is a three-stage pipeline that bridges the gap between fast but potentially infeasible machine learning predictions and the strict physical constraints required for power system operations.

The methodology employs a transformer architecture with 288 million parameters that uses multi-head self-attention to capture long-range temporal dependencies across the 72-hour window. Zero-initialized learnable positional embeddings allow the model to discover periodic patterns in load and renewable generation curves. The neural network predictions are refined through three deterministic post-processing algorithms that enforce minimum up/down time constraints, minimize excess online capacity through localized economic dispatch, and optimize generator utilization by trimming unnecessary commitment periods. The refined predictions then serve as warm starts for a MILP solver, with a confidence-based variable fixation strategy that fixes high-confidence predictions to reduce the combinatorial search space.

The framework was validated on a single-bus system representing the Irish power system with 51 thermal generators, finishing fourth among 2,300 submissions in EPRI's AI-ccelerating Unit Commitment competition. Results demonstrate significant computational speedups when using ML predictions as warm starts while maintaining solution quality. The authors acknowledge limitations including the assumption of perfect forecasts and the absence of transmission network constraints.
original_abstract: Maintaining instantaneous balance between electricity supply and demand is critical for reliability and grid instability. System operators achieve this through solving the task of Unit Commitment (UC),ca high dimensional large-scale Mixed-integer Linear Programming (MILP) problem that is strictly and heavily governed by the grid physical constraints. As grid integrate variable renewable sources, and new technologies such as long duration storage in the grid, UC must be optimally solved for multi-day horizons and potentially with greater frequency. Therefore, traditional MILP solvers increasingly struggle to compute solutions within these tightening operational time limits. To bypass these computational bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework utilizing a transformer-based architecture to predict generator commitment schedules over a 72-hour horizon. Also, because raw predictions in highly dimensional spaces often yield physically infeasible results, the pipeline integrates the self-attention network with deterministic post-processing heuristics that systematically enforce minimum up/down times and minimize excess capacity. Finally, these refined predictions are utilized as a warm start for a downstream MILP solver, while employing a confidence-based variable fixation strategy to drastically reduce the combinatorial search space. Validated on a single-bus test system, the complete multi-stage pipeline achieves 100\% feasibility and significantly accelerates computation times. Notably, in approximately 20\% of test instances, the proposed model reached a feasible operational schedule with a lower overall system cost than relying solely on the solver.

title: EVENT5Ws: A Large Dataset for Open-Domain Event Extraction from Documents
generated_summary:
This paper introduces EVENT5Ws, one of the largest manually annotated datasets for document-level open-domain event extraction, containing 10,000 news documents annotated with the 5Ws framework (where, when, what, who, and why). Unlike existing closed-domain datasets that rely on predefined event schemas limited to specific event types, EVENT5Ws supports unconstrained event types, addressing the need for algorithms that generalize to diverse real-world events.

The authors employ a systematic annotation pipeline using university students as coders, validated through inter-coder reliability measures. They adopt a one-event-per-document approach, annotating the 5Ws for the main event in each document. The dataset is sourced from news reports across seven newspapers and split into training (8,000), validation (1,000), and test (1,000) sets.

Extensive benchmarking with state-of-the-art large language models—including Gemma 3, Llama 3.1, Qwen 3, Mistral, and T5 Large—under zero-shot and five-shot prompting reveals that all models struggle with document-level event extraction. Models perform relatively better on entity-based aspects (where, when, who) but poorly on what and why, which require deeper contextual reasoning. title: Revisiting Non-Verbatim Memorization in Large Language Models: The Role of Entity Surface Forms

Across 13 LLMs, we examine surface-conditioned factual memorization and find that prediction outcomes often change when only the entity surface form changes. This inconsistency is category-dependent: models are more robust to minor orthographic variations than to larger lexical variations such as aliases and abbreviations. title: Addressing Image Authenticity When Cameras Use Generative AI

title: Gradual Voluntary Participation: A Framework for Participatory AI Governance in Journalism

original_abstract: The integration of AI into journalism challenges participatory design (PD), particularly with respect to stakeholder influence, workplace perceptions, and organizational dynamics. title: Grounding Video Reasoning in Physical Signals

original_abstract: Physical video understanding requires more than naming an event correctly. title: Machine Behavior in Relational Moral Dilemmas: Moral Rightness, Predicted Human Behavior, and Model Decisions

original_abstract: Human moral judgment is context-dependent and modulated by interpersonal relationships. By analyzing the reasoning processes, we identify a clear cross-perspective divergence: while moral rightness remains consistently fairness-oriented, predicted human behavior shifts significantly toward loyalty as relational closeness increases. title: FAccT-Checked: A Narrative Review of Authority Reconfigurations and Retention in AI-Mediated Journalism
