This paper introduces Reshoot-Anything, a self-supervised framework for video reshooting that addresses the critical lack of paired multi-view video data needed to train such models. The main contribution is a scalable, domain-agnostic data pipeline that generates pseudo multi-view training triplets (source, anchor, and target videos) from single monocular videos, eliminating the need for explicit 3D annotations or synthetic datasets.

The methodology works by extracting two distinct clips from a monocular video using smooth random-walk crop trajectories to simulate different camera perspectives. An anchor video is then synthesized by forward-warping the source video's first frame using dense 2D tracking, simulating the artifacts typical of point-cloud-based rendering. The model, built upon a pre-trained Diffusion Transformer (WAN 2.2), processes both source and anchor videos as tokens within self-attention layers using an Offset RoPE mechanism. Targeted augmentations—including 3D-aware noise injection, fluorescent background masking, and random reference frame selection—enhance robustness to inference-time artifacts.

Extensive evaluations on 100 diverse test videos demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in temporal consistency, camera control accuracy, and view synchronization compared to existing methods. The approach successfully handles complex camera motions and preserves fine details where baselines fail.

This work is significant because it shows that implicit 4D scene understanding can emerge from purely 2D self-supervised training, offering a practical and scalable alternative to synthetic data or explicit 4D reconstruction pipelines for video reshooting.
original_abstract: Precise camera control for reshooting dynamic videos is bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of paired multi-view data for non-rigid scenes. We overcome this limitation with a highly scalable self-supervised framework capable of leveraging internet-scale monocular videos. Our core contribution is the generation of pseudo multi-view training triplets, consisting of a source video, a geometric anchor, and a target video. We achieve this by extracting distinct smooth random-walk crop trajectories from a single input video to serve as the source and target views. The anchor is synthetically generated by forward-warping the first frame of the source with a dense tracking field, which effectively simulates the distorted point-cloud inputs expected at inference. Because our independent cropping strategy introduces spatial misalignment and artificial occlusions, the model cannot simply copy information from the current source frame. Instead, it is forced to implicitly learn 4D spatiotemporal structures by actively routing and re-projecting missing high-fidelity textures across distinct times and viewpoints from the source video to reconstruct the target. At inference, our minimally adapted diffusion transformer utilizes a 4D point-cloud derived anchor to achieve state-of-the-art temporal consistency, robust camera control, and high-fidelity novel view synthesis on complex dynamic scenes.

title: Adversarial Robustness of Near-Field Millimeter-Wave Imaging under Waveform-Domain Attacks
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first systematic evaluation of adversarial robustness for near-field millimeter-wave (mmWave) imaging algorithms against waveform-domain physical attacks. The work addresses a critical security gap: while mmWave imaging is widely deployed in safety-critical applications like airport screening, the vulnerability of image reconstruction algorithms to adversarial waveform injection has remained unexplored.

The authors develop a differential imaging attack (DIA) framework that treats the entire mmWave imaging pipeline as a differentiable mapping from received waveforms to reconstructed images, enabling gradient-based optimization of adversarial attack waveforms. They construct a dataset of real measured imaging and attack waveforms using a testbed with two mmWave radars—one serving as the imaging sensor and another as an adversarial transmitter. Three attack strategies are evaluated: target conceal (hiding objects), target swap (replacing objects with fake ones), and randomization attacks.

The framework is applied to 10 representative imaging algorithms spanning classical and learning-based approaches. Results demonstrate that all algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial waveform injection, with attackers achieving high-fidelity manipulation of reconstructed images. Notably, learning-based algorithms exhibit greater robustness than classical algorithms, particularly under power-constrained attacks—a finding that contradicts common assumptions.

These findings carry significant security implications, as adversaries could potentially conceal weapons or inject false targets during screening. The work motivates the development of waveform-domain defense mechanisms, including signal authentication, anomaly detection, and adversarially robust reconstruction algorithms.
original_abstract: Near-field millimeter-wave (mmWave) imaging is widely deployed in safety-critical applications such as airport passenger screening, yet its own security remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a systematic study of the adversarial robustness of mmWave imaging algorithms under waveform-domain physical attacks that directly manipulate the image reconstruction process. We propose a practical white-box adversarial model and develop a differential imaging attack framework that leverages the differentiable imaging pipeline to optimize attack waveforms. We also construct a real measured dataset of clean and attack waveforms using a mmWave imaging testbed. Experiments on 10 representative imaging algorithms show that mmWave imaging is highly vulnerable to such attacks, enabling an adversary to conceal or alter targets with moderate transmission power. Surprisingly, deep-learning-based imaging algorithms demonstrate higher robustness than classical algorithms. These findings expose critical security risks and motivate the development of robust and secure mmWave imaging systems.

title: Back to Source: Open-Set Continual Test-Time Adaptation via Domain Compensation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Open-set Continual Test-Time Adaptation (OCTTA), a realistic setting where deployed models must simultaneously handle continuously shifting domains and unexpected novel classes, both subject to the same domain corruptions. The authors demonstrate that existing methods fail because severe domain shifts collapse feature spaces, making known and unknown class samples inseparable.

To address this, the authors propose DOCO (DOmain COmpensation), a framework built on visual prompt tuning for Vision Transformers. DOCO operates through a self-reinforcing cycle with three components: (1) Back-to-Source Prompt Learning, which updates lightweight prompts using likely in-distribution samples to align target features with source statistics, neutralizing domain shift; (2) Intra-Batch Prompt Propagation, which applies the learned prompts to out-of-distribution samples within the same batch, isolating their semantic novelty for better detection; and (3) Adaptation-Conditioned Sample Splitting, which leverages prompt-adapted features for more accurate ID/OOD separation, creating a virtuous feedback loop.

Extensive experiments on ImageNet-C and LAION-C benchmarks demonstrate DOCO's superiority, achieving a state-of-the-art H-score of 70.1% on ImageNet-C—surpassing the next-best method by 4.7%. The method shows robust performance across varying OOD ratios, domain orderings, and batch sizes, while also excelling in closed-set settings. DOCO's parameter-efficient design, updating only prompt tokens while freezing backbone weights, makes it practical for real-world deployment where computational resources are constrained.
original_abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) aims to mitigate distributional shifts between training and test domains during inference time. However, existing TTA methods fall short in the realistic scenario where models face both continually changing domains and the simultaneous emergence of unknown semantic classes, a challenging setting we term Open-set Continual Test-Time Adaptation (OCTTA). The coupling of domain and semantic shifts often collapses the feature space, severely degrading both classification and out-of-distribution detection. To tackle this, we propose DOmain COmpensation (DOCO), a lightweight and effective framework that robustly performs domain adaptation and OOD detection in a synergistic, closed loop. DOCO first performs dynamic, adaptation-conditioned sample splitting to separate likely ID from OOD samples. Then, using only the ID samples, it learns a domain compensation prompt by aligning feature statistics with the source domain, guided by a structural preservation regularizer that prevents semantic distortion. This learned prompt is then propagated to the OOD samples within the same batch, effectively isolating their semantic novelty for more reliable detection. Extensive experiments on multiple challenging benchmarks demonstrate that DOCO outperforms prior CTTA and OSTTA methods, establishing a new state-of-the-art for the demanding OCTTA setting.

title: Generalizing Test Cases for Comprehensive Test Scenario Coverage
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel three-stage framework for generalizing a single developer-written test case into multiple tests that comprehensively cover diverse test scenarios for a focal method. Unlike existing code coverage-driven approaches, addresses the challenge that meaningful test scenarios often do not align with control-flow branches and are instead implicitly embedded in project design and developer intent.

The framework operates in three stages: (1) enhancing the LLM's understanding of test scenarios through multiple-choice "exams" derived from oracle mutations, which also guide retrieval of relevant project knowledge; (2) generating test scenario templates with variation points that are crystallized into concrete test scenario instances, aided by a prompt auto-tuning technique that automatically learns rules for accurate variation point identification; and (3) generating executable tests from scenario instances with iterative refinement using compiler and runtime feedback.

Evaluated on 506 focal methods from 12 open-source Java projects encompassing 1,637 test scenarios, improves mutation-based and LLM-assessed scenario coverage by 31.66% and 23.08% over ChatTester, respectively. In a field study, 16 of 27 submitted pull request tests were accepted and merged into official repositories, demonstrating practical value.

This work represents a paradigm shift from coverage-driven to scenario-driven test generation, offering a complementary approach that helps developers systematically discover overlooked test scenarios aligned with behavioral intent.
original_abstract: Test cases are essential for software development and maintenance. In practice, developers derive multiple test cases from an implicit pattern based on their understanding of requirements and inference of diverse test scenarios, each validating a specific behavior of the focal method. However, producing comprehensive tests is time-consuming and error-prone: many important tests that should have accompanied the initial test are added only after a significant delay, sometimes only after bugs are triggered. Existing automated test generation techniques largely focus on code coverage. Yet in real projects, practical tests are seldom driven by code coverage alone, since test scenarios do not necessarily align with control-flow branches. Instead, test scenarios originate from requirements, which are often undocumented and implicitly embedded in a project's design and implementation. However, developer-written tests are frequently treated as executable specifications; thus, even a single initial test that reflects the developer's intent can reveal the underlying requirement and the diverse scenarios that should be validated. In this work, we propose TestGeneralizer, a framework for generalizing test cases to comprehensively cover test scenarios. TestGeneralizer orchestrates three stages: (1) enhancing the understanding of the requirement and scenario behind the focal method and initial test; (2) generating a test scenario template and crystallizing it into various test scenario instances; and (3) generating and refining executable test cases from these instances. We evaluate TestGeneralizer against three state-of-the-art baselines on 12 open-source Java projects. TestGeneralizer achieves significant improvements: +31.66% and +23.08% over ChatTester, in mutation-based and LLM-assessed scenario coverage, respectively.

title: Who Defines "Best"? Towards Interactive, User-Defined Evaluation of LLM Leaderboards
generated_summary:
This paper reframes LLM leaderboard evaluation as an interactive sensemaking process rather than a fixed comparison, arguing that users should be able to explore and reweight evaluation data slices according to their own needs and contexts. The authors contend that aggregate rankings obscure meaningful variation across topics, domains, and task types, reflecting dataset composition choices made by benchmark creators rather than the diverse priorities of leaderboard consumers.

The methodology involves three components: an empirical analysis of the LMArena (formerly Chatbot Arena) dataset revealing substantial skews in prompt coverage and significant variability in model rankings across data slices; the design of an interactive visualization tool that allows users to select prompt categories, adjust their relative weights, and observe resulting changes in model rankings; and a qualitative user study (N=10) examining how practitioners engage with this interface.

Key findings show that the LMArena dataset is heavily skewed toward developer- and AI-related topics (30% of prompts), and model rankings diverge sharply across categories such as data processing and mathematics. The user study demonstrates that participants actively use slice-based exploration to critically interpret rankings in relation to their specific use cases, moving beyond reliance on global scores.

The work's significance lies in making evaluation assumptions explicit and manipulable, highlighting that leaderboard outcomes are contingent and value-laden. The authors caution that interactive evaluation does not guarantee fairness or correctness but serves as a mechanism for surfacing and negotiating the inherent contingencies in LLM evaluation.
original_abstract: LLM leaderboards are widely used to compare models and guide deployment decisions. However, leaderboard rankings are shaped by evaluation priorities set by benchmark designers, rather than by the diverse goals and constraints of actual users and organizations. A single aggregate score often obscures how models behave across different prompt types and compositions. In this work, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the dataset used in the LMArena (formerly Chatbot Arena) benchmark and investigate this evaluation challenge by designing an interactive visualization interface as a design probe. Our analysis reveals that the dataset is heavily skewed toward certain topics, that model rankings vary across prompt slices, and that preference-based judgments are used in ways that blur their intended scope. Building on this analysis, we introduce a visualization interface that allows users to define their own evaluation priorities by selecting and weighting prompt slices and to explore how rankings change accordingly. A qualitative study suggests that this interactive approach improves transparency and supports more context-specific model evaluation, pointing toward alternative ways to design and use LLM leaderboards.

title: Misinformation Span Detection in Videos via Audio Transcripts
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the novel task of misinformation span detection in videos, which involves identifying the specific temporal segments within a video where misinformation occurs, rather than simply classifying entire videos as misinformative or not. The authors present two Portuguese-language datasets: BOL4Y, containing 538 videos of Brazil's former president Jair Bolsonaro with 2,355 annotated false claims, and EI22, comprising 77 videos with 78 electoral fraud claims from the 2022 Brazilian presidential election.

The methodology employs a pipeline approach: extracting audio transcripts using OpenAI's Whisper model, segmenting transcripts into text segments, generating embeddings via BERTimbau (a Portuguese BERT model), semantically matching segments to fact-checked claims using cosine similarity, and then training classifiers to distinguish misinformative from non-misinformative segments. The authors benchmark BERTimbau and PTT5 classifiers with various undersampling ratios to address severe class imbalance.

Key results show that BERTimbau achieves the best Macro F1 score of 0.68 with a 1-to-75 undersampling ratio, while cross-dataset evaluation yields a promising 0.72 Macro F1 score. Temporal analyses reveal performance fluctuations across political periods, with notable decreases during the 2022 election period. The work demonstrates that automated misinformation span detection is feasible and provides publicly available datasets and benchmarks to enable future research supporting fact-checkers and content moderation on video platforms.
original_abstract: Online misinformation is one of the most challenging issues lately, yielding severe consequences, including political polarization, attacks on democracy, and public health risks. Misinformation manifests in any platform with a large user base, including online social networks and messaging apps. It permeates all media and content forms, including images, text, audio, and video. Distinctly, video-based misinformation represents a multifaceted challenge for fact-checkers, given the ease with which individuals can record and upload videos on various video-sharing platforms. Previous research efforts investigated detecting video-based misinformation, focusing on whether a video shares misinformation or not on a video level. While this approach is useful, it only provides a limited and non-easily interpretable view of the problem given that it does not provide an additional context of when misinformation occurs within videos and what content (i.e., claims) are responsible for the video's misinformation nature. In this work, we attempt to bridge this research gap by creating two novel datasets that allow us to explore misinformation detection on videos via audio transcripts, focusing on identifying the span of videos that are responsible for the video's misinformation claim (misinformation span detection). We present two new datasets for this task. We transcribe each video's audio to text, identifying the video segment in which the misinformation claims appears, resulting in two datasets of more than 500 videos with over 2,400 segments containing annotated fact-checked claims. Then, we employ classifiers built with state-of-the-art language models, and our results show that we can identify in which part of a video there is misinformation with an F1 score of 0.68. We make publicly available our annotated datasets. We also release all transcripts, audio and videos.

title: AUDITA: A New Dataset to Audit Humans vs. AI Skill at Audio QA
generated_summary:
This paper introduces AUDITA, a large-scale benchmark dataset for audio question answering (AQA) comprising 9,690 human-authored audio trivia questions sourced from real-world domains including quizzes, media, and cultural knowledge. Unlike existing AQA benchmarks that rely on synthetic audio, templated questions, or closed-set classification, AUDITA features crafted questions requiring multi-cue auditory reasoning and world knowledge, making it resistant to language priors and shallow shortcuts.

The authors evaluate both human experts and state-of-the-art audio-language models under controlled conditions, employing Item Response Theory (IRT) to jointly model question difficulty and respondent ability. They also conduct ablation studies using text-only and transcript-only settings to verify that the benchmark genuinely requires audio understanding.

Key results reveal a substantial and persistent gap between human and model performance. Expert human participants achieve strong accuracy (up to 69.17% on free-form and 86.67% on multiple-choice questions), while current models perform below chance in many settings. IRT analysis shows clear separation between human and model ability distributions, with models declining more sharply on difficult items. Text-only and transcript-only conditions confirm near-zero performance, demonstrating that AUDITA cannot be solved without genuine audio comprehension.

The findings suggest that model scaling alone is insufficient to close the auditory reasoning gap, highlighting the need for improved audio-language alignment, entity-level reasoning, and multi-step inference capabilities. The accompanying IRT-based diagnostic framework provides fine-grained insights into failure modes across categories and difficulty levels.
original_abstract: Existing audio question answering benchmarks largely emphasize sound event classification or caption-grounded queries, often enabling models to succeed through shortcut strategies, short-duration cues, lexical priors, dataset-specific biases, or even bypassing audio via metadata and captions rather than genuine reasoning Thus, we present AUDITA (Audio Understanding from Diverse Internet Trivia Authors), a large-scale, real-world benchmark to rigorously evaluate audio reasoning beyond surface-level acoustic recognition. AUDITA comprises carefully curated, human-authored trivia questions grounded in real-world audio, designed to stress robust auditory reasoning through challenging distractors and long-range temporal dependencies, using probing queries that cannot be answered from isolated text or sound cues alone. Human average accuracy of 32.13% shows both the challenge of the task while demonstrating meaningful comprehension of the audio. In stark contrast, state of-the-art audio question answering models perform poorly, with average accuracy below 8.86%. Beyond raw accuracy, we apply Item Response Theory (IRT) to estimate latent proficiency, question difficulty, and expose systematic deficiencies of the models and data.

title: PrismaDV: Automated Task-Aware Data Unit Test Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces PrismaDV, a task-aware data validation system that automatically generates specialized data unit tests by jointly analyzing dataset profiles and downstream task code. The key insight is that existing data validation frameworks like Deequ and TensorFlow Data Validation rely solely on data profiling, ignoring implicit assumptions embedded in the code that consumes the data, leading to both missed errors and false alarms.

PrismaDV is designed as a compound AI system that decomposes test generation into multiple steps: data profiling, column access detection, assumption inference from code, and constraint code generation. It leverages LLMs' code understanding capabilities to build a bipartite "data-code assumption" graph connecting accessed columns to implicit data assumptions expressed in natural language. The paper also proposes SIFTA (Selective Informative Feedback for Task Adaptation), a lightweight prompt optimization approach that uses scarce execution outcomes from data unit tests and downstream tasks as supervision signals, backtracing constraint failures to underlying code assumptions.

Two novel benchmarks are introduced: one for individual constraint discovery from data-code pairs (63 cases) and one for end-to-end error impact detection across five datasets and 60 tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PrismaDV outperforms strong baselines by over 20 F1 points on constraint discovery and over 26 F1 points on end-to-end evaluation, while SIFTA outperforms general prompt optimizers.

This work shifts data validation from a reactive paradigm—where tests are updated after production incidents—toward proactive, automated test generation tailored to specific downstream consumers.
original_abstract: Data is a central resource for modern enterprises, and data validation is essential for ensuring the reliability of downstream applications. However, existing automated data unit testing frameworks are largely task-agnostic: they validate datasets without considering the semantics and requirements of the code that consumes the data. We present PrismaDV, a compound AI system that analyzes downstream task code together with dataset profiles to identify data access patterns, infer implicit data assumptions, and generate task-aware executable data unit tests. To further adapt the data unit tests over time to specific datasets and downstream tasks, we propose "Selective Informative Feedback for Task Adaptation" (SIFTA), a prompt-optimization framework that leverages the scarce outcomes from the execution of data unit tests and downstream tasks. We evaluate PrismaDV on two new benchmarks spanning 60 tasks across five datasets, where it consistently outperforms both task-agnostic and task-aware baselines in generating unit tests that reflect the end-to-end impact of data errors. Furthermore, we show that with SIFTA, we can automatically learn prompts for PrismaDV's modules that outperform prompts written by hand or generated from a generic prompt optimizer. We publicly release our benchmarks and prototype implementation.

title: Thinking with Reasoning Skills: Fewer Tokens, More Accuracy
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Thinking with Reasoning Skills (TRS), a training-free framework that improves the efficiency of large reasoning models by shifting from "reasoning from scratch" to "reasoning with recalled experience." The main contribution is breaking the typical trade-off between inference efficiency and accuracy that plagues existing prompt-engineering approaches designed to reduce token usage.

The methodology operates in three stages. First, a reasoning model solves source problems, generating lengthy reasoning trajectories. Second, a summarizer model distills these trajectories into compact, reusable "skill cards"—extracting essential solution patterns from correct trajectories and diagnostic lessons from incorrect ones. These skills are stored in a retrieval library. At inference time, when a new problem is presented, relevant skills are retrieved based on similarity and injected into the prompt, guiding the model toward direct solution paths rather than redundant trial-and-error reasoning.

Key results across mathematical and coding benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements. For instance, Gemini-3-Flash gains +0.7 accuracy with 17.5% cost reduction, Doubao Seed achieves 53.8% cost savings with negligible accuracy loss, and GPT-OSS-120B improves coding pass@1 by +4.1 points. Notably, the experience repository and test set are independent, confirming that TRS generalizes through abstract knowledge rather than problem memorization.

The significance lies in providing a practical, black-box compatible deployment pipeline that enables open-source models to achieve more accurate reasoning with substantially fewer tokens, offering a scalable solution for cost-sensitive real-world applications.
original_abstract: Reasoning LLMs often spend substantial tokens on long intermediate reasoning traces (e.g., chain-of-thought) when solving new problems. We propose to summarize and store reusable reasoning skills distilled from extensive deliberation and trial-and-error exploration, and to retrieve these skills at inference time to guide future reasoning. Unlike the prevailing \emph{reasoning from scratch} paradigm, our approach first recalls relevant skills for each query, helping the model avoid redundant detours and focus on effective solution paths. We evaluate our method on coding and mathematical reasoning tasks, and find that it significantly reduces reasoning tokens while improving overall performance. The resulting lower per-request cost indicates strong practical and economic potential for real-world deployment.

title: Transferable Physics-Informed Representations via Closed-Form Head Adaptation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Pi-PINN, a framework for learning transferable physics-informed neural network representations that enables rapid adaptation to new PDE instances through closed-form head adaptation rather than costly gradient-based retraining. The core methodology decouples learning into two components: a shared deep embedding trained across related PDE instances via multi-task learning, and a task-specific output head adapted through a least-squares-optimal pseudoinverse computation under PDE constraints. The authors propose three variants—MLP+[Pi]², HYDRA+[Pi]² (featuring concatenative skip connections for more expressive embeddings), and PiL-PINN (which incorporates the pseudoinverse computation within the training loop for better handling of nonlinear PDEs).

Experiments across Poisson, Helmholtz, and Burgers equations demonstrate that Pi-PINN achieves 100–1000× faster prediction times compared to conventional PINNs while obtaining 10–100× lower relative errors than purely data-driven models in sparse-data regimes with as few as 2–4 training samples. The physics-informed pseudoinverse step yields up to two orders of magnitude error reduction over data-driven baselines. The HYDRA architecture proves particularly beneficial for linear PDEs, while PiL-PINN shows superior performance on nonlinear problems through iterative linearization.

This work demonstrates that combining data-driven multi-task learning with physics-informed constraints produces reusable PINN models capable of zero-shot generalization to unseen PDE instances, addressing critical limitations of standard PINNs regarding training efficiency and transferability.
original_abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have garnered significant interest for their potential in solving partial differential equations (PDEs) that govern a wide range of physical phenomena. By incorporating physical laws into the learning process, PINN models have demonstrated the ability to learn physical outcomes reasonably well. However, current PINN approaches struggle to predict or solve new PDEs effectively when there is a lack of training examples, indicating they do not generalize well to unseen problem instances. In this paper, we present a transferable learning approach for PINNs premised on a fast Pseudoinverse PINN framework (Pi-PINN). Pi-PINN learns a transferable physics-informed representation in a shared embedding space and enables rapid solving of both known and unknown PDE instances via closed-form head adaptation using a least-squares-optimal pseudoinverse under PDE constraints. We further investigate the synergies between data-driven multi-task learning loss and physics-informed loss, providing insights into the design of more performant PINNs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Pi-PINN on various PDE problems, including Poisson's equation, Helmholtz equation, and Burgers' equation, achieving fast and accurate physics-informed solutions without requiring any data for unseen instances. Pi-PINN can produce predictions 100-1000 times faster than a typical PINN, while producing predictions with 10-100 times lower relative error than a typical data-driven model even with only two training samples. Overall, our findings highlight the potential of transferable representations with closed-form head adaptation to enhance the efficiency and generalization of PINNs across PDE families and scientific and engineering applications.

title: Neural surrogates for crystal growth dynamics with variable supersaturation: explicit vs. implicit conditioning
generated_summary:
This paper systematically compares two convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) architectures for accelerating phase-field simulations of crystal growth: an implicit approach that infers the supersaturation parameter from short input sequences, and an explicit approach that receives the supersaturation value directly as an additional input channel. The study uses a two-dimensional Allen-Cahn model with anisotropic kinetics producing hexagonally faceted crystals, where variable supersaturation controls both growth rate and morphological details.

The authors train both architectures on datasets of varying sizes and evaluate them extensively on independent test sets of 2,500 simulations. The key finding is that explicit conditioning dramatically improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency. The best explicit model achieves less than 1.8% pixel error for over 90% of test cases, while the implicit model requires approximately 15 times more training data to reach comparable accuracy. The implicit model particularly struggles at low supersaturation values, where small inter-frame differences limit its ability to infer the driving parameter.

Both architectures successfully generalize to computational domains up to 2048×2048 pixels (16 times the training size), simulation durations 10 times longer than training sequences, and varied initial seed densities. The results establish that explicit parameter conditioning should be preferred whenever driving parameters are known, while implicit inference remains viable for scenarios with unknown driving forces, albeit at higher data cost. These findings provide practical guidance for developing neural surrogates for parametrically dependent materials evolution problems.
original_abstract: Simulations of crystal growth are performed by using Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network surrogate models, trained on a dataset of time sequences computed by numerical integration of Allen-Cahn dynamics including faceting via kinetic anisotropy. Two network architectures are developed to take into account the effects of a variable supersaturation value. The first infers it implicitly by processing an input mini-sequence of a few evolution frames and then returns a consistent continuation of the evolution. The second takes the supersaturation parameter as an explicit input along with a single initial frame and predicts the entire sequence. The two models are systematically tested to establish strengths and weaknesses, comparing the prediction performance for models trained on datasets of different size and, in the first architecture, different lengths of input mini-sequence. The analysis of point-wise and mean absolute errors shows how the explicit parameter conditioning guarantees the best results, reproducing with high-fidelity the ground-truth profiles. Comparable results are achievable by the mini-sequence approach only when using larger training datasets. The trained models show strong conditioning by the supersaturation parameter, consistently reproducing its overall impact on growth rates as well as its local effect on the faceted morphology. Moreover, they are perfectly scalable even on 256 times larger domains and can be successfully extended to more than 10 times longer sequences with limited error accumulation. The analysis highlights the potential and limits of these approaches in view of their general exploitation for crystal growth simulations.

title: Why are all LLMs Obsessed with Japanese Culture? On the Hidden Cultural and Regional Biases of LLMs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating cultural and regional biases in Large Language Models by prompting them with open-ended cultural questions containing masked geographic information, forcing models to implicitly select a location. The authors construct CROQ, a dataset of 31,680 cultural questions spanning 24 languages, 11 major topics, and 66 subtopics. Eight frontier LLMs are prompted with these questions, and a secondary LLM-as-a-judge extracts the geographic references from responses, achieving 98% accuracy.

The key findings reveal that models' regional preferences are primarily driven by the input language, with responses tending to reference countries where the prompted language is officially spoken. Strikingly, across all models, languages, and topics, there is a strong and consistent inclination toward countries like Japan, the United States, and India, challenging prior assumptions that LLM biases favor exclusively Western or Anglocentric perspectives. Analysis of diversity and entropy metrics shows that models exhibit limited geographic coverage, with responses concentrated around a small set of culturally prominent nations.

Further experiments comparing base and instruction-tuned model variants suggest that these cultural biases are predominantly introduced during the post-training or instruction-tuning phase rather than being inherent in pretraining data. This finding is particularly significant because post-training is traditionally intended to improve model alignment and reduce bias, yet it appears to amplify cultural concentration in unexpected directions, opening new research avenues into understanding how fine-tuning shapes cultural representation in LLMs.
original_abstract: LLMs have been showing limitations when it comes to cultural coverage and competence, and in some cases show regional biases such as amplifying Western and Anglocentric viewpoints. While there have been works analysing the cultural capabilities of LLMs, there has not been specific work on highlighting LLM regional preferences when it comes to cultural-related questions. In this work, we propose a new dataset based on a comprehensive taxonomy of Culture-Related Open Questions (CROQ). The results show that, contrary to previous cultural bias work, LLMs show a clear tendency towards countries such as Japan. Moveover, our results show that when prompting in languages such as English or other high-resource ones, LLMs tend to provide more diverse outputs and show less inclinations towards answering questions highlighting countries for which the input language is an official language. Finally, we also investigate at which point of LLM training this cultural bias emerges, with our results suggesting that the first clear signs appear after supervised fine-tuning, and not during pre-training.

title: Multistakeholder Impacts of Profile Portability in a Recommender Ecosystem
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how profile portability policies affect stakeholder outcomes in a multi-algorithm recommender ecosystem, examining the interplay between two regulatory dimensions: exclusivity (whether user data transfers between platforms) and permanence (whether platforms retain data after users leave). These dimensions yield four conditions—Algorithm-Specific, Cold Start, User Ownership, and Universal Profile—relevant to GDPR provisions on data portability and minimization.

Using the SMORES simulation framework, the authors model an ecosystem with two recommenders: a Generic one serving all users and a Niche one specializing in underserved content. Experiments span three datasets (Amazon Video Games, Goodreads, MovieLens), three collaborative filtering algorithms (ALS, BPR, ItemKNN), and five random seeds per configuration. Consumer and provider utilities are tracked across simulation cycles.

Contrary to expectations, exclusive conditions (Algorithm-Specific and Cold Start) generally produce the largest utility gains for niche consumers, while the supposedly desirable User Ownership condition does not consistently outperform others. Provider utility shows no clear patterns across portability conditions. The authors explain that non-exclusivity can dilute a niche recommender's focus by introducing irrelevant profiles from mainstream users, and permanence allows this noise to persist.

The findings have significant policy implications, suggesting that while user data rights should be honored, niche recommender systems should practice data minimization and be selective when integrating transferred profiles, rather than wholesale data retention.
original_abstract: Optimizing outcomes for multiple stakeholders in recommender systems has historically focused on algorithmic interventions, such as developing multi-objective models or re-ranking results from existing algorithms. However, structural changes to the recommendation ecosystem itself remain understudied. This paper explores the implications of algorithmic pluralism (also known as "middleware" in the governance literature), in which recommendation algorithms are decoupled from platforms, enabling users to select their preferred algorithm. Prior simulation work demonstrates that algorithmic choice benefits niche consumers and providers. Yet this approach raises critical questions about user modeling in the context of data portability: when users switch algorithms, what happens to their data? Noting that multiple data portability regulations have emerged to strengthen user data ownership and control. We examine how such policies affect user models and stakeholders' outcomes in recommendation setting. Our findings reveal that data portability scenarios produce varying effects on user utility across different recommendation algorithms. We highlight key policy considerations and implications for designing equitable recommendation ecosystems.

title: CuRast: Cuda-Based Software Rasterization for Billions of Triangles
generated_summary:
CuRast presents a CUDA-based software rasterization pipeline optimized for rendering dense, opaque triangle meshes without requiring precomputed spatial acceleration structures or hierarchical levels of detail. This design choice makes it particularly suited for editable or animated geometry, such as photogrammetry reconstructions, where preprocessing would need to be repeated after every modification.

The methodology employs a three-stage pipeline that adapts processing granularity to triangle size: single threads handle small (pixel-sized) triangles, warps of 32 threads process medium triangles, and workgroups of 64 threads handle large triangles. The system uses 64-bit atomic min operations for depth testing and adopts visibility buffer rendering, storing only triangle identifiers during rasterization and deferring full shading to a resolve pass. original_abstract: Previous work shows that small triangles can be rasterized efficiently with compute shaders. Building on this insight, we explore how far this can be pushed for massive triangle datasets without the need to construct acceleration structures in advance. Method: A 3-stage rasterization pipeline first rasterizes small triangles directly in stage 1, using atomicMin to store the closest fragments. Larger triangles are forwarded to stages 2 and 3. Results: CuRast can render models with hundreds of millions of triangles up to 2-5x (unique) or up to 12x (instanced) faster than Vulkan. Vulkan remains an order of magnitude faster for low-poly meshes. Limitations: We currently focus on dense, opaque meshes that you would typically obtain from photogrammetry/3D reconstruction. Blending/Transparency is not yet supported, and scenes with thousands of low-poly meshes are not implemented efficiently. Future Work: To make it suitable for games and a wider range of use cases, future work will need to (1) optimize handling of scenes with tens of thousands of nodes/meshes, (2) add support for hierarchical clustered LODs such as those produced by Meshoptimizer, (3) add support for transparency, likely in its own stage so as to keep opaque rasterization untouched and fast. Source Code: https://github.com/m-schuetz/CuRast

title: StructMem: Structured Memory for Long-Horizon Behavior in LLMs

By temporally anchoring dual perspectives and performing periodic semantic consolidation, StructMem improves temporal reasoning and multi-hop performance on \texttt{LoCoMo}, while substantially reducing token usage, API calls, and runtime compared to prior memory systems, see https://github.com/zjunlp/LightMem .

title: Less Is More: Measuring How LLM Involvement affects Chatbot Accuracy in Static Analysis

original_abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to make static analysis tools accessible through natural language, yet existing systems differ in how much they delegate to the LLM without treating the degree of delegation as an independent variable. We compare three architectures along a spectrum of LLM involvement for translating natural language to Joern's query language \cpgql{}: direct query generation (\approach{1}), generation of a schema-constrained JSON intermediate representation (\approach{2}), and tool-augmented agentic generation (\approach{3}). These are evaluated on a benchmark of 20 code analysis tasks across three complexity tiers, using four open-weight models in a 2\(\times\)2 design (two model families \(\times\) two scales), each with three repetitions. The structured intermediate representation (\approach{2}) achieves the highest result match rates, outperforming direct generation by 15--25 percentage points on large models and surpassing the agentic approach despite the latter consuming 8\(\times\) more tokens. title: A Brief History of Fréchet Distances: From Curves and Probability Laws to FID

Key findings reveal that both branches share a common structural instinct: comparing complex mathematical objects by embedding them in abstract spaces where distance, limit, and continuity are well-defined. original_abstract: This note provides a chronological account of Fréchet distances, starting with Maurice Fréchet's 1906 doctoral thesis on distances in abstract sets and tracing the Fréchet distance between polygonal curves and its algorithmic computation in the 1990s. It then continues with his 1957 paper on a coupling-based distance between probability laws with a brief glimpse of Wasserstein distance and optimal transport. We further attempt to draw connections between the distributional, coupling-based facet of Fréchet distances on probability laws and the geometric facet on curves. The note ends with a modern use case, the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) in the era of deep generative model evaluation, interpretable as the Wasserstein-2 distance between multivariate Gaussians in a learned feature space. title: Bridging the Training-Deployment Gap: Gated Encoding and Multi-Scale Refinement for Efficient Quantization-Aware Image Enhancement

Experiments on the DPED benchmark demonstrate that the INT8 QAT model recovers +0.474 dB PSNR and +0.111 SSIM over post-training quantization, achieving near full-precision quality. On Qualcomm's QNN HTP accelerator, INT8 inference achieves a 3.6× speedup (41.8 ms versus 151 ms for FP16), validating practical mobile deployment. The model achieved second place in the Mobile AI 2026 RGB Image Enhancement Challenge, establishing a scalable paradigm for high-fidelity, quantization-robust edge-based image enhancement.
original_abstract: Image enhancement models for mobile devices often struggle to balance high output quality with the fast processing speeds required by mobile hardware. While recent deep learning models can enhance low-quality mobile photos into high-quality images, their performance is often degraded when converted to lower-precision formats for actual use on mobile phones. To address this training-deployment mismatch, we propose an efficient image enhancement model designed specifically for mobile deployment. Our approach uses a hierarchical network architecture with gated encoder blocks and multiscale refinement to preserve fine-grained visual features. Moreover, we incorporate Quantization-Aware Training (QAT) to simulate the effects of low-precision representation during the training process. This allows the network to adapt and prevents the typical drop in quality seen with standard post-training quantization (PTQ). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method produces high-fidelity visual output while maintaining the low computational overhead needed for practical use on standard mobile devices. The code will be available at https://github.com/GenAI4E/QATIE.git.

title: Hi-WM: Human-in-the-World-Model for Scalable Robot Post-Training
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Human-in-the-World-Model (Hi-WM), a post-training framework that shifts the human corrective intervention loop from physical robot execution into an action-conditioned world model. The key insight is that the most valuable supervision for policy improvement lies near failure states, and collecting such corrections in a learned world model rather than the real world dramatically reduces costs associated with hardware deployment, scene resets, and manual monitoring.

The methodology centers on three mechanisms: state caching allows intermediate rollout states to be stored and revisited; trajectory branching enables multiple corrective continuations from a single failure point; and a hardware-agnostic intervention interface decouples human operators from physical robot access. A pretrained policy runs inside the world model, and human operators intervene only when rollouts become failure-prone, providing targeted corrective actions that are then used for post-training.

Evaluated on three real-world manipulation tasks (towel folding, T-block pushing, and rope routing) with two policy architectures, Hi-WM improves success rates by an average of 37.9 percentage points over base policies and 19.0 points over a world-model closed-loop baseline without human correction. The world model shows strong alignment with real-world execution (Pearson correlation r = 0.953 for task success). Performance scales monotonically with additional virtual intervention data, and the framework yields substantial cost savings that grow with scene diversity.

Hi-WM represents a practical paradigm shift for scalable robot post-training, transforming hardware-bound corrective loops into efficient, reusable interactive processes.
original_abstract: Post-training is essential for turning pretrained generalist robot policies into reliable task-specific controllers, but existing human-in-the-loop pipelines remain tied to physical execution: each correction requires robot time, scene setup, resets, and operator supervision in the real world. Meanwhile, action-conditioned world models have been studied mainly for imagination, synthetic data generation, and policy evaluation. We propose \textbf{Human-in-the-World-Model (Hi-WM)}, a post-training framework that uses a learned world model as a reusable corrective substrate for failure-targeted policy improvement. A policy is first rolled out in closed loop inside the world model; when the rollout becomes incorrect or failure-prone, a human intervenes directly in the model to provide short corrective actions. Hi-WM caches intermediate states and supports rollback and branching, allowing a single failure state to be reused for multiple corrective continuations and yielding dense supervision around behaviors that the base policy handles poorly. The resulting corrective trajectories are then added back to the training set for post-training. We evaluate Hi-WM on three real-world manipulation tasks spanning both rigid and deformable object interaction, and on two policy backbones. Hi-WM improves real-world success by 37.9 points on average over the base policy and by 19.0 points over a world-model closed-loop baseline, while world-model evaluation correlates strongly with real-world performance (r = 0.953). These results suggest that world models can serve not only as generators or evaluators, but also as effective corrective substrates for scalable robot post-training.

title: A Case Study in Recovery of Drones using Discrete-Event Systems
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a decentralized recovery framework for drone swarms based on supervisory control theory (SCT) and discrete-event systems (DES), addressing the problem of regrouping a lost drone with its swarm after a fault or adversarial attack causes separation. The key novelty lies in formalizing the unintended separation of a drone as a desynchronization between a plant and its supervisor, then applying a recovery strategy originally designed for plant-supervisor resynchronization.

The methodology employs a two-phase approach: a primary recovery supervisor, synthesized using a Recovery Bipartite Transition System (RBTS), guides the lost drone from an uncertain state estimate back to the operational region while guaranteeing avoidance of unsafe states; a secondary supervisor then reconnects the drone with the patrolling swarm. The environment is modeled as a grid map with operational, buffer, and no-fly zones, and drone behavior is captured through deterministic automata representing navigation, exploration, and directional scanning layers.

Simulation results across four trials demonstrate that recovery supervisors were successfully synthesized for three scenarios, while the fourth proved unrecoverable due to an overly uncertain state estimate encompassing unsafe regions. Recovery times varied with the size and composition of state estimates, illustrating how uncertainty influences computational complexity and path efficiency.

The framework provides formally guaranteed safe recovery for swarm robotics, though scalability challenges related to exponential RBTS growth and real-time hardware implementation remain subjects for future investigation.
original_abstract: Discrete-event systems and supervisory control theory provide a rigorous framework for specifying correct-by-construction behavior. However, their practical application to swarm robotics remains largely underexplored. In this paper, we investigate a topological recovery method based on discrete-event-systems within a swarm robotics context. We propose a hybrid architecture that combines a high-level discrete event systems supervisor with a low-level continuous controller, allowing lost drones to safely recover from fault or attack events and re-enter a controlled region. The method is demonstrated using ten simulated UAVs in the py-bullet-drones framework. We show recovery performance across four distinct scenarios, each with varying initial state estimates. Additionally, we introduce a secondary recovery supervisor that manages the regrouping process for a drone after it has re-entered the operational region.

title: A Compact Peristaltic Pump Based on Magneto-Elastic Hysteresis with Single Pneumatic Control
generated_summary:
This study introduces the Magneto-Elastic Hysteresis Peristaltic Pump (MEHPP), a compact pumping mechanism that achieves unidirectional fluid flow using only a single pneumatic control input. The key innovation lies in combining an elastic membrane with embedded permanent magnets, where the difference between the membrane's elastic restoring force and the magnetic interaction force creates hysteresis during pressurization and depressurization cycles, producing asymmetric peristaltic motion without requiring valves or complex control systems.

The authors develop an analytical model of the MEHPP and validate the magneto-elastic hysteresis behavior through fluid-structure interaction simulations using COMSOL. An asymmetric configuration demonstrates that the side with magneto-elastic hysteresis closes and detaches at different times than the side without, breaking symmetry and generating net flow. Control simulations without hysteresis confirm perfectly symmetric deformation and zero net flow, verifying that the hysteresis mechanism is essential. A physical prototype is fabricated and experimentally tested to demonstrate unidirectional flow generation.

Simulation results show that despite some backflow during transitions, the forward flow dominates, yielding positive net fluid transport. However, the simulations were limited to a single cycle due to convergence issues. The authors note that the system's minimalistic design—functioning as a regular tube when inactive—reduces risks such as thrombosis, making it particularly promising for medical applications in physiological biofluid systems, including cardiovascular, lymphatic, and cerebrospinal fluid circulation. Future work should address continuous flow conditions and diverse biofluid properties.
original_abstract: Pumping fluids is fundamental to a wide range of industrial, environmental, and biomedical applications. Among various pumping mechanisms, peristaltic pumps enable efficient and safe fluid transport by deforming an elastic tube without direct contact with the working fluid. Although previous studies have introduced mechanical, pneumatic, or magnetic actuations to drive membrane deformation, these approaches often lead to complex pump architectures and control schemes. In this study, we present a soft membrane pump that achieves peristaltic motion through a single pneumatic input combined with an embedded passive magnet. The actuation mechanism and system dynamics were analyzed and simplified through modeling. Numerical simulations were conducted to predict the internal fluid flow, and the magneto-elastic hysteresis behavior observed in the simulations was successfully validated by experiments with a proof-of-concept prototype.

title: Ramen: Robust Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models with Active Sample Selection
generated_summary:

Ramen addresses this through active sample selection, constructing a customized support set for each test sample based on two criteria: domain consistency, which retrieves samples from similar domains using image embedding similarity, and prediction balance, which ensures balanced class representation to prevent adaptation bias. To maintain computational efficiency, Ramen employs an embedding-gradient cache that stores embeddings and sample-level gradients of previously seen test images, enabling model updates through gradient aggregation without additional forward or backward passes, achieving a 490× speedup over naive implementation.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that entropy minimization performs feature reweighting based on variance, and that domain-relevant features can be mistakenly amplified under mixed-domain shifts—a problem mitigated by Ramen's sample selection strategy. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10-C, CIFAR-100-C, ImageNet-C, and DomainNet demonstrate consistent improvements, with Ramen achieving +1.3% to +3.4% accuracy gains over the strongest baselines while maintaining computational efficiency comparable to existing TTA methods.
