original_abstract: Pretrained vision-language models such as CLIP exhibit strong zero-shot generalization but remain sensitive to distribution shifts. Test-time adaptation adapts models during inference without access to source data or target labels, offering a practical way to handle such shifts. However, existing methods typically assume that test samples come from a single, consistent domain, while in practice, test data often include samples from mixed domains with distinct characteristics. Consequently, their performance degrades under mixed-domain settings. To address this, we present Ramen, a framework for robust test-time adaptation through active sample selection. For each incoming test sample, Ramen retrieves a customized batch of relevant samples from previously seen data based on two criteria: domain consistency, which ensures that adaptation focuses on data from similar domains, and prediction balance, which mitigates adaptation bias caused by skewed predictions. To improve efficiency, Ramen employs an embedding-gradient cache that stores the embeddings and sample-level gradients of past test images. The stored embeddings are used to retrieve relevant samples, and the corresponding gradients are aggregated for model updates, eliminating the need for any additional forward or backward passes. Our theoretical analysis provides insight into why the proposed adaptation mechanism is effective under mixed-domain shifts. Experiments on multiple image corruption and domain-shift benchmarks demonstrate that Ramen achieves strong and consistent performance, offering robust and efficient adaptation in complex mixed-domain scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/baowenxuan/Ramen .

title: AEL: Agent Evolving Learning for Open-Ended Environments
generated_summary:
Agent Evolving Learning (AEL) introduces a two-timescale framework for enabling LLM-based agents to improve as coordinated systems in open-ended environments, addressing the multi-module credit assignment problem that arises when planning, tool use, and memory modules change simultaneously. Unlike prior methods that evolve only a single module while holding others fixed, AEL treats the agent as a coupled system.

At the fast timescale, a Thompson Sampling bandit selects among memory retrieval policies episode-by-episode, adapting how the agent accesses past experience. At the slow timescale, LLM-driven reflection aggregates trajectories to produce causal diagnoses of failure patterns, injecting insights into the agent's prompt and generating new retrieval policies only when existing ones prove inadequate. This "diagnose-before-prescribe" architecture prevents changes triggered by noisy signals.

Evaluated on a sequential portfolio allocation benchmark (10 tickers, 208 episodes, 5 seeds), AEL achieves a Sharpe ratio of 2.13 ± 0.47, outperforming all baselines including prior self-improving methods like EvoTool (1.37 ± 1.74) and Reflexion (-0.59 ± 1.33), while exhibiting the lowest variance among LLM methods. An incremental study reveals that memory contributes a 24% improvement over the stateless baseline, while reflection adds a further 27%, demonstrating that the bottleneck is self-diagnosis rather than experience accumulation. A comprehensive ablation yields a striking "less is more" finding: every addition to the base configuration degrades performance, establishing that simplicity is optimal in high-noise, short-horizon domains.
original_abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate in open-ended environments spanning hundreds of sequential episodes, yet they remain largely stateless: each task is solved from scratch without converting past experience into better future behavior. The central obstacle is not \emph{what} to remember but \emph{how to use} what has been remembered, including which retrieval policy to apply, how to interpret prior outcomes, and when the current strategy itself must change. We introduce \emph{Agent Evolving Learning} (\ael{}), a two-timescale framework that addresses this obstacle. At the fast timescale, a Thompson Sampling bandit learns which memory retrieval policy to apply at each episode; at the slow timescale, LLM-driven reflection diagnoses failure patterns and injects causal insights into the agent's decision prompt, giving it an interpretive frame for the evidence it retrieves. On a sequential portfolio benchmark (10 sector-diverse tickers, 208 episodes, 5 random seeds), \ael{} achieves a Sharpe ratio of 2.13$\pm$0.47, outperforming five published self-improving methods and all non-LLM baselines while maintaining the lowest variance among all LLM-based approaches. A nine-variant ablation reveals a ``less is more'' pattern: memory and reflection together produce a 58\% cumulative improvement over the stateless baseline, yet every additional mechanism we test (planner evolution, per-tool selection, cold-start initialization, skill extraction, and three credit assignment methods) \emph{degrades} performance. This demonstrates that the bottleneck in agent self-improvement is \emph{self-diagnosing how to use} experience rather than adding architectural complexity. Code and data: https://github.com/WujiangXu/AEL.

title: Beyond N-gram: Data-Aware X-GRAM Extraction for Efficient Embedding Parameter Scaling
generated_summary:
This paper introduces X-GRAM, a data-aware framework for efficient token-indexed lookup-based scaling of language models that addresses two fundamental limitations of naive lookup table expansion: long-tail under-training due to Zipf-like token frequency distributions and representational collapse across parallel fixed slots.

The methodology comprises three key innovations. First, probability-balanced hybrid hashing assigns dedicated capacity to high-frequency tokens while routing rare tokens into shared hash buckets, improving training balance across table rows. Second, a lightweight ShortConv refinement module converts static 1-gram retrievals into variable-length local n-gram features, breaking symmetry across slots and encouraging representational diversity. Third, a mixed injection design targets attention content pathways—particularly the value stream—with depth-aware gating to modulate injection strength across layers.

In experiments at 0.73B and 1.15B model scales, X-GRAM consistently outperforms strong baselines including Retoken, MoRT, and Engram under matched training budgets. At 0.73B scale with 50% table compression, X-GRAM achieves 48.5 average downstream accuracy, surpassing all baselines while using substantially smaller lookup tables. At 1.15B scale, it reaches 50.8 accuracy with 4× capacity, exceeding baselines by 2.3 points. Crucially, X-GRAM demonstrates continued improvement as tables grow, whereas baselines plateau.

These results establish that token-indexed memory can serve as a practical scaling axis when designed to be trainable under realistic data distributions, diversity-preserving, and demand-aware across model depth.
original_abstract: Large token-indexed lookup tables provide a compute-decoupled scaling path, but their practical gains are often limited by poor parameter efficiency and rapid memory growth. We attribute these limitations to Zipfian under-training of the long tail, heterogeneous demand across layers, and "slot collapse" that produces redundant embeddings. To address this, we propose X-GRAM, a frequency-aware dynamic token-injection framework. X-GRAM employs hybrid hashing and alias mixing to compress the tail while preserving head capacity, and refines retrieved vectors via normalized SwiGLU ShortConv to extract diverse local n-gram features. These signals are integrated into attention value streams and inter-layer residuals using depth-aware gating, effectively aligning static memory with dynamic context. This design introduces a memory-centric scaling axis that decouples model capacity from FLOPs. Extensive evaluations at the 0.73B and 1.15B scales show that X-GRAM improves average accuracy by as much as 4.4 points over the vanilla backbone and 3.2 points over strong retrieval baselines, while using substantially smaller tables in the 50% configuration. Overall, by decoupling capacity from compute through efficient memory management, X-GRAM offers a scalable and practical paradigm for future memory-augmented architectures. Code aviliable in https://github.com/Longyichen/X-gram.

title: From If-Statements to ML Pipelines: Revisiting Bias in Code-Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel framework for evaluating bias in LLM-generated code by examining feature selection in machine learning pipeline generation, moving beyond the overtly discriminatory conditional statements assessed in prior work. The authors argue that real-world bias in code manifests covertly through subtle design decisions rather than explicit rules, and that ML pipeline generation represents a more realistic and consequential evaluation setting.

The study evaluates ten LLMs across seven fairness-sensitive datasets (including credit scoring, recidivism prediction, and employment assessment), each containing sensitive attributes (e.g., race, sex), non-sensitive attributes, and deliberately irrelevant attributes. Bias is measured using the Code Bias Score, quantifying how frequently models include sensitive attributes as predictive features in generated pipelines. Fifty prompt variants per task are constructed, and results are compared against a conditional statement baseline.

The findings reveal that LLMs systematically include sensitive attributes in 88.3% of generated ML pipelines, compared to only 58.7% in conditional statements—a 28.5 percentage point gap. Critically, models consistently exclude obviously irrelevant attributes, demonstrating that sensitive attribute inclusion reflects selective decision-making rather than indiscriminate retention. This bias persists across mitigation strategies, varying pipeline complexities, and different attribute set sizes.

The work highlights that current bias evaluation methodologies, focused on simplistic code patterns, provide a false sense of safety, and calls for assessments grounded in realistic programming tasks to prevent the automation of discriminatory design patterns at scale.
original_abstract: Prior work evaluates code generation bias primarily through simple conditional statements, which represent only a narrow slice of real-world programming and reveal solely overt, explicitly encoded bias. We demonstrate that this approach dramatically underestimates bias in practice by examining a more realistic task: generating machine learning (ML) pipelines. Testing both code-specialized and general-instruction large language models, we find that generated pipelines exhibit significant bias during feature selection. Sensitive attributes appear in 87.7% of cases on average, despite models demonstrably excluding irrelevant features (e.g., including "race" while dropping "favorite color" for credit scoring). This bias is substantially more prevalent than that captured by conditional statements, where sensitive attributes appear in only 59.2% of cases. These findings are robust across prompt mitigation strategies, varying numbers of attributes, and different pipeline difficulty levels. Our results challenge simple conditionals as valid proxies for bias evaluation and suggest current benchmarks underestimate bias risk in practical deployments.

title: Unlocking the Power of Critical Factors for 3D Visual Geometry Estimation
generated_summary:
This paper presents CARVE, a framework for accurate 3D visual geometry estimation from monocular video, developed through systematic ablation studies of critical training factors. The main contribution is a rigorous investigation of why multi-frame methods often underperform per-frame methods in accuracy, yielding several counterintuitive insights: spatial gradient losses and learnable confidence weighting can degrade performance, while simple inverse-depth weighting proves more effective; scaling data diversity and quality continues to improve even well-pretrained models; and per-frame alignment helps but local region alignment hurts.

Building on these insights, the authors introduce two key technical innovations. First, a consistency loss enforces geometric coherence among predicted depth maps, camera parameters, and 3D point clouds through perspective projection constraints. Second, an efficient high-resolution feature fusion mechanism uses cross-attention with zero-initialized gating to integrate high-resolution ViT features into the low-resolution processing branch, preserving pretrained knowledge while requiring substantially less computation than direct high-resolution input processing—achieving approximately 6× higher inference speed with 0.3–0.4× memory usage.

CARVE achieves strong performance across seven benchmark datasets on point cloud reconstruction, video depth estimation, camera pose estimation, and intrinsics estimation, outperforming or matching state-of-the-art methods including VGGT, MoGe v2, Spann3R, and Fast3R. The work provides practical guidelines for training visual geometry models and demonstrates that careful optimization of training components can yield significant improvements without architectural overhauls.
original_abstract: Feed-forward visual geometry estimation has recently made rapid progress. However, an important gap remains: multi-frame models usually produce better cross-frame consistency, yet they often underperform strong per-frame methods on single-frame accuracy. This observation motivates our systematic investigation into the critical factors driving model performance through rigorous ablation studies, which reveals several key insights: 1) Scaling up data diversity and quality unlocks further performance gains even in state-of-the-art visual geometry estimation methods; 2) Commonly adopted confidence-aware loss and gradient-based loss mechanisms may unintentionally hinder performance; 3) Joint supervision through both per-sequence and per-frame alignment improves results, while local region alignment surprisingly degrades performance. Furthermore, we introduce two enhancements to integrate the advantages of optimization-based methods and high-resolution inputs: a consistency loss function that enforces alignment between depth maps, camera parameters, and point maps, and an efficient architectural design that leverages high-resolution information. We integrate these designs into CARVE, a resolution-enhanced model for feed-forward visual geometry estimation. Experiments on point cloud reconstruction, video depth estimation, and camera pose/intrinsic estimation show that CARVE achieves strong and robust performance across diverse benchmarks.

title: Fairness under uncertainty in sequential decisions
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a taxonomy and diagnostic framework for identifying how uncertainty enters sequential decision-making pipelines, with implications for algorithmic fairness. Rather than proposing a novel fairness algorithm, the authors provide a structured vocabulary for reasoning about how different forms of uncertainty—particularly prediction uncertainty and feedback uncertainty—interact across the machine learning lifecycle and disproportionately affect marginalized groups in reinforcement learning settings.

The authors use synthetic lending data generated through a configurable bias simulation framework to evaluate several uncertainty-aware exploration strategies, including naïve exploration, probability-weighted exploration, uncertainty-aware exploration, and counterfactual utility maximization. These deliberately simple methods isolate distinct uncertainty mechanisms to illustrate how accounting for unobserved outcomes can affect fairness metrics. Logistic regression serves as the base model, with parametric confidence intervals quantifying prediction uncertainty.

Key results demonstrate that counterfactual utility maximization effectively mitigates bias under historical and measurement bias conditions without explicit fairness constraints, though its performance varies across bias types. Probability-weighted exploration achieves the highest utility across conditions. No single method dominates all bias scenarios, underscoring the context-dependent nature of fairness interventions.

The work's significance lies in bridging technical fairness research with legal and governance considerations, highlighting how unequal epistemic uncertainty can compound disparities under selective labels. The framework equips practitioners and policymakers with tools for auditing sequential decision systems where standard supervised fairness metrics prove inadequate.
original_abstract: Fair machine learning (ML) methods help identify and mitigate the risk that algorithms encode or automate social injustices. Algorithmic approaches alone cannot resolve structural inequalities, but they can support socio-technical decision systems by surfacing discriminatory biases, clarifying trade-offs, and enabling governance. Although fairness is well studied in supervised learning, many real ML applications are online and sequential, with prior decisions informing future ones. Each decision is taken under uncertainty due to unobserved counterfactuals and finite samples, with dire consequences for under-represented groups, systematically under-observed due to historical exclusion and selective feedback. A bank cannot know whether a denied loan would have been repaid, and may have less data on marginalized populations. This paper introduces a taxonomy of uncertainty in sequential decision-making -- model, feedback, and prediction uncertainty -- providing shared vocabulary for assessing systems where uncertainty is unevenly distributed across groups. We formalize model and feedback uncertainty via counterfactual logic and reinforcement learning, and illustrate harms to decision makers (unrealized gains/losses) and subjects (compounding exclusion, reduced access) of policies that ignore the unobserved space. Algorithmic examples show it is possible to reduce outcome variance for disadvantaged groups while preserving institutional objectives (e.g. expected utility). Experiments on data simulated with varying bias show how unequal uncertainty and selective feedback produce disparities, and how uncertainty-aware exploration alters fairness metrics. The framework equips practitioners to diagnose, audit, and govern fairness risks. Where uncertainty drives unfairness rather than incidental noise, accounting for it is essential to fair and effective decision-making.

title: Effects of Swarm Size Variability on Operator Workload
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how changes in swarm size affect operator workload and performance in Human-Swarm Interaction, focusing on the cognitive effects of transitioning between different numbers of agents. The authors propose three hypotheses: that workload residue persists after swarm size reductions (H1), that gradual increases in swarm size produce lower workload than abrupt jumps (H2), and that larger changes in swarm size produce a "shocking" effect that overwhelms the first two phenomena (H3).

The methodology employs a monitoring task where participants observe simulated drone swarms of varying sizes using the boids flocking algorithm. During each seven-second episode, one drone disappears, and the operator must identify its color. Accuracy and self-reported workload (on a 1-7 scale) are measured across two studies with different magnitudes of swarm size changes, treating performance as dependent on both the current and immediately preceding swarm size.

Results across both studies show that small decreases in swarm size leave residual workload above baseline, supporting H1, while small increases "ease in" operators, supporting H2. However, both effects hold only for small changes (delta of 2-4 agents) and collapse at larger magnitudes, supporting H3. Subjective responses strongly endorse the shock-severity hypothesis, with participants reporting surprise and disorientation from large jumps.

These findings carry significant implications for swarm interface design, suggesting that gradual transitions in swarm size should be preferred and that operators need support mechanisms when large, abrupt changes are unavoidable.
original_abstract: Real-world deployments of human--swarm teams depend on balancing operator workload to leverage human strengths without inducing overload. A key challenge is that swarm size is often dynamic: robots may join or leave the mission due to failures or redeployment, causing abrupt workload fluctuations. Understanding how such changes affect human workload and performance is critical for robust human--swarm interaction design. This paper investigates how the magnitude and direction of changes in swarm size influence operator workload. Drawing on the concept of workload history, we test three hypotheses: (1) workload remains elevated following decreases in swarm size, (2) small increases are more manageable than large jumps, and (3) sufficiently large changes override these effects by inducing a cognitive reset. We conducted two studies (N = 34) using a monitoring task with simulated drone swarms of varying sizes. By varying the swarm size between episodes, we measured perceived workload relative to swarm size changes. Results show that objective performance is largely unaffected by small changes in swarm size, while subjective workload is sensitive to both change direction and magnitude. Small increases preserve lower workload, whereas small decreases leave workload elevated, indicating workload residue; large changes in either direction attenuate these effects, suggesting a reset response. These findings offer actionable guidance for managing swarm-size transitions to support operator workload in dynamic human--swarm systems.

title: Phonological Subspace Collapse Is Aetiology-Specific and Cross-Lingually Stable: Evidence from 3,374 Speakers
generated_summary:
This study provides large-scale validation and extension of a training-free method for dysarthria characterization based on phonological subspace analysis of self-supervised learning (SSL) speech representations. The method measures d-prime separation between phonological category pairs (e.g., nasal vs. oral) in frozen SSL embeddings, using feature directions estimated solely from healthy control speech. The authors scale the analysis from 890 to 3,374 speakers across 25 datasets, 12 languages, and 6 SSL backbones.

Three key findings emerge. First, phonological degradation profiles are aetiology-specific: 10 of 13 features yield large effect sizes in distinguishing Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, ALS, Down syndrome, and stroke. Parkinson's disease is separable from the articulatory execution group (cerebral palsy, Down syndrome, stroke) with mean Cohen's d of 0.84, consistent with distinct neuroanatomical substrates. Second, aetiology-specific profile shapes are cross-lingually stable, with cosine similarities exceeding 0.97 across typologically diverse languages, suggesting degradation patterns reflect neuromuscular impairment rather than language-specific phonology. Third, results replicate across all six SSL backbones tested, with inter-model correlations exceeding 0.77, demonstrating architecture independence.

These findings establish phonological subspace analysis as a robust, interpretable, and generalizable framework for population-level dysarthria phenotyping that requires no pathological training data, though individual-level aetiology classification remains limited by within-group variability.
original_abstract: We previously introduced a training-free method for dysarthria severity assessment based on d-prime separability of phonological feature subspaces in frozen self-supervised speech representations, validated on 890 speakers across 5 languages with HuBERT-base. Here, we scale the analysis to 3,374 speakers from 25 datasets spanning 12 languages and 5 aetiologies (Parkinson's disease, cerebral palsy, ALS, Down syndrome, and stroke), plus healthy controls, using 6 SSL backbones. We report three findings. First, aetiology-specific degradation profiles are distinguishable at the group level: 10 of 13 features yield large effect sizes (epsilon-squared > 0.14, Holm-corrected p < 0.001), with Parkinson's disease separable from the articulatory execution group at Cohen's d = 0.83; individual-level classification remains limited (22.6% macro F1). Second, profiles show cross-lingual profile-shape stability: cosine similarity of 5-dimensional consonant d-prime profiles exceeds 0.95 across the languages available for each aetiology. Absolute d-prime magnitudes are not cross-lingually calibrated, so the method supports language-independent phenotyping of degradation patterns but requires within-corpus calibration for absolute severity interpretation. Third, the method is architecture-independent: all 6 backbones produce monotonic severity gradients with inter-model agreement exceeding rho = 0.77. Fixed-token d-prime estimation preserves the severity correlation (rho = -0.733 at 200 tokens per class), confirming that the signal is not a token-count artefact. These results support phonological subspace analysis as a robust, training-free framework for aetiology-aware dysarthria characterisation, with evidence of cross-lingual profile-shape stability and cross-backbone robustness in the represented sample.

title: Stealthy Backdoor Attacks against LLMs Based on Natural Style Triggers
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel backdoor attack framework targeting generative large language models (LLMs) that addresses three key limitations of existing approaches: detectable trigger patterns, unreliable backdoor injection in long-form generation, and unclear threat models for realistic applications.

The framework weaponizes LLMs themselves as poisoned sample generators, using style transfer to rewrite clean text into style-altered variants (e.g., Biblical, Shakespearean, or legal styles) that carry imperceptible triggers while preserving semantics and fluency. To improve injection reliability, the authors introduce an auxiliary target loss that provides stronger optimization signals for attacker-specified content during parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). The approach is evaluated under both prompt-induced and PEFT-based injection strategies across seven victim LLMs, including GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-3.1, and Phi-4.

Key results demonstrate that style-level triggers achieve high attack success rates—for instance, Bible style reaches 97.0% ASR with only 2.5% false positive rate across all evaluated models in downstream deployment scenarios unknown during injection. The auxiliary target loss improves ASR by up to 83.0% over standard poisoned fine-tuning. Critically, the style-level triggers exhibit substantially lower perplexity than explicit triggers, easily bypassing perplexity-based filtering and ONION detection, while a simple camouflage strategy reduces the effectiveness of state-of-the-art output-level defenses by nearly 60%.

These findings highlight urgent security risks posed by stealthy style-level backdoors in generative LLM applications, underscoring the need for more robust defense mechanisms.
original_abstract: The growing application of large language models (LLMs) in safety-critical domains has raised urgent concerns about their security. Many recent studies have demonstrated the feasibility of backdoor attacks against LLMs. However, existing methods suffer from three key shortcomings: explicit trigger patterns that compromise naturalness, unreliable injection of attacker-specified payloads in long-form generation, and incompletely specified threat models that obscure how backdoors are delivered and activated in practice. To address these gaps, we present BadStyle, a complete backdoor attack framework and pipeline. BadStyle leverages an LLM as a poisoned sample generator to construct natural and stealthy poisoned samples that carry imperceptible style-level triggers while preserving semantics and fluency. To stabilize payload injection during fine-tuning, we design an auxiliary target loss that reinforces the attacker-specified target content in responses to poisoned inputs and penalizes its emergence in benign responses. We further ground the attack in a realistic threat model and systematically evaluate BadStyle under both prompt-induced and PEFT-based injection strategies. Extensive experiments across seven victim LLMs, including LLaMA, Phi, DeepSeek, and GPT series, demonstrate that BadStyle achieves high attack success rates (ASRs) while maintaining strong stealthiness. The proposed auxiliary target loss substantially improves the stability of backdoor activation, yielding an average ASR improvement of around 30% across style-level triggers. Even in downstream deployment scenarios unknown during injection, the implanted backdoor remains effective. Moreover, BadStyle consistently evades representative input-level defenses and bypasses output-level defenses through simple camouflage.

title: Can Large Language Models Assist the Comprehension of ROS2 Software Architectures?
generated_summary:
This study presents the first empirical evaluation of large language models' ability to assist in comprehending the software architecture of ROS2 robotics systems. The authors conduct a controlled experiment involving nine commercial LLMs and three third-party ROS2 systems of varying complexity. They develop an automated question-generation algorithm that, combined with a structured prompt design methodology, systematically produces questions about system topologies. From 29,406 generated prompts, 1,230 questions are sampled and posed to each LLM, yielding 11,070 responses evaluated against predefined ground truth and analyzed for accuracy, perplexity, output length, and topic coherence.

The results demonstrate that LLMs achieve high accuracy in architecture comprehension tasks (mean 98.22%), with Gemini-2.5-Pro achieving perfect accuracy across all systems. However, performance degrades with system complexity, particularly for the most complex system (Panda). Nearly all incorrect answers (297 of 300) involve a single question type concerning message exchange detection, where models struggle with implicit communication paths through the system-wide '/parameter_events' topic. Perplexity scores vary substantially across models, ranging from 19.6 to 103.6, reflecting differences in response consistency. Topic modeling reveals six distinct themes in LLM explanations, with models favoring structural enumeration over abstract reasoning.

These findings establish that LLMs can reliably support ROS2 architecture comprehension for explicit structural queries while highlighting limitations in reasoning about implicit communication patterns, providing actionable guidance for both developers and researchers.
original_abstract: Context. The most used development framework for robotics software is ROS2. ROS2 architectures are highly complex, with thousands of components communicating in a decentralized fashion. Goal. We aim to evaluate how LLMs can assist in the comprehension of factual information about the architecture of ROS2 systems. Method. We conduct a controlled experiment where we administer 1,230 prompts to 9 LLMs containing architecturally-relevant questions about 3 ROS2 systems with incremental size. We provide a generic algorithm that systematically generates architecturally-relevant questions for a ROS2 system. Then, we (i) assess the accuracy of the answers of the LLMs against a ground truth established via running and monitoring the 3 ROS2 systems and (ii) qualitatively analyse the explanations provided by the LLMs. Results. Almost all questions are answered correctly across all LLMs (mean=98.22%). gemini-2.5-pro performs best (100% accuracy across all prompts and systems), followed by o3 (99.77%), and gemini-2.5-flash (99.72%); the least performing LLM is gpt-4.1 (95%). Only 300/1,230 prompts are incorrectly answered, of which 249 are about the most complex system. The coherence scores in LLM's explanations range from 0.394 for "service references" to 0.762 for "communication path". The mean perplexity varies significantly across models, with chatgpt-4o achieving the lowest score (19.6) and o4-mini the highest (103.6). Conclusions. There is great potential in the usage of LLMs to aid ROS2 developers in comprehending non-trivial aspects of the software architecture of their systems. Nevertheless, developers should be aware of the intrinsic limitations and different performances of the LLMs and take those into account when using them.

title: Fixation Sequences as Time Series: A Topological Approach to Dyslexia Detection
generated_summary:
This paper introduces novel topological data analysis (TDA) methods for time series classification and applies them to dyslexia detection from eye-tracking data. The main contribution is twofold: the authors propose non-horizontal filtrations (sloped, sigmoid, and arctan) for computing persistent homology of time series, which unlike standard horizontal filtrations explicitly capture temporal information, and they demonstrate the utility of these topological features for analyzing fixation sequences during reading.

The methodology involves decomposing fixation sequences into horizontal and vertical coordinate time series, computing persistent homology using the proposed filtrations, vectorizing the resulting persistence diagrams into persistence images, and reducing dimensionality via PCA. These topological features are evaluated alone (TSH-models), combined with traditional hand-crafted features (hybrid models), and compared against established baseline models using the CopCo corpus of Danish reading data from 53 participants, including 18 diagnosed with dyslexia.

Key results show that hybrid models combining topological and traditional features consistently achieve the highest ROC AUC scores across all experimental settings. The newly introduced non-horizontal filtrations generally outperform existing horizontal filtrations. Notably, models using only topological features perform comparably to established baselines, despite relying solely on geometric and temporal structure without linguistic alignment.

These findings suggest that persistent homology captures complementary information about reading behavior—specifically higher-order temporal and structural patterns in eye movements—that traditional aggregate measures miss, establishing topological features as a viable addition to dyslexia detection pipelines and eye-tracking analysis more broadly.
original_abstract: Persistent homology, a method from topological data analysis, extracts robust, multi-scale features from data. It produces stable representations of time series by applying varying thresholds to their values (a process known as a \textit{filtration}). We develop novel filtrations for time series and introduce topological methods for the analysis of eye-tracking data, by interpreting fixation sequences as time series, and constructing ``hybrid models'' that combine topological features with traditional statistical features. We empirically evaluate our method by applying it to the task of dyslexia detection from eye-tracking-while-reading data using the Copenhagen Corpus, which contains scanpaths from dyslexic and non-dyslexic L1 and L2 readers. Our hybrid models outperform existing approaches that rely solely on traditional features, showing that persistent homology captures complementary information encoded in fixation sequences. The strength of these topological features is further underscored by their achieving performance comparable to established baseline methods. Importantly, our proposed filtrations outperform existing ones.

title: Towards Universal Tabular Embeddings: A Benchmark Across Data Tasks
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the first comprehensive benchmarking framework for evaluating tabular embedding models across multiple granularity levels—cell, row, column, and table—spanning 69 datasets and diverse tasks including similarity search, prediction, and retrieval. Inspired by text embedding benchmarks like MTEB, the framework addresses the lack of standardized evaluation protocols for tabular representations, which has hindered meaningful comparison of emerging table foundation models.

The methodology evaluates a wide range of embedding approaches, from general-purpose text embeddings to specialized tabular models, using task-specific metrics aggregated through rank-based scoring. The framework also measures computational costs including execution time, RAM, and GPU memory consumption. Additionally, controlled variation studies assess model sensitivity to schema modifications, column removal, and data characteristics.

Key findings reveal that no single embedding model consistently excels across all tasks. Instead, two distinct model categories emerge: semantic similarity-oriented models and prediction-oriented models, which encode fundamentally different information. Surprisingly, general-purpose text embedding models (GritLM, IBM Granite R2, MiniLM) achieve the highest aggregate rankings, outperforming specialized tabular models on similarity-based tasks. Resource consumption varies dramatically, with larger models requiring substantially more time and GPU memory.

The framework's significance lies in establishing a standardized evaluation foundation for tabular embeddings, demonstrating that achieving truly universal table representations remains an open challenge requiring hybrid approaches combining similarity and prediction capabilities.
original_abstract: Tabular foundation models aim to learn universal representations of tabular data that transfer across tasks and domains, enabling applications such as table retrieval, semantic search and table-based prediction. Despite the growing number of such models, it remains unclear which approach works best in practice, as existing methods are often evaluated under task-specific settings that make direct comparison difficult. To address this, we introduce TEmBed, the Tabular Embedding Test Bed, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating tabular embeddings across four representation levels: cell, row, column, and table. Evaluating a diverse set of tabular representation learning models, we show that which model to use depends on the task and representation level. Our results offer practical guidance for selecting tabular embeddings in real-world applications and lay the groundwork for developing more general-purpose tabular representation models.

title: Efficient Logic Gate Networks for Video Copy Detection
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first application of differentiable Logic Gate Networks (LGNs) to video copy detection, introducing a framework that replaces conventional deep neural networks with compact, Boolean logic-based models for highly efficient video similarity computation. The approach processes videos by selecting representative frames, downscaling them to low resolutions (8×8 or 32×32 pixels), binarizing pixel intensities using fixed thresholds, and feeding the resulting binary vectors into single-layer LGN architectures. These networks, trained using differentiable relaxations of Boolean gates, learn both gate functions and inter-layer connectivity, then are discretized into purely combinatorial circuits for inference. Two connectome strategies are evaluated: fully learnable dense connections and sparse Top-K connections.

Experiments on a movie trailer dataset with 3,000 near-duplicate and 3,000 non-similar pairs across 12 cross-validation folds demonstrate that LGN models achieve median F1 scores above 0.98 and micro average precision near 1.0. A frame-pair max-pooling similarity strategy proves most effective, and coarser 8×8 resolution outperforms 32×32. Ablation studies confirm that learned logical structure substantially improves performance beyond preprocessing alone.

The significance lies in the models' extreme efficiency: LGN-based descriptors occupy less than 1 kilobyte and achieve inference throughput exceeding 11,000 samples per second, offering orders-of-magnitude advantages over conventional CNN and 3D architectures while maintaining competitive detection accuracy, making them well-suited for large-scale, resource-constrained deployment.
original_abstract: Video copy detection requires robust similarity estimation under diverse visual distortions while operating at very large scale. Although deep neural networks achieve strong performance, their computational cost and descriptor size limit practical deployment in high-throughput systems. In this work, we propose a video copy detection framework based on differentiable Logic Gate Networks (LGNs), which replace conventional floating-point feature extractors with compact, logic-based representations. Our approach combines aggressive frame miniaturization, binary preprocessing, and a trainable LGN embedding model that learns both logical operations and interconnections. After training, the model can be discretized into a purely Boolean circuit, enabling extremely fast and memory-efficient inference. We systematically evaluate different similarity strategies, binarization schemes, and LGN architectures across multiple dataset folds and difficulty levels. Experimental results demonstrate that LGN-based models achieve competitive or superior accuracy and ranking performance compared to prior models, while producing descriptors several orders of magnitude smaller and delivering inference speeds exceeding 11k samples per second. These findings indicate that logic-based models offer a promising alternative for scalable and resource-efficient video copy detection.

title: SLAM as a Stochastic Control Problem with Partial Information: Optimal Solutions and Rigorous Approximations
generated_summary:
This paper formulates active simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with rigorous mathematical foundations. The main contribution is establishing a general stochastic control framework for active SLAM that guarantees the existence of optimal policies and provides provably near-optimal finite approximations through quantization-based discretization of the belief space.

The authors define the SLAM problem over general state, action, and observation spaces, encompassing both occupancy and landmark-based map representations. They introduce a novel belief-dependent cost function incorporating Wasserstein-based Rao entropy alongside traditional Shannon entropy for exploration. Key theoretical results establish weak continuity properties of the transition kernels and observation models under physically motivated assumptions, which in turn guarantee the existence of optimal policies and the convergence of finite model approximations to near-optimal performance.

A simulation case study involving a mobile robot with a range-bearing sensor validates the theoretical framework. Comparing Shannon entropy and Wasserstein-based Rao entropy as exploration costs, the results show that Rao entropy achieves superior tail-risk performance (lower CVaR at the 90th percentile) in 8 of 12 noise settings, with the largest improvements occurring at moderate bearing noise levels. However, neither cost uniformly dominates the other.

The significance of this work lies in providing the first rigorous optimality and approximation guarantees for active SLAM formulated as a continuous-space POMDP, bridging the gap between practical SLAM algorithms and formal stochastic control theory.
original_abstract: Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a foundational state estimation problem in robotics in which a robot accurately constructs a map of its environment while also localizing itself within this construction. We study the active SLAM problem through the lens of optimal stochastic control, thereby recasting it as a decision-making problem under partial information. After reviewing several commonly studied models, we present a general stochastic control formulation of active SLAM together with a rigorous treatment of motion, sensing, and map representation. We introduce a new exploration stage cost that encodes the geometry of the state when evaluating information-gathering actions. This formulation, constructed as a nonstandard partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), is then analyzed to derive rigorously justified approximate solutions that are near-optimal. To enable this analysis, the associated regularity conditions are studied under general assumptions that apply to a wide range of robotics applications. For a particular case, we conduct an extensive numerical study in which standard learning algorithms are used to learn near-optimal policies.

title: Evaluating Post-hoc Explanations of the Transformer-based Genome Language Model DNABERT-2
generated_summary:
This paper adapts AttnLRP, a post-hoc attribution method for Transformer models, to explain predictions of DNABERT-2, a BERT-style genome language model, and systematically evaluates the resulting explanations. The key methodological contributions include extending AttnLRP to handle DNABERT-2's specific components (ALiBi positional encoding and gated linear units) and proposing four aggregation/disaggregation strategies to convert between token-level and nucleotide-level relevance scores, enabling direct comparison between Transformer and CNN explanations.

The authors fine-tune DNABERT-2 on two genomic classification tasks—human nontata promoter detection and Drosophila enhancer identification—and compare AttnLRP explanations against LRP explanations from baseline CNNs. Evaluation encompasses multiple metrics: similarity between model explanations, sparsity and complexity of attributions, faithfulness through systematic input perturbation, and biological localization via motif database comparison using TF-MoDISco and JASPAR.

Results demonstrate that AttnLRP produces reliable explanations for DNABERT-2 comparable in quality to established LRP explanations for CNNs, with faithful attributions confirmed through perturbation experiments and recovered motifs matching known biological annotations. Moderate similarity between DNABERT-2 and CNN explanations suggests the models capture partially overlapping but distinct features.

This work is significant for the genomics community as it establishes that Transformer-based genome language models, despite their architectural complexity, can yield trustworthy post-hoc explanations suitable for biological hypothesis generation and regulatory mechanism discovery.
original_abstract: Explaining deep neural network predictions on genome sequences enables biological insight and hypothesis generation-often of greater interest than predictive performance alone. While explanations of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been shown to capture relevant patterns in genome sequences, it is unclear whether this transfers to more expressive Transformer-based genome language models (gLMs). To answer this question, we adapt AttnLRP, an extension of layer-wise relevance propagation to the attention mechanism, and apply it to the state-of-the-art gLM DNABERT-2. Thereby, we propose strategies to transfer explanations from token and nucleotide level. We evaluate the adaption of AttnLRP on genomic datasets using multiple metrics. Further, we provide an extensive comparison between the explanations of DNABERT-2 and a baseline CNN. Our results demonstrate that AttnLRP yields reliable explanations corresponding to known biological patterns. Hence, like CNNs, gLMs can also help derive biological insights. This work contributes to the explainability of gLMs and addresses the comparability of relevance attributions across different architectures.

title: StyleID: A Perception-Aware Dataset and Metric for Stylization-Agnostic Facial Identity Recognition
generated_summary:
This paper introduces StyleID, a perception-aware framework for evaluating and modeling facial identity preservation under creative stylization. The central contribution addresses a critical gap: existing face recognition models and identity encoders, trained on natural photographs, fail to reliably assess identity consistency in stylized portraits such as cartoons, sketches, and artistic renderings, often disagreeing with human perception.

The authors construct two complementary datasets: StyleBench-H, a human-annotated benchmark capturing identity judgments across multiple diffusion-based stylization methods at varying strengths, and StyleBench-S, a large-scale synthetic training set derived from human-calibrated recognition-strength curves. These curves model how identity recognition degrades as stylization intensifies, enabling the generation of training pairs anchored to perceptual thresholds. Using StyleBench-S, the authors fine-tune a CLIP-L vision encoder with LoRA adapters, combining contrastive learning with angular margin losses to align similarity orderings with human judgments.

StyleID substantially outperforms widely used baselines including ArcFace, AdaFace, CLIP, SigLIP2, and StylizedFace across verification metrics on both StyleBench-H and the out-of-distribution artist-drawn SKSF-A dataset, achieving over 0.9 true positive rate in several evaluation splits. The model also demonstrates superior performance in cross-domain retrieval and pose robustness tasks. Lightweight variants reduce computational cost by up to 20× while still surpassing conventional face recognition models.

This work provides both an evaluation foundation and a practical modeling direction for human-aligned identity recognition in generative and creative applications.
original_abstract: Creative face stylization aims to render portraits in diverse visual idioms such as cartoons, sketches, and paintings while retaining recognizable identity. However, current identity encoders, which are typically trained and calibrated on natural photographs, exhibit severe brittleness under stylization. They often mistake changes in texture or color palette for identity drift or fail to detect geometric exaggerations. This reveals the lack of a style-agnostic framework to evaluate and supervise identity consistency across varying styles and strengths. To address this gap, we introduce StyleID, a human perception-aware dataset and evaluation framework for facial identity under stylization. StyleID comprises two datasets: (i) StyleBench-H, a benchmark that captures human same-different verification judgments across diffusion- and flow-matching-based stylization at multiple style strengths, and (ii) StyleBench-S, a supervision set derived from psychometric recognition-strength curves obtained through controlled two-alternative forced-choice (2AFC) experiments. Leveraging StyleBench-S, we fine-tune existing semantic encoders to align their similarity orderings with human perception across styles and strengths. Experiments demonstrate that our calibrated models yield significantly higher correlation with human judgments and enhanced robustness for out-of-domain, artist drawn portraits. All of our datasets, code, and pretrained models are publicly available at https://kwanyun.github.io/StyleID_page/

title: A-IC3: Learning-Guided Adaptive Inductive Generalization for Hardware Model Checking
generated_summary:
This paper introduces A-IC3, a lightweight, learning-guided framework that adaptively selects inductive generalization strategies within the IC3 hardware model checking algorithm. The key insight is that no single generalization strategy is uniformly optimal—the effectiveness of conservative versus aggressive generalization depends on the evolving proof context, including CTI characteristics, frame saturation, and proof-obligation dynamics.

The authors formulate generalization strategy selection as a contextual multi-armed bandit problem. Before each generalization step, a proof-aware context vector capturing both local features (CTI cube size, depth, activity score) and global features (frame level, saturation, queue length) is extracted from IC3's internal state. A LinUCB agent then selects among seven predefined generalization strategies of varying aggressiveness. After observing a reward based on clause size reduction and propagation success, the agent updates its parameters online with negligible computational overhead, requiring no offline training or pre-collected datasets.

Evaluated on 914 benchmarks from HWMCC'20, HWMCC'24, and HWMCC'25 using the state-of-the-art rIC3 solver, A-IC3 solves 50 more instances than the standard configuration and achieves the best PAR-2 scores across all metrics, with particularly strong improvements on safety proofs. The method also reduces termination frame levels, indicating more efficient proof trajectories.

This work demonstrates that even simple online learning mechanisms can meaningfully enhance formal verification tools, opening a new direction for integrating lightweight machine learning into symbolic model checking without the overhead of neural network inference.
original_abstract: The IC3 algorithm represents the state-of-the-art (SOTA) hardware model checking technique, owing to its robust performance and scalability. A significant body of research has focused on enhancing the solving efficiency of the IC3 algorithm, with particular attention to the inductive generalization process: a critical phase wherein the algorithm seeks to generalize a counterexample to inductiveness (CTI), which typically is a state leading to a bad state, into a broader set of states. This inductive generalization is a primary source of clauses in IC3 and thus plays a pivotal role in determining the overall effectiveness of the algorithm. Despite its importance, existing approaches often rely on fixed inductive generalization strategies, overlooking the dynamic and context-sensitive nature of the verification environment in which spurious counterexamples arise. This rigidity can limit the quality of generated clauses and, consequently, the performance of IC3. To address this limitation, we propose a lightweight machine-learning-based framework that dynamically selects appropriate inductive generalization strategies in response to the evolving verification context. Specifically, we employ a multi-armed bandit (MAB) algorithm to adaptively choose inductive generalization strategies based on real-time feedback from the verification process. The agent is updated by evaluating the quality of generalization outcomes, thereby refining its strategy selection over time. Empirical evaluation on a benchmark suite comprising 914 instances, primarily drawn from the latest HWMCC collection, demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. When implemented on the state-of-the-art model checker rIC3, our method solves 26 to 50 more cases than the baselines and improves the PAR-2 score by 194.72 to 389.29.

title: WorldMark: A Unified Benchmark Suite for Interactive Video World Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces WorldMark, the first standardized benchmark designed for evaluating interactive image-to-video world models, addressing a critical gap where existing models are each evaluated on proprietary benchmarks with incomparable conditions. The core contribution is a unified evaluation framework that enables apples-to-apples comparison across six world models with heterogeneous control interfaces.

The methodology centers on two pillars: a unified test infrastructure and a default evaluation toolkit. The test infrastructure includes a shared WASD-style action vocabulary with an action-mapping layer that translates standardized inputs into each model's native control format (caption prompts, pose parameters, action tensors, etc.). A curated test suite of 500 cases spans 50 reference images across first-person/third-person perspectives and photorealistic/stylized scenes at three difficulty tiers. The evaluation toolkit covers three dimensions: Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency, combining geometric trajectory metrics with VLM-based scoring.

Key findings reveal that visual quality and world consistency are largely uncorrelated—YUME 1.5 produces the most aesthetically pleasing frames but ranks poorly on coherence, while Genie 3 maintains the most consistent worlds with moderate visual fidelity. Third-person generation exposes severe weaknesses, with rotation errors degrading by nearly an order of magnitude compared to first-person settings. Human preference studies confirm strong alignment with automated metrics (Spearman correlation exceeding 0.9).

WorldMark provides the community with actionable insights and a modular, extensible evaluation platform for advancing interactive world model development.
original_abstract: Interactive video generation models such as Genie, YUME, HY-World, and Matrix-Game are advancing rapidly, yet every model is evaluated on its own benchmark with private scenes and trajectories, making fair cross-model comparison impossible. Existing public benchmarks offer useful metrics such as trajectory error, aesthetic scores, and VLM-based judgments, but none supplies the standardized test conditions -- identical scenes, identical action sequences, and a unified control interface -- needed to make those metrics comparable across models with heterogeneous inputs. We introduce WorldMark, the first benchmark that provides such a common playing field for interactive Image-to-Video world models. WorldMark contributes: (1) a unified action-mapping layer that translates a shared WASD-style action vocabulary into each model's native control format, enabling apples-to-apples comparison across six major models on identical scenes and trajectories; (2) a hierarchical test suite of 500 evaluation cases covering first- and third-person viewpoints, photorealistic and stylized scenes, and three difficulty tiers from Easy to Hard spanning 20-60s; and (3) a modular evaluation toolkit for Visual Quality, Control Alignment, and World Consistency, designed so that researchers can reuse our standardized inputs while plugging in their own metrics as the field evolves. We will release all data, evaluation code, and model outputs to facilitate future research. Beyond offline metrics, we launch World Model Arena (warena.ai), an online platform where anyone can pit leading world models against each other in side-by-side battles and watch the live leaderboard.

title: Sapiens2
generated_summary:
