original_abstract: We present Sapiens2, a model family of high-resolution transformers for human-centric vision focused on generalization, versatility, and high-fidelity outputs. Our model sizes range from 0.4 to 5 billion parameters, with native 1K resolution and hierarchical variants that support 4K. Sapiens2 substantially improves over its predecessor in both pretraining and post-training. First, to learn features that capture low-level details (for dense prediction) and high-level semantics (for zero-shot or few-label settings), we combine masked image reconstruction with self-distilled contrastive objectives. Our evaluations show that this unified pretraining objective is better suited for a wider range of downstream tasks. Second, along the data axis, we pretrain on a curated dataset of 1 billion high-quality human images and improve the quality and quantity of task annotations. Third, architecturally, we incorporate advances from frontier models that enable longer training schedules with improved stability. Our 4K models adopt windowed attention to reason over longer spatial context and are pretrained with 2K output resolution. Sapiens2 sets a new state-of-the-art and improves over the first generation on pose (+4 mAP), body-part segmentation (+24.3 mIoU), normal estimation (45.6% lower angular error) and extends to new tasks such as pointmap and albedo estimation. Code: https://github.com/facebookresearch/sapiens2

title: A Sociotechnical, Practitioner-Centered Approach to Technology Adoption in Cybersecurity Operations: An LLM Case
generated_summary:
This study presents a sociotechnical, practitioner-centered framework for co-creating and integrating large language model (LLM)-based companion tools within a live Security Operations Center (SOC). The main contribution is a structured co-creation methodology that bridges the persistent gap between academic research and operational cybersecurity practice, extending the Tool-Oriented SECI (Socialization, Externalization, Combination, Internalization) knowledge conversion model to account for LLM-specific dynamics.

The methodology involved embedding two PhD researchers within a major commercial organization's SOC over six months. Through participant observation, fieldwork, and iterative co-creation with 18 SOC analysts and security professionals, the researchers progressed through SECI-informed phases: acquiring tacit operational knowledge through immersion, externalizing workflow pain points through structured reflection, developing LLM-based tools addressing tasks like root cause analysis and query building, and deploying these tools through trust-calibrated internalization. Thematic analysis of field notes, transcripts, and observational artifacts systematically identified workflow bottlenecks and analyst reception patterns.

Key findings demonstrate that adoption success depends critically on analysts actively shaping tool behavior, constraints, and deployment boundaries rather than receiving externally designed solutions. The study identifies two novel dynamics in LLM-mediated knowledge conversion: generative recombination, where LLM tools actively produce new explicit artifacts beyond simply encoding existing knowledge, and trust-calibrated internalization, where analysts incrementally validate and incorporate AI-generated outputs into workflows. These findings carry significant implications for designing AI-augmented cybersecurity systems that align with practitioner expertise and operational realities.
original_abstract: Technology for security operations centers (SOCs) has a storied history of slow adoption due to concerns about trust and reliability. These concerns are amplified with artificial intelligence, particularly large language models (LLMs), which exhibit issues such as hallucinations and inconsistent outputs. To assess whether LLM-based tools can improve SOC efficiency, we embedded two PhD researchers within a multinational company SOC for six months of ethnographic fieldwork. We identified recurring challenges, such as repetitive tasks, fragmented/unclear data, and tooling bottlenecks, and collaborated directly with practitioners to develop LLM companion tools aligned with their operational needs. Iterative refinement reduced workflow disruption and improved interpretability, leading from skepticism to sustained adoption. Ethnographic analysis indicates that this shift was enabled by our sociotechnical co-creation process consistent with Nonaka's SECI model. This framework explains the common challenges in traditional SOC technology adoption, including workflow misalignment, rigidity against evolving threats and internal requirements, and stagnation over time. Our findings show that the co-creation approach can overcome these old barriers and create a new paradigm for creating usable technology for cybersecurity operations.

title: Counterfactual Multi-task Learning for Delayed Conversion Modeling in E-commerce Sales Pre-Promotion
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CM-DCM (Counterfactual Multi-task Learning for Delayed Conversion Model), a novel framework designed to address the unique delayed conversion challenge during e-commerce sales pre-promotion periods, where users actively browse and add items to carts but deliberately delay purchases until the promotion day. This creates a distinct delayed feedback problem where approximately 45% of promotion-day orders originate from pre-promotion clicks, yet conventional CVR models fail to capture this behavior shift.

CM-DCM integrates three key components: a multi-task architecture that jointly models direct (same-day) and delayed (promotion-day) conversions using historical pre-promotion data; a counterfactual causal regularizer based on a Doubly Robust estimator that explicitly models the causal effect of add-to-cart actions on delayed conversions while addressing confounding factors; and a personalized gated transfer mechanism that adaptively transfers knowledge from pre-trained daily CVR and ATC models based on real-time user behavior.

Extensive experiments on public datasets (Taobao and Tmall) and proprietary industrial data demonstrate that CM-DCM significantly outperforms all baselines in delayed-CVR ranking metrics. Online A/B tests during Double 11 and Double 12 promotions yielded a 7.87% increase in online revenue, 4.24% gain in delayed GMV, and 1.42% improvement in overall GMV, with only 2ms additional inference latency. This work represents the first research specifically targeting delayed conversion modeling for the sales pre-promotion phase, offering substantial practical value for e-commerce advertising platforms.
original_abstract: Sales promotions, as short-term incentives to stimulate product purchases, play a pivotal role in modern e-commerce marketing strategies. During promotional events, user behavior patterns exhibit distinct characteristics compared to regular periods. In the pre-promotion phase, users typically engage in product search and browsing without immediate purchases, adding items to carts in anticipation of promotional discounts. This behavior leads to delayed conversions, resulting in significantly lower conversion rates (CVR) before the promotion day. Although existing research has made progress in CVR prediction for promotion days using historical data, it largely overlooks the critical pre-promotion period. And delayed feedback modeling has been extensively studied, current approaches fail to account for the unique distribution shifts in conversion behavior before promotional events, where delayed conversions predominantly occur on the promotion day rather than over continuous time windows. To address these limitations, we propose the Counterfactual Multi-task Delayed Conversion Model (CM-DCM), which leverages historical pre-promotion data to enhance CVR prediction for both delayed and direct conversions. Our model incorporates three key innovations: (i) A multi-task architecture that jointly models direct and delayed conversions using historical pre-promotion data; (ii) A personalized user behavior gating module to mitigate data sparsity issues during brief pre-promotion periods; (iii) A counterfactual causal approach to model the transition probability from add-to-cart (ATC) to delayed conversion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CM-DCM outperforms baselines in pre-promotion scenarios. Online A/B tests during major promotional events showed significant improvements in advertising revenue, delayed conversion GMV, and overall GMV, validating the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Hierarchical Joint Source-Channel Coding with Constrained Information Leakage
generated_summary:
This paper investigates hierarchical joint source-channel coding where a source must be transmitted through two discrete memoryless channels in successive stages, with the receiver not fully trusted during the first stage. The key challenge is controlling information leakage at the receiver while maintaining a required level of source reconstruction quality across both phases, with degraded side information available at the receiver.

The authors model the problem by introducing an information leakage constraint alongside traditional distortion requirements. The encoder transmits a source description in two phases: the first phase allows coarse reconstruction subject to both distortion and leakage constraints, while the second phase enables refined reconstruction with better side information. The coding scheme employs three auxiliary random variables to partition information strategically. A novel aspect is the use of secret keys derived from correlated source and side information, combined with random bits from unused second-channel capacity, to encrypt information sent in the first phase that cannot be decoded until the second phase.

The main results are inner and outer bounds on the achievable distortion-leakage region for given bandwidth expansion factors. These bounds are shown to coincide when the second channel's capacity exceeds the first, yielding an optimal characterization. The information leakage decomposes into a necessary component (from side information and first-phase decoding) and an excess component (from undecoded information present in the first phase).

This work bridges successive refinement, joint source-channel coding, and information-theoretic security, addressing the unique scenario where the legitimate receiver and potential adversary are the same entity at different trust levels.
original_abstract: This paper studies the hierarchical joint source-channel coding with information leakage constraint in the first-phase reconstruction and distortion constraints. The receiver's access to the data varies and is evaluated by the quality of the side information. Due to the consideration of channel capacity limitation or the efficiency of the system performance, the encoder may send some additional information in Phase 1 that can only be decoded in Phase 2 with higher-quality side information. While this can optimize the overall performance, the additional information causes excessive information leakage. We provide general inner and outer bounds for the conditions such that a given distortion-leakage pair $(D_1,D_2,L)$ is achievable, together with a capacity-achieving condition.

title: Encoder-Free Human Motion Understanding via Structured Motion Descriptions
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Structured Motion Description (SMD), a deterministic, rule-based method for converting skeletal motion data into structured natural language text, enabling large language models (LLMs) to understand human motion without learned motion encoders or cross-modal alignment modules. Drawing on biomechanical conventions, SMD computes joint angles along kinematic chains and extracts global trajectory information, then converts these into descriptive text segments organized hierarchically by body part, trajectory, and temporal intervals. This text is fed directly to pretrained LLMs, which are adapted using only lightweight LoRA fine-tuning.

The approach is evaluated on motion question answering (BABEL-QA, HuMMan-QA) and motion captioning (HumanML3D), achieving state-of-the-art results that surpass both dedicated motion models and encoder-based LLM approaches. The method demonstrates strong backbone portability, with consistent performance across eight LLMs from six model families using the same textual input and identical LoRA configuration. Zero-shot experiments confirm that LLMs can partially interpret SMD without any fine-tuning, validating that the representation leverages pretrained linguistic knowledge. Attention analysis over human-readable SMD tokens reveals which body parts and motion segments drive model predictions, providing built-in interpretability.

The significance of this work lies in dramatically simplifying the motion understanding pipeline—replacing multi-stage encoder training with a single fine-tuning step—while achieving superior performance and offering interpretability and flexibility advantages over existing approaches.
original_abstract: The world knowledge and reasoning capabilities of text-based large language models (LLMs) are advancing rapidly, yet current approaches to human motion understanding, including motion question answering and captioning, have not fully exploited these capabilities. Existing LLM-based methods typically learn motion-language alignment through dedicated encoders that project motion features into the LLM's embedding space, remaining constrained by cross-modal representation and alignment. Inspired by biomechanical analysis, where joint angles and body-part kinematics have long served as a precise descriptive language for human movement, we propose \textbf{Structured Motion Description (SMD)}, a rule-based, deterministic approach that converts joint position sequences into structured natural language descriptions of joint angles, body part movements, and global trajectory. By representing motion as text, SMD enables LLMs to apply their pretrained knowledge of body parts, spatial directions, and movement semantics directly to motion reasoning, without requiring learned encoders or alignment modules. We show that this approach goes beyond state-of-the-art results on both motion question answering (66.7\% on BABEL-QA, 90.1\% on HuMMan-QA) and motion captioning (R@1 of 0.584, CIDEr of 53.16 on HumanML3D), surpassing all prior methods. SMD additionally offers practical benefits: the same text input works across different LLMs with only lightweight LoRA adaptation (validated on 8 LLMs from 6 model families), and its human-readable representation enables interpretable attention analysis over motion descriptions. Code, data, and pretrained LoRA adapters are available at https://yaozhang182.github.io/motion-smd/.

title: Fine-Grained Perspectives: Modeling Explanations with Annotator-Specific Rationales
generated_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in perspectivist NLP by explicitly integrating annotator-specific rationales into both label prediction and explanation generation for natural language inference (NLI). Rather than treating explanations as post-hoc justifications, the authors model them as expressions of individual annotator perspectives, conditioning explanation generation on annotator-specific representations.

The methodology employs two key components: an annotator-aware classifier built on DeBERTa-v3-base that incorporates learnable annotator embeddings and metadata representations, and two explanation generation variants using Flan-T5-base—a prompt-based post-hoc explainer and a representation-prefix bridge architecture. The bridge model explicitly connects prediction and explanation modules by transferring classifier representations enriched with annotator information into the generative model. The system is trained on the VariErrNLI dataset, which contains disaggregated NLI labels with annotator-provided explanations.

Key results demonstrate that the bridge architecture improves macro-level stability and inferential alignment across annotators, with particular gains in semantically complex categories. The approach strengthens semantic consistency and predictive robustness, with annotator-specific improvements observed in both predictive performance and explanation quality metrics including lexical overlap and semantic fidelity.

The significance of this work lies in demonstrating that jointly modeling annotator perspectives with explanation generation produces more faithful representations of human disagreement. This contributes to developing more transparent, perspective-sensitive NLP systems that capture not only label outcomes but also the underlying reasoning patterns of individual annotators.
original_abstract: Beyond exploring disaggregated labels for modeling perspectives, annotator rationales provide fine-grained signals of individual perspectives. In this work, we propose a framework for jointly modeling annotator-specific label prediction and corresponding explanations, fine-tuned on the annotators' provided rationales. Using a dataset with disaggregated natural language inference (NLI) annotations and annotator-provided explanations, we condition predictions on both annotator identity and demographic metadata through a representation-level User Passport mechanism. We further introduce two explainer architectures: a post-hoc prompt-based explainer and a prefixed bridge explainer that transfers annotator-conditioned classifier representations directly into a generative model. This design enables explanation generation aligned with individual annotator perspectives. Our results show that incorporating explanation modeling substantially improves predictive performance over a baseline annotator-aware classifier, with the prefixed bridge approach achieving more stable label alignment and higher semantic consistency, while the post-hoc approach yields stronger lexical similarity. These findings indicate that modeling explanations as expressions of fine-grained perspective provides a richer and more faithful representation of disagreement. The proposed approaches advance perspectivist modeling by integrating annotator-specific rationales into both predictive and generative components.

title: Transferable SCF-Acceleration through Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SAIL (Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning), a method that trains machine learning models to generate initial guesses for self-consistent field (SCF) calculations by backpropagating through the SCF solver itself, rather than fitting to ground-state targets. The authors also propose the Effective Relative Iteration Count (ERIC), a metric that accounts for hidden computational costs in different initialization ansätze, correcting the commonly used RIC metric.

The methodology employs an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network backbone with different readout heads for predicting density matrices, Fock matrices, or auxiliary basis coefficients. Models are first pretrained on surrogate ground-state losses, then fine-tuned by differentiating through SCF iterations using a gradient-norm loss that directly penalizes slow convergence. This process is label-free, requiring only molecular geometries.

Key results demonstrate that conventionally trained matrix-based models decelerate SCF convergence when extrapolating to larger molecules, confirming prior findings. SAIL resolves this failure, which the authors attribute to misalignment between ground-state supervision and solver dynamics—models can accurately predict ground-state quantities while producing poor initial guesses. SAIL-trained density matrix prediction achieves 27–33% iteration reductions across PBE, SCAN, and B3LYP functionals, maintaining a 1.25× wall-time speedup on B3LYP for drug-like molecules up to 10× larger than training examples.

The significance lies in extending reliable ML-based SCF acceleration to hybrid functionals and large molecules, a practically important regime for computational organic chemistry that previous approaches could not robustly address.
original_abstract: Machine learning methods that predict initial guesses from molecular geometry can reduce this cost, but matrix-prediction models fail when extrapolating to larger molecules, degrading rather than accelerating convergence [Liu et al. 2025]. We show that this failure is a supervision problem, not an extrapolation problem: models trained on ground-state targets fit those targets well out of distribution, yet produce initial guesses that slow convergence. Solver-Aligned Initialization Learning (SAIL) resolves this for both Hamiltonian and density matrix models by differentiating through the SCF solver end-to-end. We introduce the Effective Relative Iteration Count (ERIC), a correction to the commonly used RIC that accounts for hidden Fock-build overhead. On QM40, containing molecules up to 4$\times$ larger than the training distribution, SAIL reduces ERIC by 37% (PBE), 33% (SCAN), and 27% (B3LYP), more than doubling the previous state-of-the-art reduction on B3LYP (10%). On QMugs molecules 10$\times$ the training size, SAIL delivers a 1.25$\times$ wall-time speedup at the hybrid level of theory, extending ML SCF acceleration to large drug-like molecules.

title: Causal Disentanglement for Full-Reference Image Quality Assessment
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel full-reference image quality assessment (FR-IQA) method based on causal inference and decoupled representation learning that eliminates the need for costly subjective quality annotations. The main contribution is a framework that disentangles degradation features from image content using structural causal models, while explicitly modeling how image content influences perceived degradation through the visual masking effect.

The methodology employs a Vision Transformer encoder to extract degradation features from distorted images, a causal layer using ResNet18 to model content-dependent modulation of degradation visibility, and a U-Net decoder with FiLM modulation for reconstruction supervision. The model is pre-trained on synthetic degradation datasets without quality labels. For prediction, it offers three modes: supervised regression with MOS labels, few-shot learning with minimal annotations, and a fully unsupervised zero-shot approach using UMAP to project learned features onto a one-dimensional quality manifold.

Experiments across ten datasets—including five standard IQA benchmarks and five domain-specific datasets (infrared, neutron radiography, screen content, medical, and remote sensing)—demonstrate state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance. The method shows particular strength in cross-domain scenarios where existing training-free methods suffer significant performance degradation due to domain shift from ImageNet pretraining.

The significance lies in enabling practical IQA deployment in specialized domains where obtaining subjective quality annotations is prohibitively expensive, while maintaining robust performance across supervised, few-shot, and label-free settings.
original_abstract: Existing deep network-based full-reference image quality assessment (FR-IQA) models typically work by performing pairwise comparisons of deep features from the reference and distorted images. In this paper, we approach this problem from a different perspective and propose a novel FR-IQA paradigm based on causal inference and decoupled representation learning. Unlike typical feature comparison-based FR-IQA models, our approach formulates degradation estimation as a causal disentanglement process guided by intervention on latent representations. We first decouple degradation and content representations by exploiting the content invariance between the reference and distorted images. Second, inspired by the human visual masking effect, we design a masking module to model the causal relationship between image content and degradation features, thereby extracting content-influenced degradation features from distorted images. Finally, quality scores are predicted from these degradation features using either supervised regression or label-free dimensionality reduction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves highly competitive performance on standard IQA benchmarks across fully supervised, few-label, and label-free settings. Furthermore, we evaluate the approach on diverse non-standard natural image domains with scarce data, including underwater, radiographic, medical, neutron, and screen-content images. Benefiting from its ability to perform scenario-specific training and prediction without labeled IQA data, our method exhibits superior cross-domain generalization compared to existing training-free FR-IQA models.

title: GS-Quant: Granular Semantic and Generative Structural Quantization for Knowledge Graph Completion
generated_summary:
This paper introduces GS-Quant, a framework that bridges the modality gap between Knowledge Graphs (KGs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) by generating hierarchically structured discrete codes for KG entities to improve Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC). The core insight is that entity representations should mirror the hierarchical nature of language, progressing from coarse-grained semantic categories to fine-grained distinctions, thereby aligning with the autoregressive generation process of LLMs.

Built upon a Residual Quantized Variational Autoencoder (RQ-VAE), GS-Quant introduces two key modules. The Granular Semantic Enhancement (GSE) module injects hierarchical knowledge derived from clustering into codebook learning, ensuring that successive quantization levels capture progressively finer semantic granularity. The Generative Structural Reconstruction (GSR) module employs a lightweight GPT-style Transformer decoder to reconstruct entities and their ancestors from code sequences, imposing causal dependencies that render the codes structurally isomorphic to natural language. The learned discrete codes are then integrated into the LLM's vocabulary for fine-tuning on KGC tasks.

Extensive experiments on WN18RR and FB15k-237 benchmarks demonstrate that GS-Quant achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing the strongest LLM-based baselines by approximately 1.7% in MRR and 2.4% in Hits@1 on WN18RR, with similar gains on FB15k-237. Ablation studies confirm that both modules and the quantized representations are essential. This work establishes that hierarchical semantic quantization provides a more effective paradigm for integrating structured knowledge into LLM reasoning than prior flat quantization or continuous embedding approaches.
original_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown immense potential in Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC), yet bridging the modality gap between continuous graph embeddings and discrete LLM tokens remains a critical challenge. While recent quantization-based approaches attempt to align these modalities, they typically treat quantization as flat numerical compression, resulting in semantically entangled codes that fail to mirror the hierarchical nature of human reasoning. In this paper, we propose GS-Quant, a novel framework that generates semantically coherent and structurally stratified discrete codes for KG entities. Unlike prior methods, GS-Quant is grounded in the insight that entity representations should follow a linguistic coarse-to-fine logic. We introduce a Granular Semantic Enhancement module that injects hierarchical knowledge into the codebook, ensuring that earlier codes capture global semantic categories while later codes refine specific attributes. Furthermore, a Generative Structural Reconstruction module imposes causal dependencies on the code sequence, transforming independent discrete units into structured semantic descriptors. By expanding the LLM vocabulary with these learned codes, we enable the model to reason over graph structures isomorphically to natural language generation. Experimental results demonstrate that GS-Quant significantly outperforms existing text-based and embedding-based baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mikumifa/GS-Quant.

title: Large-Scale Data Parallelization of Product Quantization and Inverted Indexing Using Dask
generated_summary:
This paper presents a distributed parallel computing approach for scaling Product Quantization (PQ) and Reconfigurable Inverted Index (Rii) approximate nearest neighbor search to large-scale datasets using the Dask Python library. The main contribution is a method to overcome memory and computational limitations when applying similarity search algorithms to datasets that exceed single-system capacity.

The methodology involves dividing data row-wise into chunks, processing each chunk with PQ in parallel, and addressing the challenge of maintaining global centroid scope across distributed computations. Rather than combining locally encoded data directly, the authors propose decoding local centroids and returning their actual values, which are then combined into a new centroid dataset to train a global PQ model. The approach is evaluated using a 6.7-million-row, 48-column dataset sampled from Soil Grids 250 meter data, split into 400 chunks and tested across three configurations: a single-system baseline, a single-node Dask system with 88 threads, and a 10-node Dask cluster with 440 threads.

Key results demonstrate that parallelization produces negligible differences in reconstruction error compared to single-process PQ, with RMSE differences within 1/10th to 1/100th margins. Significant runtime improvements are observed for large-scale data, particularly with multi-node configurations. However, the authors note that parallelization overhead makes it unsuitable for small and medium-scale datasets. The work establishes a foundation for scaling approximate nearest neighbor search to billion-scale geospatial datasets.
original_abstract: Large-scale Nearest Neighbor (NN) search, though widely utilized in the similarity search field, remains challenged by the computational limitations inherent in processing large scale data. In an effort to decrease the computational expense needed, Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search is often used in applications that do not require the exact similarity search, but instead can rely on an approximation. Product Quantization (PQ) is a memory-efficient ANN effective for clustering all sizes of datasets. Clustering large-scale, high dimensional data requires a heavy computational expense, in both memory-cost and execution time. This work focuses on a unique way to divide and conquer the large scale data in Python using PQ, Inverted Indexing and Dask, combining the results without compromising the accuracy and reducing computational requirements to the level required when using medium-scale data.

title: Task-specific Subnetwork Discovery in Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Underwater Navigation
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the internal structure of contextual multi-task reinforcement learning (MTRL) networks for autonomous underwater vehicle navigation, aiming to improve interpretability and trust in deployment. The authors seek to determine whether MTRL networks effectively share knowledge across tasks and how context variables enable task differentiation.

The methodology involves pruning a pretrained Double DQN value network to extract task-specific subnetworks for individual navigation objectives, such as locating different marine species. The approach is first validated in a simplified MiniGrid environment and then applied to underwater navigation tasks in the HoloOcean simulator. Subnetwork overlap analysis reveals the distribution of shared versus task-specific parameters, while context variable connectivity is examined to understand task differentiation mechanisms.

Key results show that globally shared parameters constitute approximately 96–98% of network weights across both environments, while task-specific parameters account for only about 1.5%. Within these task-specific parameters, over 80% correspond to connections from context variables, confirming their critical role in distinguishing tasks. The extracted subnetworks preserve task-relevant performance with minimal degradation compared to the full network.

These findings demonstrate that contextual MTRL effectively leverages shared representations across related tasks while relying primarily on context variables for task specialization. This understanding supports more interpretable, efficient, and trustworthy autonomous navigation policies, contributing to safer real-world deployment of underwater vehicles.
original_abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles are required to perform multiple tasks adaptively and in an explainable manner under dynamic, uncertain conditions and limited sensing, challenges that classical controllers struggle to address. This demands robust, generalizable, and inherently interpretable control policies for reliable long-term monitoring. Reinforcement learning, particularly multi-task RL, overcomes these limitations by leveraging shared representations to enable efficient adaptation across tasks and environments. However, while such policies show promising results in simulation and controlled experiments, they yet remain opaque and offer limited insight into the agent's internal decision-making, creating gaps in transparency, trust, and safety that hinder real-world deployment. The internal policy structure and task-specific specialization remain poorly understood. To address these gaps, we analyze the internal structure of a pretrained multi-task reinforcement learning network in the HoloOcean simulator for underwater navigation by identifying and comparing task-specific subnetworks responsible for navigating toward different species. We find that in a contextual multi-task reinforcement learning setting with related tasks, the network uses only about 1.5% of its weights to differentiate between tasks. Of these, approximately 85% connect the context-variable nodes in the input layer to the next hidden layer, highlighting the importance of context variables in such settings. Our approach provides insights into shared and specialized network components, useful for efficient model editing, transfer learning, and continual learning for underwater monitoring through a contextual multi-task reinforcement learning method.

title: Geometric Characterisation and Structured Trajectory Surrogates for Clinical Dataset Condensation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a geometric characterization of trajectory matching (TM) for dataset condensation, revealing that the matching residual is fundamentally lower bounded by the projection error of real-data parameter changes onto the synthetic dataset's reachable gradient span. This analysis exposes a conditional representability bottleneck: when supervision signals from standard SGD training are spectrally broad—as commonly occurs in low-prevalence clinical settings—compact synthetic datasets cannot fully reproduce the required training dynamics.

To address this limitation, the authors propose Bézier Trajectory Matching (BTM), which replaces stored SGD trajectories with task-optimized quadratic Bézier curve surrogates connecting initial and final model states through a learned control point. These surrogates produce smoother, lower-rank supervision signals better aligned with the representational constraints of small synthetic datasets, while reducing trajectory storage by up to 33×.

BTM is evaluated on five real-world clinical datasets spanning tabular and time-series modalities, including three NHS emergency department cohorts and two public ICU benchmarks. Results demonstrate consistent improvements over trajectory-matching baselines, with the most pronounced gains in AUPRC under low-prevalence and low-budget regimes—for example, 15–18% AUPRC improvement on the most imbalanced Birmingham cohort. BTM also exhibits robust cross-architecture generalization and maintains strong performance in multi-label phenotyping tasks.

The work offers both theoretical insight into why trajectory matching struggles in clinical settings and a practical solution that improves dataset condensation where it matters most—in data-scarce, governance-constrained clinical environments.
original_abstract: Dataset condensation constructs compact synthetic datasets that retain the training utility of large real-world datasets, enabling efficient model development and potentially supporting downstream research in governed domains such as healthcare. Trajectory matching (TM) is a widely used condensation approach that supervises synthetic data using changes in model parameters observed during training on real data, yet the structure of this supervision signal remains poorly understood. In this paper, we provide a geometric characterisation of trajectory matching, showing that a fixed synthetic dataset can only reproduce a limited span of such training-induced parameter changes. When the resulting supervision signal is spectrally broad, this creates a conditional representability bottleneck. Motivated by this mismatch, we propose Bezier Trajectory Matching (BTM), which replaces SGD trajectories with quadratic Bezier trajectory surrogates between initial and final model states. These surrogates are optimised to reduce average loss along the path while replacing broad SGD-derived supervision with a more structured, lower-rank signal that is better aligned with the optimisation constraints of a fixed synthetic dataset, and they substantially reduce trajectory storage. Experiments on five clinical datasets demonstrate that BTM consistently matches or improves upon standard trajectory matching, with the largest gains in low-prevalence and low-synthetic-budget settings. These results indicate that effective trajectory matching depends on structuring the supervision signal rather than reproducing stochastic optimisation paths.

title: Multilinguality at the Edge: Developing Language Models for the Global South
generated_summary:
This survey examines what the authors term "the last mile" challenge in language technology: the intersection of multilinguality and edge deployment, where language models must both understand low-resource languages and run efficiently on hardware-constrained devices common in the Global South. The work argues that addressing efficiency and multilingual coverage in isolation is insufficient, as communities most in need of language technology face simultaneous constraints in data availability and computational resources.

The authors conduct a systematic survey of papers published from 2021 onwards, collected from NLP and machine learning venues using the Semantic Scholar API. Through a combination of LM-assisted and human annotation, they classify papers along the language modeling pipeline, identifying whether each addresses multilinguality, edge deployment, or both.

Key findings reveal that research on edge LMs and multilinguality rarely overlaps within individual pipeline stages, with only full-stack approaches showing substantial integration of both concerns. The survey demonstrates that technical requirements for edge deployment (memory, compute, and energy constraints) often compete with requirements for multilingual capability (data, representation, and alignment). Countries with the highest linguistic diversity tend to have the most limited network connectivity, underscoring the urgency of the problem.

The work provides actionable recommendations for researchers and stakeholders and releases a public dataset of surveyed papers, aiming to stimulate development of more equitable language technologies that serve underrepresented language communities.
original_abstract: Where and how language models (LMs) are deployed determines who can benefit from them. However, there are several challenges that prevent effective deployment of LMs in non-English-speaking and hardware constrained communities in the Global South. We call this challenge the last mile: the intersection of multilinguality and edge deployment, where the goals are aligned but the technical requirements often compete. Studying these two fields together is both a need, as linguistically diverse communities often face the most severe infrastructure constraints, and an opportunity, as edge and multilingual NLP research remain largely siloed. To understand the state of the art and the challenges of combining the two areas, we survey 232 papers that tackle this problem across the language modelling pipeline, from data collection to development and deployment. We also discuss open questions and provide actionable recommendations for different stakeholders in the NLP ecosystem. Finally, we hope that this work contributes to the development of inclusive and equitable language technologies.

title: To See the Unseen: on the Generalization Ability of Transformers in Symbolic Reasoning
generated_summary:
This paper investigates why decoder-only transformers struggle to generalize symbolic reasoning to previously unseen tokens. The authors identify a critical phenomenon termed **embedding collapse**, where the embeddings of unseen tokens converge to nearly identical vectors during training, making distinct symbolic variables indistinguishable. They prove theoretically that this collapse is inevitable when training with SGD, weight decay, and layer normalization, since gradient updates on unseen tokens only come from the regularization term, driving their embeddings toward a common direction.

The authors conduct extensive experiments on synthetic propositional logic tasks requiring forward-chaining reasoning. They evaluate models on problems where query variables or all predicate names are replaced with unseen tokens. To address the identified issues, they propose combining three interventions: a **copy attention** mechanism that provides a shortcut from input embeddings to output predictions (enabling generation of unseen tokens), high symbolic diversity in training data, and either freezing or periodically resetting embeddings to prevent collapse.

Key results demonstrate that no single intervention suffices alone—copy attention without collapse prevention fails with multiple unseen variables, and frozen embeddings without copy attention cannot generate unseen tokens. The authors further show that embedding collapse occurs in practice in the Gemma 3 model family's deliberately reserved unused tokens, significantly slowing downstream finetuning compared to using familiar tokens.

These findings clarify prior conflicting results in the literature, explain why active forgetting strategies help, and provide practical guidance for building transformers capable of abstract symbolic reasoning with novel symbols.
original_abstract: We investigate the ability of decoder-only transformer models to perform abstract symbolic reasoning; specifically solving propositional logic reasoning problems given in-context. Previous work demonstrated that models fail to generalize to problems involving variable names that were not observed during training, and it was shown that one reason behind this is the difficulty of copying (or generating) unseen tokens. We show both theoretically and empirically that a particular representational collapse also has a crucial role: the unembeddings (last-layer weights) of unseen tokens collapse to nearly the same vector during training. The collapse makes distinguishing multiple unseen variables difficult for the model (especially when the embedding and unembedding parameters are shared), and provides a mechanistic explanation for the effectiveness of existing heuristic interventions like "active forgetting", which periodically reset the token (un)embeddings. Based on these observations, we devise a combination of techniques, involving a small architecture change facilitating copying, data diversity, and freezing or resetting (un)embeddings, that achieves generalization to unseen tokens. We support our claims with extensive controlled experiments on propositional logic reasoning problems. Beyond synthetic experiments, we also observe evidence of (un)embedding collapse in the open-weight models in the Gemma 3 family, which includes 99 unused tokens reserved for downstream use. Empirically we find that the correlated embeddings of these tokens are a poor initialization for finetuning applications.

title: DualSplat: Robust 3D Gaussian Splatting via Pseudo-Mask Bootstrapping from Reconstruction Failures
generated_summary:
DualSplat introduces a "Failure-to-Prior" paradigm for robust 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that addresses the circular dependency between transient object detection and static scene reconstruction. The key insight is that transient objects produce characteristic reconstruction failures—incomplete, blurred fragments—that can be mined as explicit priors rather than treated merely as artifacts to suppress.

The method operates in two stages. In Stage I, a conservative 3DGS reconstruction is performed to expose failure patterns caused by view-inconsistent transients. These failures are then converted into object-level pseudo-masks by consolidating photometric residuals, feature inconsistency from FiT3D embeddings, and SAM2 instance boundaries. In Stage II, these high-recall pseudo-masks guide a second reconstruction, where a lightweight per-pixel MLP refines the masks online using a curriculum strategy that gradually shifts from pseudo-mask supervision to self-consistency regularization as scene geometry stabilizes. Depth residuals provide complementary geometric cues for transient detection.

Comprehensive experiments on the RobustNeRF and NeRF On-the-go benchmarks demonstrate that DualSplat achieves the best overall average performance compared to recent 3DGS-based baselines. Ablation studies confirm that pseudo-mask application contributes the largest performance gain (+3.56 dB over vanilla 3DGS), while stratified analysis shows improvements are concentrated in transient regions rather than from generic reconstruction sharpening. The approach decouples transient discovery from scene optimization, offering a principled solution to transient-robust novel view synthesis.
original_abstract: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves real-time photorealistic rendering, its performance degrades significantly when training images contain transient objects that violate multi-view consistency. Existing methods face a circular dependency: accurate transient detection requires a well-reconstructed static scene, while clean reconstruction itself depends on reliable transient masks. We address this challenge with DualSplat, a Failure-to-Prior framework that converts first-pass reconstruction failures into explicit priors for a second reconstruction stage. We observe that transients, which appear in only a subset of views, often manifest as incomplete fragments during conservative initial training. We exploit these failures to construct object-level pseudo-masks by combining photometric residuals, feature mismatches, and SAM2 instance boundaries. These pseudo-masks then guide a clean second-pass 3DGS optimization, while a lightweight MLP refines them online by gradually shifting from prior supervision to self-consistency. Experiments on RobustNeRF and NeRF On-the-go show that DualSplat outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating particularly clear advantages in transient-heavy scenes and transient regions.

title: Promoting Simple Agents: Ensemble Methods for Event-Log Prediction
generated_summary:
This paper investigates whether ensembles of simple language models can match or outperform complex monolithic models for next-activity prediction in streaming event logs. The main contribution is a novel Promotion Algorithm that requires only two agents active in parallel during inference, significantly reducing computational overhead compared to traditional ensemble methods like majority voting while maintaining high prediction accuracy.

The methodology centers on combining simple n-gram models into ensembles for predicting the next activity in case-based event logs. The authors first analyze the impact of window size—a critical parameter for streaming algorithms—on prediction accuracy. They then propose the Promotion Algorithm, which dynamically selects between a lower-order and higher-order n-gram model based on a promotion threshold, effectively balancing model complexity with data availability. The approach is evaluated on synthetic datasets designed to test specific properties like counting and interleaving, as well as five real-world event-log datasets ranging from approximately 15,000 to 2.5 million events.

Key results demonstrate that while LSTM networks can outperform individual n-gram models, ensembles of simple n-gram agents consistently match or exceed the accuracy of neural models across a wide range of window sizes. The Promotion Algorithm achieves this with minimal computational overhead beyond a single n-gram model. These findings are significant for real-time process mining applications, suggesting that lightweight, interpretable ensemble methods can replace resource-intensive deep learning approaches without sacrificing predictive performance.
original_abstract: We compare lightweight automata-based models (n-grams) with neural architectures (LSTM, Transformer) for next-activity prediction in streaming event logs. Experiments on synthetic patterns and five real-world process mining datasets show that n-grams with appropriate context windows achieve comparable accuracy to neural models while requiring substantially fewer resources. Unlike windowed neural architectures, which show unstable performance patterns, n-grams provide stable and consistent accuracy. While we demonstrate that classical ensemble methods like voting improve n-gram performance, they require running many agents in parallel during inference, increasing memory consumption and latency. We propose an ensemble method, the promotion algorithm, that dynamically selects between two active models during inference, reducing overhead compared to classical voting schemes. On real-world datasets, these ensembles match or exceed the accuracy of non-windowed neural models with lower computational cost.

title: Time vs. Layer: Locating Predictive Cues for Dysarthric Speech Descriptors in wav2vec 2.0
generated_summary:
This paper systematically investigates whether layer-wise or time-wise attentive statistics pooling (ASP) of wav2vec 2.0 (W2V2) features better predicts clinically relevant dysarthric speech descriptors. Using a W2V2-large-XLSR model with frozen weights, the authors compare two pooling strategies: layer-wise ASP, which aggregates information across 24 transformer layers after temporal mean pooling, and time-wise ASP, which aggregates across time frames after averaging or selecting specific layers. Both approaches feed into a regression head to predict five Mayo Clinic speech descriptors—intelligibility, imprecise consonants, inappropriate silences, harsh voice, and monoloudness—using the Speech Accessibility Project dataset of speakers with various neurological conditions.

Key results reveal that the optimal pooling strategy depends on the descriptor: intelligibility is better modeled through layer-wise representations, while imprecise consonants, harsh voice, and monoloudness benefit from time-wise modeling that preserves temporal structure. Inappropriate silences show no clear advantage for either approach. Analysis of attention weight distributions demonstrates that layer-wise attention patterns vary with descriptor severity, indicating that different severity levels activate distinct transformer layers.

These findings are significant for clinical speech assessment, demonstrating that no single pooling strategy is universally optimal and motivating future work on combining layer-wise and time-wise attentive pooling to capture complementary information for pathological speech evaluation.
original_abstract: Wav2vec 2.0 (W2V2) has shown strong performance in pathological speech analysis by effectively capturing the characteristics of atypical speech. Despite its success, it remains unclear which components of its learned representations are most informative for specific downstream tasks. In this study, we address this question by investigating the regression of dysarthric speech descriptors using annotations from the Speech Accessibility Project dataset. We focus on five descriptors, each addressing a different aspect of speech or voice production: intelligibility, imprecise consonants, inappropriate silences, harsh voice and monoloudness. Speech representations are derived from a W2V2-based feature extractor, and we systematically compare layer-wise and time-wise aggregation strategies using attentive statistics pooling. Our results show that intelligibility is best captured through layer-wise representations, whereas imprecise consonants, harsh voice and monoloudness benefit from time-wise modeling. For inappropriate silences, no clear advantage could be observed for either approach.

title: DCMorph: Face Morphing via Dual-Stream Cross-Attention Diffusion
generated_summary:
This paper introduces DCMorph, a dual-stream face morphing framework that exploits identity-conditioned latent diffusion models to generate highly effective morphing attacks against face recognition (FR) systems. The main contribution is a novel approach that simultaneously manipulates both the conditioning pathway and the latent space of diffusion models, enabling more precise identity blending than existing methods.

DCMorph operates through two complementary mechanisms: decoupled cross-attention interpolation, which injects identity-specific features from two source faces into the denoising process via linearly interpolated cross-attention outputs, and spherical interpolation of DDIM-inverted latents, which provides geometrically consistent initialization preserving global structural attributes. Together, these streams guide the diffusion model toward generating morphs that blend characteristics from both identities.

Evaluations across four state-of-the-art FR systems demonstrate that DCMorph achieves near-perfect attack success rates (MMPMR of 0.965–0.995 at FMR 0.1%), consistently outperforming GAN-based and other diffusion-based morphing methods. Crucially, DCMorph morphs prove extremely difficult to detect, with EER values reaching 77.60% and 69.20% against unsupervised and supervised morph attack detection systems, respectively, substantially exceeding all baselines. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic benefit of combining both streams over single-stream variants.

These findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in current FR and morph detection systems, underscoring the need for developing more robust defensive mechanisms against advanced diffusion-based morphing attacks.
original_abstract: Advancing face morphing attack techniques is crucial to anticipate evolving threats and develop robust defensive mechanisms for identity verification systems. This work introduces DCMorph, a dual-stream diffusion-based morphing framework that simultaneously operates at both identity conditioning and latent space levels. Unlike image-level methods suffering from blending artifacts or GAN-based approaches with limited reconstruction fidelity, DCMorph leverages identity-conditioned latent diffusion models through two mechanisms: (1) decoupled cross-attention interpolation that injects identity-specific features from both source faces into the denoising process, enabling explicit dual-identity conditioning absent in existing diffusion-based methods, and (2) DDIM inversion with spherical interpolation between inverted latent representations from both source faces, providing geometrically consistent initial latent representation that preserves structural attributes. Vulnerability analyses across four state-of-the-art face recognition systems demonstrate that DCMorph achieves the highest attack success rates compared to existing methods at both operational thresholds, while remaining challenging to detect by current morphing attack detection solutions.

title: A-THENA: Early Intrusion Detection for IoT with Time-Aware Hybrid Encoding and Network-Specific Augmentation
generated_summary:
