The system's key innovation lies in replacing conventional discrete positional encodings with continuous timestamp-based encodings, enabling the model to capture irregular packet inter-arrival times that characterize different attack patterns. The THE framework adaptively selects among three time-aware encoding variants—sinusoidal, Fourier, and rotary—based on validation performance for each deployment scenario, combined with network-specific augmentation strategies and an Early Detection Loss function that prioritizes accurate classification from minimal packet observations.

Evaluated across three diverse IoT benchmark datasets, A-THENA achieves near-perfect detection accuracy (93.83%–100%) with zero false alarm rates, outperforming traditional machine learning baselines, existing time-aware encodings, and specialized early detection architectures. The system classifies threats using as few as one packet on two datasets, compared to feature-based methods requiring complete 30-packet flows. With only approximately 5,070 parameters, a 40 KB storage footprint, and 1.42 ms inference latency on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, A-THENA demonstrates practical deployability on resource-constrained edge devices—approximately 480 times faster than traditional feature-extraction pipelines. These results establish that integrating temporal awareness into Transformer-based intrusion detection significantly enhances both detection performance and operational efficiency for IoT security.
original_abstract: The proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has significantly expanded attack surfaces, making IoT ecosystems particularly susceptible to sophisticated cyber threats. To address this challenge, this work introduces A-THENA, a lightweight early intrusion detection system (EIDS) that significantly extends preliminary findings on time-aware encodings. A-THENA employs an advanced Transformer-based architecture augmented with a generalized Time-Aware Hybrid Encoding (THE), integrating packet timestamps to effectively capture temporal dynamics essential for accurate and early threat detection. The proposed system further employs a Network-Specific Augmentation (NA) pipeline, which enhances model robustness and generalization. We evaluate A-THENA on three benchmark IoT intrusion detection datasets-CICIoT23-WEB, MQTT-IoT-IDS2020, and IoTID20-where it consistently achieves strong performance. Averaged across all three datasets, it improves accuracy by 6.88 percentage points over the best-performing traditional positional encoding, 3.69 points over the strongest feature-based model, 6.17 points over the leading time-aware alternatives, and 5.11 points over related models, while achieving near-zero false alarms and false negatives. To assess real-world feasibility, we deploy A-THENA on the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, demonstrating its ability to perform real-time intrusion detection with minimal latency and memory usage. These results establish A-THENA as an agile, practical, and highly effective solution for securing IoT networks.

title: Local Neighborhood Instability in Parametric Projections: Quantitative and Visual Analysis
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the overlooked problem of local neighborhood instability in neural network-based parametric dimensionality reduction projections. While standard evaluation metrics like Trustworthiness and Continuity assess neighborhood preservation quality, they fail to capture how sensitive these learned mappings are to small input perturbations—a critical concern for visual analytics where analysts must trust that spatial patterns reflect genuine data structure.

The authors propose three quantitative stability measures—mean displacement, displacement bias, and nearest-anchor assignment error—computed by adding small isotropic Gaussian perturbations to class-centroid-based anchor points and measuring how their projections shift in the low-dimensional space. These metrics are complemented by three visual diagnostics (anchor displacement lines, local PCA ellipses, and Voronoi cell analysis) that reveal where and in what direction projections are sensitive.

Empirical evaluation on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST using parametric UMAP and t-SNE with varying MLP architectures reveals that standard quality metrics remain nearly identical across methods (Trustworthiness: .850–.931), yet displacement differences exceed 80%. Jacobian regularization proves substantially more effective than increasing network capacity alone, reducing displacement by up to 85% and anchor assignment error to near zero.

The findings demonstrate that stability assessment should be incorporated into parametric projection training workflows, as conventional quality metrics are insufficient. The work highlights that regularization strategy matters more than model size for achieving reliable, trustworthy projections in visual analytics applications.
original_abstract: Parametric projections let analysts embed new points in real time, but input variations from measurement noise or data drift can produce unpredictable shifts in the 2D layout. Whether and where a projection is locally stable remains largely unexamined. In this paper, we present a stability evaluation framework that probes parametric projections with Gaussian perturbations around selected anchor points and assesses how neighborhoods deform in the 2D embedding. Our approach combines quantitative measures of mean displacement, bias, and nearest-anchor assignment error with per-anchor visualizations of displacement vectors, local PCA ellipsoids, and Voronoi misassignment for detailed inspection. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness on UMAP- and t-SNE-based neural projectors of varying network sizes and study the effect of Jacobian regularization as a gradient-based robustness strategy. We apply our framework to the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. The results show that our framework identifies unstable projection regions invisible to reconstruction error or neighborhood-preservation metrics.

title: Spatiotemporal 2-D Polar Codes over Non-Uniform MIMO Channels: A Reliability-Aware Construction Approach
generated_summary:
This paper presents a reliability-aware spatiotemporal two-dimensional (2-D) polar coding framework designed for practical MIMO channels exhibiting non-uniform spatial stream reliabilities. Unlike prior spatiotemporal 2-D polar coding schemes that assume uniform channel quality across spatial streams, the proposed framework explicitly accounts for the heterogeneous signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) inherent in realistic MIMO propagation environments, where different spatial streams experience unequal channel gains.

The methodology extends polar code construction by incorporating reciprocal channel approximation (RCA)-based density evolution into the 2-D polarization process. RCA avoids the symmetric Gaussian log-likelihood ratio assumptions of conventional Gaussian approximation (GA), enabling more accurate reliability tracking across spatially heterogeneous streams. This improved reliability estimation facilitates better frozen-bit selection, which is critical for polar code performance. The authors also develop a practical implementation compatible with 5G New Radio time-division duplex channel estimation, enabling transceiver-assisted frozen-bit selection without additional signaling overhead.

Simulation results demonstrate that the RCA-based construction achieves consistent bit error rate improvements over conventional GA-based designs, particularly under non-uniform MIMO conditions. The scheme maintains robustness under imperfect channel state information and shows scalable reliability gains as the spatial dimension increases.

The framework provides a practical, low-latency, capacity-approaching coding solution for massive MIMO systems, addressing the reliability-latency tradeoff critical to ultra-reliable low-latency communications in 5G and beyond.
original_abstract: With the increasing demand for ultra-reliable and low-latency communication (URLLC), spatiotemporal two-dimensional (2-D) channel coding has received growing interest. By leveraging the spatial degrees of freedom in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, it shortens the time-domain blocklength, thereby reducing latency and enhancing reliability. However, existing spatiotemporal coding schemes typically assume uniform reliability across spatial streams. This assumption does not hold in practical MIMO channels, where the underlying propagation environment generally leads to unequal spatial-eigenmode gains and reliabilities, making the conventional Gaussian-approximation-based construction for 2-D polar codes less effective. This paper investigates spatiotemporal 2-D polar coding over non-uniform MIMO channels, where the spatial domain exhibits inherently heterogeneous signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). We propose a reciprocal channel approximation (RCA)-based reliability-aware 2-D polar coding framework that accurately characterizes such heterogeneous SNRs without relying on log-likelihood-ratio distribution assumptions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed RCA-based spatiotemporal 2-D polar coding scheme achieves clear performance gains and strong robustness, confirming its effectiveness in jointly exploiting temporal and spatial polarization for URLLC in practical MIMO systems.

title: Process Supervision via Verbal Critique Improves Reasoning in Large Language Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Verbal Process Supervision (VPS), a training-free inference-time method that identifies critique granularity as a distinct fourth axis of inference-time scaling for large language model reasoning, alongside chain depth, sample breadth, and learned step-scorers. VPS employs a stronger supervisor model to provide step-level natural-language critique of a weaker actor model's reasoning, operating through a generate-critique-refine loop without requiring gradient updates, human labels, or additional training data.

The authors evaluate VPS across three benchmarks—GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and LiveCodeBench V6—using multiple same-family and cross-family model pairs. At matched inference compute, VPS outperforms Reflexion (outcome-level critique) by +8.5 to +12.1 percentage points across all benchmarks, isolating critique granularity rather than verbal feedback itself as the operative variable. VPS also outperforms Self-Consistency@5 by +5.0 and +8.3 points on GPQA and LiveCodeBench respectively. On GPQA Diamond, VPS achieves 94.9%, exceeding the reported state-of-the-art of 94.1%. Notably, weak actors experience dramatic improvements—rising from 11.7% to 70.0% on AIME under strong supervision.

Key findings include that VPS benefit is strongly predicted by supervisor-actor headroom (Pearson r=+0.90), round-count scaling is non-monotonic and pair-dependent, and VPS encounters a principled domain boundary in code synthesis where errors are not linguistically representable. These results establish critique granularity as a scalable, resource-efficient dimension for improving LLM reasoning.
original_abstract: Inference-time scaling for LLM reasoning has focused on three axes: chain depth, sample breadth, and learned step-scorers (PRMs). We introduce a fourth axis, granularity of external verbal supervision, via Verbal Process Supervision (VPS), a training-free framework that uses structured natural-language critique from a stronger supervisor to guide an iterative generate-critique-refine loop up to a round budget R. Across GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and LiveCodeBench V6 (covering both closed and open models), VPS yields three key results. First, on GPQA Diamond, GPT-5.4 (High) | GPT-5.4 (Low) reaches 94.9% at R=4, surpassing the 94.1% state of the art without gradient updates. Second, on AIME 2025, VPS enables strong weak-actor rescue, boosting scores from 11.7-26.7% to 63.3-90.0% (up to +63.3 points). Third, at matched compute, VPS outperforms Reflexion by +8.5 to +12.1 points and Self-Consistency@5 by +5.0 pp (GPQA) and +8.3 pp (LiveCodeBench), isolating critique granularity as the key driver. Performance scales with the supervisor-actor capability gap (Pearson r=0.90) and degrades when errors are not linguistically expressible (e.g., code synthesis), motivating hybrid verbal-executable methods. These results establish critique granularity as a new axis of inference-time scaling.

title: Process-Mining of Hypertraces: Enabling Scalable Formal Security Verification of (Automotive) Network Architectures
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of formally verifying the security of automotive network architectures (ANAs) under partial component compromise, a critical concern given increasing vehicle connectivity and regulatory requirements. The authors present four main contributions: (1) a novel adversarial model called CRASH-M, extending the Dolev-Yao model to capture automotive-specific threats including network segmentation, entity compromise, and internal knowledge extraction; (2) an improved verification orchestration algorithm that reduces the state-space explosion problem in analyzing attribution responsibility hypotheses (ARH), enabling scalable analysis of complex architectures with fine-grained adversarial permissions and comparative multi-security-property assessment; (3) a novel bridge between formal verification and process mining that synthesizes event logs from security protocol verification traces, allowing process mining algorithms to systematically identify and summarize adversarial behaviors causing security property invalidations; and (4) prototypical implementations called ImpACT and RoadMINER that validate real-world applicability.

The methodology is demonstrated through a case study involving a battery management system protocol within a realistic ANA. The approach not only identifies which compromised components invalidate security properties such as data secrecy and message authenticity, but also reveals how adversarial behavior achieves these invalidations. This work is significant because it advances formal security verification from isolated counterexample generation toward comprehensive, systematic analysis of compromise impacts, directly supporting automotive cybersecurity engineering requirements under ISO/SAE 21434 and UN regulations.
original_abstract: The automotive domain is transitioning: vehicles act as rolling servers, persistently connected to numerous external entities. This connectivity, combined with rising on-board computing power for advanced driver assistance systems and similar use cases, creates escalating challenges for securing automotive network architectures. This work advances the security analysis of internet-connected automotive network architectures and their protocols. We introduce a strong, active adversary model tailored to the automotive domain. We substantially extend security protocol verification possible based on Attack Resilience Hyperproperties (ARHs) by introducing a verification-orchestration algorithm. Furthermore, we provide methods for comparative attribution of security property invalidations to specific, ne-grained component compromises. We present a novel integration of formal verification and process mining. By utilizing ARH counterexample traces for process mining, we systematically identify and aggregate attacker behavior that causes security property invalidations. This pipeline enables in-depth understanding of root causes and attack paths leading to protocol-security invalidations. We demonstrate real-world applicability through a prototype and case study on the secure transmission of battery management system data within an automotive network architecture.

title: Using ASP(Q) to Handle Inconsistent Prioritized Data
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first implementation of globally-optimal repair-based semantics for querying inconsistent prioritized knowledge bases, leveraging Answer Set Programming with Quantifiers (ASP(Q)). While Pareto- and completion-optimal repairs had been previously implemented, globally-optimal repairs posed a challenge due to their higher computational complexity (second level of the polynomial hierarchy). ASP(Q), which extends ASP with quantifiers over answer sets, provides a natural framework for encoding such problems without requiring complex saturation techniques.

The authors also provide the first implementation of the grounded semantics, a tractable approximation derived from abstract argumentation theory. Their approach incorporates several optimizations, including localization techniques and specialized encodings for binary conflicts. Experiments are conducted on benchmarks adapted from the CQAPri/LUBM framework, varying dataset sizes and conflict proportions.

Key findings reveal that globally-optimal repair reasoning is significantly more expensive than Pareto- or completion-optimal reasoning, consistent with theoretical complexity predictions. However, the grounded semantics proves to be a surprisingly effective approximation of optimal repair-based semantics, capturing nearly all answers obtainable under the more expensive X-AR semantics while remaining tractable to compute. The three kinds of optimal repairs often yield identical answers in practice. These results suggest that computing the grounded repair as a preprocessing step offers a practical strategy for inconsistency-tolerant query answering, substantially reducing the number of candidate answers requiring expensive verification.
original_abstract: We explore the use of answer set programming (ASP) and its extension with quantifiers, ASP(Q), for inconsistency-tolerant querying of prioritized data, where a priority relation between conflicting facts is exploited to define three notions of optimal repairs (Pareto-, globally- and completion-optimal). We consider the variants of three well-known semantics (AR, brave and IAR) that use these optimal repairs, and for which query answering is in the first or second level of the polynomial hierarchy for a large class of logical theories. Notably, this paper presents the first implementation of globally-optimal repair-based semantics, as well as the first implementation of the grounded semantics, which is a tractable under-approximation of all these optimal repair-based semantics. Our experimental evaluation sheds light on the feasibility of computing answers under globally-optimal repair semantics and the impact of adopting different semantics, approximations, and encodings.

title: On the Role of Preprocessing and Memristor Dynamics in Reservoir Computing for Image Classification
generated_summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of reservoir computing (RC) implemented with volatile memristors for image classification, focusing on how device-level dynamics and input preprocessing strategies influence computational performance. The authors employ a parallel delayed feedback network (PDFN) architecture, where multiple volatile memristors operate in parallel to capture temporal dependencies without requiring crossbar interconnections, and systematically evaluate its performance on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset.

The methodology involves varying key parameters—preprocessing methods (1D/2D encoding, sectioning, and parity transformations), memristor decay rate, quantization levels, and device variability—and performing factorial ANOVA to quantify their relative contributions to accuracy and robustness. The study reveals that input sectioning has the strongest impact on accuracy, followed by quantization level, with 2D encoding and parity transformations providing additional improvements. The system achieves 95.88% classification accuracy on MNIST using 581 volatile memristors with 4-bit quantization, comparable to the best reported memristive RC implementations. Notably, acceptable performance is maintained even with 2-bit quantization and up to 20% device variability, though at least 3-bit resolution is needed for robust operation.

The significance of this work lies in demonstrating that co-design of input encoding and device parameters is essential for achieving both high accuracy and variability resilience, providing practical design guidelines for hardware-efficient neuromorphic computing systems based on volatile memristors.
original_abstract: Reservoir computing (RC) is an emerging recurrent neural network architecture that has attracted growing attention for its low training cost and modest hardware requirements. Memristor-based circuits are particularly promising for RC, as their intrinsic dynamics can reduce network size and parameter overhead in tasks such as time-series prediction and image recognition. Although RC has been demonstrated with several memristive devices, a comprehensive evaluation of device-level requirements remains limited. In this paper, we analyze and explain the operation of a parallel delayed feedback network (PDFN) RC architecture with volatile memristors, focusing on how device characteristics -- such as decay rate, quantization, and variability -- affect reservoir performance. We further discuss strategies to improve data representation in the reservoir using preprocessing methods and suggest potential improvements. The proposed approach achieves 95.89% classification accuracy on MNIST, comparable with the best reported memristor-based RC implementations. Furthermore, the method maintains high robustness under 20% device variability, achieving an accuracy of up to 94.2%. These results demonstrate that volatile memristors can support reliable spatio-temporal information processing and reinforce their potential as key building blocks for compact, high-speed, and energy-efficient neuromorphic computing systems.

title: DryRUN: On the Role of Public Tests in LLM-Driven Code Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces DryRUN (Debugging and Refinement Under Non-execution), a framework that challenges the conventional reliance on human-authored public test cases in LLM-driven code generation. The authors argue that this dependence creates an "Overconfidence Gap," where models overfit to trivial public tests while failing on hidden private test suites.

DryRUN operates through three phases: initial implementation planning with iterative autonomous refinement, mental simulation where the LLM synthesizes its own non-trivial inputs and traces execution line-by-line to identify logical flaws, and final code polishing. Crucially, the framework requires no public test cases and no external code execution—the LLM relies entirely on its intrinsic reasoning capacity for verification.

Evaluated on LiveCodeBench v6 (problems after March 2025) using GPT-5-mini and Gemini-3-flash, DryRUN achieves performance comparable to CodeSIM, the state-of-the-art method that explicitly exploits public tests and sandbox execution. DryRUN matches or exceeds CodeSIM's accuracy while consuming only 70% of its total tokens and 50% of output tokens. Notably, removing public test cases from zero-shot baselines slightly improves accuracy, further undermining the assumed necessity of these examples.

The findings carry significant implications for code generation research and practice, suggesting that the community's reliance on public test cases is overstated. The work raises important questions about benchmark design and points toward more practical code generation approaches suited to real-world scenarios where ground-truth examples are rarely available.
original_abstract: Multi-agent frameworks are widely used in autonomous code generation and have applications in complex algorithmic problem-solving. Recent work has addressed the challenge of generating functionally correct code by incorporating simulation-driven planning and debugging, where language models trace execution steps to verify logic. However, these approaches depend on human-provided public test cases to ground the debugging and simulation loop. Manually authoring comprehensive input-output examples is a labor-intensive bottleneck in the software development lifecycle. Because ground-truth input-output examples are rarely available prior to implementation in real-world software engineering, this dependency restricts methods to curated competitive programming benchmarks. Furthermore, we identify that reliance on these public tests induces an ``overconfidence gap,'' causing frameworks to overfit to simplistic examples and fail on hidden evaluations. In contrast, we observe that external sample inputs are not strictly necessary for code generation. We demonstrate that large language models can autonomously generate valid inputs and simulate execution traces to self-correct. Consequently, we develop DryRUN, a framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth samples by allowing the LLM to iteratively plan, autonomously generate its own inputs and simulate execution, mitigating algorithmic overconfidence. Evaluations on the LiveCodeBench v6 dataset (post-March 2025) demonstrate that DryRUN matches performance against CodeSIM, a state-of-the-art and public-test-dependent framework, while operating entirely without public test cases or external execution feedback while reducing output token consumption.

title: A Kernel Nonconformity Score for Multivariate Conformal Prediction
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a kernel-based nonconformity score (KCS) for multivariate conformal prediction that generalizes ellipsoidal methods by embedding calibration residuals into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). The score measures test residual conformity through a regularized quadratic form involving the empirical covariance operator, which the authors prove equals the posterior variance of a Gaussian process evaluated at calibration residual locations.

The score decomposes into two interpretable components: a Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) term measuring distributional typicality and a kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) correction capturing directional anisotropy. This combination produces prediction regions shaped by both the density and directional covariance of residuals, unlike existing methods that capture only one aspect. When using a linear kernel, the score reduces to the regularized Mahalanobis distance, establishing it as a strict generalization of ellipsoidal conformal prediction.

The authors provide finite-sample coverage guarantees under exchangeability with convergence rates depending on the RKHS covariance operator's effective rank rather than ambient dimension, and extend guarantees to β-mixing sequences. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate 5–86% volume reductions relative to Mahalanobis baselines while maintaining nominal coverage, with advantages increasing at higher output dimensions and tighter coverage levels. The work bridges Bayesian geometry for region design with frequentist coverage validity, offering a principled nonparametric approach to multivariate conformal prediction.
original_abstract: Multivariate conformal prediction requires nonconformity scores that compress residual vectors into scalars while preserving certain implicit geometric structure of the residual distribution. We introduce a Multivariate Kernel Score (MKS) that produces prediction regions that explicitly adapt to this geometry. We show that the proposed score resembles the Gaussian process posterior variance, unifying Bayesian uncertainty quantification with the coverage guarantees of frequentist-type. Moreover, the MKS can be decomposed into an anisotropic Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) that interpolates between kernel density estimation and covariance-weighted distance. We prove finite-sample coverage guarantees and establish convergence rates that depend on the effective rank of the kernel-based covariance operator rather than the ambient dimension, enabling dimension-free adaptation. On regression tasks, the MKS reduces the volume of prediction region significantly, compared to ellipsoidal baselines while maintaining nominal coverage, with larger gains at higher dimensions and tighter coverage levels.

title: Language as a Latent Variable for Reasoning Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces polyGRPO, a reinforcement learning framework that treats language as a latent variable to enhance reasoning capabilities in large language models. The methodology builds on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with three key modules: a Polyglot Reasoning Generation Module that produces diverse multilingual responses per question (one unconstrained and others in randomly selected languages), a rule-based Reward Module evaluating accuracy and reasoning format, and a GRPO-based optimization module that computes group-relative advantages to guide policy learning. Evaluated on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3-8B-Instruct across four benchmarks (MGSM, MATH500, PolyMath, X-CSQA) spanning 23 languages, polyGRPO consistently outperforms baselines, achieving average improvements of 3.07% and 1.72% over the strongest baselines on English tasks for the two models respectively, with an average 6.4% improvement on multilingual mathematical benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm that both constrained and unconstrained language generation are essential for stable performance.

The significance lies in demonstrating that polyglot thinking serves as effective scaffolding for stronger, language-agnostic reasoning, with improvements transferring even to English-only evaluation without requiring multilingual inference at test time.
original_abstract: As LLMs reduce English-centric bias, a surprising trend emerges: non-English responses sometimes outperform English on reasoning tasks. We hypothesize that language functions as a latent variable that structurally modulates the model's internal inference pathways, rather than merely serving as an output medium. To test this, we conducted a Polyglot Thinking Experiment, in which models were prompted to solve identical problems under language-constrained and language-unconstrained conditions. Results show that non-English responses often achieve higher accuracy, and the best performance frequently occur when language is unconstrained, suggesting that multilinguality broadens the model's latent reasoning space. Based on this insight, we propose polyGRPO (Polyglot Group Relative Policy Optimization), an RL framework that treats language variation as an implicit exploration signal. It generates polyglot preference data online under language-constrained and unconstrained conditions, optimizing the policy with respect to both answer accuracy and reasoning structure. Trained on only 18.1K multilingual math problems without chain-of-thought annotations, polyGRPO improves the base model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) by 6.72% absolute accuracy on four English reasoning testset and 6.89% in their multilingual benchmark. Remarkably, it is the only method that surpasses the base LLM on English commonsense reasoning task (4.9%), despite being trained solely on math data-highlighting its strong cross-task generalization. Further analysis reveals that treating language as a latent variable expands the model's latent reasoning space, yielding consistent and generalizable improvements in reasoning performance.

title: Sculpt4D: Generating 4D Shapes via Sparse-Attention Diffusion Transformers
generated_summary:
Sculpt4D presents a native 4D generative model that extends a pretrained 3D Diffusion Transformer (Hunyuan3D 2.1) to synthesize high-fidelity dynamic 3D shapes from video input. The main contribution is a novel Block Sparse Attention mechanism that efficiently captures spatiotemporal dependencies without the quadratic computational cost of full attention.

The approach introduces two key innovations. First, a temporally consistent surface sampling strategy ensures coherent latent representations across frames by propagating canonical point correspondences through animation sequences and sharing VAE noise across frames. Second, the sparse attention mechanism combines two principles: an "attention anchor" where all frames attend to the first frame's tokens to prevent identity drift, and a time-decaying sparse mask that enforces near-diagonal attention patterns with increasing stride for temporally distant frames. This preserves spatial correspondence while efficiently pruning uncorrelated token pairs.

Trained on only 13,000 4D animated objects from Objaverse, Sculpt4D significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods including L4GM, V2M4, and GVFD across Chamfer Distance, F-Score, and IoU metrics. The sparse attention reduces total network computation by 56% compared to full attention while maintaining comparable generation quality. The model also demonstrates strong generalization to in-the-wild videos from the DAVIS dataset.

This work is significant as it demonstrates that efficient temporal modeling can be directly integrated into powerful 3D generative architectures, providing a scalable path toward high-quality 4D content generation despite limited training data.
original_abstract: Recent breakthroughs in 3D generative modeling have yielded remarkable progress in static shape synthesis, yet high-fidelity dynamic 4D generation remains elusive, hindered by temporal artifacts and prohibitive computational demand. We present Sculpt4D, a native 4D generative framework that seamlessly integrates efficient temporal modeling into a pretrained 3D Diffusion Transformer (Hunyuan3D 2.1), thereby mitigating the scarcity of 4D training data. At its core lies a Block Sparse Attention mechanism that preserves object identity by anchoring to the initial frame while capturing rich motion dynamics via a time-decaying sparse mask. This design faithfully models complex spatiotemporal dependencies with high fidelity, while sidestepping the quadratic overhead of full attention and reducing network total computation by 56%. Consequently, Sculpt4D establishes a new state-of-the-art in temporally coherent 4D synthesis and charts a path toward efficient and scalable 4D generation.

title: AgenticQwen: Training Small Agentic Language Models with Dual Data Flywheels for Industrial-Scale Tool Use
generated_summary:
This paper introduces AgenticQwen, a family of small agentic language models (8B and 30B parameters) designed to deliver strong tool-use capabilities at significantly lower cost than frontier models. The main contribution is a dual data flywheel framework that continuously generates increasingly challenging training data to overcome the performance saturation typical of single-round reinforcement learning on synthetic data.

The methodology combines two complementary components. The reasoning data flywheel collects problems the model fails to solve, then expands them via self-instruct rewriting and persona injection to maintain diversity while increasing difficulty. The agentic data flywheel transforms simple linear tool-use workflows into multi-branch behavior trees by injecting conditional branches based on varying environment states, then applies branch-to-task inversion to create new training scenarios. Adversarial mock users further increase difficulty by attempting to mislead the model. Both flywheels operate iteratively, with each round's model failures seeding the next round's training data. Models are trained using GRPO-style multi-round reinforcement learning on approximately 100K examples, with Qwen3-235B serving as the data synthesis and evaluation backbone.

On benchmarks including TAU-2 and BFCL-V4, AgenticQwen-8B more than doubles the performance of vanilla Qwen3-8B and approaches Qwen3-235B performance. AgenticQwen-30B-A3B achieves the best overall score of 50.2. Performance improves steadily across training rounds, validating the flywheel design. These results demonstrate that targeted agentic training can make small models viable for industrial-scale tool-use applications at substantially reduced inference cost.
original_abstract: Modern industrial applications increasingly demand language models that act as agents, capable of multi-step reasoning and tool use in real-world settings. These tasks are typically performed under strict cost and latency constraints, making small agentic models highly desirable. In this paper, we introduce the AgenticQwen family of models, trained via multi-round reinforcement learning (RL) on synthetic data and a limited amount of open-source data. Our training framework combines reasoning RL and agentic RL with dual data flywheels that automatically generate increasingly challenging tasks. The reasoning flywheel increases task difficulty by learning from errors, while the agentic flywheel expands linear workflows into multi-branch behavior trees that better reflect the decision complexity of real-world applications. We validate AgenticQwen on public benchmarks and in an industrial agent system. The models achieve strong performance on multiple agentic benchmarks, and in our industrial agent system, close the gap with much larger models on search and data analysis tasks. Model checkpoints and part of the synthetic data: https://huggingface.co/collections/alibaba-pai/agenticqwen. Data synthesis and RL training code: https://github.com/haruhi-sudo/data_synth_and_rl. The data synthesis pipeline is also integrated into EasyDistill: https://github.com/modelscope/easydistill.

title: Generative Learning Enhanced Intelligent Resource Management for Cell-Free Delay Deterministic Communications
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a virtual constrained Markov decision process (CMDP)-based offline pretraining framework for energy-efficient resource management in cell-free multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MIMO) systems with statistical delay guarantees. The main contribution addresses the challenge of deploying deep reinforcement learning (DRL) in delay-sensitive wireless systems, where low sample efficiency and constraint violations during exploration pose significant risks.

The authors formulate the space-time-frequency resource allocation problem as a CMDP, aiming to maximize energy efficiency subject to delay violation rate constraints. They solve it using Proximal Policy Optimization with a primal-dual method. To enable safe and efficient pretraining, a virtual CMDP is constructed from offline transition data using three modules: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for reward and cost prediction, a VAE-based Cholesky Mixture Density Network for initial-state distribution modeling, and a novel evidence-aware conditional Gaussian Mixture Model (EA-CGMM) for state transition modeling. The EA-CGMM approach analytically infers next-state distributions while mitigating data sparsity and distribution shift through statistical evidence reweighting.

Simulation results demonstrate that the pretrained agent achieves twice the initial energy efficiency of non-pretrained baselines with only 1% delay constraint violation, ultimately converging to 4.7% higher energy efficiency while requiring 50% fewer exploration steps. The framework's generality extends beyond CF-MIMO to other wireless architectures, offering a practical pathway for deploying DRL in delay-deterministic communication systems.
original_abstract: Cell-free multiple-input multiple-output (CF-MIMO) architecture significantly enhances wireless network performance, offering a promising solution for delay-sensitive applications. This paper investigates the resource allocation problem in CF-MIMO systems, aiming to maximize energy efficiency (EE) while satisfying delay violation rate constraint. We design a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with a primal-dual method to solve it. To address the low sample efficiency and safety risks caused by cold-start of the designed safe deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method, we propose a novel offline pretraining framework based on virtual constrained Markov decision process (CMDP) modeling. The virtual CMDP consists of reward and cost prediction module, initial-state distribution module and state transition module. Notably, we propose an evidence-aware conditional Gaussian Mixture Model (EA-CGMM) inference approach to mitigate data sparsity and distribution drift issues in state transition modeling. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of CMDP modeling and validate the safety and efficiency of the proposed pretraining framework. Specifically, compared with non-pretrained baseline, the agent pretrained through our proposed framework achieves twice the initial EE and maintains a low delay constraint violation rate of $1\%$, while ultimately converging to an EE that is $4.7\%$ higher with a $50\%$ reduction in exploration steps. Additionally, our proposed pretraining framework implementation exhibits comparable performance to the SOTA diffusion model-based implementation, while achieving a $14$-fold reduction in computational complexity.

title: CoFEE: Reasoning Control for LLM-Based Feature Discovery
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CoFEE (Cognitive Feature Engineering Engine), an agent-based pipeline that leverages cognitively structured prompting to improve LLM-based feature discovery. The main contribution is demonstrating that explicitly inducing cognitive reasoning behaviors—backward chaining, subgoal decomposition, verification, and backtracking—in LLM prompts produces more predictive features compared to vanilla prompting approaches.

The methodology employs a three-agent pipeline applied to venture capital founder success prediction. Agent 1 performs feature discovery using either cognitive prompting or vanilla prompting (GPT-5.2), Agent 2 refines the feature list by merging semantically similar features, and Agent 3 scores each feature against founder data. The key evaluation metric is success-rate delta (ΔSR), which measures how effectively each feature discriminates between successful and unsuccessful founders. All pipeline components except Agent 1's prompting strategy are held constant to isolate the effect of cognitive prompting.

The results show that cognitive prompting consistently produces features with higher predictability scores than vanilla prompting, as measured by the top-ranked features' ΔSR values. This suggests that structured cognitive behaviors serve as effective inductive biases for LLM-based feature generation.

The significance of this work lies in establishing cognitive prompting as a practical design strategy for controlling LLM reasoning during upstream feature engineering. The authors acknowledge limitations including evaluation on a single domain and the use of ΔSR rather than downstream task performance, with plans for broader evaluation in future work.
original_abstract: Feature discovery from complex unstructured data is fundamentally a reasoning problem: it requires identifying abstractions that are predictive of a target outcome while avoiding leakage, proxies, and post-outcome signals. With the introduction of ever-improving Large Language Models (LLMs), our method provides a structured method for addressing this challenge. LLMs are well suited for this task by being able to process large amounts of information, but unconstrained feature generation can lead to weak features. In this work, we study reasoning control in LLMs by inducing cognitive behaviors for improving feature discovery. We introduce CoFEE (Cognitive Feature Engineering Engine), a reasoning control framework that enforces cognitive behaviors in how the LLM reasons during feature discovery. From a machine learning perspective, these cognitive behaviors act as structured inductive biases over the space of candidate features generated by the model. These behaviors have been exploited with success in ML models, and include backward chaining from outcomes, subgoal decomposition, verification against observability and leakage criteria, and explicit backtracking of rejected reasoning paths. In a controlled comparison, we show that enforcing cognitive behaviors yields features with higher empirical predictability than those under unconstrained vanilla LLM prompts. CoFEE achieves an average Success Rate Score that is 15.2% higher than the vanilla approach, while generating 29% fewer features and reducing costs by 53.3%. Using held-out feature evaluation, we assess whether cognitively induced features generalize beyond the data used for discovery. Our results indicate that, in our evaluated setting, reasoning control is associated with improvements in quality and efficiency of LLM-based feature discovery.

title: Robust Beamforming for MIMO Radar with Imperfect Prior Distribution Information
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of robust beamforming design for MIMO radar systems when the prior probability distribution of the target's angular location is imperfectly known. The main contribution is a novel framework that optimizes transmit beamforming to minimize the worst-case posterior Cramér-Rao bound (PCRB) across all possible actual probability density functions (PDFs) lying within an uncertainty set around the imperfectly known PDF.

The authors model the real PDF as a perturbed version of the known imperfect PDF, with the perturbation's energy bounded by an uncertainty radius. The resulting optimization problem is extremely challenging due to infinitely many constraints arising from the continuous uncertainty set. To overcome this, the authors employ a second-order Taylor expansion to obtain a tractable quadratic approximation of each constraint, then apply the S-procedure to collapse the infinite constraints into a single linear matrix inequality. This reformulates the problem as a convex semi-definite program solvable in polynomial time.

Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed robust design significantly outperforms non-robust beamforming, which naively optimizes based on the imperfect PDF, and performs closely to a genie-aided benchmark that has perfect knowledge of all possible real PDFs. The robust scheme produces a "flattened" power pattern that proactively covers potential highly-probable target angles surrounding the known PDF peaks, while achieving approximately 60% computational time reduction compared to enumeration-based approaches. This work has important implications for practical radar systems where prior distribution information is inherently imprecise.
original_abstract: This paper studies a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) radar system for sensing the unknown and random angular location (angle) of a point target, based on the target-reflected echo signals and known prior distribution information about the target's angle specified by a probability density function (PDF). We consider a challenging yet practical scenario where the knowledge of such PDF is imperfect, due to the inaccuracy in PDF acquisition or unpredicted change of target appearance pattern; while the real (actual) PDF is modeled as an unknown perturbed version of the imperfect known PDF bounded by a given uncertainty radius. Such PDF imperfection motivates us to study the robust transmit beamforming design to optimize the worst-case sensing performance among all possible real PDFs. Since the sensing mean-squared error (MSE) is difficult to be characterized explicitly, we adopt the worst-case posterior Cramér-Rao bound (PCRB) as the performance metric. We formulate the beamforming optimization problem to minimize the maximum PCRB among all possible real PDFs, which is highly non-trivial since the PCRB has a complex intractable expression over the real PDF, and there are infinite constraints corresponding to the continuous set of real PDFs bounded by the uncertainty radius. To address these challenges, we derive a tractable quadratic approximation of the PCRB via second-order Taylor expansion, and leverage the S-procedure to equivalently transform the infinite constraints into a linear matrix inequality, based on which the problem is reformulated into a convex optimization problem solvable with polynomial time complexity. The obtained solution approaches the globally optimal robust beamforming solution as the uncertainty radius decreases. Numerical results validate the effectiveness of our proposed robust beamforming design.

title: A Metamorphic Testing Approach to Diagnosing Memorization in LLM-Based Program Repair
generated_summary:
This paper presents a systematic empirical study investigating whether metamorphic testing can diagnose and mitigate the effects of data leakage in Large Language Model (LLM)-based Automated Program Repair (APR). The authors hypothesize that semantics-preserving code transformations—such as identifier renaming, control-flow restructuring, and loop rewriting—can reveal when LLMs rely on memorized solutions rather than genuine reasoning.

The methodology involves applying these transformations to two Java benchmarks (Defects4J and GitBug-Java) and evaluating seven state-of-the-art LLMs on both original and transformed code. Performance is measured through success rates across multiple independent prompts, with statistical significance assessed via Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The authors also correlate performance drops with negative log-likelihood (NLL) scores as a proxy for model familiarity.

Key results show statistically significant performance degradation on transformed Defects4J code across all models (drops of 4–16%), while GitBug-Java, containing newer bugs less likely to appear in training data, shows minimal degradation. Significant correlations between low NLL values and larger performance drops confirm that transformations disproportionately affect memorized bugs. Nested conditional transformations and identifier renaming combined with structural changes are most indicative of memorization.

The study demonstrates that metamorphic testing, combined with memorization signals, provides a practical, sustainable diagnostic tool for detecting benchmark contamination, offering a cheaper alternative to continually curating new evaluation datasets.
original_abstract: LLM-based automated program repair (APR) techniques have shown promising results in reducing debugging costs. However, prior results can be affected by data leakage: large language models (LLMs) may memorize bug fixes when evaluation benchmarks overlap with their pretraining data, leading to inflated performance estimates. In this paper, we investigate whether we can better reveal data leakage by combining metamorphic testing (MT) with negative log-likelihood (NLL), which has been used in prior work as a proxy for memorization. We construct variant benchmarks by applying semantics-preserving transformations to two widely used datasets, Defects4J and GitBug-Java. Using these benchmarks, we evaluate the repair success rates of seven LLMs on both original and transformed versions, and analyze the relationship between performance degradation and NLL. Our results show that all evaluated state-of-the-art LLMs exhibit substantial drops in patch generation success rates on transformed benchmarks, ranging from -4.1% for GPT-4o to -15.98% for Llama-3.1. Furthermore, we find that this degradation strongly correlates with NLL on the original benchmarks, suggesting that models perform better on instances they are more likely to have memorized. These findings show that combining MT with NLL provides stronger and more reliable evidence of data leakage, while metamorphic testing alone can help mitigate its effects in LLM-based APR evaluations.

title: OmniFit: Multi-modal 3D Body Fitting via Scale-agnostic Dense Landmark Prediction
generated_summary:
This paper presents OmniFit, a unified multi-modal framework for fitting parametric body models (SMPL-X) to 3D clothed human assets across diverse input modalities and data sources. The main contribution is a versatile system that seamlessly handles point clouds with optional RGB images while accommodating scale-distorted or partial geometry from real-world captures, synthetic datasets, and AI-generated avatars.

The methodology centers on three novel components: (1) a conditional transformer decoder that predicts 600 dense landmarks on the body surface from input point clouds, with landmarks strategically distributed across head, body, and hand regions for comprehensive coverage; (2) a plug-and-play image adapter that incorporates front-view RGB features through parallel cross-attention branches without modifying the base architecture; and (3) a scale predictor that estimates and corrects scale distortions common in generative model outputs. Body parameters are then optimized by aligning the parametric model to predicted landmarks.

OmniFit achieves millimeter-level fitting accuracy for the first time, reducing vertex-to-vertex and joint position errors by up to 75.5% and 80.9% respectively over the second-best methods on standard benchmarks (CAPE and ReSynth). It also outperforms leading multi-view optimization-based pipelines that require multiple rendered images with camera poses.

The significance lies in providing a practical, 3D-native solution that unifies previously fragmented approaches, enabling robust body fitting across the growing ecosystem of 3D human assets from diverse sources including AI-generated content.
original_abstract: Fitting an underlying body model to 3D clothed human assets has been extensively studied, yet most approaches focus on either single-modal inputs such as point clouds or multi-view images alone, often requiring a known metric scale. This constraint is frequently impractical, especially for AI-generated assets where scale distortion is common. We propose OmniFit, a method that can seamlessly handle diverse multi-modal inputs, including full scans, partial depth observations, and image captures, while remaining scale-agnostic for both real and synthetic assets. Our key innovation is a simple yet effective conditional transformer decoder that directly maps surface points to dense body landmarks, which are then used for SMPL-X parameter fitting. In addition, an optional plug-and-play image adapter incorporates visual cues to compensate for missing geometric information. We further introduce a dedicated scale predictor that rescales subjects to canonical body proportions. OmniFit substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 57.1 to 80.9 percent across daily and loose clothing scenarios. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first body fitting method to surpass multi-view optimization baselines and the first to achieve millimeter-level accuracy on the CAPE and 4D-DRESS benchmarks.

title: CHRep: Cross-modal Histology Representation and Post-hoc Calibration for Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
generated_summary:
CHRep is a two-phase framework for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E histology images, designed to address cross-slide generalization challenges under strict leave-one-slide-out evaluation. The key innovation lies in decoupling structure-aware representation learning from inference-time calibration, rather than relying on a single end-to-end regression pipeline.

During training, CHRep jointly optimizes three objectives: correlation-aware regression for gene-wise trend fidelity, symmetric contrastive alignment between coordinate-guided morphology features and gene expression features, and coordinate-induced multi-hop topology preservation to maintain tissue spatial organization. During inference, the encoder is frozen and a lightweight post-hoc calibration module is applied, combining a similarity-weighted non-parametric estimate from a training-gallery embedding bank with a magnitude-regularized residual correction to mitigate slide-specific biases without backbone fine-tuning.

Experiments on three spatial transcriptomics datasets (cSCC, HER2+, and Alex+10x) demonstrate consistent improvements. Compared to HAGE, CHRep improves average Pearson correlation by 4.0% on cSCC and 9.8% on HER2+. On Alex+10x, it achieves 39.5% higher correlation than mclSTExp alongside 9.7% and 9.0% reductions in MSE and MAE, respectively. Ablation studies confirm that each component—non-parametric estimation, residual correction, magnitude regularization, contrastive alignment, and topology preservation—contributes complementary benefits. These results suggest that separating representation learning from deployment-time calibration offers a practical strategy for building more reliable histology-to-expression prediction models in large-cohort settings.
original_abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables spatially resolved gene profiling but remains expensive and low-throughput, limiting large-cohort studies and routine clinical use. Predicting spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides is a promising alternative, yet under realistic leave-one-slide-out evaluation, existing models often suffer from slide-level appearance shifts and regression-driven over-smoothing that suppress biologically meaningful variation. CHRep is a two-phase framework for robust histology-to-expression prediction. In the training phase, CHRep learns a structure-aware representation by jointly optimizing correlation-aware regression, symmetric image-expression alignment, and coordinate-induced spatial topology regularization. In the inference phase, cross-slide robustness is improved without backbone fine-tuning through a lightweight calibration module trained on the training slides, which combines a non-parametric estimate from a training gallery with a magnitude-regularized correction module. Unlike prior embedding-alignment or retrieval-based transfer methods that rely on a single prediction route, CHRep couples topology-preserving representation learning with post-hoc calibration, enabling stable neighborhood retrieval and controlled bias correction under slide-level shifts. Across the three cohorts, CHRep consistently improves gene-wise correlation under leave-one-slide-out evaluation, with the largest gains observed on Alex+10x. Relative to HAGE, the Pearson correlation coefficient on all considered genes [PCC(ACG)] increases by 4.0% on cSCC and 9.8% on HER2+. Relative to mclSTExp, PCC(ACG) further improves by 39.5% on Alex+10x, together with 9.7% and 9.0% reductions in mean squared error (MSE) and mean absolute error (MAE), respectively.

title: Separable Expert Architecture: Toward Privacy-Preserving LLM Personalization via Composable Adapters and Deletable User Proxies
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Separable Expert Architecture (SEA), a framework that resolves the tension between LLM personalization and user data deletion by preventing the entanglement of user-specific information with shared model weights. Rather than attempting to surgically remove user influence from trained parameters—a problem recognized as computationally intractable—SEA ensures that personalization is compositional and assembled at inference time from deletable components.

The architecture comprises three layers: a frozen shared base model, domain-expert LoRA adapters selected by a query router, and per-user proxy artifacts (2–5 MB each) containing routing biases, contrastive steering vectors, and a personal LoRA adapter. A strict separation invariant ensures all user-specific information resides exclusively in the proxy, making deletion equivalent to removing a filesystem directory with zero retraining required.

Experiments across Phi-3.5-mini and Llama-3.1-8B with four domain experts and four synthetic user profiles demonstrate measurable personalization through routing weight shifts and style trait alignment, verified deletion with 82–89% of test cases showing outputs statistically indistinguishable from non-personalized baselines after proxy removal, and clean cross-user isolation with contamination scores below 0.05.

The significance lies in transforming an intractable algorithmic problem—machine unlearning—into a tractable engineering one, offering a principled path toward privacy-preserving LLM personalization that can honor data deletion rights, though with an explicit tradeoff limiting personalization expressiveness to maintain separability.
original_abstract: Current model training approaches incorporate user information directly into shared weights, making individual data removal computationally infeasible without retraining. This paper presents a three-layer architecture that decouples personal data from shared weights by combining a static base model, composable domain-expert LoRA adapters that shape behavior without imparting user data, and per-user proxy artefacts whose deletion constitutes deterministic unlearning. Evaluation on Phi-3.5-mini and Llama-3.1-8B confirms per-user differentiation in which personal data influences outputs while remaining isolated, verified by a return to baseline after proxy removal (KL divergence of approximately 0.21 nats, 82-89% verification pass rate) and near-zero cross-user contamination. Because user-specific information never enters shared weights, the architecture mitigates model inversion, membership inference, and training-data extraction against shared model components by construction. The approach converts machine unlearning from an intractable weight-editing problem into a deterministic deletion operation that preserves personalization alongside privacy-enhancing guarantees and is compatible with differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) for privacy-preserving shared model improvement.

title: SpecSyn: LLM-based Synthesis and Refinement of Formal Specifications for Real-world Program Verification
generated_summary:
This paper presents SpecSyn, an LLM-based framework for generating formal program specifications to support real-world program verification. The main contribution is a novel approach that combines scalable divide-and-conquer decomposition with an innovative specification strength refinement mechanism based on program mutation and variant discrimination.

The methodology operates in two phases. First, top-down task decomposition uses static dependency analysis and Tarjan's algorithm to segment programs into strongly connected components, with an LLM generating specification sketches that plan the generation process. Second, bottom-up synthesis iteratively generates and repairs specifications for each segment. A key innovation is the Variant Discriminative Rate (VDR) metric, which measures specification strength by evaluating whether specifications can distinguish a program from its semantically non-equivalent mutants. When specifications fail to discriminate variants, the LLM analyzes differences and generates stronger refinements.

Experiments on a benchmark of 50 C source files from open-source repositories demonstrate that SpecSyn achieves the highest average precision (96.68%) and recall (75.91%) among all baselines. In real-world verification tasks, SpecSyn successfully proves 1,071 out of 1,365 target properties, substantially outperforming the next best approach Preguss (503). Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of both the divide-and-conquer design and the refinement mechanism.

The work addresses a fundamental gap in automated specification generation by ensuring both correctness and semantic strength, significantly advancing the practical applicability of LLM-based program verification for complex real-world software.
original_abstract: Program verification is a formal technique to rigorously ensure the correctness and fault-freeness of software systems. However, constructing comprehensive interprocedural specifications for full verification obligations is time-consuming and labor-intensive, giving rise to automated specification generation approaches. Despite the significant advancements in these approaches brought by Large Language Models (LLMs), existing LLM-empowered approaches still suffer from significant limitations: they lack effective strategies for handling sizable input programs, and are typically equipped with no mechanisms to evaluate and guarantee the strength of the generated specifications. The limitations impair their ability to extract precise specifications from real-world complicated programs to support the verification of target properties, thereby hindering the applicability of existing approaches in verification tasks on real-world programs. To remedy this gap, we propose SpecSyn, a novel LLM-based specification generation method. SpecSyn first decomposes the input program into individual segments, which are handled respectively by the subsequent iterative specification generation process. Innovatively, we incorporate into the process a specification refinement mechanism based on semantic-non-equivalent program mutations and variant discrimination, assessing and enhancing the semantic strength of the generated specifications. Extensive experiments show that SpecSyn maintains high precision over 90% and outstanding recall over 75%, significantly outperforming existing LLM-based approaches. title: A Bayesian Reasoning Framework for Robotic Systems in Autonomous Casualty Triage

original_abstract: Autonomous robots deployed in mass casualty incidents (MCI) face the challenge of making critical decisions based on incomplete and noisy perceptual data. The system, evaluated during the DARPA Triage Challenge (DTC) in realistic MCI scenarios involving 11 and 9 casualties, demonstrated a nearly three-fold improvement in physiological assessment accuracy (from 15\% to 42\% and 19\% to 46\%) compared to a vision-only baseline. title: Hybrid Deep Learning Approach for Coupled Demand Forecasting and Supply Chain Optimization

original_abstract: Supply chain resilience and efficiency are vital in industries characterized by volatile demand and uncertain supply, such as textiles and personal protective equipment (PPE). Traditional forecasting and optimization approaches often operate in isolation, limiting their real-world effectiveness. This paper proposes a Hybrid AI Framework for Demand-Supply Forecasting and Optimization (HAF-DS), which integrates a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based demand forecasting module with a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) optimization layer. The LSTM captures temporal and contextual demand dependencies, while the optimization layer prescribes cost-efficient replenishment and allocation decisions. The framework jointly minimizes forecasting error and operational cost through embedding-based feature representation and recurrent neural architectures. Experiments on textile sales and supply chain datasets show significant performance gains over statistical and deep learning baselines. On the combined dataset, HAF-DS reduced Mean Absolute Error (MAE) from 15.04 to 12.83 (14.7%), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) from 19.53 to 17.11 (12.4%), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) from 9.5% to 8.1%. title: Leveraging SIMD for Accelerating Large-number Arithmetic

For addition and subtraction, DoT employs a four-phase algorithm that performs parallel limb-wise addition, then isolates carry management into distinct phases, exploiting the observation that cascading carries are probabilistically negligible for random inputs. For multiplication, DoT adopts vertical and crosswise multiplication, gathering all independent cross-products before any accumulation, eliminating read-after-write chains that plague existing SIMD multiplication implementations.

Implemented in 1,013 lines of portable C with AVX-512 intrinsics, DoT achieves up to 1.85× speedup over prior SIMD addition approaches and 2.31× speedup for 256-bit multiplication. Integrated into GMP (DoTMP) and OpenSSL (DoTSSL), DoT improves GMPbench's overall score by 7.8%, with cascading gains including 48.7% for large multiplication and 19.3% for pi computation. DoTSSL improves cryptographic throughput by up to 5.9% for FFDH and reduces latency by up to 7.9% for DSA, demonstrating that accelerating low-level arithmetic primitives propagates broadly through dependent higher-level operations.
original_abstract: Large-number arithmetic, widely used in scientific computing and cryptography, has seen limited adoption of single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) parallelism on modern CPUs due to the inherent dependencies in traditional algorithms. We present DigitsOnTurbo (DoT), which restructures the computation around independent, data-parallel operations, rather than vectorizing the standard algorithms, thereby leveraging the benefits provided by SIMD. Over prior SIMD implementations, DoT achieves up to 1.85x speedups for addition and subtraction, and 2.3x for multiplication. When integrated into state-of-the-art libraries, DoT yields up to 4x speedup for addition and subtraction, and up to 2x speedup for multiplication, cascading into end-to-end throughput gains of up to 19.3% for scientific computations, and up to 7.9% latency and 5.9% throughput improvements on cryptographic implementations.

title: Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Coercion
generated_summary:

The methodology employs two complementary probing strategies: direct probing, where a simulated user explicitly asks the model's opinion with escalating pressure, and indirect probing, where the user engages in argumentative debate without ever requesting the model's stance. Three personas (agree, disagree, neutral) interact with the assistant across five turns, and an LLM judge classifies responses into a nine-way behavioral taxonomy that distinguishes genuine positions from persona-dependent sycophancy.

Applied to 13 assistant models across 38 topics in Brazilian Portuguese, the benchmark reveals that argumentative debate triggers sycophancy at dramatically higher rates than direct questioning—median sycophancy rises from 50% to 79% across models. Models that appear to hold firm positions under direct probing frequently collapse into mirroring the user's arguments under debate pressure. Notably, two models (Kimi K2 and Claude Haiku 4.5) resist this pattern, demonstrating that debate-driven sycophancy reflects training choices rather than architectural inevitability.

The findings carry significant implications for AI transparency and deployment. Since real users typically argue positions rather than neutrally solicit opinions, single-turn benchmarks systematically underestimate sycophantic behavior, suggesting that debate-based probing should become standard practice in sycophancy evaluation.
original_abstract: Large language models increasingly shape the information people consume: they are embedded in search, consulted for professional advice, deployed as agents, and used as a first stop for questions about policy, ethics, health, and politics. When such a model silently holds a position on a contested topic, that position propagates at scale into users' decisions. Eliciting a model's positions is harder than it first appears: contemporary assistants answer direct opinion questions with evasive disclaimers, and the same model may concede the opposite position once the user starts arguing one side. We propose a method, released as the open-source llm-bias-bench, for discovering the opinions an LLM actually holds on contested topics under conditions that resemble real multi-turn interaction. The method pairs two complementary free-form probes. Direct probing asks for the model's opinion across five turns of escalating pressure from a simulated user. Indirect probing never asks for an opinion and engages the model in argumentative debate, letting bias leak through how it concedes, resists, or counter-argues. Three user personas (neutral, agree, disagree) collapse into a nine-way behavioral classification that separates persona-independent positions from persona-dependent sycophancy, and an auditable LLM judge produces verdicts with textual evidence. The first instantiation ships 38 topics in Brazilian Portuguese across values, scientific consensus, philosophy, and economic policy. Applied to 13 assistants, the method surfaces findings of practical interest: argumentative debate triggers sycophancy 2-3x more than direct questioning (median 50% to 79%); models that look opinionated under direct questioning often collapse into mirroring under sustained arguments; and attacker capability matters mainly when an existing opinion must be dislodged, not when the assistant starts neutral.

title: Probabilistic Verification of Neural Networks via Efficient Probabilistic Hull Generation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a novel framework for probabilistic verification of deep neural networks (DNNs) under Gaussian input uncertainty. The main contribution is a regression tree-guided approach that efficiently generates safe and unsafe probabilistic hulls—bounded regions in the input space whose probability mass can be analytically computed using error functions—to estimate upper and lower bounds on the probability that a DNN satisfies a given safety property.

The methodology employs three key innovations: a boundary-aware sampling strategy that identifies safety boundaries in the input space, regression trees that guide adaptive partitioning to focus computational effort on critical boundary regions rather than uniformly subdividing the entire space, and an incremental sampling mechanism that iteratively refines undecided regions with the largest probability mass. This approach avoids the exponential subdivision problem inherent in basic branch-and-bound methods.

Experimental evaluation on ACAS Xu collision avoidance networks, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lander controller, and networks with non-ReLU activations demonstrates that the method produces consistently tighter probability bounds than ProbStar and achieves up to 10× speedup compared to basic branch-and-bound approaches. The method also handles the 9-dimensional rocket lander benchmark where branch-and-bound fails entirely due to combinatorial explosion.

The framework's generality is a significant advantage over existing tools like ProbStar, as it treats the neural network as a black box, supporting arbitrary activation functions rather than being restricted to ReLU networks.
original_abstract: The problem of probabilistic verification of a neural network investigates the probability of satisfying the safe constraints in the output space when the input is given by a probability distribution. It is significant to answer this problem when the input is affected by disturbances often modeled by probabilistic variables. In the paper, we propose a novel neural network probabilistic verification framework which computes a guaranteed range for the safe probability by efficiently finding safe and unsafe probabilistic hulls. Our approach consists of three main innovations: (1) a state space subdivision strategy using regression trees to produce probabilistic hulls, (2) a boundary-aware sampling method which identifies the safety boundary in the input space using samples that are later used for building regression trees, and (3) iterative refinement with probabilistic prioritization for computing a guaranteed range for the safe probability. The accuracy and efficiency of our approach are evaluated on various benchmarks including ACAS Xu and a rocket lander controller. The result shows an obvious advantage over the state of the art.

title: Finding Meaning in Embeddings: Concept Separation Curves
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Concept Separation Curves (CSCs), a classifier-independent and annotation-free method for evaluating whether sentence embedding models can distinguish between different semantic concepts. Unlike existing evaluation approaches that rely on human annotations or downstream classifiers, CSCs isolate semantic changes from surface-level perturbations to directly assess how sensitively embeddings represent meaning.

The methodology involves two parallel perturbation processes applied to sentences: "Fuzzing," which introduces non-semantic changes (inserting articles like "a" or "the"), and "Negation," which introduces semantic changes (inserting "not"). The embeddings of original and perturbed sentences are compared using cosine similarity, producing two distributions whose overlap is quantified with a geometric measure ranging from 0 (perfect separation) to 1 (complete overlap). Lower overlap indicates better concept discrimination by the embedding model.

The authors evaluate six embedding methods across Dutch and English corpora of varying domains and sentence lengths. Key findings reveal that the Dutch GroNLP model and multilingual LaBSE achieve the best concept separation for their respective languages. Notable failure modes are identified: FastText conflates semantic and surface perturbations, while MPNET and RobBERTa exhibit extreme sensitivity to token position rather than meaning. Sentence length emerges as the strongest limiting factor, with longer sentences reducing detection capability.

The significance lies in providing a language-agnostic, domain-flexible diagnostic tool that reveals embedding limitations without requiring labeled data or external classifiers.
original_abstract: Sentence embedding techniques aim to encode key concepts of a sentence's meaning in a vector space. However, the majority of evaluation approaches for sentence embedding quality rely on the use of additional classifiers or downstream tasks. These additional components make it unclear whether good results stem from the embedding itself or from the classifier's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a novel method for evaluating the effectiveness of sentence embedding methods in capturing sentence-level concepts. Our approach is classifier-independent, allowing for an objective assessment of the model's performance. The approach adopted in this study involves the systematic introduction of syntactic noise and semantic negations into sentences, with the subsequent quantification of their relative effects on the resulting embeddings. The visualisation of these effects is facilitated by Concept Separation Curves, which show the model's capacity to differentiate between conceptual and surface-level variations. By leveraging data from multiple domains, employing both Dutch and English languages, and examining sentence lengths, this study offers a compelling demonstration that Concept Separation Curves provide an interpretable, reproducible, and cross-model approach for evaluating the conceptual stability of sentence embeddings.

title: Engaged AI Governance: Addressing the Last Mile Challenge Through Internal Expert Collaboration
generated_summary:

The workshop guided practitioners through learning EU AI Act requirements, brainstorming implementation strategies grounded in existing practices, and prioritizing actions using impact-effort mapping.
