original_abstract: Since software performance requirements are documented in natural language, quantifying them into mathematical forms is essential for software engineering. Yet, the vagueness in performance requirements and uncertainty of human cognition have caused highly uncertain ambiguity in the interpretations, rendering their automated quantification an unaddressed and challenging problem. In this paper, we formalize the problem and propose IRAP, an approach that quantifies performance requirements into mathematical functions via interactive retrieval-augmented preference elicitation. IRAP differs from the others in that it explicitly derives from problem-specific knowledge to retrieve and reason the preferences, which also guides the progressive interaction with stakeholders, while reducing the cognitive overhead. Experiment results against 10 state-of-the-art methods on four real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of IRAP on all cases with up to 40x improvements under as few as five rounds of interactions.

title: Active Inference of Extended Finite State Machine Models with Registers and Guards
generated_summary:
This paper presents an algorithm for inferring Extended Finite State Machine (EFSM) models from reactive software systems without requiring system resets, extending previous work by supporting registers in transition guards. The key contribution is a fully black-box inference approach that learns EFSM models—including guards, register updates, and output functions—from a single continuous trace of inputs and outputs, with no prior knowledge beyond the system's interface.

The methodology follows a two-stage approach. First, an extension of the hW algorithm infers the control structure (finite state machine) of the system without resets, building a "sampled FSM" that associates observed concrete input-output values with each transition. Second, genetic programming via symbolic regression infers the mathematical expressions for transition guards, output functions, and register update functions from the collected data samples. The approach assumes register observability and some level of behavioral boundedness when exercising the system with a subset of inputs.

The algorithm is demonstrated through a proof-of-concept application to a drinks vending machine example, showing how the complete EFSM with register-based guards can be recovered. The significance of this work lies in avoiding the state explosion problem inherent in treating all parameter values as separate inputs, which is especially critical for infinite domains. By inferring symbolic expressions rather than pointwise functions, the approach produces compact, generalizable models applicable to software testing, verification, and reverse engineering tasks where system resets are infeasible or costly.
original_abstract: Extended finite state machines (EFSMs) model stateful systems with internal data variables and have numerous applications in software engineering. A major advantage of this type of model lies in its ability to model both the data flow and the data-dependent control behaviour. In the absence of such models, it is desirable to reverse-engineer them by observing the system's behaviour. However, existing approaches generally require the ability to reset the system during inference, or can only handle situations where the control flow depends exclusively on the input parameters, and not on the values of the stored data. In this work, we present a black-box active learning algorithm that infers EFSMs with guards and registers, and which significantly relaxes the assumptions that have to be made about the system in comparison to previous attempts.

title: A formal proof of the Sands-Sauer-Woodrow theorem using the Rocq prover and mathcomp/ssreflect
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first formal verification of the Sands-Sauer-Woodrow (SSW) theorem for infinite graphs using the Rocq prover (formerly Coq) with the MathComp/ssreflect library. The SSW theorem states that in a directed graph whose edges are colored with two colors and containing no monochromatic infinite outward path, there exists an independent set S such that every vertex outside S can reach S via a monochromatic path. This theorem generalizes the classical Gale-Shapley marriage theorem and is foundational in kernel theory for digraphs.

The authors formalize the theorem using binary relations to model the two-colored directed graph, closely following the original combinatorial proof. A key contribution is the identification and proof of a strengthened version of the theorem that replaces the original assumption of no monochromatic infinite outward paths with a weaker condition: that the asymmetric parts of the transitive closures of each color's relation admit no infinite outward paths. This strictly broadens the theorem's applicability, as demonstrated through an example involving symmetric relations where the original SSW theorem cannot be applied but the strengthened version can.

Establishing the logical equivalence between the strengthened and classical formulations required proving that an infinite path in the asymmetric part of a transitive closure yields an infinite path in the original relation—a technically demanding component of the formalization. The accompanying MathComp library for binary relations and graph paths is designed to be reusable for further formalizations in infinite graph theory.
original_abstract: We present a formal proof of the Sands-Sauer-Woodrow (SSW) theorem using the Rocq proof assistant and the MathComp/SSReflect library. The SSW theorem states that in a directed graph whose edges are colored with two colors and that contains no monochromatic infinite outward path, there exists an independent set S of vertices such that every vertex outside S can reach S by a monochromatic path. We formalize the graph using two binary relations Eb and Er , representing the blue and red edges respectively, and we develop a dedicated library for binary relations represented as classical sets. Beyond formalizing the original SSW theorem, we establish a strictly stronger version in which the assumption ''no monochromatic infinite outward path'' is replaced by the weaker condition that the asymmetric parts of the transitive closures of Eb and Er admit no infinite outward paths. The original SSW theorem is then recovered as a corollary via a lemma showing that an infinite path for the asymmetric part of the transitive closure of a relation implies an infinite path for the relation.

title: VLAA-GUI: Knowing When to Stop, Recover, and Search, A Modular Framework for GUI Automation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces VLAA-GUI, a modular framework for autonomous GUI agents that addresses two persistent challenges: premature task completion and repetitive action loops. The framework integrates three key components: a Completeness Verifier that enforces UI-observable success criteria before accepting any task completion claim, a Loop Breaker with multi-tier escalation rules that detects and recovers from repetitive behavioral patterns, and an on-demand Search Agent that queries an LLM with search grounding to provide procedural knowledge for unfamiliar workflows.

The system is evaluated on OSWorld-Verified and WindowsAgentArena benchmarks across five backbone models spanning Claude and Gemini families. With Claude Opus 4.6, VLAA-GUI achieves 77.5% on OSWorld, surpassing human-level performance (72.4%) for the first time, with three of five backbones exceeding this threshold. On WindowsAgentArena, the framework reaches 61.0%, outperforming the strongest baseline by over 4%. Notably, with only 15 action steps, the system already surpasses the best published 50-step systems.

Ablation studies confirm each component's contribution, while analysis reveals that false completion accounts for over 86% of failures—the dominant failure mode in GUI agents. The Completeness Verifier reduces false completion rates by up to 3.9%, and the Loop Breaker nearly halves wasted steps for loop-prone backbones. These results demonstrate that targeted verification and recovery mechanisms substantially improve GUI agent reliability and efficiency across model families and platforms.
original_abstract: Autonomous GUI agents face two fundamental challenges: early stopping, where agents prematurely declare success without verifiable evidence, and repetitive loops, where agents cycle through the same failing actions without recovery. We present VLAA-GUI, a modular GUI agentic framework built around three integrated components that guide the system on when to Stop, Recover, and Search. First, a mandatory Completeness Verifier enforces UI-observable success criteria and verification at every finish step -- with an agent-level verifier that cross-examines completion claims with decision rules, rejecting those lacking direct visual evidence. Second, a mandatory Loop Breaker provides multi-tier filtering: switching interaction mode after repeated failures, forcing strategy changes after persistent screen-state recurrence, and binding reflection signals to strategy shifts. Third, an on-demand Search Agent searches online for unfamiliar workflows by directly querying a capable LLM with search ability, returning results as plain text. We additionally integrate a Coding Agent for code-intensive actions and a Grounding Agent for precise action grounding, both invoked on demand when required. We evaluate VLAA-GUI across five top-tier backbones, including Opus 4.5, 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, on two benchmarks with Linux and Windows tasks, achieving top performance on both (77.5% on OSWorld and 61.0% on WindowsAgentArena). Notably, three of the five backbones surpass human performance (72.4%) on OSWorld in a single pass. Ablation studies show that all three proposed components consistently improve a strong backbone, while a weaker backbone benefits more from these tools when the step budget is sufficient. Further analysis also shows that the Loop Breaker nearly halves wasted steps for loop-prone models.

title: MKJ at SemEval-2026 Task 9: A Comparative Study of Generalist, Specialist, and Ensemble Strategies for Multilingual Polarization
generated_summary:
This paper presents a language-adaptive modeling framework for multilingual polarization detection across 22 languages as part of SemEval-2026 Task 9. The main contribution is a systematic empirical methodology for selecting between generalist models, monolingual specialists, and hybrid ensembles on a per-language basis, rather than imposing a single universal architecture.

The approach proceeds in three phases. First, XLM-RoBERTa-Base serves as a universal baseline, against which monolingual specialists and high-capacity generalists like mDeBERTa-v3 are evaluated per language track, with alternatives adopted only when they yield meaningful improvements. Second, weighted soft-voting ensembles with threshold calibration are constructed for languages where candidate models exhibit complementary error profiles. Third, cross-lingual data augmentation via machine translation is explored but ultimately abandoned due to inconsistent results.

The system achieves a macro-averaged F1 of 0.796 and accuracy of 0.826 across the 22 test tracks, remaining within four F1 points of the top leaderboard score on 13 tracks. Monolingual specialists outperformed XLM-RoBERTa in 18 of 22 languages, with gains up to 10.6% in Odia. However, failure modes emerged from development-set overfitting, majority-class collapse, and domain mismatch between formal pretraining corpora and informal social media text.

The findings demonstrate that multilingual polarization detection resists universal solutions, highlighting the importance of tokenizer efficiency, domain alignment, and calibration under limited supervision over model scale alone.
original_abstract: We present a systematic study of multilingual polarization detection across 22 languages for SemEval-2026 Task 9 (Subtask 1), contrasting multilingual generalists with language-specific specialists and hybrid ensembles. While a standard generalist like XLM-RoBERTa suffices when its tokenizer aligns with the target text, it may struggle with distinct scripts (e.g., Khmer, Odia) where monolingual specialists yield significant gains. Rather than enforcing a single universal architecture, we adopt a language-adaptive framework that switches between multilingual generalists, language-specific specialists, and hybrid ensembles based on development performance. Additionally, cross-lingual augmentation via NLLB-200 yielded mixed results, often underperforming native architecture selection and degrading morphologically rich tracks. Our final system achieves an overall macro-averaged F1 score of 0.796 and an average accuracy of 0.826 across all 22 tracks. Code and final test predictions are publicly available at: https://github.com/Maziarkiani/SemEval2026-Task9-Subtask1-Polarization.

title: Channel-Free Human Activity Recognition via Inductive-Bias-Aware Fusion Design for Heterogeneous IoT Sensor Environments
generated_summary:
This paper formalizes "channel-free" human activity recognition (HAR) as a new problem setting where a single model processes heterogeneous sensor inputs with varying numbers and compositions of channels without assuming a fixed channel template. This capability is argued to be essential for building HAR foundation models that can leverage diverse IoT sensor datasets.

The authors systematically analyze fusion strategies—early, middle, and late fusion—under channel-free constraints, examining their inductive biases. They propose a late-fusion architecture combining shared per-channel encoding via a 1D ResNet backbone, metadata conditioning through conditional batch normalization (injecting sensor location, modality, and axis information), and a combination loss that jointly supervises fused and channel-wise predictions.

Extensive experiments across six HAR datasets and five backbone architectures demonstrate that the proposed method maintains strong performance under clean conditions while exhibiting substantially greater robustness to channel perturbations (shuffling, missing channels) compared to conventional channel-fixed baselines. The late-fusion design alone proves to be a strong channel-free baseline, with metadata conditioning and combination loss providing incremental improvements. Cross-dataset transfer learning experiments confirm that the channel-free design enables pretraining across datasets with different sensor configurations, with single-source transfer improving target performance.

The work establishes architectural foundations for scalable, heterogeneous HAR systems, though the authors note that more principled multi-dataset pretraining strategies and robust metadata handling remain important future directions.
original_abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) in Internet of Things (IoT) environments must cope with heterogeneous sensor settings that vary across datasets, devices, body locations, sensing modalities, and channel compositions. This heterogeneity makes conventional channel-fixed models difficult to reuse across sensing environments because their input representations are tightly coupled to predefined channel structures. To address this problem, we investigate strict channel-free HAR, in which a single shared model performs inference without assuming a fixed number, order, or semantic arrangement of input channels, and without relying on sensor-specific input layers or dataset-specific channel templates. We argue that fusion design is the central issue in this setting. Accordingly, we propose a channel-free HAR framework that combines channel-wise encoding with a shared encoder, metadata-conditioned late fusion via conditional batch normalization, and joint optimization of channel-level and fused predictions through a combination loss. The proposed model processes each channel independently to handle varying channel configurations, while sensor metadata such as body location, modality, and axis help recover structural information that channel-independent processing alone cannot retain. In addition, the joint loss encourages both the discriminability of individual channels and the consistency of the final fused prediction. Experiments on PAMAP2, together with robustness analysis on six HAR datasets, ablation studies, sensitivity analysis, efficiency evaluation, and cross-dataset transfer learning, demonstrate three main findings...

title: mcdok at SemEval-2026 Task 13: Finetuning LLMs for Detection of Machine-Generated Code
generated_summary:
This paper presents mcdok, a system developed for SemEval-2026 Task 13 on detecting machine-generated code across three subtasks: binary detection, multi-class authorship attribution among 11 classes, and hybrid code detection among 4 classes. The main contribution lies in demonstrating that generic machine-generated text detectors can be effectively transferred to the code detection domain through careful selection and finetuning of large language models.

The methodology builds upon the existing mdok text detection framework, adapting it for code by exploring various base models ranging from 0.5B to 70B parameters. The authors employed strategic data subsampling and class balancing, using out-of-distribution validation data for checkpoint selection. A notable finding is that setting the classification threshold to 100% confidence significantly boosted binary detection performance. Different models proved optimal for each subtask: Gemma-3-27B-PT for binary detection, CodeGemma-7B for authorship attribution, and Qwen2.5-Coder-14B for hybrid detection.

The systems outperformed both CodeBERT and random baselines across all subtasks, ranking 10th of 81 submissions in subtask A, 13th of 34 in subtask B, and 5th of 32 in subtask C. Interestingly, a general-purpose model outperformed code-specialized models in binary detection. Analysis revealed stable cross-language performance, with the highest confusion occurring between machine-generated and hybrid code classes, highlighting the inherent difficulty of distinguishing partially AI-assisted code.
original_abstract: Multi-domain detection of the machine-generated code snippets in various programming languages is a challenging task. SemEval-2026 Task~13 copes with this challenge in various angles, as a binary detection problem as well as attribution of the source. Specifically, its subtasks also cover generator LLM family detection, as well as a hybrid code co-generated by humans and machines, or adversarially modified codes hiding its origin. Our submitted systems adjusted the existing mdok approach (focused on machine-generated text detection) to these specific kinds of problems by exploring various base models, more suitable for code understanding. The results indicate that the submitted systems are competitive in all three subtasks. However, the margins from the top-performing systems are significant, and thus further improvements are possible.

title: A Deployable Embodied Vision-Language Navigation System with Hierarchical Cognition and Context-Aware Exploration
generated_summary:
This paper presents HiCo-Nav, a deployable vision-language navigation (VLN) system that addresses the challenge of balancing high-level reasoning with real-time execution on resource-constrained robotic platforms. The main contribution is a hierarchical, asynchronous architecture that decouples navigation intelligence into three layers: a real-time perception-action layer for high-frequency sensing, a memory layer that incrementally constructs a cognitive memory graph (CMG) organizing semantic entities and visual evidence, and a reasoning layer that leverages vision-language models asynchronously over structured subgraphs of the CMG without blocking real-time control.

The system introduces a context-aware frontier exploration strategy that integrates structural-semantic propagation within explored regions and visual evidence beyond map boundaries. Goal selection is formulated as a Weighted Traveling Repairman Problem, enabling globally optimized exploration that minimizes expected time-to-discovery rather than relying on greedy local decisions.

Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. HiCo-Nav achieves 48.5% success rate on MP3D, 61.0% on HM3D for object navigation, and 52.4% on HM3D-OVON for open-vocabulary navigation, consistently outperforming existing methods. Real-world deployment on a quadruped robot with embedded hardware achieves 95% success rate for large objects while maintaining real-time operation, demonstrating the system's practical viability for embodied robotic applications.
original_abstract: Bridging the gap between embodied intelligence and embedded deployment remains a key challenge in intelligent robotic systems, where perception, reasoning, and planning must operate under strict constraints on computation, memory, energy, and real-time execution. In vision-language navigation (VLN), existing approaches often face a fundamental trade-off between strong reasoning capabilities and efficient deployment on real-world platforms. In this paper, we present a deployable embodied VLN system that achieves both high efficiency and robust high-level reasoning on real-world robotic platforms. To achieve this, we decouple the system into three asynchronous modules: a real-time perception module for continuous environment sensing, a memory integration module for spatial-semantic aggregation, and a reasoning module for high-level decision making. We incrementally construct a cognitive memory graph to encode scene information, which is further decomposed into subgraphs to enable reasoning with a vision-language model (VLM). To further improve navigation efficiency and accuracy, we also leverage the cognitive memory graph to formulate the exploration problem as a context-aware Weighted Traveling Repairman Problem (WTRP), which minimizes the weighted waiting time of viewpoints. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic platforms demonstrate improved navigation success and efficiency over existing VLN approaches, while maintaining real-time performance on resource-constrained hardware.

title: KD-CVG: A Knowledge-Driven Approach for Creative Video Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces KD-CVG, a knowledge-driven framework for automatically generating advertising creative videos (ACVs) from product selling point texts in e-commerce scenarios. The work addresses two key challenges that prevent general text-to-video models from being directly applicable to advertising: ambiguous semantic alignment between selling points and video content, and inadequate motion adaptability for producing physically realistic product-specific movements.

The methodology centers on an Advertising Creative Knowledge Base (ACKB) containing 10,000 text-video pairs across 377 product categories, along with two core modules. The Semantic-Aware Retrieval (SAR) module employs a Graph Attention Network to model semantic correlations among selling points and retrieve relevant references from the ACKB, optimized through policy gradient reinforcement learning. The Multimodal Knowledge Reference (MKR) module uses a hierarchical generation pipeline comprising progressive script generation via LLM prompting with retrieved references and motion prior distillation through a differential motion encoding scheme with parameter-efficient Low-Rank Adaptation (MR-LoRA).

Experiments demonstrate that KD-CVG outperforms state-of-the-art video generation models including VideoCrafter2 and Show-1 across automated metrics for textual alignment, temporal consistency, and motion smoothness, while also achieving superior user study ratings. The framework maintains competitive inference time (102 seconds) while delivering substantially better generation quality. This work represents the first automated pipeline for converting selling point texts directly into advertising videos, offering a practical and efficient solution for e-commerce content production.
original_abstract: Creative Generation (CG) leverages generative models to automatically produce advertising content that highlights product features, and it has been a significant focus of recent research. However, while CG has advanced considerably, most efforts have concentrated on generating advertising text and images, leaving Creative Video Generation (CVG) relatively underexplored. This gap is largely due to two major challenges faced by Text-to-Video (T2V) models: (a) \textbf{ambiguous semantic alignment}, where models struggle to accurately correlate product selling points with creative video content, and (b) \textbf{inadequate motion adaptability}, resulting in unrealistic movements and distortions. To address these challenges, we develop a comprehensive Advertising Creative Knowledge Base (ACKB) as a foundational resource and propose a knowledge-driven approach (KD-CVG) to overcome the knowledge limitations of existing models. KD-CVG consists of two primary modules: Semantic-Aware Retrieval (SAR) and Multimodal Knowledge Reference (MKR). SAR utilizes the semantic awareness of graph attention networks and reinforcement learning feedback to enhance the model's comprehension of the connections between selling points and creative videos. Building on this, MKR incorporates semantic and motion priors into the T2V model to address existing knowledge gaps. Extensive experiments have demonstrated KD-CVG's superior performance in achieving semantic alignment and motion adaptability, validating its effectiveness over other state-of-the-art methods. The code and dataset will be open source at https://kdcvg.github.io/KDCVG/.

title: Time, Causality, and Observability Failures in Distributed AI Inference Systems
generated_summary:
This paper demonstrates that distributed AI inference pipelines can silently lose causal observability due to small clock skew across nodes, even while continuing to produce correct outputs at stable throughput. The central contribution is identifying and experimentally validating a failure mode where timestamp-based reasoning—used for logging, tracing, auditing, and incident reconstruction—becomes logically inconsistent without triggering conventional alarms.

The authors construct a multi-stage distributed inference pipeline with independent clocks communicating via message-oriented middleware, testing across both Kafka and ZeroMQ transports. They inject controlled clock skew values and measure causal consistency by detecting negative timing spans (where effects appear to precede causes). They also introduce a binary causality health signal to surface this failure at runtime.

Key results reveal an onset region between 3 ms and 5 ms of clock skew where causal violations begin appearing while throughput and functional correctness remain unaffected. The failure mode is consistent across both messaging platforms, confirming it stems from time alignment rather than transport specifics. Notably, violation behavior evolves dynamically in longer runs, with partial self-recovery driven by relative clock drift between nodes.

The findings carry significant implications for multi-tenant AI platforms, autonomous agents, regulated decision systems, and incident response, where reliable causal reasoning is essential. The work underscores that observability correctness depends critically on time synchronization and cannot be assumed from functional health alone.
original_abstract: Distributed AI inference pipelines rely heavily on timestamp-based observability to understand system behavior. This work demonstrates that even small clock skew between nodes can cause observability to become causally incorrect while the system itself remains functionally correct and performant. We present controlled experiments on a multi-node AI inference pipeline, where clock skew is introduced at a single stage. Results show that no violations are observed under synchronized conditions and up to 3 ms skew, while clear causality violations emerge by 5 ms. Despite this, system throughput and output correctness remain largely unaffected. We further observe that violation behavior is not strictly static. In longer runs, negative span rates may stabilize or decrease over time, indicating that effective skew evolves due to relative clock drift between nodes. Experiments were conducted using Kafka and ZeroMQ transports, with consistent results across both. Aeron is under active exploration but is not yet included in the completed validation set. These findings suggest that observability correctness depends not only on system functionality but also on precise time alignment, and that timing must be treated as a first-class concern in distributed AI systems.

title: Prototype-Based Test-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Prototype-based Test-Time Adaptation (PTA), a backpropagation-free and cache-free method for adapting vision-language models like CLIP to distribution shifts at test time. The key contribution addresses critical limitations of existing cache-based test-time adaptation methods, including high inference latency in large-scale settings, cold-start problems with sparse caches, and error accumulation from heuristic filtering.

PTA maintains class-specific knowledge prototypes that continuously accumulate visual features from streaming test samples using a dynamic exponential moving average mechanism. Each incoming sample's visual features are weighted by an adaptive decay rate derived from its zero-shot classification confidence, enabling all test samples to contribute proportionally to prototype updates. To prevent drift from CLIP's pretrained embedding space, text-anchored prototypes initialized from CLIP's text embeddings are interpolated with the knowledge prototypes, and the final prediction combines prototype-based and zero-shot logits.

Evaluated across 15 image recognition datasets and 4 robust point cloud analysis benchmarks, PTA achieves state-of-the-art performance among backpropagation-free methods, outperforming cache-based approaches like TDA, SCA, and ADAPT by 0.64–1.63% on cross-domain benchmarks. Crucially, PTA operates at 81.83 FPS on ImageNet-1K—92% of original CLIP speed—compared to only 14.5% for cache-based ADAPT. These results establish PTA as a practical, efficient solution for deploying vision-language models in latency-sensitive, resource-constrained environments.
original_abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a promising paradigm for vision-language models (VLMs) to bridge the distribution gap between pre-training and test data. Recent works have focused on backpropagation-free TTA methods that rely on cache-based designs, but these introduce two key limitations. First, inference latency increases as the cache grows with the number of classes, leading to inefficiencies in large-scale settings. Second, suboptimal performance occurs when the cache contains insufficient or incorrect samples. In this paper, we present Prototype-Based Test-Time Adaptation (PTA), an efficient and effective TTA paradigm that uses a set of class-specific knowledge prototypes to accumulate knowledge from test samples. Particularly, knowledge prototypes are adaptively weighted based on the zero-shot class confidence of each test sample, incorporating the sample's visual features into the corresponding class-specific prototype. It is worth highlighting that the knowledge from past test samples is integrated and utilized solely in the prototypes, eliminating the overhead of cache population and retrieval that hinders the efficiency of existing TTA methods. This endows PTA with extremely high efficiency while achieving state-of-the-art performance on 15 image recognition benchmarks and 4 robust point cloud analysis benchmarks. For example, PTA improves CLIP's accuracy from 65.64% to 69.38% on 10 cross-domain benchmarks, while retaining 92% of CLIP's inference speed on large-scale ImageNet-1K. In contrast, the cache-based TDA achieves a lower accuracy of 67.97% and operates at only 50% of CLIP's inference speed.

title: ReaGeo: Reasoning-Enhanced End-to-End Geocoding with LLMs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces ReaGeo, the first end-to-end geocoding framework based on large language models (LLMs) that directly maps textual location descriptions to geographic coordinates, eliminating the need for traditional multi-stage pipelines relying on geographic knowledge bases. The approach converts coordinate prediction into a generative task by having an LLM autoregressively decode geohash sequences from input queries.

The methodology employs a two-stage training process built on Qwen2.5-3B. The first stage uses supervised fine-tuning with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which incorporates neighboring address relationships as intermediate reasoning steps to improve handling of ambiguous queries. The second stage applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning with a novel reward function based on geodesic distance deviation between predicted and ground-truth coordinates, enhancing spatial reasoning for relative location descriptions.

Experiments on 239,918 samples from Beijing covering both rural and urban areas demonstrate that ReaGeo significantly outperforms traditional methods including NER-based matching, vector retrieval, commercial geocoding APIs (Baidu Maps, Tencent Maps), and general-purpose LLMs (Qwen3-Max) across all metrics. The model shows particular robustness on anchor offset data containing relative positional descriptions. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of both CoT and reinforcement learning components. Additionally, beam search enables non-point geometry prediction for roads and administrative regions.

ReaGeo represents a paradigm shift in geocoding by leveraging LLMs' semantic understanding and spatial reasoning, with significant implications for industrial-scale digital map services.
original_abstract: This paper proposes ReaGeo, an end-to-end geocoding framework based on large language models, designed to overcome the limitations of traditional multi-stage approaches that rely on text or vector similarity retrieval over geographic databases, including workflow complexity, error propagation, and heavy dependence on structured geographic knowledge bases. The method converts geographic coordinates into geohash sequences, reformulating the coordinate prediction task as a text generation problem, and introduces a Chain-of-Thought mechanism to enhance the model's reasoning over spatial relationships. Furthermore, reinforcement learning with a distance-deviation-based reward is applied to optimize the generation accuracy. Comprehensive experiments show that ReaGeo can accurately handle explicit address queries in single-point predictions and effectively resolve vague relative location queries. In addition, the model demonstrates strong predictive capability for non-point geometric regions, highlighting its versatility and generalization ability in geocoding tasks.

title: SparseGF: A Height-Aware Sparse Segmentation Framework with Context Compression for Robust Ground Filtering Across Urban to Natural Scenes
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SparseGF, a deep learning framework for ground filtering of airborne laser scanning point clouds that addresses two persistent challenges: the context-detail dilemma in block-wise processing and random misclassification of tall objects. The framework incorporates three synergistic innovations: a convex-mirror-inspired context compression module that condenses expansive spatial context into compact representations while preserving geometrically intact central details; a hybrid sparse voxel-point network architecture that leverages compressed peripheral context for elevation cues while restricting classification to undistorted central regions; and a height-aware loss function that enforces topographic elevation priors during training to penalize misclassification of tall objects without requiring height-above-ground as input, thereby avoiding circular dependency issues.

Evaluated on two large-scale public datasets, SparseGF demonstrates a clear performance gradient across terrain types. It substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in complex urban scenes (95.75% overall accuracy, 0.08 m RMSE), achieves competitive results on mixed terrains, and maintains reasonable accuracy in densely forested mountainous areas. The framework also exhibits strong cross-dataset generalization without fine-tuning and reduces overall processing time compared to its backbone baseline through voxel reduction from compression.

SparseGF represents a significant methodological advancement in deep learning-based ground filtering, enabling more reliable digital terrain model generation across diverse landscapes for large-scale environmental monitoring applications including flood analysis, ecological monitoring, and geomorphological hazard assessment.
original_abstract: High-quality digital terrain models derived from airborne laser scanning (ALS) data are essential for a wide range of geospatial analyses, and their generation typically relies on robust ground filtering (GF) to separate point clouds across diverse landscapes into ground and non-ground parts. Although current deep-learning-based GF methods have demonstrated impressive performance, especially in specific challenging terrains, their cross-scene generalization remains limited by two persistent issues: the context-detail dilemma in large-scale processing due to limited computational resources, and the random misclassification of tall objects arising from classification-only optimization. To overcome these limitations, we propose SparseGF, a height-aware sparse segmentation framework enhanced with context compression. It is built upon three key innovations: (1) a convex-mirror-inspired context compression module that condenses expansive contexts into compact representations while preserving central details; (2) a hybrid sparse voxel-point network architecture that effectively interprets compressed representations while mitigating compression-induced geometric distortion; and (3) a height-aware loss function that explicitly enforces topographic elevation priors during training to suppress random misclassification of tall objects. Extensive evaluations on two large-scale ALS benchmark datasets demonstrate that SparseGF delivers robust GF across urban to natural terrains, achieving leading performance in complex urban scenes, competitive results on mixed terrains, and moderate yet non-catastrophic accuracy in densely forested steep areas. This work offers new insights into deep-learning-based GF research and encourages further exploration toward truly cross-scene generalization for large-scale environmental monitoring.

title: RPG: Robust Policy Gating for Smooth Multi-Skill Transitions in Humanoid Fighting
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Robust Policy Gating (RPG), a framework for enabling smooth multi-skill transitions in humanoid robot fighting, allowing seamless switching between dynamic combat actions such as punching, jumping, sword swings, and kicking.

The methodology consists of three main stages. First, individual expert policies are trained for each fighting skill using imitation learning with Proximal Policy Optimization. During training, two novel randomization strategies are introduced: policy-transition randomization, which stochastically interrupts and switches between skills mid-episode, and temporal randomization, which introduces discontinuities in reference motion sequences. These techniques force each expert to develop robustness against out-of-domain states encountered during skill transitions. Second, the trained expert policies are frozen, and a lightweight gating network is trained to produce weighted combinations of expert outputs, with separate weights for upper and lower body actions, regularized with smoothness constraints. Third, the system integrates a locomotion policy, creating a game-like control interface.

Ablation studies demonstrate that RPG significantly improves transition success rates and control smoothness across diverse skill combinations without substantially compromising individual motion tracking accuracy. The framework is validated both in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot, confirming successful sim-to-real transfer of high-agility fighting motions.

RPG provides a practical solution for dynamic multi-skill control in humanoid robots, addressing a critical gap in robust policy switching for complex whole-body behaviors requiring rapid, interruptible skill transitions.
original_abstract: Humanoid robots have demonstrated impressive motor skills in a wide range of tasks, yet whole-body control for humanlike long-time, dynamic fighting remains particularly challenging due to the stringent requirements on agility and stability. While imitation learning enables robots to execute human-like fighting skills, existing approaches often rely on switching among multiple single-skill policies or employing a general policy to imitate input reference motions. These strategies suffer from instability when transitioning between skills, as the mismatch of initial and terminal states across skills or reference motions introduces out-of-domain disturbances, resulting in unsmooth or unstable behaviors. In this work, we propose RPG, a hybrid expert policy framework, for smooth and stable humanoid multi-skills transition. Our approach incorporates motion transition randomization and temporal randomization to train a unified policy that generates agile fighting actions with stability and smoothness during skill transitions. Furthermore, we design a control pipeline that integrates walking/running locomotion with fighting skills, allowing humanlike long-time combat of arbitrary duration that can be seamlessly interrupted or transit action policies at any time. Extensive experiments in simulation demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, and real-world deployment on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot further validates its robustness and applicability.

title: Decoupled Travel Planning with Behavior Forest
generated_summary:

Second, the planning problem is decoupled into independent subtasks (transportation, dining, attractions, accommodation), with constraints partitioned into local (task-specific) and global (cross-task) categories. original_abstract: Behavior sequences, composed of executable steps, serve as the operational foundation for multi-constraint planning problems such as travel planning. In such tasks, each planning step is not only constrained locally but also influenced by global constraints spanning multiple subtasks, leading to a tightly coupled and complex decision process. Existing travel planning methods typically rely on a single decision space that entangles all subtasks and constraints, failing to distinguish between locally acting constraints within a subtask and global constraints that span multiple subtasks. Consequently, the model is forced to jointly reason over local and global constraints at each decision step, increasing the reasoning burden and reducing planning efficiency. To address this problem, we propose the Behavior Forest method. Specifically, our approach structures the decision-making process into a forest of parallel behavior trees, where each behavior tree is responsible for a subtask. A global coordination mechanism is introduced to orchestrate the interactions among these trees, enabling modular and coherent travel planning. Within this framework, large language models are embedded as decision engines within behavior tree nodes, performing localized reasoning conditioned on task-specific constraints to generate candidate subplans and adapt decisions based on coordination feedback. The behavior trees, in turn, provide an explicit control structure that guides LLM generation. This design decouples complex tasks and constraints into manageable subspaces, enabling task-specific reasoning and reducing the cognitive load of LLM. Experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 6.67% on the TravelPlanner and by 11.82% on the ChinaTravel benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in increasing LLM performance for complex multi-constraint travel planning.

title: CARE: Counselor-Aligned Response Engine for Online Mental-Health Support
generated_summary:

The work demonstrates that longitudinal user modeling through full-history fine-tuning can enable effective domain-specific personalization in high-stakes, low-resource conversational settings, offering a practical decision-support tool for overburdened crisis counselors.
original_abstract: Mental health challenges are increasing worldwide, straining emotional support services and leading to counselor overload. This can result in delayed responses during critical situations, such as suicidal ideation, where timely intervention is essential. While large language models (LLMs) have shown strong generative capabilities, their application in low-resource languages, especially in sensitive domains like mental health, remains underexplored. Furthermore, existing LLM-based agents often struggle to replicate the supportive language and intervention strategies used by professionals due to a lack of training on large-scale, real-world datasets. To address this, we propose CARE (Counselor-Aligned Response Engine), a GenAI framework that assists counselors by generating real-time, psychologically aligned response recommendations. CARE fine-tunes open-source LLMs separately for Hebrew and Arabic using curated subsets of real-world crisis conversations. The training data consists of sessions rated as highly effective by professional counselors, enabling the models to capture interaction patterns associated with successful de-escalation. By training on complete conversation histories, CARE maintains the evolving emotional context and dynamic structure of counselor-help-seeker dialogue. In experimental settings, CARE demonstrates stronger semantic and strategic alignment with gold-standard counselor responses compared to non-specialized LLMs. These findings suggest that domain-specific fine-tuning on expert-validated data can significantly support counselor workflows and improve care quality in low-resource language contexts.

title: Learn Weightlessness: Imitate Non-Self-Stabilizing Motions on Humanoid Robot
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a human-inspired weightlessness mechanism (WM) that enables humanoid robots to perform non-self-stabilizing (NSS) motions—movements requiring external support such as sitting on chairs, lying on beds, and leaning against walls. The authors identify that existing imitation learning methods produce "fake" behaviors where robots adopt visually correct postures without establishing functional contact with supporting objects.

The methodology involves four key components. First, video demonstrations are collected and processed to extract SMPL motions and reconstruct environmental geometry. Second, a weightlessness-state auto-labeling strategy automatically annotates which joints should relax and when, based on center-of-mass projection and contact analysis. Third, an LSTM-based WM network is trained to predict continuous joint-specific relaxation levels from motion history and future trends. Finally, an imitation learning policy trained via asymmetric PPO is fine-tuned with the WM network, enabling controlled free-fall during NSS motions.

Experiments on the Unitree G1 robot demonstrate that the WM significantly improves task success rates across sitting on chairs of varying heights, lying on surfaces at different inclinations, and leaning against walls via shoulder or elbow. The fine-tuning approach outperforms synchronous WM training. The framework generalizes across diverse environmental configurations without task-specific engineering and transfers successfully from simulation to real-world deployment, representing an important advance toward natural, physically grounded humanoid robot behaviors.
original_abstract: The integration of imitation and reinforcement learning has enabled remarkable advances in humanoid whole-body control, facilitating diverse human-like behaviors. However, research on environment-dependent motions remains limited. Existing methods typically enforce rigid trajectory tracking while neglecting physical interactions with the environment. We observe that humans naturally exploit a "weightless" state during non-self-stabilizing (NSS) motions--selectively relaxing specific joints to allow passive body--environment contact, thereby stabilizing the body and completing the motion. Inspired by this biological mechanism, we design a weightlessness-state auto-labeling strategy for dataset annotation; and we propose the Weightlessness Mechanism (WM), a method that dynamically determines which joints to relax and to what level, together enabling effective environmental interaction while executing target motions. We evaluate our approach on 3 representative NSS tasks: sitting on chairs of varying heights, lying down on beds with different inclinations, and leaning against walls via shoulder or elbow. Extensive experiments in simulation and on the Unitree G1 robot demonstrate that our WM method, trained on single-action demonstrations without any task-specific tuning, achieves strong generalization across diverse environmental configurations while maintaining motion stability. Our work bridges the gap between precise trajectory tracking and adaptive environmental interaction, offering a biologically-inspired solution for contact-rich humanoid control.

title: Trust-SSL: Additive-Residual Selective Invariance for Robust Aerial Self-Supervised Learning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Trust-SSL, a self-supervised learning framework for aerial imagery that addresses a critical failure mode in uncertainty-gated contrastive learning. The main contribution is identifying that multiplicatively scaling alignment losses by learned trust weights starves the backbone of contrastive gradients during early training when trust estimates are uncalibrated, and proposing an additive-residual formulation with gradient-detached trust weights as the solution.

The methodology builds upon standard contrastive SSL by decomposing backbone features into augmentation-anchored factor subspaces, computing per-factor evidential belief states via Dempster-Shafer fusion, and deriving conflict and ignorance signals that form trust gates. Crucially, the trust-weighted selective alignment is added as a residual on top of the unmodified contrastive loss with stop-gradient applied to trust weights, preventing the gate from weakening the base learning signal.

Evaluated on three aerial benchmarks with a ResNet-50 backbone, Trust-SSL achieves the highest mean linear-probe accuracy (90.20%) and delivers substantial gains on information-erasing corruptions, notably +19.9 points over SimCLR on severe haze in EuroSAT. Cross-domain transfer to BDD100K driving scenes shows 1-3 point AUROC improvements over baselines. Ablations reveal that the additive-residual training recipe, rather than the specific trust function, drives the gains—simpler gate variants achieve comparable performance.

The findings establish a broadly applicable design principle: learned reliability signals in SSL should modulate objectives additively with detached gradients rather than multiplicatively, with particular relevance for corruption-prone aerial and remote-sensing applications.
original_abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a standard approach for representation learning in aerial imagery. Existing methods enforce invariance between augmented views, which works well when augmentations preserve semantic content. However, aerial images are frequently degraded by haze, motion blur, rain, and occlusion that remove critical evidence. Enforcing alignment between a clean and a severely degraded view can introduce spurious structure into the latent space. This study proposes a training strategy and architectural modification to enhance SSL robustness to such corruptions. It introduces a per-sample, per-factor trust weight into the alignment objective, combined with the base contrastive loss as an additive residual. A stop-gradient is applied to the trust weight instead of a multiplicative gate. While a multiplicative gate is a natural choice, experiments show it impairs the backbone, whereas our additive-residual approach improves it. Using a 200-epoch protocol on a 210,000-image corpus, the method achieves the highest mean linear-probe accuracy among six backbones on EuroSAT, AID, and NWPU-RESISC45 (90.20% compared to 88.46% for SimCLR and 89.82% for VICReg). It yields the largest improvements under severe information-erasing corruptions on EuroSAT (+19.9 points on haze at s=5 over SimCLR). The method also demonstrates consistent gains of +1 to +3 points in Mahalanobis AUROC on a zero-shot cross-domain stress test using BDD100K weather splits. Two ablations (scalar uncertainty and cosine gate) indicate the additive-residual formulation is the primary source of these improvements. An evidential variant using Dempster-Shafer fusion introduces interpretable signals of conflict and ignorance. These findings offer a concrete design principle for uncertainty-aware SSL. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/WadiiBoulila/trust-ssl.

title: Symbolic Grounding Reveals Representational Bottlenecks in Abstract Visual Reasoning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Componential-Grammatical (C-G) paradigm to diagnose representational bottlenecks in abstract visual reasoning. The authors decouple perception from reasoning on Bongard-LOGO, a benchmark requiring models to infer latent geometric rules from positive and negative example images. Instead of feeding raw pixels to vision-language models (VLMs), the C-G interface provides language models with the underlying procedural LOGO programs or natural-language descriptions that generated each image, transforming the task into purely symbolic inference.

The study evaluates 12 language models across multiple conditions, including formal grammar strings, natural-language action descriptions, concept-conditioned prompts, grounded variants with visual anchors, and token-randomization controls. A strong VLM baseline (Gemini-2.5-Flash) achieves near-chance accuracy (~50%) on raw images, while the same tasks reframed symbolically yield 60–80% accuracy across models, with Phi-4-Reasoning reaching 96.2% on Free-form problems—a 25–30 percentage point gain from representational format alone. Token randomization experiments confirm that models exploit genuine compositional structure rather than surface-level heuristics. Adding visual anchors to symbolic input provides only marginal benefits, and the optimal representation format varies by task complexity.

These findings demonstrate that the primary bottleneck in current multimodal systems for abstract reasoning lies not in reasoning capacity but in visual representations that fail to capture geometric and relational structure. The results support modular architectures that explicitly separate perception from reasoning through intermediate symbolic representations.
original_abstract: Vision--language models (VLMs) often fail on abstract visual reasoning benchmarks such as Bongard problems, raising the question of whether the main bottleneck lies in reasoning or representation. We study this on Bongard-LOGO, a synthetic benchmark of abstract concept learning with ground-truth generative programs, by comparing end-to-end VLMs on raw images with large language models (LLMs) given symbolic inputs derived from those images. Using symbolic inputs as a diagnostic probe rather than a practical multimodal architecture, our \emph{Componential--Grammatical (C--G)} paradigm reformulates Bongard-LOGO as a symbolic reasoning task based on LOGO-style action programs or structured descriptions. LLMs achieve large and consistent gains, reaching mid--90s accuracy on Free-form problems, while a strong visual baseline remains near chance under matched task definitions. Ablations on input format, explicit concept prompts, and minimal visual grounding show that these factors matter much less than the shift from pixels to symbolic structure. These results identify representation as a key bottleneck in abstract visual reasoning and show how symbolic input can serve as a controlled diagnostic upper bound.

title: Beyond Single Plots: A Benchmark for Question Answering on Multi-Charts
generated_summary:
This paper introduces PolyChartQA, a benchmark dataset specifically designed for question answering over multi-chart images—composite figures containing multiple sub-charts. Unlike existing datasets such as MultiChartQA and CharXiv, PolyChartQA omits explicit chart references in questions, forcing models to localize relevant sub-charts independently, and includes rich annotations for chart type, homogeneity, question difficulty, and question type.

The dataset comprises 534 multi-chart images sourced from peer-reviewed computer science papers, containing 2,297 sub-charts and 2,694 question-answer pairs (519 human-authored, 2,175 MLM-generated and manually verified). The authors evaluate nine state-of-the-art multimodal language models (MLMs) and propose a Visual Decomposition and Self-Verification Pipeline (VDSP) that decomposes multi-chart reasoning into sub-chart identification, reasoning, and verification stages.

Key findings reveal that MLMs perform substantially worse on multi-chart images compared to single-chart settings, with accuracy drops up to 36.98%. Performance consistently declines with increasing question difficulty, sub-chart count, and chart homogeneity. Data retrieval questions prove most challenging across models. Human-authored questions are significantly harder than MLM-generated ones, with gaps up to 27.4% in accuracy. The VDSP pipeline improves accuracy by up to 5.39% over zero-shot prompting while enhancing interpretability by making failure points transparent.

These results highlight critical limitations of current MLMs in multi-chart reasoning and establish PolyChartQA as a valuable resource for advancing research in complex chart understanding.
original_abstract: Charts are widely used to present complex information. Deriving meaningful insights in real-world contexts often requires interpreting multiple related charts together. Research on understanding multi-chart images has not been extensively explored. We introduce PolyChartQA, a mid-scale dataset specifically designed for question answering over multi-chart images. PolyChartQA comprises 534 multi-chart images (with a total of 2,297 sub-charts) sourced from peer-reviewed computer science research publications and 2,694 QA pairs. We evaluate the performance of nine state-of-the-art Multimodal Language Models (MLMs) on PolyChartQA across question type, difficulty, question source, and key structural characteristics of multi-charts. Our results show a 27.4% LLM-based accuracy (L-Accuracy) drop on human-authored questions compared to MLM-generated questions, and a 5.39% L-accuracy gain with our proposed prompting method.

title: Latent Denoising Improves Visual Alignment in Large Multimodal Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a training-time latent denoising framework for Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) that strengthens internal visual representations without adding inference overhead. The key insight is that corrupting projected visual tokens and training the model to recover clean features can serve as effective visual supervision during multimodal instruction tuning.

The methodology applies saliency-guided corruption to projected image tokens through a mixture of Gaussian noising (applied preferentially to salient patches) and masking (applied to less salient patches). The model then recovers aligned teacher features from an intermediate LLM layer using three complementary objectives: a normalized reconstruction loss, a relational alignment loss preserving pairwise feature geometry, and a contrastive loss encouraging patch-level distinctiveness. All corruption and auxiliary decoding operate only during training.

Evaluated across three LMM architectures (LLaVA with CLIP, LLaVA with SigLIP, and Qwen-2.5-VL) on 18 benchmarks, the framework consistently improves performance, with the largest gains on tasks requiring fine-grained visual reasoning such as GQA (+1.6 to +4.4) and MMStar (+1.2 to +3.1). The authors also introduce a systematic corruption evaluation protocol for LMMs, demonstrating that latent denoising reduces performance degradation under noisy, blurred, and otherwise corrupted inputs. Internal analysis reveals improved cross-modal alignment, higher feature discriminability, and more spatially grounded attention patterns, confirming that the method produces measurably better visual representations throughout the network.
original_abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) such as LLaVA are typically trained with an autoregressive language modeling objective, providing only indirect supervision to visual tokens. This often yields weak internal visual representations and brittle behavior under distribution shift. Inspired by recent progress on latent denoising for learning high-quality visual tokenizers, we show that the same principle provides an effective form of visual supervision for improving internal visual feature alignment and multimodal understanding in LMMs. We propose a latent denoising framework that corrupts projected visual tokens using a saliency-aware mixture of masking and Gaussian noising. The LMM is trained to denoise these corrupted tokens by recovering clean teacher patch features from hidden states at a selected intermediate LLM layer using a decoder. To prevent representation collapse, our framework also preserves the teacher's intra-image similarity structure and applies intra-image contrastive patch distillation. During inference, corruption and auxiliary heads are disabled, introducing no additional inference-time overhead. Across a broad suite of standard multimodal benchmarks, our method consistently improves visual understanding and reasoning over strong baselines, and yields clear gains on compositional robustness benchmarks (e.g., NaturalBench). Moreover, under ImageNet-C-style non-adversarial common corruptions applied to benchmark images, our method maintains higher accuracy and exhibits reduced degradation at both moderate and severe corruption levels. Our code is available at https://github.com/dhruvashp/latent-denoising-for-lmms.

title: "If We Had the Information That We Need to Interpret the World Around Us, We Wouldn't Be Disabled:" Barriers and Opportunities in Information Work among Blind and Sighted Colleagues
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how blind and low-vision (BLV) workers and their sighted colleagues navigate information representation challenges in professional mixed-visual-ability teams. The authors conduct a qualitative study comprising a five-day diary study with follow-up interviews (teams T1–T5) and focus groups (teams T6–T7), involving 30 participants across seven professional teams in sectors including legal, nonprofit, consulting, and academia.

The study's main contribution is a novel characterization of four types of representational inaccessibility: invisible visual content, inaccessible visual structure, inadequate system feedback during editing, and lost cognitive support. For each type, the authors document workarounds that teams employ, such as linearizing structured content, adding semantic labels, manually tracking edits, and relying on verbal mediation with sighted colleagues. These workarounds often involve trade-offs, sacrificing functionality, efficiency, or visual quality for basic access.

Beyond technical failures, the findings reveal that organizational culture and productivity-focused metrics often deprioritize accessibility. The authors identify a progressive awareness framework through which team members move from ignorance to interdependence regarding colleagues' representational needs, driven by advocacy, inquiry, and relationship-building.

The paper argues that accessibility emerges through collective negotiation rather than purely technical fixes, advocating for modality-free information architectures that render representations adaptively. These findings have significant implications for designing inclusive collaborative tools and reshaping workplace cultures to treat accessibility as integral to knowledge work productivity.
original_abstract: Despite recognition of the value of diversity, the way work takes place can fail to support blind or low-vision employees, especially in collaborative work settings. This paper examines how professional teams with diverse visual abilities use information representations (e.g., PDF documents, spreadsheets and charts). A diary study with follow-up individual interviews (23 participants with mixed abilities from 5 teams) and 2 separate focus groups (7 participants from 2 other teams) allowed us to characterize key dimensions of the role of representations in the workplace into four types of interrelated failures and workarounds, influenced by workplace stigmas and shaped by evolving social dynamics towards interdependent information work. We contribute this new empirically supported conceptual understanding of representation use in workplaces that can help design and improve the experiences of mixed-ability teams doing knowledge work in the current technological landscape.

title: PREVENT-JACK: Context Steering for Swarms of Long Heavy Articulated Vehicles
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Prevent-Jack, a decentralized, purely reactive control algorithm for coordinating swarms of Heavy Articulated Vehicles (HAVs) — trucks towing multiple passive trailers — with provable guarantees against jackknifing and inter-vehicle collisions. The key novelty lies in transferring context steering, a multi-behavior merging strategy from computer games, to robotics. Unlike standard behavior fusion approaches that combine output velocity vectors, context steering merges the decision contexts of multiple competing objectives, enabling more intuitive design and reducing parameter tuning requirements.

The methodology employs a scalable kinematic simulation framework, validated against physics-based Gazebo simulations, to evaluate performance across 15,000 randomized scenarios. Vehicles feature up to ten trailers with randomly sampled configurations, and experiments span varying swarm sizes (1–10 HAVs) and collision densities.

Results demonstrate that Prevent-Jack eliminates jackknifing and collisions entirely across all tested scenarios, while increasing task completion rates compared to the prior Avoid-Jack baseline (from 65.1% to 73.2% for two-vehicle swarms). However, deadlocks and livelocks increase with swarm size and density, with even the most challenging configurations still allowing approximately 70% of individual HAVs to reach their goals.

This work is significant as one of the first to address highly kinematically constrained articulated vehicles in swarm robotics, bridging the gap between idealized swarm models and real-world platforms such as airport baggage trains, mining vehicles, and articulated buses.
original_abstract: In this paper, we aim to extend the traditional point-mass-like robot representation in swarm robotics and instead study a swarm of long Heavy Articulated Vehicles (HAVs). HAVs are kinematically constrained, elongated, and articulated, introducing unique challenges. Local, decentralized coordination of these vehicles is motivated by many real-world applications. Our approach, Prevent-Jack, introduces the sparsely covered context steering framework in robotics. It fuses six local behaviors, providing guarantees against jackknifing and collisions at the cost of potential dead- and livelocks, tested for vehicles with up to ten trailers. We highlight the importance of the Evade Attraction behavior for deadlock prevention using a parameter study, and use 15,000 simulations to evaluate the swarm performance. Our extensive experiments and the results show that both the dead- and livelocks occur more frequently in larger swarms and denser scenarios, affecting a peak average of 27%/31% of vehicles. We observe that larger swarms exhibit increased waiting, while smaller swarms show increased evasion.

title: Sub-Token Routing in LoRA for Adaptation and Query-Aware KV Compression
generated_summary:
This paper introduces sub-token routing, a fine-grained control mechanism for KV-cache compression in LoRA-adapted transformers. The key insight is that relevant tokens need not be internally uniform—not every part of a token's value representation is equally useful—so KV compression need not be an all-or-nothing decision at the token level. Instead, individual groups within value vectors can be selectively preserved or dropped.

The authors propose two complementary designs. The query-independent design combines routed subspace LoRA adaptation with value-group routing on the KV path, where a lightweight router selects which value groups to cache and a reconstructor estimates dropped groups. The query-aware design uses a predictor-based selector that scores context-token/value-group pairs using query-conditioned relevance, allocating a global retention budget so that important tokens preserve more value groups while less relevant tokens retain fewer or none.

Experiments across the Qwen 2.5 family (7B–72B) demonstrate that the query-independent design improves language-modeling perplexity over standard LoRA while retaining only 75% of the KV cache. The query-aware design preserves downstream MMLU accuracy well under reduced budgets. Crucially, sub-token routing complements token-level selection methods: their combination achieves 37.5% total KV retention while maintaining over 99% baseline accuracy on larger models. This demonstrates that token-level and sub-token-level routing provide orthogonal compression axes, enabling deeper KV compression without meaningful accuracy loss.
original_abstract: Sub-token routing offers a finer control axis for transformer efficiency than the coarse units used in most prior work, such as tokens, pages, heads, or layers. In this paper, we study routing within a token representation itself in LoRA-adapted transformers. The motivation is that a relevant token need not be internally uniform: under a retention budget, preserved value groups are distributed unevenly both across tokens and within tokens, which suggests that KV compression need not be an all-or-nothing decision at token level. We study this fine-grained routing mechanism in two settings. For compression-aware language modeling, we introduce a query-independent design that combines routed subspace LoRA with value-group routing on the KV path. For downstream-task-preserving KV compression, we introduce a query-aware design in which a predictor-based selector allocates a global retention budget over context-token/value-group pairs using query-conditioned relevance. Experiments show that the query-independent design improves the quality-compression tradeoff for language modeling, while the query-aware design preserves downstream behavior under reduced KV budgets. We further examine the relation between token-level and sub-token-level query-aware routing, and show that they form complementary compression axes: token-level methods determine which tokens survive globally, while sub-token routing determines how the surviving tokens are compressed internally.

title: Ideological Bias in LLMs' Economic Causal Reasoning
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first systematic analysis of ideological bias in large language models' economic causal reasoning. The authors leverage the EconCausal benchmark dataset of 10,490 context-annotated causal triplets from top-tier economics and finance journals, identifying 1,056 ideologically contested triplets where market-oriented and intervention-oriented economic frameworks predict divergent causal directions. They evaluate 20 state-of-the-art LLMs on their ability to predict causal signs, comparing accuracy when empirical ground truth aligns with intervention-oriented versus market-oriented expectations, and introduce directional bias metrics to quantify systematic asymmetries.

The key finding is a striking and consistent asymmetry: across 18 of 20 models, accuracy is substantially higher when empirical truth aligns with intervention-oriented expectations, with average gaps of 9.7 to 15.1 percentage points. This pattern persists after controlling for item difficulty and is not eliminated by one-shot in-context steering, suggesting it reflects deep-seated tendencies rather than superficial prompting artifacts. Base-versus-instruct comparisons indicate the bias originates partly in pretraining and can be amplified by instruction tuning.

These findings carry significant implications for LLM-assisted policy analysis, economic reporting, and decision support. The authors demonstrate that aggregate accuracy metrics are insufficient, as models can appear broadly competent while being systematically less reliable on one side of contested economic questions, potentially introducing invisible ideological tilt into downstream policy recommendations.
original_abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) exhibit systematic ideological bias when reasoning about economic causal effects? As LLMs are increasingly used in policy analysis and economic reporting, where directionally correct causal judgments are essential, this question has direct practical stakes. We present a systematic evaluation by extending the EconCausal benchmark with ideology-contested cases - instances where intervention-oriented (pro-government) and market-oriented (pro-market) perspectives predict divergent causal signs. From 10,490 causal triplets (treatment-outcome pairs with empirically verified effect directions) derived from top-tier economics and finance journals, we identify 1,056 ideology-contested instances and evaluate 20 state-of-the-art LLMs on their ability to predict empirically supported causal directions. We find that ideology-contested items are consistently harder than non-contested ones, and that across 18 of 20 models, accuracy is systematically higher when the empirically verified causal sign aligns with intervention-oriented expectations than with market-oriented ones. Moreover, when models err, their incorrect predictions disproportionately lean intervention-oriented, and this directional skew is not eliminated by one-shot in-context prompting. These results highlight that LLMs are not only less accurate on ideologically contested economic questions, but systematically less reliable in one ideological direction than the other, underscoring the need for direction-aware evaluation in high-stakes economic and policy settings.

title: FingerViP: Learning Real-World Dexterous Manipulation with Fingertip Visual Perception
generated_summary:
This paper presents FingerViP, a learning system for real-world dexterous manipulation that embeds miniature cameras in each fingertip of a multi-fingered robotic hand, providing close-range, multi-view visual perception that mitigates occlusion challenges inherent to external and wrist-mounted cameras. The vision-enhanced fingertip modules are compact, low-cost, and modular, preserving the hand's form factor while capturing fine-grained interaction cues near contact points.

The system employs a transformer-based diffusion policy trained on human demonstrations collected via teleoperation with an Apple Vision Pro. The policy fuses five fingertip camera views with a third-view camera, incorporating fingertip camera pose encodings computed via forward kinematics and per-finger joint current encodings to enhance spatial awareness and contact sensitivity. Cross-attention mechanisms in the transformer capture semantic correspondences between multi-view visual tokens and action tokens across the 26-DoF arm-hand system.

FingerViP is evaluated on four challenging real-world tasks—confined-box button pressing, unstable-support stick retrieval, curtain-occluded object retrieval, and closed-cabinet object retrieval—achieving success rates of 73.8%, 75.7%, 90.0%, and 83.6% respectively, consistently outperforming baselines using wrist-mounted, third-view, or combined camera configurations. Ablation studies confirm the importance of both camera pose and joint current encodings. The work demonstrates that fingertip visual perception offers a scalable, occlusion-robust approach for contact-rich dexterous manipulation in confined, unstructured environments.
original_abstract: The current practice of dexterous manipulation generally relies on a single wrist-mounted view, which is often occluded and limits performance on tasks requiring multi-view perception. In this work, we present FingerViP, a learning system that utilizes a visuomotor policy with fingertip visual perception for dexterous manipulation. Specifically, we design a vision-enhanced fingertip module with an embedded miniature camera and install the modules on each finger of a multi-fingered hand. The fingertip cameras substantially improve visual perception by providing comprehensive, multi-view feedback of both the hand and its surrounding environment. Building on the integrated fingertip modules, we develop a diffusion-based whole-body visuomotor policy conditioned on a third-view camera and multi-view fingertip vision, which effectively learns complex manipulation skills directly from human demonstrations. To improve view-proprioception alignment and contact awareness, each fingertip visual feature is augmented with its corresponding camera pose encoding and per-finger joint-current encoding. We validate the effectiveness of the multi-view fingertip vision and demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of FingerViP on various challenging real-world tasks, including pressing buttons inside a confined box, retrieving sticks from an unstable support, retrieving objects behind an occluding curtain, and performing long-horizon cabinet opening and object retrieval, achieving an overall success rate of 80.8%. All hardware designs and code will be fully open-sourced.

title: Teacher-Guided Routing for Sparse Vision Mixture-of-Experts
generated_summary:
This paper introduces TGR-MoE, a teacher-guided routing framework that addresses the gradient blocking problem in sparse Vision Mixture-of-Experts (VMoE) models. title: Role of diversity in team performance: the case of missing expertise, an agent based simulation

original_abstract: Theory and empirical research on management teams' influence on firm performance have witnessed continuous development, and by now incorporate numerous details. Classic, experiment-based studies examining social systems collect vast amount of data, but often times investigate only the first one or two modes of the distribution of measured variables, and experience difficulty in analyzing the effect of context.
