Modeling results show that depending on the context, such as communication scheme among interacting agents, or their functional composition, intrapersonal functional diversity (IFD), and dominant function diversity (DFD) might enhance or reduce performance and communication among agents. title: Understanding and Mitigating Spurious Signal Amplification in Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for Math Reasoning
generated_summary:

To address these issues, the authors propose Debiased and Denoised Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (DDRL), comprising three components: (1) balanced confidence-aware sampling that filters ambiguous medium-frequency samples while maintaining balanced positive and negative examples; (2) debiased advantage estimation that replaces group-relative normalization with fixed, label-dependent advantages to eliminate frequency-dependent amplification; and (3) a lightweight consensus-based off-policy refinement stage using rejection sampling and supervised fine-tuning to consolidate high-confidence behaviors.

Experiments across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME 2024, AMC, MATH-500) and three models demonstrate that DDRL consistently outperforms TTRL, achieving relative improvements of 15.3% on Qwen2.5-MATH-1.5B and 12.7% on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct. Ablation studies confirm each component's contribution, while analysis of advantage dynamics reveals DDRL's adaptive behavior—initially suppressing unreliable positive signals and gradually shifting toward reinforcing correct responses as pseudo-label quality improves. original_abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) always adapts models at inference time via pseudo-labeling, leaving it vulnerable to spurious optimization signals from label noise. Through an empirical study, we observe that responses with medium consistency form an ambiguity region and constitute the primary source of reward noise. Crucially, we find that such spurious signals can be even amplified through group-relative advantage estimation. Motivated by these findings, we propose a unified framework, Debiased and Denoised test-time Reinforcement Learning (DDRL), to mitigate spurious signals. Concretely, DDRL first applies a frequency-based sampling strategy to exclude ambiguous samples while maintaining a balanced set of positive and negative examples. It then adopts a debiased advantage estimation with fixed advantages, removing the bias introduced by group-relative policy optimization. Finally, DDRL incorporates a consensus-based off-policy refinement stage, which leverages the rejection-sampled dataset to enable efficient and stable model updates. Experiments on three large language models across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that DDRL consistently outperforms existing TTRL baselines. The code will soon be released at https://github.com/yuyongcan/DDRL.

title: MiMIC: Mitigating Visual Modality Collapse in Universal Multimodal Retrieval While Avoiding Semantic Misalignment
generated_summary:
This paper identifies and addresses two critical failure modes in Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR): visual modality collapse in early-fusion models, where visual features are disregarded in favor of textual cues, and semantic misalignment in late-fusion models, where document positions in embedding space are disproportionately influenced by modality type.

The authors propose MiMIC, which introduces a Fusion-in-Decoder (FiD) architecture that encodes different modalities separately and uses cross-attention in a language model decoder to dynamically aggregate multimodal information. This is complemented by a robust training strategy consisting of two components: single-modality mix-in, which preserves modality-specific signals by explicitly maintaining individual modality representations alongside fused embeddings, and random caption dropout, which forces the model to optimize visual embeddings rather than over-relying on textual features. The authors also extend existing benchmarks (WebQA and EVQA) to create WebQA+ and EVQA+ datasets that include missing-modality scenarios.

Experimental results demonstrate that MiMIC-ANCE achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving R@100 by 6.77 points on WebQA+ and 7.07 points on EVQA+ over the strongest baseline. Notably, MiMIC maintains balanced performance across text-to-text and text-to-image retrieval tasks, whereas competing methods show severe modality bias. Ablation studies confirm that both the FiD architecture and training strategies are essential. This work represents the first systematic investigation of modality collapse in UMR, with practical implications for building robust multimodal search systems.
original_abstract: Universal Multimodal Retrieval (UMR) aims to map different modalities (e.g., visual and textual) into a shared embedding space for multi-modal retrieval. Existing UMR methods can be broadly divided into two categories: early-fusion approaches, such as Marvel, which projects visual features into the language model (LM) space for integrating with text modality, and late-fusion approaches, such as UniVL-DR, which encode visual and textual inputs using separate encoders and obtain fused embeddings through addition. Our pilot study reveals that Marvel exhibits visual modality collapse, which is characterized by the model's tendency to disregard visual features while depending excessively on textual cues. In contrast, although UniVL-DR is less affected by this issue, it is more susceptible to semantic misalignment, where semantically related content is positioned far apart in the embedding space. To address these challenges, we propose MiMIC, which introduces two key innovations: (1) a fusion-in-decoder architecture for effective multimodal integration, and (2) robust training through single modality mixin and random caption dropout. Experiments on the WebQA+ and EVQA+ datasets, where image in documents or queries might lack captions, indicate that MiMIC consistently outperforms both early- and late-fusion baselines.

title: Temporal Prototyping and Hierarchical Alignment for Unsupervised Video-based Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification
generated_summary:

HiTPro comprises four components: a Temporal-aware Feature Encoder (TFE) that aggregates frame-level features via temporal attention; Intra-Camera Tracklet Prototyping (ICTP), which exploits the structural prior that tracklets within a single camera represent distinct identities to construct reliable prototypes without clustering; Hierarchical Cross-Prototype Alignment (HCPA), which progressively mines positive pairs first across cameras within a modality, then across modalities, using dynamic thresholds and soft weight assignment for reliability; and Hierarchical Contrastive Learning (HCL), which progressively optimizes alignment from intra-camera discrimination to cross-modality matching through curriculum-based loss scheduling.

Experiments on HITSZ-VCM and BUPTCampus datasets demonstrate that HiTPro significantly outperforms all unsupervised baselines, achieving 12.10% and 19.03% Rank-1 improvements over the second-best methods, respectively, and even surpasses several supervised approaches. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic contribution of each component. This work establishes a strong baseline for unsupervised video-based VI-ReID, addressing a practical yet previously unexplored setting in cross-modal surveillance.
original_abstract: Visible-infrared person re-identification (VI-ReID) enables cross-modality identity matching for all-day surveillance, yet existing methods predominantly focus on the image level or rely heavily on costly identity annotations. While video-based VI-ReID has recently emerged to exploit temporal dynamics for improved robustness, existing studies remain limited to supervised settings. Crucially, the unsupervised video VI-ReID problem, where models must learn from RGB and infrared tracklets without identity labels, remains largely unexplored despite its practical importance in real-world deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose HiTPro (Hierarchical Temporal Prototyping), a prototype-driven framework without explicit hard pseudo-label assignment for unsupervised video-based VI-ReID. HiTPro begins with an efficient Temporal-aware Feature Encoder that first extracts discriminative frame-level features and then aggregates them into a robust tracklet-level representation. Building upon these features, HiTPro first constructs reliable intra-camera prototypes via Intra-Camera Tracklet Prototyping by aggregating features from temporally partitioned sub-tracklets. Through Hierarchical Cross-Prototype Alignment, we perform a two-stage positive mining process: progressing from within-modality associations to cross-modality matching, enhanced by Dynamic Threshold Strategy and Soft Weight Assignment. Finally, {Hierarchical Contrastive Learning} progressively optimizes feature-prototype alignment across three levels: intra-camera discrimination, cross-camera same-modality consistency, and cross-modality invariance. Extensive experiments on HITSZ-VCM and BUPTCampus demonstrate that HiTPro achieves state-of-the-art performance under fully unsupervised settings, significantly outperforming adapted baselines and establishes a strong baseline for future research.

title: FryNet: Dual-Stream Adversarial Fusion for Non-Destructive Frying Oil Oxidation Assessment
generated_summary:
FryNet is a dual-stream RGB-thermal architecture for non-destructive frying oil quality assessment that simultaneously performs segmentation, classification, and regression of chemical oxidation indices. The paper's central contribution is identifying and addressing a camera-fingerprint shortcut problem, where deep learning models memorize sensor-specific signatures rather than learning oxidation chemistry, causing five backbone architectures to collapse to 54–62% mIoU under video-disjoint evaluation.

The methodology employs a ThermalMiT-B2 backbone with thermal channel and spatial attention for processing FLIR images, paired with a lightweight RGB-MAE Encoder that learns chemically grounded representations through masked autoencoding and chemical alignment losses. Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) fuses the two streams efficiently. Critically, Gradient Reversal Layers applied to both encoders via a Dual-Encoder Domain-Adversarial Neural Network suppress camera-fingerprint shortcuts in both streams, forcing domain-invariant feature learning. Fused regression routing enables chemical prediction heads to benefit from cross-modal context.

On a held-out test set of 1,005 frames from four unseen oil batches, FryNet achieves 98.97% mIoU, 100% classification accuracy, and a mean regression MAE of 2.32—a 3.2× improvement over the best single-modal baseline—using only 31M parameters. The authors also release a dataset of 7,226 paired RGB-thermal frames with segmentation masks and chemical annotations. This work demonstrates that adversarial domain adaptation is essential for reliable multi-modal fusion in industrial food safety monitoring.
original_abstract: Monitoring frying oil degradation is critical for food safety, yet current practice relies on destructive wet-chemistry assays that provide no spatial information and are unsuitable for real-time use. We identify a fundamental obstacle in thermal-image-based inspection, the camera-fingerprint shortcut, whereby models memorize sensor-specific noise and thermal bias instead of learning oxidation chemistry, collapsing under video-disjoint evaluation. We propose FryNet, a dual-stream RGB-thermal framework that jointly performs oil-region segmentation, serviceability classification, and regression of four chemical oxidation indices (PV, p-AV, Totox, temperature) in a single forward pass. A ThermalMiT-B2 backbone with channel and spatial attention extracts thermal features, while an RGB-MAE Encoder learns chemically grounded representations via masked autoencoding and chemical alignment. Dual-Encoder DANN adversarially regularizes both streams against video identity via Gradient Reversal Layers, and FiLM fusion bridges thermal structure with RGB chemical context. On 7,226 paired frames across 28 frying videos, FryNet achieves 98.97% mIoU, 100% classification accuracy, and 2.32 mean regression MAE, outperforming all seven baselines.

title: LLM-Steered Power Allocation for Parallel QPSK-AWGN Channels
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a dual-process architecture for LLM-steered power allocation in parallel QPSK-AWGN channels, inspired by Kahneman's System 1/System 2 cognitive framework. The main contribution is a framework where a fast projected-gradient optimizer (System 1) continuously maximizes a weighted sum mutual information objective under power constraints, while a large language model (System 2) periodically interprets natural-language operator policies and adjusts the optimization weights and power budget accordingly. Crucially, the LLM steers the optimizer indirectly through bounded control parameters rather than directly setting power allocations, ensuring feasibility by construction regardless of erratic LLM outputs. Additional guardrails including normalization, exponential moving average smoothing, and fallback mechanisms further mitigate unreliable LLM behavior.

Experiments on an 8-channel QPSK system demonstrate that a single LLM, using an unchanged system prompt, produces qualitatively distinct allocation strategies for four different natural-language policies—including sum-rate maximization, channel prioritization, rate targeting, and channel deactivation—without any per-policy reimplementation. In a resilience test involving abrupt channel-gain reversal, LLM steering reduces mutual information spread by 60% compared to an equal-weight baseline, demonstrating reactive homeostasis. The architecture also provides explainable reasoning outputs for human oversight. This work establishes a promising design pattern for integrating LLM-based semantic reasoning into real-time wireless optimization loops while maintaining safety guarantees.
original_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored as high-level decision modules in closed-loop systems, but their stochastic nature makes safe integration challenging. In this paper, we propose LLM-Steered Power Allocation, a dual-process architecture for parallel QPSK channels inspired by Kahneman's System 1/System 2 framework. A fast numerical optimizer (System 1) continuously performs projected gradient ascent on a weighted mutual-information objective, while an LLM navigator (System 2) periodically interprets natural-language policies and updates only the channel weights and the operational power budget. The LLM never manipulates the power-allocation variables directly, and constraint satisfaction is enforced structurally by the optimizer. To mitigate LLM unreliability, we further incorporate multi-layer guardrails including normalization, exponential moving-average smoothing, and fallback mechanisms. Numerical experiments on an 8-channel system show that, with a fixed optimization core and unchanged system prompt, different natural-language policies induce qualitatively different operating points, including throughput-oriented allocation, channel prioritization, power-aware operation, and channel shutdown. In addition, under an abrupt channel-gain reversal, the proposed system autonomously reconfigures its steering signals and reduces the final mutual-information spread by 60% compared with the optimizer alone. These results suggest that LLMs can serve as policy interpreters for safe, flexible reconfiguration of communication-system optimizers without controller reimplementation.

title: TopoStyle: Supporting Iterative Design with Generative AI for 2.5D Topology Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper presents TopoStyle, an interactive design tool that leverages generative AI (diffusion models) to enable iterative 2.5D topology optimization within 3D modeling environments. The main contribution is reframing topology optimization from a one-shot engineering solver into an iterative design medium that supports both structural performance and aesthetic exploration.

TopoStyle builds upon an open-source diffusion model (TopoDiff) and introduces an image-to-image generation strategy to support arbitrary geometric shapes, rather than being limited to square domains. The tool offers two complementary workflows integrated into Rhino/Grasshopper: a sketch-based DRAWER method, where users draw physical constraints directly on a 2D canvas, and a geometry-based GEO method, where constraints are specified through precise 3D point placement. Both workflows support masking functionality, allowing users to selectively apply topology optimization to specific regions.

Quantitative evaluation across three benchmark tasks demonstrates that TopoStyle generates structures with minimum compliance values comparable to traditional finite-element-analysis ground truth, though volume fractions tend to be slightly higher. Keystroke-Level Model analysis reveals that the DRAWER workflow requires less total interaction time and lower cognitive overhead than the GEO workflow, making it particularly suited for rapid iterative exploration. Three application cases—a chair, robot gripper, and wall hook—illustrate the tool's capacity for balancing performance requirements with aesthetic customization.

TopoStyle represents a meaningful step toward integrating generative AI-driven structural optimization into practical design workflows, enabling designers to efficiently explore diverse structural solutions through intuitive interaction.
original_abstract: Topology optimization(TO) is widely used in engineering because of its ability to save material and optimize structural performance. Although prior work has explored 2D human-centered design tool for TO, the results are often limited in variety and offer weak customizability. Meanwhile, due to the high computational and time costs of TO, researchers have attempted to address these issues using generative AI; however, such methods often provide limited interactivity. In addition, topology optimization in many cases needs to balance structural performance and aesthetic qualities through iterative design, a perspective that has rarely been emphasized in traditional TO. We present TopoStyle, an iterative design tool for 2.5D topology optimization using a 2D diffusion model. We explore two interaction methods. The first exports 3D parts to a graphical interface for hand-drawn interaction. The second enables direct interaction within 3D modeling software using points. Our tool also supports the use of masks to apply topology optimization to specific regions, allowing users to address customized design needs. We compare and evaluate both performance and interaction methods, and investigate how TopoStyle can balance performance and aesthetics while improving design efficiency through customization and iterative design. Finally, we demonstrate the application scenarios of TopoStyle through several design cases.

title: PLAS-Net: Pixel-Level Area Segmentation for UAV-Based Beach Litter Monitoring
generated_summary:
This paper presents PLAS-Net (Pixel-level Litter Area Segmentor), an instance segmentation framework designed for UAV-based beach litter monitoring that extracts precise pixel-level masks rather than relying on bounding boxes, which overestimate debris footprints. Built upon the YOLOv26n-seg architecture, PLAS-Net incorporates three custom modules: C3kDFF for suppressing complex background noise from sand and vegetation, CPCAA for repairing mask fragmentation caused by partial burial and occlusion, and DMSSF for preserving structural integrity of thin, elongated objects like fishing lines across multiple scales.

Evaluated on 1,300 UAV image tiles from Aow Luek Bay, Koh Tao, Thailand, PLAS-Net achieves the highest mAP among eleven benchmark models while maintaining minimal parameters and competitive inference speed. Ablation studies confirm each module's contribution: C3kDFF improves precision by over 10 percentage points, CPCAA enhances mask continuity, and DMSSF boosts overall segmentation performance.

The authors demonstrate that improved mask quality directly benefits three downstream environmental analyses: power-law fragmentation modeling yielding physically consistent scaling exponents, area-weighted ecological risk mapping that identifies concentrated pollution hotspots missed by count-based indices, and source composition analysis revealing that fishing gear imposes disproportionate spatial footprints despite low abundance. These applications illustrate how pixel-level geometric fidelity can bridge computer vision and quantitative environmental assessment, supporting evidence-based coastal conservation in monsoon-driven environments.
original_abstract: Accurate quantification of the physical exposure area of beach litter, rather than simple item counts, is essential for credible ecological risk assessment of marine debris. However, automated UAV-based monitoring predominantly relies on bounding-box detection, which systematically overestimates the planar area of irregular litter objects. To address this geometric limitation, we develop PLAS-Net (Pixel-level Litter Area Segmentor), an instance segmentation framework that extracts pixel-accurate physical footprints of coastal debris. Evaluated on UAV imagery from a monsoon-driven pocket beach in Koh Tao, Thailand, PLAS-Net achieves a mAP_50 of 58.7% with higher precision than eleven baseline models, demonstrating improved mask fidelity under complex coastal conditions. To illustrate how the accuracy of the masking affects the conclusions of environmental analysis, we conducted three downstream demonstrations: (i) power-law fitting of normalized plastic density (NPD) to characterize fragmentation dynamics; (ii) area-weighted ecological risk index (ERI) to map spatial pollution hotspots; and (iii) source composition analysis revealing the abundance-area paradox: fishing gear constitutes a small proportion of the total number of items, but has the largest physical area per unit item. Pixel-level area extraction can provide more valuable information for coastal monitoring compared to methods based solely on counting.

title: Adversarial Evasion in Non-Stationary Malware Detection: Minimizing Drift Signals through Similarity-Constrained Perturbations
generated_summary:
This paper investigates whether adversarial malware samples can simultaneously evade deep learning classifiers and remain undetectable by concept drift monitoring mechanisms in non-stationary malware detection environments. The authors propose a novel framework that generates targeted adversarial examples in standardized feature space by augmenting cross-entropy loss with similarity-constrained regularizers—specifically KL divergence, ℓ₂ distance, and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD)—to maintain distributional similarity between adversarial and clean malware samples. The framework is implemented using iterative FGSM and Projected Gradient Descent optimizers and evaluated on the BODMAS dataset containing over 134,000 Windows PE files. Drift detectability is assessed through a comprehensive protocol employing six complementary metrics: Jensen-Shannon divergence, Hellinger distance, Wasserstein distance, KS statistic, PSI, and output-based MMD.

Key findings reveal that under constrained low-budget settings, KL and ℓ₂ regularization effectively reduce output-distribution drift across statistical metrics but paradoxically do not improve attack success rates, which remain around 3%. MMD regularization introduces substantially larger distributional shifts, making attacks more detectable. The perturbation budget emerges as the dominant factor jointly driving both evasion success and drift magnitude. These results highlight the fundamental tension between adversarial evasion effectiveness and drift detectability, underscoring the importance of multi-metric evaluation for assessing adversarial robustness in evolving malware detection systems.
original_abstract: Deep learning has emerged as a powerful approach for malware detection, demonstrating impressive accuracy across various data representations. However, these models face critical limitations in real-world, non-stationary environments where both malware characteristics and detection systems continuously evolve. Our research investigates a fundamental security question: Can an attacker generate adversarial malware samples that simultaneously evade classification and remain inconspicuous to drift monitoring mechanisms? We propose a novel approach that generates targeted adversarial examples in the classifier's standardized feature space, augmented with sophisticated similarity regularizers. By carefully constraining perturbations to maintain distributional similarity with clean malware, we create an optimization objective that balances targeted misclassification with drift signal minimization. We quantify the effectiveness of this approach by comprehensively comparing classifier output probabilities using multiple drift metrics. Our experiments demonstrate that similarity constraints can reduce output drift signals, with $\ell_2$ regularization showing the most promising results. We observe that perturbation budget significantly influences the evasion-detectability trade-off, with increased budget leading to higher attack success rates and more substantial drift indicators.

title: When Bigger Isn't Better: A Comprehensive Fairness Evaluation of Political Bias in Multi-News Summarisation
generated_summary:
This study presents the first comprehensive fairness evaluation of political bias in multi-document news summarization using large language models. The authors introduce FairNews, a novel dataset of multi-document news articles annotated with political orientation labels, alongside a multi-dimensional fairness evaluation framework comprising five metrics: Neutralisation, Equal Fairness, Ratio Fairness, Entity Coverage, and Entity Sentiment Similarity. These metrics capture both coarse-grained political balance and fine-grained entity-level sentiment preservation.

The researchers evaluate 13 LLMs across three model families (Gemma-3, Llama-3, and Qwen2.5) at varying scales, testing baseline performance, prompt-based debiasing strategies, and agent-based debiasing approaches. The evaluation examines how model size, architecture, and intervention strategies affect fairness outcomes.

Key findings reveal that larger models do not consistently improve fairness; medium-sized variants often achieve the best balance of performance, fairness, and computational efficiency. No single debiasing strategy universally addresses all fairness dimensions, and effectiveness varies significantly across model architectures. Notably, Entity Sentiment Similarity proves highly resistant to prompt-based interventions, suggesting that sentiment toward entities is encoded deeply within model representations and requires approaches beyond surface-level prompting. Input document positioning shows no significant effect on fairness outcomes.

These results underscore the necessity of multi-dimensional fairness evaluation frameworks and highlight critical trade-offs between different fairness dimensions, challenging the assumption that scaling alone resolves bias in automated news summarization systems.
original_abstract: Multi-document news summarisation systems are increasingly adopted for their convenience in processing vast daily news content, making fairness across diverse political perspectives critical. However, these systems can exhibit political bias through unequal representation of viewpoints, disproportionate emphasis on certain perspectives, and systematic underrepresentation of minority voices. This study presents a comprehensive evaluation of such bias in multi-document news summarisation using FairNews, a dataset of complete news articles with political orientation labels, examining how large language models (LLMs) handle sources with varying political leanings across 13 models and five fairness metrics. We investigate both baseline model performance and effectiveness of various debiasing interventions, including prompt-based and judge-based approaches. Our findings challenge the assumption that larger models yield fairer outputs, as mid-sized variants consistently outperform their larger counterparts, offering the best balance of fairness and efficiency. Prompt-based debiasing proves highly model dependent, while entity sentiment emerges as the most stubborn fairness dimension, resisting all intervention strategies tested. These results demonstrate that fairness in multi-document news summarisation requires multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks and targeted, architecture-aware debiasing rather than simply scaling up.

title: CI-Work: Benchmarking Contextual Integrity in Enterprise LLM Agents
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CI-Work, a benchmark grounded in Contextual Integrity (CI) theory for evaluating the privacy-utility trade-off of LLM agents operating in enterprise workflows. Unlike prior benchmarks that focus on simple, isolated assistant tasks, CI-Work simulates realistic corporate environments where agents must navigate dense retrieval contexts containing both essential and sensitive information across five organizational communication directions (e.g., upward, lateral, diagonal). The benchmark employs a rigorous construction pipeline combining human-in-the-loop seed generation with automated self-iterative refinement to ensure scenarios reflect authentic business logic and hierarchical constraints.

The authors evaluate nine frontier LLMs, including GPT-5, Grok-4, DeepSeek-R1, and others, across CI-Work's scenarios. Key findings reveal a persistent privacy-utility trade-off that intensifies with realistic data scale and density. While models demonstrate understanding of high-level organizational boundaries, they fail at fine-grained information flow adjudication, frequently leaking sensitive data embedded within retrieval contexts. Even unintentional user pressure causes a dual collapse where agents simultaneously leak more sensitive information while failing to convey essential data. Notably, the study identifies an "inverse scaling" phenomenon: larger models and increased reasoning effort paradoxically worsen privacy violations rather than mitigating them.

These results underscore fundamental limitations in current safety alignment approaches for professional domains, highlighting the urgent need for context-aware privacy mechanisms specifically designed for enterprise LLM agents.
original_abstract: Enterprise LLM agents can dramatically improve workplace productivity, but their core capability, retrieving and using internal context to act on a user's behalf, also creates new risks for sensitive information leakage. We introduce CI-Work, a Contextual Integrity (CI)-grounded benchmark that simulates enterprise workflows across five information-flow directions and evaluates whether agents can convey essential content while withholding sensitive context in dense retrieval settings. Our evaluation of frontier models reveals that privacy failures are prevalent (violation rates range from 15.8%-50.9%, with leakage reaching up to 26.7%) and uncovers a counterintuitive trade-off critical for industrial deployment: higher task utility often correlates with increased privacy violations. Moreover, the massive scale of enterprise data and potential user behavior further amplify this vulnerability. Simply increasing model size or reasoning depth fails to address the problem. We conclude that safeguarding enterprise workflows requires a paradigm shift, moving beyond model-centric scaling toward context-centric architectures.

title: Finding Pareto frontier for one-sided matching
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of computing the complete Pareto-efficient frontier—the set of all Pareto-optimal matchings—in one-sided matching problems, where agents submit strict ordinal preferences over items without monetary transfers. Rather than finding a single Pareto-optimal allocation, the authors argue that enumerating all such allocations enables secondary optimizations for fairness or welfare criteria.

The main contribution is the Inverse-TTC Enumeration Algorithm (ITEA), which systematically inverts the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) mapping to partition the space of all initial endowments into equivalence classes, each corresponding to a unique Pareto-optimal outcome. A brute-force approach requires running TTC on all n! possible initial allocations at O(n!·n³) cost, with massive redundancy since many allocations converge to the same outcome. ITEA eliminates this redundancy by reconstructing, for each discovered Pareto-optimal allocation, the complete set of initial allocations that map to it, then pruning them from further exploration. The inverse reconstruction uses a tagging system with breadth-first search to systematically identify valid predecessor configurations.

Experiments on 700 randomly generated instances (n = 3 to 9) demonstrate that ITEA's advantage grows substantially with problem size. The ratio of Pareto front size to n! drops from 46% at n = 3 to 0.13% at n = 9, yielding over 700× speedup in TTC invocations. The authors position ITEA as a foundational tool enabling principled selection of Pareto-optimal allocations that satisfy additional desiderata such as envy minimization or welfare maximization.
original_abstract: One-sided matching problems with ordinal preferences, such as hostel room allocation, are commonly solved using the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) mechanism, which guarantees Pareto-optimal (PO) outcomes. However, TTC does not yield a unique solution: multiple PO allocations may exist, and many distinct initial endowments can converge to the same outcome. Focusing on a single TTC result obscures the structure of the Pareto-efficient frontier and limits principled secondary optimization over fairness or welfare objectives. Therefore, the goal is to find the entire set of PO allocations for a given preference profile. We prove the soundness and completeness of the proposed algorithm and analyze its computational complexity. title: GraphLeap: Decoupling Graph Construction and Convolution for Vision GNN Acceleration on FPGA

title: Cross-Entropy Is Load-Bearing: A Pre-Registered Scope Test of the K-Way Energy Probe on Bidirectional Predictive Coding

original_abstract: Software Bills of Material (SBOMs) have emerged as an important technology for vulnerability management amid rising supply-chain attacks. title: Do LLM Decoders Listen Fairly? Benchmarking How Language Model Priors Shape Bias in Speech Recognition

original_abstract: As pretrained large language models replace task-specific decoders in speech recognition, a critical question arises: do their text-derived priors make recognition fairer or more biased across demographic groups? title: Optimizing High-Throughput Distributed Data Pipelines for Reproducible Deep Learning at Scale

original_abstract: Training massive-scale deep learning models on datasets spanning tens of terabytes presents critical challenges in hardware utilization and training reproducibility. Through systematic profiling, we demonstrate that network I/O and CPU-bound data transformations (e.g., PyArrow to NumPy) constrain GPU utilization to as low as 10-15%. To address this, we propose an optimized architecture that features push-down worker-level transformations coupled with local-disk caching via Fanout-Cache, minimizing redundant I/O and CPU overhead across training epochs. Furthermore, we eliminate race conditions in multi-worker shared queues by implementing dedicated round-robin ventilator and result queues, alongside modernized RNG handling, achieving strict deterministic data loading. Our optimizations yield a 6x speedup, reducing end-to-end training time from 22 hours to 3 hours, increasing GPU utilization to over 60%, and drastically reducing run-to-run variance, enabling robust, high-throughput, and reproducible large-scale model training.

title: Random Access Codes: Explicit Constructions, Optimality, and Classical-Quantum Gaps
generated_summary:

The authors formulate the construction of optimal RACs as geometric optimization problems: finding an average-optimal (L,k)-RAC corresponds to minimizing a directed Chamfer dissimilarity over subsets of binary strings, while finding a worst-case optimal RAC corresponds to minimizing a directed Hausdorff distance. These formulations are solved as mixed-integer linear programs for small parameter values.

The authors provide explicit constructions of optimal (L,L-1)-RACs and demonstrate that optimal (L,L-1)-QRACs can be derived from their classical counterparts. For QRACs, they employ gradient-based optimization over parameterized density operators and POVMs, along with tensor product constructions from smaller optimal QRACs.

The key finding is that while the gap between RACs and QRACs in average decoding success probability is relatively small, a substantial separation emerges in worst-case decoding success probability. For RACs, the worst-case performance falls markedly below the average, whereas QRACs maintain worst-case probabilities close to their averages. This gap persists for moderately small parameters but vanishes asymptotically as L grows.

These results suggest that the primary quantum advantage in random access coding manifests in the worst-case regime rather than the average case, providing new insight into the nature of classical-quantum separations in information compression tasks.
original_abstract: A random access code (RAC) encodes an $L$-bit string into a $k$-bit $(L>k)$ message from which any designated source bit can be recovered with high probability. Its quantum counterpart, a quantum random access code (QRAC), replaces the $k$-bit message with $k$ qubits. While upper bounds on the decoding success probability have long been studied in both classical and quantum settings, explicit constructions of optimal codes are known only in special cases, even for classical RACs. In this paper, we develop a constructive framework for classical $(L,k)$-RACs under both average- and worst-case criteria. We show that optimal code design reduces to selecting $2^k$ points in $\{0,1\}^L$ and $[0,1]^L$ for the average- and worst-case criteria, respectively, so as to minimize a distance-like objective. This characterization yields explicit constructions for general $(L,k)$. For $k=L-1$, we further obtain closed-form optimal encoders and decoders for both criteria, and show that the resulting classical $(L,L-1)$-RACs attain the corresponding proved upper bounds. We also show that these optimal classical codes induce $(L,L-1)$-QRACs that attain a conjectured upper bound on the decoding success probability. Numerical optimization suggests little difference between RACs and QRACs in the average-case setting, but a potentially large classical-quantum gap in the worst-case nonasymptotic regime.

title: Downlink Channel Matrix Estimation from PMI-Only Feedback in FDD Systems: Maximum Likelihood and Sharp Excess Risk Bound

original_abstract: We study downlink channel estimation in a frequency-division duplex (FDD) massive MIMO system from PMI-only feedback under a 5G NR-type limited-feedback architecture. In this architecture, the user selects a preferred codeword from a shared codebook based on the reduced-dimensional channel and only reports its index (known as the precoding matrix indicator, PMI) back to the base station. Therefore, the channel must be estimated from these highly quantized, nonlinear PMI observations. Based on a probabilistic perturbation model, a constrained maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) is proposed for this estimation problem, whose objective can also be interpreted as a relaxation of the hard empirical decision error. The Cramér--Rao bound is derived for the complex-valued model, with the global phase ambiguity handled via gauge-fixing. For the real-valued setting, a global excess-risk bound of order $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ is established, which is then refined to a sharp local rate of order $O(1/T)$ under suitable identifiability conditions. Numerical results show that the MLE asymptotically attains the Cramér--Rao bound and outperforms several baseline methods on both synthetic data and realistic FDD channels.

title: CLT-Optimal Parameter Error Bounds for Linear System Identification

For Frobenius norm analysis, the inner-product structure makes this tractable, while operator norm analysis requires non-commutative Burkholder inequalities. original_abstract: There has been remarkable progress over the past decade in establishing finite-sample, non-asymptotic bounds on recovering unknown system parameters from observed system behavior. Surprisingly, however, we show that the current state-of-the-art bounds do not accurately capture the statistical complexity of system identification, even in the most fundamental setting of estimating a discrete-time linear dynamical system (LDS) via ordinary least-squares regression (OLS). Informed by this discrepancy, we then sharpen the OLS parameter error bounds via a novel second-order decomposition of the parameter error, where crucially the lower-order term is a matrix-valued martingale that we show correctly captures the CLT scaling. From our analysis we obtain finite-sample bounds for both (i) stable systems and (ii) the many-trajectories setting that match the instance-specific optimal rates up to constant factors in Frobenius norm, and polylogarithmic state-dimension factors in spectral norm.

title: Listen and Chant Before You Read: The Ladder of Beauty in LM Pre-Training

original_abstract: We show that pre-training a Transformer on music before language significantly accelerates language acquisition. Using piano performances (MAESTRO dataset), a developmental pipeline -- music $\to$ poetry $\to$ prose -- yields a $17.5\%$ perplexity improvement over random initialization ($p < 0.001$, 5 seeds), with music and poetry improving orthogonal model components (internal computation and embeddings, respectively). Convergence tests confirm that this is not a transient head start: at $d\!=\!64$, multi-seed validation (5 seeds) shows a persistent 5.5\% gap at plateau ($p = 0.017$), with the pipeline converging faster and to a lower loss in every run. Real music matches the transfer ceiling of synthetic patterns with one-third the data, and scaling experiments reveal that optimal pre-training data volume shifts with model capacity ($-3\% \to +3\% \to +6\%$ advantage of larger datasets from $d\!=\!16$ to $d\!=\!64$). Across the scales we study ($d\!\in\!\{16,32,64\}$, up to ${\sim}400$K parameters), these results suggest a capacity-dependent data curation principle and indicate that structured human creative outputs can provide an efficient pre-training substrate for small language models; stronger conclusions at modern pre-training scale will require substantially larger experiments.

title: Enhancing Online Recruitment with Category-Aware MoE and LLM-based Data Augmentation

original_abstract: Person-Job Fit (PJF) is a critical component for online recruitment. Existing approaches face several challenges, particularly in handling low-quality job descriptions and similar candidate-job pairs, which impair model performance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a large language model (LLM) based method with two novel techniques: (1) LLM-based data augmentation, which polishes and rewrites low-quality job descriptions by leveraging chain-of-thought (COT) prompts, and (2) category-aware Mixture of Experts (MoE) that assists in identifying similar candidate-job pairs. This MoE module incorporates category embeddings to dynamically assign weights to the experts and learns more distinguishable patterns for similar candidate-job pairs. We perform offline evaluations and online A/B tests on our recruitment platform. Our method relatively surpasses existing methods by 2.40% in AUC and 7.46% in GAUC, and boosts click-through conversion rate (CTCVR) by 19.4% in online tests, saving millions of CNY in external headhunting expenses.

title: ECCFROG522PP: An Enhanced 522 bit Weierstrass Elliptic Curve

original_abstract: This paper presents ECCFROG522PP, a 522-bit prime-field elliptic curve in short Weierstrass form, designed with a focus on deterministic generation and public reproducibility. The central design principle is that all critical parameters are derived from a fixed public seed through a transparent and verifiable procedure. While many deployed systems rely on NIST P-256 and secp256k1, which target approximately 128-bit classical security, higher security applications typically consider curves such as NIST P-521, Curve448, and Brainpool P512. ECCFROG522PP is intended for the same general classical security range as P-521, with emphasis on transparency, auditability, and reproducibility rather than performance optimization. The curve parameters are generated through a BLAKE3-based deterministic pipeline with publicly specified indices. The resulting construction has prime order, cofactor one, and a deterministically derived base point of full order. The quadratic twist has a large proven prime factor, and the construction includes a documented lower bound on the embedding degree together with standard sanity checks against low embedding degree reductions and basic CM discriminant anomalies. The full generation and validation procedure can be reproduced end to end from public artifacts and reference scripts, enabling independent verification of all parameters and checks.

title: Calibeating Prediction-Powered Inference
generated_summary:
This paper introduces calibrated prediction-powered inference (PPI), a framework for semisupervised mean estimation that applies post-hoc calibration to black-box prediction scores before using them for debiased estimation. The key insight is that prediction scores used in standard PPI and AIPW estimators may rank observations well but be poorly scaled numerically, leaving substantial efficiency gains unrealized due to inflated residual variance.

The authors propose calibrating prediction scores using standard methods—particularly linear calibration and isotonic regression—before incorporating them into semisupervised estimators. They develop asymptotic theory showing that linearly calibrated PPI is asymptotically equivalent to PPI++, while isotonic-calibrated PPI achieves the smallest asymptotic variance among estimators based on monotone transformations of the original score. The isotonic-calibrated score additionally satisfies a "calibeating" property, meaning it cannot be improved by further post-processing for either prediction or functional estimation.

Experiments on synthetic data, reproduced PPI benchmarks, and an LLM evaluation benchmark demonstrate that calibration transforms poorly scaled proxy scores into practically useful regression adjustments. In LLM evaluation, raw PPI and AIPW can perform dramatically worse than labeled-only estimation, while linearly calibrated PPI consistently improves efficiency, achieving 3–10% label savings. The authors position calibration not as a marginal refinement but as an essential step for safely leveraging cheap prediction scores in semisupervised inference.
original_abstract: We study semisupervised mean estimation with a small labeled sample, a large unlabeled sample, and a black-box prediction model whose output may be miscalibrated. A standard approach in this setting is augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) [Robins et al., 1994], which protects against prediction-model misspecification but can be inefficient when the prediction score is poorly aligned with the outcome scale. We introduce Calibrated Prediction-Powered Inference, which post-hoc calibrates the prediction score on the labeled sample before using it for semisupervised estimation. This simple step requires no retraining and can improve the original score both as a predictor of the outcome and as a regression adjustment for semisupervised inference. We study both linear and isotonic calibration. For isotonic calibration, we establish first-order optimality guarantees: isotonic post-processing can improve predictive accuracy and estimator efficiency relative to the original score and simpler post-processing rules, while no further post-processing of the fitted isotonic score yields additional first-order gains. For linear calibration, we show first-order equivalence to PPI++. We also clarify the relationship among existing estimators, showing that the original PPI estimator is a special case of AIPW and can be inefficient when the prediction model is accurate, while PPI++ is AIPW with empirical efficiency maximization [Rubin et al., 2008]. In simulations and real-data experiments, our calibrated estimators often outperform PPI and are competitive with, or outperform, AIPW and PPI++. We provide an accompanying Python package, ppi_aipw, at https://larsvanderlaan.github.io/ppi-aipw/.

title: Robustness Analysis of POMDP Policies to Observation Perturbations
