This paper introduces the **POMDP Robustness Problem**, which seeks the maximum admissible deviation in a POMDP's observation model that guarantees a policy's value remains above a specified threshold. Unlike robust policy synthesis, which designs policies for known uncertainty sets, this work quantifies the observation uncertainty a given policy can tolerate—applicable to any policy including heuristic, MDP, or hand-specified policies.

The authors formulate the problem as a bi-level optimization and analyze two variants: a *sticky* variant where observation deviations are fixed across timesteps, and a *non-sticky* variant where deviations may depend on history. A key theoretical insight is that worst-case policy value is monotonic in the deviation size, enabling efficient bisection search. For the non-sticky variant, the authors prove that finite-state controller nodes suffice to represent history-dependent deviations, reducing the problem to polynomial-time interval Markov chain evaluation. They present the Robust Interval Search algorithm with convergence and soundness guarantees.

Empirical results demonstrate scalability to POMDPs with tens of thousands of states and Markov chain representations with millions of states. Case studies in rover navigation, cancer diagnosis, and manufacturing quality control illustrate practical applications, showing how the framework quantifies tolerable sensor degradation and informs policy selection based on robustness properties. This work provides practitioners with formal tools for validating policy robustness before real-world deployment.
original_abstract: Policies for Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) are often designed using a nominal system model. In practice, this model can deviate from the true system during deployment due to factors such as calibration drift or sensor degradation, leading to unexpected performance degradation. This work studies policy robustness against deviations in the POMDP observation model. We introduce the Policy Observation Robustness Problem: to determine the maximum tolerable deviation in a POMDP's observation model that guarantees the policy's value remains above a specified threshold. We analyze two variants: the sticky variant, where deviations are dependent on state and actions, and the non-sticky variant, where they can be history-dependent. We show that the Policy Observation Robustness Problem can be formulated as a bi-level optimization problem in which the inner optimization is monotonic in the size of the observation deviation. This enables efficient solutions using root-finding algorithms in the outer optimization. For the non-sticky variant, we show that when policies are represented with finite-state controllers (FSCs) it is sufficient to consider observations which depend on nodes in the FSC rather than full histories. We present Robust Interval Search, an algorithm with soundness and convergence guarantees, for both the sticky and non-sticky variants. We show this algorithm has polynomial time complexity in the non-sticky variant and at most exponential time complexity in the sticky variant. We provide experimental results validating and demonstrating the scalability of implementations of Robust Interval Search to POMDP problems with tens of thousands of states. We also provide case studies from robotics and operations research which demonstrate the practical utility of the problem and algorithms.

title: When Agents Look the Same: Quantifying Distillation-Induced Similarity in Tool-Use Behaviors
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a systematic framework for quantifying distillation-induced behavioral similarity among LLM-based tool-use agents, addressing the observation that many independently developed models exhibit suspiciously similar behaviors. The authors propose two complementary metrics: Response Pattern Similarity (RPS), which measures verbal similarity by segmenting trajectories into canonical interaction stages and scoring style, structure, and alignment dimensions; and Action Graph Similarity (AGS), which analyzes tool invocation patterns through three sub-metrics capturing optional tool agreement, sequential execution habits, and dependency patterns. Crucially, the framework distinguishes mandatory behaviors dictated by task requirements from non-mandatory behaviors reflecting autonomous model preferences.

Evaluating 18 models from 8 providers against Claude Sonnet 4.5 as a reference, the authors find that Anthropic models show strong internal consistency, as expected. More notably, Kimi-K2 achieves the highest similarity among non-Anthropic models on both metrics (AGS 82.7%, RPS 3.65), exceeding even some within-family Anthropic pairs on sub-metrics like optional tool agreement and dependency patterns. A controlled distillation experiment validates that AGS produces directional signals, increasing toward the teacher model while decreasing toward a non-teacher control, unlike baseline metrics that lack this discriminative ability.

The work provides essential tools for ecosystem transparency, enabling researchers to assess whether model diversity is genuine or reflects convergent distillation from dominant teachers, with implications for robustness and independent verification in AI systems.
original_abstract: Model distillation is a primary driver behind the rapid progress of LLM agents, yet it often leads to behavioral homogenization. Many emerging agents share nearly identical reasoning steps and failure modes, suggesting they may be distilled echoes of a few dominant teachers. Existing metrics, however, fail to distinguish mandatory behaviors required for task success from non-mandatory patterns that reflect a model's autonomous preferences. We propose two complementary metrics to isolate non-mandatory behavioral patterns: \textbf{Response Pattern Similarity (RPS)} for verbal alignment and \textbf{Action Graph Similarity (AGS)} for tool-use habits modeled as directed graphs. Evaluating 18 models from 8 providers on $τ$-Bench and $τ^2$-Bench against Claude Sonnet 4.5 (thinking), we find that within-family model pairs score 5.9 pp higher in AGS than cross-family pairs, and that Kimi-K2 (thinking) reaches 82.6\% $S_{\text{node}}$ and 94.7\% $S_{\text{dep}}$, exceeding Anthropic's own Opus 4.1. A controlled distillation experiment further confirms that AGS distinguishes teacher-specific convergence from general improvement. RPS and AGS capture distinct behavioral dimensions (Pearson $r$ = 0.491), providing complementary diagnostic signals for behavioral convergence in the agent ecosystem. Our code is available at https://github.com/Syuchin/AgentEcho.

title: Hyperloop Transformers
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Hyperloop Transformer, a parameter-efficient language model architecture that combines looped Transformers with hyper-connections to outperform standard Transformers while using approximately half the parameters. The key insight is that while looped Transformers (which share parameters across depth by repeating a middle block) are parameter-efficient, they typically underperform depth-matched baselines. The authors address this by incorporating hyper-connections—which expand the residual stream into multiple parallel streams—applied only at the loop level rather than at every layer, thereby incurring minimal additional parameters and compute overhead.

The architecture organizes layers into begin, middle, and end blocks, looping only the middle block three times, and uses a simple data-dependent diagonal transition matrix for the parallel residual streams. Experiments at 240M, 1B, and 2B parameter scales on FineWeb-Edu demonstrate that Hyperloop Transformers achieve lower perplexity than depth-matched vanilla Transformers despite using 50% fewer parameters, with only 150-300K additional parameters over vanilla looped models. These gains persist under INT4 post-training quantization and in overtrained settings. Analysis reveals that hyper-connections allow representations across loop iterations to diverge more flexibly, and logit lens analysis shows stronger alignment with vocabulary distributions, suggesting potential for early-exit inference strategies.

The work positions Hyperloop Transformers as particularly attractive for memory-constrained edge deployments where model size is a primary bottleneck.
original_abstract: LLM architecture research generally aims to maximize model quality subject to fixed compute/latency budgets. However, many applications of interest such as edge and on-device deployment are further constrained by the model's memory footprint, thus motivating parameter-efficient architectures for language modeling. This paper describes a simple architecture that improves the parameter-efficiency of LLMs. Our architecture makes use of looped Transformers as a core primitive, which reuse Transformer layers across depth and are thus more parameter-efficient than ordinary (depth-matched) Transformers. We organize the looped Transformer into three blocks--begin, middle, and end blocks--where each block itself consists of multiple Transformer layers, and only the middle block is applied recurrently across depth. We augment the looped middle block with hyper-connections (Xie et al., 2026), which expand the residual stream into matrix-valued residual streams. Hyper-connections are applied only after each loop, and therefore add minimal new parameters and compute cost. Across various model scales, we find that our Hyper-Connected Looped Transformer (Hyperloop Transformer) is able to outperform depth-matched Transformer and mHC Transformer baselines despite using approximately 50% fewer parameters. The outperformance persists through post-training weight quantization, thus positioning Hyperloop Transformers as an attractive architecture for memory-efficient language modeling.

title: Planning Beyond Text: Graph-based Reasoning for Complex Narrative Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces PLOTTER, a framework that transforms complex narrative generation from a sequential text planning problem into a dynamic graph generation and refinement problem. The core contribution is the insight that planning narratives on explicit graph structures—rather than directly on text—enables more effective long-range causal reasoning for story generation.

PLOTTER operates in three stages. First, it constructs two interacting graph structures from a premise: an Event Graph capturing causal plot dependencies and a Character Graph modeling inter-character relationships. Second, it applies an iterative Evaluate-Plan-Revise cycle through a multi-agent critique module, where specialized agents (Theme, Character, and Plot critics) diagnose structural issues such as causal discontinuities and unmotivated character transitions. A Constrained Graph Editor then executes atomic graph operations to repair these issues while enforcing deterministic constraints ensuring causal acyclicity and narrative completeness. Third, the optimized graphs are serialized and used to condition a state-aware generator that produces the final script.

Experiments across 50 diverse premises using GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-R1, and Qwen3 backbones demonstrate that PLOTTER consistently outperforms strong baselines (Dramatron, DOC, LLM Plan-and-Write) in narrative coherence, characterization, thematic expression, and dramatic engagement. Human evaluation corroborates these findings with strong machine-human agreement. Ablation studies reveal a significant synergy effect among the critique agents, where joint optimization yields gains substantially exceeding the sum of individual module contributions, underscoring the importance of structural graph-based reasoning for complex narrative generation.
original_abstract: While LLMs demonstrate remarkable fluency in narrative generation, existing methods struggle to maintain global narrative coherence, contextual logical consistency, and smooth character development, often producing monotonous scripts with structural fractures. To this end, we introduce PLOTTER, a framework that performs narrative planning on structural graph representations instead of the direct sequential text representations used in existing work. Specifically, PLOTTER executes the Evaluate-Plan-Revise cycle on the event graph and character graph. By diagnosing and repairing issues of the graph topology under rigorous logical constraints, the model optimizes the causality and narrative skeleton before complete context generation. Experiments demonstrate that PLOTTER significantly outperforms representative baselines across diverse narrative scenarios. These findings verify that planning narratives on structural graph representations-rather than directly on text-is crucial to enhance the long context reasoning of LLMs in complex narrative generation.

title: Improving Performance in Classification Tasks with LCEN and the Weighted Focal Differentiable MCC Loss
generated_summary:
This paper extends the LASSO-Clip-EN (LCEN) algorithm, originally developed for regression tasks, to classification problems by replacing linear regression components with logistic regression counterparts and introducing a hyperparameter for harmonizing feature sets across classes in multiclass settings. The study also systematically evaluates the weighted focal differentiable MCC (diffMCC) loss function for training neural networks across diverse classification tasks beyond its original biological applications.

The modified LCEN algorithm and diffMCC-trained MLPs are tested on four real datasets spanning binary and multiclass classification in physical, biological, and social sciences, compared against multiple baselines including logistic regression variants, random forests, gradient-boosted trees, SVMs, and standard MLPs. Performance is assessed using macro F₁ scores and Matthews correlation coefficients with 5-fold cross-validation across multiple seeds.

LCEN demonstrates consistently strong performance, achieving metrics only 7.3% lower in macro F₁ and 15.0% lower in MCC than the best model per dataset, while maintaining interpretability and sparsity by eliminating an average of 56% of input features. When other models are retrained using only LCEN-selected features, average performance improves in three of four datasets. MLPs trained with the diffMCC loss consistently outperform those trained with weighted cross-entropy, achieving 4.9% higher macro F₁ scores and 8.5% higher MCCs on average.

These findings establish LCEN as an effective interpretable classification and feature selection method and demonstrate the broad applicability of the diffMCC loss function beyond biological domains.
original_abstract: The LASSO-Clip-EN (LCEN) algorithm was previously introduced for nonlinear, interpretable feature selection and machine learning. However, its design and use was limited to regression tasks. In this work, we create a modified version of the LCEN algorithm that is suitable for classification tasks and maintains its desirable properties, such as interpretability. This modified LCEN algorithm is evaluated on four widely used binary and multiclass classification datasets. In these experiments, LCEN is compared against 10 other model types and consistently reaches high test-set macro F$_1$ score and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) metrics, higher than that of the majority of investigated models. LCEN models for classification remain sparse, eliminating an average of 56% of all input features in the experiments performed. Furthermore, LCEN-selected features are used to retrain all models using the same data, leading to statistically significant performance improvements in three of the experiments and insignificant differences in the fourth when compared to using all features or other feature selection methods. Simultaneously, the weighted focal differentiable MCC (diffMCC) loss function is evaluated on the same datasets. Models trained with the diffMCC loss function are always the best-performing methods in these experiments, and reach test-set macro F$_1$ scores that are, on average, 4.9% higher and MCCs that are 8.5% higher than those obtained by models trained with the weighted cross-entropy loss. These results highlight the performance of LCEN as a feature selection and machine learning algorithm also for classification tasks, and how the diffMCC loss function can train very accurate models, surpassing the weighted cross-entropy loss in the tasks investigated.

title: CAP: Controllable Alignment Prompting for Unlearning in LLMs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Controllable Alignment Prompting (CAP), a novel prompt-driven framework for machine unlearning in large language models that operates without modifying the base model's parameters. The key contribution is framing unlearning as an inference-time control problem, where a lightweight small language model (SLM) generates input-conditioned prefix prompts that steer a frozen LLM to selectively suppress targeted knowledge while preserving general capabilities.

The methodology employs a two-stage pipeline. In the optimization stage, the SLM serves as a policy network trained via a novel Beam PPO algorithm, which maintains multiple anchor policies to enhance exploration and avoid premature convergence. The SLM generates dual prompt types—forgetting and retaining prompts—optimized through a diversity-promoting contrastive objective based on a variational information bottleneck. This objective simultaneously maximizes information suppression for forget targets and information preservation for retained knowledge. During inference, the trained SLM generates candidate prompts, refined through a self-check mechanism.

Experiments across multiple LLMs (LLaMA, GPT-4.1, Qwen, Zephyr) on the RWKU and WMDP benchmarks demonstrate that CAP significantly outperforms baselines in both forgetting effectiveness and utility retention. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of the information bottleneck objective and Beam PPO, while the framework generalizes across different SLM architectures and LLM scales.

CAP's significance lies in its reversibility, model-agnostic nature, and applicability to closed-source models, making it practically viable for regulatory compliance scenarios where parameter access is unavailable and full retraining is infeasible.
original_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) trained on unfiltered corpora inherently risk retaining sensitive information, necessitating selective knowledge unlearning for regulatory compliance and ethical safety. However, existing parameter-modifying methods face fundamental limitations: high computational costs, uncontrollable forgetting boundaries, and strict dependency on model weight access. These constraints render them impractical for closed-source models, yet current non-invasive alternatives remain unsystematic and reliant on empirical experience. To address these challenges, we propose the Controllable Alignment Prompting for Unlearning (CAP) framework, an end-to-end prompt-driven unlearning paradigm. CAP decouples unlearning into a learnable prompt optimization process via reinforcement learning, where a prompt generator collaborates with the LLM to suppress target knowledge while preserving general capabilities selectively. This approach enables reversible knowledge restoration through prompt revocation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CAP achieves precise, controllable unlearning without updating model parameters, establishing a dynamic alignment mechanism that overcomes the transferability limitations of prior methods.

title: Reasoning About Traversability: Language-Guided Off-Road 3D Trajectory Planning
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of off-road trajectory planning by proposing a language-grounded framework that aligns natural language supervision with vehicle motion and terrain geometry. The authors identify that existing language annotations for off-road driving datasets are too generic and poorly correlated with actual driving actions, limiting their utility for trajectory planning.

The methodology centers on three contributions. First, a language annotation refinement pipeline transforms scene-level descriptions into action-aligned, terrain-aware annotations by jointly inspecting front-view images, trajectory plots, and elevation profiles, with scene-based normalization to contextualize directional and slope-related expressions. Second, a vision-language model built on Qwen3-VL-2B with LoRA adaptation autoregressively generates structured scene descriptions followed by 3D trajectory waypoints in a "reasoning-before-acting" paradigm. Third, Odds Ratio Preference Optimization (ORPO) with geometry-aware hard negatives—trajectories that match horizontally but diverge vertically—further enforces terrain elevation consistency. The authors also introduce novel off-road evaluation metrics assessing traversability compliance and elevation consistency, arguing that conventional planar metrics are insufficient.

Experiments on the ORAD-3D benchmark demonstrate that refined language supervision substantially reduces L2 displacement errors and failure rates compared to raw annotations and state-of-the-art open VLMs. Terrain-aware ORPO further improves traversability compliance and elevation consistency. These results validate that carefully constructed language-action alignment and terrain-aware optimization are essential for reliable off-road autonomous planning in unstructured environments.
original_abstract: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable high-level semantic reasoning for end-to-end autonomous driving, particularly in unstructured environments, existing off-road datasets suffer from language annotations that are weakly aligned with vehicle actions and terrain geometry. To address this misalignment, we propose a language refinement framework that restructures annotations into action-aligned pairs, enabling a VLM to generate refined scene descriptions and 3D future trajectories directly from a single image. To further encourage terrain-aware planning, we introduce a preference optimization strategy that constructs geometry-aware hard negatives and explicitly penalizes trajectories inconsistent with local elevation profiles. Furthermore, we propose off-road-specific metrics to quantify traversability compliance and elevation consistency, addressing the limitations of conventional on-road evaluation. Experiments on the ORAD-3D benchmark demonstrate that our approach reduces average trajectory error from 1.01m to 0.97m, improves traversability compliance from 0.621 to 0.644, and decreases elevation inconsistency from 0.428 to 0.322, highlighting the efficacy of action-aligned supervision and terrain-aware optimization for robust off-road driving.

title: An Efficient Wireless iBCI Headstage with Adaptive ADC Sample Rate
generated_summary:
This paper presents a wireless implantable brain-computer interface (iBCI) headstage that reduces data throughput and power consumption by adapting ADC sampling rates and spike detection thresholds on a per-electrode basis, shifting neural data compression from the conventional post-digitization digital domain directly to the physical acquisition layer.

The framework operates through a server-driven, hardware-software co-design approach. During offline calibration, spike templates extracted from each electrode are sent to a server, where a lightweight multilayer perceptron predictor estimates spike detection errors for candidate sampling rate and threshold configurations. The server then selects the minimum sampling rate per electrode that satisfies a user-defined error budget. During online streaming, these optimized configurations are wirelessly delivered to the headstage, where an FPGA-based scheduler controls ADC sampling using simple counter logic, ensuring unnecessary samples are never digitized.

Evaluated across macaque, rat, and human neural datasets with an FPGA prototype, the system achieves 24–40 mW power savings and 2.8–3.2× reduction in FPGA resource utilization compared to conventional digital compression baselines (DCT and compressive sensing), while maintaining comparable compression ratios and approximately 2% lower spike detection error. Downstream motor and visual decoding tasks demonstrate preserved or improved accuracy.

This work represents a significant advance toward practical, fully wireless iBCI systems by eliminating the energy waste of the "digitize-then-compress" paradigm, making it particularly suitable for large-scale, closed-loop neural interfaces intended for long-term clinical use.
original_abstract: Implantable Brain-Computer Interfaces (iBCIs) are increasingly pivotal in clinical and daily applications. However, wireless iBCIs face severe constraints in power consumption and data throughput. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose a wireless iBCI headstage featuring adaptive ADC sampling and spike detection. Distinguishing our design from traditional application-layer compression, we employ a server-driven architecture that achieves source-level efficiency. Specifically, the server learns an optimal, electrode-specific sample rate vector to dynamically reconfigure the ADC hardware. This strategy reduces data volume directly at the acquisition layer (ADC and amplifier) rather than relying on computationally intensive post-digitization processing. Extensive experiments across diverse subjects and arrays demonstrate a power reduction of up to 40 mW and a 3.2$\times$ decrease in FPGA resource utilization, all while maintaining or exceeding decoding accuracy in both motor and visual tasks. This design offers a highly practical solution for long-term in-vivo recording.Our prototype is open-sourced in: https://github.com/liuhongyao99cs/32-Channel-Wireless-BCI-Headstage.

title: CorridorVLA: Explicit Spatial Constraints for Generative Action Heads via Sparse Anchors
generated_summary:
CorridorVLA introduces a method for improving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by predicting sparse future spatial anchors as text-style physical quantities and using them to impose explicit tolerance-region constraints on action generation. Unlike prior approaches that encode spatial guidance through image-based or latent visual intermediates, CorridorVLA expresses spatial cues as simple end-effector position increments that directly constrain the generative action head at the objective level.

The method works by appending a small number of learnable anchor slots to the vision-language backbone, which predict sparse end-effector displacement increments at key timesteps within an action chunk. These anchors define a "corridor"—a tolerance band around the predicted trajectory—that penalizes generated actions deviating beyond this region while permitting minor execution noise. The corridor regularizer complements a flow-matching velocity regression objective, incorporating noise-aware weighting and in-corridor consistency terms that together function like a smooth-L1 objective providing fast correction outside the corridor and gradual refinement within.

Evaluated on the LIBERO benchmark using SmolVLA as a baseline, CorridorVLA achieves a 4.45% success rate improvement with negligible computational overhead, and a 12.4% gain on the more challenging LIBERO-Plus benchmark. Cross-backbone validation on GR00T yields a 7.98% improvement. These results demonstrate that explicit, action-aligned spatial constraints represent a viable and complementary design axis for VLA policies, offering interpretable spatial guidance without requiring substantial architectural modifications.
original_abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models often use intermediate representations to connect multimodal inputs with continuous control, yet spatial guidance is often injected implicitly through latent features. We propose $CorridorVLA$, which predicts sparse spatial anchors as incremental physical changes (e.g., $Δ$-positions) and uses them to impose an explicit tolerance region in the training objective for action generation. The anchors define a corridor that guides a flow-matching action head: trajectories whose implied spatial evolution falls outside it receive corrective gradients, while minor deviations from contacts and execution noise are permitted. On the more challenging LIBERO-Plus benchmark, CorridorVLA yields consistent gains across both SmolVLA and GR00T, improving success rate by $3.4\%$--$12.4\%$ over the corresponding baselines; notably, our GR00T-Corr variant reaches a success rate of $83.21\%$. These results indicate that action-aligned physical cues can provide direct and interpretable constraints for generative action policies, complementing spatial guidance encoded in visual or latent forms. Code is available at https://github.com/corridorVLA.

title: Unlocking the Power of Large Language Models for Multi-table Entity Matching
generated_summary:
This paper introduces LLM4MEM, a novel framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to address multi-table entity matching (MEM), the task of identifying equivalent entities across more than two heterogeneous data sources simultaneously. Unlike prior work that primarily focuses on dual-table matching, LLM4MEM tackles challenges of semantic inconsistency, computational scalability, and noise in multi-source settings.

The framework comprises three modules. First, the Multi-style Prompt-enhanced LLM Attribute Coordination module uses LLMs to normalize and standardize entity attributes (e.g., numerical formats, units) across heterogeneous schemas, eliminating the need for manual alignment rules. Second, the Transitive Consensus Embedding Matching module generates entity embeddings using Sentence-BERT, performs approximate nearest neighbor search via HNSW indexing, and constructs equivalence classes through transitive closures to produce pre-matched entity tuples. Third, a Density-aware Pruning module refines results by classifying entities as core, reachable, or noise based on spatial density constraints, removing semantically deviant matches.

Experiments across six benchmark datasets from diverse domains demonstrate that LLM4MEM achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving F1 scores by 5.1% over existing methods while maintaining linear complexity. Ablation studies confirm that the attribute coordination module contributes most significantly, with its removal causing a 15.15% F1 drop. The framework's unsupervised, schema-agnostic design enhances its practical applicability for real-world multi-source data integration scenarios.
original_abstract: Multi-table entity matching (MEM) addresses the limitations of dual-table approaches by enabling simultaneous identification of equivalent entities across multiple data sources without unique identifiers. However, existing methods relying on pre-trained language models struggle to handle semantic inconsistencies caused by numerical attribute variations. Inspired by the powerful language understanding capabilities of large language models (LLMs), we propose a novel LLM-based framework for multi-table entity matching, termed LLM4MEM. Specifically, we first propose a multi-style prompt-enhanced LLM attribute coordination module to address semantic inconsistencies. Then, to alleviate the matching efficiency problem caused by the surge in the number of entities brought by multiple data sources, we develop a transitive consensus embedding matching module to tackle entity embedding and pre-matching issues. Finally, to address the issue of noisy entities during the matching process, we introduce a density-aware pruning module to optimize the quality of multi-table entity matching. We conducted extensive experiments on 6 MEM datasets, and the results show that our model improves by an average of 5.1% in F1 compared with the baseline model. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ymeki/LLM4MEM.

title: Learning Dynamic Representations and Policies from Multimodal Clinical Time-Series with Informative Missingness
generated_summary:
This paper introduces OPL-MT-MNAR, a framework for learning dynamic patient representations from multimodal electronic health records that explicitly leverages informative missingness—the principle that observation patterns themselves encode clinically meaningful information about patient acuity. The key insight is that missing data in clinical settings is not random: sicker patients receive more frequent laboratory tests, vital sign monitoring, and clinical documentation, and these patterns differ systematically across data modalities.

The methodology operates in two stages. The first stage learns a latent patient state through a multimodal encoder that incorporates missingness-aware features (time since last observation, observation counts, documentation density) for both structured data and clinical text, combined with Bayesian filtering to capture treatment-conditioned dynamics via variational inference. The second stage uses the learned representation for joint offline policy optimization via expectile regression and clinical outcome prediction.

Evaluated on three ICU datasets (MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU) for sepsis management, OPL-MT-MNAR achieves FQE scores of 0.679, 0.634, and 0.604 respectively, substantially exceeding clinician behavior (0.528, 0.521, 0.534) and outperforming recent baselines. The framework also achieves 0.886 AUROC for post-72-hour mortality prediction on MIMIC-III. Notably, the largest improvements appear in the highest-acuity subgroups where observation processes are most informative.

This work demonstrates that treating clinical observation patterns as informative signals rather than nuisance artifacts meaningfully improves both representation quality and downstream clinical decision support.
original_abstract: Multimodal clinical records contain structured measurements and clinical notes recorded over time, offering rich temporal information about the evolution of patient health. Yet these observations are sparse, and whether they are recorded depends on the patient's latent condition. Observation patterns also differ across modalities, as structured measurements and clinical notes arise under distinct recording processes. While prior work has developed methods that accommodate missingness in clinical time series, how to extract and use the information carried by the observation process itself remains underexplored. We therefore propose a patient representation learning framework for multimodal clinical time series that explicitly leverages informative missingness. The framework combines (1) a multimodal encoder that captures signals from structured and textual data together with their observation patterns, (2) a Bayesian filtering module that updates a latent patient state over time from observed multimodal signals, and (3) downstream modules for offline treatment policy learning and patient outcome prediction based on the learned patient state. We evaluate the framework on ICU sepsis cohorts from MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU. It improves both offline treatment policy learning and adverse outcome prediction, achieving FQE 0.679 versus 0.528 for clinician behavior and AUROC 0.886 for post-72-hour mortality prediction on MIMIC-III.

title: Assessing Emulator Design and Training for Modal Aerosol Microphysics Parameterizations in E3SMv2
generated_summary:
This study systematically investigates design decisions affecting the accuracy of machine learning emulators for aerosol microphysics parameterizations in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 2 (E3SMv2). The authors address a gap in understanding why prior emulator studies reported widely varying performance (R² from 0.48 to 0.99) by conducting controlled experiments that isolate the effects of architecture, training configuration, and data preprocessing.

The methodology employs feedforward neural networks with residual connections to emulate the one-timestep evolution of 20 aerosol and gas mixing ratios under cloud-free conditions. The authors systematically explore network depth (1–8 hidden layers) and width (32–512 neurons), using data from a boreal winter E3SMv2 simulation. A key methodological contribution is the application of power transformations to handle mixing ratios spanning many orders of magnitude, combined with z-score normalization.

Results demonstrate that a modest architecture (3 hidden layers, 256 neurons each) achieves R² values of approximately 0.99 across all 20 target variables. The study reveals that width matters more than depth beyond 2–3 layers, that proper training convergence requires sufficient epochs with appropriate optimizer settings, and that variable transformations are essential for balanced performance across value ranges.

These findings establish a reproducible baseline for aerosol microphysics emulation and provide generalizable strategies—including convergence monitoring, systematic complexity assessment, and nonlinear variable transformations—applicable to emulating other Earth system model parameterizations.
original_abstract: Toward the goal of using Scientific Machine Learning (SciML) emulators to improve the numerical representation of aerosol processes in global atmospheric models, we explore the emulation of aerosol microphysics processes under cloud-free conditions in the 4-mode Modal Aerosol Module (MAM4) within the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 2 (E3SMv2). To develop an in-depth understanding of the challenges and opportunities in applying SciML to aerosol processes, we begin with a simple feedforward neural network architecture that has been used in earlier studies, but we systematically examine key emulator design choices, including architecture complexity and variable normalization, while closely monitoring training convergence behavior. Our results show that optimization convergence, scaling strategy, and network complexity strongly influence emulation accuracy. When effective scaling is applied and convergence is achieved, the relatively simple architecture, used together with a moderate network size, can reproduce key features of the microphysics-induced aerosol concentration changes with promising accuracy. These findings provide practical clues for the next stages of emulator development; they also provide general insights that are likely applicable to the emulation of other aerosol processes, as well as other atmospheric physics involving multi-scale variability.

title: ReCAPA: Hierarchical Predictive Correction to Mitigate Cascading Failures
generated_summary:
ReCAPA (Hierarchical Predictive Correction to Mitigate Cascading Failures) addresses the critical problem of semantic drift and cascading errors in vision-language-action agents performing long-horizon tasks in embodied environments. The framework's main contribution is a Hierarchical Predictive Correction mechanism that organizes trajectory representations across three levels—action, subgoal, and trajectory—where lower levels predict higher-level representations and receive corrective signals when mismatches are detected. This is complemented by prompt-trajectory alignment through two modules: a Sinkhorn-based optimal transport module for global distributional alignment and a Score-field module providing step-wise corrective gradients toward task intent.

The authors also introduce two novel diagnostic metrics—Error Propagation Rate (EPR) and Propagation Attenuation Coefficient (PAC)—that quantify how errors compound across steps and how quickly their effects dissipate, filling an evaluation gap in long-horizon reasoning benchmarks.

ReCAPA demonstrates consistent improvements over strong baselines including proprietary LLMs, achieving gains of +5.65% on VisualAgentBench, +9% on MineDojo, and +7% on AI2-THOR in success rate. Crucially, it achieves the lowest EPR and highest PAC values, indicating superior error containment and faster recovery. Ablation studies confirm that all three hierarchical levels and both alignment modules contribute meaningfully, with trajectory-level representations serving as essential global semantic references that prevent locally plausible but globally misaligned actions from accumulating into irreversible failures.
original_abstract: Vision-Language-Action systems follow instructions to execute multi-step tasks in multimodal environments. Recent VLA approaches typically rely on post-hoc correction mechanisms or operate under fixed task decompositions and alignment schemes. However, once an intermediate step is mis-specified, local errors propagate through subsequent steps and eventually accumulate into cascading failures. To mitigate this compounding effect, we propose Predictive Alignment and Planning Architecture, a framework that uses prediction and contrast to adjust deviations across three levels: actions, subgoals, and trajectories. Semantic alignment is enforced at all levels using a Sinkhorn-based module and a Score-field module. The predictive correction and alignment jointly update the action generator during training, enabling it to adjust fine-grained steps to remain aligned with the overall intent. We further introduce two new metrics to quantify error propagation and recovery processes in tasks, capturing how mistakes spread and fade over long-horizon execution. original_abstract: Efficient inference for on-device Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging due to limited hardware resources and the high cost of the prefill stage, which processes the full input context to construct Key-Value (KV) caches. We present SparKV, an adaptive KV loading framework that combines cloud-based KV streaming with on-device computation. SparKV models the cost of individual KV chunks and decides whether each chunk should be streamed or computed locally, while overlapping the two execution paths to reduce latency. To handle fluctuations in wireless connectivity and edge resource availability, SparKV further refines offline-generated schedules at runtime to rebalance communication and computation costs. original_abstract: Large language model assistants are increasingly expected to retain and reason over information accumulated across many sessions. We introduce EngramaBench, a benchmark for long-term conversational memory built around five personas, one hundred multi-session conversations, and one hundred fifty queries spanning factual recall, cross-space integration, temporal reasoning, adversarial abstention, and emergent synthesis. We evaluate Engrama, a graph-structured memory system, against GPT-4o full-context prompting and Mem0, an open-source vector-retrieval memory system. All three use the same answering model (GPT-4o), isolating the effect of memory architecture. GPT-4o full-context achieves the highest composite score (0.6186), while Engrama scores 0.5367 globally but is the only system to score higher than full-context prompting on cross-space reasoning (0.6532 vs. 0.6291, n=30). title: UAU-Net: Uncertainty-aware Representation Learning and Evidential Classification for Facial Action Unit Detection

An asymmetric Beta loss is derived to address severe class imbalance by down-weighting easy negatives while emphasizing positive instances.

Experiments on BP4D and DISFA benchmarks demonstrate that UAU-Net achieves state-of-the-art average F1-scores of 66.8% and 66.6%, respectively. original_abstract: Facial action unit (AU) detection remains challenging because it involves heterogeneous, AU-specific uncertainties arising at both the representation and decision stages. Recent methods have improved discriminative feature learning, but they often treat the AU representations as deterministic, overlooking uncertainty caused by visual noise, subject-dependent appearance variations, and ambiguous inter-AU relationships, all of which can substantially degrade robustness. Meanwhile, conventional point-estimation classifiers often provide poorly calibrated confidence, producing overconfident predictions, especially under the severe label imbalance typical of AU datasets. We propose UAU-Net, an Uncertainty-aware AU detection framework that explicitly models uncertainty at both stages. At the representation stage, we introduce CV-AFE, a conditional VAE (CVAE)-based AU feature extraction module that learns probabilistic AU representations by jointly estimating feature means and variances across multiple spatio-temporal scales; conditioning on AU labels further enables CV-AFE to capture uncertainty associated with inter-AU dependencies. At the decision stage, we design AB-ENN, an Asymmetric Beta Evidential Neural Network for multi-label AU detection, which parameterizes predictive uncertainty with Beta distributions and mitigates overconfidence via an asymmetric loss tailored to highly imbalanced binary labels. Extensive experiments on BP4D and DISFA show that UAU-Net achieves strong AU detection performance, and further analyses indicate that modeling uncertainty in both representation learning and evidential prediction improves robustness and reliability.

title: Zero-Shot Detection of LLM-Generated Text via Implicit Reward Model

Given a text, the method computes the difference between log-probabilities assigned by an instruction-tuned model and its corresponding base model, where higher scores indicate greater likelihood of LLM generation. Evaluated on the DetectRL benchmark, which covers multiple domains, LLMs, and adversarial attack scenarios, IRM achieves strong performance. Using the Llama-3.2-1B family, it attains an average score of 91.77%, surpassing zero-shot baselines including Log-Likelihood (77.46%), Log-Rank (77.42%), and Binoculars (87.67%), and even outperforming the supervised reward-based method ReMoDetect (85.86%). The method demonstrates robust generalization across different domains, source LLMs, and attack types, though performance varies with text length due to reward score accumulation effects.

original_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks. However, their ability to generate human-like text has raised concerns about potential misuse. This underscores the need for reliable and effective methods to detect LLM-generated text. In this paper, we propose IRM, a novel zero-shot approach that leverages Implicit Reward Models for LLM-generated text detection. Such implicit reward models can be derived from publicly available instruction-tuned and base models. Previous reward-based method relies on preference construction and task-specific fine-tuning. In comparison, IRM requires neither preference collection nor additional training. We evaluate IRM on the DetectRL benchmark and demonstrate that IRM can achieve superior detection performance, outperforms existing zero-shot and supervised methods in LLM-generated text detection.

title: Sparse Forcing: Native Trainable Sparse Attention for Real-time Autoregressive Diffusion Video Generation
generated_summary:

Building on these observations, Sparse Forcing maintains a structured memory decomposition consisting of a persistent set of spatiotemporal anchor blocks preserving long-range semantic information and a local sliding window with block-sparse attention for recent context. The persistent memory is updated through coarse block-level scoring using compressed representations, while local computation is restricted to dynamically selected top-K blocks. The authors develop Persistent Block-Sparse Attention (PBSA) GPU kernels to efficiently support this irregular sparsity pattern during both training and inference.

Evaluated on the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model, Sparse Forcing achieves higher VBench scores than baselines across short (5-second) and long-horizon (20-second, 1-minute) generation while reducing peak KV cache memory by 42% and improving decoding throughput. The PBSA kernel delivers 1.16× to 11.11× speedups over FlashAttention-2. Ablation studies confirm that each component—persistent memory, block-sparse local attention, and training-time alignment—contributes meaningfully. The work demonstrates that well-designed sparsity can serve as both a computational optimization and a quality improvement by controlling error propagation pathways during autoregressive rollouts.
original_abstract: We introduce Sparse Forcing, a training-and-inference paradigm for autoregressive video diffusion models that improves long-horizon generation quality while reducing decoding latency. Sparse Forcing is motivated by an empirical observation in autoregressive diffusion rollouts: attention concentrates on a persistent subset of salient visual blocks, forming an implicit spatiotemporal memory in the KV cache, and exhibits a locally structured block-sparse pattern within sliding windows. Building on this observation, we propose a trainable native sparsity mechanism that learns to compress, preserve, and update these persistent blocks while restricting computation within each local window to a dynamically selected local neighborhood. To make the approach practical at scale for both training and inference, we further propose Persistent Block-Sparse Attention (PBSA), an efficient GPU kernel that accelerates sparse attention and memory updates for low-latency, memory-efficient decoding. Experiments show that Sparse Forcing improves the VBench score by +0.26 over Self-Forcing on 5-second text-to-video generation while delivering a 1.11-1.17x decoding speedup and 42% lower peak KV-cache footprint. The gains are more pronounced on longer-horizon rollouts, delivering improved visual quality with +0.68 and +2.74 VBench improvements, and 1.22x and 1.27x speedups on 20-second and 1-minute generations, respectively.

title: The Recurrent Transformer: Greater Effective Depth and Efficient Decoding
generated_summary:
The paper introduces the Recurrent Transformer, a modification to standard Transformers where each layer's key-value pairs are computed from that layer's own outputs rather than from the previous layer's representations, creating temporal recurrence within each layer. This allows later positions to attend to representations that have already undergone attention and MLP processing at the current layer, effectively increasing the computational depth without adding parameters.

The authors motivate the design from three perspectives: representational capacity (the architecture can emulate standard Transformers while also implementing token-to-token recurrence), training stability (multi-hop paths through recurrence combined with direct attention connections mitigate vanishing gradients), and computational efficiency. They develop an exact IO-aware tiling algorithm that reduces memory traffic from O(N²) to O(N√N) during training and prefill, making the approach practical despite the inherently sequential nature of the recurrence.

Experiments on 300M-parameter models pretrained on C4 demonstrate meaningful cross-entropy improvements over standard Transformers, with a 0.03 reduction at matched depth (12 layers). Crucially, a 6-layer Recurrent Transformer performs comparably to a 12-layer standard Transformer at the same parameter count, reducing KV cache size by approximately 30% and lowering decode-time memory traffic.

The work demonstrates that layerwise recurrence offers a principled mechanism for increasing effective depth while enabling favorable depth-width tradeoffs that translate directly into improved inference efficiency.
original_abstract: Transformers process tokens in parallel but are temporally shallow: at position $t$, each layer attends to key-value pairs computed based on the previous layer, yielding a depth capped by the number of layers. Recurrent models offer unbounded temporal depth but suffer from optimization instability and historically underutilize modern accelerators. We introduce the Recurrent Transformer, a simple architectural change where each layer attends to key-value pairs computed off its own activations, yielding layerwise recurrent memory while preserving standard autoregressive decoding cost. We show that the architecture can emulate both (i) a conventional Transformer and (ii) token-to-token recurrent updates under mild assumptions, while avoiding optimization instability. Naively, prefill/training appears bandwidth-bound with effective arithmetic intensity near $1$ because keys and values are revealed sequentially; we give an exact tiling-based algorithm that preserves the mathematical computation while reducing HBM traffic from $Θ(N^2)$ to $Θ(N\log N)$, increasing effective arithmetic intensity to $Θ(N/\log N)$ for sequence length $N$. On 150M and 300M parameter C4 pretraining, Recurrent Transformers improve cross-entropy over a parameter-matched Transformer baseline and achieve the improvement with fewer layers (fixed parameters), suggesting that recurrence can trade depth for width, thus reducing KV cache memory footprint and inference latency.

title: SQLyzr: A Comprehensive Benchmark and Evaluation Platform for Text-to-SQL
generated_summary:

The platform addresses four critical shortcomings of current benchmarks. Second, it enables evaluation under scaled database settings, moving beyond the fixed, small-scale databases typical of existing benchmarks to capture how generated queries perform under realistic, large-scale conditions. Third, it incorporates workload augmentation to better reflect real-world SQL usage patterns. Fourth, it provides diagnostic capabilities including error analysis and fixing suggestions, making it suitable for integration into iterative development workflows rather than serving as a static evaluation tool.

The platform features a graphical user interface for configuring evaluations, comparing models, and exploring results through visualization plots and error analysis.

The significance of this work lies in its potential to facilitate more meaningful evaluation and continuous improvement of text-to-SQL systems as they approach deployment readiness in real-world settings.
original_abstract: Text-to-SQL models have significantly improved with the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs), leading to their increasing use in real-world applications. Although many benchmarks exist for evaluating the performance of text-to-SQL models, they often rely on a single aggregate score, lack evaluation under realistic settings, and provide limited insight into model behaviour across different query types. In this work, we present SQLyzr, a comprehensive benchmark and evaluation platform for text-to-SQL models. SQLyzr incorporates a diverse set of evaluation metrics that capture multiple aspects of generated queries, while enabling more realistic evaluation through workload alignment with real-world SQL usage patterns and database scaling. It further supports fine-grained query classification, error analysis, and workload augmentation, allowing users to better diagnose and improve text-to-SQL models. This demonstration showcases these capabilities through an interactive experience. Through SQLyzr's graphical interface, users can customize evaluation settings, analyze fine-grained reports, and explore additional features of the platform. We envision that SQLyzr facilitates the evaluation and iterative improvement of text-to-SQL models by addressing key limitations of existing benchmarks. The source code of SQLyzr is available at https://github.com/sepideh-abedini/SQLyzr.

title: Subject-level Inference for Realistic Text Anonymization Evaluation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SEPIA (Subject-level PII Inference Assessment), the first benchmark and evaluation framework that shifts text anonymization assessment from span-based metrics to subject-level inference-based evaluation. Recognizing that real-world documents contain multiple identifiable individuals and that masking explicit mentions alone cannot prevent privacy breaches, the framework evaluates whether personal information remains inferable for every individual mentioned in a document.

The methodology employs a two-stage approach: first identifying all data subjects within a document, then inferring 15 categories of personally identifiable information (PII) for each subject from the anonymized text. The benchmark comprises 675 documents spanning legal and online domains, encompassing 1,712 subjects. Two novel metrics—Collective Protection Rate (CPR) and Individual Protection Rate (IPR)—quantify privacy protection across all subjects in a document.

Experiments across four anonymization methods and six LLM backbones reveal critical findings: span-based metrics dramatically overestimate protection, with two-thirds of PIIs remaining inferable even at 99.7% entity recall; single-subject-focused anonymization leaves non-target subjects up to 11 percentage points less protected; and anonymization effectiveness varies substantially across document types.

These results demonstrate that current evaluation paradigms are fundamentally inadequate for assessing real-world privacy protection. The framework provides a more realistic foundation for developing anonymization techniques that ensure equitable protection for all individuals mentioned in textual data.
original_abstract: Current text anonymization evaluation relies on span-based metrics that fail to capture what an adversary could actually infer, and assumes a single data subject, ignoring multi-subject scenarios. To address these limitations, we present SPIA (Subject-level PII Inference Assessment), the first benchmark that shifts the unit of evaluation from text spans to individuals, comprising 675 documents across legal and online domains with novel subject-level protection metrics. Extensive experiments show that even when over 90% of PII spans are masked, subject-level inference protection drops as low as 33%, leaving the majority of personal information recoverable through contextual inference. Furthermore, target-subject-focused anonymization leaves non-target subjects substantially more exposed than the target subject. We show that subject-level inference-based evaluation is essential for ensuring safe text anonymization in real-world settings.

title: When Constraints Limit and Inspire: Characterizing Presentation Authoring Practices for Evolving Narratives

Two subsequent studies—a within-subjects comparison with 12 participants and an exploratory two-session study with 8 professionals—evaluated the framework's utility.

Results show that ReSlide significantly outperformed a baseline tool on usability, constraint awareness, narrative coherence, and reuse metrics, without increasing cognitive workload. Participants shifted from treating constraints as mental checkpoints to actively using them as design drivers. The section-based structure supported both top-down and bottom-up authoring workflows, while the repository enabled exploratory and intentional reuse strategies across sessions.

The work's significance lies in reframing presentation authoring as a constraint-driven, multi-session process, offering a theoretical foundation and practical design implications for future AI-assisted presentation tools that can provide context-aware, timely support aligned with presenters' evolving needs.
original_abstract: Authoring presentation slides involves navigating contextual constraints that shape how content is structured, adapted, and reused. While prior work frames constraints as limitations, little is known about how presenters actively reason about them. We conducted a formative study with ten presenters to examine how constraints emerge, are interpreted, and influence authoring decisions, leading to the Constraint-based Multi-session Presentation Authoring (CMPA) framework. CMPA treats time, audience, and communicative intent as key constraints shaping authoring. We instantiated CMPA in ReSlide, a research prototype for constraint-aware slide creation and reuse, and conducted two user studies on (1) single-session behaviors and (2) multi-session workflows. Compared to a baseline tool, ReSlide helped presenters treat constraints as active design drivers that guide narrative construction. The second study further shows how presenters flexibly reuse and adapt content across authoring cycles as constraints evolve. We then propose design implications for future constraint-aware presentation tools.

title: On Reasoning Behind Next Occupation Recommendation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a reasoning-augmented framework for next occupation prediction that integrates explicit rationale generation with occupation forecasting, aiming to produce transparent and actionable career transition recommendations. The framework is instantiated in two designs: a two-model approach with separate reason generator and occupation predictor, and a joint model that generates both reasoning and predictions simultaneously.

The methodology involves constructing high-quality "oracle reasons" through multi-attempt LLM generation filtered by a rationality-based LLM-as-a-Judge that evaluates factuality, coherence, and utility. These oracle reasons serve as supervision for fine-tuning Qwen3-8B models using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). The framework leverages the standardized O*NET-SOC taxonomy for occupation classification and evaluates predictions using exact match accuracy and related occupation match accuracy metrics.

Key results demonstrate that reasoning-augmented models significantly outperform both zero-shot LLM approaches (including GPT-4.1) and traditional transformer-based sequential recommenders such as SASRec and BERT4Rec. The joint model achieves the best performance, and prediction quality correlates strongly with reason quality—more factual, coherent, and utility-aligned reasoning leads to more accurate predictions.

The significance of this work lies in bridging predictive accuracy with interpretability in career trajectory modeling. By providing explicit rationales for occupation transitions, the framework enables job seekers to understand recommended career paths and take actionable steps toward skill development, while offering workforce planners transparent insights into labor market dynamics.
original_abstract: In this work, we develop a novel reasoning approach to enhance the performance of large language models (LLMs) in future occupation prediction. In this approach, a reason generator first derives a ``reason'' for a user using his/her past education and career history. The reason summarizes the user's preference and is used as the input of an occupation predictor to recommend the user's next occupation. This two-step occupation prediction approach is, however, non-trivial as LLMs are not aligned with career paths or the unobserved reasons behind each occupation decision. We therefore propose to fine-tune LLMs improving their reasoning and occupation prediction performance. We first derive high-quality oracle reasons, as measured by factuality, coherence and utility criteria, using a LLM-as-a-Judge. These oracle reasons are then used to fine-tune small LLMs to perform reason generation and next occupation prediction. Our extensive experiments show that: (a) our approach effectively enhances LLM's accuracy in next occupation prediction making them comparable to fully supervised methods and outperforming unsupervised methods; (b) a single LLM fine-tuned to perform reason generation and occupation prediction outperforms two LLMs fine-tuned to perform the tasks separately; and (c) the next occupation prediction accuracy depends on the quality of generated reasons. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sarasarahhhhh/job_prediction.

title: Refining Covariance Matrix Estimation in Stochastic Gradient Descent Through Bias Reduction
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a de-biased covariance matrix estimator for averaged stochastic gradient descent (SGD) that significantly improves upon existing online, Hessian-free estimation approaches. The main contribution is a novel bias-reduction technique that achieves a convergence rate of n^(κ−1)/2 for the estimation error, representing a substantial improvement over the previously best-known rate of n^(κ−1)/4, where κ ∈ (0.5, 1) is the step-size decay parameter.

The methodology builds on a key insight: rather than adjusting the inherently biased sample covariance structure used in batch-means estimators, the authors construct an estimator that more directly mirrors the theoretical definition of the running average's variance. The estimator employs a block-based batching scheme that enables fully online computation, requiring only O(d²) operations per iteration—the minimal cost for estimating a d×d matrix. The approach operates on a single SGD trajectory without requiring Hessian evaluations or access to raw data.

Numerical experiments across linear, logistic, and expectile regression models demonstrate that the de-biased estimator consistently outperforms the online batch-means estimator in both estimation accuracy and confidence interval coverage across various dimensions. The method achieves near-nominal coverage rates while maintaining computational efficiency.

This work has significant implications for uncertainty quantification in large-scale machine learning, enabling practitioners to construct more reliable confidence intervals for SGD-based parameter estimates while preserving the computational advantages that make SGD attractive.
original_abstract: We study online inference and asymptotic covariance estimation for the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. While classical methods (such as plug-in and batch-means estimators) are available, they either require inaccessible second-order (Hessian) information or suffer from slow convergence. To address these challenges, we propose a novel, fully online de-biased covariance estimator that eliminates the need for second-order derivatives while significantly improving estimation accuracy. Our method employs a bias-reduction technique to achieve a convergence rate of $n^{(α-1)/2} \sqrt{\log n}$, outperforming existing Hessian-free alternatives.

title: Participation and Representation in Local Government Speech
generated_summary:
This paper presents the most comprehensive empirical study of local democratic participation to date, constructing a novel dataset of over 25,000 city council meetings across 115 California municipalities from 2015 to 2024. The authors transcribe and analyze more than 75,000 hours of audio using state-of-the-art speech recognition, speaker diarization, and large language models to identify speakers, extract discussion topics, and classify approximately 320,000 discrete policy issues. They link identified speakers to voter registration and property ownership records to assess demographic representativeness.

The analysis reveals significant representation gaps: meeting participants are systematically older, more male, whiter, more Democratic, and more likely to be homeowners than the registered voter population. Topic composition matters for participation, with land use and zoning issues drawing substantially more public engagement. Most council votes are unanimous, and cities show modest variation in discussion topics.

Leveraging quasi-experimental variation from the staggered removal of remote participation options introduced during COVID-19, the authors find that eliminating remote access reduces participation rates in the short term but does not clearly alter the demographic composition of speakers.

These findings have important implications for local governance design, suggesting that the participant pool providing input to city councils is systematically unrepresentative of the broader electorate, potentially undermining local governments' ability to effectively aggregate community preferences.
original_abstract: Local government meetings are the most common formal channel through which residents speak directly with elected officials, contest policies, and shape local agendas. However, data constraints typically limit the empirical study of these meetings to agendas, single cities, or short time horizons. We collect and transcribe a massive new dataset of city council meetings from 115 California cities over the last decade, using advanced transcription and diarization techniques to analyze the speech content of the meetings themselves. We document two sets of descriptive findings: First, city council meetings are frequent, long, and vary modestly across towns and time in topical content. Second, public participants are substantially older, whiter, more male, more liberal, and more likely to own homes than the registered voter population, and public participation surges when topics related to land use and zoning are included in meeting agendas. Given this skew, we examine the main policy lever municipalities have to shift participation patterns: meeting access costs. Exploiting pandemic-era variation in remote access, we show that eliminating remote options reduces the number of speakers, but does not clearly change the composition of speakers. Collectively, these results provide the most comprehensive empirical portrait to date of who participates in local democracy, what draws them in, and how institutional design choices shape both the volume and composition of public input.

title: ARFBench: Benchmarking Time Series Question Answering Ability for Software Incident Response
generated_summary:
This paper introduces ARFBench, a multimodal multiple-choice question-answering benchmark designed to evaluate time series reasoning capabilities in the context of software incident response. The benchmark comprises 750 question-answer pairs derived from 63 real-world incidents and 142 observability time series from a leading observability platform, with questions organized into three tiers of increasing difficulty: anomaly detection, anomaly property identification, and cross-series anomaly reasoning.

The authors evaluate a wide range of foundation models, including LLMs, vision-language models (VLMs), and time series LLMs, and propose a novel hybrid architecture (Toto-1.0-QA-Experimental) that jointly trains a time series foundation model with a VLM using a three-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data, supervised fine-tuning on real data, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

Key findings reveal that frontier VLMs substantially outperform existing baselines, with GPT-5 achieving 62.7% accuracy and 51.9% macro F1. The hybrid TSFM-VLM model achieves comparable performance (63.9% accuracy), demonstrating that combining time series encoders with vision-language models is a promising direction. Notably, models and human domain experts exhibit complementary error profiles, with a theoretical model-expert oracle achieving 87.2% accuracy, establishing a superhuman frontier.

ARFBench addresses a critical gap in evaluating compositional time series reasoning for operational contexts and provides an open-source resource for advancing AI-assisted incident response.
original_abstract: Time series question-answering (TSQA), in which we ask natural language questions to infer and reason about properties of time series, is a promising yet underexplored capability of foundation models. In this work, we present ARFBench, a TSQA benchmark that evaluates the understanding of multimodal foundation models (FMs) on time series anomalies prevalent in software incident data. ARFBench consists of 750 questions across 142 time series and 5.38M data points from 63 production incidents sourced exclusively from internal telemetry at Datadog. We evaluate leading proprietary and open-source LLMs, VLMs, and time series FMs and observe that frontier VLMs perform markedly better than existing baselines; the leading model (GPT-5) achieves a 62.7% accuracy and 51.9% F1. We next demonstrate the promise of specialized multimodal approaches. We develop a novel TSFM + VLM hybrid prototype which we post-train on a small set of synthetic and real data that yields comparable overall F1 and accuracy with frontier models. Lastly, we find models and human domain experts exhibit complementary strengths. We define a model-expert oracle, a best-of-2 oracle selector over model and expert answers, yielding 82.8% F1 and 87.2% accuracy and establishing a new superhuman frontier for future TSQA models. The benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Datadog/ARFBench.

title: A Probabilistic Framework for Improving Dense Object Detection in Underwater Image Data via Annealing-Based Data Augmentation

original_abstract: Object detection models typically perform well on images captured in controlled environments with stable lighting, water clarity, and viewpoint, but their performance degrades substantially in real-world underwater settings characterized by high variability and frequent occlusions. In this work, we address these challenges by introducing a novel data augmentation framework designed to improve robustness in dense and unconstrained underwater scenes. Using the DeepFish dataset, which contains images of fish in natural environments, we first generate bounding box annotations from provided segmentation masks to construct a custom detection dataset. We then propose a pseudo-simulated annealing-based augmentation algorithm, inspired by the copy-paste strategy of Deng et al. [1], to synthesize realistic crowded fish scenarios. Our approach improves spatial diversity and object density during training, enabling better generalization to complex scenes. Experimental results show that our method significantly outperforms a baseline YOLOv10 model, particularly on a challenging test set of manually annotated images collected from live-stream footage in the Florida Keys. title: Toward Efficient Membership Inference Attacks against Federated Large Language Models: A Projection Residual Approach

To address this gap, we propose ProjRes, the first projection residuals-based passive MIA tailored for FedLLMs. ProjRes leverages hidden embedding vectors as sample representations and analyzes their projection residuals on the gradient subspace to uncover the intrinsic link between gradients and inputs. It requires no shadow models, auxiliary classifiers, or historical updates, ensuring efficiency and robustness. Experiments on four benchmarks and four LLMs show that ProjRes achieves near 100% accuracy, outperforming prior methods by up to 75.75%, and remains effective even under strong differential privacy defenses. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked privacy vulnerability in FedLLMs and call for a re-examination of their security assumptions. title: Trust but Verify: Introducing DAVinCI -- A Framework for Dual Attribution and Verification in Claim Inference for Language Models

Results demonstrate consistent improvements across all models and metrics when DAVinCI is applied. original_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable fluency and versatility across a wide range of NLP tasks, yet they remain prone to factual inaccuracies and hallucinations. This limitation poses significant risks in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, law, and scientific communication, where trust and verifiability are paramount. In this paper, we introduce DAVinCI - a Dual Attribution and Verification framework designed to enhance the factual reliability and interpretability of LLM outputs. DAVinCI operates in two stages: (i) it attributes generated claims to internal model components and external sources; (ii) it verifies each claim using entailment-based reasoning and confidence calibration. We evaluate DAVinCI across multiple datasets, including FEVER and CLIMATE-FEVER, and compare its performance against standard verification-only baselines. Through an extensive ablation study, we isolate the contributions of evidence span selection, recalibration thresholds, and retrieval quality. title: How VLAs (Really) Work In Open-World Environments

original_abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have been extensively used in robotics applications, achieving great success in various manipulation problems. More recently, VLAs have been used in long-horizon tasks and evaluated on benchmarks, such as BEHAVIOR1K (B1K), for solving complex household chores. The common metric for measuring progress in such benchmarks is success rate or partial score based on satisfaction of progress-agnostic criteria, meaning only the final states of the objects are considered, regardless of the events that lead to such states. In this paper, we argue that using such evaluation protocols say little about safety aspects of operation and can potentially exaggerate reported performance, undermining core challenges for future real-world deployment. To this end, we conduct a thorough analysis of state-of-the-art models on the B1K Challenge and evaluate policies in terms of robustness via reproducibility and consistency of performance, safety aspects of policies operations, task awareness, and key elements leading to the incompletion of tasks. We then propose evaluation protocols to capture safety violations to better measure the true performance of the policies in more complex and interactive scenarios. title: Prefix Parsing is Just Parsing
generated_summary:
