The key finding is that Europe-only pretraining consistently outperforms all other strategies, including globally balanced pretraining, across multiple downstream tasks (scene classification, population density estimation, landcover segmentation, and GEO-Bench), evaluation protocols (kNN, linear probing, full finetuning), and geographic regions. This contradicts the intuition that geographic alignment between pretraining and downstream data, or globally diverse pretraining, should yield optimal performance. Performance differences due to pretraining data source rival or exceed those from hyperparameter tuning, and persist even when finetuning on datasets as large as the pretraining set.

To explain these patterns, the authors analyze correlations between downstream performance and various diversity measures. Coarse geographic diversity metrics (continent, biome, landcover entropy) show weak correlations, while per-sample spectral entropy exhibits a strong correlation (ρ = 0.84, p = 0.002), suggesting that individual sample complexity drives pretraining quality more than geographic coverage. These findings provide practical guidance for constructing pretraining datasets and highlight that data design choices deserve attention comparable to architectural innovations.
original_abstract: New geospatial foundation models introduce a new model architecture and pretraining dataset, often sampled using different notions of data diversity. Performance differences are largely attributed to the model architecture or input modalities, while the role of the pretraining dataset is rarely studied. To address this research gap, we conducted a systematic study on how the geographic composition of pretraining data affects a model's downstream performance. We created global and per-continent pretraining datasets and evaluated them on global and per-continent downstream datasets. We found that the pretraining dataset from Europe outperformed global and continent-specific pretraining datasets on both global and local downstream evaluations. To investigate the factors influencing a pretraining dataset's downstream performance, we analysed 10 pretraining datasets using diversity across continents, biomes, landcover and spectral values. We found that only spectral diversity was strongly correlated with performance, while others were weakly correlated. This finding establishes a new dimension of diversity to be accounted for when creating a high-performing pretraining dataset. We open-sourced 7 new pretraining datasets, pretrained models, and our experimental framework at https://github.com/kerner-lab/pretrain-where.

title: AI Governance under Political Turnover: The Alignment Surface of Compliance Design
generated_summary:
This paper identifies a fundamental tension in AI governance: the same compliance infrastructure designed to make AI-assisted public administration accountable can become a vulnerability after political turnover. The authors introduce the concept of the "alignment surface"—the inherited pass-or-flag boundary created by standardized review processes—arguing that it can serve as a learnable map for bad-faith successor governments seeking to pursue procedurally compliant but democratically erosive actions.

The authors develop a three-stage formal model in which safeguards are established first, institutions adopt AI-mediated administrative processes under modernization pressure, and a successor executive inherits the resulting architecture. Using a Poisson benchmark for within-form exploitation, they derive three key results: a threshold condition under which inherited compliance architecture becomes politically exploitable; a "codification dilemma" showing that once overt violations are deterred, further standardization can shift from protective to risk-increasing by making approval boundaries more learnable to insiders; and a persistence result demonstrating that temporary modernization pressure can create durable vulnerability because later democratic governments only partially unwind inherited workflows.

The paper's significance lies in reframing AI governance design criteria. Rather than simply maximizing transparency and auditability, institutions must preserve oversight visibility while limiting insider learnability—distinguishing between oversight-facing auditability and insider-facing boundary standardization. This challenges conventional assumptions that more procedural regularity necessarily strengthens democratic control, offering concrete design principles for safeguards including throughput constraints, evaluation-deployment decoupling, and enhanced contestation capacity.
original_abstract: Governments are increasingly interested in using AI to make administrative decisions cheaper, more scalable, and more consistent. But for probabilistic AI to be incorporated into public administration it must be embedded in a compliance layer that makes decisions reviewable, repeatable, and legally defensible. That layer can improve oversight by making departures from law easier to detect. But it can also create a stable approval boundary that political successors learn to navigate while preserving the appearance of lawful administration. We develop a formal model in which institutions choose the scale of automation, the degree of codification, and safeguards on iterative use. The model shows when these systems become vulnerable to strategic use from within government, why reforms that initially improve oversight can later increase that vulnerability, and why expansions in AI use may be difficult to unwind. Making AI usable can thus make procedures easier for future governments to learn and exploit.

title: Leveraging Multimodal LLMs for Built Environment and Housing Attribute Assessment from Street-View Imagery
generated_summary: This paper presents a framework for automated building condition assessment from Google Street View imagery using multimodal large language models, addressing the challenge of scalable housing quality evaluation across the United States. The methodology employs GroundingDINO for building isolation from street-view scenes, followed by evaluation using multimodal LLMs prompted with structured rating criteria on a 1–5 scale. The authors benchmark multiple open-source models, identifying Gemma 3 27B as the most practical single-GPU option, achieving Spearman rank correlation of 0.77 with human mean opinion scores. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning using QLoRA on just 500 labeled images improves alignment to surpass individual human rater consistency. Knowledge distillation transfers the fine-tuned model's capabilities to smaller architectures—including EfficientNetV2 and Gemma 3 4B—achieving comparable performance with over 30× faster inference, enabling million-scale deployment. The framework further extends to comprehensive built environment attribute assessment through a human–AI alignment study and includes an interactive visualization dashboard for stakeholder decision-making. Key findings demonstrate that multimodal LLMs can effectively replicate expert-level building assessments with minimal annotation, and that pseudo-labeled datasets generated by the teacher model consistently outperform human-labeled datasets for training student models. This work has significant implications for scalable, cost-effective housing condition monitoring to support passive retrofit strategies nationwide.
original_abstract: We present a novel framework for automatically evaluating building conditions nationwide in the United States by leveraging large language models (LLMs) and Google Street View (GSV) imagery. By fine-tuning Gemma 3 27B on a modest human-labeled dataset, our approach achieves strong alignment with human mean opinion scores (MOS), outperforming even individual raters on SRCC and PLCC relative to the MOS benchmark. To enhance efficiency, we apply knowledge distillation, transferring the capabilities of Gemma 3 27B to a smaller Gemma 3 4B model that achieves comparable performance with a 3x speedup. Further, we distill the knowledge into a CNN-based model (EfficientNetV2-M) and a transformer (SwinV2-B), delivering close performance while achieving a 30x speed gain. Furthermore, we investigate LLMs' capabilities for assessing an extensive list of built environment and housing attributes through a human-AI alignment study and develop a visualization dashboard that integrates LLM assessment outcomes for downstream analysis by homeowners. Our framework offers a flexible and efficient solution for large-scale building condition assessment, enabling high accuracy with minimal human labeling effort.

title: A Hybridizable Neural Time Integrator for Stable Autoregressive Forecasting
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a hybridizable neural time integrator (HNODE) that embeds autoregressive transformer dynamics within a structure-preserving mixed finite element framework based on finite element exterior calculus (FEEC). The central contribution is demonstrating that this architectural scaffold provides provable stability guarantees—including discrete energy preservation and uniformly bounded gradients independent of rollout length—addressing the notorious exploding gradient problem that plagues neural ODEs and the lack of stability analysis for standard transformers.

The methodology partitions the time domain into rollout segments, each discretized using mixed finite elements with staggered variable arrangements analogous to geometric integrators. A novel temporal mortar formulation, extending mortar methods to initial value problems for the first time, couples segments via Lagrange multipliers that stably transfer energy across domains. A transformer learns nonlinear dynamics within this scaffold, and the entire system can be jointly trained with vision transformer encoders for spatiotemporal data.

Key results include stable forecasting of the Lorenz attractor for 10,000 Lyapunov times while reproducing its invariant measure, matching state-of-the-art accuracy on a shear flow benchmark with 65× fewer parameters than PhysiX, and building a real-time pulsed power fusion surrogate from only 12 simulations achieving a 9,000× speedup.

The work demonstrates that encoding physical structure into neural architectures can substitute for data scale, offering a principled path toward sample-efficient scientific foundation models with mathematically guaranteed stability.
original_abstract: For autoregressive modeling of chaotic dynamical systems over long time horizons, the stability of both training and inference is a major challenge in building scientific foundation models. We present a hybrid technique in which an autoregressive transformer is embedded within a novel shooting-based mixed finite element scheme, exposing topological structure that enables provable stability. For forward problems, we prove preservation of discrete energies, while for training we prove uniform bounds on gradients, provably avoiding the exploding gradient problem. Combined with a vision transformer, this yields latent tokens admitting structure-preserving dynamics. We outperform modern foundation models with a $65\times$ reduction in model parameters and long-horizon forecasting of chaotic systems. A "mini-foundation" model of a fusion component shows that 12 simulations suffice to train a real-time surrogate, achieving a $9{,}000\times$ speedup over particle-in-cell simulation.

title: Preconditioned DeltaNet: Curvature-aware Sequence Modeling for Linear Recurrences
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Preconditioned DeltaNet (PDN) and its variants, incorporating second-order curvature information into linear recurrent sequence models through approximate preconditioning. Viewing existing delta-rule recurrences (DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, Kimi Delta Attention) through the test-time regression framework, the authors observe that these models perform first-order gradient descent on an in-context least-squares objective, ignoring the problem's curvature. While exact preconditioning is either unparallelizable or numerically unstable, the authors derive a key theoretical result: under exact preconditioning, linear attention and DeltaNet become equivalent. Leveraging this insight, they propose a diagonal approximation to the preconditioner that admits efficient chunkwise parallel computation, enabling practical implementation via custom Triton kernels with only approximately 10% overhead compared to unpreconditioned counterparts.

The authors introduce a DGPS (decay, gain, preconditioner, solve) taxonomy that systematically classifies existing linear recurrent models and reveals the preconditioner as a previously unexplored design axis. Empirically, preconditioned variants consistently outperform their base recurrences on synthetic multi-query associative recall tasks, commonsense reasoning benchmarks, and in-context retrieval tasks at 340M and 1B parameter scales. Analysis of recurrent dynamics shows that preconditioning introduces distinct read and write keys, enabling richer eigenvalue distributions in the transition matrix and improving long-context retrieval capabilities. This work opens a new dimension in the design space of efficient subquadratic sequence models.
original_abstract: To address the increasing long-context compute limitations of softmax attention, several subquadratic recurrent operators have been developed. This work includes models such as Mamba-2, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet (GDN), and Kimi Delta Attention (KDA). As the space of recurrences grows, a parallel line of work has arisen to taxonomize them. One compelling view is the test-time regression (TTR) framework, which interprets recurrences as performing online least squares updates that learn a linear map from the keys to values. Existing delta-rule recurrences can be seen as first-order approximations to this objective, but notably ignore the curvature of the least-squares loss during optimization. In this work, we address this by introducing preconditioning to these recurrences. Starting from the theory of online least squares, we derive equivalences between linear attention and the delta rule in the exactly preconditioned case. Next, we realize this theory in practice by proposing a diagonal approximation: this enables us to introduce preconditioned variants of DeltaNet, GDN, and KDA alongside efficient chunkwise parallel algorithms for computing them. Empirically, we find that our preconditioned delta-rule recurrences yield consistent performance improvements across synthetic recall benchmarks and language modeling at the 340M and 1B scale.

title: Propensity Inference: Environmental Contributors to LLM Behaviour
generated_summary:
This pre-registered study provides a more rigorous methodology for investigating factors that drive unsanctioned behavior in large language models, addressing criticisms of existing propensity research as anecdotal and lacking proper controls. The authors distinguish between "strategic" factors (e.g., goal conflicts between AI and humans, threats of replacement) and "non-strategic" factors (e.g., dispositional instructions, filler content), aiming to assess whether models' undesired behaviors reflect strategic reasoning—a prerequisite for loss-of-control scenarios.

The researchers constructed 11 evaluation environments where 12 environmental factors could be independently varied, collected over 600,000 samples across 23 language models, and applied Bayesian logistic regressions to quantify effect sizes. Key methodological contributions include studying relative rather than absolute behavior rates, principled statistical quantification via odds ratios, and measures against circular analysis artifacts.

Results show that strategic and non-strategic factors have approximately equal explanatory power for unsanctioned behavior, with no clear trend of strategic factors becoming more important as model capabilities increase. The strongest individual effects come from goal instructions, goal conflicts, anti-misalignment instructions, and independence instructions. More capable models show increased sensitivity to goal conflict, though with substantial variation across models.

This work represents an important step toward bridging theoretical frameworks about AI misalignment with empirical evidence, though the authors acknowledge significant limitations regarding ecological validity and the need for explicit cognitive models of language model decision-making.
original_abstract: Motivated by loss of control risks from misaligned AI systems, we develop and apply methods for measuring language models' propensity for unsanctioned behaviour. We contribute three methodological improvements: analysing effects of changes to environmental factors on behaviour, quantifying effect sizes via Bayesian generalised linear models, and taking explicit measures against circular analysis. We apply the methodology to measure the effects of 12 environmental factors (6 strategic in nature, 6 non-strategic) and thus the extent to which behaviour is explained by strategic aspects of the environment, a question relevant to risks from misalignment. Across 23 language models and 11 evaluation environments, we find approximately equal contributions from strategic and non-strategic factors for explaining behaviour, do not find strategic factors becoming more or less influential as capabilities improve, and find some evidence for a trend for increased sensitivity to goal conflicts. Finally, we highlight a key direction for future propensity research: the development of theoretical frameworks and cognitive models of AI decision-making into empirically testable forms.

title: Learning to Emulate Chaos: Adversarial Optimal Transport Regularization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces adversarial optimal transport (OT) regularization for training neural network emulators of chaotic dynamical systems. The key insight is that standard mean squared error (MSE) training degrades catastrophically for long-term forecasting of chaotic systems due to exponential sensitivity to initial conditions, while distributional objectives remain well-behaved by capturing invariant measure statistics rather than individual trajectories.

The methodology combines a one-step MSE prediction loss with an OT regularization term that matches the distribution of learned summary statistics between emulator-generated and true trajectories. Crucially, the summary statistics are not handcrafted but learned adversarially: a summary map is trained to maximize the OT discrepancy while the emulator minimizes it, ensuring optimally discriminative statistics are discovered automatically. The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that MSE blows up exponentially with rollout horizon under noise, while the Wasserstein-based objective stabilizes due to the mixing properties of chaotic systems.

Experiments on Lorenz-96, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Kolmogorov flow demonstrate that the adversarial OT methods (Sinkhorn and WGAN variants) consistently outperform MSE-only training and match or exceed handcrafted OT regularization, particularly in spectral distance metrics not explicitly enforced during training. The approach also better captures dynamical properties like Lyapunov exponents. This work is significant for data-driven scientific modeling, providing a principled framework for learning faithful emulators of chaotic systems from single noisy trajectories.
original_abstract: Chaos arises in many complex dynamical systems, from weather to power grids, but is difficult to accurately model using data-driven emulators, including neural operator architectures. For chaotic systems, the inherent sensitivity to initial conditions makes exact long-term forecasts theoretically infeasible, meaning that traditional squared-error losses often fail when trained on noisy data. Recent work has focused on training emulators to match the statistical properties of chaotic attractors by introducing regularization based on handcrafted local features and summary statistics, as well as learned statistics extracted from a diverse dataset of trajectories. In this work, we propose a family of adversarial optimal transport objectives that jointly learn high-quality summary statistics and a physically consistent emulator. We theoretically analyze and experimentally validate a Sinkhorn divergence formulation (2-Wasserstein) and a WGAN-style dual formulation (1-Wasserstein). Our experiments across a variety of chaotic systems, including systems with high-dimensional chaotic attractors, show that emulators trained with our approach exhibit significantly improved long-term statistical fidelity.

title: Multilingual and Domain-Agnostic Tip-of-the-Tongue Query Generation for Simulated Evaluation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a multilingual and domain-agnostic method for generating simulated Tip-of-the-Tongue (ToT) queries to evaluate retrieval systems. ToT retrieval involves users attempting to refind known items using partial, indirect, or noisy recollections rather than precise identifiers. Existing ToT benchmarks are predominantly English-centric and skewed toward entertainment domains, limiting their generalizability.

The authors leverage large language model-based query generation to systematically expand ToT evaluation beyond English to three East Asian languages—Chinese, Japanese, and Korean—while covering general-domain content rather than narrow topical categories. They empirically evaluate multiple query generation strategies and validate simulation fidelity through system rank correlation analysis, a well-established meta-evaluation methodology that compares system rankings produced by simulated queries against those from real queries.

Key results demonstrate that the proposed method maintains high system rank correlation across all evaluated languages, confirming the robustness of the simulation approach. Importantly, the findings reveal that multilingual ToT query simulation requires language-specific design choices: both prompt language and source Wikipedia language significantly influence simulation quality, and their effects vary across languages and entity types. Non-English Wikipedia content proves generally essential for capturing culturally specific ToT behavior.

The work contributes a publicly released multilingual, general-domain ToT retrieval test collection integrated into the ir_datasets framework, supporting future research on complex query understanding, multilingual retrieval, cross-lingual benchmarking, and culturally diverse information access evaluation through the NTCIR evaluation forum.
original_abstract: Tip-of-the-Tongue (ToT) retrieval benchmarks have largely focused on English, limiting their applicability to multilingual information access. In this work, we construct multilingual ToT test collections for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and English, using an LLM-based query simulation framework. We systematically study how prompt language and source document language affect the fidelity of simulated ToT queries, validating synthetic queries through system rank correlation against real user queries. Our results show that effective ToT simulation requires language-aware design choices: non-English language sources are generally important, while English Wikipedia can be beneficial when non-English sources provide insufficient information for query generation. Based on these findings, we release four ToT test collections with 5,000 queries per language across multiple domains. This work provides the first large-scale multilingual ToT benchmark and offers practical guidance for constructing realistic ToT datasets beyond English.

title: Spectral Embeddings Leak Graph Topology: Theory, Benchmark, and Adaptive Reconstruction
generated_summary: This paper presents a unified framework addressing two interconnected challenges in graph learning: understanding how fragmentation and privacy constraints affect GNN performance, and quantifying the privacy risks of sharing spectral embeddings. The authors make three main contributions. First, they introduce LoGraB (Local Graph Benchmark), a systematic benchmark exploring fragmentation, spectral truncation, and noise across 486 scenarios on 9 diverse datasets, with three evaluation tasks and tailored metrics. Second, they propose Adaptive Fidelity-driven Reconstruction (AFR), an algorithm that reconstructs graph topology from fragmented spectral embeddings by assigning fidelity scores to patches based on spectral stability and structural entropy, then adaptively assembling them through RANSAC-Procrustes alignment, Bundle Adjustment refinement, and cross-voting link inference. Third, they establish the Spectral Leakage Proposition, an information-theoretic result showing polynomial-time graph recovery is feasible when sufficiently many eigenvectors are shared. Experiments across 9 datasets demonstrate that AFR consistently outperforms six baselines in graph reconstruction, achieving notably stronger results on large-scale graphs. The benchmark reveals that local view structure (neighborhood radius and coverage) dominates GNN performance under fragmentation, while no single architecture excels universally. Privacy analysis shows that per-embedding differential privacy requires substantial utility sacrifice to meaningfully degrade AFR's reconstruction capability. This work provides essential tools for developing privacy-aware graph learning systems and designing defenses against topology reconstruction attacks.
original_abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on relational data, but standard benchmarks unrealistically assume the graph is centrally available. In practice, settings such as Federated Graph Learning, distributed systems, and privacy-sensitive applications involve graph data that are localized, fragmented, noisy, and privacy-leaking. We present a unified framework for this setting. We introduce LoGraB (Local Graph Benchmark), which decomposes standard datasets into fragmented benchmarks using three strategies and four controls: neighborhood radius $d$, spectral quality $k$, noise level $σ$, and coverage ratio $p$. LoGraB supports graph reconstruction, localized node classification, and inter-fragment link prediction, with Island Cohesion. We propose AFR (Adaptive Fidelity-driven Reconstruction), a method for noisy spectral fragments. AFR scores patch quality via a fidelity measure combining a gap-to-truncation stability ratio and structural entropy, then assembles fragments using RANSAC-Procrustes alignment, adaptive stitching, and Bundle Adjustment. Rather than forcing a single global graph, AFR recovers large faithful islands. We prove heat-kernel edge recovery under a separation condition, Davis--Kahan perturbation stability, and bounded alignment error. We establish a Spectral Leakage Proposition: under a spectral-gap assumption, polynomial-time Bayesian recovery is feasible once enough eigenvectors are shared, complementing AFR's deterministic guarantees. Experiments on nine benchmarks show that LoGraB reveals model strengths and weaknesses under fragmentation, AFR achieves the best F1 on 7/9 datasets, and under per-embedding $(ε,δ)$-Gaussian differential privacy, AFR retains 75% of its undefended F1 at $ε=2$. Our anonymous code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/JMLR_submission

title: Mind the Prompt: Self-adaptive Generation of Task Plan Explanations via LLMs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces COMPASS (COgnitive Modelling for Prompt Automated SynthesiS), a self-adaptive approach that formalizes prompt engineering as a cognitive and probabilistic decision-making process to generate tailored task plan explanations via Large Language Models. The core contribution is the integration of a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) to model users' latent cognitive states—including attention and understanding—alongside observable interaction feedback, enabling dynamic synthesis of optimal prompt policies that adjust explanation tone, detail level, and format to individual stakeholder profiles and evolving cognitive conditions.

The methodology combines probabilistic reasoning with cognitive modeling within a MAPE-K adaptation loop. COMPASS first translates natural language problem descriptions into valid planner inputs using LLMs, generates task plans, and then produces explanations adapted to user profiles (AI experts, domain experts, non-experts). The system continuously refines explanations based on acceptance rates, user feedback, and predicted cognitive states informed by Prospect Theory.

Evaluation across construction and agriculture cyber-physical system domains using GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 demonstrates that LLMs reliably generate syntactically valid planner inputs. A user study with 32 participants shows that adapted explanations improve perceived appropriateness and understanding for non-experts and AI experts, and that personalisation cues are identified above chance levels.

COMPASS represents a significant step toward principled, cognitively-grounded prompt engineering for explainable AI planning systems, addressing the critical need for transparent, user-adaptive explanations in complex human-AI collaborative environments.
original_abstract: Integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into complex software systems enables the generation of human-understandable explanations of opaque AI processes, such as automated task planning. However, the quality and reliability of these explanations heavily depend on effective prompt engineering. The lack of a systematic understanding of how diverse stakeholder groups formulate and refine prompts hinders the development of tools that can automate this process. We introduce COMPASS (COgnitive Modelling for Prompt Automated SynthesiS), a proof-of-concept self-adaptive approach that formalises prompt engineering as a cognitive and probabilistic decision-making process. COMPASS models unobservable users' latent cognitive states, such as attention and comprehension, uncertainty, and observable interaction cues as a POMDP, whose synthesised policy enables adaptive generation of explanations and prompt refinements. We evaluate COMPASS using two diverse cyber-physical system case studies to assess the adaptive explanation generation and their qualities, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of COMPASS integrating human cognition and user profile's feedback into automated prompt synthesis in complex task planning systems.

title: Structural Quality Gaps in Practitioner AI Governance Prompts: An Empirical Study Using a Five-Principle Evaluation Framework
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a five-principle evaluation framework for assessing the structural quality of AI governance prompts, treating them as a new class of requirements engineering artefact. The five principles—Success Definition, Assessment Rubric, Scope Boundary, Data Classification, and Quality Gate—are theoretically grounded in Rice's theorem, the Curry-Howard correspondence, and Bayesian epistemology, establishing necessary conditions for verifiable agent governance.

The authors apply this framework to a corpus of 34 publicly available AGENTS.md files from GitHub, scored independently by three LLM evaluators on a three-point scale (0, 0.5, 1.0) per principle. The mean total score across the corpus is 2.81 out of 5.0, indicating widespread structural incompleteness. Data Classification emerges as the weakest principle (mean 0.34), while Scope Boundary and Quality Gate are the strongest. No file achieves full structural completeness across all evaluators. Three dominant archetypes emerge: operational guides that specify tasks without evaluation criteria, constrained executors with partial rubrics, and minimal pointers that redirect to other documents without containing governance content themselves.

The findings reveal that practitioners conceptualize governance prompts as operational instructions rather than formal specifications, systematically omitting evaluative and classificatory elements. The framework is directly operationalizable as automated static analysis tooling, enabling a shift-left approach to AI governance quality—catching specification gaps at authorship rather than after deployment failures. The work opens a research programme applying established requirements engineering methods to this increasingly consequential artefact class.
original_abstract: AI governance programmes increasingly rely on natural language prompts to constrain and direct AI agent behaviour. These prompts function as executable specifications: they define the agent's mandate, scope, and quality criteria. Despite this role, no systematic framework exists for evaluating whether a governance prompt is structurally complete. We introduce a five-principle evaluation framework grounded in computability theory, proof theory, and Bayesian epistemology, and apply it to an empirical corpus of 34 publicly available AGENTS.md governance files sourced from GitHub. Our evaluation reveals that 37% of evaluated file-model pairs score below the structural completeness threshold, with data classification and assessment rubric criteria most frequently absent. These results suggest that practitioner-authored governance prompts exhibit consistent structural patterns that automated static analysis could detect and remediate. We discuss implications for requirements engineering practice in AI-assisted development contexts, identify a previously undocumented artefact classification gap in the AGENTS.md convention, and propose directions for tool support.

title: A rigorous quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm for SYK thermal expectations
generated_summary:
This paper presents a rigorous quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm for estimating local thermal expectations of the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model, a random quantum Hamiltonian ensemble widely considered a candidate for quantum computational advantage. The SYK model exhibits properties—including a sign problem, high entanglement, large magic, and circuit complexity lower bounds—that obstruct common classical simulation techniques, making this result particularly surprising.

The authors' approach proceeds in two main steps. First, they establish that the SYK partition function has no complex zeros within a constant-radius disk around the origin, rigorously ruling out phase transitions above a certain constant temperature. This is achieved through a novel cluster expansion whose polymers are constructed from Wick pairs, directly exploiting the noncommutative structure of Majorana fermion operators—a departure from prior classical cluster expansion techniques that fail for noncommuting Hamiltonians. Second, they combine this zero-freeness result with Barvinok's interpolation method to estimate perturbed partition functions, using finite difference approximations to recover thermal expectations.

The resulting algorithm estimates local, bounded-norm observables of the SYK Gibbs state to arbitrary inverse polynomial additive error in quasipolynomial time for temperatures above an explicit constant threshold, succeeding with high probability over the random disorder. This work provides the first rigorous control of complex zeros for a mean-field quantum spin glass and rigorously confirms physics conjectures about the replica-symmetric regime of SYK, challenging the model's status as a quantum advantage candidate for thermal property estimation.
original_abstract: Estimating local observables in Gibbs states is a central problem in quantum simulation. While this task is BQP-complete at asymptotically low temperatures, the possibility of quantum advantage at constant temperature remains open. The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model is a natural candidate: at any constant temperature, its Gibbs states have polynomial quantum circuit complexity and are not described by Gaussian states. Rigorous analyses of the SYK model are difficult due to the failure of known techniques using random matrix theory, cluster expansions, and rigorous formulations of the quantum path integral and replica trick. Despite this, we give a rigorous proof of a quasipolynomial-time classical algorithm that estimates SYK local thermal expectations at sufficiently high constant temperature. Our result introduces a new Wick-pair cluster expansion that we expect to be broadly useful for disordered quantum many-body systems.

title: climt-paraformer: Stable Emulation of Convective Parameterization using a Temporal Memory-aware Transformer
generated_summary:
This paper introduces climt-paraformer, a temporal memory-aware Transformer architecture designed to emulate the Emanuel convective parameterization scheme in climate models. The key contribution is demonstrating that attention-based sequence models can effectively capture temporal correlations in convective processes, addressing the limitation of conventional memory-less neural network emulators that assume convection depends only on the instantaneous atmospheric state.

The methodology involves training neural network emulators using data generated from a single-column model (SCM) under radiative-convective equilibrium. The Transformer architecture processes sequences of consecutive atmospheric states (temporal windows) to learn dependencies across multiple time steps. The authors impose hard physical constraints by suppressing convective tendencies above an optimized cutoff level and compare performance against baseline models including multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs).

Key results show that a Transformer with a temporal window of five time steps achieves the lowest offline errors across temperature tendency, specific humidity tendency, and convective precipitation rate. However, excessive temporal context (windows of 15-20 steps) degrades performance due to error accumulation. In online simulations, the Transformer maintains stable 10-year integrations, while the MLP and LSTM exhibit instabilities and eventual crashes.

This work provides proof of concept that attention-based temporal modeling improves both accuracy and numerical stability of machine learning-based convective parameterization, offering a promising pathway toward more reliable climate model emulation.
original_abstract: Accurate representation of moist convective sub-grid-scale processes remains a major challenge in global climate models, as traditional parameterization schemes are both computationally expensive and difficult to scale. Neural network (NN) emulators offer a promising alternative by learning efficient mappings between atmospheric states and convective tendencies while retaining fidelity to the underlying physics. However, most existing NN-based parameterizations are memory-less and rely only on instantaneous inputs, even though convection evolves over time and depends on prior atmospheric states. Recent studies have begun to incorporate convective memory, but they often treat past states as independent features rather than modeling temporal dependencies explicitly. In this work, we develop a temporal memory-aware Transformer emulator for the Emanuel convective parameterization and evaluate it in a single-column climate model (SCM) under both offline and online configurations. The Transformer captures temporal correlations and nonlinear interactions across consecutive atmospheric states. Compared with baseline emulators, including a memory-less multilayer perceptron and a recurrent long short-term memory model, the Transformer achieves lower offline errors. Sensitivity analysis indicates that a memory length of approximately 100 minutes yields the best performance, whereas longer memory degrades performance. We further test the emulator in long-term coupled simulations and show that it remains stable over 10 years. Overall, this study demonstrates the importance of explicit temporal modeling for NN-based parameterizations.

title: Deductive Verification of Weak Memory Programs with View-based Protocols (extended version)
generated_summary:
This paper presents VerCors-relaxed, an approach for deductive verification of programs under weak memory models using view-based protocols. This combination enables modular reasoning about reordered and speculative writes while verifying threads individually in sequentially-consistent order.

The methodology encodes relaxed memory accesses using view-based protocols within VerCors, a deductive verifier based on permission-based separation logic. The authors formalize the SLR program logic, a state-of-the-art logic for weak memory concurrency, using their view-based protocol framework. Protocols define valid state transitions for writes to shared locations, while views track each thread's knowledge of other threads' progress, constraining which values can be read.

Future work includes supporting release/acquire memory orders, improving scalability, reducing annotation overhead, and targeting additional weak memory models.
original_abstract: Concurrent programming under weak memory concurrency faces substantial challenges to ensure correctness due to program behaviors that cannot be explained by thread interleaving, a.k.a. sequential consistency. While several program logics are proposed to reason about weak memory concurrency, their usage has been limited to intricate manual proofs. On the other hand, the VerCors verifier provides a rich toolset for automated deductive verification for sequential consistency. In this paper, we bridge this gap for automated deductive verification of weak memory concurrent programs with the VerCors deductive verification tool. We propose an approach to encode weak memory concurrency in VerCors. We develop VerCors-relaxed, where we extend the VerCors atomics support and bring concepts from several protocol automata to encode permission-based separation logics for weak memory concurrency models. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we encode the relaxed fragment of the SLR program logic, a recent state-of-the-art permission-based separation logic for weak memory concurrency in VerCors-relaxed, our extension of VerCors. We use the SLR encoding on VerCors-relaxed to automatically verify several examples from the literature within realistic performance.

title: Behavioral Consistency and Transparency Analysis on Large Language Model API Gateways
generated_summary:

GateScope evaluates gateway behavior across four dimensions: response content analysis using structured probing queries to detect model substitution, multi-turn conversational consistency to identify context truncation or model switching, billing accuracy by comparing expected versus actual charges, and latency characteristics to quantify variability in response times. The framework trains binary classifiers on behavioral signatures from 24 LLMs, achieving an average F1 score of 0.968 in controlled validation on official vendor APIs, while avoiding misclassification of unseen models.

Applied to 10 commercial gateways, GateScope reveals significant discrepancies: several gateways appear to substitute cheaper models for requested ones, multi-turn memory degrades substantially compared to official baselines, billing deviations reach up to 62.8% on one platform, and latency variability suggests heterogeneous backend behavior. These findings demonstrate that current LLM gateways lack meaningful transparency guarantees, highlighting the need for client-side auditing tools. GateScope provides a practical, lightweight approach to hold gateway intermediaries accountable.
original_abstract: Third-party Large Language Model (LLM) API gateways are rapidly emerging as unified access points to models offered by multiple vendors. However, the internal routing, caching, and billing policies of these gateways are largely undisclosed, leaving users with limited visibility into whether requests are served by the advertised models, whether responses remain faithful to upstream APIs, or whether invoices accurately reflect public pricing policies. To address this gap, we introduce GateScope, a lightweight black-box measurement framework for evaluating behavioral consistency and operational transparency in commercial LLM gateways. GateScope is designed to detect key misbehaviors, including model downgrading or switching, silent truncation, billing inaccuracies, and instability in latency by auditing gateways along four critical dimensions: response content analysis, multi-turn conversation performance, billing accuracy, and latency characteristics. Our measurements across 10 real-world commercial LLM API gateways reveal frequent gaps between expected and actual behaviors, including silent model substitutions, degraded memory retention, deviations from announced pricing, and substantial variation in latency stability across platforms.

title: Weighting What Matters: Boosting Sample Efficiency in Medical Report Generation via Token Reweighting
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training vision-language models for medical report generation in data-constrained settings, where paired image-report datasets are limited and costly to obtain. The methodology involves defining three curated sets of clinically relevant keywords: quantitative terms describing severity or extent (e.g., "thick," "several"), diagnostic terms related to biomarkers and disease concepts (e.g., "drusen," "fluid"), and a combined set. During training, the standard per-token cross-entropy loss is replaced with a weighted objective that assigns higher loss weights to tokens matching these predefined clinical keywords, while normalizing to maintain consistent loss scale across reports with varying keyword density. This approach increases the penalty for errors on semantically important terms relative to non-diagnostic tokens.

Key results demonstrate that the weighted loss formulation improves generated report quality with respect to age-related macular degeneration staging and biomarker identification accuracy across various dataset sizes. Notably, models trained with token reweighting frequently outperform standard training with three times more data, highlighting substantial gains in sample efficiency.

The significance of this work lies in providing a simple yet effective strategy for data-efficient training of medical vision-language models, particularly valuable for smaller medical subdisciplines where annotated data is scarce and expensive to curate.
original_abstract: Training vision-language models (VLMs) for medical report generation is often hindered by the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. This work evaluates the use of a weighted loss function to improve data efficiency. Compared to standard cross-entropy loss, which treats all token prediction errors equally, the reweighted loss shifts the focus to semantically salient tokens with outsized clinical importance. In experiments on ophthalmological report generation, we show that this simple method improves efficiency across multiple data scales, achieving similar report quality with up to ten times less training data.

title: Foveated Reasoning: Stateful, Action-based Visual Focusing for Vision-Language Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a foveated reasoning framework for vision-language models (VLMs) that integrates non-linguistic, action-based visual focusing with textual reasoning within a single, stateful autoregressive decoding pass. Inspired by human foveation, the approach addresses limitations of existing visual focusing methods—namely the compute overhead and interrupted reasoning states of multi-pass methods, and the token overhead and format brittleness of text-grounded methods.

The method formulates VLM decoding as a partially observable Markov decision process where the model can either emit text tokens or trigger continuous foveation actions to acquire high-resolution visual evidence from task-relevant regions. A dedicated foveation policy network predicts bounding box coordinates directly from the model's hidden state, and retrieved evidence is injected into the ongoing decoding stream without restarting generation. Training proceeds in two stages: coldstart supervised fine-tuning to bootstrap foveation behavior, followed by reinforcement learning using group-relative policy optimization with a region regularizer that discourages excessive evidence acquisition.

Experiments on Visual CoT benchmarks and V* Bench demonstrate that the approach outperforms prior visual focusing methods across document understanding, general VQA, and fine-grained perception tasks while consuming substantially fewer visual tokens (averaging 307 tokens versus 1,152 for baselines). The framework adaptively allocates foveation budget based on task difficulty, using minimal evidence for simple queries and multiple foveations for visually demanding cases. This work offers a principled approach to the resolution-efficiency trade-off in VLMs under constrained compute budgets.
original_abstract: Vision-language models benefit from high-resolution images, but the increase in visual-token count incurs high compute overhead. Humans resolve this tension via foveation: a coarse view guides "where to look", while selectively acquired high-acuity evidence refines "what to think". We introduce Foveated Reasoner, an autoregressive vision-language framework that unifies foveation and reasoning within a single decoding trajectory. Starting from a low-resolution view, the model triggers foveation only when needed, retrieves high-resolution evidence from selected regions, and injects it back into the same decoding trajectory. We train the method with a two-stage pipeline: coldstart supervision to bootstrap foveation behavior, followed by reinforcement learning to jointly improve evidence acquisition and task accuracy while discouraging trivial "see-everything" solutions. Experiments show that the method learns effective foveation policies and achieves stronger accuracy under tight visual-token budgets across multiple vision-language benchmarks.

title: Impact-Aware Model Predictive Control for UAV Landing on a Heaving Platform
generated_summary:

The key contribution is the explicit incorporation of rigid-body impact dynamics into the MPC formulation through a Linear Complementarity Problem (LCP) approach that accounts for the coefficient of restitution between the UAV and the landing surface.

The methodology models the landing event as a complementarity-constrained contact problem, where the controller anticipates velocity discontinuities at impact and actively regulates the pre-impact relative velocity between the UAV and the heaving deck. The framework introduces a restitution-aware cost that penalizes approach conditions likely to produce rebounds, while respecting actuator and state constraints. The authors assume known platform vertical position and model contact as a single frictionless point.

Indoor experiments using a Crazyflie 2.1 UAV landing on a custom heaving platform demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves an 86.2% reduction in average rebound height and a 166.7% increase in landing success rate compared to a baseline tracking MPC. The restitution-aware strategy achieves 80% landing success versus 30% for the baseline across varying heave amplitudes and frequencies.

This work represents an important step toward enabling persistent UAV operations in maritime environments by ensuring safe autonomous landings on moving vessels, though extensions to full six-degree-of-freedom dynamics and realistic sea conditions remain as future work.
original_abstract: Landing UAVs on heaving marine platforms is challenging because relative vertical motion can generate large impact forces and cause rebound on touchdown. To address this, we develop an impact-aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that models landing as a velocity-level rigid-body impact governed by Newton's restitution law. We embed this as a linear complementarity problem (LCP) within the MPC dynamics to predict the discontinuous post-impact velocity and suppress rebound. In simulation, restitution-aware prediction reduces pre-impact relative velocity and improves landing robustness. Experiments on a heaving-deck testbed show an 86.2% reduction in post-impact deflection compared to a tracking MPC.

title: Serialisation Strategy Matters: How FHIR Data Format Affects LLM Medication Reconciliation
generated_summary:
This paper systematically investigates how the serialisation format of FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) electronic health record data affects large language model performance on medication reconciliation, the task of identifying a patient's currently active medications. The authors construct a controlled benchmark of 200 synthetic patients generated via Synthea, four serialisation strategies (Raw JSON, Markdown Table, Clinical Narrative, and Chronological Timeline), and five open-weight models ranging from 3.8B to 70B parameters, yielding 4,000 total inference runs evaluated on precision, recall, and F1.

Key findings reveal that serialisation choice has statistically significant, clinically meaningful effects on performance, particularly for smaller models. For models up to 8B parameters, Clinical Narrative format yields the best results, boosting Mistral-7B's F1 from 0.72 (Raw JSON) to 0.91 with no retraining required. At 70B parameters, this ranking reverses, with Raw JSON achieving near-perfect F1 of 0.9956. Across all conditions, omission dominates hallucination as the primary failure mode, and smaller models exhibit a sharp performance ceiling around 7–10 concurrent medications, systematically underserving the highest-risk polypharmacy patients. BioMistral-7B, a domain-pretrained but non-instruction-tuned model, produces zero usable output, demonstrating that instruction-following capability is prerequisite to domain knowledge.

These results establish that serialisation is a consequential deployment decision, offering cost-free performance gains through preprocessing choices alone.
original_abstract: Medication reconciliation at clinical handoffs is a high-stakes, error-prone process. Large language models are increasingly proposed to assist with this task using FHIR-structured patient records, but a fundamental and largely unstudied variable is how the FHIR data is serialised before being passed to the model. We present the first systematic comparison of four FHIR serialisation strategies (Raw JSON, Markdown Table, Clinical Narrative, and Chronological Timeline) across five open-weight models (Phi-3.5-mini, Mistral-7B, BioMistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B) on a controlled benchmark of 200 synthetic patients, totalling 4,000 inference runs. We find that serialisation strategy has a large, statistically significant effect on performance for models up to 8B parameters: Clinical Narrative outperforms Raw JSON by up to 19 F1 points for Mistral-7B (r = 0.617, p < 10^{-10}). This advantage reverses at 70B, where Raw JSON achieves the best mean F1 of 0.9956. In all 20 model and strategy combinations, mean precision exceeds mean recall: omission is the dominant failure mode, with models more often missing an active medication than fabricating one, which changes how clinical safety auditing priorities should be set. Smaller models plateau at roughly 7-10 concurrent active medications, leaving polypharmacy patients, the patients most at risk from reconciliation errors, systematically underserved. BioMistral-7B, a domain-pretrained model without instruction tuning, produces zero usable output in all conditions, showing that domain pretraining alone is not sufficient for structured extraction. These results offer practical, evidence-based format recommendations for clinical LLM deployment: Clinical Narrative for models up to 8B, Raw JSON for 70B and above. The complete pipeline is reproducible on open-source tools running on an AWS g6e.xlarge instance (NVIDIA L40S, 48 GB VRAM).

title: Generative Discovery of Magnetic Insulators under Competing Physical Constraints
generated_summary:
This paper introduces MagMatLLM, a constraint-first generative discovery framework for identifying magnetic insulators—materials that are inherently rare because magnetism and insulating behavior impose competing requirements on electronic structure. Unlike conventional stability-first approaches that generate candidates broadly and apply functional filters post hoc, MagMatLLM embeds target properties—stability, magnetism, and insulating behavior—directly into the generative and selection loop through multi-objective ranking.

The methodology couples a large language model (8B-parameter LLaMA) with an evolutionary search strategy, where the LLM proposes crystal structure modifications guided by explicit physical constraints encoded in structured prompts. Candidates are iteratively generated, evaluated using machine-learning surrogate models, and refined through multi-objective selection. Promising candidates undergo first-principles validation including phonon dispersion calculations for dynamical stability and spin-polarized density functional theory for electronic and magnetic characterization.

From 1,000 parent structures, the framework generates 82 unique, previously unreported candidates, of which 12 pass surrogate-level stability screening. First-principles analysis confirms that 10 of these are dynamically stable, exhibiting finite band gaps and nonzero magnetic moments, including notable compounds Tm₄Co₂Cr₂O₁₂ and Cr₄Nb₂O₁₂. Benchmarking demonstrates that MagMatLLM achieves the highest joint magnetic-insulator success rate at the lowest computational cost compared to baseline methods.

This work establishes a transferable paradigm for multi-constraint materials discovery in data-scarce regimes, applicable beyond magnetic insulators to other material classes governed by competing physical criteria.
original_abstract: Discovering materials that must simultaneously satisfy multiple competing constraints remains a central challenge in computational materials design, particularly in data-scarce regimes where conventional data-driven approaches are least effective. Magnetic insulators represent a stringent example: the electronic conditions that favor magnetic order often also promote metallicity, while insulating behavior suppresses the interactions that stabilize magnetism. As a result, experimentally viable magnetic insulators are rare and difficult to identify through conventional screening. Here, we introduce MagMatLLM, a constraint-guided generative discovery framework that integrates language-model-based crystal generation with evolutionary selection, surrogate screening, and first-principles validation to target simultaneous stability, magnetism, and insulating behavior. Unlike stability-first approaches, the framework enforces functional constraints during generation and selection, steering the search toward sparsely populated regions of materials space defined by competing physical requirements. Using this workflow, we identify twelve previously unreported candidate magnetic insulators, including Tm$_4$Co$_2$Cr$_2$O$_{12}$ and Cr$_4$Nb$_2$O$_{12}$. Of these, ten are dynamically stable by phonon analysis and exhibit finite band gaps and nonzero magnetic moments in spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. Beyond the specific compounds identified here, this work establishes a general constraint-guided paradigm for multi-objective materials discovery in sparse chemical spaces and provides a transferable strategy for the design of quantum materials under competing physical constraints.

title: Distributed Generative Inference of LLM at Internet Scales with Multi-Dimensional Communication Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Bloombee, a geo-distributed large language model inference system designed for Internet-scale deployments where low network bandwidth between nodes becomes the primary performance bottleneck rather than computation. The main contribution is a multi-dimensional communication optimization framework that jointly coordinates several techniques: layer assignment across heterogeneous GPUs, micro-batching to overlap communication with computation, tensor offloading to CPU memory to reduce required GPU count, lossless activation compression, and speculative decoding with learned pruning.

The authors formulate the coordination of these interacting techniques as an optimization problem solved via dynamic programming, accounting for heterogeneous GPU capabilities and network conditions. They introduce a custom lossless compression method that reorganizes floating-point activation data layouts to expose repeated byte patterns, improving compression ratios. For speculative decoding in bandwidth-constrained settings, they deploy a learned classifier that prunes candidate tokens before transmission, reducing communication volume by 60% while preserving 96% of the acceptance rate.

Evaluated across multiple network environments (20-500 Mbps) using LLaMA models (13B-65B), Bloombee achieves up to 1.76× throughput improvement and 43.20% latency reduction compared to state-of-the-art decentralized inference systems Petals and Helix. The system adaptively selects optimal technique combinations based on available bandwidth and model size.

This work demonstrates that communication-centric optimization is essential for making decentralized LLM inference practical, enabling utilization of fragmented GPU resources across the public internet.
original_abstract: Decentralized LLM inference distributes computation among heterogeneous nodes across the internet, offering a performant and cost-efficient solution, alternative to traditional centralized inference. However, the low cross-node network bandwidth makes communication the primary bottleneck. In this paper, we introduce BloomBee, an internet-scale distributed LLM inference framework. BloomBee integrates LLM-layer assignment, micro-batching and tensor offloading to optimize communication from multiple dimensions. Additionally, BloomBee formulates the coordination of these techniques as an optimization problem and solves it using dynamic programming. BloomBee also customizes lossless compression and speculative decoding according to low-bandwidth network settings to reduce communication overhead. We evaluate BloomBee across a spectrum of network environments and show that it improves service throughput by up to 1.76x. It also reduces average latency by up to 43.20% compared to state-of-the-art decentralized LLM inference systems. BloomBee is open-sourced.

title: DWTSumm: Discrete Wavelet Transform for Document Summarization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces DWTSumm, a novel summarization framework that applies the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)—a signal processing technique—to compress document representations for more effective LLM-based summarization of long and domain-specific texts. The framework operates by encoding sentences into embeddings using domain-specific models, then applying DWT to decompose these representations into approximation and detail components that capture global semantic structure and local information variations, respectively. This multiresolution decomposition achieves compression ratios exceeding 60-87.5% while preserving essential semantic content.

The authors evaluate their approach on clinical summarization (MultiClinSum dataset) and legal summarization (CaseSumm dataset) using GPT-4o as the base LLM. Two configurations are tested: DWT-only summaries and a hybrid DWT+GPT model where DWT-compressed representations guide GPT generation. Results demonstrate that both configurations outperform baseline GPT-4o across BERTScore, semantic fidelity, factual consistency, and METEOR metrics. The hybrid model achieves gains of over 2% in BERTScore and 4% in fidelity on clinical tasks while maintaining strong factual consistency. The framework also proves robust across multiple embedding models and decomposition levels, with deeper decompositions maintaining semantic quality despite aggressive compression.

The significance of this work lies in offering a representation-agnostic compression mechanism that reduces hallucinations and information loss in domain-specific summarization without requiring recursive LLM inference, addressing key limitations of hierarchical summarization approaches.
original_abstract: Summarizing long, domain-specific documents with large language models (LLMs) remains challenging due to context limitations, information loss, and hallucinations, particularly in clinical and legal settings. We propose a Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT)-based multi-resolution framework that treats text as a semantic signal and decomposes it into global (approximation) and local (detail) components. Applied to sentence- or word-level embeddings, DWT yields compact representations that preserve overall structure and critical domain-specific details, which are used directly as summaries or to guide LLM generation. Experiments on clinical and legal benchmarks demonstrate comparable ROUGE-L scores. Compared to a GPT-4o baseline, the DWT based summarization consistently improve semantic similarity and grounding, achieving gains of over 2% in BERTScore, more than 4\% in Semantic Fidelity, factual consistency in legal tasks, and large METEOR improvements indicative of preserved domain-specific semantics. Across multiple embedding models, Fidelity reaches up to 97%, suggesting that DWT acts as a semantic denoising mechanism that reduces hallucinations and strengthens factual grounding. Overall, DWT provides a lightweight, generalizable method for reliable long-document and domain-specific summarization with LLMs.

title: Optimizing Diffusion Priors with a Single Observation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a principled framework for addressing misspecified diffusion model priors in imaging inverse problems by forming product-of-experts combinations of multiple priors and optimizing their exponents using Bayesian evidence. The key insight is that rather than fine-tuning diffusion models directly—which risks overfitting to measurement noise—the method restricts adaptation to a small number of interpretable exponent parameters that control the temperature and relative influence of each prior.

The authors propose two strategies for exponent optimization: an evidence scalar field reconstruction method that computes evidence gradients on a grid and solves for the underlying landscape, and a generalized expectation-maximization approach that iteratively maximizes evidence. Both methods require only a single observation and avoid overfitting by limiting degrees of freedom.

Validation on a 1000-dimensional Gaussian toy problem demonstrates that reconstructed evidence fields closely match analytic solutions and that EM trajectories converge to true evidence maximizers. For black hole imaging with Event Horizon Telescope data, combining physics-based GRMHD priors with generic space image priors yields higher evidence than either prior alone, suggesting real observations extend beyond simulation-based assumptions. In text-conditioned image deblurring, the method automatically identifies semantically correct condition weightings, such as discovering a dog image is a golden retriever-corgi mix.

This work reframes prior selection as an inference problem, enabling principled, data-driven balancing of prior strength that improves reconstruction trustworthiness in scientific imaging applications.
original_abstract: While diffusion priors generate high-quality posterior samples across many inverse problems, they are often trained on limited training sets or purely simulated data, thus inheriting the errors and biases of these underlying sources. Current approaches to finetuning diffusion models rely on a large number of observations with varying forward operators, which can be difficult to collect for many applications, and thus lead to overfitting when the measurement set is small. We propose a method for tuning a prior from only a single observation by combining existing diffusion priors into a single product-of-experts prior and identifying the exponents that maximize the Bayesian evidence. We validate our method on real-world inverse problems, including black hole imaging, where the true prior is unknown a priori, and image deblurring with text-conditioned priors. We find that the evidence is often maximized by priors that extend beyond those trained on a single dataset. By generalizing the prior through exponent weighting, our approach enables posterior sampling from both tempered and combined diffusion models, yielding more flexible priors that improve the trustworthiness of the resulting posterior image distribution.

title: InVitroVision: a Multi-Modal AI Model for Automated Description of Embryo Development using Natural Language
generated_summary:
This study introduces InVitroVision, the first application of vision-language models adapted through Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for generating natural language descriptions of embryo morphology in IVF workflows. The approach addresses the inherent subjectivity and inter-observer variability in embryo assessment by producing standardized, clinically meaningful textual descriptions from embryo images.

The authors fine-tuned PaliGemma-2, a pretrained multi-modal model, on 400, 700, and 1,000 annotated embryo images spanning all developmental stages from oocyte to blastocyst, sourced from a public time-lapse dataset. A novel expert-based evaluation metric was developed, assessing embryo recognition, embryonic cell cycle identification, morphological detail accuracy, and positional information correctness, weighted by clinical priority. Two experienced embryologists scored model outputs in a blinded manner.

Results demonstrate that performance improved consistently with training data size, with InVitroVision-1000 achieving the highest overall score (0.66) across evaluation criteria. All fine-tuned models outperformed both the pretrained base model (0.29) and ChatGPT 5.2 (0.50). The domain-adapted model generated more clinically grounded descriptions, appropriately expressing uncertainty and using correct terminology, whereas ChatGPT tended toward over-specification and imprecise language, particularly for compacting and blastocyst-stage embryos.

These findings demonstrate that parameter-efficient domain adaptation of vision-language models can enhance interpretability and standardization in embryo assessment, with potential applications in clinical documentation, quality assurance, and retrieval-augmented decision support systems in reproductive medicine.
original_abstract: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in IVF has shown promise in improving consistency and standardization of decisions, but often relies on annotated data and does not make use of the multimodal nature of IVF data. We investigated whether foundational vision-language models can be fine-tuned to predict natural language descriptions of embryo morphology and development. Using a publicly available embryo time-lapse dataset, we fine-tuned PaliGemma-2, a multi-modal vision-language model, with only 1,000 images and corresponding captions, describing embryo morphology, embryonic cell cycle and developmental stage. Our results show that the fine-tuned model, InVitroVision, outperformed a commercial model, ChatGPT 5.2, and base models in overall metrics, with performance improving with larger training datasets. This study demonstrates the potential of foundational vision-language models to generalize to IVF tasks with limited data, enabling the prediction of natural language descriptions of embryo morphology and development. This approach may facilitate the use of large language models to retrieve information and scientific evidence from relevant publications and guidelines, and has implications for few-shot adaptation to multiple downstream tasks in IVF.

title: Clinically-Informed Modeling for Pediatric Brain Tumor Classification from Whole-Slide Histopathology Images
generated_summary:
This paper introduces an expert-guided contrastive learning (EGCL) framework for weakly supervised classification of pediatric brain tumors from whole-slide histopathology images, addressing challenges of data scarcity, class imbalance, and fine-grained diagnostic heterogeneity unique to pediatric neuro-oncology.

The methodology employs a frozen UNI2-h pathology foundation model for patch-level feature extraction, followed by CLAM-based multiple instance learning for slide-level aggregation. The key innovation lies in integrating contrastive learning at the slide-representation level during MIL fine-tuning, with an expert-guided variant that up-weights clinically confusable tumor subtypes as hard negatives in a queue-based supervised contrastive loss. The framework is evaluated across multiple classification granularities (2-, 3-, 6-, and 7-class tasks) using patient-stratified 10-fold cross-validation.

Key results demonstrate that contrastive learning variants reduce systematic confusions between diagnostically adjacent classes, with performance following an inverted-U trend relative to contrastive loss weight. Expert-guided error analysis reveals complementary strengths: contrastive learning corrects errors caused by superficial morphologic overlap but can introduce new confusions by overweighting features like cellular density. Some cases remain intrinsically ambiguous on H&E alone, requiring molecular or clinical context for resolution.

The work is significant as one of the first systematic studies of contrastive representation shaping for pediatric brain tumor computational pathology, demonstrating that incorporating clinical domain knowledge into learning objectives can improve fine-grained diagnostic separation under realistic low-sample conditions.
original_abstract: Accurate diagnosis of pediatric brain tumors, starting with histopathology, presents unique challenges for deep learning, including severe data scarcity, class imbalance, and fine-grained morphologic overlap across diagnostically distinct subtypes. While pathology foundation models have advanced patch-level representation learning, their effective adaptation to weakly supervised pediatric brain tumor classification under limited data remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce an expert-guided contrastive fine-tuning framework for pediatric brain tumor diagnosis from whole-slide images (WSI). Our approach integrates contrastive learning into slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL) to explicitly regularize the geometry of slide-level representations during downstream fine-tuning. We propose both a general supervised contrastive setting and an expert-guided variant that incorporates clinically informed hard negatives targeting diagnostically confusable subtypes. Through comprehensive experiments on pediatric brain tumor WSI classification under realistic low-sample and class-imbalanced conditions, we demonstrate that contrastive fine-tuning yields measurable improvements in fine-grained diagnostic distinctions. Our experimental analyses reveal complementary strengths across different contrastive strategies, with expert-guided hard negatives promoting more compact intra-class representations and improved inter-class separation. This work highlights the importance of explicitly shaping slide-level representations for robust fine-grained classification in data-scarce pediatric pathology settings.

title: TRACES: Tagging Reasoning Steps for Adaptive Cost-Efficient Early-Stopping
generated_summary:
This paper introduces TRACES, an interpretable early-stopping framework for Language Reasoning Models (LRMs) that reduces excessive token generation during inference while preserving accuracy. The core contribution is a novel approach to monitoring reasoning steps in real-time by classifying their semantic content to determine when generation can be safely terminated.

The methodology centers on two components. First, the authors propose ReasonType, a fine-grained taxonomy of reasoning step types that categorizes steps into distinct classes (e.g., answer construction versus answer evaluation). Second, they develop a lightweight Step-Tagging classifier that identifies the type of each reasoning step as it is generated. Through analysis of step-type distributions, the authors discover that LRMs exhibit a characteristic transition pattern after generating a correct answer, shifting from constructive reasoning steps to evaluative ones. TRACES exploits this transition signal to trigger early stopping dynamically.

The framework is evaluated across three open-source LRMs (DeepSeek-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-Qwen-14B, and QwQ-32B) on five reasoning benchmarks including GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA, and MMLU-Pro. Results demonstrate 20–50% reduction in token count with minimal accuracy loss, with the largest efficiency gains observed on more complex tasks.

The significance of this work lies in providing an interpretable, model-agnostic approach to inference efficiency that leverages semantic understanding of reasoning processes rather than relying on static budgets or opaque compression methods, offering practical cost and latency savings for deploying reasoning models.
original_abstract: The field of Language Reasoning Models (LRMs) has been very active over the past few years with advances in training and inference techniques enabling LRMs to reason longer, and more accurately. However, a growing body of studies show that LRMs are still inefficient, over-generating verification and reflection steps. Additionally, the high-level role of each reasoning step and how different step types contribute to the generation of correct answers, is largely underexplored. To address this challenge, we introduce TRACES (Tagging of the Reasoning steps enabling Adaptive Cost-Efficient early-Stopping), a lightweight framework that tags reasoning steps in real-time, and enable adaptive, cost-efficient early stopping of large-language-model inferences. Building on this framework we monitor reasoning behaviors during inferences, and we find that LRMs tend to shift their reasoning behavior after reaching a correct answer. We demonstrate that the monitoring of the specific type of steps can produce effective interpretable early stopping criteria. title: StyleVAR: Controllable Image Style Transfer via Visual Autoregressive Modeling
