Participants scored significantly higher on informedness quizzes after using KUBO (p = 0.010), suggesting enhanced comprehension and recall. Subjectively, KUBO was rated higher on ease of use, satisfaction, and perceived effectiveness, with 19 of 20 participants preferring its clarity of information. Order effects analysis revealed that starting with KUBO helped participants build clearer mental models of information.

The study demonstrates that purpose-built hyperlocal platforms emphasizing verified sources and structured content can meaningfully improve community information access, though the authors acknowledge limitations including the prototype's comparison against a live application and the digitally native participant sample.
original_abstract: Effective hyperlocal communication is critical in the Philippines, where delayed or algorithm-filtered updates can leave residents uninformed about emergency advisories and community events. We conducted a user-centered study consisting of contextual inquiry and semi-structured interviews to identify four key barriers: delayed alerts, algorithm-driven noise, language gaps, and digital divides. Guided by these insights, we designed KUBO (Kumunidad at Balitang Opisyal), a prototype that integrates a home module for verified local government unit advisories and curated headlines, and a community module for resident-powered neighborhood reports and discussions. Using a within-subjects evaluation design, KUBO significantly reduced task completion times (p-value < 0.001), improved information recall on post-task quizzes (p-value = 0.010), and yielded higher user satisfaction ratings for ease of use, overall satisfaction, and perceived effectiveness compared to Facebook, the commonly used communication platform in the Philippines. These results demonstrate that a dual-channel, inclusive platform can substantially enhance real-time information access, comprehension, and civic engagement in hyperlocal settings.

title: Escaping the Agreement Trap: Defensibility Signals for Evaluating Rule-Governed AI
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Defensibility Framework for evaluating AI systems operating under explicit governance rules, addressing what the authors term the "Agreement Trap"—the problem that standard agreement-based metrics like F₁ systematically mischaracterize policy-compliant decisions as errors when multiple valid outcomes exist under ambiguous rules.

The framework formalizes policy-grounded correctness through three defensibility levels (Robustly Defensible, Plausibly Defensible, and Indefensible) and introduces two core metrics: the Defensibility Index (DI), measuring the rate of policy-defensible decisions, and the Ambiguity Index (AI), quantifying normative underspecification in rule structures. A structured audit model evaluates whether decisions are logically derivable from explicit rules rather than simply matching human labels. The authors also introduce the Policy Defensibility Score (PDS), a logprob-based stability signal extracted at zero additional cost from reasoning traces, and a Governance Gate that restricts automation to high-confidence decision cohorts.

Validated on over 193,000 Reddit moderation decisions across 270+ communities, the framework reveals a 33–46 percentage point gap between F₁ and DI, with 79.8–80.6% of false negatives being policy-grounded decisions rather than true errors. Fleet-level diagnostics distinguish communities exhibiting model error from those with genuine policy ambiguity, enabling targeted interventions.

The framework's significance lies in shifting AI evaluation from agreement-based scoring to policy-grounded verification, enabling safer automation deployment while preserving human judgment where rules are deliberately flexible.
original_abstract: Content moderation systems are typically evaluated by measuring agreement with human labels. In rule-governed environments this assumption fails: multiple decisions may be logically consistent with the governing policy, and agreement metrics penalize valid decisions while mischaracterizing ambiguity as error -- a failure mode we term the Agreement Trap. We formalize evaluation as policy-grounded correctness and introduce the Defensibility Index (DI) and Ambiguity Index (AI). To estimate reasoning stability without additional audit passes, we introduce the Probabilistic Defensibility Signal (PDS), derived from audit-model token logprobs. We harness LLM reasoning traces as a governance signal rather than a classification output by deploying the audit model not to decide whether content violates policy, but to verify whether a proposed decision is logically derivable from the governing rule hierarchy. We validate the framework on 193,000+ Reddit moderation decisions across multiple communities and evaluation cohorts, finding a 33-46.6 percentage-point gap between agreement-based and policy-grounded metrics, with 79.8-80.6% of the model's false negatives corresponding to policy-grounded decisions rather than true errors. We further show that measured ambiguity is driven by rule specificity: auditing 37,286 identical decisions under three tiers of the same community rules reduces AI by 10.8 pp while DI remains stable. Repeated-sampling analysis attributes PDS variance primarily to governance ambiguity rather than decoding noise. A Governance Gate built on these signals achieves 78.6% automation coverage with 64.9% risk reduction. Together, these results show that evaluation in rule-governed environments should shift from agreement with historical labels to reasoning-grounded validity under explicit rules.

title: SpeechParaling-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Paralinguistic-Aware Speech Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SpeechParaling-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating paralinguistic-aware speech generation in Large Audio Language Models (LALMs). Unlike traditional benchmarks that focus primarily on text-to-speech consistency, this benchmark assesses models' ability to generate speech with appropriate non-verbal features such as tone, emotion, pace, and speaking style.

The benchmark covers over 100 distinct paralinguistic features across more than 1,000 English-Chinese parallel speech queries, significantly expanding coverage compared to existing benchmarks that typically address fewer than 50 features. The evaluation is structured around three progressively complex tasks: Paralanguage Control (generating speech with specific paralinguistic features), Dynamic Variation (modulating features within utterances), and Situational Adaptation (context-aware paralinguistic alignment with users). To address the inherent subjectivity of paralinguistic evaluation, the authors propose a pairwise comparison framework that evaluates candidate responses against a fixed baseline, yielding more stable and reliable assessments than absolute scoring approaches.

Extensive evaluations of leading LALMs reveal several key findings: comprehensive control across diverse paralinguistic dimensions remains challenging, dynamic regulation of paralinguistic features represents a common bottleneck, and misinterpretation of paralinguistic cues in user speech accounts for 43.3% of failures in situational dialogue tasks. These findings highlight critical gaps in current voice assistants' capabilities and underscore the need for enhanced paralinguistic modeling to achieve more natural, human-aligned spoken interactions.
original_abstract: Paralinguistic cues are essential for natural human-computer interaction, yet their evaluation in Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) remains limited by coarse feature coverage and the inherent subjectivity of assessment. To address these challenges, we introduce SpeechParaling-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for paralinguistic-aware speech generation. It expands existing coverage from fewer than 50 to over 100 fine-grained features, supported by more than 1,000 English-Chinese parallel speech queries, and is organized into three progressively challenging tasks: fine-grained control, intra-utterance variation, and context-aware adaptation. To enable reliable evaluation, we further develop a pairwise comparison pipeline, in which candidate responses are evaluated against a fixed baseline by an LALM-based judge. By framing evaluation as relative preference rather than absolute scoring, this approach mitigates subjectivity and yields more stable and scalable assessments without costly human annotation. Extensive experiments reveal substantial limitations in current LALMs. Even leading proprietary models struggle with comprehensive static control and dynamic modulation of paralinguistic features, while failure to correctly interpret paralinguistic cues accounts for 43.3% of errors in situational dialogue. These findings underscore the need for more robust paralinguistic modeling toward human-aligned voice assistants.

title: DeVI: Physics-based Dexterous Human-Object Interaction via Synthetic Video Imitation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces DeVI (Dexterous Video Imitation), a framework that enables physics-based dexterous human-object interaction (HOI) by imitating synthetic videos generated from text-conditioned video diffusion models, eliminating the need for expensive 3D motion capture demonstrations.

The core methodological innovation is a hybrid imitation target that combines 3D reconstructed references for the human body with 2D trajectory tracking for objects. This design addresses the fundamental challenge that reconstructing accurate 3D object poses from 2D video remains unreliable, particularly for hand-object spatial alignment. The framework renders an initial scene containing a humanoid and objects, generates an HOI video using an image-to-video diffusion model conditioned on text prompts, then extracts imitation targets through world-grounded human mesh recovery enhanced by a visual HOI alignment optimization. A humanoid control policy is trained via reinforcement learning using Proximal Policy Optimization with a hybrid tracking reward combining 3D human tracking and 2D object tracking.

Evaluated against state-of-the-art methods (PhysHOI, SkillMimic, InterMimic) on the GRAB dataset, DeVI outperforms all baselines across human and object tracking metrics, despite using only 2D object trajectories rather than 6D poses. The framework demonstrates generalization across 20 diverse objects and multi-object scenes with varied interactions.

DeVI's significance lies in democratizing physics-based HOI simulation by leveraging video generation models as interaction-aware motion planners, enabling zero-shot generalization to novel objects and scenarios without costly 3D data collection.
original_abstract: Recent advances in video generative models enable the synthesis of realistic human-object interaction videos across a wide range of scenarios and object categories, including complex dexterous manipulations that are difficult to capture with motion capture systems. While the rich interaction knowledge embedded in these synthetic videos holds strong potential for motion planning in dexterous robotic manipulation, their limited physical fidelity and purely 2D nature make them difficult to use directly as imitation targets in physics-based character control. We present DeVI (Dexterous Video Imitation), a novel framework that leverages text-conditioned synthetic videos to enable physically plausible dexterous agent control for interacting with unseen target objects. To overcome the imprecision of generative 2D cues, we introduce a hybrid tracking reward that integrates 3D human tracking with robust 2D object tracking. Unlike methods relying on high-quality 3D kinematic demonstrations, DeVI requires only the generated video, enabling zero-shot generalization across diverse objects and interaction types. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeVI outperforms existing approaches that imitate 3D human-object interaction demonstrations, particularly in modeling dexterous hand-object interactions. We further validate the effectiveness of DeVI in multi-object scenes and text-driven action diversity, showcasing the advantage of using video as an HOI-aware motion planner.

title: Dynamic Construction of the Lovász Local Lemma
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the first systematic study of the Lovász Local Lemma (LLL) in a fully dynamic setting, where constraints (flaws) can be inserted or deleted over time, and the algorithm must maintain a flawless object after each update. The main contribution is a general framework that extends the powerful static LLL machinery to dynamic settings while achieving only polylogarithmic overhead per update, even against adaptive and clairvoyant adversaries.

The methodology builds upon the Moser–Tardos resampling framework and the general Achlioptas–Iliopoulos–Sinclair (AIS) framework. The authors design resampling algorithms that, upon each flaw update, efficiently repair the current solution by iteratively addressing violated constraints. They analyze convergence by leveraging existing LLL convergence criteria and extend guarantees to clairvoyant adversaries through union bounds over all possible update sequences.

The framework yields several concrete dynamic algorithms: maintaining satisfying assignments for dynamic k-CNF formulas in O(dk²) amortized time, triangle-free list coloring under edge updates in O(Δ³) amortized time, Leighton–Maggs–Rao packet scheduling under path updates in O(1) amortized time for constant congestion and dilation, and (1+ε)Δ-edge coloring in polylogarithmic amortized time. Several of these are the first known dynamic algorithms for their respective problems.

The significance lies in establishing the LLL as a general-purpose dynamic algorithmic tool, enabling near-black-box transformation of static LLL applications into efficient dynamic algorithms resilient to the strongest adversarial models.
original_abstract: This paper proves that a wide class of local search algorithms extend as is to the fully dynamic setting with an adaptive adversary, achieving an amortized $\tilde{O}(1)$ number of local-search steps per update. A breakthrough by Moser (2009) introduced the witness-tree and entropy compression techniques for analyzing local resampling processes for the Lovász Local Lemma. These methods have since been generalized and expanded to analyze a wide variety of local search algorithms that can efficiently find solutions to many important local constraint satisfaction problems. These algorithms either extend a partial valid assignment and backtrack by unassigning variables when constraints become violated, or they iteratively fix violated constraints by resampling their variables. These local resampling or backtracking procedures are incredibly flexible, practical, and simple to specify and implement. Yet, they can be shown to be extremely efficient on static instances, typically performing only (sub)-linear number of fixing steps. The main technical challenge lies in proving conditions that guarantee such rapid convergence. This paper extends these convergence results to fully dynamic settings, where an adaptive adversary may add or remove constraints. We prove that applying the same simple local search procedures to fix old or newly introduced violations leads to a total number of resampling steps near-linear in the number of adversarial updates. Our result is very general and yields several immediate corollaries. For example, letting $Δ$ denote the maximum degree, for a constant $ε$ and $Δ= \text{poly}(\log n)$, we can maintain a $(1+ε) Δ$-edge coloring in $\text{poly}(\log n)$ amortized update time against an adaptive adversary. The prior work for this regime has exponential running time in $\sqrt{\log n}$ [Christiansen, SODA '26].

title: Parallel-SFT: Improving Zero-Shot Cross-Programming-Language Transfer for Code RL
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of zero-shot cross-programming-language (PL) transfer in reinforcement learning (RL) for code, where a model trained via RL on one source PL is evaluated on a different target PL. The authors find that Llama-3.1 exhibits poor cross-PL transferability, with RL gains in a source language failing to generalize—or even degrading performance—in target languages.

To overcome this limitation, the authors propose Parallel-SFT, a supervised fine-tuning approach that incorporates synthetically generated "parallel programs"—functionally equivalent code solutions across multiple programming languages—into the SFT data mixture. These parallel programs are created by translating Python solutions into seven other languages using a large language model, then filtering translations through test-case verification to ensure execution equivalence. Three SFT mixtures are compared: monolingual, multilingual non-parallel (no question overlap across languages), and multilingual parallel (same questions across all languages).

Experiments on code generation and code validation tasks demonstrate that Parallel-SFT consistently achieves the best cross-PL transfer performance during downstream RL, outperforming both monolingual and non-parallel multilingual baselines. Remarkably, Parallel-SFT sometimes surpasses the oracle setting where both SFT and RL use target-language data directly. Analysis reveals that Parallel-SFT induces higher representational similarity between functionally equivalent programs across languages, even for unseen PLs, supporting the hypothesis that it creates more language-general code representations that enable better propagation of RL-learned policy improvements across programming languages.
original_abstract: Modern language models demonstrate impressive coding capabilities in common programming languages (PLs), such as C++ and Python, but their performance in lower-resource PLs is often limited by training data availability. In principle, however, most programming skills are universal across PLs, so the capability acquired in one PL should transfer to others. In this work, we propose the task of zero-shot cross-programming-language transfer for code RL. We find that, for Llama-3.1, RL training for code generation in a source PL fails to improve, and sometimes even degrades, the performance on other target PLs. To address this, we hypothesize that effective RL transfer requires a generalizable SFT initialization before RL. We thus propose **Parallel-SFT**, an SFT strategy that incorporates "parallel programs" -- functionally equivalent code implemented in multiple PLs -- into the data mixture. We demonstrate that this improves transferability: when we subsequently perform RL on our Parallel-SFT model, we observe better generalization to unseen PLs. Analysis of the model internal representations reveals that Parallel-SFT leads to a more functionality-centric latent space, where equivalent programs across PLs are more tightly clustered, which we hypothesize to contribute to the improved transferability.

title: PokeVLA: Empowering Pocket-Sized Vision-Language-Action Model with Comprehensive World Knowledge Guidance
generated_summary:

The approach employs a two-stage training framework. In the first stage, a compact embodied vision-language model (PokeVLM) is pre-trained on a curated multimodal dataset of approximately 2.4 million samples spanning visual question answering, spatial grounding, affordance learning, and embodied reasoning. In the second stage, manipulation-relevant representations are learned through multi-view consistent semantic segmentation of manipulation targets using a learnable special token, along with geometric feature alignment via a feed-forward geometry foundation model. Action queries then aggregate these visual, semantic, and spatial features through cross-attention and inject them into the action expert for precise action prediction.

Despite using only a 1.22 billion parameter backbone, PokeVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, outperforming OpenVLA-OFT and VLA-Adapter by 4.0% and 2.5% in success rate respectively. In generalization experiments, it surpasses these baselines by 9.7% and 20.2%. Real-world evaluations show 12.5% improvement over comparable methods, extending to 20.0% under environmental perturbations.

This work demonstrates that compact VLA models enriched with comprehensive embodied priors and manipulation-relevant representations can achieve robust, generalizable robotic manipulation without requiring massive model scales.
original_abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have opened new avenues for robot manipulation, yet existing methods exhibit limited efficiency and a lack of high-level knowledge and spatial awareness. To address these challenges, we propose PokeVLA, a lightweight yet powerful foundation model for embodied manipulation that effectively infuses vision-language understanding into action learning. Our framework introduces a two-stage training paradigm: first, we pre-train a compact vision-language model (PokeVLM) on a curated multimodal dataset of 2.4M samples encompassing spatial grounding, affordance, and embodied reasoning tasks; second, we inject manipulation-relevant representations into the action space through multi-view goal-aware semantics learning, geometry alignment, and a novel action expert. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark and in real-world deployment, outperforming comparable baselines in success rate and robustness under diverse perturbations. To foster reproducibility and community progress, we will open-source our code, model weights, and the scripts for the curated pre-training dataset. Project page: https://getterupper.github.io/PokeVLA

title: AVISE: Framework for Evaluating the Security of AI Systems
generated_summary:

The framework supports black-box, white-box, and grey-box testing approaches and accounts for the stochastic nature of AI models by allowing multiple test executions under identical conditions for statistically robust assessments.

To demonstrate the framework's capabilities, the authors develop an automated SET based on the multi-turn jailbreak attack "Red Queen," augmented with an Adversarial Language Model (ALM) that dynamically adapts attack prompts based on target model responses. This SET is evaluated against several recently released language models. Key results reveal that while target models demonstrate robustness against static template-based attacks, ALM-augmented attacks expose significant vulnerabilities across all tested models. Failure rates range from 0.08 to 0.84, with Nemotron 3 Super 120B and Qwen 3.5 35B proving most robust, while Ministral 3.2 14B is most vulnerable. The Evaluation Language Model achieves 92% accuracy and 0.91 F1-score when classifying ALM-augmented test outcomes.

The findings underscore that multi-turn adversarial attacks remain a persistent challenge despite safety alignment efforts, validating the need for systematic, automated security evaluation tools like AVISE to help identify and address AI vulnerabilities before deployment.
original_abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed across critical domains, their security vulnerabilities pose growing risks of high-profile exploits and consequential system failures. Yet systematic approaches to evaluating AI security remain underdeveloped. In this paper, we introduce AVISE (AI Vulnerability Identification and Security Evaluation), a modular open-source framework for identifying vulnerabilities in and evaluating the security of AI systems and models. As a demonstration of the framework, we extend the theory-of-mind-based multi-turn Red Queen attack into an Adversarial Language Model (ALM) augmented attack and develop an automated Security Evaluation Test (SET) for discovering jailbreak vulnerabilities in language models. The SET comprises 25 test cases and an Evaluation Language Model (ELM) that determines whether each test case was able to jailbreak the target model, achieving 92% accuracy, an F1-score of 0.91, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.83. We evaluate nine recently released language models of diverse sizes with the SET and find that all are vulnerable to the augmented Red Queen attack to varying degrees. AVISE provides researchers and industry practitioners with an extensible foundation for developing and deploying automated SETs, offering a concrete step toward more rigorous and reproducible AI security evaluation.

title: An Analysis of Attack Vectors Against FIDO2 Authentication
generated_summary:
This paper presents a systematic analysis of attack vectors targeting FIDO2-based authentication (passkeys), evaluating the feasibility, complexity, and prerequisites of each potential attack. The main contribution is a comprehensive threat taxonomy that classifies attacks against FIDO2 into categories including victim key extraction, victim impersonation, Bluetooth man-in-the-middle, authenticator deception, attacker passkey registration, passkey reduction, infected authenticator, and relying party impersonation—each rated by difficulty level.

The authors employ both theoretical analysis and practical experimentation. Two attacks are demonstrated: an infected authenticator attack, where KeePassXC's source code is modified to generate known key pairs, enabling the attacker to authenticate as the victim on a Google account; and an authenticator deception attack, combining DNS spoofing, ARP poisoning, and a fraudulent TLS certificate to relay authentication challenges from a legitimate relying party (linear.app) through a phishing site to the victim's authenticator.

Key findings reveal that all identified attack vectors require either prior compromise of the victim's device or close physical proximity—no remote exploitation of FIDO2 without device compromise is demonstrated. Every attack demands substantial effort and multiple preconditions, significantly raising the bar compared to password-based attacks.

The work confirms that FIDO2 largely fulfills its security promises, as passkeys cannot be phished through conventional techniques. However, the authors note that fallback password authentication and device-level compromises remain potential weaknesses, suggesting future research into automating these attacks and exploring remote exploitation possibilities.
original_abstract: Phishing attacks remain one of the most prevalent threats to online security, with the Anti-Phishing Working Group reporting over 890,000 attacks in Q3 2025 alone. Traditional password-based authentication is particularly vulnerable to such attacks, prompting the development of more secure alternatives. This paper examines passkeys, also known as FIDO2, which claim to provide phishing-resistant authentication through asymmetric cryptography. In this approach, a private key is stored on a user's device, the authenticator, while the server stores the corresponding public key. During authentication, the server generates a challenge that the user signs with the private key; the server then verifies the signature and establishes a session. We present passkey workflows and review state-of-the-art attack vectors from related work alongside newly identified approaches. Two attacks are implemented and evaluated: the Infected Authenticator attack, which generates attacker-known keys on a corrupted authenticator, and the Authenticator Deception attack, which spoofs a target website by modifying the browser's certificate authority store, installing a valid certificate, and intercepting user traffic. An attacker relays a legitimate challenge from the real server to a user, who signs it, allowing the attacker to authenticate as the victim. Our results demonstrate that successful attacks on passkeys require substantial effort and resources. The claim that passkeys are phishing-resistant largely holds true, significantly raising the bar compared to traditional password-based authentication.

title: FedSIR: Spectral Client Identification and Relabeling for Federated Learning with Noisy Labels
generated_summary:
This paper introduces FedSIR, a multi-stage federated learning framework that addresses the challenge of noisy labels by leveraging the spectral geometry of client feature representations, offering a novel alternative to conventional loss-dynamics or prediction-based approaches. The framework operates in three stages: first, it identifies clean and noisy clients by analyzing class-wise feature subspaces through singular value decomposition, where clean clients exhibit low between-class similarity in their principal directions while noisy clients show higher cross-class mixing. Second, it constructs spectral reference subspaces from clean clients' dominant directions and residual subspaces to conservatively relabel potentially corrupted samples on noisy clients, requiring agreement between complementary spectral criteria. Third, it integrates noise-aware federated optimization combining logit-adjusted loss, knowledge distillation for noisy clients using the global model as a teacher, and distance-aware aggregation that downweights noisy client updates based on their deviation from clean clients.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 under symmetric label noise rates ranging from 30% to 90% and varying levels of data heterogeneity demonstrate that FedSIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including FedELC, FedNoRo, and FedNed. The framework proves particularly effective under severe noise and high non-IID conditions. Importantly, FedSIR requires no centralized clean data, no noise transition matrix estimation, and minimal communication overhead, making it practically suitable for privacy-preserving federated settings with unreliable annotations.
original_abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data; however, the presence of noisy labels across distributed clients can severely degrade the learning performance. In this paper, we propose FedSIR, a multi-stage framework for robust FL under noisy labels. Different from existing approaches that mainly rely on designing noise-tolerant loss functions or exploiting loss dynamics during training, our method leverages the spectral structure of client feature representations to identify and mitigate label noise. Our framework consists of three key components. First, we identify clean and noisy clients by analyzing the spectral consistency of class-wise feature subspaces with minimal communication overhead. Second, clean clients provide spectral references that enable noisy clients to relabel potentially corrupted samples using both dominant class directions and residual subspaces. Third, we employ a noise-aware training strategy that integrates logit-adjusted loss, knowledge distillation, and distance-aware aggregation to further stabilize federated optimization. Extensive experiments on standard FL benchmarks demonstrate that FedSIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods for FL with noisy labels. The code is available at https://github.com/sinagh72/FedSIR.

title: Closing the Domain Gap in Biomedical Imaging by In-Context Control Samples
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CS-ARM-BN, a control-stabilized meta-learning method that leverages negative control samples—unperturbed reference samples routinely included in biomedical experiments—to address batch effects in microscopy imaging. Batch effects arise from non-biological variations across experimental conditions and severely degrade deep learning model generalization.

The authors frame batch effect correction as a multi-source domain adaptation problem and build upon Adaptive Risk Minimization with Batch Normalization (ARM-BN), a meta-learning approach that adapts normalization statistics at test time. The key innovation is using negative control samples, rather than all available test samples, to compute batch normalization statistics during both training and inference. This decouples the adaptation signal from the class composition of the test batch.

Experiments on the large-scale JUMP-CP microscopy dataset demonstrate that while existing methods like AdaBN, TENT, and ARM-BN perform well under mild domain shift, they degrade significantly under label shift—when the class distribution of test data differs from training data—a common scenario in drug screening. CS-ARM-BN maintains robust performance across varying degrees of label shift and small batch sizes, nearly closing the generalization gap between in-domain and unseen-batch performance.

The significance of this work lies in exploiting an existing experimental design feature—negative controls—to stabilize domain adaptation without retraining, making the approach practical for real-world biomedical imaging pipelines where new experimental batches arrive sequentially with unpredictable class compositions.
original_abstract: The central problem in biomedical imaging are batch effects: systematic technical variations unrelated to the biological signal of interest. These batch effects critically undermine experimental reproducibility and are the primary cause of failure of deep learning systems on new experimental batches, preventing their practical use in the real world. Despite years of research, no method has succeeded in closing this performance gap for deep learning models. We propose Control-Stabilized Adaptive Risk Minimization via Batch Normalization (CS-ARM-BN), a meta-learning adaptation method that exploits negative control samples. Such unperturbed reference images are present in every experimental batch by design and serve as stable context for adaptation. We validate our novel method on Mechanism-of-Action (MoA) classification, a crucial task for drug discovery, on the large-scale JUMP-CP dataset. The accuracy of standard ResNets drops from 0.939 $\pm$ 0.005, on the training domain, to 0.862 $\pm$ 0.060 on data from new experimental batches. Foundation models, even after Typical Variation Normalization, fail to close this gap. We are the first to show that meta-learning approaches close the domain gap by achieving 0.935 $\pm$ 0.018. If the new experimental batches exhibit strong domain shifts, such as being generated in a different lab, meta-learning approaches can be stabilized with control samples, which are always available in biomedical experiments. Our work shows that batch effects in bioimaging data can be effectively neutralized through principled in-context adaptation, which also makes them practically usable and efficient.

title: From Meme to Method: Rethinking Animal Adoption Platforms through the Cat Distribution System
generated_summary:
This study demonstrates how the internet meme known as the "Cat Distribution System" (CDS)—which humorously frames cat adoption as cats "choosing" their owners through serendipitous encounters—can be translated into a meaningful design framework for digital animal adoption platforms. The authors argue that conventional adoption platforms rely on rigid search-and-filter mechanisms that overlook the informal, community-driven, and proximity-based dynamics that characterize real-world adoption experiences.

The researchers employed a qualitative methodology combining semi-structured interviews with eight participants involved in animal welfare in the Philippines and observational analysis of 30 publicly available social media videos depicting spontaneous human-cat encounters. Using thematic analysis, they identified four key dimensions shaping adoption behavior: serendipity, proximity, environment, and decision-making. These themes informed the development of the Serendipitous Adoption Framework, which served as the basis for a prototype platform called Meowtify, incorporating features such as location-based matchmaking, community reporting, and playful discovery mechanisms. Evaluation with 35 users yielded consistently high usability ratings, with participants praising the platform's simplicity, convenience, and community orientation.

The study's significance lies in demonstrating that culturally resonant narratives—even those originating from internet folklore—can serve as legitimate foundations for design research in human-computer interaction, offering pathways toward adoption systems that are both effective and contextually grounded in users' lived experiences.
original_abstract: The internet folklore of the Cat Distribution System (CDS) humorously suggests that cats are "assigned" to people rather than intentionally sought. Beyond its playful origins, CDS reflects a culturally resonant way people perceive and engage in adoption, and this user context can guide the redesign and improvement of adoption systems. In the Philippines, where an estimated 13.11 million stray cats and dogs place the country sixth worldwide in overpopulation, this framing offers a novel way to rethink adoption platforms. We developed a prototype application inspired by CDS principles, focusing on features such as algorithmic matchmaking, community reporting, and proximity-based discovery. An initial evaluation with potential users (n=35) indicated that the system was positively received for its ease of use and its alignment with users' intuitive expectations, though participants highlighted areas for improvement in transparency of matchmaking and owner-adopter communication. The findings suggest that culturally embedded metaphors like CDS can shape mental models, making adoption processes feel more serendipitous and less transactional.

title: Early Detection of Latent Microstructure Regimes in Limit Order Books
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the fundamental limitation that conventional market stress detectors—based on order flow imbalance, spread widening, and volatility—are inherently reactive, firing only after stress has already manifested in limit order books (LOBs). The authors propose that a latent "build-up" phase of liquidity deterioration precedes observable stress and can be detected early.

The methodology centers on a three-regime causal model (stable, latent build-up, stress) where build-up produces persistent but weak drift in LOB features before stress onset. The authors prove identifiability of the latent regime sequence and derive two theoretical guarantees: a sufficient drift-to-noise condition for positive expected lead-time, and a closed-form lower bound on early detection probability. They construct a trigger-based detector combining MAX-channel aggregation, a rising-edge condition, and adaptive threshold calibration.

Across 200 simulation runs, the adaptive trigger achieves mean lead-time of +18.6 timesteps with perfect precision and 54% coverage, while traditional imbalance and volatility detectors exhibit negative lead-times. The 46% missed detection rate concentrates in low-SNR, short build-up episodes, consistent with theoretical predictions. Depth erosion and HMM entropy drive detection, accounting for all first triggers. A preliminary application on BTC/USDT order book data shows +38-second mean lead-time while all baselines remain reactive.

This work establishes that pre-stress liquidity deterioration is detectable before observable dislocations, arguing that depth-based structural signals are more causally proximate to stress onset than flow-based observables, with implications for financial early warning system design.
original_abstract: Limit order books can transition rapidly from stable to stressed conditions, yet standard early-warning signals such as order flow imbalance and short-term volatility are inherently reactive. We formalise this limitation via a three-regime causal data-generating process (stable $\to$ latent build-up $\to$ stress) in which a latent deterioration phase creates a prediction window prior to observable stress. Under mild assumptions on temporal drift and regime persistence, we establish identifiability of the latent build-up regime and derive guarantees for strictly positive expected lead-time and non-trivial probability of early detection. We propose a trigger-based detector combining MAX aggregation of complementary signal channels, a rising-edge condition, and adaptive thresholding. Across 200 simulations, the method achieves mean lead-time $+18.6 \pm 3.2$ timesteps with perfect precision and moderate coverage, outperforming classical change-point and microstructure baselines. A preliminary application to one week of BTC/USDT order book data shows consistent positive lead-times while baselines remain reactive. Results degrade in low signal-to-noise and short build-up regimes, consistent with theory.

title: Global Offshore Wind Infrastructure: Deployment and Operational Dynamics from Dense Sentinel-1 Time Series
generated_summary:
This study advances offshore wind infrastructure monitoring by shifting from static spatial mapping to dynamic temporal characterization at global scale. The authors compile dense Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) time series for 15,606 offshore wind infrastructure locations worldwide, spanning 2016 to 2025, yielding 14.8 million analysis-ready 1D backscatter profiles that capture deployment and operational phases.

The methodology involves a two-stage YOLOv10-based detection pipeline trained on synthetic data to identify wind farm regions and individual infrastructure units from Sentinel-1 composites. Detected locations are then used to extract temporally dense SAR backscatter profiles via Google Earth Engine, achieving revisit intervals as frequent as one day in European waters and 12 days elsewhere. A multi-stage rule-based classifier assigns semantic labels—water, turbine foundation, deployed turbine, support platform, vessel, and mooring/construction—to each event in the time series.

The detection system achieves a macro-averaged F1 score of 98.1% across three global validation sites. Time series classification yields a macro F1 of 0.84 and a collapsed edit similarity AUC of 0.785, with stronger performance for turbine-related classes than transient vessel events. Regional analysis reveals significantly shorter deployment durations in China compared to Europe, and a case study at Hywind Scotland demonstrates the dataset's sensitivity to individual maintenance events.

This openly available dataset and benchmark establish a foundation for spatiotemporal monitoring of the rapidly expanding global offshore wind sector.
original_abstract: The offshore wind energy sector is expanding rapidly, increasing the need for independent, high-temporal-resolution monitoring of infrastructure deployment and operation at global scale. While Earth Observation based offshore wind infrastructure mapping has matured for spatial localization, existing open datasets lack temporally dense and semantically fine-grained information on construction and operational dynamics. We introduce a global Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) time series data corpus that resolves deployment and operational phases of offshore wind infrastructure from 2016Q1 to 2025Q1. Building on an updated object detection workflow, we compile 15,606 time series at detected infrastructure locations, with overall 14,840,637 events as analysis-ready 1D SAR backscatter profiles, one profile per Sentinel-1 acquisition and location. To enable direct use and benchmarking, we release (i) the analysis ready 1D SAR profiles, (ii) event-level baseline semantic labels generated by a rule-based classifier, and (iii) an expert-annotated benchmark dataset of 553 time series with 328,657 event labels. The baseline classifier achieves a macro F1 score of 0.84 in event-wise evaluation and an area under the collapsed edit similarity-quality threshold curve (AUC) of 0.785, indicating temporal coherence. We demonstrate that the resulting corpus supports global-scale analyses of deployment dynamics, the identification of differences in regional deployment patterns, vessel interactions, and operational events, and provides a reference for developing and comparing time series classification methods for offshore wind infrastructure monitoring.

title: Stream-CQSA: Avoiding Out-of-Memory in Attention Computation via Flexible Workload Scheduling
generated_summary:
Stream-CQSA introduces a framework for enabling exact self-attention computation on arbitrarily long sequences without exceeding GPU memory, addressing a fundamental limitation where even optimized attention methods like FlashAttention fail because the full Q, K, and V tensors cannot fit in memory.

The methodology builds on cyclic quorum set (CQS) theory to define "CQS Divide," a combinatorial decomposition that partitions full-sequence attention into mutually exclusive subsequence computations whose results can be recombined to yield exact full-sequence attention. This decomposition is recursively applicable, allowing fine-grained, memory-adaptive control. The Stream-CQSA framework treats these subsequences as schedulable tasks, streaming them through the GPU and trading computation time for reduced peak memory usage. The approach is kernel-agnostic, compatible with any attention implementation that accepts CQS masks and returns softmax numerators and denominators.

Experiments on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80 GiB) demonstrate that Stream-CQSA successfully scales to sequences of one billion tokens without out-of-memory failures. Memory scaling is highly predictable, with each CQS Divide reducing memory by a factor proportional to the number of chunks. The framework shifts attention from a memory-bound to a kernel-bound regime, where performance depends on the underlying attention kernel's efficiency.

The significance lies in enabling exact long-context attention on memory-constrained hardware without architectural modifications or approximation error, making extreme-length sequence processing practically feasible on commodity GPUs.
original_abstract: The scalability of long-context large language models is fundamentally limited by the quadratic memory cost of exact self-attention, which often leads to out-of-memory (OOM) failures on modern hardware. Existing methods improve memory efficiency to near-linear complexity, while assuming that the full query, key, and value tensors fit in device memory. In this work, we remove this assumption by introducing CQS Divide, an operation derived from cyclic quorum sets (CQS) theory that decomposes attention into a set of independent subsequence computations whose recomposition yields exactly the same result as full-sequence attention. Exploiting this decomposition, we introduce Stream-CQSA, a memory-adaptive scheduling framework that partitions attention into subproblems that fit within arbitrary memory budgets. This recasts attention from a logically monolithic operation into a collection of schedulable tasks, enabling flexible execution across devices without inter-device communication. Experiments demonstrate predictable memory scaling and show that exact attention over billion-token sequences can be executed on a single GPU via streaming, without changing the underlying mathematical definition of attention or introducing approximation error.

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
generated_summary:
This paper investigates why language models develop periodic (Fourier) representations for number tokens, revealing a two-tiered convergence phenomenon. The authors distinguish between "spectral convergence" — the emergence of Fourier spikes at periods T = 2, 5, and 10 — and "geometric convergence" — the linear separability of modular arithmetic classes in embeddings. Drawing an analogy to biological convergent evolution, they argue these representations arise from shared constraints in training data and tokenization.

Through controlled experiments with 300M-parameter models trained on identical data, the authors systematically isolate the roles of data distribution, architecture, and optimizer. They demonstrate that spectral convergence is universal, appearing across Transformers, LSTMs, linear RNNs, classical word embeddings, and even raw token frequency distributions. However, geometric convergence is selective: Transformers and linear RNNs (Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2) achieve strong modular arithmetic probing, while LSTMs — despite exhibiting more prominent Fourier spikes — remain at chance level. Data perturbation experiments show that text-number co-occurrence and sufficient context length are necessary for geometric convergence, while Fourier spikes persist even when all co-occurrence structure is destroyed.

The central finding — that visible representational structure does not guarantee functional organization — carries significant implications for interpretability research. It cautions against using Fourier analysis or similar spectral diagnostics alone as evidence that models have learned meaningful numerical structure, and provides a framework for distinguishing superficial statistical artifacts from genuinely learned representations.
original_abstract: Language models trained on natural text learn to represent numbers using periodic features with dominant periods at $T=2, 5, 10$. In this paper, we identify a two-tiered hierarchy of these features: while Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings trained in different ways all learn features that have period-$T$ spikes in the Fourier domain, only some learn geometrically separable features that can be used to linearly classify a number mod-$T$. To explain this incongruity, we prove that Fourier domain sparsity is necessary but not sufficient for mod-$T$ geometric separability. Empirically, we investigate when model training yields geometrically separable features, finding that the data, architecture, optimizer, and tokenizer all play key roles. In particular, we identify two different routes through which models can acquire geometrically separable features: they can learn them from complementary co-occurrence signals in general language data, including text-number co-occurrence and cross-number interaction, or from multi-token (but not single-token) addition problems. Overall, our results highlight the phenomenon of convergent evolution in feature learning: A diverse range of models learn similar features from different training signals.

title: ParetoSlider: Diffusion Models Post-Training for Continuous Reward Control
generated_summary:
ParetoSlider introduces a multi-objective reinforcement learning framework for diffusion and flow-matching models that enables continuous, inference-time control over competing reward trade-offs using a single trained model. The key contribution is eliminating the need to train separate models for each desired balance between objectives, instead conditioning a single model on a preference vector that specifies the desired trade-off.

The methodology builds upon DiffusionNFT, an RL fine-tuning framework for flow-matching models. A critical design choice is late scalarization: rather than combining multiple rewards into a single scalar before computing policy updates, ParetoSlider computes independent losses for each reward objective and normalizes per-reward advantages separately before aggregating them with the preference vector. This prevents rewards with larger magnitudes from dominating the learning signal. The preference vector is injected into the diffusion transformer through modulation-based conditioning.

Evaluated across three state-of-the-art backbones—Stable Diffusion 3.5 for text-to-image, FluxKontext for image editing, and LTX-2 for text-to-video—ParetoSlider consistently matches or exceeds multiple separately trained fixed-weight baselines while producing smooth, continuous transitions across the full preference spectrum. The method dominates baselines including classifier-free guidance scaling, prompt rewriting, and Pareto-based selection approaches in Pareto front coverage.

This work establishes a scalable paradigm for multi-objective alignment of visual generative models, enabling intuitive user control over complex reward trade-offs without retraining.
original_abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training has become the standard for aligning generative models with human preferences, yet most methods rely on a single scalar reward. When multiple criteria matter, the prevailing practice of ``early scalarization'' collapses rewards into a fixed weighted sum. This commits the model to a single trade-off point at training time, providing no inference-time control over inherently conflicting goals -- such as prompt adherence versus source fidelity in image editing. We introduce ParetoSlider, a multi-objective RL (MORL) framework that trains a single diffusion model to approximate the entire Pareto front. By training the model with continuously varying preference weights as a conditioning signal, we enable users to navigate optimal trade-offs at inference time without retraining or maintaining multiple checkpoints. We evaluate ParetoSlider across three state-of-the-art flow-matching backbones: SD3.5, FluxKontext, and LTX-2. Our single preference-conditioned model matches or exceeds the performance of baselines trained separately for fixed reward trade-offs, while uniquely providing fine-grained control over competing generative goals.

title: Adapting TrOCR for Printed Tigrinya Text Recognition: Word-Aware Loss Weighting for Cross-Script Transfer Learning

Starting from a pre-trained model, we extend the byte-level BPE tokenizer to cover 230 Ge'ez characters and introduce Word-Aware Loss Weighting to resolve systematic word-boundary failures that arise when applying Latin-centric BPE conventions to a new script. The unmodified model produces no usable output on Ge'ez text. After adaptation, the TrOCR-Printed variant achieves 0.22% Character Error Rate and 97.20% exact match accuracy on a held-out test set of 5,000 synthetic images from the GLOCR dataset. An ablation study confirms that Word-Aware Loss Weighting is the critical component, reducing CER by two orders of magnitude compared to vocabulary extension alone. title: Diagnosing CFG Interpretation in LLMs
generated_summary:

We introduce RoboGrid, a framework that disentangles syntax, behavior, and semantics through controlled stress-tests of recursion depth, expression complexity, and surface styles. Our experiments reveal a consistent hierarchical degradation: LLMs often maintain surface syntax but fail to preserve structural semantics. Despite the partial mitigation provided by CoT reasoning, performance collapses under structural density, specifically deep recursion and high branching, with semantic alignment vanishing at extreme depths. Furthermore, "Alien" lexicons reveal that LLMs rely on semantic bootstrapping from keywords rather than pure symbolic induction. These findings pinpoint critical gaps in hierarchical state-tracking required for reliable, grammar-agnostic agents.

title: Can Virtual Agents Care? Designing an Empathetic and Personalized LLM-Driven Conversational Agent

title: DNA storage approaching the information-theoretic ceiling

This paper presents Mahoraga, a DNA storage codec that preserves soft probabilistic information from sequencer output through to final decoding, closing a significant gap between achieved and theoretical information density. The methodology employs a profile hidden Markov model to compute per-position posterior distributions jointly with read-to-reference alignment, combining posteriors across multiple reads via log-product fusion into soft log-likelihood ratios. These feed a progressive-edge-growth LDPC inner code decoded by ordered-statistics decoding, with CRC-32 flagging inner failures as erasures for a Reed-Solomon outer code. No hard decision is taken until the LDPC decoding stage.

Benchmarked on the DT4DDS channel simulator, Mahoraga achieved 155.8 exabytes per gram on the high-fidelity channel and 25.9 exabytes per gram on the low-fidelity channel, exceeding the best prior codec (DNA-Aeon) by 11% and 52% respectively, while requiring lower physical redundancy and sequencing depth. At matched outer-code parity, Mahoraga exceeded DNA-Aeon by 1.42-fold on both channels, operating at 68% of the theoretical alphabet ceiling versus 48% for the best prior codec.

These results demonstrate that preserving sequencer-emitted posterior probabilities through the decoding pipeline yields substantial density gains, particularly under high-noise conditions where the information advantage of soft decisions over hard calls is greatest.
original_abstract: Synthetic DNA approaches 227.5 exabytes per gram of storage density with stability over millennial timescales. Realising this capacity requires error-correction codes that recover data from substantial synthesis and sequencing errors. Existing codecs convert noisy sequencer output into discrete base calls before error correction, discarding probabilistic information about which positions are reliable. Here we present a coding scheme that retains the sequencer's per-position posterior distributions through an integrated decoder of profile hidden Markov model alignment, log-product fusion across reads, and ordered-statistics decoding. On the DT4DDS channel simulator, the codec recovers 155.8 and 25.9 exabytes per gram of dsDNA under high- and low-fidelity conditions, exceeding the highest prior-art density on each channel by 11 and 52 percent. Under a single-encode-then-degrade protocol mapped to depurination kinetics at 25 °C in the dry state, the codec projects 282 years of decodable storage at 17.1 exabytes per gram. These results place DNA storage density within reach of the Shannon bound of the underlying channel.

title: Formal Primal-Dual Algorithm Analysis
generated_summary:

For instance, the combinatorial proofs for RANKING's correctness and Berge's Lemma involve extensive case analyses and higher complexity, whereas primal-dual arguments are primarily algebraic and more tractable for formalization. original_abstract: We present an ongoing effort to build a framework and a library in Isabelle/HOL for formalising primal-dual arguments for the analysis of algorithms. We discuss a number of example formalisations from the theory of matching algorithms, covering classical algorithms like the Hungarian Method, widely considered the first primal-dual algorithm, and modern algorithms like the Adwords algorithm, which models the assignment of search queries to advertisers in the context of search engines.

title: OMIBench: Benchmarking Olympiad-Level Multi-Image Reasoning in Large Vision-Language Model

The authors also assess enhancement strategies including long chain-of-thought prompting, test-time scaling, in-context learning, and think-with-image approaches, finding only modest improvements. These results suggest that meaningful progress will require fundamental advances in model architecture and training rather than prompting techniques alone, establishing multi-image Olympiad-level reasoning as an important open challenge.
original_abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have made substantial advances in reasoning tasks at the Olympiad level. Nevertheless, current Olympiad-level multimodal reasoning benchmarks for these models often emphasize single-image analysis and fail to exploit contextual information across multiple images. We present OMIBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate Olympiad-level reasoning when the required evidence is distributed over multiple images. It contains problems from biology, chemistry, mathematics, and physics Olympiads, together with manually annotated rationales and evaluation protocols for both exact and semantic answer matching. Across extensive experiments on OMIBench, we observe meaningful performance gaps in existing models. Even the strongest LVLMs, such as Gemini-3-Pro, attain only about 50% on the benchmark. title: Autonomous LLM-generated Feedback for Student Exercises in Introductory Software Engineering Courses
generated_summary:

The regression model controls for baseline ability, written exercise completion, and face-to-face meeting attendance to isolate NAILA's effect.

Key findings reveal that 37% of active students voluntarily adopted NAILA, primarily for exam preparation. Students rated perceived ease of use, usefulness, and learning at approximately 4.1 out of 5. Critically, the regression analysis shows that students who used NAILA's confirmatory feedback—validating mastery before progressing—achieved significantly higher exam scores. However, students who relied on iterative remedial feedback did not demonstrate measurable performance gains, suggesting possible surface-level compliance rather than deep learning.

These results demonstrate that AI-generated feedback can effectively serve as a scalable "green light" mechanism for self-regulated learning, though its remedial function requires redesign toward Socratic questioning approaches. The paper also provides a thorough discussion of regulatory compliance under GDPR and the EU AI Act.
original_abstract: Introductory Software Engineering (SE) courses face rapidly increasing student enrollment numbers, participants with diverse backgrounds and the influence of Generative AI (GenAI) solutions. High teacher-to-student ratios often challenge providing timely, high-quality, and personalized feedback a significant challenge for educators. To address these challenges, we introduce NAILA, a tool that provides 24/7 autonomous feedback for student exercises. Utilizing GenAI in the form of modern LLMs, NAILA processes student solutions provided in open document formats, evaluating them against teacher-defined model solutions through specialized prompt templates. We conducted an empirical study involving 900+ active students at the University of Duisburg-Essen to assess four main research questions investigating (1) the underlying motivations that drive students to either adopt or reject NAILA, (2) user acceptance by measuring perceived usefulness and ease of use alongside subjective learning progress, (3) how often and how consistently students engage with NAILA, and (4) how using NAILA to receive AI feedback impacts on academic performance compared to human feedback.

title: Synthesizing Multi-Agent Harnesses for Vulnerability Discovery
generated_summary:
This paper introduces AgentFlow, a system for automatically synthesizing multi-agent harnesses—the orchestration programs that coordinate teams of language model agents for vulnerability discovery. The main contribution is a typed graph domain-specific language (DSL) that unifies five harness dimensions (agent roles, communication topology, message schemas, tool bindings, and coordination protocols) into a single searchable representation, combined with a feedback-driven optimization loop that uses structured runtime diagnostics rather than binary pass/fail signals.

The methodology centers on an iterative propose-execute-score-diagnose cycle. At each step, an LLM proposes edits to the harness program, which are validated through a type system that cheaply eliminates structurally broken candidates. The harness is then executed, and rich feedback—including coverage maps, sanitizer reports, and agent action traces—enables precise diagnosis of why failures occurred, guiding subsequent proposals.

On the TerminalBench-2 benchmark of 89 long-horizon tasks, AgentFlow achieves 84.3% pass rate with Claude Opus 4.6, the highest score on the public leaderboard, surpassing the best hand-engineered system by 2.9 percentage points. Applied to Google Chrome's 35-million-line codebase using the open-weight Kimi K2.5 model, the system discovers ten previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities, including two Critical sandbox-escape CVEs confirmed through Chrome's Vulnerability Reward Program.

These results demonstrate that automated harness synthesis can surpass hand-engineered multi-agent systems and generalize across domains, models, and scales for practical security applications.
original_abstract: LLM agents have begun to find real security vulnerabilities that human auditors and automated fuzzers missed for decades, in source-available targets where the analyst can build and instrument the code. In practice the work is split among several agents, wired together by a harness: the program that fixes which roles exist, how they pass information, which tools each may call, and how retries are coordinated. When the language model is held fixed, changing only the harness can still change success rates by several-fold on public agent benchmarks, yet most harnesses are written by hand; recent harness optimizers each search only a narrow slice of the design space and rely on coarse pass/fail feedback that gives no diagnostic signal about why a trial failed. AgentFlow addresses both limitations with a typed graph DSL whose search space jointly covers agent roles, prompts, tools, communication topology, and coordination protocol, paired with a feedback-driven outer loop that reads runtime signals from the target program itself to diagnose which part of the harness caused the failure and rewrite it accordingly. We evaluate AgentFlow on TerminalBench-2 with Claude Opus 4.6 and on Google Chrome with Kimi K2.5. AgentFlow reaches 84.3% on TerminalBench-2, the highest score in the public leaderboard snapshot we evaluate against, and discovers ten previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities in Google Chrome, including two Critical sandbox-escape vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-5280 and CVE-2026-6297).

title: LEXIS: LatEnt ProXimal Interaction Signatures for 3D HOI from an Image
generated_summary:
## Summary

This paper introduces LEXIS, a framework for reconstructing 3D human-object interactions (HOI) from single images that moves beyond sparse, binary contact representations by leveraging dense, continuous Interaction Fields (InterFields), which encode surface-to-surface proximity distances across entire body and object meshes. The key contribution is a learned lexicon of latent interaction signatures (LEXIS) that compactly captures action- and object-specific proximity patterns through a VQ-VAE architecture with TriPlane-based decoding.

The methodology comprises two main components. First, a VQ-VAE learns a discrete codebook of interaction signatures from 3D interaction datasets, encoding body pose and proximal relationships into compact tokens that can be decoded into full InterFields. Second, a dual-stream Flow-Matching transformer (LEXISDiff) jointly estimates 3D human and object meshes alongside their InterField tokens from a single image. Crucially, predicted InterFields guide the generative sampling process through gradient-based refinement at inference time, eliminating the need for separate post-hoc optimization stages.

Experiments on the Open3DHOI benchmark demonstrate that LEXIS achieves the lowest object Chamfer Distance (22.96 cm) and highest Contact F1 (0.451), outperforming all baselines. Dense InterFields consistently outperform binary contacts in both fitting and generative settings. A perceptual study shows LEXIS reconstructions are preferred 75.8% of the time over competing methods. These results demonstrate that continuous proximity representations provide substantially richer geometric constraints than binary contact for physically plausible 3D interaction reconstruction.
original_abstract: Reconstructing 3D Human-Object Interaction from an RGB image is essential for perceptive systems. Yet, this remains challenging as it requires capturing the subtle physical coupling between the body and objects. While current methods rely on sparse, binary contact cues, these fail to model the continuous proximity and dense spatial relationships that characterize natural interactions. We address this limitation via InterFields, a representation that encodes dense, continuous proximity across the entire body and object surfaces. However, inferring these fields from single images is inherently ill-posed. To tackle this, our intuition is that interaction patterns are characteristically structured by the action and object geometry. We capture this structure in LEXIS, a novel discrete manifold of interaction signatures learned via a VQ-VAE. We then develop LEXIS-Flow, a diffusion framework that leverages LEXIS signatures to estimate human and object meshes alongside their InterFields. Notably, these InterFields help in a guided refinement that ensures physically-plausible, proximity-aware reconstructions without requiring post-hoc optimization. Evaluation on Open3DHOI and BEHAVE shows that LEXIS-Flow significantly outperforms existing SotA baselines in reconstruction, contact, and proximity quality. Our approach not only improves generalization but also yields reconstructions perceived as more realistic, moving us closer to holistic 3D scene understanding. Code & models will be public at https://anticdimi.github.io/lexis.

title: A Hough transform approach to safety-aware scalar field mapping using Gaussian Processes
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the GP-HT algorithm, an adaptive sampling strategy for safely mapping unknown scalar fields by integrating Gaussian Process (GP) regression with the Hough Transform (HT) for online detection and avoidance of high-intensity regions. The approach addresses scenarios where a mobile robot must map hazardous fields—such as nuclear radiation, forest fires, or hostile radar signals—while maintaining safe distance from dangerous zones.

The methodology employs GP regression to estimate the scalar field from noisy measurements and compute predictive uncertainty, while the HT extracts geometric approximations of high-intensity regions from thresholded GP posterior estimates. Maximum variance sampling optimizes measurement locations for information gain, and a systematic relocation algorithm replaces unsafe candidate locations with admissible safe alternatives. Path planning via RRT* generates collision-free trajectories that avoid estimated hazardous zones. The paper provides formal analysis of information loss incurred by safety-constrained sampling compared to unconstrained approaches, along with convergence guarantees showing prediction error converges to a bounded value.

The algorithm is validated through two numerical simulations (2D and 3D scalar fields) and indoor experiments using a wheeled robot mapping light intensity. Results demonstrate effective field estimation while dynamically avoiding high-intensity regions, though early-stage measurements may occur in hazardous zones before sufficient data is collected. This work fills an important gap by formally integrating safety constraints into GP-based field mapping, with implications for autonomous environmental monitoring and hazardous area characterization.
original_abstract: This paper presents a framework for mapping unknown scalar fields using a sensor-equipped autonomous robot operating in unsafe environments. The unsafe regions are defined as regions of high-intensity, where the field value exceeds a predefined safety threshold. For safe and efficient mapping of the scalar field, the sensor-equipped robot must avoid high-intensity regions during the measurement process. In this paper, the scalar field is modeled as a sample from a Gaussian process (GP), which enables Bayesian inference and provides closed-form expressions for both the predictive mean and the uncertainty. Concurrently, the spatial structure of the high-intensity regions is estimated in real-time using the Hough transform (HT), leveraging the evolving GP posterior. A safe sampling strategy is then employed to guide the robot towards safe measurement locations, using probabilistic safety guarantees on the evolving GP posterior. The estimated high-intensity regions also facilitate the design of safe motion plans for the robot. The effectiveness of the approach is verified through two numerical simulation studies and an indoor experiment for mapping a light-intensity field using a wheeled mobile robot.

title: Gauge-Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for Lattice Gauge Theories
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a gauge-equivariant graph neural network framework for lattice gauge theories that enforces local non-Abelian gauge symmetry exactly at the architectural level through matrix-valued message passing. Unlike standard equivariant neural networks designed for global symmetries, this approach operates directly on gauge-covariant degrees of freedom, with node and edge features transforming consistently under independent, site-dependent gauge transformations. The methodology employs iterative message-passing updates where information propagation implicitly constructs gauge-covariant transport along lattice paths, allowing Wilson lines and loop-like structures to emerge from local operations without explicit construction.

The framework is validated across three representative settings. In pure SU(3) gauge theory in 3+1 dimensions, the network accurately reconstructs both the gauge action (R² = 0.994) and local topological charge (R² = 0.99) from covariant inputs. In SU(2) and SU(3) gauge-matter systems, it captures fermion-mediated nonlocal correlations, predicting energy densities and local fermion densities with high accuracy. In dynamical settings, the network learns gauge-covariant force fields for semiclassical SU(2) quantum link model dynamics, faithfully reproducing statistical properties including Wilson loop autocorrelation functions.

The significance of this work lies in establishing gauge-equivariant message passing as a unified, scalable paradigm extending equivariant machine learning from global to local symmetry structures, with potential applications spanning lattice QCD acceleration, neural quantum states for gauge-constrained systems, and quantum simulation platforms.
original_abstract: Local gauge symmetry underlies fundamental interactions and strongly correlated quantum matter, yet existing machine-learning approaches lack a general, principled framework for learning under site-dependent symmetries, particularly for intrinsically nonlocal observables. Here we introduce a gauge-equivariant graph neural network that embeds non-Abelian symmetry directly into message passing via matrix-valued, gauge-covariant features and symmetry-compatible updates, extending equivariant learning from global to fully local symmetries. In this formulation, message passing implements gauge-covariant transport across the lattice, allowing nonlocal correlations and loop-like structures to emerge naturally from local operations. We validate the approach across pure gauge, gauge-matter, and dynamical regimes, establishing gauge-equivariant message passing as a general paradigm for learning in systems governed by local symmetry.

title: LLaDA2.0-Uni: Unifying Multimodal Understanding and Generation with Diffusion Large Language Model

original_abstract: We present LLaDA2.0-Uni, a unified discrete diffusion large language model (dLLM) that supports multimodal understanding and generation within a natively integrated framework. Its architecture combines a fully semantic discrete tokenizer, a MoE-based dLLM backbone, and a diffusion decoder. By discretizing continuous visual inputs via SigLIP-VQ, the model enables block-level masked diffusion for both text and vision inputs within the backbone, while the decoder reconstructs visual tokens into high-fidelity images. Inference efficiency is enhanced beyond parallel decoding through prefix-aware optimizations in the backbone and few-step distillation in the decoder. Supported by carefully curated large-scale data and a tailored multi-stage training pipeline, LLaDA2.0-Uni matches specialized VLMs in multimodal understanding while delivering strong performance in image generation and editing. Its native support for interleaved generation and reasoning establishes a promising and scalable paradigm for next-generation unified foundation models. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/LLaDA2.0-Uni.

title: Can "AI" Be a Doctor? A Study of Empathy, Readability, and Alignment in Clinical LLMs
generated_summary:
This study presents a large-scale empirical evaluation of LLM-generated clinical communication compared to physician-authored responses, assessing three dimensions: semantic fidelity, readability, and affective resonance (empathy and sentiment). The work addresses a critical gap in understanding how well AI systems align with clinical communication norms beyond factual accuracy.

The authors evaluate multiple LLMs (Mixtral, Med-PaLM 2, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5) across two datasets—MedQuAD (institutionally curated medical explanations) and iCliniqQAs (real physician-patient consultations)—using three prompting strategies: baseline, empathy-enhanced, and collaborative rewriting. Semantic similarity is measured via BioBERT embeddings, readability through Flesch-Kincaid and Gunning Fog metrics, and affective tone through sentiment and fine-grained emotion classifiers.

Key findings reveal that no single LLM configuration consistently outperforms physicians across all dimensions. LLMs systematically amplify affiliative emotions like "caring" while attenuating corrective cues, deviating from physician affective norms rather than faithfully replicating them. Baseline LLM outputs do not inherently improve readability; GPT-5 and Claude produce significantly more complex text than physicians. However, collaborative rewriting emerges as the most effective strategy, consistently improving readability, emotional appropriateness, and semantic fidelity across both datasets without degrading clinical accuracy.

These findings carry significant implications for deploying LLMs in healthcare, supporting their use as communication enhancers in human-AI collaborative workflows rather than autonomous clinical communicators, while emphasizing that alignment properties are controllable through prompting strategies rather than intrinsic to model architecture.
original_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in healthcare, yet their communicative alignment with clinical standards remains insufficiently quantified. We conduct a multidimensional evaluation of general-purpose and domain-specialized LLMs across structured medical explanations and real-world physician-patient interactions, analyzing semantic fidelity, readability, and affective resonance. Baseline models amplify affective polarity relative to physicians (Very Negative: 43.14-45.10% vs. 37.25%) and, in larger architectures such as GPT-5 and Claude, produce substantially higher linguistic complexity (FKGL up to 16.91-17.60 vs. 11.47-12.50 in physician-authored responses). Empathy-oriented prompting reduces extreme negativity and lowers grade-level complexity (up to -6.87 FKGL points for GPT-5) but does not significantly increase semantic fidelity. Collaborative rewriting yields the strongest overall alignment. original_abstract: Internal ice layers imaged by radar provide key evidence of snow accumulation and ice dynamics, but radar-derived layer boundary observations are often incomplete, with discontinuous traces and sometimes entirely missing layers, due to limited resolution, sensor noise, and signal loss. title: Efficient Multi-Cohort Inference for Long-Term Effects and Lifetime Value in A/B Testing with User Learning

original_abstract: Retrieval quality is the primary bottleneck for accuracy and robustness in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
