original_abstract: Space-time self-similarity (STSS), which captures visual correspondences across frames, provides an effective way to represent temporal dynamics for video understanding. original_abstract: The development of visual analytics (VA) systems has traditionally been a labor-intensive process, balancing design methodologies with complex software engineering practices. In domain-specific fields like urban VA, this challenge is amplified by heterogeneous data streams and a reliance on complex, multi-service architectures that hinder fast development, deployment, and reproducibility. Despite the richness of the urban VA literature, the field lacks a consolidated toolkit that encapsulates the core components of these systems, such as spatial data management, analytical processing, and visualization, into a unified, lightweight framework. In this paper, we introduce Autark, a serverless toolkit designed for the rapid prototyping of urban VA systems. Autark provides domain-aware abstractions through a self-contained architecture, enabling researchers to transition from design intention to deployed, shareable systems within hours. Furthermore, Autark's structured, tightly scoped interfaces make it well-suited for AI-assisted coding workflows, where LLMs produce more reliable code when composing from well-defined abstractions rather than generating complex solutions from scratch. Our contributions are: (1) the Autark toolkit, a serverless architecture for rapid prototyping of urban VA; (2) a comparative study of LLM coding effectiveness with and without Autark; and (3) a series of usage scenarios demonstrating its capability to streamline the creation of robust, shareable urban VA prototypes. Autark is available at https://autarkjs.org/.

title: V-tableR1: Process-Supervised Multimodal Table Reasoning with Critic-Guided Policy Optimization
generated_summary:
V-tableR1 introduces a process-supervised reinforcement learning framework that addresses a fundamental limitation of vision-language models in tabular reasoning: their reliance on outcome-only supervision, which rewards correct final answers regardless of whether intermediate reasoning steps are valid. This leads to visual hallucinations and shortcut guessing in multi-step table comprehension tasks.

The framework comprises three core components. First, a Visual Chain-of-Thought dataset provides step-level reasoning annotations that explicitly ground logical operations to visual anchors such as cell coordinates. Second, a critic VLM trained on both pristine and synthetically corrupted reasoning trajectories evaluates the structural fidelity of each reasoning step, producing dense process scores that dynamically gate outcome rewards. Third, Process-Guided Direct Alignment Policy Optimization (PGPO), a novel reinforcement learning algorithm, integrates decoupled policy constraints, length-aware dynamic sampling, and critic-generated step-level feedback to optimize the policy model toward verifiable reasoning rather than mere answer guessing.

Evaluated across seven tabular reasoning benchmarks spanning fact verification and question answering, V-tableR1 at just 4 billion parameters achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source models, consistently outperforming models up to 72 billion parameters. Ablation studies confirm that process supervision provides the largest performance gain, improving accuracy by approximately 4.6% over standard GRPO on question answering tasks. These results demonstrate that explicit step-level verification fundamentally shifts multimodal reasoning from opaque pattern matching to rigorous logical derivation, establishing a new paradigm for structured visual reasoning.
original_abstract: We introduce V-tableR1, a process-supervised reinforcement learning framework that elicits rigorous, verifiable reasoning from multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Current MLLMs trained solely on final outcomes often treat visual reasoning as a black box, relying on superficial pattern matching rather than performing rigorous multi-step inference. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards could enforce transparent reasoning trajectories, extending it to visual domains remains severely hindered by the ambiguity of grounding abstract logic into continuous pixel space. We solve this by leveraging the deterministic grid structure of tables as an ideal visual testbed. V-tableR1 employs a specialized critic VLM to provide dense, step-level feedback on the explicit visual chain-of-thought generated by a policy VLM. To optimize this system, we propose Process-Guided Direct Alignment Policy Optimization (PGPO), a novel RL algorithm integrating process rewards, decoupled policy constraints, and length-aware dynamic sampling. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that V-tableR1 explicitly penalizes visual hallucinations and shortcut guessing. By fundamentally shifting multimodal inference from black-box pattern matching to verifiable logical derivation, V-tableR1 4B establishes state-of-the-art accuracy among open-source models on complex tabular benchmarks, outperforming models up to 18x its size and improving over its SFT baseline

title: Termination of Innermost-Terminating Right-Linear Overlay Term Rewrite Systems (Full Version)
generated_summary:
This paper establishes that right-linear overlay term rewrite systems (TRSs) are terminating if and only if they are innermost terminating, extending the previously known maximum class for which this equivalence holds—locally confluent overlay TRSs. The key advantage is that both right-linearity and the overlay property are purely syntactic and efficiently decidable, unlike local confluence, which is a semantic property sometimes requiring termination proofs itself.

The methodology centers on the dependency pair framework. The authors prove that for a non-collapsing right-linear TRS where the combined system forms an overlay system, there is no infinite minimal dependency-pair chain if and only if there is no infinite innermost minimal dependency-pair chain. The proof strategy involves showing that any finite minimal chain of length *n* can be simulated by an innermost minimal chain of the same length, leveraging a known result that rewrite sequences ending in normal forms can be simulated by innermost reduction in terminating right-linear overlay systems. A contradiction argument then extends this from finite to infinite chains.

The main result also yields a practical dependency pair processor that converts DP problems from full to innermost evaluation strategy when the system is a right-linear overlay TRS. This is significant for termination analysis tools, as innermost termination provers can employ weaker sufficient conditions than those required for general termination, potentially enabling more termination proofs. The purely syntactic characterization makes the applicability check computationally inexpensive.
original_abstract: It has been shown that, regarding a terminating right-linear overlay term rewrite system (TRS), any rewrite sequence ending with a normal form can be simulated by the innermost reduction. In this paper, using this simulation property, we show that for a right-linear overlay TRS, there is no infinite minimal dependency-pair chain if and only if there is no infinite innermost minimal dependency-pair chain. This implies that a right-linear overlay TRS is terminating if and only if it is innermost terminating.

title: Where and What: Reasoning Dynamic and Implicit Preferences in Situated Conversational Recommendation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Situated Preference Reasoning (SPR), a novel framework for situated conversational recommendation (SCR) that addresses two key challenges: reasoning about dynamic scene transitions and inferring implicit user preferences within visually grounded environments. The framework integrates two core mechanisms. First, Scene Transition Estimation (STE) employs a generative-retrieval approach where a multimodal large language model generates a semantic profile of the desired target scene, followed by coarse-to-fine retrieval to identify the optimal real scene from a candidate pool. Second, Bayesian Inverse Inference (BI-INF) formalizes preference discovery as an inverse planning problem, treating user utterances as observable actions generated by latent goals. By comparing competing hypotheses (like vs. dislike) for each candidate item using likelihood ratios computed from fine-tuned MLLM logits, the system probabilistically identifies what the user truly desires.

Evaluated on the SIMMC 2.1 and SCREEN datasets, SPR achieves average improvements of 10.9% and 10.6% over baselines, respectively. Notably, it surpasses GPT-4o in both recommendation accuracy and response quality despite using a smaller 7B backbone. Ablation studies confirm that both components are essential, with STE removal causing the largest performance degradation. Human evaluation further validates SPR's superiority in coherence, informativeness, and situatedness. This work represents one of the first systematic framework-level approaches to SCR, offering a foundation for developing proactive, context-aware recommendation agents in real-world situated environments.
original_abstract: Situated conversational recommendation (SCR), which utilizes visual scenes grounded in specific environments and natural language dialogue to deliver contextually appropriate recommendations, has emerged as a promising research direction due to its close alignment with real-world scenarios. Compared to traditional recommendations, SCR requires a deeper understanding of dynamic and implicit user preferences, as the surrounding scene often influences users' underlying interests, while both may evolve across conversations. This complexity significantly impacts the timing and relevance of recommendations. To address this, we propose situated preference reasoning (SiPeR), a novel framework that integrates two core mechanisms: (1) Scene transition estimation, which estimates whether the current scene satisfies user needs, and guides the user toward a more suitable scene when necessary; and (2) Bayesian inverse inference, which leverages the likelihood of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to predict user preferences about candidate items within the scene. Extensive experiments on two representative benchmarks demonstrate SiPeR's superiority in both recommendation accuracy and response generation quality. The code and data are available at https://github.com/DongdingLin/SiPeR.

title: Amodal SAM: A Unified Amodal Segmentation Framework with Generalization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Amodal SAM, a framework that extends the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to perform amodal segmentation—predicting complete object shapes including occluded regions—while preserving SAM's strong zero-shot generalization capabilities. The key contribution lies in addressing the open-world amodal segmentation problem, where models must generalize to unseen object categories and domains.

The methodology encompasses three synergistic adaptations. First, a lightweight Spatial Completion Adapter (SCA) using gated convolutions is integrated into SAM's image encoder to enable reconstruction of occluded regions while maintaining core segmentation abilities. Second, a Target-Aware Occlusion Synthesis (TAOS) pipeline automatically generates large-scale amodal training data from existing segmentation datasets like SA-1B by synthesizing diverse occlusion patterns without manual annotation. Third, composite learning objectives incorporating regional consistency and holistic topological regularization guide training.

Extensive experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate that Amodal SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance in both closed-domain and open-world settings, significantly outperforming existing methods such as pix2gestalt and SAMBA on zero-shot cross-dataset evaluations. The framework also extends to video amodal segmentation through adaptation of SAM-2, marking the first successful implementation of open-world video amodal segmentation. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component. This work establishes a strong foundation for generalizable amodal perception in real-world applications.
original_abstract: Amodal segmentation is a challenging task that aims to predict the complete geometric shape of objects, including their occluded regions. Although existing methods primarily focus on amodal segmentation within the training domain, these approaches often lack the generalization capacity to extend effectively to novel object categories and unseen contexts. This paper introduces Amodal SAM, a unified framework that leverages SAM (Segment Anything Model) for both amodal image and amodal video segmentation. Amodal SAM preserves the powerful generalization ability of SAM while extending its inherent capabilities to the amodal segmentation task. The improvements lie in three aspects: (1) a lightweight Spatial Completion Adapter that enables occluded region reconstruction, (2) a Target-Aware Occlusion Synthesis (TAOS) pipeline that addresses the scarcity of amodal annotations by generating diverse synthetic training data, and (3) novel learning objectives that enforce regional consistency and topological regularization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Amodal SAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks, while simultaneously exhibiting robust generalization to novel scenarios. We anticipate that this research will advance the field toward practical amodal segmentation systems capable of operating effectively in unconstrained real-world environments.

title: Realistic Virtual Flood Experience System Using 360° Videos and 3D City Models Constructed from Building Footprints
generated_summary: This paper presents a novel virtual flood experience framework that integrates 360° walkthrough videos with 3D city models automatically generated from widely available 2D building footprints, enabling photorealistic flood visualizations without requiring pre-existing detailed 3D city models. The key insight is that precise building heights are unnecessary for flood visualization; only the lower portions of buildings that interact with floodwaters need to be modeled. The methodology involves three steps: extruding 2D building footprints to constant heights to create simplified 3D geometries, spatially aligning these models with 360° videos using a novel ground-region-based alignment approach combined with Visual SLAM-derived 3D points (rather than relying on accurate building heights), and dynamically projecting video frames onto the aligned geometries to render realistic flood scenes. This approach significantly reduces the data collection and processing burden compared to methods requiring CAD models, photogrammetry, or pre-existing CityGML data. The framework is demonstrated in Memuro, Hokkaido, Japan, an area vulnerable to river flooding. A user study conducted with local residents through a workshop shows that the system enhances participants' ability to understand and envision location-specific flood evacuation scenarios. The framework represents a scalable, practical tool for disaster risk communication and education, with potential for broader deployment across regions where detailed 3D urban models are unavailable but building footprint data exists.
original_abstract: Virtual flood experience systems, which enable users to vividly experience flooding, are attracting increasing attention as effective tools for communicating flood risks. However, existing systems typically rely on virtual cities that do not correspond to real locations and often lack sufficient photorealism, limiting users' ability to relate scenarios to their own surroundings. Although 360° video-based virtual environments offer a simple and scalable way to visually replicate real-world scenes, effective 3D flood visualization in these environments typically requires 3D building geometry of the target area, which is not readily available in many regions. To address this limitation, we propose a new virtual flood experience framework that integrates 360° videos with 3D models automatically constructed from widely available 2D building footprints. By extruding footprints to plausible heights and spatially aligning the constructed models with 360° videos, our framework enables 3D flood visualization in photorealistic environments without relying on pre-existing city models such as CityGML. We demonstrate the framework in Memuro, Hokkaido, Japan, an area vulnerable to river flooding. A user study with local residents showed that the proposed system enhances users' ability to envision location-specific flood evacuation situations, demonstrating its potential as an effective tool for disaster risk communication and education.

title: Lifecycle-Aware Federated Continual Learning in Mobile Autonomous Systems
generated_summary:
This paper presents a lifecycle-aware Federated Continual Learning (FCL) framework designed for mobile autonomous systems, specifically targeting Mars terrain segmentation by rover fleets. The framework addresses catastrophic forgetting at two temporal scales: training-time forgetting during local updates and long-term degradation from repeated federated aggregation under non-IID conditions.

The methodology comprises two complementary components. Layer-Selective Rehearsal (LSR) operates during training, employing learned generators that apply stratified corrections to different network layers based on their empirically observed forgetting sensitivities—minimal intervention for shallow layers, moderate guidance for deep layers, and strong stabilization for the segmentation head, which contributes 87.1% of total forgetting. Rapid Knowledge Recovery (RKR) addresses long-term cumulative drift through a meta-learned recovery function trained once during the initial task, which efficiently restores degraded segmentation head states without retraining.

Evaluated on three Mars terrain datasets (MarsScapes, S5Mars, AI4MARS), the framework achieves up to 8.3% mIoU improvement over the strongest federated baseline and up to 31.7% over conventional fine-tuning. RKR restores performance in 5–8 epochs compared to 11–18 epochs for full retraining. Physical deployment on a four-rover testbed with Raspberry Pi edge devices validates system-level robustness under extreme non-IID conditions and heterogeneous resource constraints.

This work provides a principled dual-timescale defense against forgetting in distributed autonomous systems, with theoretical foundations and practical validation bridging simulation-to-deployment gaps.
original_abstract: Federated continual learning (FCL) allows distributed autonomous fleets to adapt collaboratively to evolving terrain types across extended mission lifecycles. However, current approaches face several key challenges: 1) they use uniform protection strategies that do not account for the varying sensitivities to forgetting on different network layers; 2) they focus primarily on preventing forgetting during training, without addressing the long-term effects of cumulative drift; and 3) they often depend on idealized simulations that fail to capture the real-world heterogeneity present in distributed fleets. In this paper, we propose a lifecycle-aware dual-timescale FCL framework that incorporates training-time (pre-forgetting) prevention and (post-forgetting) recovery. Under this framework, we design a layer-selective rehearsal strategy that mitigates immediate forgetting during local training, and a rapid knowledge recovery strategy that restores degraded models after long-term cumulative drift. We present a theoretical analysis that characterizes heterogeneous forgetting dynamics and establishes the inevitability of long-term degradation. Our experimental results show that this framework achieves up to 8.3\% mIoU improvement over the strongest federated baseline and up to 31.7\% over conventional fine-tuning. We also deploy the FCL framework on a real-world rover testbed to assess system-level robustness under realistic constraints; the testing results further confirm the effectiveness of our FCL design.

title: AAC: Admissible-by-Architecture Differentiable Landmark Compression for ALT
generated_summary:
This paper introduces AAC (Architecturally Admissible Compressor), a differentiable landmark selector for the ALT (A*, Landmarks, Triangle inequality) shortest-path framework that guarantees admissibility by architectural design rather than through loss regularization or post-hoc calibration. AAC uses a row-stochastic Gumbel-softmax compressor to select a subset of landmarks from a larger teacher pool generated by farthest-point sampling (FPS). Since each compressed heuristic term is a convex combination of admissible teacher terms, admissibility holds for every parameter setting, including under early stopping or training divergence. At deployment, hard argmax reduces the module to classical ALT on a learned subset.

The authors evaluate AAC against FPS-ALT under a rigorous matched per-vertex memory protocol across road networks, synthetic graphs, and citation networks, using pre-registered hypotheses and FDR-corrected statistical tests. The key finding is a structural negative result: FPS's Gonzalez 2-approximation on covering radius is already near-optimal on tested graphs, leaving minimal headroom for any selector. FPS-ALT leads AAC on expansion count across nearly all tested configurations, though AAC achieves faster query latency due to better cache locality. A controlled ablation traces the gap to training-objective drift under default initialization rather than architectural limitations.

The work's significance lies in demonstrating that architectural admissibility is achievable at zero cost within differentiable pipelines, establishing the first differentiable admissible landmark compressor while rigorously characterizing the theoretical ceiling that limits improvement over classical methods.
original_abstract: We introduce \textbf{AAC} (Architecturally Admissible Compressor), a differentiable landmark-selection module for ALT (A*, Landmarks, and Triangle inequality) shortest-path heuristics whose outputs are admissible by construction: each forward pass is a row-stochastic mixture of triangle-inequality lower bounds, so the heuristic is admissible for \emph{every} parameter setting without requiring convergence, calibration, or projection. At deployment, the module reduces to classical ALT on a learned subset, composing end-to-end with neural encoders while preserving the classical toolchain. The construction is the first differentiable instance of the compress-while-preserving-admissibility tradition in classical heuristic search. Under a matched per-vertex memory protocol, we establish that ALT with farthest-point-sampling landmarks (FPS-ALT) has provably near-optimal coverage on metric graphs, leaving at most a few percentage points of headroom for \emph{any} selector. AAC operates near this ceiling: the gap is $0.9$--$3.9$ percentage points on 9 road networks and ${\leq}1.3$ percentage points on synthetic graphs, with zero admissibility violations across $1{,}500+$ queries and all logged runs. At matched memory, AAC is also $1.2$--$1.5{\times}$ faster than FPS-ALT at the median query on DIMACS road networks, amortizing its offline cost within $170$--$1{,}924$ queries. A controlled ablation isolates the binding constraint: training-objective drift under default initialization, not architectural capacity; identity-on-first-$m$ initialization closes the expansion-count gap entirely. We release the module, a reusable matched-memory benchmarking protocol with paired two-one-sided-test (TOST) equivalence and pre-registration, and a reference compressed-differential-heuristics baseline.

title: Evaluating Software Defect Prediction Models via the Area Under the ROC Curve Can Be Misleading
generated_summary:
This paper presents a methodological critique of using the Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) as an evaluation metric for Software Defect Prediction (SDP) models. The authors argue that traditional interpretations of ROC curves and AUC can be misleading because they ignore the threshold values used to classify software modules as faulty or non-faulty.

The core observation is that ROC curves represent model performance across all possible thresholds but do not explicitly encode threshold information. By introducing "threshold-aware" ROC curves—where specific threshold values are mapped onto curve points—the authors demonstrate that models with seemingly good AUC values often perform poorly at practical threshold settings. Specifically, many models that appear to outperform the random classifier may actually have worse True Positive Rate or False Positive Rate than random classification for certain threshold ranges. Similarly, when comparing two models, one with a higher AUC may perform worse than the other at specific thresholds.

Through empirical analysis using real-world SDP datasets with multiple classifiers (including Bayesian Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and SVM), the authors show that these misleading indications occur frequently in practice. They also examine how class imbalance affects ROC curve interpretation.

The authors recommend replacing AUC-based evaluation with threshold-aware approaches, such as plotting TPR and FPR as functions of the threshold, enabling researchers to assess trade-offs at operationally meaningful threshold values. This finding has significant implications, suggesting that many published SDP model evaluations relying on AUC may require reconsideration.
original_abstract: Background: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves are widely used to evaluate the performance of Software Defect Prediction (SDP) models that estimate module fault-proneness, i.e., the probability that a module is faulty. A ROC curve maps a model's performance in terms of True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate for any possible threshold set on fault-proneness. The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) summarizes the performance of a model across all possible thresholds. Traditionally, ROC curves completely above the bisector of the ROC space are considered better than random, and high AUC values are associated with good performance. Aim: We investigate whether these beliefs are correct, hence if SDP model evaluation based on ROC curves and AUC is reliable. Method: We decorate ROC curves by highlighting the points corresponding to threshold values. We also represent True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate as functions of the threshold. Thus, we can evaluate whether a model classifies both faulty and non-faulty modules better than the random model. Results: We show that commonly used evaluation criteria may lead to wrong conclusions. Conclusions: A high value of AUC does not guarantee that both the True Positive Rate and the False Positive Rate of a model are better than the random model's for all possible thresholds. Either decorated ROC curves or alternative representations are needed to appreciate all the relevant aspects of SDP models.

title: RespondeoQA: a Benchmark for Bilingual Latin-English Question Answering
generated_summary:
This paper introduces RespondeoQA, the first bilingual benchmark for evaluating large language models on Latin-English question answering and translation tasks. The dataset comprises approximately 7,800 question-answer pairs drawn from diverse pedagogical sources spanning the 1800s to the present, including standardized exams, quizbowl trivia, and textbooks. Questions are annotated with fine-grained metadata including format (multiple choice or short answer), content category (across 10 types), language pairing, multihop reasoning requirements, and translation constraints. The taxonomy distinguishes knowledge-based questions (history, mythology, literature) from skill-based ones (grammar, scansion, translation).

Three LLMs are evaluated: LLaMA 3.3 (70B), Qwen QwQ (32B), and OpenAI's o3-mini. Overall accuracy ranges from 68% to 72%, with all models performing substantially better on multiple choice questions (approximately 91%) than short answer ones. All models score higher on knowledge-based questions than skill-based ones, with scansion proving particularly challenging (best accuracy only 25%). Reasoning-focused models show modest advantages on literary and metrical tasks but do not outperform LLaMA overall. Question language affects performance inconsistently across models.

The benchmark fills a critical gap in evaluating LLMs for historical and low-resource languages, providing a structured framework for assessing both factual recall and linguistic reasoning. The authors release the dataset publicly to support future research in multilingual and historical language understanding.
original_abstract: We introduce a benchmark dataset for question answering and translation in bilingual Latin and English settings, containing about 7,800 question-answer pairs. The questions are drawn from Latin pedagogical sources, including exams, quizbowl-style trivia, and textbooks ranging from the 1800s to the present. After automated extraction, cleaning, and manual review, the dataset covers a diverse range of question types: knowledge- and skill-based, multihop reasoning, constrained translation, and mixed language pairs. To our knowledge, this is the first QA benchmark centered on Latin. As a case study, we evaluate three large language models -- LLaMa 3, Qwen QwQ, and OpenAI's o3-mini -- finding that all perform worse on skill-oriented questions. Although the reasoning models perform better on scansion and literary-device tasks, they offer limited improvement overall. QwQ performs slightly better on questions asked in Latin, but LLaMa3 and o3-mini are more task dependent. This dataset provides a new resource for assessing model capabilities in a specialized linguistic and cultural domain, and the creation process can be easily adapted for other languages. The dataset is available at: https://github.com/slanglab/RespondeoQA

title: Decoupling Speculation from Merit: The Identity-Bound Asset Integrity Model (IBAIM) for Sustainable Web3 Gaming
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the systemic economic failures plaguing Web3 Play-to-Earn gaming ecosystems, which commonly experience hyperinflationary death spirals due to unchecked speculation, bot exploitation, and perpetual asset oversupply. The authors identify three necessary and sufficient conditions for sustainable open game economies: Anti-Sybil Resilience, Anti-Capital Dominance, and Anti-Inflationary Saturation, arguing that the absence of any single condition guarantees economic collapse.

To satisfy these conditions, the paper introduces the Identity-Bound Asset Integrity Model (IBAIM), a comprehensive technical and economic architecture that decouples financial speculation from in-game merit. The model employs three core mechanisms: Zero-Knowledge biometric hashing combined with Account Abstraction to anchor asset production to verified unique human identities, preventing Sybil attacks; an Asymmetric Utility Decay mechanism that imposes significant performance penalties on assets transferred through secondary markets, thereby limiting capital dominance and Pay-to-Win dynamics; and a dual-factor thermodynamic degradation system where assets decay through both time and usage, introducing digital entropy that counteracts inflationary oversupply and requires continuous human labor for maintenance.

The comparative analysis demonstrates that these mechanisms collectively create meaningful friction against speculation while preserving meritocratic gameplay. The authors acknowledge a deliberate trade-off: sacrificing absolute asset liquidity to preserve systemic integrity. This framework represents a significant paradigmatic contribution, offering a scalable blueprint for transitioning decentralized gaming economies from unsustainable speculative models toward labor-centric value systems with long-term viability.
original_abstract: The rapid collapse of decentralized game economies, often characterized by the \textit{death spiral,} remains the most formidable barrier to the mass adoption of Web3 gaming. This paper proposes that the sustainability of an open game economy is predicated on three necessary and sufficient conditions: Anti-Sybil Resilience, Anti-Capital Dominance, and Anti-Inflationary Saturation. The first section establishes a theoretical proof of these conditions, arguing that the absence of any single dimension leads to systemic failure. The second section explores the dialectical relationship between these dimensions, illustrating how unchecked automation and capital-driven monopolies accelerate asset hyperinflation. In the third section, we introduce the Identity-Bound Asset Integrity Model (IBAIM) as a comprehensive technical solution. IBAIM utilizes Zero-Knowledge (ZK) biometric hashing and Account Abstraction (AA) to anchor asset utility to unique human identities through a privacy-preserving and regulatory-compliant architecture. By exogenizing biometric verification to trusted local environments and utilizing Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Identity (zk-PoI), the model ensures absolute user privacy. Furthermore, by implementing an Asymmetric Utility Decay (AUD) engine-whereby assets suffer a vertical 50% utility cliff upon secondary transfer-and an entropy-driven thermodynamic degradation mechanism., the model successfully decouples financial speculation from in-game merit. Finally, we apply this framework to analyze prominent historical failures in the GameFi sector, demonstrating that their collapse was an inevitable consequence of violating these core economic constraints. Our findings suggest that trading a degree of asset liquidity for system integrity is the only viable path toward long-term economic viability in decentralized virtual worlds.

title: F\textsuperscript{2}LP-AP: Fast \& Flexible Label Propagation with Adaptive Propagation Kernel
generated_summary:
This paper introduces F²LP-AP (Free-from-training Label Propagation with Adaptive Propagation), a training-free framework for semi-supervised node classification that addresses two critical limitations of traditional Graph Neural Networks: computational inefficiency from gradient-based training and poor performance on heterophilic graphs.

The methodology comprises three stages. First, robust class prototypes are constructed using the geometric median of training features via the Weiszfeld algorithm, which resists outlier influence far better than arithmetic means. Second, an adaptive feature propagation mechanism leverages the Local Clustering Coefficient (LCC) to dynamically assign node-specific propagation depth and teleport probability—nodes in dense homophilic communities undergo shallower, more thorough smoothing, while nodes in sparse heterophilic regions retain more of their original features through deeper but more conservative propagation. Third, classification is performed analytically through cosine similarity between evolved node representations and class prototypes, entirely bypassing learnable parameters.

Experiments across eight benchmarks spanning diverse homophily levels demonstrate that F²LP-AP achieves state-of-the-art results among training-free methods, reaching 0.842 accuracy on Texas (heterophilic) and 0.835 on Cora (homophilic), while matching or surpassing supervised GNNs. Notably, inference latency on PubMed is approximately 3% of GCN's. Ablation studies confirm that both the adaptive propagation mechanism and geometric median prototypes contribute significantly, with the latter providing an average 5.8% accuracy improvement over arithmetic mean prototypes. The framework offers a compelling solution where both accuracy and computational efficiency are critical.
original_abstract: Semi-supervised node classification is a foundational task in graph machine learning, yet state-of-the-art Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are hindered by significant computational overhead and reliance on strong homophily assumptions. Traditional GNNs require expensive iterative training and multi-layer message passing, while existing training-free methods, such as Label Propagation, lack adaptability to heterophilo\-us graph structures. This paper presents \textbf{F$^2$LP-AP} (Fast and Flexible Label Propagation with Adaptive Propagation Kernel), a training-free, computationally efficient framework that adapts to local graph topology. Our method constructs robust class prototypes via the geometric median and dynamically adjusts propagation parameters based on the Local Clustering Coefficient (LCC), enabling effective modeling of both homophilous and heterophilous graphs without gradient-based training. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that \textbf{F$^2$LP-AP} achieves competitive or superior accuracy compared to trained GNNs, while significantly outperforming existing baselines in computational efficiency.

title: Fast Bayesian equipment condition monitoring via simulation based inference: applications to heat exchanger health
generated_summary:
This study presents a scalable probabilistic framework for real-time condition monitoring of industrial heat exchangers by applying Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) as a computationally efficient alternative to traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) Bayesian methods. The framework targets the inference of latent health parameters—including fouling resistance, leakage rates, and failure onset times—that cannot be directly measured during operation.

The methodology employs a stochastic heat exchanger model incorporating two failure mechanisms: fouling (modeled as a compound Poisson process) and internal leakage (modeled as exponential growth). Sequential Neural Posterior Estimation with Neural Spline Flows is trained offline on 50,000 forward simulations, learning a mapping from 25-dimensional summary statistics of sensor data to approximate posterior distributions over failure modes and degradation parameters.

Evaluated across six benchmark scenarios with 500 synthetic datasets each, SBI achieves diagnostic accuracy comparable to MCMC for both failure-mode classification and continuous parameter estimation, as confirmed by Wasserstein distances, CRPS scores, and posterior predictive checks. Critically, SBI reduces inference time by several orders of magnitude—becoming more efficient than MCMC after approximately six inference calls—enabling near-instantaneous posterior characterization during deployment.

The significance lies in enabling real-time, uncertainty-aware Bayesian diagnostics for industrial systems. The model-agnostic, likelihood-free nature of SBI makes it applicable to black-box simulators and legacy systems, offering a practical pathway toward scalable predictive maintenance across multiple industrial assets simultaneously.
original_abstract: Accurate condition monitoring of industrial equipment requires inferring latent degradation parameters from indirect sensor measurements under uncertainty. While traditional Bayesian methods like Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) provide rigorous uncertainty quantification, their heavy computational bottlenecks render them impractical for real-time process control. To overcome this limitation, we propose an AI-driven framework utilizing Simulation-Based Inference (SBI) powered by amortized neural posterior estimation to diagnose complex failure modes in heat exchangers. By training neural density estimators on a simulated dataset, our approach learns a direct, likelihood-free mapping from thermal-fluid observations to the full posterior distribution of degradation parameters. We benchmark this framework against an MCMC baseline across various synthetic fouling and leakage scenarios, including challenging low-probability, sparse-event failures. The results show that SBI achieves comparable diagnostic accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification, while accelerating inference time by a factor of82$\times$ compared to traditional sampling. The amortized nature of the neural network enables near-instantaneous inference, establishing SBI as a highly scalable, real-time alternative for probabilistic fault diagnosis and digital twin realization in complex engineering systems.

title: Near-Future Policy Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Near-Future Policy Optimization (NPO), a mixed-policy reinforcement learning framework that enhances reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by using trajectories from near-future checkpoints along the same training run to guide the current policy. The authors formalize a quality-variance trade-off: auxiliary trajectory sources offer signal quality Q (ability to solve problems the current policy cannot) but incur variance cost V from distribution mismatch. The effective learning signal S = Q/V has a unique optimum at an intermediate checkpoint distance, where the future policy is strong enough to provide useful guidance yet close enough to remain learnable.

NPO operates by replacing one rollout slot in the standard group-based RL objective with a verified-correct trajectory from a near-future checkpoint when the current policy struggles on a given prompt. The authors further propose AutoNPO, which automatically detects intervention opportunities through online monitoring of reward stagnation and entropy decline, selecting the optimal checkpoint distance by maximizing an empirical estimate of S.

Experiments on Qwen3-VL-8B across eight multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that NPO outperforms pure on-policy GRPO and existing mixed-policy baselines including LUFFY, ExGRPO, and RLEP. AutoNPO achieves the highest average score of 63.15 (+5.27 over baseline), accelerates early-stage convergence, breaks through late-stage performance plateaus, and maintains higher policy entropy, preventing premature exploration collapse. original_abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a core post-training recipe. Existing mixed-policy methods either import trajectories from external teachers (high-quality but distributionally far) or replay past training trajectories (close but capped in quality), and neither simultaneously satisfies the strong enough (higher $Q$ , more new knowledge to learn) and close enough (lower $V$ , more readily absorbed) conditions required to maximize the effective learning signal $\mathcal{S} = Q/V$. We propose \textbf{N}ear-Future \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization (\textbf{NPO}), a simple mixed-policy scheme that learns from a policy's own near-future self: a later checkpoint from the same training run is a natural source of auxiliary trajectories that is both stronger than the current policy and closer than any external source, directly balancing trajectory quality against variance cost. We validate NPO through two manual interventions, early-stage bootstrapping and late-stage plateau breakthrough, and further propose \textbf{AutoNPO},an adaptive variant that automatically triggers interventions from online training signals and selects the guide checkpoint that maximizes $S$. On Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with GRPO, NPO improves average performance from 57.88 to 62.84, and AutoNPO pushes it to 63.15, raising the final performance ceiling while accelerating convergence.

title: Anchor-and-Resume Concession Under Dynamic Pricing for LLM-Augmented Freight Negotiation
generated_summary:

The adaptive strategy achieves 68.4% agreement in narrow spreads and the highest savings (0.764) in wide spreads, matching a 20-billion-parameter unconstrained LLM broker's performance at negligible computational cost. These results suggest the framework enables scalable, auditable deployment across large freight brokerage operations handling hundreds of thousands of annual negotiations.
original_abstract: Freight brokerages negotiate thousands of carrier rates daily under dynamic pricing conditions where models frequently revise targets mid-conversation. Classical time-dependent concession frameworks use a fixed shape parameter $β$ that cannot adapt to these updates. Deriving $β$ from the live spread enables adaptation but introduces a new problem: a pricing shift can cause the formula to retract a previous offer, violating monotonicity. LLM-powered brokers offer flexibility but require expensive reasoning models, produce non-deterministic pricing, and remain vulnerable to prompt injection. We propose a two-index anchor-and-resume framework that addresses both limitations. A spread-derived $β$ maps each load's margin structure to the correct concession posture, while the anchor-and-resume mechanism guarantees monotonically non-decreasing offers under arbitrary pricing shifts. All pricing decisions remain in a deterministic formula; the LLM, when used, serves only as a natural-language translation layer. Empirical evaluation across 115,125 negotiations shows that the adaptive $β$ tailors behavior by regime: in narrow spreads, it concedes quickly to prioritize deal closure and load coverage; in medium and wide spreads, it matches or exceeds the best fixed-$β$ baselines in broker savings. Against an unconstrained 20-billion-parameter LLM broker, it achieves similar agreement rates and savings. Against LLM-powered carriers as more realistic stochastic counterparties, it maintains comparable savings and higher agreement rates than against rule-based opponents. By decoupling the LLM from pricing logic, the framework scales horizontally to thousands of concurrent negotiations with negligible inference cost and transparent decision-making.

title: CO$_2$ sequestration hybrid solver using isogeometric alternating-directions and collocation-based robust variational physics informed neural networks (IGA-ADS-CRVPINN)
generated_summary:

The methodology exploits the strengths of each component: IGA-ADS uses B-spline-based discretization with L² projections for time-stepping the saturation field, while CRVPINN—a PINN variant using Kronecker delta test functions and a Gram matrix-based robust loss function—efficiently computes pressure updates. The CRVPINN model is pretrained for 20,000 epochs on the initial configuration, then continuously trained for only 100 epochs at each subsequent time step.

The solver is validated on three reservoir configurations with both uniform and non-uniform permeability maps on a 50m × 50m 2D domain. Critically, the hybrid IGA-ADS-CRVPINN solver achieves over three times speedup compared to the IGA-ADS-MUMPS baseline (3,400 versus 10,800 seconds for 128² mesh resolution), demonstrating significant computational advantages for CO₂ sequestration modeling with potential extensions to hydrogen storage and inverse problem formulations.
original_abstract: This paper presents the hybrid solver for a $CO_2$ sequestration problem. The solver uses the IGA-ADS (IsoGeometric Analysis Alternating Directions solver) to compute the saturation scalar field update using the explicit method, and CRVPINN (Collocation-based Robust Variational Physics Informed Neural Networks solver) to compute the pressure scalar field. The study focuses on simulating the physical behavior of $CO_2$ in porous structures, excluding chemical reactions. The mathematical model is based on Darcy's Law. The CRVPINN is pretrained on the initial pressure configuration, and the time step pressure updates require only 100 iterations of the Adam method per time step. We compare our hybrid IGA-ADS solver, coupled with the CRVPINN method, with a baseline of the IGA-ADS solver coupled with the MUMPS direct solver. Our hybrid solver is over 3 times faster on a single computational node from the ARES cluster of ACK CYFRONET. title: Render-in-the-Loop: Vector Graphics Generation via Visual Self-Feedback
generated_summary:

The methodology comprises three components: Visual Self-Feedback (VSF) training, which constructs dense multi-step visual trajectories through fine-grained path decomposition to train the model on interleaved code-and-canvas sequences; a Render-and-Verify (RaV) inference strategy that detects and filters degenerate or redundant generation steps; and careful data preprocessing that decomposes complex SVG paths into atomic subpaths for denser visual feedback.

Built on Qwen3-VL-8B, the model achieves highly competitive performance on the MMSVGBench benchmark for both Text-to-SVG and Image-to-SVG tasks. Notably, training on only 0.85M samples, it surpasses OmniSVG (trained on 2M samples) and InternSVG (trained on 16M samples), demonstrating exceptional data efficiency. Ablation studies confirm that both VSF training and RaV are essential, as naive visual feedback without specialized training actually degrades performance. The paradigm suggests that explicit visual feedback is more critical than data scaling for high-quality vector graphics generation.
original_abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promising capabilities in generating Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) via direct code synthesis. However, existing paradigms typically adopt an open-loop "blind drawing" approach, where models generate symbolic code sequences without perceiving intermediate visual outcomes. This methodology severely underutilizes the powerful visual priors embedded in MLLMs vision encoders, treating SVG generation as a disjointed textual sequence modeling task rather than an integrated visuo-spatial one. Consequently, models struggle to reason about partial canvas states and implicit occlusion relationships, which are visually explicit but textually ambiguous. To bridge this gap, we propose Render-in-the-Loop, a novel generation paradigm that reformulates SVG synthesis as a step-wise, visual-context-aware process. By rendering intermediate code states into a cumulative canvas, the model explicitly observes the evolving visual context at each step, leveraging on-the-fly feedback to guide subsequent generation. However, we demonstrate that applying this visual loop naively to off-the-shelf models is suboptimal due to their inability to leverage incremental visual-code mappings. To address this, we first utilize fine-grained path decomposition to construct dense multi-step visual trajectories, and then introduce a Visual Self-Feedback (VSF) training strategy to condition the next primitive generation on intermediate visual states. Furthermore, a Render-and-Verify (RaV) inference mechanism is proposed to effectively filter degenerate and redundant primitives. Our framework, instantiated on a multimodal foundation model, outperforms strong open-weight baselines on the standard MMSVGBench. This result highlights the remarkable data efficiency and generalization capability of our Render-in-the-Loop paradigm for both Text-to-SVG and Image-to-SVG tasks.

title: On the regularity index of the minimum distance function in projective nested Cartesian codes
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the regularity index of the minimum distance function for projective nested Cartesian codes, a family of linear codes that generalizes classical projective Reed-Muller codes. The regularity index determines the degree beyond which the minimum distance equals one, making it critical for identifying potentially useful error-correcting codes.

The authors employ indicator functions—homogeneous polynomials that vanish at all points of a projective nested product of fields except one designated point—as their primary tool. They construct explicit indicator functions for each point and establish a vanishing criterion that leverages the footprint bound and the algebraic structure of the vanishing ideal. A key methodological insight is that determining the minimal degree of indicator functions for all points reduces to analyzing indicator functions at the canonical basis vectors, since local v-numbers are invariant within certain equivalence classes of points.

The main results provide an explicit formula for the local v-number at each point, showing it depends on which coordinate position contains the first nonzero entry. The regularity index of the minimum distance function is shown to equal the sum of all field cardinalities minus the number of fields, matching the Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity of the quotient ring. Additionally, the authors derive an arithmetical criterion characterizing when the projective nested Cartesian set satisfies the Cayley-Bacharach property, proving this holds if and only if all subfields in the tower are equal.

These results enable efficient computation of code parameters and provide theoretical foundations for identifying degree ranges where projective nested Cartesian codes have meaningful error-correcting capability.
original_abstract: Let $X$ be a projective nested product of fields and let $δ_X(d)$ be the minimum distance in degree $d\geq 1$ of the projective nested Cartesian code $C_X(d)$. The regularity index ${\rm reg}(δ_X)$ of the minimum distance function $δ_X$ is the minimum integer $d_0\geq 0$ such that $δ_X(d)=1$ for $d\geq d_0$. We give a formula for ${\rm reg}(δ_X)$ by determining an indicator function of least degree for each point of $X$ and using the fact that ${\rm reg}(δ_X)$ is the ${\rm v}$-number of the vanishing ideal $I_X$ of $X$. Then we give an arithmetical criterion that characterizes when $X$ is Cayley--Bacharach.

title: Interval POMDP Shielding for Imperfect-Perception Agents
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a shielding framework for autonomous agents with imperfect perception, modeled as Interval Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (IPOMDPs). The key contribution is a method that lifts perfect-perception safety shields to the imperfect-perception setting by using confidence intervals on emission probabilities rather than point estimates, providing robustness to both control-based and deployment distributional shifts with PAC-style correctness guarantees.

The methodology constructs confidence bounds on perception uncertainty from finite labeled data, defining an IPOMDP whose observation model uses interval-valued probabilities. At runtime, the shield propagates over-approximations of reachable belief states (belief envelopes) and tests action admissibility through worst-case linear programming, admitting only actions whose safety score exceeds a threshold under all beliefs in the envelope.

Evaluation across four benchmarks (TaxiNet, Obstacle, CartPole, Refuel) demonstrates that interval belief envelopes occupy a useful middle ground: they outperform point-estimate belief shields when observations are ambiguous and remain usable where support-based shields collapse entirely. However, they incur higher computational costs and greater conservatism, sometimes blocking too many actions. A forward-sampling approximation provides a scalable alternative when exact envelope propagation is infeasible.

The work is significant because it provides formally grounded safety shielding for learned-perception systems under finite-data uncertainty, addressing a critical gap in deploying autonomous agents in safety-critical domains.
original_abstract: Autonomous systems that rely on learned perception can make unsafe decisions when sensor readings are misclassified. We study shielding for this setting: given a proposed action, a shield blocks actions that could violate safety. We consider the common case where system dynamics are known but perception uncertainty must be estimated from finite labeled data. From these data we build confidence intervals for the probabilities of perception outcomes and use them to model the system as a finite Interval Partially Observable Markov Decision Process with discrete states and actions. We then propose an algorithm to compute a conservative set of beliefs over the underlying state that is consistent with the observations seen so far. This enables us to construct a runtime shield that comes with a finite-horizon guarantee: with high probability over the training data, if the true perception uncertainty rates lie within the learned intervals, then every action admitted by the shield satisfies a stated lower bound on safety. Experiments on four case studies show that our shielding approach (and variants derived from it) improves the safety of the system over state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Exploiting LLM-as-a-Judge Disposition on Free Text Legal QA via Prompt Optimization
generated_summary:

The results demonstrate that automatic prompt optimization consistently outperforms LEXam's human-crafted baseline, yielding absolute score gains of 2.79% to 6.74%. Critically, the study reveals an asymmetric transfer pattern: prompts optimized with lenient judge feedback transfer more effectively to strict judges than the reverse. Qualitative analysis explains this asymmetry—strict feedback produces narrow, case-specific prompts prone to overfitting, while lenient feedback encourages generalizable structural frameworks that capture essential legal reasoning processes. Ensemble optimization using both judges yields only modest gains due to conflicting feedback signals.

These findings carry practical significance for practitioners employing LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation: optimizing with permissive judges maximizes both performance gains and cross-judge transferability. The work also highlights that judge evaluative disposition, rather than model size, is the primary determinant of optimization effectiveness, offering actionable guidance for designing robust automated evaluation pipelines in specialized domains.
original_abstract: This work explores the role of prompt design and judge selection in LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations of free text legal question answering. We examine whether automatic task prompt optimization improves over human-centered design, whether optimization effectiveness varies by judge feedback style, and whether optimized prompts transfer across judges. We systematically address these questions on the LEXam benchmark by optimizing task prompts using the ProTeGi method with feedback from two judges (Qwen3-32B, DeepSeek-V3) across four task models, and then testing cross-judge transfer. Automatic optimization consistently outperforms the baseline, with lenient judge feedback yielding higher and more consistent gains than strict judge feedback. Prompts optimized with lenient feedback transfer better to strict judges than the reverse direction. Analysis reveals that lenient judges provide permissive feedback, yielding prompts with broader applicability, whereas strict judges produce restrictive feedback, leading to judge-specific overfitting. Our findings demonstrate algorithmically optimizing prompts on training data can outperform human-centered prompt design and that judges' dispositions during optimization shape prompt generalizability.

title: Supplement Generation Training for Enhancing Agentic Task Performance
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Supplement Generation Training (SGT), a framework that trains a small, open-source language model (1.7B parameters) to generate instance-specific textual supplements that enhance the performance of large, frozen actor models without modifying their weights. This addresses the practical constraint that many powerful language models are accessible only through APIs without gradient access.

The methodology employs a two-phase training pipeline: a warm-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT) phase that teaches the generator to produce supplements in correct formats across eight predefined types (such as chain-of-thought reasoning, mistake warnings, and contrastive examples), followed by an iterative Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) phase that refines supplement quality and type selection using proxy rewards from the actor model's task outcomes. The DPO phase implements a search-and-focus strategy, initially exploring diverse supplement types before converging on the most effective ones for each task.

Evaluated across five benchmarks spanning text-to-SQL, code generation, multi-hop reasoning, and frontier knowledge tasks, SGT achieves a 21% average improvement over baselines without supplements, outperforming prompt optimization methods like DSPy and TextGrad. The framework generalizes across different actor models from distinct model families, including Claude and GPT variants.

The significance of SGT lies in its demonstration that a compact model can serve as an effective, interpretable intermediary that dynamically tailors contextual information to improve large model reasoning, offering a cost-efficient alternative to fine-tuning or scaling inference compute.
original_abstract: Training large foundation models for agentic tasks is increasingly impractical due to the high computational costs, long iteration cycles, and rapid obsolescence as new models are continuously released. Instead of post-training massive models for every new task or domain, we propose Supplement Generation Training (SGT), a more efficient and sustainable strategy. SGT trains a smaller LLM to generate useful supplemental text that, when appended to the original input, helps the larger LLM solve the task more effectively. These lightweight models can dynamically adapt supplements to task requirements, improving performance without modifying the underlying large models. This approach decouples task-specific optimization from large foundation models and enables more flexible, cost-effective deployment of LLM-powered agents in real-world applications.

title: Tokenised Flow Matching for Hierarchical Simulation Based Inference
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Tokenised Flow Matching Posterior Estimation (TFMPE) with likelihood factorisation (LF) sampling, a novel approach for simulation-efficient Bayesian inference in hierarchical models where simulators are expensive and observations may be function-valued or irregularly sampled.

The key methodological contribution is LF sampling, a two-stage training strategy that factorises the likelihood rather than the posterior. In the first stage, a per-site neural surrogate is trained from single-site simulations, reducing simulator calls to one per training sample regardless of the number of sites. In the second stage, this surrogate generates synthetic multi-site observations to train an amortised posterior estimator. The posterior estimator uses an encoder-only transformer architecture with a novel tokenisation scheme incorporating group identifiers for site membership, variable identifiers, and functional inputs, enabling flexible handling of irregular and variable-length observations. Flow matching provides stable training dynamics for learning the conditional density.

Evaluated on a newly developed hierarchical SBI benchmark suite, TFMPE with LF sampling achieves superior sample efficiency over non-hierarchical baselines and competitive performance against posterior factorisation methods, particularly when many sites make simulation costs prohibitive. Applied to seasonal infectious disease modeling (100 sites) and computational fluid dynamics for haemodynamics, TFMPE produces well-calibrated posteriors while reducing computational costs by orders of magnitude—achieving an 1850× speedup per synthetic observation in the haemodynamics setting. This represents the first application of functional observations within hierarchical SBI.
original_abstract: The cost of simulator evaluations is a key practical bottleneck for Simulation Based Inference (SBI). In hierarchical settings with shared global parameters and exchangeable site-level parameters and observations, this structure can be exploited to improve simulation efficiency. Existing hierarchical SBI approaches factorise the posterior yet still simulate across multiple sites per training sample; We instead explore likelihood factorisation (LF) to train from single-site simulations. In LF sampling we learn a per-site neural surrogate of the simulator and then assemble synthetic multi-site observations to amortise inference for the full hierarchical posterior. Building on this, we propose Tokenised Flow Matching for Posterior Estimation (TFMPE), a tokenised flow matching approach that supports function-valued observations through likelihood factorisation. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce a benchmark for hierarchical SBI. We validate TFMPE on this benchmark and on realistic infectious disease and computational fluid dynamics models, finding well-calibrated posteriors while reducing computational cost.

title: ALAS: Adaptive Long-Horizon Action Synthesis via Async-pathway Stream Disentanglement
generated_summary:

This functional disentanglement addresses critical limitations of existing methods, which tightly couple environmental perception with self-state representation, hindering cross-domain transfer and skill reuse.

Evaluated on three progressively challenging long-horizon tasks involving humanoid control, ALAS achieves a 42% improvement over CML and 17% over TokenHSI in overall task completion on foundational benchmarks. For generalization tasks, it improves long-horizon success rates by 28% and 21% over TokenHSI while reducing execution times. Ablation studies confirm that both the dual-stream disentanglement and adaptive fusion mechanism are individually essential for robust performance.

ALAS represents a promising step toward scalable embodied intelligence, demonstrating that biologically motivated functional separation of perception streams enables superior cross-domain adaptation and modular skill reuse in complex HSI scenarios.
original_abstract: Long-Horizon (LH) tasks in Human-Scene Interaction (HSI) are complex multi-step tasks that require continuous planning, sequential decision-making, and extended execution across domains to achieve the final goal. However, existing methods heavily rely on skill chaining by concatenating pre-trained subtasks, with environment observations and self-state tightly coupled, lacking the ability to generalize to new combinations of environments and skills, failing to complete various LH tasks across domains. To solve this problem, this paper presents ALAS, a cross-domain learning framework for LH tasks via biologically inspired dual-stream disentanglement. Inspired by the brain's "where-what" dual pathway mechanism, ALAS comprises two core modules: i) an environment learning module for spatial understanding, which captures object functions, spatial relationships, and scene semantics, achieving cross-domain transfer through complete environment-self disentanglement; ii) a skill learning module for task execution, which processes self-state information including joint degrees of freedom and motor patterns, enabling cross-skill transfer through independent motor pattern encoding. We conducted extensive experiments on various LH tasks in HSI scenes. Compared with existing methods, ALAS can achieve an average subtasks success rate improvement of 23\% and average execution efficiency improvement of 29\%.

title: COMPASS: COntinual Multilingual PEFT with Adaptive Semantic Sampling
generated_summary:

Language-specific adapters are then fine-tuned using weight-decomposed low-rank adaptation (DoRA), enabling efficient multi-language deployment from a single base model.

Evaluated across three model architectures (Phi4-Mini, LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B) on benchmarks including Global-MMLU, MMLU-ProX, XQuAD, XNLI, and MGSM, COMPASS consistently outperforms monolingual fine-tuning, random sampling, and linguistically-informed baselines like LangRank and LangSim, with statistically significant improvements. The method automatically detects and exploits language synergies without prior linguistic knowledge, achieving greatest gains for low-resource languages. A continual learning extension, COMPASS-ECDA, addresses distribution shifts over time through distributional anchors and elastic regularization, achieving Pareto-optimal learning-forgetting trade-offs across multiple temporal transitions.

The work's significance lies in demonstrating that strategically aligning training data distributions with target usage patterns provides superior cross-lingual transfer compared to linguistic similarity heuristics, offering a scalable, modular framework for reducing linguistic inequality in deployed multilingual systems.
original_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit performance disparities across languages, with naive multilingual fine-tuning frequently degrading performance due to negative cross-lingual interference. To address this, we introduce COMPASS (COntinual Multilingual PEFT with Adaptive Semantic Sampling), a novel data-centric framework for adapting LLMs to target languages. COMPASS leverages parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) by training lightweight, language-specific adapters on a judiciously selected subset of auxiliary multilingual data. The core of our method is a distribution-aware sampling strategy that uses multilingual embeddings and clustering to identify semantic gaps between existing training data and a target usage distribution. By prioritizing auxiliary data from under-represented semantic clusters, COMPASS maximizes positive cross-lingual transfer while minimizing interference. We extend this into a continual learning framework, COMPASS-ECDA, which monitors for data distribution shifts in production and dynamically updates adapters to prevent model staleness, balancing adaptation to new data with the preservation of existing knowledge. Across three different model architectures (Phi-4-Mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B) and multiple challenging multilingual benchmarks (Global-MMLU, MMLU-ProX), including unseen long-context tasks (OneRuler), we demonstrate that COMPASS consistently outperforms baseline methods guided by linguistic similarity, providing an effective, efficient, and sustainable solution for developing and maintaining high-performing multilingual models in dynamic environments.

title: ONOTE: Benchmarking Omnimodal Notation Processing for Expert-level Music Intelligence
generated_summary:
This paper introduces ONOTE, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate Omnimodal Notation Processing (ONP) capabilities of large language models across three music notation systems: standard staff notation, Jianpu (numbered musical notation), and Guitar Tablature. The benchmark addresses the fragmented nature of existing music AI evaluations and the unreliability of subjective "LLM-as-a-judge" approaches for assessing musical understanding.

ONOTE encompasses four complementary task tracks: Visual Score Understanding, Cross-Format Notation Conversion, Audio-to-Symbolic Transcription, and Symbolic Music Generation and Aesthetics. A key methodological contribution is the deterministic evaluation pipeline that projects all model outputs into a unified canonical pitch space using absolute scientific pitches, then employs Levenshtein Edit Distance-based sequence alignment to calculate exact accuracy. This approach eliminates subjective scoring biases and specifically penalizes common LLM failures such as hallucinated notes and temporal drift. The benchmark comprises 1,120 high-quality test samples constructed through a rigorous three-stage pipeline involving data extraction, cross-modal alignment, and targeted question design.

Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art omnimodal models reveal a significant discrepancy between perceptual and reasoning capabilities: while current systems perform adequately on visual recognition tasks, they exhibit substantial limitations in music-theoretic reasoning, temporal alignment, and structured symbolic generation. ONOTE provides a scalable, reproducible testbed that highlights fundamental challenges in processing highly structured musical domains, aiming to drive development of more musically aware AI systems.
original_abstract: Omnimodal Notation Processing (ONP) represents a unique frontier for omnimodal AI due to the rigorous, multi-dimensional alignment required across auditory, visual, and symbolic domains. Current research remains fragmented, focusing on isolated transcription tasks that fail to bridge the gap between superficial pattern recognition and the underlying musical logic. This landscape is further complicated by severe notation biases toward Western staff and the inherent unreliability of "LLM-as-a-judge" metrics, which often mask structural reasoning failures with systemic hallucinations. To establish a more rigorous standard, we introduce ONOTE, a multi-format benchmark that utilizes a deterministic pipeline--grounded in canonical pitch projection--to eliminate subjective scoring biases across diverse notation systems. Our evaluation of leading omnimodal models exposes a fundamental disconnect between perceptual accuracy and music-theoretic comprehension, providing a necessary framework for diagnosing reasoning vulnerabilities in complex, rule-constrained domains.

title: GeoRelight: Learning Joint Geometrical Relighting and Reconstruction with Flexible Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformers
generated_summary:
GeoRelight introduces a unified generative framework that jointly performs single-image portrait relighting and 3D geometry reconstruction, arguing that these tasks are mutually beneficial rather than sequential. The key insight is that accurate geometry enables physically plausible shadow and shading generation, while shading cues in images provide shape-from-shading information that refines geometry estimation.

The framework employs a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer that repurposes the temporal dimension of a pretrained video DiT as a modality dimension, simultaneously denoising five outputs: relit images, albedo, surface normals, 3D geometry, and segmentation masks. A flexible modality switch mask enables each modality to serve as either a generation target or conditioning input. The authors propose isotropic Normalized Orthographic Depth (iNOD), a novel geometry representation that isotropically normalizes 3D shapes before orthographic projection, avoiding the distortion artifacts that standard depth maps or point maps exhibit when compressed through pretrained VAE encoders. A strategic mixed-data training procedure combines fully-labeled synthetic data with auto-labeled light stage and in-the-wild images to bridge the synthetic-real domain gap.

Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across relighting, geometry reconstruction, and intrinsic estimation tasks, outperforming both specialized single-task methods and general-purpose baselines. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic benefits of joint modeling, validating that geometry improves relighting fidelity and appearance cues enhance geometric detail. The framework represents a significant advance toward unified, physically-grounded image understanding and manipulation.
original_abstract: Relighting a person from a single photo is an attractive but ill-posed task, as a 2D image ambiguously entangles 3D geometry, intrinsic appearance, and illumination. Current methods either use sequential pipelines that suffer from error accumulation, or they do not explicitly leverage 3D geometry during relighting, which limits physical consistency. Since relighting and estimation of 3D geometry are mutually beneficial tasks, we propose a unified Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that jointly solves for both: GeoRelight. We make this possible through two key technical contributions: isotropic NDC-Orthographic Depth (iNOD), a distortion-free 3D representation compatible with latent diffusion models; and a strategic mixed-data training method that combines synthetic and auto-labeled real data. By solving geometry and relighting jointly, GeoRelight achieves better performance than both sequential models and previous systems that ignored geometry.

title: Learning to Evolve: A Self-Improving Framework for Multi-Agent Systems via Textual Parameter Graph Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Textual Parameter Graph Optimization (TPGO), a framework that reconceptualizes multi-agent system (MAS) optimization as a graph evolution problem, enabling automated refinement of complex agent architectures. The key insight is that agent configurations can be decomposed into a Textual Parameter Graph (TPG), where agents, tools, and logic units are modular nodes connected by directed edges representing dependencies and information flow. title: Kinematic Optimization of Phalanx Length Ratios in Robotic Hands Using Potential Dexterity

title: MGDA-Decoupled: Geometry-Aware Multi-Objective Optimisation for DPO-based LLM Alignment

original_abstract: Aligning large language models (LLMs) to desirable human values requires balancing multiple, potentially conflicting objectives such as helpfulness, truthfulness, and harmlessness, which presents a multi-objective optimisation challenge. Most alignment pipelines rely on a fixed scalarisation of these objectives, which can introduce procedural unfairness by systematically under-weighting harder-to-optimise or minority objectives. To promote more equitable trade-offs, we introduce MGDA-Decoupled, a geometry-based multi-objective optimisation algorithm that finds a shared descent direction while explicitly accounting for each objective's convergence dynamics. In contrast to prior methods that depend on reinforcement learning (e.g., GAPO) or explicit reward models (e.g., MODPO), our approach operates entirely within the lightweight Direct Preference Optimisation (DPO) paradigm. Experiments on the UltraFeedback dataset show that geometry-aware methods -- and MGDA-Decoupled in particular -- achieve the highest win rates against golden responses, both overall and per objective.

title: CKM Beyond Channel Gain: Spatial Correlation Map Construction with Deep Learning

original_abstract: Channel knowledge map (CKM) is a promising technique to achieve environment-aware wireless communication and sensing. title: Variance Is Not Importance: Structural Analysis of Transformer Compressibility Across Model Scales
