original_abstract: We present a systematic empirical study of transformer compression through over 40 experiments on GPT-2 (124M parameters) and Mistral 7B (7.24B parameters). Our analysis covers spectral compression, block-level function replacement, rotation-based quantization, activation geometry, and adaptive early exit. We identify five structural properties relevant to compression. (1) Variance is not importance: high-variance activation directions are approximately 96 percent uncorrelated with predictive directions (measured via CCA), and projecting onto these subspaces preserves over 90 percent of variance while degrading perplexity. (2) Block linearity is conditional: transformer blocks are approximately linear (R^2 ~ 0.95 on GPT-2, 0.93 on Mistral block 31) only under the correct upstream distribution; modifying earlier blocks induces distribution shift that degrades downstream approximations. (3) The reconstruction wall: approaches that factor weights into quantized components amplify errors through cross-terms, making direct quantization strictly superior. (4) Linearity increases with depth: Mistral 7B exhibits a progression from R^2 = 0.17 (block 0) to R^2 = 0.93 (block 31), indicating a division between nonlinear feature construction and linear refinement. (5) Approximately 30 percent of tokens are computationally easy, confirmed via exit heads and KL divergence sensitivity. We demonstrate that single-block linear replacement achieves 34x compression with a 1.71 perplexity increase on the final block of Mistral 7B, while multi-block replacement fails due to residual error accumulation and distribution shift. These findings suggest fundamental limits to static post-training compression and motivate adaptive, per-token computation as a more effective direction.

title: Learning Hippo: Multi-attractor Dynamics and Stability Effects in a Biologically Detailed CA3 Extension of Hopfield Networks

original_abstract: We present a biologically detailed extension of the classical Hopfield/Marr auto-associative memory model for CA3, implementing ten populations (two asymmetric pyramidal subtypes, eight GABAergic interneuron classes), forty-seven compartments, multi-rule plasticity (recurrent Hebb, BCM anti-saturation, mossy-fiber short-term, endocannabinoid iLTD, burst-gated Hebb), and a bimodal cholinergic encoding/consolidation cycle. Evaluated on pattern completion across auto-associative, associative, and temporal regimes, and on a controlled inhibitory-proportion manipulation at $N{=}256$, the full architecture exhibits \emph{three qualitative signatures absent from a minimal Hopfield baseline}: (i)~multi-attractor cross-seed behaviour at $K{=}5$ with biologically realistic inhibitory proportions, where two of five seeds converge to positive attractors with margin ${+}0.10{-}0.22$ (Cohen's $d{=}0.71$, one-sided $p{=}0.08$); (ii)~target-selective associative recall in paired $(A, B)$ memory at $K{\geq}5$, where the full model retrieves $B$ from a partial cue of $A$ while the minimal model echoes $A$ (Pearson margin $Δ{=}{+}0.163$ at $K{=}5$); (iii)~reduced cross-seed variance of the full model below the minimal baseline under clean upstream, with ratios $1.0{-}3.0$. title: Intersectional Fairness in Large Language Models
generated_summary:

In disambiguated contexts, accuracy is systematically influenced by stereotype alignment, with models performing better when correct answers reinforce stereotypes, particularly in race-gender intersections. Although some fairness metrics suggest low disparity, outcome distributions remain uneven across intersectional groups. Consistency analysis shows that no model achieves fully stable behavior across repeated prompts, with LLaMA-3 exhibiting the greatest instability and highest stereotyped error rates, while even better-performing models like Claude-Sonnet-4 demonstrate occasional failures.

These findings underscore that fairness assessment in LLMs requires multi-metric, multi-context evaluation accounting for intersectional subgroup structure, stereotype alignment, and output stability, rather than relying on aggregate accuracy alone—particularly critical for high-stakes deployment scenarios.
original_abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in socially sensitive settings, raising concerns about fairness and biases, particularly across intersectional demographic attributes. In this paper, we systematically evaluate intersectional fairness in six LLMs using ambiguous and disambiguated contexts from two benchmark datasets. We assess LLM behavior using bias scores, subgroup fairness metrics, accuracy, and consistency through multi-run analysis across contexts and negative and non-negative question polarities. Our results show that while modern LLMs generally perform well in ambiguous contexts, this limits the informativeness of fairness metrics due to sparse non-unknown predictions. In disambiguated contexts, LLM accuracy is influenced by stereotype alignment, with models being more accurate when the correct answer reinforces a stereotype than when it contradicts it. This pattern is especially pronounced in race-gender intersections, where directional bias toward stereotypes is stronger. Subgroup fairness metrics further indicate that, despite low observed disparity in some cases, outcome distributions remain uneven across intersectional groups. Across repeated runs, responses also vary in consistency, including stereotype-aligned responses. Overall, our findings show that apparent model competence is partly associated with stereotype-consistent cues, and no evaluated LLM achieves consistently reliable or fair behavior across intersectional settings. These findings highlight the need for evaluation beyond accuracy, emphasizing the importance of combining bias, subgroup fairness, and consistency metrics across intersectional groups, contexts, and repeated runs.

title: Improving clinical interpretability of linear neuroimaging models through feature whitening
generated_summary:

The methodology applies regularized ZCA-cor whitening (with a tunable parameter controlling decorrelation strength) as a preprocessing step before logistic regression classification. Whitening matrices are computed on training data and applied to test data within cross-validation folds to prevent data leakage. The approach is evaluated on two psychiatric classification tasks: bipolar disorder versus healthy controls (861 participants) and schizophrenia versus healthy controls (604 participants), using ROI-based voxel-based morphometry measures from multi-site datasets.

Results demonstrate that whitening preserves classification performance (no significant differences in ROC-AUC or balanced accuracy) while substantially improving the alignment of model-derived region importance rankings with established ENIGMA consortium meta-analytic findings for both disorders. The approach provides a principled, structure-informed framework for improving the biological plausibility of linear neuroimaging models and lays groundwork for extending whitening-based interpretability methods to deep learning architectures in neuroimaging.
original_abstract: Linear models are widely used in computational neuroimaging to identify biomarkers associated with brain pathologies. However, interpreting the learned weights remains challenging, as they do not always yield clinically meaningful insights. This difficulty arises in part from the inherent correlation between brain regions, which causes linear weights to reflect shared rather than region-specific contributions. In particular, some groups of regions, including homologous structures in the left and right hemispheres, are known to exhibit strong anatomical correlations. In this work, we leverage this prior neuroanatomical knowledge to introduce a whitening approach applied to groups of regions with known shared variance, designed to disentangle overlapping information across correlated brain measures. We additionally propose a regularized variant that allows controlled tuning of the degree of decorrelation. We evaluate this method using region-of-interest features in two psychiatric classification tasks, distinguishing individuals with bipolar disorder or schizophrenia from healthy controls. Importantly, unlike PCA or ICA which use whitening as a dimensionality reduction step, our approach decorrelates anatomically informed pairs of neuroanatomical regions while retaining the full input signal, making it specifically suited for feature interpretation rather than feature selection. Our findings demonstrate that whitening improves the interpretability of model weights while preserving predictive performance, providing a robust framework for linking linear model outputs to neurobiological mechanisms.

title: Short-time, Wavelet-inspired Mouse Submovement Detection
generated_summary:

An iterative decomposition loop identifies candidate submovements, then refines their parameters (amplitude, width, and location) using a novel wavelet-weighted loss metric that prioritizes fit accuracy around speed peaks rather than weighting all time points equally. This work provides researchers with a principled tool for studying overlapping submovements, enabling deeper analysis of human motor planning strategies in computerized tasks.
original_abstract: Submovements are ballistic components of human motion constituting a large part of motor interaction and arising from the cyclical and overlapping cognitive processes of perception, motor planning, and motor execution. Extracting submovements is challenging as the motions tend to overlap, or start before the previous ends. We propose and evaluate use of a wavelet-inspired technique to accurately locate and parameterize submovements from one-dimensional speed time series. Our method employs a self-weighted loss refinement step to identify and improve regions of poor quality of fit, a challenge for simpler wavelet transforms. We demonstrate the accuracy of our method by presenting analysis of ~6,400 1-2s trials of synthetic egocentric camera (first-person shooter) aim data for which we know ground truth, modeled from a similarly sized real data set of 13 users. title: GRPO-VPS: Enhancing Group Relative Policy Optimization with Verifiable Process Supervision for Effective Reasoning
generated_summary:

The methodology leverages the model's own evolving belief in the correct answer as a supervision signal. Specifically, the approach segments a model's reasoning trace into discrete steps and appends the correct final answer at each segment boundary. By computing the conditional probability of the correct answer at these positions, the method derives probability increments between adjacent segments, which serve as dense, interpretable process supervision signals quantifying each segment's contribution to reaching the correct solution. These segment-wise signals complement trajectory-level advantages during policy optimization.

Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 7B models demonstrate substantial improvements across four math reasoning benchmarks, achieving up to +2.6 points Pass@1 over GRPO while reducing reasoning length by 11–14%. The method outperforms both outcome-only baselines and process-supervised approaches relying on costly Monte Carlo rollouts or auxiliary reward models. These findings highlight that confidence-driven, verifier-free process supervision offers a scalable and effective direction for improving both reasoning accuracy and efficiency in language models without requiring auxiliary models or additional computational overhead.
original_abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has advanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) by leveraging direct outcome verification instead of learned reward models. Building on this paradigm, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) eliminates the need for critic models but suffers from indiscriminate credit assignment for intermediate steps, which limits its ability to identify effective reasoning strategies and incurs overthinking. In this work, we introduce a model-free and verifiable process supervision via probing the model's belief in the correct answer throughout its reasoning trajectory. By segmenting the generation into discrete steps and tracking the conditional probability of the correct answer appended at each segment boundary, we efficiently compute interpretable segment-wise progress measurements to refine GRPO's trajectory-level feedback. This approach enables more targeted and sample-efficient policy updates, while avoiding the need for intermediate supervision derived from costly Monte Carlo rollouts or auxiliary models. Experiments on mathematical and general-domain benchmarks show consistent gains over GRPO across diverse models: up to 2.6-point accuracy improvements and 13.7% reasoning-length reductions on math tasks, and up to 2.4 points and 4% on general-domain tasks, demonstrating strong generalization.

title: Cooperative Profiles Predict Multi-Agent LLM Team Performance in AI for Science Workflows
generated_summary:

The authors evaluate 35 open-weight LLMs (ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters) across six established games—including Weakest-Link, Common-Pool Resource, Collective Risk, O-Ring, and Public Goods—each capturing distinct cooperation challenges with known Nash equilibria and Pareto optima as behavioral benchmarks.

The study employs a two-part methodology. First, models are profiled based on their cooperative behavior across the six games. Second, the same models are deployed as specialized agent teams performing collaborative AI-for-Science tasks under shared budget constraints. Bayesian hierarchical measurement-error models then assess whether game-derived cooperative profiles predict downstream scientific workflow outcomes.

Key results show that LLMs exhibit systematic differences in cooperative behavior only partially explained by model size or general capability. Models demonstrating higher coordination effort and greater contributions to collective goods produce more accurate scientific reports, while those withdrawing from joint production perform worse. Notably, theory-of-mind prompting improves game cooperation but reduces task completion in realistic workflows, revealing a divergence between stylized and applied cooperation.

The framework offers a practical screening tool for multi-agent deployment, reducing evaluation costs by up to 44 times in speed and 27 times in token usage compared to full workflow evaluation, enabling efficient assessment of LLMs' collaborative potential.
original_abstract: Multi-agent systems built from teams of large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for collaborative scientific reasoning and problem-solving. These systems require agents to coordinate under shared constraints, such as GPUs or credit balances, where cooperative behavior matters. Behavioral economics provides a rich toolkit of games that isolate distinct cooperation mechanisms, yet it remains unknown whether a model's behavior in these stylized settings predicts its performance in realistic collaborative tasks. Here, we benchmark 35 open-weight LLMs across six behavioral economics games and show that game-derived cooperative profiles robustly predict downstream performance in AI-for-Science tasks, where teams of LLM agents collaboratively analyze data, build models, and produce scientific reports under shared budget constraints. Models that effectively coordinate games and invest in multiplicative team production (rather than greedy strategies) produce better scientific reports across three outcomes, accuracy, quality, and completion. These associations hold after controlling for multiple factors, indicating that cooperative disposition is a distinct, measurable property of LLMs not reducible to general ability. Our behavioral games framework thus offers a fast and inexpensive diagnostic for screening cooperative fitness before costly multi-agent deployment.

title: MAPRPose: Mask-Aware Proposal and Amodal Refinement for Multi-Object 6D Pose Estimation
generated_summary:

First, the Mask-Aware Pose Proposal (MAPP) module constrains feature correspondences to visible foreground regions, pruning the hypothesis space from hundreds of templates to a compact set of top-K candidates. original_abstract: 6D object pose estimation in cluttered scenes remains challenging due to severe occlusion and sensor noise. We propose MAPRPose, a two-stage framework that leverages mask-aware correspondences for pose proposal and amodal-driven Region-of-Interest (ROI) prediction for robust refinement. In the Mask-Aware Pose Proposal (MAPP) stage, we lift 2D correspondences into 3D space to establish reliable keypoint matches and generate geometrically consistent pose hypotheses based on correspondence-level scoring, from which the top-$K$ candidates are selected. In the refinement stage, we introduce a tensorized render-and-compare pipeline integrated with an Amodal Mask Prediction and ROI Re-Alignment (AMPR) module. By reconstructing complete object geometry and dynamically adjusting the ROI, AMPR mitigates localization errors and spatial misalignment under heavy occlusion. Furthermore, our GPU-accelerated RGB-XYZ reprojection enables simultaneous refinement of all $N \times B$ pose hypotheses in a single forward pass. Evaluated on the BOP benchmark, MAPRPose achieves a state-of-the-art Average Recall (AR) of 76.5%, outperforming FoundationPose by 3.1% AR while delivering a 43x speedup in multi-object inference.

title: Fully Dynamic Algorithms for Coloring Triangle-Free Graphs

This paper presents the first non-trivial fully dynamic algorithms for coloring triangle-free graphs, addressing a gap in the dynamic graph algorithms literature. The methodology centers on two key innovations. First, the authors develop a *dynamic entropy compression* technique, adapting the entropy compression method (rooted in algorithmic Lovász Local Lemma) to the dynamic setting. This is achieved by jointly modeling the interaction between the randomized algorithm and the adversary as a compression scheme, logging both standard compression information and dynamic graph changes. Second, they design a recursive hierarchy of vertex partitions that reduces the triangle-free coloring problem to dynamic (Δ+1)-coloring at its base case, rather than relying on Reed's list-coloring reduction used in static settings.

The key results include a base algorithm achieving O(Δ²√n) amortized update time for (1+ε)Δ/ln Δ coloring, which through the recursive framework improves to Δ^{o(1)}√n update time for O(Δ/log Δ) coloring. Against oblivious adversaries, the update times improve further.

The significance extends beyond the specific coloring result: the paper demonstrates that entropy compression serves as a natural potential function for analyzing randomized dynamic algorithms against adaptive adversaries, offering a fundamentally new analytical tool for the dynamic algorithms community.
original_abstract: A celebrated result of Johansson in graph theory states that every triangle-free graph of maximum degree $Δ$ can be properly colored with $O(Δ/\lnΔ)$ colors, improving upon the "greedy bound" of $Δ+1$ coloring in general graphs. This coloring can also be found in polynomial time. We present an algorithm for maintaining an $O(Δ/\lnΔ)$ coloring of a dynamically changing triangle-free graph that undergoes edge insertions and deletions. The algorithm is randomized and on $n$-vertex graphs has amortized update time of $Δ^{o(1)}\log{n}$ per update with high probability, even against an adaptive adversary. A key to the analysis of our algorithm is an application of the entropy compression method that to our knowledge is new in the context of dynamic algorithms. This technique appears general and is likely to find other applications in dynamic problems and thus can be of its own independent interest.

title: Minimum Energy per Bit of Unsourced Multiple Access with Location-Based Codebook Partitioning
generated_summary:

The authors consider a simplified Gaussian UMA channel with two user clusters experiencing different deterministic path losses. They derive finite-blocklength random-coding achievability bounds on the minimum energy per bit for three strategies: location-based codebook partitioning, common codebook with joint decoding, and common codebook with successive interference cancellation. Additionally, they perform replica-method large-system analysis, revealing that codebook partitioning effectively decomposes the UMA problem into two equivalent scalar Gaussian channels with distinct signal-to-noise ratios, whereas a single codebook yields an equivalent fading channel with unknown instantaneous fading. Practical validation is provided through simulations using coded compressive sensing with multisource approximate message passing decoding.

Numerical results demonstrate that location-based codebook partitioning consistently achieves lower minimum energy per bit compared to both alternative approaches, with the advantage growing as the number of active users increases. Interference cancellation with a common codebook performs particularly poorly, showing approximately 6 dB degradation relative to the partitioning approach. These findings suggest that exploiting readily available path-loss information through codebook partitioning offers meaningful energy-efficiency improvements for practical massive IoT systems.
original_abstract: We derive finite-blocklength bounds on the minimum achievable energy per bit over a Gaussian unsourced multiple access (UMA) channel in the presence of heterogeneous path-loss conditions. We consider a setting in which the path loss is known to the users, which enables the use of location-based codebook partitioning [Çakmak et al., 2025]. Through numerical simulations and a large-system analysis based on the replica method, we quantify the performance gain of this strategy relative to the conventional UMA approach in which all users employ a common codebook.

title: A Universal Quantum Information Preserving Photonic Switch for Scalable Quantum Networks

The UQS addresses a critical gap in quantum networking by enabling dynamic, coherence-preserving quantum state routing, essential for distributed quantum computing, entanglement-as-a-service, and the emerging heterogeneous quantum internet.
original_abstract: Quantum networks are a keystone of the quantum internet. However, existing implementations remain largely confined to static point-to-point links due to the absence of a switching paradigm capable of dynamically routing fragile quantum entanglement without introducing decoherence. Here, we propose the Universal Quantum Switch, a foundational building block allowing on-demand, non-blocking, and encoding-agnostic routing of quantum information, as well as seamless modality conversion between disparate quantum platforms. We develop a prototype in thin-film lithium niobate and experimentally demonstrate robust switching with $\le 4\%$ decoherence via thermo-optic modulation and high-speed electro-optic switching of arbitrary entangled states at 1 MHz. Moreover, we show that our platform can support reconfiguration speeds up to 1 GHz. To our knowledge, this work represents the first demonstration of multi-node dynamic entanglement distribution at these speeds. Complementing these experimental results, we project the architecture's scalability, showing dimension-independent decoherence, and provide a scalable, interoperable building block for heterogeneous quantum network fabrics.

title: Ion Channel Dynamics in Temperature-Dependent Weibel Instability Saturation

Using the Gkeyll framework with a discontinuous Galerkin scheme, the authors perform noise-free continuum kinetic simulations of counter-streaming electron-ion plasma beams, complemented by analytical and numerical solutions of the kinetic dispersion relation. The simulations employ a 1D spatial, 2D velocity-space configuration with realistic mass ratio.

Key findings reveal that electron temperature governs the linear growth rate across all cases, while ion temperature primarily affects nonlinear saturation timescales and mechanisms. Hot electron cases exhibit magnetic trapping as the dominant saturation mechanism, whereas cold electron cases show comparable contributions from both electrostatic and magnetic trapping regardless of ion temperature. Critically, electrons rapidly thermalize and merge into single broadened populations, while ions maintain distinct bulk velocities in shielded current channels and undergo much slower thermalization. The authors validate these findings against Wind/SWE and MMS1 spacecraft observations showing analogous temperature anisotropy signatures at collisionless shocks.

These results have significant implications for understanding magnetic field generation in astrophysical collisionless shocks and large-scale structure formation, where ion channel merging drives late-time magnetic energy growth.
original_abstract: We present 1X2V continuum Vlasov-Maxwell simulations of interpenetrating plasma beams with mobile ions. While the early-time evolution is similar to the stationary-ion case, the late-time dynamics are dominated by the ion-Weibel instability. As ion channels merge, the magnetic energy increases and the magnetic structures extend further along the beam direction. Electrons rapidly reach thermal equilibrium, whereas ions retain distinct bulk velocities for much longer and thermalize more slowly. These results are relevant to collisionless shock formation in astrophysical compact objects and laser-plasma experiments. Wind/SWE observations place all four simulated cases in the firehose/Weibel-unstable region of the proton temperature anisotropy diagram, and MMS1 observations of a quasi-perpendicular bow shock ($θ_{Bn}\approx83^\circ$, $M_A\approx27$) show a similar electron-ion thermalization disparity.

title: Meshless $h$-adaptive Solution for non-Newtonian Natural Convection in a Differentially Heated Cavity
generated_summary:
This paper presents an automatic h-adaptive meshless discretization procedure for solving non-Newtonian natural convection problems in differentially heated cavities using the Radial Basis Function-generated Finite Difference (RBF-FD) method. The main contribution is a lightweight variability indicator that quantifies the dissimilarity of approximated differential operator values within local stencils, enabling automatic identification of regions requiring refinement or coarsening without a priori knowledge of solution features.

The methodology begins with a coarse initial node distribution, allowing the flow to develop before iteratively adjusting node density based on the variability indicator. When the indicator exceeds a refinement threshold, local internodal distances are decreased; when it falls below a derefinement threshold, they are increased. The procedure is applied to power-law non-Newtonian fluid natural convection in both a classical de Vahl Davis square cavity and a spherical cavity at various Rayleigh numbers.

Key results demonstrate that the adaptive approach achieves comparable accuracy to uniform fine discretizations while requiring significantly less computational time—approximately 35% less than manually refined static discretizations and an order of magnitude less than constant-density approaches. The adaptivity parameters transfer effectively between different geometries. Convergence studies show the average Nusselt number settling to values consistent with established reference solutions.

The significance lies in eliminating the need for manual, problem-specific refinement patterns in meshless simulations, though the authors identify remaining issues including spurious refinement in stagnant regions and divergence introduced during field re-interpolation.
original_abstract: One of the main challenges in numerically solving partial differential equations is finding a discretisation for the computational domain that balances the accurate representation of the underlying field with computational efficiency. Meshless methods approximate differential operators based on the values of the field in computational nodes, offering a natural approach to adaptivity. The density of computational nodes can either be increased to enhance accuracy or decreased to reduce the number of numerical operations, depending on the properties of the intermediate solution. In this paper, we utilise an adaptive discretisation approach for the numerical simulation of natural convection in non-Newtonian fluid flow. The shear-thinning behaviour is interesting both due to its numerous occurrences in nature, blood being a prime example, and due to its properties, as the decreasing viscosity with increasing shear rate results in sharper flow structures. We focus on the de Vahl Davis test case, a natural convection driven flow in a differentially heated rectangular cavity. The thin boundary layer flow along the vertical boundaries makes this an ideal test case for refinement. We demonstrate that adaptively refining the node density enhances computational efficiency and examine how the parameters for adaptive refinement affect the solution.

title: Hierarchical organization of critical brain dynamics
generated_summary:
This study investigates how signatures of criticality—the hypothesis that the brain operates near a phase transition—are distributed across brain regions and relate to anatomical hierarchy. Using large-scale Neuropixels recordings from mouse visual cortex and hippocampus (Allen Brain Institute dataset), the authors apply the phenomenological renormalization group (PRG) framework to coarse-grain neural spiking activity and introduce the Jensen-Shannon distance from a Gaussian distribution as a robust measure of distance from trivial dynamics.

The key finding is that criticality signatures are not uniform across the brain but follow a gradient aligned with known anatomical hierarchies. In the visual cortex, the primary visual area exhibits the strongest critical signatures, which systematically decay along higher-order regions. A similar gradient appears in the hippocampus. However, a notable dissociation emerges: static scaling exponents (α, β) suggest lower hierarchical regions are closer to criticality, while the dynamical exponent z shows the opposite trend, with higher-order regions exhibiting longer temporal correlations. The scaling exponents closely obey a theoretically predicted relation across all regions. Remarkably, temporal correlations between criticality signatures across regions accurately reconstruct the brain's anatomical hierarchy, and this functional network is modulated by task engagement.

These results demonstrate that critical dynamics possess rich spatial organization mirroring morphological hierarchy, establishing a quantitative link between collective neural dynamics and structural brain architecture.
original_abstract: The hierarchical organization of the brain is a fundamental structural principle, while brain criticality is a leading hypothesis for its collective dynamics. However, the connection between structure and signatures of criticality remains an open question. Here, we address this issue by applying phenomenological renormalization group approaches to large-scale neuronal spiking activity from the mouse visual cortex and hippocampus. We find that signatures of criticality are not uniform, but instead vary systematically along the known anatomical hierarchy in both brain systems. Strikingly, the direction along this gradient is inconsistent across different criticality exponents, revealing a nontrivial, measure-dependent organization: exponents based on static properties point to a gradient in one direction, while the exponent based on dynamic properties points in the opposite direction. Moreover, the signatures across the visual system are strongly modulated by the engagement in a visual task. We show that the correlations among criticality markers of different brain regions during active engagement are sufficient to reconstruct the anatomical hierarchy from the dynamics. Scaling exponents closely follow a theoretically predicted scaling relation among them, and covary with the hierarchical position. Our findings provide a direct link between the collective dynamics of neurons and the macroscopic architecture of the brain.

title: The clock ambiguity is back with a vengeance
generated_summary:
This paper reexamines the clock ambiguity problem in the Page-Wootters proposal, which attempts to explain how time emerges from a fundamentally timeless quantum universe satisfying the constraint equation Ĥ|Ψ⟩ = 0. The Page-Wootters mechanism posits that time arises from entanglement between a clock subsystem and the rest of the world, but Albrecht and Iglesias showed that different choices of clock degrees of freedom yield all possible states and dynamics, undermining the proposal's predictive power.

The author critically evaluates Marletto and Vedral's claim that imposing a noninteraction condition between clock and world eliminates this ambiguity. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, the author identifies a key incorrect assumption in their proof and demonstrates that the clock ambiguity persists and is in fact maximal for both continuous and discrete ideal clocks, even with the noninteraction condition imposed. The technical reason is that the clock Hamiltonian's spectrum washes out information contained in the world Hamiltonian's spectrum, leaving only the dimension of the world's Hilbert space recoverable.

The paper further establishes that some ambiguity is actually necessary to preserve spacetime symmetries including relativity of simultaneity and diffeomorphism invariance, while maximal ambiguity destroys all predictive power. The resolution lies in accepting that operators must have definite associations with the physical properties they represent, meaning the clock ambiguity arises from an incomplete description of reality rather than representing a fundamental perspectival freedom.
original_abstract: Page and Wootters (1983) showed how time and dynamics can emerge in a stationary system containing a clock. Albrecht (1995) later showed, for discrete time, that within this framework any dynamical evolution can be obtained simply by choosing a different clock. Marletto and Vedral (2017) claimed that this ambiguity disappears assuming that the clock and the rest of the world do not interact. I show that their proof relies on an incorrect mathematical assumption. Also, eliminating the ambiguity completely would obstruct spacetime symmetries. Whereas the original clock ambiguity concerns all possible histories of a discrete-time system evolving under arbitrary Hamiltonians, but not the Hamiltonians themselves, I prove a stronger version for continuous and discrete unbounded time: the ambiguity extends to both histories and Hamiltonians, including noninteracting ones. Only the dimension of the Hilbert space remains. One might hope to dismiss the ambiguity as merely perspectival, but I show that this would predict incorrect correlations between outcomes and their records, making even knowledge impossible. Purely relational approaches therefore face both the stronger and the original clock ambiguity problems. The ambiguity is removed by taking into account the physical meaning of the operators.

title: Phenomenological Detector Design and Optimization in Vertically-Integrated Differentiable Full Simulations with Agentic-AI
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first application of agentic AI to phenomenological detector design optimization, using a dual-readout segmented crystal electromagnetic calorimeter for future colliders as a case study. The authors introduce a modular bilevel optimization framework that couples DD4HEP/Geant4 full detector simulations with downstream reconstruction algorithms, enabling simultaneous optimization of detector geometry parameters and digitization/reconstruction parameters against physics-driven objectives.

The methodology employs the SciFi agentic framework powered by Claude Code Opus 4.6 to autonomously navigate an 11-dimensional parameter space encompassing detector geometry (crystal width, length, projective offset), digitization settings (ADC bit depth, sampling rate), and waveform reconstruction parameters. The agent iteratively proposes parameter configurations, executes simulations, interprets results, and adaptively refines its search strategy through reasoning and trial-and-feedback loops.

Key results demonstrate that the agent successfully decomposed the 11-dimensional problem into tractable subspaces by identifying decoupled metrics and nuisance parameters, reducing optimization to two sequential two-dimensional scans. However, the study also reveals important limitations: the agent mischaracterized the projective offset as a nuisance parameter due to lacking higher-level experimental context about realistic crystal granularity scales, highlighting that physics-informed human guidance remains essential.

This work demonstrates that agentic AI can significantly accelerate complex detector optimization workflows and reduce human labor, while establishing that domain expertise is critical for ensuring physically meaningful results—positioning this approach as a practical tool for next-generation experiment design.
original_abstract: We present the first implementation of AI agents into the design and optimization of detectors in high-energy physics experiments via a bilevel optimization framework that vertically integrates detector geometry, front-end digitization, and high-level reconstruction algorithm parameters in differentiable full simulations. Using the example of a dual-readout, segmented crystal EM calorimeter with a baseline resolution of $3\%/\sqrt{E}$, we investigate the capabilities and value propositions of AI agents in the identification and reduction of key detector parameters and in the nonlinear traversal of a given detector design's full parameter space. We find that LLM-based reasoning models today, without being given additional experiment-specific context, are able to effectively execute complex workflows and proactively suggest generic but relevant avenues for further study or improvement. Here, we demonstrate an AI agent's ability to use the workflow to simultaneously optimize a representative subset of vertically integrated detector parameters: crystal granularity and length, number of ADC bits and sampling rate, and center-of-gravity hit-clustering radius. We find that effective integration of agents into the complex workflows of frontier areas of research not only significantly reduces labor and compute, but opens up efficient avenues for computational validation of first-principles design choices. While the ability to make autonomous leaps of physics-motivated judgment or insight is not demonstrated in this work, this study defines the current frontier of experimental design methods in high-energy physics.

title: Turbulent mixing of a hydrogen jet in crossflow: direct numerical simulation and model assessment
generated_summary:
This study presents the first direct numerical simulation (DNS) of a hydrogen jet in air crossflow, designed to represent port fuel injection conditions in hydrogen-fueled heavy-duty internal combustion engines. The authors generate a high-fidelity DNS dataset using the spectral element code Nek5000 with approximately 93 million grid points, and use it to systematically assess the performance of large eddy simulation (LES) and Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approaches for predicting turbulent mixing.

The results demonstrate that LES provides excellent agreement with DNS for both mean velocity fields, Reynolds stresses, and hydrogen mass fraction distributions. In contrast, RANS significantly under-predicts all Reynolds stress components and the hydrogen mixing process, producing smaller fuel clouds with higher peak concentrations. By extracting turbulent transport properties directly from DNS data, the authors identify two root causes for RANS deficiencies: substantial under-prediction of turbulent viscosity and an overly high default turbulent Schmidt number (0.78 versus a DNS-derived most probable value of 0.44). Furthermore, analysis of anisotropic Schmidt number components and misalignment angles between DNS-derived and model-predicted species fluxes reveals that the isotropic turbulent diffusivity assumption underlying the commonly used Gradient Diffusion Hypothesis is fundamentally invalid for this configuration, with misalignment angles peaking around 37 degrees. These findings provide critical guidance for improving RANS turbulent mixing models for hydrogen engine applications and establish a benchmark DNS dataset for future model development.
original_abstract: A numerical study for a hydrogen (H2) jet in an air crossflow (JICF) was performed using direct numerical simulation (DNS), large eddy simulation (LES), and Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) approaches, based on a geometry representative of key aspects of port fuel injection (PFI) in a H2-fueled heavy-duty internal combustion engine. The focus was placed on the H2 mixing process and the turbulent species flux model used in the latter two approaches. Based on the DNS data, the performance of LES and RANS on predicting the turbulent flow fields and mixing process was comprehensively evaluated. Results showed that LES performs very well in predicting both the mean velocity and the Reynolds stress. In contrast, RANS significantly under-predicts all Reynolds stress components, while predicting the mean flow field relatively well. Regarding the H2 mixing prediction, LES shows an excellent agreement with DNS, while RANS significantly under-predicts the mixing process. The underlying reasons for the poor performance of RANS were identified by extracting turbulent transport properties used in RANS approach from DNS data. It was found that the turbulent diffusivity used in RANS is much smaller than that derived from DNS, which is attributed to the over-prediction on turbulent Schmidt number (Sct), as well as the under-prediction on turbulent viscosity. By further analyzing the anisotropic components of Sct and the misalignment angle between turbulent species fluxes directly obtained from DNS and those predicted by the RANS mixing model, the commonly used assumption of isotropic turbulent diffusivity in RANS was demonstrated to be invalid for the present configuration. This study provided a unique DNS dataset for H2 jet in a crossflow relevant to H2 PFI engines and generated new insights on improved modeling of turbulent mixing.

title: Exact formulas for arbitrary order velocity-gradient moments in isotropic turbulence
generated_summary:
This paper develops an analytical framework for deriving exact expressions of arbitrary-order statistical moments of both longitudinal and transverse velocity gradients in homogeneous isotropic turbulence, applicable to compressible and incompressible flows. The key novelty lies in circumventing the prohibitively complex linear systems traditionally required for high-order isotropic tensor representations, which grow as (2n−1)!! independent contractions for nth-order moments.

The methodology combines isotropic tensor representations with orientational averaging, expressing velocity-gradient moments directly in terms of scalar invariants of the velocity gradient tensor. This approach yields closed-form expressions without solving large systems of equations, extending beyond previous work that was limited to longitudinal gradients in incompressible flows. The authors obtain a general formula for longitudinal moments valid at arbitrary order and derive corresponding expressions for transverse gradients.

Validation through direct numerical simulations of both incompressible and compressible turbulence demonstrates excellent agreement. For incompressible turbulence, relative errors for longitudinal moments (up to eighth order) remain generally below 5%, while transverse moment errors (up to sixth order) stay below 0.5%. For compressible turbulence, errors remain below 8.5% and 5%, respectively, despite slight anisotropy from shocklets. Analysis of individual invariant term contributions reveals that terms involving powers of the strain-rate tensor dominate, while rotation-rate contributions, though smaller, cannot be neglected.

These exact expressions provide physical constraints for velocity gradient modeling, tools for assessing flow isotropy, and benchmarks for validating high-order statistics in numerical simulations.
original_abstract: Statistical moments of velocity gradients provide fundamental information on the small-scale properties of turbulence. In this work, we propose a systematic method to derive exact expressions for statistical moments of arbitrary order for both longitudinal and transverse velocity gradients in isotropic turbulence. The approach is applicable to both compressible and incompressible flows and expresses the moments in terms of invariants of the velocity gradient tensor. The derivation combines isotropic tensor theory, orientational averaging, and an algorithmic implementation, enabling the computation of high-order moments in a unified framework. We show that longitudinal velocity gradient moments of order higher than three depend not only on $\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{S}^2)$, which is proportional to the dissipation rate, but also on $\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{S}^3)$, which reflects strain self-amplification, where $\boldsymbol{S}$ denotes the strain-rate tensor. The resulting theoretical expressions are validated through comparisons with existing theoretical results and direct numerical simulations.

title: Nearly Complete Charge--Spin Conversion via Strain-Eliminated Fermi Pockets in a $d$-Wave Altermagnet
generated_summary:
This study demonstrates that the charge-to-spin conversion efficiency (CSE) in the d-wave altermagnet KV₂Se₂O can be driven to nearly 100% through in-plane equibiaxial tensile strain engineering. The central insight is that residual elliptical Fermi pockets near the X and Y points in momentum space act as parasitic conduction channels that enhance charge conductivity while suppressing spin conductivity, thereby limiting CSE well below the theoretical maximum.

The authors employ first-principles density functional theory calculations combined with an effective two-orbital tight-binding model to systematically track the strain-dependent evolution of the Fermi surface topology and spin transport properties. The tight-binding model reveals that suppressing next-nearest-neighbor hopping parameters—mimicking tensile strain effects—progressively eliminates the parasitic pockets, restoring the ideal orthogonal flat Fermi surface geometry characteristic of a perfect d-wave altermagnet.

At 4% tensile strain, the in-plane CSE reaches a record 95–96%, up from 84% in the unstrained material, with quantitative agreement between DFT and model calculations. Additionally, an unconventional out-of-plane spin current component is identified, achieving approximately 55% conversion efficiency at optimal crystallographic orientations, potentially enabling field-free perpendicular magnetization switching.

These findings establish strain engineering as a clean, continuously tunable alternative to chemical doping for maximizing spin-current generation in altermagnets, positioning KV₂Se₂O as a promising platform for next-generation spintronic devices compatible with epitaxial thin-film fabrication.
original_abstract: The room-temperature altermagnet \mathrm{KV_2Se_2O} possesses nearly orthogonal flat Fermi surfaces, which in an idealized $d$-wave limit enable complete spin-channel separation and a theoretical charge-to-spin conversion efficiency (CSE) of 100%. Realistic samples, however, host residual elliptical Fermi pockets that enhance charge conductivity while suppressing spin conductivity, drastically reducing the CSE. Here we show that in-plane equibiaxial tensile strain systematically eliminates these parasitic pockets, restoring the flat-band geometry. Our first-principles calculations reveal that the CSE increases monotonically with strain, reaching a record value of approximately 96% at 4% strain. An effective tight-binding model fitted to the computed band structure accurately captures the evolution of the Fermi surface and confirms that the suppression of the pockets -- governed by reduced next-nearest-neighbor hoppings -- is the dominant mechanism for the strain-enhanced CSE. We further identify an unconventional out-of-plane spin current that emerges under tilted electric fields and achieves a CSE of nearly 55% at optimal orientations, offering a promising pathway for field-free perpendicular magnetization switching. Our work establishes strain engineering as a practical route to approach the ultimate conversion limit in altermagnets and provides a design principle for high-efficiency spintronic devices.

title: Molecular dynamics simulations of Nafion thin films at a platinum catalyst surface: Correlating structure with charging behaviour
generated_summary:
This study presents molecular dynamics simulations of a platinum(111)–water–Nafion thin-film interface to characterize the structural and electrostatic properties of the local reaction environment in polymer electrolyte fuel cells. The main contribution is establishing a coherent picture connecting water film thickness, ionomer structure, and catalyst charging state to the electrostatic behavior at the interface, including the computation of differential capacitance as a diagnostic fingerprint.

The authors construct a dense Nafion skin layer using Voronoi tessellation to determine optimal strand packing, then simulate systems with varying water content (0–9000 water molecules) at two temperatures using the LAMMPS code. Surface charging is implemented via the fixed charge method, with charge neutrality maintained by adjusting hydronium ion numbers. Electrostatic potentials are obtained by double integration of planar-averaged charge densities.

Key results indicate that a thermodynamically stable water film of less than 13 Å forms between platinum and Nafion, consistent with experimental neutron scattering data. Hydronium ions strongly accumulate at the platinum surface, with a second adsorption layer forming under negative surface charging due to crowding effects. Differential capacitances range from 4–12 μF/cm² and exhibit asymmetric, water-content-dependent behavior around the potential of zero charge.

These findings provide atomistic insight into how water content and electrode charging reshape the interfacial electrolyte structure, establishing a computational framework applicable to evaluating alternative PFAS-free ionomer materials.
original_abstract: Electrocatalysis is greatly influenced by the local reaction environment, which is governed by the structure of the catalyst, the distribution of the electrolyte, and the local electric field. In catalytic systems comprised of complex molecular species like ionomers, the distribution of electrolyte can vary substantially, resulting in divers local reaction environments. In order to gain atom-scale insight into this micro-environment we construct a model system consisting of a platinum surface, varying levels of water, and a Nafion thin film and conduct molecular dynamics simulations. We employ a construction based on Voronoi tesselation to assemble a dense film of ionomer that fully covers the platinum substrate. An energy analysis reveals that water film configurations with thickness of less then 1.3 nm are stable. Simulations with charged platinum surfaces are analysed in view of electrostatic conditions and differential capacitance of the interface configuration. Trends observed in these properties can be interpreted in view of the crowding of hydronium ions or the Nafion film at the platinum surface. The presented workflow can be easily applied to investigate novel ionomers for use in PEMFCs.

title: Entanglement of two optical emitters mediated by a terahertz channel
generated_summary:
This paper presents a theoretical protocol for generating steady-state entanglement between two polar optical emitters mediated by a terahertz (THz) quantum channel, establishing a hybrid visible-THz quantum interface. The authors address the gap in THz quantum technologies by leveraging polar, optically-active emitters with permanent dipole moments, which enable radiative transitions between laser-dressed states tunable to THz frequencies.

The methodology employs a driven-dissipative approach where two non-identical emitters are driven by carrier and sideband optical fields while coupled to a shared lossy THz cavity mode. The carrier laser creates dressed states with THz-scale Rabi splittings, while the sideband drive induces secondary dressing that enables collective dissipation through overlapping Mollow triplets. Through a generalized rotating wave approximation and adiabatic elimination of the cavity, the authors derive analytical conditions for stabilizing an entangled dark state, revealing a fundamental trade-off between entanglement purity and stabilization rate governed by the doubly-dressed mixing angle.

Numerical simulations predict high steady-state concurrence exceeding 0.9 across a broad THz spectral window (0.5–3.0 THz) and wide ranges of cavity parameters. The authors also propose a purely optical quantum state tomography protocol with error mitigation, demonstrating faithful state reconstruction under realistic detection efficiencies.

This work establishes a foundational primitive for THz quantum networks, where entanglement is mediated by THz modes while all control and measurement operations remain in the mature visible regime.
original_abstract: Quantum technologies in the terahertz (THz) require a coherent interface between addressable qubits and THz quantum channels -- a capacity that so far, remains largely underdeveloped. Here, we propose and demonstrate the generation of steady-state entanglement between polar quantum emitters, mediated by THz photons. We exploit strong visible-light driving of the emitters to create Rabi-split dressed eigenstates whose energy separation can be optically tuned into the THz regime. The polar nature of the emitters activates THz transitions within these eigenstates, allowing them to couple to a THz photonic mode that induces collective dissipative dynamics. A coherent driving and control of these effective THz emitters is achieved by using a sideband optical drive with detuning close to the THz transition frequency. The resulting interplay of collective dissipation and driving activates a mechanism to generate steady-state entanglement with high values of the concurrence ($C>0.9$), attainable under experimentally feasible parameters. Crucially, both coherent manipulation and quantum state tomography are implemented entirely through optical means, avoiding direct THz control and detection. This establishes a hybrid visible-THz quantum interface in which a THz channel mediates qubit-qubit entanglement (a key operational requirement for THz quantum technologies) while remaining optically accessible.

title: Towards hybrid kinetic/drift-kinetic simulations in 6d Vlasov codes
generated_summary:
This paper presents a novel implicit field solver for hybrid kinetic ion/drift-kinetic electron simulations within the BSL6D Vlasov code, addressing a critical challenge in magnetic confinement fusion research. The key problem is that coupling fully kinetic ions with drift-kinetic electrons via the Vlasov-Poisson system introduces high-frequency modes (Langmuir and upper hybrid waves) that impose prohibitively restrictive time-step constraints, preventing ion-scale turbulence studies.

The authors enforce quasi-neutrality to eliminate these fast waves, but determining the corresponding electric potential is non-trivial in fully kinetic frameworks where ion polarization is implicitly embedded in the distribution function. Their solution derives the quasi-neutral electric potential directly from the semi-Lagrangian advection algorithm, focusing on the massless electron limit. The approach features an automatic error-balancing mechanism and spectral correction techniques that maintain the quasi-neutrality constraint even in the presence of steep gradients characteristic of tokamak edge plasmas.

The authors rigorously prove that the implicitly determined potential preserves the global second-order convergence of the underlying Strang-splitting scheme. Numerical experiments confirm this O(Δt²) convergence and successfully verify two branches of ion Bernstein waves. Without the introduced interpolation error corrections, unphysical density drifts lead to numerical instabilities in edge-relevant parameter regimes.

This work establishes a foundational framework for future full-f, two-species simulations of tokamak edge turbulence, ultimately targeting phenomena such as the L-H transition that govern plasma confinement quality.
original_abstract: Simulating fully kinetic, two-species plasmas is computationally challenging due to the stiff multiscale dynamics of electrons and ions. While enforcing a quasi-neutral time evolution mitigates this stiffness, it requires an electric potential that consistently maintains this constraint. In this work, we present an implicit approach to determine this electric field self-consistently within the semi-Lagrangian, fully kinetic BSL6D code. We employ a hybrid two-species model that couples kinetic ions with massless, drift-kinetic electrons, enabling an implicit treatment of the latter. Notably, the model captures the generation of ion-scale zonal flows. Beyond the algorithmic description, we provide a proof of second-order time-splitting error convergence under specific regularity assumptions. A key feature of our approach is an error-balancing mechanism: we demonstrate that the field solver achieves the required accuracy of the electric field by automatically adjusting the error of certain moments of the distribution function. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of semi-Lagrangian interpolation errors to ensure robustness against the steep density and temperature gradients characteristic of tokamak edge plasmas.

title: Performance characterisation of the Hamamatsu R760 photomultiplier tube for the PLUME detector
generated_summary:
This paper presents comprehensive performance characterization of Hamamatsu R760 photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used in the PLUME detector, the luminometer of the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. PLUME is a hodoscope of 48 PMTs designed to monitor luminosity in real time during LHC Runs 3 and 4, where luminosity levels are approximately five times higher than in previous runs.

The characterization methodology employs a picosecond diode laser as a light source within a light-tight enclosure, with measurements of gain, transit-time drift, linearity, and dark current performed using instruments including a picoammeter, DRS4 digitizer board, and calibrated photodiodes. An ageing campaign using LED illumination assessed long-term PMT durability.

Key results show an average absolute gain of 1.5 × 10⁷ at the maximum supply voltage of 1250 V. Transit-time variation across the full operating voltage range remains below 7 ns (less than 11% relative variation). The PMT response is linear to within 10% for integrated charges below 10 pC, corresponding to approximately three detected particles at nominal gain. Dark currents remain below 20 nA at the highest operating voltage. The ageing campaign accumulated 340 C of integrated charge, demonstrating that despite an initial fourfold gain reduction, the PMTs can sustain operation throughout Runs 3 and 4 by adjusting the supply voltage from approximately 800 V to 1035 V, well within the allowable maximum. These results confirm the suitability of the R760 PMTs for reliable long-term luminosity monitoring at LHCb.
original_abstract: The Probe for Luminosity Measurement detector is a novel luminometer designed to monitor the luminosity and beam conditions of the Large Hadron Collider at the interaction point of the LHCb experiment, starting from Run 3. The detector is based on a hodoscope composed of 48 Hamamatsu R760 photomultiplier tubes, which detect the Cherenkov light produced by charged particles originating from the interaction region. The accurate and stable operation of these sensors is essential to ensure reliable luminosity measurements throughout the full data-taking period. This paper presents a detailed characterisation of the photomultiplier tubes currently installed in the detector. In particular, their absolute gain, transit-time drift, linearity, dark current, and ageing behaviour are systematically studied under controlled laboratory conditions. The results provide a comprehensive assessment of the performance of the detection modules and establish the optimal operating conditions required to ensure stable and precise measurements throughout Run 3 and Run 4.

title: Flexible Piezoresistive Yarn Sensor for Human Physiological Signal Measurement
generated_summary:
This study presents the development and optimization of a flexible piezoresistive yarn (FPY) sensor based on conductive thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) filament containing graphene particles for measuring multiple human physiological signals. The main contribution lies in the sensor's design optimization, achieving both wide working range and high sensitivity through a tight triangular bonding pattern configured on parallel polyester yarns, enabling dual-mode operation as both strain and pressure sensor.

The FPY was fabricated using a simple extrusion technique via 3D printing. Preliminary experiments evaluated the effects of pattern density and yarn length on sensitivity, establishing that tighter patterns with minimal FPY length yield optimal performance. The final sensor design was tested on a healthy male subject for measuring neck motion (coughing, swallowing, talking), finger bending at various angles, respiratory signals (normal, deep, and rapid breathing), and arterial blood pressure waveforms at the wrist.

Key results demonstrate that all measured signals exhibit morphological characteristics consistent with established physiological references. The sensor achieved low baseline drift across measurements, with mean absolute errors remaining minor and relative baseline drift percentages below 20% for most signals. The arterial blood pressure waveform measurement successfully resolved low-magnitude features including systolic peaks, dicrotic notches, and dicrotic peaks, confirming high sensitivity.

The sensor's ability to detect diverse physiological signals spanning different magnitudes and frequencies highlights its potential for continuous, non-invasive health monitoring in personalized healthcare and wearable applications.
original_abstract: Continuous monitoring of physiological signals is essential for the early detection of health problems. A measurement system that ensures high sensitivity, accuracy, and user comfort is needed. In this study, we designed and optimized a flexible piezoresistive yarn (FPY) sensor to achieve a high sensitivity and wide working range for detecting physiological signals. The representative sensor design was constructed by applying an FPY bonding pattern, utilizing tightly arranged triangular patterns and using minimal FPY. The prototype sensor operates in two measurement modes, strain and pressure, and was evaluated for measuring neck motion, finger bending, respiratory signals, and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms. A qualitative evaluation, performed by comparing the characteristics of the measurement results of each physiological signal with those from related studies, indicates a high similarity in its morphological characteristics. Then, a quantitative evaluation through baseline drift analysis demonstrates that the FPY sensor displays high measurement stability. The ABP waveform measurement shows the most stable baseline, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of $0.0051 \pm 0.0029$ in terms of baseline drift, using normalized values from 0 to 1. Based on our results, the prototype sensor can be used as an innovative solution for physiological signal monitoring and can be further enhanced for personalized healthcare and sports applications.

title: A microwave super-resolution imaging approach towards breast cancer margin mapping
generated_summary:
This paper presents a novel microwave single-pixel imaging approach for intraoperative breast cancer margin assessment, addressing the critical challenge of determining whether sufficient healthy tissue surrounds an excised tumor during breast-conserving surgery. The technique overcomes the inherent spatial resolution limitations of radiofrequency imaging by employing near-field photo-generated masks on a passivated silicon photomodulator, enabling deeply sub-wavelength resolution.

The methodology combines a portable vector network analyzer operating at 11–20 GHz with a digital micromirror device that projects Hadamard basis patterns onto the silicon modulator. The photoexcited patterns locally modulate microwave reflectivity, and computational single-pixel imaging reconstructs complex-valued hyperspectral images. Margin depth is determined by fitting the measured spectral response to transfer matrix method simulations, exploiting quarter-wavelength Fabry-Pérot resonances that maximize sensitivity to tissue thickness variations in the 0–2 mm range relevant to clinical margin guidelines.

Using tissue-mimicking hydrogel phantoms with spatially varying margin depths, the authors demonstrate quantitative margin depth mapping over a 100 mm × 100 mm field of view at 1.5 mm lateral resolution, successfully identifying localized positive margins. Simulations confirm robustness to inter-patient variations in tissue hydration. The approach offers a safe, non-ionizing, low-cost alternative to existing techniques, with imaging times compatible with surgical workflows and significant potential to reduce reoperation rates currently affecting up to 40% of breast-conserving surgery patients.
original_abstract: Accurate characterisation of margins in excised breast cancer tumours is critical to the success of surgical interventions, yet margin status is typically confirmed post-operatively using histopathology. Here we present a new approach to intraoperative margin assessment based on microwave single pixel imaging, demonstrating tissue phantom hydration mapping across large areas (~10 cm x 10 cm) at ~1 mm resolution. By leveraging the photo-induced change in microwave transparency of a silicon modulator placed under the sample, we map the microwave reflectivity and identify positive margins with deeply sub-wavelength resolution. We test the discriminatory capabilities of our approach using gelatine-based tumour phantoms with variations in water density representative of the margin and cancerous tissues of a resected tumour. We demonstrate the capability to identify, locate and quantify inadequate margins up to the typically targeted minimum thickness of 2 mm. Furthermore, using numerical modelling, we show that our approach is expected to be resilient to patient-specific tissue differences. Our technique has potential for future deployment as a real-time intraoperative tissue margin analysis tool.

title: Weighted complement graphs of spatial networks with functional connections reveal nodes with high potential for new links
generated_summary:
This study introduces a novel methodology for constructing weighted complement graphs of spatial networks with functional connections, applied to public transport networks (PTNs) in P-space representation. The complement graph captures all unrealized connections between existing stops, with edge weights estimated from geographical distances between nodes and network-specific distributions of effective velocities and waiting times.

The authors compute degree and eigenvector centrality in both original P-space graphs and their weighted complements for 31 metro networks worldwide. They identify nodes with the highest potential for new connections by analyzing centrality in the complement graph. A key finding is that the relationship between node centrality in the original and complement graphs shifts from the expected negative linear correlation in unweighted networks to a predominantly positive correlation in weighted versions, driven by the interplay between network topology and spatial embedding. Testing against multiple null models that decouple topology from geography confirms that this reversal is attributable to spatial effects.

The most central nodes in the weighted complement graph are not peripheral nodes but rather geographically central nodes with relatively low topological connectedness—indicating high potential for new links. This challenges conventional planning approaches focused on existing hubs. The results carry implications for transport network planning, suggesting that densifying connections through geographically central but poorly connected nodes could efficiently improve network accessibility and robustness.
original_abstract: In this study, we take a systematic look at the unrealised part of public transport networks (PTNs) with functional connections. We consider their complement graphs and study their structure. The complement graph $\bar G$ of an unweighted graph $G$ is a straightforward concept, yielding a graph on the same set of nodes, and an edge exists in $\bar G$ if and only if it is not present in $G$. In contrast, a weighted complement graph cannot be uniquely determined. However, if we consider PTNs with travel times as edge weights, there are physical constraints on the possible weight ranges. We propose a method to construct weighted complement graphs of operational PTN graph representations based on the geographical distances between nodes (representing stops) and assign weights to edges based on distance, combined with network-specific distributions of effective velocities and waiting times. We observe that the most central nodes in the weighted complement graph do not correspond to the least central nodes in the original network but are, remarkably, those in the geographical centre of the network that lack topological connectedness. Testing against null models on a dataset of 31 metro networks worldwide confirms that this is a fundamentally spatial effect.

title: How to quantify long-time rotational motion in molecular systems
generated_summary:
This paper addresses fundamental limitations in existing methods for quantifying long-time rotational diffusion in molecular systems, particularly supercooled liquids approaching the glass transition. The authors identify two conventional approaches—the Euler vector method, which tracks molecular orientation between two time points but produces bounded angular displacements preventing extraction of a diffusion constant, and the integral method, which accumulates angular velocity over time but introduces systematic errors because it incorrectly assumes three-dimensional rotation matrices commute. This latter error causes the integral method to yield finite rotational diffusion constants even in glasses where rotation is completely arrested.

To overcome these limitations, the authors propose a novel "threshold method" that combines advantages of both approaches. This method monitors the amplitude of the Euler rotation vector and resets the measurement each time a threshold angular displacement is crossed, accumulating unbounded angular displacements while maintaining mathematical consistency with the non-commutative nature of rotations.

The method is validated against a series of analytically tractable models of increasing complexity, including free diffusion, confined dynamics, intermittent cage-escape dynamics, and anomalous sub-diffusion. In all cases, the threshold method correctly captures the expected long-time behavior, including proper diffusion constants, sub-diffusive exponents, and van Hove angular distributions, while conventional methods fail qualitatively.

These results have significant implications for understanding rotational-translational coupling and the Debye-Stokes-Einstein relation in supercooled liquids, suggesting that previous numerical studies may have drawn incorrect physical conclusions due to methodological artifacts.
original_abstract: We show that all existing methods quantifying rotational motion in molecular fluids eventually fail in systems undergoing complex rotational motion characterised by slow, heterogeneous, or intermittent dynamics. This impacts in particular the study of rotational dynamics in molecular supercooled liquids near their glass transition, as well as discussions of the decoupling between rotational and translational motion and violations of the Debye-Stokes-Einstein relation. We present a brief overview of existing methods and explain why none of them can accurately capture the evolution of rotational dynamics from a diffusive fluid to an arrested solid, thus resolving inconsistent literature results. We then introduce an empirical method that efficiently solves all issues. We benchmark our method devising a family of continuous time random walk models for rotational dynamics. Our method correctly quantifies the statistics of free and caged rotational motion, as well as non-Gaussian and non-Fickian rotational dynamics, and should allow a better characterisation of dynamic heterogeneity in the rotational motion of supercooled molecular fluids.

title: Data-Driven Thermal and Mechanical Modeling of Defective Covalent Organic Frameworks
generated_summary:
This study develops and validates QCOF, a quantum-accurate machine learning interatomic potential based on the MACE architecture, for investigating thermal and mechanical properties of defective covalent organic frameworks (COFs). The model is trained on over 36,000 DFT-derived configurations of 23 two-dimensional carbon nitride nanosheets and systematically benchmarked against general-purpose MACE models, their fine-tuned variants, and moment tensor potentials, evaluating accuracy, computational efficiency, memory footprint, and transferability.

QCOF enables simulations of systems containing up to 140,000 atoms with near-quantum accuracy, making it feasible to study experimentally relevant defect concentrations inaccessible to DFT. The authors employ non-equilibrium molecular dynamics and uniaxial tensile tests to characterize two COFs—CTF-1 and COF-LZU1—with various defect types including Stone-Wales defects, 5-8-5 defects, and grain boundaries.

Key findings reveal that defects reduce ultimate tensile strength by up to 40% even at low concentrations (~0.9%), while the 2D Young's modulus remains virtually unchanged. Thermal conductivity responses differ markedly between the two materials: stiffer CTF-1 shows reductions up to 30% with grain boundaries, whereas more compliant COF-LZU1 remains largely insensitive to defects. This contrast suggests that defect impacts on thermal transport depend strongly on intrinsic framework stiffness rather than defect density alone. These insights have important implications for designing reliable COF membranes and thin films for practical applications.
original_abstract: Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs) are versatile two-dimensional (2D) materials for flexible electronics, catalysis, and sensing, owing to their tunable architectures and large surface areas. However, like most materials, COFs inevitably contain synthesis-induced defects, which-similar to graphene-can strongly influence intrinsic properties, such as thermal transport and mechanical strength. To address this challenge, we have assessed the performance of a set of machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIP) capable of efficient large-scale simulations of COFs with quantum accuracy. In doing so, QCOF models (Quantum COF) were developed by tuning the state-of-the-art MACE architecture on an extensive dataset of non-equilibrium COF conformations generated from high-fidelity density functional theory calculations. The accuracy, computational efficiency, memory footprint, and transferability to unseen chemical environments of these models were benchmarked against general-purpose MACE models and their fine-tuned variants. Our results show that an invariant QCOF model with a small descriptor dimensionality and cutoff outperforms all other models in most validation tasks, including scalability to large systems, force prediction in defective COFs, and phonon dispersion calculations. The best-performing QCOF model was then used to run large-scale simulations of thermal conductivity for defective CTF-1 and COF-LZU1 systems via non-equilibrium MD, revealing a more pronounced sensitivity of CTF-1 to structural defects. Stress-strain curves were also investigated, showing that the mechanical response remains nearly invariant at low defect densities, while asymmetric behaviour emerges at large strains. This work thus provides a foundation for the design of robust quantum-informed MLIP for large-scale property simulations of defective of extended network materials.

title: Designing interferometers within a single optical beam
generated_summary:
This paper introduces structured light interferometers (SLIs), a novel approach to common-path interferometry that operates within a single optical beam by exploiting structured optical modes as interferometric arms. Instead of splitting light into separate spatial paths using beam splitters, the authors use mode-splitting optics—such as q-plates, geometric-phase axicons, and g-plates—to divide a beam into co-propagating structured and unstructured modes that separate spatially in the transverse plane. One mode serves as a reference while the other probes a sample, and a reciprocal transformation recombines them for interference.

The authors demonstrate three SLI architectures using vortex, Bessel, and displaced beam structures for quantitative phase imaging of transparent azopolymer samples with various topographic reliefs. They further show that phase information can be encoded into either intensity or polarization distributions, depending on how the recombination step is implemented. Polarization encoding enables potential single-shot real-time measurements using polarization-sensitive cameras.

Experimental results show excellent agreement with atomic force microscopy benchmarks across all configurations, achieving root mean square errors below 72 nm and similarities above 95%. The framework is inherently versatile, compatible with diverse optical platforms including spatial light modulators, liquid crystal devices, and metasurfaces. This compact, robust interferometric paradigm offers a promising platform for high-precision phase sensing applicable to materials science, biology, and industrial diagnostics.
original_abstract: Interferometry provides highly sensitive access to optical phase and is central to much of modern metrology and phase imaging methods. Conventional implementations, however, often face trade-offs between mechanical stability and experimental or computational complexity. Here, we present a general framework for designing custom interferometers within a single optical beam by exploiting structured light.
