This paper investigates whether jointly optimizing the optical input and readout layers of a photonic reservoir computer can reduce the node count required for effective equalization in intensity-modulation/direct-detection optical links. The authors address the challenge that scaling integrated photonic reservoirs incurs significant hardware costs, as node count directly determines the number of interferometric elements and recurrent interconnects.

Using a hybrid VPIphotonics-Photontorch simulation framework, the authors model a four-port silicon photonic reservoir equalizer processing on-off keyed signals across varying fiber lengths, launch powers, and reservoir sizes. They compare jointly optimized input-readout architectures against readout-only variants under matched conditions, including matched total parameter counts, and evaluate different input-node injection policies.

The central finding is that joint optimization yields a substantial node-scaling advantage. An 8-node jointly optimized reservoir consistently outperforms its 8-node readout-only counterpart by one to two orders of magnitude in bit-error rate and approaches the performance of a 16-node readout-only system across short-to-intermediate fiber lengths. At a challenging 200 km operating point, jointly optimized systems scale far more effectively with node count, with the "all" input-node policy providing the strongest improvement. Crucially, this advantage persists when comparing systems with equal trainable degrees of freedom, confirming the benefit stems from architectural allocation rather than parameter count alone.

These results suggest that trainable optical input encoding enables a factor-of-two reduction in photonic reservoir hardware while maintaining equalization performance, offering a practical pathway toward more compact integrated photonic neural equalizers.
original_abstract: Photonic reservoir computing is a machine learning paradigm in which a recurrent neural network remains fixed while only the output weights are trained. This makes it a well-suited approach for high-speed signal equalisation in optical communication systems, offering a trainable, low-power, and low-complexity solution. However, achieving strong performance typically requires relatively large network sizes, as learning is confined to the output layer. To address this, we investigate the role of trainable input mappings alongside conventional output weight optimisation. Across a range of short- and mid-reach IM/DD transmission scenarios, reaching up to 200 km for a 28 GBd NRZ signal, improvements of over two orders of magnitude in BER are achieved. This enables halving the network size while maintaining comparable performance. Furthermore, we show that this approach effectively extends the memory of the reservoir, resulting in over three orders of magnitude improvement in memory-intensive tasks. These results also show that starting at 16 nodes a performance of at least one to two magnitudes better than both a complexity matched FFE and a Volterra filter of second order are reached.

title: Nonisothermal global-pressure exactness in fractured multiphase flow with evolving fracture aperture
generated_summary:
This paper derives the nonisothermal extension of the Total-Differential exactness criterion for global-pressure formulations of multiphase Darcy flow and embeds it within a fractured-media framework with evolving fracture aperture. The central contribution is demonstrating that nonisothermal exactness requires closure of a mobility-weighted capillary one-form on the augmented state space of saturation and temperature jointly, rather than merely satisfying isothermal compatibility on each fixed-temperature slice. This yields two compatibility requirements: the classical saturation-sector condition and a genuinely new mixed saturation-temperature condition.

The authors develop the mathematical theory and embed it in a reduced-dimensional matrix-fracture model incorporating heat transport, matrix-fracture thermal exchange, and thermally driven aperture evolution. For cases where exactness fails, they introduce a fiberwise least-squares projection that provides a conservative scalar-pressure approximation along with a quantitative defect diagnostic.

Numerical benchmarks verify the three regimes predicted by the theory: fully exact, slice-wise exact but nonisothermally nonexact, and fully nonexact. The fractured-media benchmarks demonstrate that temperature evolution alone can dynamically trigger exactness loss, with defects typically stronger in fractures than in the matrix. Evolving aperture further modifies the system's trajectory through augmented state space, reshaping the history of exactness loss and recovery.

These results provide a compact framework for nonisothermal global-pressure modeling in fractured reservoirs, relevant to geothermal and thermo-hydraulic applications where thermal effects on constitutive laws and fracture transmissivity are significant.
original_abstract: Global-pressure formulations recast multiphase Darcy flow in terms of a single pressure driving the total flux. Their exact equivalence to phase-pressure formulations, however, holds only when the constitutive data satisfy the compatibility conditions required for a total-differential structure and its generalized nonisothermal extension. In this work, we derive the corresponding exactness criterion for temperature-dependent mobilities and capillary pressures. We show that equivalence is governed by the closure of a mobility-weighted capillary one-form on the augmented state space of saturation and temperature. This yields both the classical compatibility conditions within the saturation sector and a distinct mixed saturation--temperature condition that arises only in the nonisothermal setting. We then incorporate this structure into a reduced matrix--fracture model with heat transport, matrix--fracture thermal exchange, and evolving fracture aperture. Numerical benchmarks recover the three regimes predicted by the theory: globally exact, exact on each fixed-temperature slice but not on the full saturation--temperature space, and fully nonexact. In fractured systems, thermal forcing alone can drive transitions between these regimes, while aperture evolution changes the path through state space. When exactness fails, a least-squares projection performed independently on each fixed-temperature slice provides a conservative scalar-pressure surrogate together with quantitative defect diagnostics. The resulting framework unifies nonisothermal exactness theory, fractured-flow dynamics, and conservative reduced closure within a single global-pressure formulation.

title: Baudrate- and Reach-Flexible All-Optical Equalization with a Co-Packaged Photonic Reservoir and Receiver
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first demonstration of a co-packaged, receiver-side photonic reservoir computing equalizer for optical signal equalization in intensity modulation and direct detection (IM/DD) links. The key novelty lies in achieving simultaneous flexibility across both baudrate and transmission reach using a fixed-topology integrated photonic reservoir, where adaptation is accomplished solely through retraining the linear readout weights.

The demonstrator comprises a 16-node spatially multiplexed silicon nitride reservoir chip with programmable Mach-Zehnder interferometer-based optical readout, co-packaged with semiconductor optical amplifiers, photodiodes, and transimpedance amplifiers. A hardware-in-the-loop optimization approach using CMA-ES trains the readout weights directly on the physical device. The reservoir equalizer consistently achieves multi-order-of-magnitude BER improvement over a conventional digital feed-forward equalizer baseline. These results establish that a single fixed integrated photonic reservoir can serve as a flexible, reusable equalization processor across diverse link configurations, positioning photonic reservoir computing as a practical energy-efficient alternative to digital signal processing for power- and latency-constrained optical interconnects.
original_abstract: Intensity-modulation direct-detection links must support increasing baudrates and transmission distances while operating under stringent power and cost constraints. However, as data rates and reaches increase, chromatic dispersion induces stronger inter-symbol interference and, after direct detection, frequency-selective fading, thus requiring increasingly powerful equalization. In conventional receivers, this translates into digital equalization whose complexity scales unfavorably with data rate. Photonic-domain equalization offers a hardware-based alternative that operates naturally at line rate and mitigates frequency fading. However, prior demonstrations were not readily adaptable for different rate and/or reach operation. In this paper, we experimentally demonstrate all-optical equalization across 10-46 Gbaud and 10-250 km SSMF in the C-band enabled solely through retraining of the readout layer, achieving up to four orders of magnitude BER improvement over standard DSP equalization. The demonstrator comprises a 16-node spatially multiplexed reservoir, programmable on-chip readout, and co-packaged receiver front-end. To our knowledge, this is the first co-packaged photonic reservoir receiver and the first demonstration of simultaneous baudrate- and reach-flexible equalization using a fixed-topology integrated photonic circuit.

title: OpenWaveLogger v2026 (OWL-v2026): an open source, low cost, easy to build, high performance logger for wave data measurements
generated_summary:
The paper introduces the OpenWaveLogger v2026 (OWL-v2026), an open-source, low-cost wave data logger designed for high-frequency inertial measurement unit (IMU) logging at 208 or 416 Hz. The primary contribution is a purpose-built bare-metal firmware that delivers reliable, low-jitter data acquisition through interrupt-driven sensor sampling and multi-level buffering, decoupling deterministic data collection from variable SD card write latency.

The OWL-v2026 is constructed entirely from off-the-shelf maker-community breakout boards, requiring only through-hole soldering for assembly at approximately 220 USD per unit—roughly one-tenth the cost of previous high-performance wave loggers. It logs six-axis IMU data, GNSS position and velocity at 10 Hz, and Pulse Per Second timestamps for UTC synchronization. A Python decoder converts binary data to UTC-timestamped arrays using PPS-based linear regression.

Validation demonstrates zero data loss over more than 10 days of continuous logging, approximately 20 days of deployment autonomy on three D-cell lithium batteries, and absolute UTC timestamp accuracy consistently below 10 ms. The IMU sampling rate represents a 10- to 40-fold increase over previous wave loggers operating at 10–20 Hz.

The low cost and ease of assembly enable qualitatively new measurement paradigms, particularly large-scale distributed arrays of hundreds of synchronized units for two-dimensional wave field analysis in environments such as sea ice, at spatial scales previously achievable only in laboratory wave tanks.
original_abstract: Ocean wave models are critical for weather and climate forecasting, and accurate in-situ wave observations are essential for validating and improving these models. Open-source, community-driven buoys have democratized wave observations via telemetry in recent years, but these systems transmit only limited amounts of data. Full high-frequency time series, required to study detailed wave physics, can still in most cases only be collected in situ using data loggers. Yet open-source, low-cost logger solutions remain scarce compared to their telemetry-enabled counterparts. Here we present the Openlogartemis Wave Logger (OWL-v2026), an open-source, low-cost, easy-to-build, high-performance logger for wave data measurements. The OWL-v2026 is built from off-the-shelf components from the maker community, requiring only through-hole soldering for assembly, and totals approximately 220USD per unit. Custom firmware enables high-frequency, low-jitter logging of six-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU) data at 208 or 416Hz, and GNSS position and Doppler velocity at 10Hz, with Pulse Per Second (PPS) synchronization for accurate absolute UTC timestamping. We have successfully validated continuous logging over more than 10 days at 208Hz, a power consumption of approximately 80mA (approximately 20 days of autonomy with three D-cell lithium batteries), and absolute UTC timestamp accuracy typically better than 10ms. Though the OWL-v2026 is a purely technical contribution, it has the potential to substantially expand the availability and affordability of high-frequency in-situ wave time series, similar to how the OpenMetBuoy (OMB) (Rabault 2022) expanded the availability of telemetry-enabled wave observations and helped spark new developments in low-cost open-source buoys.

title: Maximum Q-factor of planar inductors
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the previously overlooked problem of establishing fundamental upper bounds on the quality factor (Q-factor) of planar inductors, complementing the extensive literature on Q-factor minimization for broadband antennas. The authors derive analytical expressions for the maximum achievable Q-factor of electrically small planar inductors, which depend only on conductor losses and the available design area, independent of any specific inductor layout.

The methodology employs a rigorous convex optimization framework, specifically semidefinite relaxation, combined with characteristic mode theory based on the Method of Moments. Although the original Q-factor maximization problem is non-convex, it is transformed into a related convex problem whose solution provides a rigorous upper bound. Both optimization approaches yield virtually identical results, validating the derived bounds.

Key findings reveal that optimal current distributions transition from single wide-loop configurations for small design areas to multi-turn solutions for larger sizes, driven by the increasing significance of radiation losses. The analysis demonstrates that square or circular geometries maximize Q-factor density, as rectangular designs with increasing axial ratios show diminishing returns. The authors also incorporate kinetic inductance effects, showing that two-dimensional materials like intercalated graphene with high relaxation times can potentially exceed Q-factors achievable with conventional metals.

These bounds serve as rigorous benchmarks for inductor design across applications including RFICs, wireless power transfer, RFID sensors, and superconducting qubits, providing designers with fundamental performance limits that can guide optimization efforts and reduce computational costs.
original_abstract: On-chip inductor design plays a critical role in the advancement of radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs). Inductors typically occupy a substantial portion of the chip area as their performance metrics, namely, inductance density and Quality factor ($Q$-factor), are fundamentally tied to the available footprint, thereby limiting miniaturization. To better understand and quantify these limitations, we employ rigorous electromagnetic analysis together with convex optimization techniques to derive a fundamental bound on the maximum achievable $Q$-factor of electrically-small planar inductors as a function of the available design area. The analysis yields analytical expressions for the bound and, via modal analysis techniques, identifies and interprets operational regimes and scaling trends with respect to design area and material conductivity. The analysis accounts for both ohmic and radiation losses, with the latter becoming significant as the inductor size increases. A broad set of state-of-the-art inductor designs from the literature is evaluated against the established $Q$-factor upper bound, identifying designs that approach the theoretical limit as well as those with potential for further improvement. The study is extended to include the effect of kinetic inductance, which offers a promising avenue toward next-generation inductors with higher inductance densities and $Q$-factors. By establishing this benchmark, this work aims to guide and inspire the design of more efficient and compact planar inductors for high-performance RF systems.

title: The physics of ELM-free regimes in EUROfusion tokamaks
generated_summary:
This paper presents the physics understanding behind two major ELM-free operational regimes—Quasi-Continuous Exhaust (QCE) and Negative Triangularity (NT)—developed across the EUROfusion tokamak program spanning TCV, ASDEX Upgrade (AUG), JET, and WEST. The central contribution is a unified conceptual framework showing that ballooning modes play a dominant role in both regimes: QCE relies on a ballooning mode at the separatrix (likely a kinetic ballooning mode) to maintain continuous edge transport, while NT avoids large ELMs by blocking access to second stability in the pedestal region.

The methodology employs a "stepladder approach," where physics mechanisms are first understood on smaller, flexible devices (TCV, AUG), validated through predictive modeling using ideal MHD stability codes, and then demonstrated on larger machines (JET). This strategy significantly shortened scenario development time, enabling successful demonstration of both QCE and NT regimes in JET, including QCE operation in deuterium-tritium plasmas.

Key results include identification of a critical separatrix density threshold for QCE access that scales with plasma shaping and poloidal magnetic field, and determination of a minimum negative triangularity needed for ELM avoidance predictable through ideal MHD calculations. Both regimes were successfully demonstrated across multiple devices with consistent physics behavior.

These findings carry significant implications for future devices, as predictions indicate QCE should be accessible in ITER, SPARC, and EU-DEMO, providing validated pathways toward safe, ELM-free reactor operation.
original_abstract: The development of operational scenarios without large Type-I ELMs is of utmost importance for the stable operation and longevity of future tokamaks. The EUROfusion tokamak exploitation program has therefore made the understanding of ELM-free regimes a major topic of exploration across all its contributing devices (ASDEX Upgrade, JET, MAST-Upgrade, TCV, and WEST). An integrated program to investigate a range of Type-I ELM-free regimes has been developed covering the enhanced D-alpha (EDA), magnetic perturbations (MP), negative triangularity (NT), quasi-continuous exhaust (QCE), quiescent H-mode (QH), the baseline small ELMs (SE), I-mode, and X-point radiator (XPR) regimes. This contribution focuses on the development and understanding of the NT and QCE regimes on ASDEX Upgrade, JET, and TCV. The importance of transport via ballooning modes in both regimes is highlighted, as well as the progress in developing access models based on ideal-MHD. In the case of the QCE, this can also be expressed as a minimum separatrix density, which corresponds well to experimentally measured separatrix densities. Particular focus is paid to the performance of the QCE in terms of the achieved pedestal top values, which, when appropriately normalised, do not differ significantly from ELMy H-mode plasmas. This, combined with the predicted minimum separatrix density for the 15 MA ITER baseline plasma, highlight the relevance of the QCE as a potential operational scenario for both ITER and future reactors.

title: Valley-Aware Optimal Control of Spin Shuttling Using Cryogenic Integrated Electronics
generated_summary:
This paper presents a hardware-embedded, valley-aware optimal control framework for spin shuttling in Si/SiGe quantum dot devices using integrated cryogenic electronics. The central contribution is an end-to-end co-simulation approach that jointly treats realistic valley disorder, transistor-level circuit non-idealities including electronic noise, and hardware-constrained optimal control—a combination not previously reported.

The methodology couples disorder-informed valley maps with transistor-level simulations of a cryogenic signal generator implemented in 22 nm FDSOI CMOS technology. The circuit generates four-phase shuttling waveforms through a programmable RC network, enabling period-wise velocity modulation via discrete resistor configurations without requiring high-resolution DAC synthesis. A genetic algorithm optimizes these discrete control parameters to maximize shuttling fidelity by compensating valley-induced spin errors.

Key results demonstrate that increasing shuttling velocity strongly suppresses noise-induced fidelity dispersion, saturating near 12 m/s—qualitatively consistent with recent experimental observations. Under cryogenic noise proxy conditions, the optimized protocol achieves an average fidelity of 99.99±0.007% over 10 μm shuttling distance, compared to 99.78±0.06% for the unoptimized baseline. The active analog power dissipation remains at the microwatt level, compatible with millikelvin operation.

This work establishes that control electronics and qubit dynamics must be treated as a coupled system for scalable quantum computing architectures, providing a practical pathway toward integrating shuttling control at cryogenic temperatures.
original_abstract: Electron shuttling is emerging as a key mechanism for enabling long-range coupling in scalable spin-qubit architectures. Bringing shuttling waveform generation into the cryostat can improve scalability, but imposes strict area and power constraints on the control electronics. Concurrently, shuttling in Si/SiGe is further limited by a spatially varying valley splitting that induces spin--valley mixing and degrades coherence. Here, we make three contributions that address these limitations jointly: (i) an end-to-end co-simulation framework that combines disorder-informed valley maps with transistor-level cryogenic circuit simulations including electronic noise; (ii) a fully integrated cryogenic shuttling-signal generator tailored to velocity modulation, enabling period-wise waveform shaping through discrete circuit settings stored in on-chip memory; and (iii) a noise-aware optimization procedure that tunes only these implementable circuit controls, using one of four discrete resistor settings per period, to generate high-fidelity shuttling sequences. Across simulated valley and noise realizations in our co-simulation framework, the optimized velocity-modulation waveforms improve transport performance, achieving an average shuttling fidelity of $99.99 \pm 0.007\%$ at $v_{\mathrm{avg}} = 20~\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ over a distance of $10~μ\mathrm{m}$, while maintaining active analog power consumption in the tens of $μ\mathrm{W}$ during shuttling. This validates on-chip storage and replay of optimized control settings as a practical strategy to mitigate valley disorder in scalable shuttling architectures.

title: Restoring the Conical Intersection Topology using Convex Density Functional Theory
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Convex Density Functional Theory (CVX-DFT), a reformulation of Kohn-Sham DFT that resolves the long-standing failure of conventional DFT in describing ground-state conical intersections. The authors identify the root cause of this failure as a loss of convexity in the orbital optimization problem near electronic degeneracies, which leads to bifurcations, discontinuities, and multiple spurious solutions in the potential energy surfaces.

The methodology employs a two-step procedure within the Tamm-Dancoff approximation. First, the lowest-curvature mode of the orbital Hessian—associated with vanishing or negative eigenvalues near degeneracies—is projected out, yielding a strictly convex optimization problem with a unique, continuous solution. Second, the excluded excitation direction is reintroduced through a configuration interaction-like diagonalization, producing consistent ground and excited state energies from a single framework.

The authors validate CVX-DFT on three benchmark photochemical systems: protonated formaldimine, azobenzene, and the retinal model PSB3. In all cases, conventional LR-TDDFT/TDA produces pathological surfaces with linear intersections, negative excitation energies, or convergence failures, while CVX-DFT recovers smooth, topologically correct conical intersection seams in qualitative agreement with multireference methods such as XMS-CASPT2 and SA-CASSCF.

The significance of this work is substantial: it demonstrates that the failure of DFT at conical intersections is not fundamental but stems from the non-convex formulation, opening the door to reliable, computationally efficient non-adiabatic dynamics simulations for large molecular systems beyond the reach of multireference methods.
original_abstract: Conical intersections are central to the description of photophysics and photochemistry. Nevertheless, in non-adiabatic molecular dynamics simulations, they are fundamentally challenging for single-reference electronic structure methods. Density functional theory (DFT) and its time-dependent extension (TDDFT) represent the most widely used theoretical approaches in physics, chemistry, and biology. However, the treatment of ground and excited states as separate problems leads to breakdowns in the topological structure of potential energy surfaces near conical intersections. In this work, we solve this long-standing issue by presenting Convex DFT (CVX-DFT), a framework that, by explicitly enforcing convexity of the variational problem within an appropriately defined subspace, guarantees a unique and continuous electronic solution across regions of degeneracies. We demonstrate that CVX-DFT yields smooth and physically meaningful intersection seams by comparison with reference methods, such as multireference wave function methods. In this way, we establish the method as a robust and computationally efficient DFT approach for treating electronically degenerate regions. These developments represent a critical step toward reliable non-adiabatic simulations beyond the limitations of conventional TDDFT.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Tool for AI Weather Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces an open-source visualization tool designed to support mechanistic interpretability research for AI weather models, currently implemented for Google DeepMind's GraphCast graph neural network. The tool addresses the critical challenge of understanding how data-driven weather models generate predictions, given that these models learn from data without explicit physical knowledge, making their internal workings opaque.

The methodology leverages mechanistic interpretability concepts to explore the model's latent space. The tool organizes and visualizes large-scale meteorological and latent data, enabling users to examine correspondences between directions in the latent space and meaningful meteorological features. It supports analyses including principal component analysis of latent activations, examination of individual latent channels across processor steps, and cosine similarity computations between latent feature vectors.

Two case studies demonstrate the tool's utility. The first reveals qualitative associations between latent space directions and mid-latitude synoptic-scale waves visible in 500 hPa geopotential fields. The second identifies correspondences between latent features and specific humidity patterns. In both cases, specific latent channels show spatial structures that align with physically meaningful meteorological phenomena.

The significance of this work lies in its potential to build trust in AI weather models for operational forecasting and to enable scientific discovery. By facilitating rapid hypothesis generation about learned representations, the tool could ultimately support construction of interpretable feature dictionaries and identification of computational circuits within these models. Development is ongoing to extend support to transformer-based architectures.
original_abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) weather models are improving rapidly, and their forecasts are already competitive with long-established traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP). To build confidence in this new methodology, it is critical that we understand how these predictions are generated. This is a huge challenge as these AI weather models remain largely black boxes. In other areas of Machine Learning (ML), mechanistic interpretability has emerged as a framework for understanding ML predictions by analysing the building blocks responsible for them. Here we present an open-source, highly adaptable tool which incorporates concepts from mechanistic interpretability. The tool organises internal latent representations from the model processor and allows for initial analyses, including cosine similarity and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), enabling the user to identify directions in latent space potentially associated with meteorological features. Applying our tool to the graph neural network GraphCast, we present preliminary case studies for mid-latitude synoptic-scale waves and specific humidity. These demonstrate the tool's ability to identify linear combinations of latent channels that appear to correspond to interpretable features.

title: Imaging the transverse component of optical near-fields in resonant photonic structures
generated_summary:
This paper demonstrates the application of ultrafast 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy (U4DSTEM) to image the transverse components of optical near-fields in resonant periodic photonic structures made of crystalline silicon. While photon-induced near-field electron microscopy (PINEM) captures longitudinal field components, U4DSTEM provides complementary information by mapping the transverse Lorentz force experienced by electrons traversing the nanostructures.

The methodology involves focusing a pulsed 28.6 keV electron beam (20 nm spot size) and scanning it across a periodic dual-pillar silicon nanostructure excited by 1930 nm femtosecond laser pulses. The resulting electron deflection patterns are recorded using a hybrid pixel detector, and the standard deviation of the transverse momentum distribution is extracted at each beam position to reconstruct spatial maps of the transverse force components.

Key results reveal qualitatively distinct near-field distributions for two orthogonal polarizations of the excitation light. When polarized along the electron trajectory, transverse deflection occurs primarily near pillar edges, while perpendicular polarization produces strong deflection within the channel between pillars. The measurements show good qualitative agreement with finite-difference time-domain simulations, and the transverse momentum change scales linearly with excitation field amplitude, confirming the linear coupling regime. The resonant periodic structure enhances electron deflection by an order of magnitude compared to single nanostructures.

These results establish that combining U4DSTEM with PINEM could enable complete three-dimensional reconstruction of optical near-fields with deep sub-wavelength resolution and suggest applications for attosecond electron experiments.
original_abstract: We report on imaging the optical near-fields in resonant periodic photonic structures with nanometer resolution using ultrafast 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy (U4DSTEM). In particular, U4DSTEM is applied to visualize the transverse component of the Lorentz force of a synchronous near-field mode excited by an infrared femtosecond pulse in a periodic silicon nanostructure designed for photonic acceleration of electrons. Our results show that in addition to the accelerating/decelerating force acting on the electrons in the longitudinal direction along the electron propagation, the structures can be efficiently used for transverse electron streaking at optical frequencies when excited by light with polarization perpendicular to the electron trajectory. The measured spatial profile of the excited near-field mode intensity is consistent with the numerical simulations performed using finite-difference time domain technique.

title: Surrogate Functionals for Machine-Learned Orbital-Free Density Functional Theory
generated_summary:
This paper introduces **surrogate functionals** for machine-learned orbital-free density functional theory (OF-DFT), reframing the problem through the lens of energy-based modeling. A surrogate functional need not reproduce the true energy surface but must yield the correct ground-state electron density when used within a specified density optimization procedure. This perspective decouples the learning objective from exact energy prediction, focusing instead on optimization outcomes.

The authors propose a **gradient-descent-improvement (GDI) loss** that requires each gradient descent step to contract the distance to the ground-state density by a guaranteed factor, providing principled convergence guarantees. Crucially, this loss requires only ground-state density labels and can be evaluated at arbitrary input densities. To ensure the model generalizes over densities encountered during optimization, the authors develop a train-time density optimization strategy inspired by persistent contrastive divergence, maintaining cached per-molecule density coefficients that evolve during training.

Empirically, surrogate functionals achieve density optimization accuracy matching or approaching state-of-the-art methods on QM9 and QMugs benchmarks while **eliminating the need for costly O(N³) Löwdin orthonormalization**, thereby improving asymptotic computational scaling. The surrogate models also converge in fewer optimization steps, yielding improved throughput.

This work demonstrates that learning functionals optimized for optimization outcomes rather than pointwise energy accuracy offers a promising paradigm for scalable, machine-learned OF-DFT with better computational complexity than conventional Kohn-Sham DFT.
original_abstract: We introduce surrogate functionals: machine-learned energy functionals for orbital-free density functional theory (OF-DFT) which are defined not by universal fidelity to a physical reference, but merely by the requirement that density optimization with a fixed procedure yields the true ground-state density. Helpfully, training surrogate functionals requires only ground-state densities, no energies or gradients away from the ground state. We here propose a gradient-descent-improvement loss that guarantees exponential convergence of the density to the ground state, and combine it with an adaptive sampling scheme that concentrates learning around the optimization trajectories actually visited during inference. On the QM9 and QMugs benchmarks, surrogate functionals achieve density errors competitive with or improving upon the state of the art for fully supervised machine-learned OF-DFT, while eliminating the need for the $O(N^3)$ orthononormalization step required by prior work, yielding improved runtime scaling for larger systems.

title: Quantum Optical Signatures of Band Topology in Solid-State High Harmonics
generated_summary:
This paper develops a fully quantum-mechanical formalism connecting the quantum statistical properties of high-harmonic generation (HHG) radiation from solids to the material's electronic band topology. The main contribution is a density-matrix framework that links photonic observables—such as squeezing, photon correlations, and entanglement—to two-time current-current correlation functions of the classically driven crystal, enabling predictions of how topologically trivial and nontrivial phases produce distinct quantum optical signatures.

The methodology employs a universal Lindblad-like master equation for the coupled reduced density matrices of the photonic field and the solid-state system. By rotating the photon space to subtract the coherent laser field, the authors decompose the problem into a classically pumped material system and quantum vacuum fluctuations, treating light-matter coupling perturbatively. The formalism naturally accommodates mixed states, thermal occupations, and band-resolved correlations through the density-matrix approach, using the velocity gauge with Peierls substitution to avoid divergence issues inherent in the length gauge for periodic systems.

Applied to the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, the results demonstrate that the topological phase produces enhanced current response, stronger photon squeezing, more pronounced sub-Poissonian statistics, and greater two-mode entanglement compared to the trivial phase. The current-current correlation tensor, which encodes quantum geometric properties including Berry connections, directly governs these non-classical photonic features.

This work establishes a pathway for probing electronic quantum correlations through quantum optical measurements and for engineering non-classical light using topological phases of matter.
original_abstract: We develop a general theory of high-harmonic generation (HHG) in solid-state systems, based on a weak-correlation expansion of photonic and matter degrees of freedom. Unlike standard HHG theories, which treat light-matter dynamics through the Schrodinger equation, our approach employs density-matrix evolution, naturally capturing the mixed-state character of both the field and the matter - a critical aspect for describing complex solid-state band structures. We show explicitly that the properties of the emitted fields are governed by the quantum statistics and quantum geometry of the underlying solid. Taking the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model in a one-sided optical cavity as a paradigmatic example and considering the dual regime, we demonstrate that in the topological phase a system exhibits a stronger HHG response and stronger quantum-light signatures than in the trivial phase. Furthermore, we show that cavity-matter interaction gives rise to squeezed high-harmonic quantum light, whose properties are directly imprinted by the current-current fluctuations in the material system. Crucially, the observed squeezing does not rely on a separate quartic Kerr mechanism. In the mesoscopic regime, the genuine quantum Kerr term is higher order in light-matter coupling strength and negligible, while the relevant non-classical effect is governed by current-current fluctuations encoded in the complex susceptibility of the material. This work establishes a direct link between band topology and photon statistics, opening new avenues for topology-sensitive quantum light generation and photon statistics based spectroscopy of solid-state systems.

title: Emergence of Transport Regimes from the Axial Field-Induced Interfacial Gradients in Uniform Surface Potential Nanopores
generated_summary:
This study investigates how ion selectivity, ionic current rectification (ICR), and electroosmotic flow rectification (EFR) emerge from a single unified mechanism in voltage-gated nanopores with uniform surface potential. The authors demonstrate that these seemingly distinct transport phenomena all originate from axial nonuniformity of the electric double layer (EDL), induced by electrostatic coupling between the externally applied transmembrane potential and the gate voltage.

Using coupled Poisson-Nernst-Planck and Navier-Stokes simulations of cylindrical nanopores, the authors systematically vary the transmembrane potential relative to the gate voltage across different electrolyte concentrations. They compare fixed surface potential (representing voltage-gated nanopores) against fixed surface charge boundary conditions to isolate the effects of electrostatic gating.

The key finding is that all three transport responses—selectivity, current rectification, and flow rectification—are governed by a single asymmetry parameter representing the ratio of transmembrane to gate potential. Consistent transitions in transport behavior occur at critical values of this parameter. The work also reveals pronounced vortical flow structures arising from nonlinear coupling between the biased axial field and spatially varying EDL charge, even without geometric asymmetry. These phenomena emerge at moderate surface potentials near thermal voltage.

The significance lies in providing a mechanistic foundation for experimental observations in gated nanopores and proposing a method-agnostic asymmetry index applicable across different symmetry-breaking strategies, with implications for programmable biosensing, energy harvesting, and nanofluidic logic applications.
original_abstract: Gate-modulated nanopores have emerged as a promising platform for achieving ion selectivity and ionic current rectification (ICR) with the advantage of active field-based control. However, the mechanistic origin of these experimentally reported phenomena, arising from electrostatic coupling between the prescribed radial pore surface potential and the axial transmembrane electric field, remains insufficiently understood. Here, using coupled Poisson--Nernst--Planck and Navier--Stokes simulations supported by asymptotic analysis, we show that a uniform surface potential inherently interacts with the axial driving field to generate a three-dimensional, axially nonuniform electric double layer (EDL). This field-induced EDL heterogeneity effectively mimics a linear axial variation in zeta potential, breaking translational symmetry within an otherwise uniform pore. As a result, the system exhibits coupled electrokinetic responses, including ion selectivity, ionic current rectification, and non-canonical electroosmotic flow, all governed by a single asymmetry parameter $α$ derived from the EDL structure. Critical transitions occur at specific values of $α$; in particular, at $α=0$, the EDL becomes axially antisymmetric, leading to reversal of ion selectivity, significant ICR and the emergence of a peculiar negative electroosmotic flow rectification accompanied by internal vortical structures. These findings establish the electrostatic mechanism for axial symmetry breaking as the underlying principle for transport in voltage-gated nanopores, enabling a unified framework for designing tunable electrokinetic functionalities beyond geometry- and chemistry-based strategies.

title: AI models of unstable flow exhibit hallucination
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the concept of "hallucination" in AI models of fluid dynamics, demonstrating that deep learning models can produce visually plausible predictions of viscous fingering that fundamentally violate physical laws. The authors identify spectral bias—where neural architectures disproportionately favor certain spatial scales over others—as the underlying cause of these physically inconsistent outputs.

To address this problem, the authors propose DeepFingers, a hybrid architecture combining Deep Operator Networks (DeepONet) with Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) and U-FNO layers. The branch network employs an FNO layer to capture global dependencies, while U-FNO layers resolve multi-scale features characteristic of fingering dynamics. The trunk network processes physical parameters including viscosity ratio and time.

Benchmarking against Vision Transformers (ViT) and DAE-LSTM models across varying viscosity ratios, the authors show that baseline models produce hallucinations: ViT generates nonphysical fluid islands at later timesteps, while DAE-LSTM produces spurious fluid patches at early times. Spectral wavelet analysis reveals that ViT overestimates high-frequency modes while DAE-LSTM underestimates them. DeepFingers maintains balanced spectral energy across all modes, closely matching direct numerical simulation results for key physical metrics including breakthrough concentration, mixing rates, and uncertainty propagation.

This work bridges the hallucination concept from large language models to scientific AI, raising critical awareness about the need for physics-based validation of deep learning models beyond visual plausibility, with implications for applications in enhanced oil recovery, CO₂ sequestration, and groundwater remediation.
original_abstract: We report the first systematic evidence of hallucination in AI models of fluid dynamics, demonstrated in the canonical problem of hydrodynamically unstable transport known as viscous fingering. AI-based modeling of flow with instabilities remains challenging because rapidly evolving, multiscale fingering patterns are difficult to resolve accurately. We identify solutions that appear visually realistic yet are physically implausible, analogous to hallucinations in large language models. These hallucinations manifest as spurious fluid interfaces and reverse diffusion that violate conservation laws. We show that their origin lies in the spectral bias of AI models, which becomes dominant at high flow rates and viscosity contrasts. Guided by this insight, we introduce DeepFingers, a new framework for AI-driven fluid dynamics that enforces balanced learning across the full spectrum of spatial modes by combining the Fourier Neural Operator with a Deep Operator Network to predict the spatiotemporal evolution of viscous fingers. By conditioning on both time and viscosity contrast, DeepFingers learns mappings between successive concentration fields across regimes. The framework accurately captures tip splitting, finger merging, and channel formation while preserving global metrics of mixing. The results open a new research direction to investigate fundamental limitations in AI models of physical systems.

title: Extrapolation from historical data cannot reliably predict the time of a potential AMOC collapse
generated_summary:
This paper critically evaluates the reliability of AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) collapse timing predictions made by Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen (2023), who estimated a tipping point around 2025–2095. The authors demonstrate that these predictions are highly sensitive to modeling assumptions, data choices, and statistical procedures, rendering them unreliable for actionable forecasting.

The methodology involves multiple lines of investigation: replacing DD23's quadratic drift model with a cubic polynomial that does not prescribe tipping, generating synthetic time series to test for spurious predictions, conducting Bayesian parameter estimation with less informative priors, evaluating the bootstrap confidence interval procedure, correcting errors in DD23's fingerprint calculation, and testing alternative SST fingerprints and observational datasets.

Key findings reveal that an equally plausible cubic drift model suggests no tipping in finite time, yet DD23's method still falsely predicts near-future collapse when applied to synthetic data from this model. The bootstrap confidence intervals are shown to have severely inadequate coverage due to biases introduced by a penalty term and parameter clipping. Correcting data processing errors eliminates the statistically significant early warning signals reported by DD23, and alternative fingerprints and datasets yield tipping times spanning several millennia.

The authors emphasize that their analysis does not preclude future AMOC collapse but demonstrates that current observational records and simplified statistical models cannot support specific collapse timeline predictions for policymakers.
original_abstract: Ditlevsen and Ditlevsen [Nature Communications, 2023] (DD23 hereafter) propose a statistical framework to estimate the timing of a potential collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) based on extrapolating information from observed sea-surface temperature (SST) variability. By fitting a stochastic one-dimensional fold-bifurcation model to an SST-based fingerprint of the AMOC using Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), they conclude that a collapse is most likely to occur in the middle of the 21st century, with a reported 95% confidence interval covering the time span from 2037 to 2109. Given the profound implications of such a claim for both climate and society, it is essential to thoroughly test the robustness of this result, to critically assess the underlying assumptions and uncertainties, and to estimate the extent to which the reported confidence interval reflects the true limits of current knowledge. Here we examine the sensitivity of DD23's results and argue that four types of uncertainty are insufficiently explored in their analysis: (i) structural uncertainty associated with the assumed low-order bifurcation model, (ii) statistical uncertainty in their model fit, (iii) uncertainty in the representativeness of SST-based fingerprints as proxies for the high-dimensional AMOC dynamics, and (iv) uncertainty in the underlying data, arising from non-stationary observational coverage and dataset preprocessing. Using synthetic experiments and a systematic analysis of alternative fingerprints and observational products, we show that the tipping times estimated by DD23 are highly sensitive to the uncertainties listed above, and extend several millennia into the future when these uncertainties are thoroughly propagated.

title: Europa's Lyman-$α$ emissions from HST/STIS observations

original_abstract: An image of Lyman-$α$ (Ly$α$) emission from Europa obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (HST/STIS) has previously provided the first evidence of localized water vapor (H$_2$O) aurora, potentially originating from outgassing. We present a comprehensive analysis of STIS Ly$α$ observations of Europa acquired in 1999 and between 2012 and 2020 to search for localized auroral emissions and constrain the properties of Europa's H exosphere. We analyze the complete dataset of STIS observations obtained when Europa was sunlit and not transiting Jupiter. A forward model is constructed to account for all known sources of Ly$α$ emission, including resonantly scattered sunlight from Europa's H exosphere. To identify localized anomalies, such as H$_2$O aurora, the modeled Ly$α$ emission is subtracted and the residuals are examined. Emission from Europa's H exosphere is detected at all observing epochs, but is attenuated by absorption in Earth's exosphere when Europa's radial velocity relative to Earth (and thus the Doppler shift) is small. From the velocity dependence of this attenuation, we estimate an H-exosphere temperature of $\sim 1000$ K and derive an upper limit of 5100 K. For the best-constrained epoch in 2014--2015, we infer a vertical H column density of $1.4x10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$ and an H source rate of $1.1x10^{27}$ s$^{-1}$. No localized emission enhancements are detected in any of the observations, including the image previously interpreted as evidence of H$_2$O aurora near Europa's south pole. The discrepancy with earlier results arises primarily from differences in the assumed position of Europa's disk on the detector, as well as from the inclusion of an H-exosphere signal in the present analysis...

title: Domain-Wall-Mediated Ultralow-Barrier Sliding and Pinning in Ferroelectric Moiré Superlattices Revealed by Machine Learning

This ultralow barrier arises from a domain-wall-mediated collective reconstruction pathway rather than rigid layer translation.

The study further shows that sulfur vacancies at concentrations as low as 0.1% act as pinning centers, converting long-range sliding into bounded oscillations due to stacking-dependent vacancy formation energies. Importantly, both the ultralow-barrier sliding and defect-induced pinning persist across a broad range of twist angles, indicating that the essential ingredient is the twist-induced multidomain structure rather than a specific moiré geometry. These findings deepen understanding of sliding ferroelectric dynamics and moiré superlattice behavior.
original_abstract: Sliding ferroelectrics built from stacked nonpolar monolayers enable out-of-plane polarization and unconventional switching via interlayer sliding, yet the microscopic sliding dynamics remain unclear. Using machine-learning molecular dynamics, we reveal spontaneous thermally driven interlayer sliding in ferroelectric MoS2 moiré superlattices, with relative velocities on the order of 1 m/s at 300 K. Instead of rigid translation of the entire bilayer, the motion appears as a global drift of the moiré pattern. Such thermally driven sliding is inconsistent with the meV/atom-scale rigid-sliding barrier. In contrast, when constrained relaxation is allowed, the sliding proceeds along an almost barrierless pathway that directly reproduces the global drift of the moiré pattern. Furthermore, sulfur vacancies trigger a sliding-to-pinning transition, with about 0.1% S vacancies already sufficient to convert the long-range sliding into localized oscillations. Notably, these phenomena are not restricted to small twist angles, but arise generically in twisting-induced multidomain structures. These results reveal that the sliding process is governed by a domain-wall-mediated collective reconstruction pathway with an ultralow barrier, rather than rigid layer translation, deepening the understanding of microscopic dynamics in moiré superlattices and sliding ferroelectrics.

title: Mesoscopic theory of flocking with alignment and anti-alignment copying

The authors derive exact mesoscopic Fokker-Planck and Langevin equations from the microscopic Master equation through a systematic 1/N expansion, comparing two implementations of interaction heterogeneity: an annealed version where each interaction is randomly alignment or anti-alignment, and a quenched version where individuals are permanently assigned as aligners or anti-aligners.

A central finding is that the deterministic drift terms are identical for both annealed and quenched implementations, meaning macroscopic mean-field dynamics are insensitive to how heterogeneity is realized. Differences emerge only at the fluctuation level, where quenched disorder introduces persistent correlations that modify finite-size noise, though these corrections are subleading in 1/N and numerically negligible for moderate system sizes. The authors also establish an exact equivalence in the nematic order parameter sector between both formulations, arising from the rotational symmetry of anti-alignment interactions. This identifies nematic order as an independent observable sensitive to competing interactions that polarization alone cannot detect.

The model reveals a critical system size below which finite-size fluctuations sustain collective order that vanishes in the thermodynamic limit, illustrating how population size and the nature of microscopic heterogeneity jointly determine collective behavior. These results provide a controlled framework for distinguishing disorder types in non-equilibrium biological and physical collectives.
original_abstract: We study a stochastic model of collective motion in which individuals update their orientation through pairwise aligning or anti-aligning copying interactions. We analyze both annealed dynamics, where interaction types are chosen probabilistically at each update, and quenched dynamics, where individuals are permanently assigned to aligning or anti-aligning subpopulations. Starting from the microscopic master equation on the circle, we derive an exact mesoscopic description via a Fourier-mode expansion and a systematic large $N$ expansion, obtaining closed Fokker-Planck equations and effective stochastic differential equations for the polarization. We show that competing alignment and anti-alignment suppress long-range polar order in the thermodynamic limit in both cases, while finite systems display nontrivial fluctuation-induced structure controlled by the interaction composition. Our results, validated by Gillespie simulations, establish an analytically tractable framework for collective dynamics characterized by competing copying rules and intrinsic noise.

title: Construction of a Battery Research Knowledge Graph using a Global Open Catalog
generated_summary:

original_abstract: Battery research is a rapidly growing and highly interdisciplinary field, making it increasingly difficult to track relevant expertise and identify potential collaborators across institutional boundaries. In this work, we present a pipeline for constructing an author-centric knowledge graph of battery research built on OpenAlex, a large-scale open bibliographic catalogue. For each author, we derive a weighted research descriptors vector that combines coarse-grained OpenAlex concepts with fine-grained keyphrases extracted from titles and abstracts using KeyBERT with ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) as the backend model, selected after evaluating multiple alternatives. Vector components are weighted by research descriptor origin, authorship position, and temporal recency. The framework is applied to a corpus of 189,581 battery-related works. The resulting vectors support author-author similarity computation, community detection, and exploratory search through a browser-based interface. The knowledge graph is then serialized in RDF and linked to Wikidata identifiers, making it interoperable with external linked open data sources and extensible beyond the battery domain. Unlike prior author-centric analyses confined to institutional repositories, our approach operates at cross-institutional scale and grounds similarity in domain semantics rather than citation or co-authorship structure alone.

title: Localized Tornado Outbreak at the Upstream of a Tropical Easterly Wave in Camarines Norte, Philippines (13 September 2025)

original_abstract: (Abridge) On 13 September 2025 around 22 UTC, a localized tornado outbreak affected eastern Philippines, causing significant damage in Camarines Norte. The event developed within an atypical easterly severe weather regime characterized by warm, moist southeasterly flow and strong low-level wind shear associated with an easterly wave trough. A vorticity convergence zone along the inverted trough enhanced low-level rotation, while highly curved streamwise hodographs indicated a favorable environment for supercells and tornadogenesis. At least five vortices were identified, including three tornadic supercells. The Magang supercell was rated IF2.5 (EF3-equivalent) with $\sim$2 km damage path, while the Cahabaan and Napilihan supercells were rated IF1 (EF1-equivalent), with Cahabaan producing $\sim$3 km damage path. The remaining vortices were rated IF0 (EF0-equivalent). These tornadoes occurred simultaneously, indicating multiple discrete supercells within the same mesoscale environment and possible inflow-outflow interactions. Dual-polarization radar observations revealed Z$_\text{DR}$ and K$_\text{DP}$ columns, a debris signature in the Magang tornado, and a bounded weak echo region (BWER) in the Cahabaan supercell. title: Incoherent light delivers skyrmionic topological resilience and transitions
generated_summary:

The methodology involves generating partially coherent skyrmion beams by imposing time-varying random phase screens on a spatial light modulator, creating two orthogonally polarized Laguerre-Gaussian modes sharing identical random realizations. Stokes polarimetry reconstructs the polarization textures, and a renormalized Stokes vector framework accounts for propagation-induced depolarization. The beams are characterized across propagation distances and under simulated turbulence conditions.

Key results show that reducing spatial coherence suppresses turbulence-induced phase singularity proliferation, stabilizing the skyrmion number at the receiver plane. Under strong turbulence, partially coherent skyrmions maintain near-integer skyrmion numbers with significantly reduced variance compared to fully coherent beams. The authors also discover coherence-driven topological transitions in the low-coherence regime: non-Gaussian spatial correlations enable skyrmion-to-skyrmionium conversion using Laguerre-Gaussian coherence structures, and skyrmion lattice formation using Hermite-Gaussian coherence structures.

These findings are significant for topology-encoded free-space optical communications, where real-time skyrmion number readout is essential. The work establishes partial coherence as both a protective mechanism against environmental randomness and a control parameter for engineering topological transitions, broadening the scope of topological photonics to realistic optical environments.
original_abstract: Optical skyrmions has recently unlocked topological quasiparticle textures of light, rising in prominence for next-generation ultra-robust information processing. However, to date, their study hasbeen mainly confined to coherent laser fields. Here we extend skyrmions to much general light sources of partially coherent, stochastic optical fields. We define stochastic optical skyrmions and uncover a hidden regime where spatial coherence acts as a primary determinant of topological stability. While environmental randomness typically degrades fully coherent states, we demonstrate that engineered partial coherence provides a self-healing mechanism that preserves topology under extreme turbulence. Moreover, we show that the coherence structure can be actively tailored to trigger on-demand topological phase transitions, such as skyrmion-to-skyrmionium conversion and skyrmion lattice splitting. These findings redefine the boundaries of topological photonics, paving the way for resilient and high-fidelity information platforms that remain operational in general, non-ideal, real-world environments.

title: Stability of Charge Collection Efficiency and Time Resolution in a Novel Ultra-fast Graphene-Optimized Silicon Carbide Detector Under X-ray Irradiation

The G/RE detectors were tested before and after exposure to 1 MGy of 160 keV X-ray irradiation.

Key results show that the G/RE detector exhibits improved time resolution compared to the RE detector, confirming graphene's effectiveness as an electrode material. After 1 MGy irradiation, the G/RE detector maintains excellent performance with leakage current below 0.2 nA and no significant degradation in CCE or time resolution. The authors attribute this radiation hardness to the fact that secondary electrons from 160 keV X-rays lack sufficient energy to create displacement damage in the SiC bulk.

These findings are significant for applications in high-energy physics, nuclear monitoring, medical dosimetry, and space exploration, where detectors must operate reliably under extreme radiation environments while maintaining fast timing and efficient charge collection.
original_abstract: A graphene-optimized silicon carbide PIN detector was fabricated and its radiation tolerance under X-ray irradiation of 160 keV was evaluated. Its electrical properties, charge collection performance and time resolution of beta-particles (90Sr) are reported. The time resolution of the graphene-optimized silicon carbide detector is 58.0 ps. The time resolution is comparable to that of state-of-the-art 4H-SiC low-gain avalanche detectors (LGADs). The G/RE 4H-SiC PIN detector exhibits outstanding time resolution performance. Compared with the time resolution of the RE 4H-SiC PIN detector, the time resolution of the G/RE 4H-SiC PIN detector has decreased by 39.6%. This demonstrates the significance of the graphene electrode design. The graphene detector exhibits a charge collection efficiency (CCE) of 99.24% after X-ray irradiation, along with excellent stability. The graphene-optimized silicon carbide detector maintains good timing resolution: 58.0ps before and 64.0ps after X-ray irradiation. These results demonstrate stable performance under extreme X-ray exposure, highlighting the detectors potential for radiation-hard applications in high-energy physics, space missions, and nuclear reactor monitoring.

title: Chromatographic Peak Shape from a Stochastic-Diffusive Model with Multiple Retention Mechanisms: Analytic Time-Domain Expression and Derivatives
generated_summary: This paper extends a stochastic-diffusive framework for chromatographic peak shapes from a single slow retention mechanism to an arbitrary number of independent slow retention mechanisms, while preserving analytic tractability in the time domain. The central challenge lies in marginalizing over multiple independent Poisson-distributed event counts, which produces a multi-index mixture of Gamma convolutions with heterogeneous scales. The author overcomes this by recasting the mixture onto a common scale using Moschopoulos's method, recovering a single-index series representation whose terms share the same functional form as the original single-mechanism case. This structure enables efficient numerical evaluation. Analytical derivatives with respect to all model parameters are also derived at comparable computational cost, facilitating gradient-based parameter estimation without finite-difference approximations. Additionally, the evaluation scheme for the basis functions replaces the previous confluent hypergeometric function approach, reducing computational cost by two to four orders of magnitude. Fits to three literature chromatographic peaks demonstrate that every tested instance of the multi-mechanism formulation yields lower root-mean-square error than the exponentially modified Gaussian, and allowing multiple slow mechanisms reduces fitting error relative to the single-mechanism case by factors ranging from approximately two to more than one order of magnitude. This work bridges the gap between mechanistic richness and practical computability, enabling direct time-domain fitting with physically interpretable kinetic and transport parameters.
original_abstract: A time-domain analytic expression for chromatographic peak shapes is derived within a stochastic-diffusive framework that incorporates axial diffusion (molecular and multipath/Eddy), finite initial spatial variance, a retention mechanism characterized by a high rate of short-duration events, and an arbitrary number of independent slow retention mechanisms, each characterized by its own rate of infrequent, long-duration events. A highly efficient evaluation scheme is derived for this expression. In the single-slow-mechanism case, it is two to four orders of magnitude faster than the previously available analytic route. Analytical derivatives with respect to all model parameters are also obtained, and each can be evaluated at computational cost comparable to that of the peak-shape expression. Illustrative fits to three literature peaks yielded full-profile RMSE values lower than those of the exponentially modified Gaussian in all tested cases, with minima ranging from 0.03 to 0.14 percent of peak height, compared with 0.43 to 5.57 percent for the reference model. Relative to the one-slow-mechanism formulation, allowing more than one slow mechanism produced a data-dependent improvement that exceeded one order of magnitude for one of the peaks.

title: A Spatial-Resolved Proton Energy Spectrometer Based on a Scintillation-Fiber Cube

This configuration provides 120 energy channels along the beam direction while enabling quasi-two-dimensional spatial reconstruction through transverse scintillation imaging, achieving a pixel size of 0.5 mm.

The SFICS was calibrated using monoenergetic, spatially uniform proton beams from a synchrotron accelerator and validated against both radiochromic film (RCF) stack measurements and Geant4 simulations. The authors developed an energy spectrum retrieval method based on the depth-dependent scintillation light yield response function. Calibration experiments demonstrated that the spectrometer achieves relative energy uncertainty better than 1% for protons above 60 MeV. The device was further tested with artificially complex proton beams created using custom-designed degraders, successfully reconstructing spatially varying energy distributions.

Compared to existing scintillator-based spectrometers, the SFICS simultaneously achieves fine spatial sampling and low energy uncertainty while enabling real-time online diagnostics. This represents a significant advancement over passive detectors like RCF stacks, which lack real-time capability, and over existing scintillator designs that sacrifice either spatial resolution or energy channels. The SFICS shows particular promise for characterizing the spatially non-uniform, energy-chirped beams produced by laser-plasma acceleration.
original_abstract: Advanced particle acceleration methods have produced high-peak-current ion beams with broad energy spread and complex spatial distribution. There is an urgent need to develop online spatial-resolved energy spectrometers for high-energy pulsed ions. This paper introduces a novel spectrometer based on a scintillation-fiber cube for online diagnosis of proton beams with broadband energy spread and complex spatial distribution. We present its working principles, experimental setup, and comprehensive calibration using monoenergetic and spatially uniform proton beams generated by a synchrotron accelerator. Calibration results confirm an energy measurement range of 6-93 MeV, a relative energy uncertainty of 0.6% at 80 MeV, and a pixel size of 0.5 mm for beam profile reconstruction. By exploiting a custom-designed energy degrader, we generated a complex proton beam and measured it with the scintillation-fiber cube spectrometer (SFICS). The results demonstrate the spectrometer's potential for online measurement of the energy spectrum and spatial distribution of complex proton beams.

title: Machine learning moment closure models for the radiative transfer equation IV: enforcing symmetrizable hyperbolicity in two dimensions
generated_summary:
This paper extends a structure-preserving machine learning moment closure framework for the radiative transfer equation from one-dimensional slab geometry (1D1V) to the substantially more challenging two-dimensional setting (2D2V). The main contribution is the derivation of explicit algebraic conditions that guarantee symmetrizable hyperbolicity of the learned closure system in 2D, where any linear combination of the x- and y-direction coefficient matrices must be diagonalizable over the reals.

The authors analyze the block tridiagonal structure of the real-valued P_N system's coefficient matrices in 2D spherical harmonics and construct a block-diagonal symmetrizer. They design a neural network architecture that parametrizes the closure through a symmetric positive definite matrix and symmetric closure blocks, ensuring hyperbolicity by construction. The closure is trained using a residual-based loss function on reference data generated from high-order P_N solutions.

Numerical experiments across three tasks of increasing complexity demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. On single-mode sine waves, the ML closure reduces relative L² errors by up to two orders of magnitude compared to the linear P_N baseline. On random multi-mode sine wave initial conditions, the ML closure consistently produces smoother, more accurate solutions and generalizes to unseen trajectories. The framework also generalizes across varying absorption and scattering parameters when trained on diverse material regimes.

This work is significant because it demonstrates that careful architectural design preserving mathematical structure enables ML closures to reliably improve classical moment methods for multidimensional kinetic equations, advancing the practical applicability of learned closures.
original_abstract: This is our fourth work in the series on machine learning (ML) moment closure models for the radiative transfer equation (RTE). In the first three papers of this series, we considered the RTE in slab geometry in 1D1V (i.e. one dimension in physical space and one dimension in angular space), and introduced a gradient-based ML moment closure [1], then enforced the hyperbolicity through a symmetrizer [2], or together with physical characteristic speeds by learning the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix [3]. Here, we extend our framework to the RTE in 2D2V (i.e. two dimensions in physical space and two dimensions in angular space). The main idea is to preserve the leading part of the classical $P_N$ model and modify only the highest-order block row. By analyzing the structural properties of the $P_N$ model, we show that its coefficient matrices are symmetric and admit a block-tridiagonal structure. Then we use this property to introduce a block-diagonal symmetrizer for the ML moment model and derive explicit algebraic conditions on the closure blocks which guarantee the symmetrizable hyperbolicity of the resulting ML system. These conditions lead to a natural parametrization of the closure in terms of a symmetric positive definite matrix together with symmetric closure blocks, which can be learned from data while automatically enforcing symmetrizable hyperbolicity by construction. The numerical results show that the proposed framework improves upon the classical $P_N$ model while maintaining hyperbolicity.

title: Autonomous operation of the DIAG0 diagnostic line for 6D phase-space monitoring at LCLS-II

Measurement data are streamed to a shared computing facility for processing, enabling reconstruction cadences of 5–10 minutes during user operation.

The system was demonstrated during multi-hour user delivery shifts at LCLS-II, autonomously performing beamline steering, focusing, and transverse deflecting cavity configuration while continuously reconstructing the 6D phase-space distribution.
