original_abstract: Multi-photon microscopy is a powerful technique for deep-tissue imaging, providing high spatial resolution at increased penetration depth. Nevertheless, imaging remains largely restricted to superficial tissue layers well below 1 mm. Adaptive optics based on indirect wavefront sensing can significantly extend the accessible imaging depth, but their iterative operation is typically time-consuming and therefore limits the correction of strong, spatially complex aberrations. Until recently, this limitation was partly due to the lack of high-speed phase modulators offering sufficiently large numbers of actuators. Recent technological advances have addressed this bottleneck with the emergence of megapixel phase modulators operating at kilohertz rates. Here, we demonstrate wavefront correction in multi-photon microscopy using a high-speed phase-only MEMS modulator combined with a rapidly converging scatter-compensation algorithm. We experimentally correct complex aberrations comprising 144 spatial modes in less than one second, resulting in signal enhancements exceeding a factor of two. Benchmarking against a fast liquid-crystal spatial light modulator reveals a sixfold increase in correction speed. We further demonstrate adaptive optics imaging in mouse brain tissue using both two-photon and three-photon excitation fluorescence microscopy. These results indicate that high-resolution MEMS-based spatial light modulators enable efficient indirect wavefront sensing and represent a promising platform for high-speed wavefront shaping in non-linear microscopy.

title: Enhanced Mid-Infrared Single-Photon Detection with Antenna-Coupled Superconducting Nanowires
generated_summary:
This study demonstrates that resonant metallic antennas coupled to superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can significantly enhance mid-infrared photon detection by concentrating incident radiation onto short nanowire segments, effectively decoupling the photon collection and sensing functions. The authors fabricated crossed bowtie gold antennas on 3 nm-thick, 80 nm-wide amorphous tungsten silicide (WSi) nanowires on silicon substrates with silicon dioxide spacer layers and characterized their performance at 7.4 μm wavelength using a filtered broadband thermal source.

Experimental measurements reveal that antenna-coupled nanowires achieve a 15.7-fold increase in photon-absorption efficiency compared to identical bare nanowires, while maintaining nearly identical dark-count rates. This enhancement arises from the antenna's ability to collect and concentrate free-space radiation into its nanoscale feed gap, enabling the nanowire's effective detection area to far exceed its geometric footprint. The authors further analyze a scalable periodic antenna array configuration spanning 50 × 50 μm² and show through simulations that it can reduce the noise-equivalent power by approximately 900-fold at 7 μm wavelength compared to a conventional meandered nanowire of identical geometric footprint, with improvements becoming more pronounced at longer wavelengths.

These results establish antenna-coupled nanowire arrays as a promising architecture for large-area, low-noise mid- and far-infrared single-photon detection, with applications in infrared astronomy, dark-matter searches, and biological sensing.
original_abstract: Scaling the photon-detection area of superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) has traditionally been achieved by nanowire meandering. However, material inhomogeneities and fabrication-induced defects, such as line-edge roughness, increase with nanowire length, leading to reduced internal photon-detection efficiency and elevated dark-count rates. This trade-off becomes increasingly pronounced as nanowires are scaled to sub-100 nm widths and sub-5 nm thicknesses required for mid- to far-infrared sensitivity. Here, we demonstrate an antenna-coupled SNSPD architecture that enhances the effective photon-detection area without increasing nanowire length. A crossed bowtie antenna integrated with an 80 nm-wide, 3 nm-thick WSi nanowire yields 15.7$\times$ increase in effective detection area at 7.4 $μ$m compared to a bare nanowire of identical geometric footprint, while maintaining the same internal detection efficiency and dark-count rate. Antenna coupling improves noise-equivalent power and provides a more scalable route to increasing photon-detection area than conventional meander geometries, offering performance benefits for applications in astronomy, biological imaging, and molecular spectroscopy.

title: Equation of State for warm Neutron Star outer crusts
generated_summary:
This study presents a finite-temperature equation of state (EoS) for the outer crust of neutron stars, relevant to core-collapse supernovae, protoneutron star evolution, and binary neutron star mergers. The main contribution is the incorporation of dynamical ionic correlations and screening effects into the outer crust EoS using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, addressing systematic biases present in existing approaches that typically treat ions as either an ideal gas or a cold crystallized phase.

The methodology employs MD simulations with finite-size Gaussian-shaped ions interacting through screened Coulomb potentials, where electron screening is parametrized via the Thomas-Fermi wave vector. The Ewald summation technique handles long-range interactions efficiently. Electrons are incorporated as a relativistic degenerate free gas using the Sommerfeld expansion. A neural network parametrization is developed to interpolate thermodynamic quantities between directly simulated density and temperature values, achieving goodness of fit R² > 0.99.

Key results show that the effective thermal adiabatic index (Γ_th), frequently used in numerical relativity simulations, is significantly quenched compared to existing literature values. Ionic thermal effects prove particularly important at higher densities approaching the inner crust boundary, producing a notable drop in Γ_th.

These findings have direct implications for numerical simulations of compact binary mergers and supernovae, where accurate low-density warm matter EoS tables are essential for predicting ejecta properties, kilonova light curves, and r-process nucleosynthesis yields.
original_abstract: We describe the equation of state (EoS) of a warm ion plasma as obtained by performing microscopic many-body simulations using Molecular Dynamics computational techniques. Using the cold one-component plasma (OCP) composition in the Neutron Star (NS) outer crust assumed in Murarka et al. (2022) with a representative heavy nucleus for each density, we refine previous calculations. We include electron screening and modeling of ions as finite-size Gaussian distributions in the interaction potential, together with an efficient Ewald energy summation procedure. From this, the EoS relation $P(n_B,T)$ is obtained as a function of baryonic density and temperature in the NS outer crust under conditions $n_B\in[7.48\times 10^{-10},2.09\times10^{-4}]$ $ \rm fm^{-3}$ , $k_{B}T\in[1,5]$ MeV. In order to improve the usability of our results we provide tabulated data values along with a neural network parametrization available in the Zenodo repository, see https://zenodo.org/records/15348712. We find that even at moderate temperatures, thermal effects of ions are key in the higher density region closer to the inner crust, when described using a thermal effective parametrization based on the thermal adiabatic index $Γ_{th}$. We compare our results with other EoS in the literature performing a critical discussion.

title: A Slow-Time Receiver Interface for Turbulent Free-Space Quantum Polarization Links
generated_summary:
This paper presents a slow-time extension of an aperture-conditioned receiver interface for turbulent free-space quantum polarization channels. The main contribution is a generative temporal framework that retains hidden atmospheric fluctuations as time-dependent stochastic processes rather than averaging them out before forming effective receiver parameters, thereby exposing the temporal structure relevant to quantum communication protocols.

The methodology promotes three hidden propagation quantities—the receiver-plane phase field, centroid displacement, and scintillation—to slow-time stochastic processes. A first-order local closure maps coarse-grained receiver-plane phase roughness to the variance of an effective polarization-mixing angle, grounded in standard spatiotemporal phase statistics and frozen-flow arguments. After aperture conditioning, this procedure yields time-dependent effective parameters: depolarization, coherence loss, and total detection probability.

Key results from weak-turbulence numerical simulations show that the polarization branch of the receiver interface remains close to the near-ideal regime, while the scalar detection branch exhibits more pronounced slow-time fluctuations. Temporal correlation analysis reveals distinct autocorrelation structures for the three output variables and measurable cross-correlations between the polarization and detection branches, indicating nontrivial temporal memory in the channel.

The significance lies in providing a compact, calibration-ready, protocol-facing temporal channel description that downstream analyses for free-space quantum key distribution or measurement-device-independent QKD can directly consume for blockwise performance evaluation, bridging the gap between atmospheric propagation physics and quantum protocol design.
original_abstract: Atmospheric turbulence makes free-space quantum polarization links intrinsically time varying, whereas receiver-side reduced interfaces are often treated as static. This paper develops a slow-time receiver interface by extending an aperture-conditioned static model to the temporal domain. The receiver-plane phase field, beam-centroid displacement, and scintillation are modeled as hidden slow-time stochastic processes, from which the reduced interface is generated at each instant. A leading-order closure maps coarse-grained phase roughness to an effective polarization-mixing variance while preserving the inherited local polarization-channel family. Aperture conditioning then yields time-dependent effective depolarization, coherence, and detection descriptors. In a representative weak-turbulence case, the polarization branch remains close to the near-ideal regime, with effective depolarization on the order of \(10^{-3}\) and effective coherence close to unity, whereas the detection branch exhibits visibly stronger fluctuations and a longer correlation time. These results show that a single static receiver-side parameterization is insufficient to characterize the temporal behavior of turbulent free-space quantum links. The resulting interface is intended for receiver-side characterization of time-varying quantum links, with MDI-QKD as one representative downstream application.

title: Shannon and Rényi entropies of molecular densities: insights into extensivity and the incomplete description of electron correlation
generated_summary:
This paper systematically examines whether Shannon and Rényi entropies derived from the electron density can effectively capture electron correlation and chemical bonding effects in molecular systems. The authors combine algebraic analysis with numerical integration to study two-electron homodiatomic molecules (H₂, N₂) and H₂O at various levels of theory—Hartree-Fock, Heitler-London, and multideterminant methods—using both minimal and extended basis sets, with particular focus on dissociation processes.

The authors derive a Mulliken-type atomic partition of Shannon and Rényi entropies into additive (net atomic and overlap) and nonadditive contributions, establishing general algebraic asymptotic limits at infinite internuclear distances. For minimal-basis calculations, they demonstrate that the Shannon entropy of the electron density fails to distinguish between correlated and uncorrelated wavefunctions, as all methods converge to the same atomic limits regardless of correlation content. Shape-function entropies and Rényi entropies violate extensivity due to persistent nonadditive contributions. With extended basis sets, only sufficiently correlated methods (e.g., full-valence CAS) recover correct large-distance limits, while Hartree-Fock consistently overestimates entropy due to variational flexibility rather than improved accuracy.

These findings demonstrate that electron-density-based entropic measures provide an incomplete description of electron correlation and chemical bonding, challenging assumptions underlying proposed entropy-correlation energy relationships. The authors advocate for more sophisticated entropic descriptors constructed from higher-dimensional Hilbert-space objects to properly capture electronic correlation effects.
original_abstract: In this work, we investigate the reliability of information-theoretic measures based on the electron-density and shape-function, specifically Shannon and Rényi entropies, as descriptors of electronic correlation. By establishing a rigorous decomposition of these entropic measures into additive and nonadditive contributions, supported on a Mulliken-like atomic partition of molecules, we systematically analyze the asymptotic behavior of the entropies at the infinite-internuclear-distance limit to assess the problem of static correlation and extensivity. Our algebraic and numerical analysis reveals several flaws in the use of these density-based descriptors. We demonstrate that for minimal-basis and different theoretical levels, the Shannon and Rényi entropies fail to encode the amount of static correlation conveyed by the underlying wavefunction. Conversely, shape-function Shannon entropies and Rényi entropies (for $α\neq 1$) violate extensivity. In larger basis sets, uncorrelated Hartree-Fock densities consistently overestimate entropy compared to sufficiently correlated (e.g., full-valence-CAS) densities. Moreover, the entropies for insufficiently correlated methods violate extensivity. These findings indicate that electron-density-based measures are insufficient for capturing static correlation, suggesting that robust entropic descriptors should be constructed from higher-dimensional Hilbert-space objects.

title: Towards a Foundation-Model Paradigm for Aerodynamic Prediction in Three-dimensional Design
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a foundation-model paradigm for aerodynamic prediction of three-dimensional wing designs, addressing the challenge of balancing reusability and accuracy in surrogate models under realistic computational constraints. The key insight is that pre-training and fine-tuning datasets can differ in geometric fidelity: a large pre-training dataset uses simplified parameterizations to capture broad aerodynamic priors, while a smaller fine-tuning dataset incorporates detailed, task-specific geometry.

The authors develop the AeroTransformer, a scalable transformer-based surrogate model, and evaluate it on large-scale transonic wing datasets. The pre-training dataset (SuperWing) contains thousands of simplified wing configurations, while fine-tuning targets the more complex NASA Common Research Model (CRM) wing. The framework maps surface meshes to a structured reference grid, enabling consistent input representations across different geometries.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that large-scale pre-training significantly improves downstream prediction accuracy for both surface pressure distributions and aerodynamic coefficients, even when pre-training and fine-tuning geometries differ substantially. The model exhibits favorable scaling behavior with increased data and model size. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning strategies prove effective, enabling adaptation with limited task-specific data. The authors also show that pre-trained models consistently outperform models trained from scratch across various data regimes.

This work provides a scalable, reusable framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling, with publicly released datasets and models intended to serve as shared community resources for accelerating three-dimensional aerodynamic design optimization.
original_abstract: Accurate machine-learning models for aerodynamic prediction are essential for accelerating shape optimization, yet remain challenging to develop for complex three-dimensional configurations due to the high cost of generating training data. This work introduces a methodology for efficiently constructing accurate surrogate models for design purposes by first pre-training a large-scale model on diverse geometries and then fine-tuning it with a few more detailed task-specific samples. A Transformer-based architecture, AeroTransformer, is developed and tailored for large-scale training to learn aerodynamics. The methodology is evaluated on transonic wings, where the model is pre-trained on SuperWing, a dataset of nearly 30000 samples with broad geometric diversity, and subsequently fine-tuned to handle specific wing shapes perturbed from the Common Research Model. Results show that, with 450 task-specific samples, the proposed methodology achieves 0.36% error on surface-flow prediction, reducing 84.2% compared to training from scratch. The influence of model configurations and training strategies is also systematically studied to provide guidance on effectively training and deploying such models under limited data and computational budgets. To facilitate reuse, we release the datasets and the pre-trained models at https://github.com/tum-pbs/AeroTransformer. An interactive design tool is also built on the pre-trained model and is available online at https://webwing.pbs.cit.tum.de.

title: Information decomposition for disentangled and interpretable manifold learning of fluid flows via variational autoencoders
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a Decomposed-KL Variational Autoencoder (DKL-VAE) framework for constructing physically interpretable low-dimensional manifolds of unsteady fluid flows. The key contribution is applying the ELBO-TC decomposition to split the standard VAE's KL-divergence term into three independently controllable components—mutual information, total correlation, and dimension-wise KL divergence—each with clear information-theoretic meaning. This decomposition enables targeted regularization of the latent space, promoting disentanglement of distinct physical effects without the information loss and posterior collapse caused by uniformly increasing KL penalty weights in conventional β-VAE approaches.

The method employs convolutional encoder-decoder architectures and is validated on two benchmark datasets: cylinder-in-channel wake flows with varying geometric parameters and NACA 0012 airfoil gust encounters at multiple angles of attack. Comparisons against PCA, ISOMAP, β-VAE, and observation-augmented autoencoders demonstrate that DKL-VAE achieves superior latent-space organization, with latent coordinates that cleanly separate physical effects such as wall confinement, vortex shedding phase, and effective angle of attack. DKL-VAE attains the lowest reconstruction errors—approximately half those of PCA—while maintaining robust performance across hyperparameter variations.

The significance of this work lies in achieving physically meaningful, disentangled latent representations through a fully unsupervised framework, without requiring auxiliary physical observables, offering a principled tool for reduced-order modeling, flow analysis, and potential applications in aerodynamic design.
original_abstract: We introduce an information-theoretic framework that uses variational autoencoders (VAEs) to extract compact, physically interpretable manifolds from high-dimensional flow-field data. To this end, the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence in the variational objective is decomposed into three complementary information-theoretic terms: the index-code mutual information, the total correlation, and the dimension-wise KL divergence. These terms explicitly regulate data compression, latent disentanglement, and geometric regularization. This establishes a principled basis for targeted latent-space design, allowing enhanced interpretability without sacrificing information capacity, a common drawback of heavily regularized VAE variants. The approach is evaluated on two synthetic unsteady flow datasets. First, we consider a flow around a cylinder in a channel with variable cylinder position, diameter, and Reynolds number. Later, we also consider the flow around a NACA 0012 airfoil at varying angles of attack and subjected to strong vortex gusts with variable intensity, position, and length scale. Comparisons with Principal Component Analysis, Isometric Feature Mapping, and $β$-VAE demonstrate clear advantages in disentanglement and physical interpretability. The learned latent coordinates successfully separate distinct physical effects. Moreover, the proposed method demonstrates strong robustness to variations in the loss-weighting parameters, despite involving a larger number of such parameters.

title: The strange mechanics of an elastic rod under null-resultant transverse loads
generated_summary:
This paper reveals that an elastic rod subjected to equal and opposite transverse dead loads applied at its extrados and intrados—a loading condition traditionally assumed to have no mechanical effect due to its null resultant—can in fact induce buckling and postcritical behavior identical to that caused by axial compression. The authors demonstrate that transverse compressive stress adds directly to axial stress in a generalized form of the Euler elastica, where both stresses play equivalent roles in governing deformation and stability.

The findings are established through four independent theoretical approaches: bifurcation analysis of an incompressible elastic layer in the thin-thickness limit, linearized governing equations using mean stresses, an Euler-Bernoulli rod model equipped with finite thickness, and homogenization of a discrete chain of rigid links with elastic hinges. All four approaches yield the same generalized elastica equation and buckling formula, in which the critical condition depends on the sum of axial and transverse stresses. Finite element numerical simulations confirm these predictions, showing excellent agreement even at large deformations. Crucially, dedicated experiments using a novel setup with dead transverse loads validate the theory, demonstrating both the linear relationship between axial buckling stress and applied transverse stress and accurate postcritical load-displacement behavior.

These results establish a new paradigm for understanding structural stability, with potential applications in deformable manipulators, thin film mechanics, and micro- and nanotechnologies where transverse loading conditions are prevalent.
original_abstract: Two equal and opposite distributed dead loads are applied orthogonally to the axis of an elastic rod in its rectilinear reference configuration, one at the extrados and the other at the intrados, such that the resultant applied force per unit length is uniformly zero. In this configuration, the rod is subjected to a transverse (tensile or compressive) stress, which is usually believed to have no significant effect on the structural response and has therefore not been considered so far. Contrary to this common belief, the asymptotic behavior of an incrementally deformed elastic layer and three different rod models (the first derived as an asymptotic approximation of the elastic layer; the second based on Euler elastica; and the third obtained by homogenization of a discrete model) reveal that this loading condition produces the same deformation in the rod as an axial load. In particular, the transverse load adds to the axial load in a generalized version of the Euler elastica, leading to buckling and nontrivial postcritical deformations when compressive. The critical transverse stress for buckling is found to have the same form as the Euler critical stress under axial force and tends to zero in the limit of vanishing rod inertia. For this reason, instability induced by transverse loading persists even when the rod thickness tends to zero. These theoretical predictions are confirmed by numerical simulations of a slender elastic layer, which show that increasing transverse load can induce buckling and drive the layer along a deformation path that closely follows that predicted by the generalized Euler elastica throughout the entire postcritical regime, even beyond self-intersection. To show that this behavior can be realized in practice, a dedicated experimental setup is developed, and the experimental results fully confirm the theoretical and numerical predictions.

title: Modeling Utah FORGE 2022 EGS Hydraulic Stimulations: Tensile Hydraulic Fractures versus Fluid-Induced Dilatant Shear Ruptures
generated_summary:
This study investigates the nature of two hydraulic stimulation stages performed in April 2022 at the Utah FORGE Enhanced Geothermal System test site, distinguishing between tensile hydraulic fracturing and fluid-induced dilatant shear rupture (hydro-shearing) mechanisms. The two stages differed primarily in fracturing fluid viscosity: a low-viscosity slick-water stage and a high-viscosity cross-linked gel stage.

The authors extract time-dependent fracture radii from located microseismic events and compare their evolution against analytical scaling relationships for radial hydraulic fractures and shear ruptures. They then employ a 3D axisymmetric fully-coupled hydro-mechanical numerical solver capable of resolving both tensile and shear failure modes, along with fluid leak-off. Uncertainty propagation of in-situ stress state and natural fracture orientations is also performed.

Key findings reveal that the cross-linked gel stage produced sustained post-shut-in microseismic growth consistent with viscosity-dominated hydraulic fracture propagation, while the slick-water stage showed immediate cessation upon shut-in. Numerical simulations confirm that shear-induced dilation alone cannot accommodate the viscous gel, necessitating tensile fracture opening, whereas the slick-water stage could potentially be explained by either mechanism depending on dilatancy assumptions and fracture orientation.

This work demonstrates that relatively simple analytical-numerical frameworks, grounded in well-established fracture mechanics, can capture first-order stimulation behavior and discriminate between fundamentally different failure mechanisms, providing valuable insights for EGS design and induced seismicity risk management.
original_abstract: We investigate two hydraulic stimulation stages performed in April 2022 at the Utah FORGE enhanced geothermal system test site using analytical and numerical models for tensile hydraulic fractures and fluid-induced dilatant shear fractures. The two injection stages differ primarily by the viscosity of the fracturing fluid. Despite similar injection rate schedules and well-head pressure responses, the two stages exhibit markedly different post-shut-in microseismic behavior. The cross-linked gel stage shows sustained microseismic activity for several hours after shut-in, whereas the slickwater stage exhibits an immediate decrease. For the cross-linked gel stage, the located microseismic events reveal the development of a planar radial fracture and allow confident retrieval of the fracture extent evolution with time. We demonstrate that this evolution follows the scalings predicted for viscosity-storage-dominated radial hydraulic fracture by analytical models, providing strong evidence for the development of a planar tensile hydraulic fracture. We further show that leak-off is required to reproduce the fracture extent. In contrast, the immediate arrest observed during the slick-water stage suggests either a transition to a toughness- or leak-off-dominated hydraulic fracture regime, or the development of a fluid-induced shear fracture. We show that the slickwater stage could plausibly correspond to a dilatant shear fracture, provided sufficient dilatancy, whereas this hypothesis is invalidated for the cross-linked gel stage. We confirm these insights using a 3D axisymmetric fully-coupled hydro-mechanical numerical model capable of resolving both tensile and shear failure modes, and including leak-off. Finally, we propagate uncertainties in the in-situ stress state and natural fracture orientations through this numerical model to assess their impact on injection pressures.

title: Unidirectional Inter-Axial Coupling and Spontaneous Cooling in a~Non-Hermitian Dynamics of a~Levitated Particle
generated_summary:
This study demonstrates tunable non-reciprocal coupling between the transverse motional modes of a single levitated silica microsphere, establishing it as a minimal platform for exploring non-Hermitian dynamics. The two perpendicular oscillation axes of a single particle serve as coupled harmonic oscillators, offering intrinsic advantages over multi-particle systems since both oscillators share identical physical properties.

The experimental platform employs counter-propagating Gaussian beams forming a standing wave trap, where a spatial light modulator controls beam ellipticity and wave plate combinations precisely tune polarization. The stiffness matrix governing inter-axial coupling is reconstructed directly from measured particle trajectories by fitting time-dependent covariance functions derived from the linearized Langevin equation.

By varying polarization from linear to circular, the authors achieve continuous transitions from reciprocal to non-reciprocal and fully unidirectional coupling regimes. Under circular polarization, the system exhibits anti-reciprocal coupling and passes through exceptional points where eigenfrequencies coalesce, leading to dynamical instabilities and limit-cycle oscillations above a power threshold. Remarkably, in the non-reciprocal regime near unidirectional coupling conditions, asymmetric energy exchange produces spontaneous cooling of one motional mode below the thermal equipartition limit, without requiring external feedback or engineered reservoirs.

These results establish levitated optomechanics as a highly controllable platform for studying non-Hermitian physics, directional energy transport, and autonomous thermalization, with potential extensions toward quantum regime applications and synthetic mechanical systems with programmable interactions.
original_abstract: Non-Hermitian dynamics in open systems can give rise to a variety of fascinating non-equilibrium phenomena, ranging from symmetry-breaking transitions to directional energy flow. Parity-time (PT) symmetry breaking determines the occurrence of dynamical instabilities, while non-reciprocal interactions enable asymmetric energy transfer between modes. Here, we present a versatile optomechanical platform based on a vacuum-levitated nanoparticle that allows full control over the coupling of its mechanical modes, including non-reciprocal and non-conservative interactions. By engineering the spatial ellipticity and polarization of the trapping beam, we continuously tune the system from a reciprocal to a strongly non-reciprocal regime. This allows us to observe PT-symmetry phase transitions and to isolate a unidirectional regime in which one mode remains effectively decoupled while driving the other. We demonstrate that elliptical polarisation of the trapping beam spanning unidirectional and reciprocal regimes induces asymmetric intermodal energy transfer. This results in the spontaneous cooling of one mechanical mode without external feedback. Both modes share identical mass, size, charge, and optical environment, providing a clean and robust setting for exploring non-Hermitian dynamics, exceptional-point physics, and energy redistribution in minimal systems. Combined with recent advances in ground-state cooling, our results provide a direct route to realising non-Hermitian phenomena in the quantum regime.

title: Advances in photocathode development for PICOSEC Micromegas precise-timing detectors
generated_summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive comparative characterization of four photocathode materials — CsI, titanium (Ti), boron carbide (B₄C), and diamond-like carbon (DLC) — for use in PICOSEC Micromegas precise-timing detectors targeting sub-nanosecond resolution for minimum ionizing particles (MIPs). While CsI offers excellent quantum efficiency, its vulnerability to ion backflow, discharges, and humidity motivates the development of more robust alternatives.

The photocathode samples were manufactured at CERN and evaluated during test beam campaigns using muon beams, with a standardized single-pad metallic detector operated in sealed mode. Performance was assessed through time resolution measurements, detection efficiency, and photoelectron yield (N_PE), with particle tracking provided by a beam telescope and timing referenced to a microchannel plate photomultiplier.

CsI achieved the best time resolution of approximately 11 ps with over 30 photoelectrons per MIP. Among alternatives, B₄C performed best at 27 ps, followed by Ti at 30.5 ps and DLC at 32.5 ps. Detection efficiency exceeded 95% for all materials. Thinner coatings generally yielded superior timing performance across all materials. Ti and B₄C produced comparable N_PE values above 5, while DLC exceeded 3.

The results establish Ti and B₄C as the most promising robust alternatives to CsI. Ti offers excellent reproducibility, conductivity, ease of production, and humidity insensitivity, while B₄C shows intriguing performance improvements after air exposure. Both materials demonstrated no degradation over multiple test beam campaigns spanning several years, confirming their suitability for large-area, long-term operation in future high-energy physics experiments.
original_abstract: The PICOSEC Micromegas detector is a precise-timing gaseous detector that combines a Cherenkov radiator, a semi-transparent photocathode and a Micromegas amplification stage, targeting time resolutions of tens of picoseconds for minimum ionising particles (MIPs). Initial single-pad prototypes achieved $σ<25$ ps, demonstrating strong potential for High Energy Physics (HEP) applications. The objective of this paper is a~comprehensive characterisation of photocathodes, with a strong focus on robust materials while preserving excellent timing performance. The study includes laboratory measurements of optical and resistive properties together with beam tests using 150 GeV/$c$ muons to evaluate time resolution and photoelectron yield for various photocathodes. The best performance was delivered by a~5\,nm Cesium Iodide (CsI) photocathode, reaching $σ= 10.9 \pm 0.3$ ps with more than 30 extracted photoelectrons, representing the most precise time resolution achieved by PICOSEC Micromegas to date. Metallic and carbon-based photocathodes, including Titanium (Ti), Boron Carbide (B$_4$C) and Diamond-Like Carbon (DLC), were also tested, with Ti and B$_4$C emerging as the most promising alternatives, achieving $σ\approx 30$ ps with about 5 extracted photoelectrons. These results demonstrate that improved robustness can be achieved while maintaining excellent time resolution, supporting the feasibility of using the PICOSEC Micromegas concept in future experiments.

title: Import-Dependent Grain Processing Hubs: The Case of Türkiye's Flour Sector
generated_summary:
This paper examines the vulnerability of trade-dependent food processing hubs to climate-driven disruptions in global agricultural supply chains, using Türkiye's flour sector as a primary case study. The main contribution is the introduction of the Biophysical Autonomy Ratio (BAR), a novel analytical indicator that measures the relationship between a country's domestic biological production capacity and its industrial processing scale. This metric serves as a diagnostic tool for identifying structural dependencies in food processing systems that rely heavily on imported agricultural inputs.

The methodology involves applying the BAR framework to Türkiye's wheat and flour industry, comparing domestic wheat production against milling capacity across two periods (2000–2004 and 2019–2023). The analysis also extends to cross-country comparisons to contextualize Türkiye's position among other nations.

Key findings reveal that Türkiye, despite being a major wheat producer and the world's largest flour exporter, operates milling capacity that significantly exceeds its domestic wheat production base. This structural imbalance creates a fundamental reliance on imported grain, rendering the sector vulnerable to supply shocks from synchronized crop failures, export restrictions, or trade disruptions—risks that are expected to intensify under climate change scenarios, including Multiple Breadbasket Failure events.

original_abstract: International commerce has long been seen as a key way to keep the global food system stable, allowing agricultural surpluses in some areas to compensate for shortages in others. This strategy has led to the rise of highly specialised processing hubs that combine significant industrial capacity with agricultural inputs sourced from throughout the world. Türkiye's flour sector -- currently the largest wheat flour exporter in the world -- represents one of the most prominent examples of this model. However, increasing climate variability and geopolitical fragmentation raise important questions regarding the long-term resilience of food systems that rely heavily on imported biological inputs. Recent research shows the growing probability of synchronised crop failures across multiple agricultural regions due to atmospheric circulation anomalies and climate-induced extreme weather events. The assumption that global markets can consistently rebalance supply disruptions through trade is challenged by such events. Using the flour industry of Türkiye as a case study, this paper investigates the susceptibility of globally integrated grain processing centres. In order to assess the correlation between the scope of industrial processing and the capacity of domestic agricultural production, we introduce the Biophysical Autonomy Ratio~(BAR). The analysis demonstrates that Türkiye's BAR has declined consistently over time, suggesting that its processing sector has expanded beyond the domestic production base. The results suggest that in order to enhance the resilience of the food system in the future, it may be necessary to establish a more precise alignment between biological production systems and industrial food infrastructure. The paper concludes by addressing the policy implications for national food security governance in the context of escalating climate instability.

title: State-Averaged Quantum Algorithms for Multiconfigurational Surface Chemistry: A Benchmark on Rh@TiO2(110)
generated_summary:

The quantum ansätze are evaluated as approximate CASCI solvers within this fixed orbital basis, isolating wavefunction accuracy from orbital optimization effects.

Key results show that SA-fUCCSD converges slowly toward the CASCI limit, requiring up to 1350 parameters across ten layers while retaining residual errors of approximately 0.11 mE_h, with notable sensitivity to parameter initialization near state crossings. In contrast, a modified SA-ADAPT protocol—incorporating multiple operators per iteration based on relative gradient magnitudes—achieves errors of approximately 1 μE_h using only around 386 operators, representing a two-order-of-magnitude improvement in accuracy with fewer parameters.

original_abstract: Accurate modeling of surface catalytic processes often requires methods capable of describing strong correlation, charge transfer, and multiple closely lying electronic states. While density functional theory remains widely used, its limitations for localized electronic states motivate the use of wavefunction-based approaches and, more recently, quantum computing algorithms. However, the performance of quantum ansätze in chemically motivated, multistate settings remains largely unexplored. Here, we benchmark state-averaged factorized unitary coupled cluster with singles and doubles (SA-fUCCSD) and the adaptive, problem-tailored ansatz (SA-ADAPT) using an embedded cluster model of NO adsorption on Rh-doped TiO2(110). The system exhibits pronounced multiconfigurational character and multiple state crossings, providing a stringent test. State-averaged CASSCF serves as a reference, and the quantum ansätze are evaluated as solvers for the corresponding CASCI problem within a fixed orbital basis. We find that SA-fUCCSD improves with increasing circuit depth but requires many parameters and shows sensitivity to initialization. In contrast, SA-ADAPT achieves near-CASSCF accuracy with significantly fewer operators. A modified operator selection scheme, incorporating multiple operators per iteration, substantially accelerates convergence. Our results demonstrate the efficiency of adaptive ansätze for multistate problems and establish a controlled benchmark for quantum algorithms in chemically motivated systems beyond minimal models.

title: Synthetic Seismograms from Particle Bed Interactions and Turbulent River Flow: Modeling and Comparison with Observations

Results show that turbulent hydrodynamic forcing dominates the seismic signal, accounting for approximately 75–80% of total energy, while particle impacts contribute 20–30%, primarily at frequencies above 10 Hz. original_abstract: We present a physics based numerical model that estimates the seismic radiation generated by water sediment flows in gravel-bed rivers. The model reproduces the trajectories of individual particles, evaluates impact and rolling forces from grain scale dynamics, and accounts for broadband turbulence and vortex shedding in the water column. Synthetic seismic signals are propagated to the receivers using the Rayleigh wave Green s function approach and synthetic ground-velocity signals are estimated. Application to a controlled test case shows how intermittent, size selective sediment transport mechanisms produce distinct spectral signatures. Comparison with seismic data from a flood event in a mountain torrent in the Tuscan Apennines displays general agreement with the observed frequency bands and clarifies the relative width of particle collisions and turbulent flow. These results show that resolved grain scale dynamics provides a framework for discriminating sediment transport and flow induced contributions to river seismic noise.

title: How to quantify direct correlations between variables
generated_summary:
This paper organizes existing nonlinear measures of direct correlation between variables into two coherent families and introduces regularized analogues to address fundamental limitations. The first family—comprising conditional mutual information (CMI), part mutual information (PMI), and independent conditional mutual information (ICMI)—removes direct correlation from distributions and measures the induced shift. The second family relies on Pearl's do-calculus to measure distributional responses to interventions, including average causal effect and do-based mutual information.

The key methodological contribution is replacing the Kullback-Leibler divergence underlying these measures with the Jensen-Shannon divergence, producing regularized versions that are bounded in [0,1] and free of the singularities that plague sparse-data applications. The authors further derive explicit achievable upper bounds for each measure that depend on observed marginals and alphabet sizes, providing the correct scale for interpreting observed values.

The measures are evaluated on a decision-making toy model and three public datasets: Titanic 1912, UCI Adult 1994, and UC Berkeley 1973. Results demonstrate consistent behavior: direct-correlation measures remain substantial for datasets with genuine direct effects (Titanic, Adult) but fall markedly below total mutual information for the Berkeley data, where marginal correlation largely reflects confounding by department. Bootstrap confidence intervals confirm these distinctions are statistically robust. The framework clarifies the relationships among disparate existing measures and provides practitioners principled guidance for selecting among them based on which aspect of direct correlation is of scientific interest.
original_abstract: Analyzing correlation between variables is often both the tool and the goal of modern science. A crucial question is whether the correlation between two variables is a direct correlation or only an indirect correlation through a confounder. We review the existing measures of direct correlation and organize them into two families, each corresponding to a systematic construction: (i) removing the direct correlation from the original joint distribution and quantifying the resulting distributional shift, and (ii) intervening on one variable via do-calculus and quantifying how the distribution of the other variable responds. For every Kullback--Leibler-based measure in either family, we propose a Jensen--Shannon-based regularized analogue. Since the square root of the Jensen--Shannon divergence is a bounded metric, the regularized measures take values in $[0,1]$ and are free of the singularity of the Kullback--Leibler divergence. We further analyze the achievable upper bound of each regularized measure under the observed marginal $p(x,z)$, which depends on the alphabet size and is in general strictly below $1$; this sets the correct scale against which observed values should be read. The properties and the differences of the proposed measures are illustrated on a decision-making toy model and on three public real datasets: Titanic survival, UCI Adult (Census Income), and the UC~Berkeley 1973 graduate admissions. Bootstrap $95\%$ confidence intervals are reported for every numerical value.

title: Coherent structures in axis-switching elliptical jets
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how axis switching—a phenomenon where the major and minor axes of an elliptical jet invert downstream—affects the large-scale coherent structures within the jet. The authors conduct three direct numerical simulations (DNS) of incompressible aspect-ratio-2 elliptical jets at Reynolds number 400, using different forcing levels to produce jets that either do not axis-switch or axis-switch at different downstream locations. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), applied with D₂ symmetry decomposition, extracts the dominant coherent structures from the simulation data.

The key finding is that axis switching significantly modifies the coherent structures, particularly in the SA symmetry family. In the pre-axis-switch region, a "wagging" mode dominates, while a new "flapping" mode emerges in the post-axis-switch region, attributable to the inverted mean flow creating favorable conditions for flapping instability along the switched major axis. The antisymmetric-symmetric (AS) flapping mode remains dominant overall but exhibits faster downstream decay in axis-switching cases. The effects of axis switching are most pronounced at lower frequencies, where coherent structures extend further downstream and thus experience the mean-flow deformation before decaying.

This work represents the first systematic characterization of how axis switching modifies wavepacket structures in elliptical jets, providing foundational understanding that could inform noise reduction and mixing enhancement strategies through nozzle geometry design. The identification of emergent post-axis-switch instabilities opens avenues for future modeling using linear stability and resolvent analysis frameworks.
original_abstract: Coherent structures in aspect ratio 2, axis-switching elliptical jets are studied using direct numerical simulation (DNS). Three different datasets are studied with varying near-nozzle forcing levels. Increasing the forcing level causes the jet to axis switch at an earlier streamwise location. Spectral proper orthogonal decomposition was applied to the dataset to extract the most-energetic coherent structures in the flow, and modes associated with the main symmetries of the flow were identified. The flapping mode was found to decay faster at the high forcing level, a feature that was linked to the axis-switching behavior. The axis-switching phenomenon causes the flapping mode to become a wagging mode relative to the new axis, lowering the growth rate of the structure. Two different coherent structures were found in the SA (dihedral group $D_2$) symmetry for the axis-switching cases: the wagging mode which was dominant in the pre-axis-switch region and a new flapping mode which is dominant in the post-axis-switch region. The new flapping mode was dominant in the low-frequency region of the full-field SPOD spectrum which was overtaken by the wagging mode at $St\approx 0.2$ for the medium-forcing case and at $St\approx 0.4$ for the high-forcing case. This new flapping mode is likely a flapping mode relative to the axis-switched mean flow, which develops due to the slower growth of the shear layer in the major axis.

title: What Do Black Holes Teach Us About Wigner's Friend?
generated_summary:

The analysis yields two principal findings. The work is significant because it uses insights from quantum gravity to constrain interpretive options in quantum foundations, and reciprocally suggests that dynamical relationalism may offer a less metaphysically radical understanding of black hole complementarity than typically assumed.
original_abstract: Recently, Hausmann and Renner have pointed out that several famous paradoxes relating to black holes have a similar character to various Extended Wigner's Friend paradoxes. In this paper I consider what the connection between these things could teach us about the Wigner's Friend scenarios. I argue that if we take the analogy between these cases seriously, the black hole paradoxes appear to favour a certain class of response to the Wigner's Friend scenario - specifically, those which posit intrinsic relationality, rather than effective and emergent relationality, and also those which posit some kind of retrocausality.

title: Inferring lunar wake potentials from electron phase space densities
generated_summary: This paper presents the Hamiltonian inversion method, a novel technique for inferring the electric potential structure of the lunar wake from electron phase space density measurements. The method employs a domain-decomposition strategy to address two key challenges: the solar wind strahl creates asymmetric distributions across the wake, and ion acoustic shocks in the central wake produce flat-top trapped electron distributions where the standard equilibrium relation breaks down. The wake is partitioned into left, middle, and right domains, with independent optimizations performed on the flanks using an L-BFGS-B algorithm on a multigrid hierarchy, while the central shock region is treated through direct inversion based on the measurable width of flat-top velocity distributions. Validation against particle-in-cell simulations at both early and late evolutionary stages demonstrates that the method accurately recovers potential profiles, including shock-associated enhancements, outperforming the Hamiltonian shift method particularly in the central wake. Application to ARTEMIS spacecraft observations of two lunar wake crossings yields potential drops of approximately 3–5 times the electron temperature. The method is broadly applicable to plasma wakes behind other unmagnetized bodies and to any environment where electrons maintain quasi-static equilibrium with field-aligned potentials.
original_abstract: Inferring electric potentials from electron phase space density measurements in the lunar wake is complicated by two challenges: the asymmetry between the sunward and anti-sunward sides of the wake driven by the solar wind strahl, and the presence of ion acoustic shocks in the central wake. We develop the Hamiltonian inversion method, which infers the full spatial electric potential profile by exploiting the quasi-static Vlasov equilibrium condition $f = f(H)$, where $H$ is the electron Hamiltonian. The method addresses both challenges through a domain-decomposition strategy: on the two sides of the wake the potential is inferred independently by minimizing the misfit between the observed phase space density and a self-consistently reconstructed $f_\mathrm{interp}(\tilde{H})$, while in the central wake where flat-top trapped electron distributions are present the potential is inferred directly from the flat-top width. We validate the method against particle-in-cell simulation data at two evolutionary stages of the lunar wake: an early stage where strahl asymmetry is strong but no shocks have formed, and a later stage where ion acoustic shocks and flat-top distributions are present. We then apply the method to two ARTEMIS lunar wake crossings at the same evolutionary stages, inferring normalized potential drops of $eΔ\varphi/T_e \sim 15$ and $\sim 5$ respectively and capturing shock-associated potential enhancements in the central wake. The method is broadly applicable to plasma environments where electrons are in quasi-static equilibrium with a field-aligned electric potential.

title: Measurement-defined control of single-particle interference
generated_summary:
This paper presents a measurement-centered framework for understanding single-particle interference, demonstrating that interference is governed by the projection of a prepared quantum state onto detector-defined photonic modes rather than by propagation-phase accumulation alone.

The experimental platform employs two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources driven by a stabilized optical frequency comb, performing stimulated parametric downconversion. This architecture enables independent control over three phase parameters: the pump phase difference and seed phase difference (controlling state preparation) and the signal interferometric phase (controlling the measurement basis). The detector at the output beam splitter defines orthogonal bright and dark collective modes, with interference arising from projection onto the bright mode.

The key experimental result demonstrates that scanning any of the three independent phases produces identical sinusoidal interference fringes with visibility approaching 0.99, confirming that interference depends solely on the detection phase—the relative angle between the prepared state and measurement basis on the Bloch sphere. The same interference law persists from the single-photon regime to high-flux operation. The idler-state overlap continuously controls fringe visibility without requiring idler detection, providing intrinsic tunability of wave-particle duality.

This work establishes measurement as an active control parameter rather than a passive readout, providing a direct operational demonstration that separates state preparation from measurement—a capability structurally absent from conventional interferometers. The framework connects to coherent population trapping in atomic systems and enables delayed-choice implementations.
original_abstract: Interference is conventionally attributed to path-accumulated phase differences, with measurement treated as a passive readout. Here we demonstrate that single-particle interference is governed by the relative phase between the prepared quantum state and the detector-defined measurement basis -- a joint quantity that is operationally inaccessible in any conventional interferometer. Using coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources, we show that independently scanning the pump phase difference, the seed phase difference, or the signal interferometric phase each produces identical sinusoidal fringes ($V\approx0.99$) -- a three-scan equivalence impossible in any two-mode interferometer. The fringe visibility is continuously controlled through the idler-state overlap, directly encoding quantum distinguishability without idler detection. The same measurement-defined interference law persists from the single-photon to the high-flux regime. The bright-dark collective-state structure demonstrated here unifies coherent population trapping and electromagnetically induced transparency in atomic $Λ$-systems, discrete photonic interference, and single-slit diffraction within a common framework differing only in dark-subspace dimensionality, establishing measurement-defined photonic modes as a fundamental resource for quantum photonics.

title: Poling-free Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion without for Silicon Carbide and Lithium Niobate photonics
generated_summary:

The methodology relies on phase-matching between a higher-order TM₂₀ pump mode and fundamental TE₀₀ signal and idler modes in standard ridge waveguides. An adiabatic directional coupler converts fiber-injected fundamental TM₀₀ modes into the required TM₂₀ modes, achieving conversion efficiencies of approximately 99% and 96% for 4H-SiC and LN platforms, respectively, as confirmed by FDTD simulations.

Key results demonstrate that phase-matching conditions support SPDC across a broad range of signal and idler wavelengths in both platforms, with the specific wavelength pairs selected by tuning the pump wavelength. Importantly, the phase-matching conditions show tolerance to fabrication-induced deviations in waveguide geometry, including etch depth and sidewall angle variations.

The significance of this work is substantial: it enables 4H-SiC to function as a fully CMOS-compatible χ⁽²⁾ nonlinear photonics platform and opens pathways to backward-wave generation and simplified photon source fabrication in integrated quantum photonic circuits.
original_abstract: State-of-the-art photon sources based on spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) currently rely on artificial structuring of the material nonlinearity to satisfy phase-matching conditions. This technique, known as periodic poling, is available only in a limited number of material platforms and introduces additional fabrication steps and errors, which are detrimental to up-scaling efforts. Here, we present a device architecture that enables SPDC of a wide range of frequencies without the need for periodic poling. We present explicit designs and calculations for 4H Silicon Carbide on-insulator, in which SPDC photon generation is so far unavailable, and thin-film Lithium Niobate on-insulator, a state-of-the-art quantum photonics platform. Our design, based on mode conversion and subsequent modal phase-matched SPDC, facilitates a CMOS compatible $χ^{(2)}$ platform, and simplifies photon sources by removing the requirement of periodic poling and the associated additional fabrication complexity.

title: Generation of Standing Waves on a Real String
generated_summary:

The author employs Green's function methods to construct general solutions to the inhomogeneous telegraph equation, then analyzes several forcing scenarios: spatially extended continuous resonant forcing, spatially distributed impulsive forcing, and spatially localized continuous forcing. Each scenario reveals distinct physical behaviors relevant to real string vibrations.

The key results demonstrate that sustaining a pure standing wave requires continuous resonant forcing with a spatial profile matching the desired normal mode, creating a steady state where energy input exactly balances dissipative losses. Analysis of impulsive forcing reproduces Mersenne's laws for the fundamental harmonic in low-stiffness and weak-damping regimes, while explaining why plucked or struck musical strings produce time-decaying sounds composed of multiple harmonics rather than pure tones. The study of localized continuous forcing reveals that the common textbook scenario of driving one end of a string inevitably excites multiple normal modes. Additionally, higher-frequency modes require stronger forcing than lower-frequency ones, consistent with the proportionality between mechanical energy and frequency squared.

These findings deepen understanding of wave phenomena governed by the telegraph equation and its extensions, which find applications ranging from electromagnetic wave propagation to quantum gravity theories.
original_abstract: We investigate the generation of standing waves in the model provided by the inhomogeneous telegraph equation under different forcing conditions. We show that sustained standing waves arise only for a specific forcing that is spatially distributed, continuous, and resonant.

title: Optimality in group-driven social dynamics on hypergraphs
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how group-level nonlinear interactions on hypergraphs lead to unexpected optimal behavior in two fundamental social dynamics models: simplicial contagion and group-driven voter models. The central contribution is demonstrating that intermediate levels of structural or dynamical group effects maximize spreading efficiency and consensus speed, rather than extreme values.

For simplicial contagion dynamics, the authors study how hyperedge nestedness—the degree to which pairwise edges are contained within larger triangular hyperedges—affects outbreak size and thresholds. They develop a novel analytical framework called the facet-based approximate master equation (FAME) method, which accurately captures dynamical correlations between local processes through nested hyperedges. Results from both Monte Carlo simulations and FAME analysis reveal that contagion spreads most efficiently at an intermediate nestedness level, arising from competition between two opposing effects: increased nestedness activates higher-order contagion pathways but simultaneously reduces pairwise connectivity between groups.

For opinion dynamics, the authors introduce the group-driven voter model (GVM) on hypergraphs, generalizing the classical voter model to incorporate within-group nonlinear interactions. Mean-field analysis and simulations demonstrate that consensus time is minimized at intermediate nonlinearity strength, reflecting a trade-off between suppression of diffusive fluctuations and delay of drift-induced ordering.

These findings provide important theoretical insight into how higher-order network structure and group-level interactions jointly shape collective social phenomena, highlighting that optimal social dynamics emerge from balanced group effects rather than maximal ones.
original_abstract: We explore the role of intrinsic structural properties of hypergraphs in governing group-driven social dynamics with social reinforcement. First, we analyze simplicial contagion dynamics on random hypergraphs in which the level of hyperedge nestedness is systematically controlled. By developing the facet-based approximate master equation (FAME) method, we demonstrate that hyperedge nestedness induces a non-monotonic change in the outbreak threshold for simplicial contagion, displaying the lowest threshold at an intermediate level of hyperedge nestedness due to competition between simple and higher-order contagion processes. Next, we formulate the group-driven voter model (GVM) and investigate the consensus time for the GVM on hypergraphs with N nodes. Focusing on a representative case of the GVM, we show that the consensus time scales logarithmically with the system size as A ln N, where the prefactor A displays the fastest consensus formation at an intermediate level of social reinforcement due to competition between group-constraint and nonlinearity factors. Taken together, our results highlight the importance of competing effects arising from higher-order interactions in shaping optimality in group-driven social dynamical processes.

title: Pulsed Optical Injection Steering in Multistable Semiconductor Laser Arrays under Correlated Noise
generated_summary:
This paper investigates pulsed optical injection steering as a state-preparation mechanism for multistable semiconductor laser arrays, specifically vertical-cavity surface-emitting laser (VCSEL) arrays coupled through delayed optical feedback. The main contribution is demonstrating that short, transient injection pulses can reliably steer small coupled laser arrays toward desired stable compound laser mode (CLM) equilibria, after which the arrays maintain the selected state through their own autonomous dynamics without requiring continuous external forcing.

They employ a Crank-Nicolson integration scheme to handle the system's stiffness and systematically test injection pulse parameters including strength, width, frequency offset, and phase.

Key findings indicate that successful steering requires injection strengths exceeding approximately five times the coupling strength with pulse widths greater than three delay times. The results are independent of injection phase, and the injection frequency can deviate by approximately ±0.1 GHz from the target equilibrium frequency while maintaining success. Under correlated noise, injection steering remains effective for most equilibrium branches, though CLMs with small basins of attraction become destabilized.

This work is significant for coherent beam combining and optical memory applications, demonstrating that minimal injection power (hundreds of microwatts) can control milliwatt-scale array outputs, offering a practical pathway toward experimental implementation of state selection in multistable photonic systems.
original_abstract: We demonstrate robust programmable state preparation in small VCSEL arrays with optical feedback using transient optical injection in the form of Gaussian pulses. In Lang--Kobayashi type models of delay-coupled 2- and 3-laser arrays, multistability gives rise to coexisting synchronized and symmetry-broken equilibrium branches. We show that short injection pulses applied to one or more lasers can steer the system from free-running operation to any stable equilibrium branch in the absence of noise by appropriate choice of pulse detuning and amplitude, after which the selected state persists without continued forcing. With correlated noise, injection steering remains effective, but branches with small basins of attraction are effectively destabilized by noise. These results validate pulsed injection as a practical mechanism for attractor selection in multistable VCSEL arrays and point to a feasible route toward experimental realization of programmable collective-state control.

title: Is segregation encoded in urban form? An entropy-based analysis
generated_summary:
This study investigates whether residential segregation patterns are systematically associated with urban morphological complexity in São Paulo, Brazil. The authors propose a novel analytical framework that places built-form entropy and income-based segregation measures on a common spatial support using a regular 3×3 km grid tessellation, enabling direct comparison between otherwise incompatible datasets.

The methodology involves three steps: quantifying urban morphology through built-form entropy (BFE) derived from building footprints using Shannon's entropy applied to two-dimensional binary matrices; measuring residential segregation using Moran's I (spatial autocorrelation) and the Gini index computed from census-tract per-capita income data; and analyzing their relationships through piecewise regression.

The key finding is a non-linear, threshold-based relationship between built-form entropy and segregation indicators. Below an entropy threshold (approximately 0.317), income decreases with increasing entropy, while above it, higher entropy corresponds to higher income, greater inequality, and stronger spatial clustering. Notably, the highest values of Moran's I occur exclusively in high-entropy cells, suggesting that morphologically complex areas facilitate the co-occurrence and local clustering of distinct income groups. Different income groups concentrate in distinct entropy bands rather than distributing randomly across the morphological spectrum.

These findings suggest that urban form and residential segregation are structurally intertwined, offering a quantitative basis for understanding how built environments encode socioeconomic spatial patterns and potentially informing urban planning interventions targeting segregation.
original_abstract: The footprints of residential segregation have long been documented, yet the role of urban form as both medium and manifestation of segregation remains under-specified. We investigate whether the configuration of the built fabric may encode residential segregation in its spatial structure, hypothesising that built-form entropy (BFE) regimes are associated with the spatial distribution of income groups and their local clustering in non-linear ways. We examine this by quantifying BFE through a Shannon-based measure computed from building footprints, characterising income-based distributions using the Gini index and Moran's I, and placing both on a common spatial footing through a regular tessellation. Applying this framework to Sao Paulo, Latin America's largest city, we find non-linear relationships between BFE, income, and segregation: income levels and residential clustering increase toward both extremes of the entropy spectrum, with a stronger rise at the high-entropy end. This asymmetry suggests that high-entropy urban forms are associated with distinct spatial processes of segregation, including elite enclaving and incremental development in lower-income settlements, while low-entropy forms reflect more selective occupation shaped by planning and market filtering. Overall, the findings suggest that built form is more than a neutral backdrop, functioning as both affordance and signal of segregation.

title: Achromatic optics using nonlinear plasma lenses for beam-quality preservation between plasma-accelerator stages
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a novel achromatic beam optics lattice based on nonlinear plasma lenses for transporting electron beams between successive plasma-accelerator stages while preserving beam quality. The central challenge addressed is chromaticity—energy-dependent focusing that causes emittance growth when refocusing highly divergent beams with finite energy spread, which is the primary obstacle to staging multiple plasma accelerators for achieving higher energies.

The proposed lattice combines the principles of local chromaticity correction (traditionally implemented with quadrupoles and sextupoles) with the compactness of plasma lenses, which provide simultaneous focusing in both transverse planes at gradients far exceeding conventional magnets. The key innovation is introducing nonlinear plasma lenses with transversely varying focusing strength, paired with magnetic dipoles that energetically disperse the beam. This combination renders the focusing achromatic while maintaining a compact footprint. The lattice also features tunable longitudinal dispersion (R₅₆) enabling self-correction of energy spread across multiple stages.

Compared to an equivalent quadrupole-based achromatic lattice, the plasma-lens solution is approximately half the length (6 meters versus 12 meters at 10 GeV), uses fewer elements, and supports larger energy bandwidths—up to several percent rms energy spread. The design scales over four orders of magnitude in energy, from 0.5 GeV to beyond 5 TeV. This work represents a potentially transformative solution to the staging problem, a critical bottleneck for realizing plasma-based particle colliders and other high-energy applications.
original_abstract: Plasma acceleration promises to deliver high-energy particle beams by combining, or staging, several low- or medium-energy accelerator stages. However, chromatic aberrations from the combination of high divergence and energy spread make it nontrivial to transport beams between plasma-accelerator stages. This paper describes a compact and achromatic lattice optimized for staging, based on a new beam-optics element; a nonlinear plasma lens. The lattice preserves emittance for energy spreads up to several percent and has a tunable $R_{56}$ that enables bunch-length preservation or a longitudinal self-correction mechanism. The performance and limitations of the plasma-lens-based solution are modeled analytically and numerically, and compared to a more conventional yet novel solution based on quadrupole and sextupole magnets. While functional, the latter is double the length, has about twice the number of elements and a narrower energy bandwidth. Lastly, a solution for scaling to TeV energies is described, in which all lengths scale with the square root of the energy and the deleterious effects of coherent and incoherent synchrotron radiation are mitigated.

title: Polarization and Integration in Global AI Research
generated_summary:
This study maps the evolving structure of international collaboration and knowledge exchange networks in artificial intelligence research from 1990 to 2023, revealing patterns of polarization and integration among countries. Using over 1.9 million AI publications from the OpenAlex database, the authors construct temporal country-level collaboration and citation networks. They employ a maximum-entropy null model (Enhanced Configuration Model) to assess the significance of bilateral relationships beyond what countries' overall research output would predict, then cluster the resulting significance trajectories using k-means with Dynamic Time Warping to identify archetypal trends.

The analysis reveals a long-run divergence between the United States and China in both collaboration and knowledge exchange, establishing them as two distinct poles of global AI research. The United Kingdom and Germany are converging toward the US while diverging from China, whereas a broad group including India, South Korea, and Brazil is gravitating toward China. Notably, several countries—France, Italy, Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, and Israel—are integrating with both poles simultaneously, positioning themselves as potential bridges. Within Europe, major AI producers are diverging from one another while converging with smaller neighbors, forming a hub-and-spoke structure.

These findings carry significant implications for AI governance, suggesting that polarization threatens regulatory coherence and scientific quality. The doubly integrated "bridge" countries, particularly in Europe, may play a crucial role in sustaining cross-bloc knowledge flows and preventing fragmentation of the global AI research system.

While the US restricts mobility and knowledge flows, challenges regulatory efforts to protect its advantage, China leads initiatives of global governance. Both strategies depend on cross-country relationships in AI innovation; yet, how this system evolves is unclear. Here, we measure the processes of polarization and integration in the global AI research over three decades by using large-scale data of scientific publications. Comparing cross-country collaboration and citation links to their random realizations, we find that the US and China have long diverged in both dimensions, forming two poles around which global AI research increasingly revolves. While the United Kingdom and Germany have integrated exclusively with the US, many European countries have converged with both poles. Developing and further developed countries, however, only integrate with China, signaling its expanding influence over the international AI research landscape. Our results inform national science policies and efforts toward global AI regulations.

title: Leaky-Wave Antenna Analysis using Multi-Modal Network Theory with Open Periodic Boundaries
generated_summary:

The methodology is hybrid and iterative, combining commercial full-wave simulations of a single unit-cell with periodic boundary conditions applied to the open region, followed by post-processing that solves a multi-modal eigenvalue problem for the guided region. Two analysis methods are derived from this framework: one for computing dispersion characteristics of transmitting LWAs (eigenmode analysis) and another for analyzing LWAs in reception under plane-wave illumination.

The framework is validated against multiple classic periodic LWAs, including slotted waveguide antennas, parallel plate antennas, metal strip gratings, and modulated metasurface antennas. Results show excellent agreement with reference solutions from finite-length antenna simulations, Method of Moments, and analytical methods. Notably, OPB-MNT requires fewer modes than existing multi-modal transfer matrix methods (e.g., one mode versus ten) and is largely independent of the open-region simulation domain size. The receiving analysis reveals that transmission and reception exhibit slightly different responses due to the lack of strict time-reversal symmetry between inhomogeneous transmitted waves and homogeneous received plane waves.

original_abstract: This paper introduces two methods for analyzing periodic leaky-wave antennas (LWAs) within a new framework denoted as multi-modal network theory (MNT) with open periodic boundaries (OPBs). The approach is hybrid, combining analytical techniques with a commercial full-wave solver. The first method computes the dispersion diagram of periodic LWAs. It is iterative and relies on the full-wave simulation of a single unit-cell of a LWA, coupled with the analytical solution of an eigenvalue problem. This method effectively captures both the phase and attenuation constants of periodic LWAs while using fewer modes than previous methods with commercial frequency-domain solvers. The method is validated by computing the dispersion of classic LWA unit-cells and comparing them to those obtained through full-wave simulations of the full-length antenna and other state-of-the-art methods. The second, also based on OPB-MNT, focuses on LWA analysis in reception. Specifically, it determines the response of a unit-cell to an incident plane wave. To validate this method, we compute the response of LWA with different unit-cell designs. By comparing these results with the corresponding dispersion analysis, we show that the receiving case and the eigenvalue problem are related but not simply time-reversed versions of each other.

title: Target Parameterization in Diffusion Models for Nonlinear Spatiotemporal System Identification

In this work, we revisit this design choice in the context of nonlinear spatiotemporal system identification. We consider a simple, self-contained patch-based transformer that operates directly on physical fields and use turbulent flow simulation as a representative testbed. Our results show that clean-state prediction consistently improves rollout stability and reduces long-horizon error relative to velocity- and noise-based objectives, with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the per-token dimensionality increases. These findings identify target parameterization as a key modeling choice in diffusion-based identification of nonlinear systems with spatial outputs in turbulent regimes.

title: Ice as a Photochemical Shield: Adsorption Energetics and Spectroscopic Modulation of Interstellar Thiocyanates HCSCN and HCSCCH in TMC-1
