original_abstract: This paper presents a hybrid switched-capacitor converter (HSCC) with a novel multi-mode modulation (3M) scheme for wide-range voltage regulation in 48-V automotive power systems. By introducing a three-state operating sequence beyond the conventional 2:1 resonant operation, the proposed converter achieves variable step-down conversion ratios while preserving soft-switching operation in most transitions. The proposed modulation supports both zero-current switching (ZCS) and zero-voltage switching (ZVS) modes, enabling efficient operation over a broad range of load and conversion conditions. To enable voltage regulation, a closed-loop control configuration is proposed with a linear proportional-integral (PI) controller, with gain tuning assisted by reinforcement learning (RL) to address the converter's nonlinear and variable-frequency nature while maintaining good transient performance. A hardware prototype was built to validate the proposed modulation scheme. The measured results verify ZCS operation over voltage conversion ratios of 0.2--0.4, with a peak efficiency exceeding 92\% at 100~W, and efficiency above 88\% over a wide operating range for 3:1 conversion. The feasibility of both ZCS and ZVS operation is also experimentally demonstrated. These results show that the proposed HSCC significantly extends the practical regulation range of resonant switched-capacitor converters while maintaining high efficiency.

title: Ultra-high-vacuum cluster tool for epitaxial synthesis and optical spectroscopy of reactive 2D materials
generated_summary:
This paper presents the design and demonstration of an all-ultra-high-vacuum (UHV) cluster tool that integrates molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) growth of two-dimensional (2D) materials with in situ optical confocal spectroscopy, addressing the critical challenge that many promising 2D semiconductors degrade rapidly upon air exposure, obscuring their intrinsic properties.

The system connects an MBE growth chamber to an optical spectroscopy chamber via a UHV transfer channel, enabling micro-photoluminescence (PL) and micro-Raman mapping of samples up to 3 inches in diameter without breaking vacuum. A pseudo-4f laser scanning technique achieves spatial resolution of 1.1 μm at room temperature, while a closed-cycle cryostat enables temperature-dependent measurements from 20 to 300 K. Cryostat-induced vibrations degrade low-temperature spatial resolution, which is partially recovered through computational deconvolution using the measured point-spread function.

The authors demonstrate the system's capabilities using epitaxially grown post-transition metal monochalcogenides, specifically GaSe and β-In₂Se₃. Wafer-scale Raman mapping reveals stoichiometric variations across a 2-inch GaSe film, while temperature-dependent PL of In₂Se₃ resolves bound and free excitonic features. Critically, GaSe samples remain pristine for over 10 weeks in the UHV environment and withstand more than one hour of continuous laser illumination without degradation.

This platform enables contamination-free, systematic investigation of intrinsic optical and structural properties of air-sensitive 2D materials, filling an important gap in the characterization of next-generation semiconductors.
original_abstract: The large-area synthesis of high-crystalline-quality two-dimensional (2D) materials is at the core of novel material integration for semiconductor technology. This effort relies on developing fabrication and characterization techniques that can uncover the material's intrinsic properties by preserving its pristine conditions. In this article, we present an all ultra-high-vacuum cluster for the growth using molecular beam epitaxy of 2D semiconductors that are unstable under ambient conditions and optical spectroscopy using low temperature (20 K) photoluminescence and Raman scattering. The optical chamber of the setup provides micrometer scale spatial resolution and the ability to scan the entire wafer. The performance of its setup regarding spatial resolution, temperature control over a temperature range of 20-300 K using a closed-cycle cryostat and long-term preservation are demonstrated using as-grown post-transition metal monochalcogenides. Furthermore, we introduce a deconvolution-based algorithm to recover spatial information under vibration using a system-specific point-spread function. This enables in situ analysis of the structural and optoelectronic properties of as-grown materials in their pristine form, providing rich and reproducible feedback for both fundamental studies and the optimization of scalable 2D material growth toward integration in advanced devices.

title: Additively manufactured Shape Memory Alloy Hybrid Composites with a polymer matrix featuring a re-entrant honeycomb structure
generated_summary:
This study presents a novel manufacturing approach for Shape Memory Alloy Hybrid Composites (SMAHCs) that combines stereolithography (SLA) 3D printing with embedded SMA-reinforced glass-fiber layers to create actuators featuring re-entrant honeycomb structures in the polymer toplayer. The composites consist of an active actuator layer, where pre-stretched Nitinol SMA wires are integrated into glass-fiber fabric, and a passive toplayer with auxetic honeycomb geometry of varying thickness (3, 4, and 5 mm). Two SMA wire integration methods are compared: manual hand-weaving (HW) and automated Tailored Fiber Placement (TFP).

Specimens were thermally activated via Joule heating over 50 cycles and evaluated using synchronized dual-camera displacement tracking and deflection angle measurements. Results demonstrate that TFP specimens consistently achieve higher deflection angles (75°–90°) compared to HW specimens (20°–55°), with significantly improved symmetry, reproducibility, and reduced tilt-to-stroke ratios. The opposite thickness-dependence of stroke amplitude between methods is explained by their distinct positions on a qualitative stiffness-deflection curve, reflecting differences in compressive stiffness of the actuator layer architectures.

This work is significant because it establishes a fully integrated, single-workflow additive manufacturing platform for functionally graded SMAHCs, enabling unprecedented geometric design freedom including architected metamaterial structures. The approach overcomes limitations of conventional hot-extrusion and solvent-based methods while demonstrating that automated TFP integration provides superior actuation control for next-generation morphing and adaptive composite systems.
original_abstract: Stereolithography (SLA) and Tailored Fiber Placement (TFP) were combined to fabricate shape memory alloy hybrid composites (SMAHC) featuring a three-layer structure and exhibiting out of plane bending deformation when activated, in a fully integrated, additive manufacturing process. SMA wires as active elements were attached to a textile reinforcement layer, which then was embedded within a UV-curable polymer matrix and combined with a geometrically tailored toplayer, featuring the re-entrant honeycomb architecture. Exploiting the design freedom of SLA, the overall mechanical response of the SMAHC can be systematically adjusted, enabling controlled out-of-plane bending during thermal activation. Two different SMA integration strategies - manual embedding and automated TFP were investigated to assess their influence on actuation behavior, reproducibility, and deformation behaviour. A total of eight geometric configurations were manufactured and experimentally characterized using synchronized optical measurements. The results demonstrate that the combination of SLA-based fabrication and textile-mediated SMA integration enables precise control over the actuation response, while the use of re-entrant honeycomb structures provides an effective approach to tailor stiffness and deformation characteristics. In particular, the automated TFP integration yields improved reproducibility and more symmetric deformation behavior compared to manual fabrication. The presented approach establishes a fully additive manufacturing route for SMAHCs, enabling the realization of structurally integrated, morphing composite systems with programmable mechanical properties.

title: A tensor invariant approach to energy flux in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence
generated_summary:
This paper establishes a framework directly linking tensor invariants of velocity and magnetic field gradient tensors to scale-by-scale energy transfer in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence. By combining spatial filtering techniques with tensor invariant analysis, the authors derive two complementary relationships. First, they prove analytically that the energy flux across scales is bounded above by functions of local tensor invariants, with the tightest bounds obtained through exact optimization. Second, they demonstrate that under conditions of preferential alignment between field structures and strain-rate eigenvectors, the strain-rate invariants serve as proxies for local energy flux, with the sign of the third invariant reliably predicting the direction of energy transfer.

The theoretical predictions are validated using pseudospectral simulations of freely decaying, incompressible three-dimensional MHD turbulence in a periodic domain, filtered at inertial-range scales. The simulations confirm that the derived bounds are tight and that conditional averages of energy flux in invariant space display the predicted statistical ordering. As a special case, purely hydrodynamic contributions to energy flux are expressible exactly in terms of velocity gradient tensor invariants.

The framework has direct applicability to multispacecraft observations, where field gradients can be estimated from measurements across spacecraft separations, enabling characterization of energy transfer in astrophysical plasmas such as the solar wind without requiring direct flux computation.
original_abstract: A scale-by-scale analysis of energy flux in the turbulent cascade can be performed using the spatially filtered magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) equations, while the gradient tensor invariants are widely used to characterise the structure of velocity and magnetic fields. Physical mechanisms responsible for energy flux require specific field configurations whose strength is quantified by these tensor invariants. We explore this requirement, showing that the tensor invariants act as proxies for mechanistic energy fluxes under quantifiable conditions. As a special case, the purely hydrodynamic contributions to energy flux can be expressed exactly in terms of the invariants of the velocity gradient tensor. We also show that the invariants bound the available energy flux for distinct physical mechanisms, formalising the idea that each transfer mechanism requires field configurations with gradients of sufficient strength to support a given energy flux. Results are illustrated using 3D simulations of freely decaying MHD turbulence.

title: Non-intrusive Learning of Physics-Informed Spatio-temporal Surrogate for Accelerating Design
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a Physics-Informed Spatio-Temporal Modeling (PISTM) framework designed to predict the spatio-temporal behavior of nonlinear dynamical systems under unseen operating conditions over specified temporal horizons. The main contribution lies in addressing a problem more challenging than classical forecasting: predicting system dynamics for unknown operating conditions rather than simply extrapolating from known temporal histories.

The methodology combines Koopman autoencoders, which incorporate dynamical system constraints, with an emulation strategy that enables predictions at untested operating conditions. The framework is non-intrusive, meaning it does not require knowledge of the underlying governing equations. Instead, it leverages training data from known operating conditions to learn physics-constrained representations that generalize to new conditions. The Koopman autoencoder captures the system's temporal dynamics within a latent space governed by linear operators, while the emulation component bridges across different operating conditions.

The framework is demonstrated on a fluid flow problem, where it is trained on 45 operating conditions characterized by Reynolds number and tested on 5 unseen conditions. Results show that the approach achieves low generalization errors, with qualitative comparisons at different timesteps confirming accurate predictions of spatial flow fields compared to ground truth data.

The significance of this work lies in its potential to substantially accelerate engineering design processes where generating simulation data at each new operating condition is computationally expensive, while maintaining physical consistency in predictions across the parameter space.
original_abstract: Most practical engineering design problems involve nonlinear spatio-temporal dynamical systems. Multi-physics simulations are often performed to capture the fine spatio-temporal scales which govern the evolution of these systems. However, these simulations are often high-fidelity in nature, and can be computationally very expensive. Hence, generating data from these expensive simulations becomes a bottleneck in an end-to-end engineering design process. Spatio-temporal surrogate modeling of these dynamical systems has been a popular data-driven solution to tackle this computational bottleneck. This is because accurate machine learning models emulating the dynamical systems can be orders of magnitude faster than the actual simulations. However, one key limitation of purely data-driven approaches is their lack of generalizability to inputs outside the training distribution. In this paper, we propose a physics-informed spatio-temporal surrogate modeling (PISTM) framework constrained by the physics of the underlying dynamical system. The framework leverages state-of-the-art advancements in the field of Koopman autoencoders to learn the underlying spatio-temporal dynamics in a non-intrusive manner, coupled with a spatio-temporal surrogate model which predicts the behavior of the Koopman operator in a specified time window for unknown operating conditions. We evaluate our framework on a prototypical fluid flow problem of interest: two-dimensional incompressible flow around a cylinder.

title: Synchrotron-cooled plasma distribution in the outer magnetosphere of a neutron star
generated_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding the dynamics and distribution of synchrotron-cooled plasma trapped in neutron star magnetospheres, analogous to Earth's van Allen belts but with much stronger radiative cooling. The main contribution is deriving evolution equations for relativistic charged particles in a magnetic bottle geometry using the guiding center formalism, where the magnetic moment is no longer conserved due to synchrotron energy losses.

The authors identify two distinct trajectory types: particles with large initial pitch angles form a stable trapped population that gradually cools near magnetic reflection points, while particles with small pitch angles undergo catastrophic energy loss and precipitate onto the stellar surface. When a sustained particle source operates on timescales exceeding a single magnetic bounce period, a steady-state "cooled-loss-cone" or "funnel" distribution emerges, characterized by sharply enhanced particle density at the loss-cone boundary and an energy-dependent opening angle scaling as γ⁻¹/⁴.

A key finding is that synchrotron losses concentrate in a well-localized magnetospheric region at hundreds to roughly a thousand stellar radii, producing potentially observable non-polar emission. The funnel distribution, being highly anisotropic, is unstable to maser emission, which the authors suggest could generate coherent radiation potentially explaining weak fast radio bursts, including FRB 200428 from the galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154. The dual-mirror magnetospheric geometry naturally accounts for observed burst pairs separated by tens of milliseconds.
original_abstract: The guiding center formalism is employed to analyze the motion of a charged relativistic particle in an inhomogeneous magnetic field, subject to magnetic mirroring and energy loss due to cooling. The governing equation for the evolution of the magnetic moment is derived. An example representing a neutron star (pulsar or magnetar) magnetosphere is presented to illustrate typical particle orbits. Notably, radiative losses are most pronounced near a trapped particle's turning point. Depending on the initial particle's pitch angle, energy loss can become catastrophic, resulting in the rapid migration of the particle into the loss cone and subsequent precipitation onto a neutron star. Conversely, particles with a larger pitch angle remain temporarily trapped and form a gradually decaying "cooled-loss-cone" or "funnel'' distribution, characterized by the maximum momentum space particle density being located at the edge of the loss cone. The size of the loss cone is energy-dependent and scales as $α_{c} \propto γ^{3/10}$. Synchrotron losses are strongest in a well-localized region of the magnetosphere, about a few hundred to a thousand star radii under typical pulsar and magnetar conditions. This region is a plausible site for synchrotron radiation originating in the outer magnetosphere, and could also be responsible for non-polar coherent pulsar emission, as well as weak fast radio bursts.

title: Timescale Separation Enables Deep Reinforcement Learning Control of Rotating Detonation Engine Mode Transitions
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first application of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to control rotating detonation engine (RDE) dynamics, specifically targeting rapid transitions between mode-locked states in a one-dimensional reduced-order model. The central methodological innovation is a moving reference frame transformation that exploits the rotational symmetry of the system to separate the fast timescale of detonation wave propagation from the slower timescale of mode transitions. This scale separation reduces the temporal credit assignment challenge inherent in controlling multiscale dynamical systems, allowing DRL agents to operate at lower actuation frequencies while maintaining effective control over fast-moving detonation structures.

The authors employ Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with segmented spatially-varying injection pressure control, testing six agent configurations combining single/multi-agent setups, uniform/segmented control, and stationary/moving reference frames. The single-agent segmented control with moving reference frame (SSM) consistently achieves the best performance across all target states, successfully transitioning between one- to four-wave configurations. The moving reference frame approach enables higher success rates across a broader range of actuation periods compared to stationary-frame counterparts, while multi-agent approaches underperform due to difficulties with global credit assignment and inter-segment coordination.

The findings demonstrate DRL's potential for RDE control and introduce a scale separation strategy that may generalize to other multiscale flow-control problems, laying groundwork for future extensions to higher-fidelity simulations and experimental implementations.
original_abstract: Rotating detonation engines (RDEs) are a promising propulsion concept that may offer higher thermodynamic efficiency and specific impulse than conventional systems, but nonlinear phenomena, including transitions to oscillatory or chaotic propagation modes, can hinder practical operation. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising method for controlling complex nonlinear dynamics such as those observed in RDEs. However, the multi-timescale nature of the RDE system makes direct application of DRL challenging. We address this challenge by reformulating the DRL problem in a moving reference frame that follows the detonation-wave pattern, making the wave structure appear quasi-steady to the agent. This reformulation enables scale separation between fast detonation propagation and slower operating-mode dynamics. We train DRL controllers to modulate spatially segmented injection pressure in a one-dimensional reduced-order RDE model and induce rapid transitions between different mode-locked states. Across a range of actuation periods, initial states, and target modes, controllers trained in the moving frame learn more reliably than those trained in a stationary frame and remain effective over a broader range of actuation periods. These results suggest that symmetry-aware moving reference frame formulations may be useful for related multiscale flow-control problems and that scale separation should be exploited whenever possible to enable DRL control of multi-timescale systems.

title: Magnet-Free Nonreciprocal frequency conversion using Sequential Temporal modulation: Theory and Simulations
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a magnet-free scheme for nonreciprocal frequency conversion based on sequential, time-gated couplings in a three-mode system. Unlike conventional approaches requiring bulky magnets or complex multi-path interference networks, directionality arises solely from the fixed temporal ordering of discrete coupling pulses, breaking time-reversal symmetry without momentum matching or velocity constraints.

The authors develop an analytical framework combining Fourier-Floquet expansion with Dyson-Born perturbation theory to describe energy transfer between three coupled modes, where couplings are activated sequentially within each modulation period. The key physical mechanism is a dwell-time asymmetry: in the forward direction, energy transfers efficiently through sequential gate activation, while in the reverse direction, excitation becomes trapped in the lossy intermediate mode during an idle interval, experiencing dissipation that suppresses back-conversion.

Time-domain simulations validate the analytical predictions across multiple parameter regimes. The authors demonstrate that isolation can be optimized by tuning duty cycles, modulation frequency, inter-gate delay, intermediate mode loss, and coupling strength. Peak isolation occurs when the intermediate mode's dissipation timescale matches the idle interval between gates, and vanishes when gates cover the full period without gaps, restoring reciprocity.

The scheme is platform-agnostic, applicable to photonic, phononic, microwave, and superconducting systems, offering practical design guidelines for CMOS-compatible, magnet-free isolators critical for scalable quantum information architectures.
original_abstract: Nonreciprocal conversion is essential for protecting sources and enabling unidirectional signal routing in photonic, phononic, electronics, and quantum systems, yet conventional implementations rely on magnetic bias that could be challenging to integrate on chip. We propose a magnet-free scheme for frequency-domain nonreciprocity based on sequential, time-gated couplings in a three-mode system. By activating interactions in a fixed temporal order, the forward and reverse frequency conversion pathways acquire unequal dwell times in a lossy intermediate mode, producing strong nonreciprocity without requiring nonlinearities or magnetic materials. Using a harmonic-balance formulation and a Dyson-Born expansion, we derive a compact analytical expression for the isolation ratio that reveals the roles of Floquet sidebands, duty-cycle control, modulation frequency, and dissipation. The results are confirmed by direct time-domain simulations over a wide parameter range. From these results, we extract practical design rules for optimizing isolation through temporal sequencing, loss engineering, and modulation timing. The framework is general and directly applicable to integrated platforms in photonics, phononics, microwave electronics, and superconducting circuits.

title: Where diverse populations gather: Transit accessibility and the spatial structure of social mixing
generated_summary:
This study presents the first spatially explicit, cross-national analysis of how public transit accessibility shapes social mixing at urban venues, comparing nine Swedish and three US cities. The authors introduce a framework distinguishing three diversity measures—residential composition, transit catchment diversity (populations reachable within 45 minutes by transit), and realized visitor diversity—to examine how transit infrastructure mediates encounters across social groups.

Using mobile phone-derived mobility data from approximately 330,000 points of interest and 2024 foot traffic records, the researchers employ OLS regression, spatial lag models with alternative weight specifications, and geographically weighted regression to assess transit's predictive role and spatial spillover effects.

Key findings reveal that transit catchment diversity consistently predicts visitor mixing, but through fundamentally different mechanisms across contexts. In US cities, transit functions as a "diversity bridge," importing heterogeneous visitors into otherwise homogeneous peripheral areas. In Swedish cities, transit amplifies pre-existing residential diversity in already-mixed neighborhoods. Spatial spillovers follow general geographic proximity rather than transit-network connectivity specifically, suggesting transit shapes mixing indirectly by delivering diverse populations to neighborhoods rather than through station-level mechanisms. The transit-mixing relationship is stronger for birth-background diversity than income diversity, with Swedish venues attracting more income-diverse visitors than their surroundings while US venues show the opposite pattern.

These findings carry important implications for context-sensitive transit planning aimed at fostering socially inclusive cities.
original_abstract: Urban venues serve as arenas for social mixing, where individuals from different socioeconomic backgrounds share space during daily activities. While residential and activity-space segregation have been extensively studied, less is known about how public transit infrastructure shapes the spatial structure of social mixing at specific locations. This study examines how transit accessibility influences visitor diversity at points of interest (POIs) in nine cities in Sweden and the United States (New York, Washington DC, Atlanta), using mobile phone GPS traces and aggregated foot traffic data in 2024. We employ spatial regression models and geographically weighted regression (GWR) to test whether transit catchment diversity, the socioeconomic heterogeneity of populations reachable by public transit, predicts visitor diversity, and the spatial heterogeneity of this relationship. Transit catchment diversity is a consistent positive predictor of visitor diversity across nearly all cities, with the strongest effects in large metropolitan areas and where transit links demographically distinct neighborhoods. However, the relationship is much more spatially clustered in US cities, where transit-mixing hotspots emerge in peripheral, lower-diversity areas, whereas in Swedish cities diversity is more spatially diffuse and hotspots occur in already-diverse neighborhoods, suggesting that transit compensates for local homogeneity in the former but amplifies existing diversity in the latter. These results suggest that transit infrastructure functions as a spatial bridge, channeling diverse populations to common destinations and reshaping the geography of social mixing in urban space, particularly for venues located farther from city centers and in less-dense areas.

title: A Fast and Physically Grounded Ocean Model for GCMs: The Dynamical Slab Ocean Model of the Generic-PCM (rev. 3423)
generated_summary:
This paper presents an updated dynamical slab ocean model integrated into the Generic Planetary Climate Model (Generic-PCM), designed to bridge the gap between computationally cheap static slab oceans and expensive fully coupled atmosphere-ocean GCMs. The model features emergent ocean heat transport through wind-driven Ekman transport, horizontal diffusion, convective adjustment, and a newly implemented Gent-McWilliams parameterization for mesoscale eddy mixing—the first such application within a slab ocean framework. Additional improvements include spectrally and thickness-dependent sea ice and snow albedos, and a Sverdrup balance scheme for more physically consistent tropical meridional transport.

The model is validated against two benchmarks: a zero-obliquity aquaplanet and modern Earth. In the aquaplanet configuration, enabling ocean heat transport reduces sea ice coverage and produces realistic equatorial cooling via Ekman-driven upwelling, replacing the unrealistic equatorial temperature peak seen without transport. For modern Earth, the model yields a global mean surface temperature of 13°C (compared to 14°C from reanalysis), with extrapolar sea surface temperatures within 0.6°C and sea ice coverage within 3 million km² of observations—substantially outperforming simulations without ocean heat transport.

The fully parallelized model enables long-timescale simulations and broad parameter space exploration at minimal additional computational cost, making it particularly valuable for exoplanet habitability studies and paleoclimate research in preparation for upcoming observational missions.
original_abstract: Ocean dynamics are often sidelined in exoplanet climate studies due to the high computational cost of fully coupled atmosphere-ocean general circulation models (GCMs). However, ocean heat transport (OHT) can play a critical role in shaping the climate and observables of terrestrial planets. As a compromise, most exoplanet GCMs rely on slab ocean models without OHT. Here, we present an improved compromise - a fast and physically grounded dynamical slab ocean model, implemented in the Generic Planetary Climate Model (Generic-PCM). The model extends previous frameworks by incorporating a Sverdrup balance formulation for wind-driven Ekman transport, the first application of the Gent-McWilliams parameterisation of mesoscale eddies in a slab ocean model, and a spectrally and thickness-dependent treatment of sea ice and snow albedo. In aquaplanet simulations, enabling OHT produces substantial changes in both surface climate and atmospheric circulation, including cooler tropical sea surface temperatures, reduced sea ice, and the emergence of a double-banded equatorial precipitation pattern driven by Ekman-induced upwelling. The resulting OHT profiles show first-order agreement with fully coupled atmosphere-ocean GCMs. Applied to modern Earth, the model reproduces key large-scale climate properties, including a global mean surface temperature of 13°C (within 1°C of observations), planetary albedo of 0.32 (within 0.01), and sea ice extent with significantly reduced seasonal biases relative to simulations without OHT. Due to model parallelisation, these improvements are achieved at almost no additional computation cost compared to OHT-disabled simulations run over the same number of model years. This enables long integrations, making the model particularly well suited for exoplanet and paleoclimate studies where broad parameter exploration is essential.

title: Warring Contextualities -- Provably Classical vs Provably Nonclassical
generated_summary:
This paper reconciles two competing definitions of contextuality in quantum mechanics — Kochen-Specker contextuality and Spekkens' generalized noncontextuality — by establishing a clear hierarchy relating them to notions of classicality and nonclassicality. Rather than viewing these frameworks as rivals, the authors demonstrate they serve complementary roles at different levels of a classicality spectrum.

The methodology combines polytope-based geometric characterizations, simplex embeddability criteria, and Abramsky's sheaf-theoretic framework to formally prove implication relationships between the two notions of contextuality and Bell nonlocality. The authors define sufficient conditions for classicality based on assumptions including tomographic completeness and measurement-independence of outcomes.

The key result is a strict hierarchy of implications: classicality implies Spekkens noncontextuality, which implies Kochen-Specker noncontextuality, which implies Bell locality — with none of the converses holding in general. By contraposition, Bell nonlocality implies Kochen-Specker contextuality, which implies Spekkens contextuality, which implies nonclassicality. The authors further show that Kochen-Specker contextuality and Bell nonlocality share a common sheaf-theoretic structure, rooted in the inability to extend empirical models to global sections.

The significance lies in clarifying that Spekkens noncontextuality serves as a sufficient condition for a system being "provably classical," while Kochen-Specker contextuality provides a sufficient condition for being "provably nonclassical." original_abstract: In the literature, there are two differing definitions of contextuality: Kochen and Specker's, and Spekkens' (or ``generalised''). However, researchers using one of these definitions rarely consider the other, meaning comparative analysis of these two notions is rare. In this paper, we advance the idea that Kochen-Specker contextuality provides a generalisation of the idea of system being fundamentally nonclassical, while Spekkens' noncontextuality provides a generalisation of the idea of a system being classical. This allows us to reconcile the two approaches, as different stages in a hierarchy of classicality/nonclassicality.

title: The Damping and Instability of Ion-acoustic Waves in the Solar Wind: Solar Orbiter Observations
generated_summary:

The authors employ the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver (ALPS), which uniquely accepts measured velocity distribution functions (VDFs) rather than idealized bi-Maxwellian approximations, to solve the linear Vlasov-Maxwell dispersion relation. Proton and alpha-particle VDFs measured by Solar Orbiter's Proton-Alpha Sensor are processed using Gaussian mixture models and a "collar" method that preserves measured fine-scale velocity-space structures while extending coverage to unmeasured regions.

The key finding is that fine-scale structures in the measured proton VDF drive IA wave instability near the proton inertial scale, even when the electron-to-proton temperature ratio is near unity. This instability arises from two concurrent mechanisms: reduced proton Landau damping due to softened velocity gradients at the resonant phase speed, and enhanced energy transfer from protons to waves through the first-order cyclotron resonance. Wavelet coherence analysis of magnetic field and density fluctuations confirms anti-correlated signatures consistent with IA waves at the predicted unstable frequencies.

These results demonstrate that realistic VDF structures, often smoothed away by parametric models, fundamentally regulate compressive wave behavior in the solar wind, challenging conventional stability predictions based on bulk plasma parameters alone.
original_abstract: Observations of solar wind velocity distribution functions (VDFs) commonly reveal fine-scale structures. These features strongly influence kinetic processes such as wave damping and instability, yet their role remains poorly understood. We use a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) to separate proton and $α$-particle (fully ionized helium) VDFs from Solar Orbiter Proton and Alpha-particle Sensor (PAS) measurements, and assess how measured VDFs affect the damping of compressive fluctuations with the Arbitrary Linear Plasma Solver (ALPS). We analyze the dispersion relation and polarization properties of ion-acoustic (IA) waves in the solar wind. Protons and $α$-particles are represented by the measured VDFs derived from PAS observations. For comparison, we also perform calculations using the bi-Maxwellian assumption for the VDFs. Fine-scale structures of the measured proton VDFs reduce the damping rate of IA waves, even when $T_e \simeq T_i$. In some cases, we find that the measured VDFs drive the IA mode unstable, while the corresponding bi-Maxwellian representations predict strong damping. These results demonstrate that resolving the fine-scale structures of VDFs is essential for accurately capturing the kinetic physics of the solar wind.

title: Single Plane Spatial Mode Sorter
generated_summary:

The methodology involves constructing a sorter mask as a coherent superposition of the target spatial modes, each modulated by a unique spatial frequency to direct different modes to spatially separated detectors in the far field. The authors validate the approach through both numerical simulations and experiments using a spatial light modulator setup, testing across Hermite-Gaussian, Laguerre-Gaussian, and Bessel-Gaussian mode families.

Key results demonstrate an average sorting efficiency of 96.6% with only 2.7% cross-talk for four-mode configurations. The power transmission scales as O(M⁻¹) with the number of modes M, which the authors prove is optimal for a single-layer design. The sorter reduces to the well-known fork grating for OAM modes, confirming its generality. It also exhibits robustness to phase noise and can function as a mode generator when operated in reverse.

The method offers a practical alternative for applications requiring moderate mode counts, including quantum key distribution, spatial-division multiplexing, and spectroscopy, where simplicity and signal fidelity are prioritized over power efficiency.
original_abstract: A mode sorter separates a set of M orthogonal spatial modes in a shared input channel into M different output channels. Here we present an analytic derivation and experimental validation of a single plane device for sorting spatial modes from a diverse variety of mode families, including Hermite-Gaussian (HG), Laguerre-Gaussian (LG), Bessel-Gaussian (BG), with almost no cross-talk. This sorting capability is required for a wide range of applications that employ classical or quantum light. We also show that applying this design in order to sort a set of Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) modes with zero radial index reproduces the well-known Fork grating configuration. Furthermore, by taking the limit of M -> inf, we present an analytical expression for sorting all the modes of a given family. By operating this device in reverse, it can be used to generate arbitrary modes, by illuminating it with a Gaussian beam. The power transmission coefficient for this sorter goes as 1/M and we provide a mathematical proof that this is optimal for any typical arrangement of the detector positions. We further study the sorter sensitivity to wavelength and random phase noise.

title: Configuration interaction extension of AGP for incorporating inter-geminal correlations
generated_summary:

The key methodological innovation is the application of border-rank approximations to these AGP-CI polynomials, yielding compact AGP-CIε representations that reduce the number of required AGP terms from O(n) to O(1), where n is the number of electron pairs. This is achieved by expressing AGP-CI monomials as finite-difference combinations of pure n-th powers using a small deformation parameter ε, enabling efficient evaluation through the existing Onishi formula machinery for LC-AGP overlaps and Hamiltonian matrix elements.

Applications to the Hubbard model and small molecules (H₂O, N₂) demonstrate that AGP-CIε maintains high accuracy as system size increases, unlike LC-AGP, which deteriorates significantly in strongly correlated regimes. For the strongly correlated Hubbard model at U/t=10, AGP-CIε shows stable accuracy with increasing electron number, while LC-AGP requires rapidly growing numbers of AGP components. For the N₂ molecule, AGP-CITε achieves high accuracy where LC-AGP with comparable or more AGP terms fails, likely due to LC-AGP becoming trapped in local minima. The approach offers systematic improvability through CI expansion levels while maintaining computational tractability, providing an effective bridge between AGP and the exponentially costly antisymmetrized product of geminals.
original_abstract: In this paper, we develop a class of antisymmetrized geminal power configuration interaction (AGP-CI) wave functions that extend the AGP framework by incorporating inter-geminal correlations through a CI expansion. To make these wavefunctions computationally tractable, we evaluate them by rewriting the AGP-CI ansatz as a linear combination of AGPs (LC-AGP), for which overlaps and Hamiltonian matrix elements can be computed with standard AGP machinery. Motivated by border-rank decompositions, we further reorganize this ansatz into a compact linear combination of AGPs depending on a small deformation parameter $τ$, which controls how closely the truncated expansion approximates the full AGP-CI state. Benchmark applications to the Hubbard model and to the small molecules H$_2$O and N$_2$ demonstrate that the proposed wavefunctions achieve consistently high accuracy and outperform the LC-AGP, particularly for systems with more electrons and in strongly correlated regimes.

title: Distributional Inverse Homogenization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces "distributional inverse homogenization," a framework for inferring the statistical properties of material microstructure from collections of macroscopic (bulk) mechanical measurements. While recovering a unique microstructure from bulk properties is severely ill-posed—since many different microstructures can yield the same macroscopic response—the authors demonstrate that recovering the *statistics* of microstructure is a well-posed and tractable problem.

The methodology employs a generative modeling approach: a parametric statistical model produces random microstructures controlled by physically interpretable parameters (e.g., volume fractions, constituent material properties, geometric features). These generated microstructures are mapped to bulk properties via homogenization theory, producing a predicted distribution on macroscopic measurements. The model parameters are then calibrated by minimizing the sliced-Wasserstein distance between this predicted distribution and the empirical distribution of observed bulk measurements. The framework is developed for both periodic and stochastic homogenization settings.

Key results include successful recovery of microstructural statistics in one-dimensional analytical settings and two-dimensional Voronoi microstructure experiments. For stochastic homogenization, the authors develop a novel concurrent surrogate learning strategy that makes the computationally expensive forward solves tractable. They also construct locally periodic and locally stationary-ergodic models that exploit natural spatial variability within single material specimens.

The significance lies in enabling non-invasive statistical characterization of microstructure—relevant to quality control in steel manufacturing, composite materials, concrete, and other applications—using only macroscopic mechanical measurements, without requiring microscopy or other intrusive techniques.
original_abstract: For many materials, macroscopic mechanical behavior is determined by an intricate microstructure. Understanding the relation between these two scales helps scientists and engineers design better materials. The relation which maps microstructure to bulk mechanical properties can be understood via the well-established theory of homogenization. However inverting the homogenization process, to recover microstructural information from measured macroscopic properties, is fraught with difficulties because of the averaging processes that underlie homogenization. Therefore, scientists and engineers usually need recourse to more invasive, often highly localized, investigations to learn about a microstructure. In this work, we develop a noninvasive methodology by which one can leverage large collections of measured bulk mechanical properties to learn information about the statistics of microstructure at a global level. We call this, distributional inverse homogenization. We study this problem in one and two dimensions, considering both periodic and stochastic homogenization. We demonstrate the methodology in the context of 2D Voronoi constructions and underpin the observed empirical success with theory in 1D. We also show how the natural spatial variability of microstructure can be exploited to gather data that enables distributional inversion. And we concurrently learn a surrogate model, approximating the homogenization map, that accelerates the resulting computations in this setting. The work formulates a new class of inverse problems, bridging ideas from probability and homogenization to facilitate the learning of microstructural material variability from macroscopic measurements.

title: Finding and characterising physical states of Euclidean Abelianized loop quantum gravity using neural quantum states
generated_summary:
This paper investigates physical states of 4-dimensional Euclidean loop quantum gravity in Smolin's weak coupling limit, where the SU(2) gauge group is replaced by an Abelian U(1)³ structure. The authors employ neural network quantum states combined with variational Monte Carlo methods to find and characterize near-kernel states of quadratic Hamiltonian constraints on the complete K₅ graph—the boundary graph of a 4-simplex—with truncated charge representations.

The central finding is that operator ordering in the quadratic constraint is physically consequential, not merely a technical choice. Two orderings generically produce distinct solution families with sharply different properties. Type-A solutions (standard ordering) exhibit non-degenerate volume, flatness on minimal loops, weak long-range correlations, and approximate isotropy consistent with a Dittrich-Geiller vacuum sector. Type-B solutions (alternative ordering) display exact volume degeneracy, non-trivial curvature, strong adjacency-enhanced correlations, and characteristics resembling the Ashtekar-Lewandowski vacuum sector. A symmetrized constraint with auxiliary regularizers produces interpolating quasi-solutions combining features of both families.

The methodology demonstrates remarkable compression efficiency, with network parameters constituting a vanishingly small fraction of the exponentially growing Hilbert space dimension, enabling simulations at cutoffs up to 100. This work establishes variational methods as a practical framework for exploring constraint solutions and their geometric content in loop quantum gravity, providing scalable tools applicable to the full SU(2) theory.
original_abstract: We study physical (near-kernel of constraints) states of 4-d Euclidean loop quantum gravity in Smolin's weak coupling limit on the complete graph $K_5$ using variational Monte Carlo with neural network quantum states. We investigate the Hamilton constraint $\hat{H}$ in the ordering proposed by Thiemann, as well as $\hat{H}^\dagger$ and $\hat{H}+\hat{H}^\dagger$. We find that the variational optimisation selects distinct solution families for $\hat{H}$ and $\hat{H}^\dagger$ across several considered cutoffs on the kinematical degrees of freedom. The solution family of $\hat{H}$ is flat on all minimal loops and has non-vanishing volume expectation values. Its edge-charge marginals delocalise with increasing cutoff, which indicates they are approximations to solutions that are non-normalisable in the kinematical inner product. The solution family for $\hat{H}^\dagger$ is normalisable, shows non-trivial charge correlations, lies in the kernel of volume and is not flat. $\hat{H}+\hat{H}^\dagger$ turns out to be much harder to solve and yields quasi-solutions combining features of both previous families. We characterise all solutions using chromaticity 1- and 2-point functions, minimal loop holonomies, geometric area and volume observables and show that the two families can be interpreted as, on the one hand, a family of states close to the Ashtekar-Lewandowski vacuum and the Dittrich-Geiller vacuum with some numerical noise on the other hand. We also present some results that link solutions of the truncated theory to solutions of the continuum theory.

title: Nonmonotonic percolation threshold in correlated networks and hypergraphs
generated_summary:
This study investigates how degree-degree correlations affect the robustness of complex networks and hypergraphs under random node percolation, revealing that the relationship between assortativity and resilience is more nuanced than previously understood. The authors employ generating function techniques and large-scale stochastic simulations to analyze percolation thresholds in trimodal networks (where nodes take one of three possible degree values), networks with Poisson and power-law degree distributions, and hypergraphs with hyperdegree-cardinality correlations.

For dyadic networks, the results confirm that assortative networks are generally more robust than disassortative ones. However, the authors discover that the percolation threshold exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on the Pearson assortativity coefficient in the disassortative regime: maximally disassortative networks are not necessarily the most fragile, and intermediate negative correlations can yield the highest percolation thresholds. This challenges the conventional assumption that robustness decreases monotonically with decreasing assortativity. For hypergraphs, the role of correlations is qualitatively reversed—assortative correlations increase fragility while disassortative configurations enhance robustness. The nonmonotonic behavior in hypergraphs occurs in the assortative regime, where intermediate positive correlations produce the most fragile configurations.

These findings demonstrate that the scalar assortativity coefficient alone is insufficient to predict network resilience, highlighting the need for more detailed characterizations of correlation structure when designing robust networked systems.
original_abstract: We study the effect of assortative and disassortative mixing on the robustness of networks under random node failures. For ordinary (dyadic) networks, by using the generating function technique and stochastic simulations, we show that the relationship between the Pearson assortativity coefficient $r$ and the percolation threshold $p_c$ is not always monotonic. More specifically, in certain regions of the parameter space of our model, moderately disassortative networks can be more fragile than either strongly disassortative or uncorrelated networks. We observe this nonmonotonic behavior for trimodal networks as well as for networks with Poisson and power-law degree distributions. We then extend our analysis to hypergraphs with correlations between node hyperdegree and hyperedge cardinality. For this case, we find that positively correlated hypergraphs tend to be more fragile than negatively correlated ones. Additionally, as in the dyadic case, the relationship between $r$ and $p_c$ is nonmonotonic, and the most fragile configuration does not correspond to the most assortative hypergraph.

title: Observation of light production by charged particles in WLS fibers
generated_summary:
This paper reports the first systematic observation and quantification of light produced directly by charged particles in wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers, a phenomenon traditionally neglected in detector simulations. The authors demonstrate that this light production is non-negligible and should be accounted for in Monte Carlo simulations of particle physics detectors.

The investigation began with observations during prototype tests at a 730 MeV/c pion beam, where Kuraray Y11(200) WLS fibers not connected to scintillators produced clear signals of approximately 3 photoelectrons. To quantify the effect more precisely, the authors conducted dedicated measurements using a strontium-90 radioactive source with three fiber types — Y11 WLS fibers, Bicron BCF-12 scintillating fibers, and Bicron BCF-98 clear fibers — read out by silicon photomultipliers at crossing angles of 45°, 90°, and 135°.

Key results show that the light yield in Y11 WLS fibers reaches approximately 23±2% of that in BCF-12 scintillating fibers, a surprisingly substantial fraction. No significant difference was found between Y11(200)MSJ and Y11(200)MS fiber variants. The clear fiber produced practically no scintillation light, though Cherenkov radiation was clearly observed at the 45° crossing angle. The Cherenkov contribution to WLS fiber signals is difficult to isolate since absorption and re-emission by the fiber dyes destroys the directional information.

These findings are significant for detectors requiring good energy or time resolution, where the direct WLS fiber light contribution could meaningfully affect performance if not properly simulated.
original_abstract: Wavelength shifting (WLS) fibers are widely used in particle physics for light collection from scintillators. Light production by charged particles directly in WLS fibers is traditionally ignored. In this study, light produced by charged particles in WLS fibers is clearly observed. The light yield of different batches of Y11(200) 1 mm diameter WLS fibers is as large as 23 $\pm$ 2% with respect to the light yield of the Bicron BCF-12 1 mm diameter scintillating fiber. In clear fibers of the same diameter, no scintillation light is produced, while Cherenkov light is clearly seen at the 45-degree crossing angle. The observed amount of light produced by charged particles in the WLS fibers is not small and should be taken into account in advanced detector simulations.

title: Demanding peer review is associated with higher impact in published science
generated_summary:
This study investigates whether demanding peer review is associated with higher scientific impact among published papers. The authors analyze the full peer review correspondence of 8,000 Nature Communications papers published between 2017 and 2024, using large language models to extract structured, issue-level comment-response pairs from unstructured review text. Seven dimensions of reviewer-author interaction are measured: opinion strength, constructiveness, comment quality, revision cost, opinion type, author response type, and persuasion success. The extraction pipeline is validated through cross-model consistency checks, keyword-based validation, and expert comparisons.

The central finding challenges the intuition that high-quality papers pass smoothly through review. Instead, papers with greater later citation impact receive stronger criticism, higher-quality comments, and require more extensive revision. These associations are strongest when scrutiny targets core claims—novelty, conceptual framing, and interpretation—rather than peripheral presentation issues. Among papers with three first-round reviewers, stronger review is associated with more reviewer disagreement, and rebuttal becomes more likely as disagreement increases. Broad author-team characteristics explain little variation in review substance, consistent with a relatively impartial process, while disciplinary differences manifest more in review style than length.

These findings suggest peer review functions not merely as a gatekeeping filter but as a substantive interactional process through which influential scientific claims are challenged, negotiated, and refined, with implications for editorial practices and review policy design.
original_abstract: Peer review shapes which scientific claims enter the published record, but its internal dynamics are hard to measure at scale because reviewer criticism and author revision are usually embedded in long, unstructured correspondence. Here we use a fixed-prompt large language model pipeline to convert the review correspondence of \textit{Nature Communications} papers published from 2017 to 2024 into structured reviewer--author interactions. We find that review pressure is concentrated in the first round and focused disproportionately on core claims rather than peripheral presentation. Higher average opinion strength is also associated with more reviewer disagreement, while review patterns vary little with broad team attributes, consistent with relatively impartial evaluation. Contrary to the intuition that stronger papers should pass review more smoothly, with greater reviewer--author agreement and less extensive revision, we find that stronger criticism, higher-quality comments, and greater revision burden are associated with higher later citation impact within accepted papers. We finally show that fields differ more in review style than in review length, pointing to disciplinary variation in how criticism is negotiated and resolved. These findings position open peer review not just as a gatekeeping mechanism but as a measurable record of how influential scientific claims are challenged, defended, and revised before entering the published record.

title: Parity-mixing interference in laser-assisted photoionization
generated_summary:
This study investigates parity-mixing interference effects in laser-assisted photoionization of helium, identifying and characterizing four distinct quantum interference pathways that arise when broad harmonics and few-cycle dressing fields are employed in attosecond measurements.

The experiment uses an Optical Parametric Chirped Pulse Amplification system delivering few-cycle (~6 fs) pulses at 830 nm with stabilized carrier-envelope phase. High-order harmonics generated in argon ionize helium atoms in the presence of an infrared probe field, while a reaction microscope provides three-dimensional electron momentum detection. The broad spectral bandwidth of the harmonics enables spectral overlap between main photoelectron bands and sidebands, which is essential for observing parity-mixing interference — interference between quantum paths leading to final states of different parity.

Through Fourier analysis of delay-dependent photoelectron oscillations, the authors spectrally distinguish four quantum pathways: two "intra-harmonic" paths involving the same harmonic and two "inter-harmonic" paths involving consecutive harmonics. A perturbation theory formalism reveals that pathways involving absorption versus emission of a probe photon are out of phase, leading to destructive interference when they spectrally overlap. Experimental results are validated by time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations.

The amplitude and phase of these parity-mixing interferences encode information about both the light fields and photoionization dynamics. With improved spectral resolution, this approach could enable complete reconstruction of XUV and infrared fields alongside detailed characterization of laser-assisted photoionization dynamics, including continuum-continuum transitions.
original_abstract: Photoionization of atoms by high-order harmonics in the presence of a laser may lead to quantum interference from which information about the photoionization dynamics or the light fields can be extracted. Traditionally, this interference arises from two-photon transitions involving the absorption of consecutive harmonics combined with the absorption and stimulated emission of a laser photon. In this process, parity is conserved. Here, we investigate interference between one- and two-photon transitions in helium using high-order harmonics generated by a few-cycle laser and three-dimensional electron detection. In this case, parity is not conserved. We identify four parity-mixing interference pathways, involving two different harmonic fields or a single harmonic, together with absorption or emission of a probe photon.

title: Mirror Surface Evaluation for the Einstein Telescope Using Virtual Mirror Maps
generated_summary:
This paper presents a framework for generating virtual mirror maps (VMMs)—synthetic digital representations of mirror surfaces—to evaluate optical performance requirements for the Einstein Telescope (ET), a proposed next-generation gravitational-wave detector whose mirrors have not yet been fabricated.

The authors develop three complementary VMM generation methods: Zernike polynomial reconstruction (capturing low-spatial-frequency structure), FFT-based synthesis (reproducing high-frequency content from measured power spectral densities), and a hybrid approach combining both. These methods are validated against measured mirror surface data from Advanced Virgo Plus (AdVirgo+), serving as a realistic baseline. The framework also introduces a scaling procedure to extrapolate maps to ET's larger mirror diameters. Additionally, the authors compare two preprocessing techniques for removing low-order distortions (piston, tilt, curvature) from mirror maps, finding that a Hermite-Gauss mode-based method is more physically appropriate than Zernike polynomial subtraction, as it weights distortions by the carrier beam intensity profile.

Key results show that the hybrid method provides the most accurate reproduction of reference mirror spatial statistics and optical losses across all spatial frequencies, while Zernike-only maps underestimate high-frequency content and FFT-only maps deviate at low frequencies. Statistical ensembles of one thousand maps per method demonstrate stable and realistic carrier-mode power losses for ET-scale simulations.

This framework provides a practical, quantitative tool for developing and testing mirror surface specifications during ET's design phase, enabling systematic exploration of fabrication tolerances before manufacturing begins.
original_abstract: The performance of mirrors in optical interferometers is critically influenced by their surface quality. Accurate metrology enables mirror surfaces to be characterized through phase maps describing their three-dimensional structure after coating. In this work, we combine Zernike polynomial decomposition and spatial frequency (PSD) analysis with numerical optical simulations to quantify the impact of surface distortions on the reflected optical field. The method is validated using metrology data from mirrors currently installed in the Advanced Virgo gravitational-wave detector. Building on this validation, we introduce a framework for generating realistic virtual mirror maps that reproduce both low order aberrations and high spatial frequency content of measured surfaces. These virtual maps are used in optical simulations to systematically explore and compare candidate surface quality specifications for future detectors, with particular focus on the Einstein Telescope. Our results show that metrology-informed virtual mirrors provide a practical design tool to assess the impact of different surface specifications on optical performance, and to relate future requirements to the performance of existing interferometers.

title: Redefining the limits of real-time noise cancellation in optical fiber links
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a technique to surpass the previously accepted fundamental limit on real-time noise cancellation in optical fiber links. The authors develop a framework based on temporal correlations between round-trip and one-way fiber noise, showing that the optimal correction signal requires a temporal advance determined by the spatial "center of mass" of the noise distribution along the fiber.

The methodology involves digitally weighting and adding delayed copies of the correction signal to achieve an effective temporal advance of the round-trip noise measurement. This is implemented using an FPGA-based digital servo that stores the correction signal history and applies parameterized weighting controlled by a single variable α. The scheme requires only minor digital signal processing modifications to standard fiber noise cancellation setups.

The authors demonstrate their technique on two systems: a 5.5 km deployed urban fiber in Boulder, Colorado, and an 8.8 km lab-based fiber with adjustable noise distribution. For spatially uniform noise (α = 1/2), they achieve approximately 6 dB improvement in phase noise over the standard limit. For localized noise sources, where α is matched to the fractional noise position, they demonstrate over 10 dB improvement.

This work has significant implications for ultrastable frequency dissemination, optical clock comparisons, and quantum networking. The technique's adaptability—allowing real-time tuning of α based on changing noise distributions—makes it particularly valuable for practical fiber links with aerial sections or other localized noise sources.
original_abstract: A broad and growing array of applications rely on the faithful transmission of ultrastable optical signals over noisy paths, requiring cancellation of environmentally induced noise. A generally accepted limit constrains how well the path length noise can be suppressed in real time. Here, we show that this standard limit is not fundamental and can be improved upon. By considering the temporal correlations between the round-trip and one-way signals, we develop a new framework for optimizing the noise cancellation feedback signal for any spatial distribution of noise along the signal path. We use this framework to surpass the standard limit in two sets of experiments. First, we demonstrate noise cancellation in a deployed urban optical fiber, where we achieve noise suppression approximately 6 dB beyond the standard limit. Then, in a reconfigurable lab-based fiber-optic testbed, we show that, for certain spatial distributions of noise, suppression of well over 10 dB beyond the standard limit is readily achievable. With the use of digital signal processing to generate the correction signal, our new technique requires no new electro-optic hardware relative to the field-standard noise cancellation scheme. This will allow for widespread adoption of these improved limits in existing systems, with applications in optical clock distribution, optical clock comparisons for fundamental physics and geodesy, and quantum networking.

title: A generative model for bipartite gene-sharing networks
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the first generative model for bipartite gene-sharing networks, which jointly captures the evolution of genome sizes and gene family sizes in viruses and prokaryotic pangenomes. The bipartite network framework connects genomes to gene families, preserving complete information about gene-sharing patterns across organisms.

The model incorporates four fundamental evolutionary processes: horizontal gene transfer (with probability proportional to gene abundance), functional innovation (capture of new genes), organismal innovation (emergence of new genomes), and gene loss. With only two free parameters—the probability of new gene capture and the probability of new genome emergence—the model recovers the empirical degree distributions observed in real viral gene-sharing networks, including power-law distributions for gene degrees and exponential-like distributions for genome degrees.

Analytical expressions for asymptotic degree distributions are derived under a no-gene-loss assumption, and numerical simulations confirm these approximations hold even for finite, transient networks. A key finding is that gene gain must dominate over gene loss to reproduce observed network properties, fundamentally distinguishing viral and pangenome evolution from individual prokaryotic genome evolution, where gene loss typically predominates. The model successfully fits networks of RNA viruses, DNA viruses, and prokaryotic pangenomes, with fitted parameters reflecting known biological differences among these systems. However, the model does not capture phylogenetic correlations, leaving the reconciliation of network structure with tree-like evolution as an important open challenge.
original_abstract: Gene-sharing networks provide a powerful framework to study the evolution of viruses and mobile genetic elements. These bipartite networks, which link genes to the genomes that contain them, exhibit characteristic degree distributions: a scale-free distribution for genes and an exponential-like decay for genomes. Here, we propose a mechanistic model that explains these patterns through fundamental evolutionary processes including horizontal gene transfer, capture of new genes, emergence of new genomes, and gene loss. Using a mean-field approximation, we derive analytical expressions for the asymptotic gene and genome degree distributions, recapitulating a power-law distribution for genes and an exponential distribution for genomes. Numerical simulations validate these predictions and yield parameter values that closely fit empirical data from dsDNA viruses, RNA viruses, and prokaryotic pangenomes. This simple model with only two parameters provides a generative framework for bipartite gene-sharing networks, offering qualitative and quantitative insights into the main evolutionary forces driving genome plasticity. Setting the gene loss rate to zero, the gene and genome degree distributions of the model closely fit the empirically observed distributions. Thus, evolution of viruses appears to be dominated by gene gain, in agreement with the results of independent reconstructions of viral evolution.

title: Symmetry-protected coexistence of a nodal surface and multiple types of Weyl fermions in $P6_3$-$\text{B}_{30}$

This study identifies P6₃-B₃₀, a light-element boron allotrope, as a multidimensional hybrid topological semimetal that simultaneously hosts a symmetry-protected nodal surface and multiple types of Weyl fermions within a single material. Unlike previous proposals that rely on heavy-element or transition-metal compounds, this work demonstrates that such rich topological physics can emerge in a simple, light-element system without spin-orbit coupling.

Using first-principles density functional theory calculations, the authors establish the dynamic, thermodynamic, and mechanical stability of P6₃-B₃₀ through phonon dispersion analysis, ab initio molecular dynamics simulations, and elastic constant evaluation. Topological properties are characterized via Wannier function-based tight-binding models, Berry curvature calculations, and surface Green's function methods.

The key findings reveal three distinct topological features coexisting in momentum space: a two-dimensional nodal surface pinned to the k_z = π plane enforced by non-symmorphic screw rotation symmetry combined with time-reversal symmetry; Type-I Weyl points at K and K′ with Chern number C = −1; Type-II Weyl points along H-K with C = +1; and an unconventional double-Weyl point at Γ with C = −2 exhibiting quadratic in-plane dispersion. These topological objects are well separated in momentum and energy space, producing clean Fermi arc signatures on the (100) surface that faithfully reflect the bulk topological charges. This material provides a pristine platform for investigating interplay between topological objects of different dimensionalities.
original_abstract: The coexistence of topological states with different dimensionalities in a single crystalline system offers a unique platform to study the interplay of distinct fermionic excitations. Here, integrating first-principles calculations with symmetry analysis, we propose the three-dimensional boron allotrope $P6_3$-$\text{B}_{30}$ as an ideal, structurally stable candidate for exploring multidimensional topological physics. Benefiting from the practically negligible spin-orbit coupling of the light-element framework, $P6_3$-$\text{B}_{30}$ operates as a pristine spinless topological semimetal. We show that the combined time-reversal and twofold screw symmetry ($\mathcal{T}S_{2z}$) enforces a robust two-dimensional nodal surface on the $k_z = π$ plane via a Kramers-like degeneracy. Concurrently, the system hosts a diverse set of zero-dimensional Weyl fermions -- including an unconventional double-Weyl point ($\mathcal{C} = -2$), conventional Type-I WPs ($\mathcal{C} = -1$), and completely tilted Type-II WPs ($\mathcal{C} = +1$) -- emerging at the high-symmetry points $Γ$ and K, as well as along the H-K path, protected by $C_6$ and $C_3$ crystalline rotational symmetries. Crucially, the substantial momentum-space separation between the nodal surface and Weyl points allows for their unambiguous independent resolution. Calculations of the (100) surface states reveal distinct, nontrivial Fermi arcs connecting Weyl nodes of opposite chirality. This work establishes $P6_3$-$\text{B}_{30}$ as a compelling material platform for investigating the physics of multidimensional hybrid topological fermions and their interplay.

title: Three-dimensional photon transport in spinodal photocatalytic aerogels: how bicontinuous morphology controls kinetic rate constants

original_abstract: Porous monolithic photocatalysts based on anatase TiO2 in silica aerogels are promising for air purification. Their bicontinuous spinodal architecture offers high surface area and strong light scattering. However, extracting intrinsic kinetic rates requires accurate optical models. Current methods replace the complex 3D pore network with a homogeneous 1D slab, an approximation whose error is unknown for spinodal geometries. We combine 3D spinodal masks from Cahn-Hilliard simulations with GPU Monte Carlo photon transport to quantify this. We introduce a solid-phase fluence estimator that accounts for catalytic site distribution, comparing it to volume averages and diffusion approximations. The solid phase receives 50% more photons than volume averages at porosity 0.70, rising to 70% at 0.90. This preferential illumination stems from quasi-ballistic paths through pore channels, termed photon channelling. The extracted kinetic descriptor differs by 34% between 3D Monte Carlo and diffusion models. Homogeneous controls show that roughly 50% of the total 73% discrepancy is intrinsic to the bicontinuous structure and cannot be fixed by effective medium theories. These results provide the first quantitative correction for kinetic extraction in such photocatalysts and establish design rules linking synthesis coarsening, pore size, and light efficiency.

title: Nested Fourier-enhanced neural operator for efficient modeling of radiation transfer in fires

The methodology builds upon the MIONet architecture by integrating Fourier layers that capture multi-scale and high-frequency features characteristic of turbulent fires. For 3D simulations utilizing locally refined meshes, a nested architecture processes four refinement levels sequentially in a coarse-to-fine manner, with each level's prediction conditioning the next. The framework is validated on 2D pool fires and 3D McCaffrey fires with both fixed and variable heat release rates (HRRs). Fourier-MIONet achieves L² relative errors of 3.70% for radiative intensity in the 2D case. For 3D cases, the Large model achieves global errors around 1-4% across HRRs from 14 to 58 kW. Inference times range from 0.012 to 0.044 seconds on a GPU, compared to 0.10-0.24 seconds for conventional solvers on multiple CPU cores.

original_abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has become an essential tool for predicting fire behavior, yet maintaining both efficiency and accuracy remains challenging. A major source of computational cost in fire simulations is the modeling of radiation transfer, which is usually the dominant heat transfer mechanism in fires. Solving the high-dimensional radiative transfer equation (RTE) with traditional numerical methods can be a performance bottleneck. Here, we present a machine learning framework based on Fourier-enhanced multiple-input neural operators (Fourier-MIONet) as an efficient alternative to direct numerical integration of the RTE. We first investigate the performance of neural operator architectures for a small-scale 2D pool fire and find that Fourier-MIONet provides the most accurate radiative solution predictions. The approach is then extended to 3D CFD fire simulations, where the computational mesh is locally refined across multiple levels. In these high-resolution settings, monolithic surrogate models for direct field-to-field mapping become difficult to train and computationally inefficient. To address this issue, a nested Fourier-MIONet is proposed to predict radiation solutions across multiple mesh-refinement levels. We validate the approach on 3D McCaffrey pool fires simulated with FireFOAM, including fixed fire sizes and a unified model trained over a continuous range of heat release rates (HRRs). The proposed method achieves global relative errors of 2-4% for 3D varying-HRR scenarios while providing faster inference than the estimated cost of one finite-volume radiation solve in FireFOAM for the 16-solid-angle case. With fast and accurate inference, the surrogate makes higher-fidelity radiation treatments practical and enables the incorporation of more spectrally resolved radiation models into CFD fire simulations for engineering applications.

title: Contrasting ultrafast light-driven electron-hole interaction dynamics in monolayer MoS$_2$ and metallic NbSe$_2$
