By integrating over these fast microscopic cycles, they derive macroscopic mean-field dynamical equations for cisternal sizes, where the fusion-fission flux kernels naturally embed size-dependent negative feedback control.

The analysis reveals a rich nonequilibrium phase diagram parameterized by fusion-fission rates and influx. For a single cisterna, the system exhibits vesicle, stable cisterna, and unbounded growth phases separated by saddle-node bifurcations. For two coupled cisternae, additional phases emerge, including limit cycle oscillations with definite phase relations. Crucially, the authors identify stable fixed-point solutions with vesicular transport, and out-of-phase oscillatory solutions with cisternal progression—demonstrating that these historically competing models of Golgi organization are distinct phenotypic outcomes within the same physical framework, occupying different regions of the phase diagram.

The authors further analyze dynamical responses to perturbations, entrainment with cell-cycle-periodic driving (producing Arnold tongues), and robustness to both intrinsic and extrinsic noise using Fokker-Planck analysis and Gillespie simulations. This work provides a unifying quantitative theory with testable predictions for organelle assembly and homeostasis in living cells.
original_abstract: Organelle patterning and its heritability remain central mysteries in cell biology, highlighting the fundamental tension between genetic inheritance and self-assembly. Here, we explore the nonequilibrium assembly and size control of the Golgi complex and endosomes, amid a continuous flux of membrane traffic, within a stochastic framework of mechanochemical fusion-fission cycles that violate detailed balance. Using a dynamical systems approach, we identify distinct, robust regimes, ranging from fixed points to limit cycles with definite phase relations. We identify these dynamical regimes with diverse phenotypes, from stable cisternae to periodic, cell-cycle-dependent dissolution/reassembly to cisternal progression. We analyse its dynamic response to systematic perturbations or driving protocols and make definite predictions that may be tested experimentally. Our analysis reveals that the two competing models of Golgi organization-vesicular transport and cisternal progression - are, in fact, two phases of the same underlying nonequilibrium process. Finally, our framework offers a strategy for controlling cisternal chemical identity and number and by modulating the interplay between glycosylation enzymes and membrane fission-fusion dynamics.

title: Efficient Implementation of Relativistic Coupled Cluster Linear Response Theory in Combination with Perturbation Sensitive Natural Spinors and Cholesky Decomposition Treatment of Two-electron Integrals
generated_summary:
This paper presents an efficient implementation of relativistic linear-response coupled-cluster singles and doubles (LR-CCSD) theory for computing static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities of systems containing heavy elements. The approach combines three key computational strategies: exact two-component Hamiltonians (X2CAMF and X2CMP) to reduce the cost of four-component relativistic calculations, perturbation-sensitive natural spinors (FNS++) to truncate the virtual orbital space, and Cholesky decomposition (CD) to compress two-electron integral storage.

The FNS++ scheme constructs natural spinors from second-order perturbed densities rather than ground-state MP2 densities, capturing response-relevant correlation effects. This enables aggressive virtual space truncation—removing approximately 73% of virtual spinors on average—while maintaining accuracy within 0.02 atomic units of four-component reference polarizabilities across diverse molecular systems. In contrast, conventional frozen natural spinors (FNS) require nearly the full virtual space for comparable accuracy.

Benchmark calculations on Group IIB atoms, hydrogen halides, dihalogens, gold compounds, and UF₆ demonstrate excellent agreement with four-component reference values and experimental data. The combined FNS++/CD approach achieves approximately 15-fold computational speedup over canonical calculations, with substantial memory savings. The successful application to UF₆, yielding a static polarizability of 55.8 a.u. in good agreement with experiment (54.4 ± 7.0 a.u.), demonstrates the method's applicability to large, strongly relativistic molecular systems that were previously computationally prohibitive.
original_abstract: We present an efficient implementation of the low-cost linear-response coupled-cluster singles and doubles (LR-CCSD) method for computing static and frequency-dependent polarizabilities in systems with significant relativistic and electron-correlation effects. The approach employs X2C-based Hamiltonians (X2CAMF and X2CMP) and incorporates Cholesky decomposition to reduce memory requirements. In the current implementation, costly three- and four-external index integrals are generated on the fly, eliminating the need for their storage. Benchmark results indicate that the X2CMP Hamiltonian provides more consistent performance than X2CAMF, particularly for large and highly augmented basis sets. The proposed FNS++CD-X2CMP-LR-CCSD method shows excellent agreement with four-component reference values across a wide range of systems. Additionally, different strategies for constructing the FNS++ basis were assessed, and an averaged density approach was found to offer a favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. On average, about 73% of the virtual spinor space is removed, demonstrating the efficiency and consistency of the FNS++ density-based truncation approach. The present implementation enables accurate and scalable relativistic response calculations for large molecular systems, as demonstrated by the calculation of the static polarizability of the Uranium Hexafluoride complex with a triple-zeta basis set more than 1400 basis functions.

title: Noise factor of Brillouin amplifiers
generated_summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical framework for calculating the noise factor of Brillouin optical amplifiers, extending beyond the commonly used non-propagating phonon (NPP) approximation to account for phonon spatial propagation. Using a traveling-wave Hamiltonian model that captures photon-phonon interactions, Heisenberg-Langevin equations of motion are derived for the coupled optical and acoustic fields, incorporating thermal-mechanical Langevin noise sources consistent with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem.

Under the NPP approximation—valid when phonon decay rates are large—the authors recover the established noise factor result of F ≈ 1 + n_th (where n_th is the thermal phonon occupation number) in the high-gain limit, consistent with prior experimental measurements. However, when phonon propagation is significant, as occurs in emerging Brillouin photonic systems, the analysis reveals markedly different behavior. For both forward intermodal and backward Brillouin scattering configurations, the noise factor can be substantially lower than the NPP prediction because thermal-mechanical noise experiences a shorter effective interaction length than the coherent signal.

The results are explored across nondimensionalized parameters capturing phonon decay, single-pass gain, and optical loss, revealing distinct noise characteristics between forward and backward scattering geometries. This work is particularly significant for the growing class of Brillouin systems—including those utilizing acoustoelectric tuning of phonon propagation—whose parameters fall outside the NPP regime, providing essential design guidance for low-noise Brillouin amplifiers and signal processing technologies.
original_abstract: Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS), an optical nonlinearity arising from photon-phonon interactions, has formed the basis for a large class of optical signal processing devices, including Brillouin amplifiers. A limiting factor of such amplifiers is the noise due to thermal-mechanical fluctuations that the phonons imprint on the optical signal. Prior work has either inferred or experimentally observed a noise factor ($F$) that depends only on the thermal occupation of the phonons ($F\approx 1+n_{th}$). We show that this noise factor results naturally from a Hamiltonian-based spatio-temporal coupled mode treatment in the limit of large Brillouin amplification and when phonon propagation is neglected. Moreover, this theoretical framework allows us to extend our treatment to a much larger and more representative parameter space for emerging SBS systems; specifically, this analysis accounts for the forward or backward nature of the scattering process and the effects of phonon propagation, optical loss, and small Brillouin gains. Our results demonstrate that the noise factor can deviate radically from $F\approx 1+n_{th}$ for a host of modern SBS devices, especially those in which phonon propagation significantly changes the coupled mode dynamics.

title: Neuron Surface Emitting Laser (NeuronSEL): Spiking Regimes and Negative Differential Resistance in Solitary Multi-junction VCSELs

The NeuronSEL's unique double-threshold characteristic around the NDR boundaries enables intrinsic XOR operation and temporal coincidence detection. Scalability is demonstrated through an emulated photonic spiking neural network comprising 20 time-multiplexed NeuronSEL nodes, achieving 94.83% accuracy on the Iris flower classification task. Compatibility with event-based vision sensors is also shown, establishing a native neuromorphic optical link.

The NeuronSEL represents a significant advance in neuromorphic photonics by combining VCSEL advantages—low cost, vertical emission, array scalability, and high efficiency—with inherent excitability, positioning it as a promising building block for large-scale spiking photonic processors and hybrid neuromorphic sensing architectures.
original_abstract: Neuromorphic photonics is emerging as a powerful platform for fast and efficient optical information processing and sensing. However, future brain-inspired photonic systems require compact and scalable light sources, capable of generating the neuro-mimetic optical signals needed for their operation. This work demonstrates a single-stack laser that delivers optical and electrical neural-like spiking emission under solitary operation. Termed the Neuron Surface-Emitting Laser (NeuronSEL), this compact, multi-junction Vertical-Cavity Surface Emitting Laser (VCSEL) exhibits non-linear Negative Differential Resistance (NDR), similar to that observed in memristive devices. Leveraging this NDR behaviour enables the novel demonstration of multiple neuronal features in the NeuronSEL including refractoriness and threshold-/integrate-and-fire dynamics. We demonstrate the NeuronSEL's behaviour as an optical spiking neuron and its ability to perform processing functions, such as coincidence detection and exclusive OR operations. Its scalability is illustrated by proposing a network based on an array of NeuronSELs, able to perform classification tasks. The NeuronSEL emerges as a strong candidate for practical and scalable neuromorphic photonic hardware, with potential impact across a range of applications in optical sensing, communications and computing technologies, whilst benefitting from the inherent advantages of VCSEL technology -low manufacturing cost, compactness, efficiency, vertical emission, and straightforward integration into large arrayed-structures and networks.

title: Building reliable 3D photonic integrated circuits and cavities at the wafer scale
generated_summary:

The work addresses two critical challenges in 3D PICs: stress-induced non-uniformity in multilayer fabrication and the efficiency-footprint trade-off in inter-layer optical transitions.

The authors employ PECVD SiN deposition combined with stress release trenches (SRT) to manage film stress during high-temperature annealing, and develop an etch-back assisted chemical mechanical polishing (E-CMP) process to achieve highly uniform vertical spacer layers across 4-inch wafers, with a coefficient of variation of only 2.06%. They further propose a novel κ-engineered taper (κ-taper) that reshapes the coupling coefficient distribution using Hermite interpolation, flattening the coupling profile around the phase-matching point to enable smoother, more efficient power transfer between layers.

The κ-taper outperforms conventional linear tapers by 75% in a reliability metric combining transition efficiency and misalignment tolerance. The platform achieves inter-layer transition losses as low as 5.56 mdB/coupler with a wafer-scale coefficient of variation of 9.69%. Waveguide propagation losses reach approximately 0.07 dB/cm, corresponding to intrinsic quality factors around 5.2 million. These ultralow transition losses enable novel 3D high-Q optical cavities spanning both layers while maintaining high quality factors across the telecom S, C, and L bands, establishing a practical pathway toward mass-manufacturable, high-density 3D photonic systems.
original_abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) photonic integrated circuits (PIC) are emerging as an indispensable scheme for high density and multifunctional photonic systems. However, the wafer-scale scaling of PICs towards a 3D configuration is constrained by two key factors: (i) the trade-off between inter-layer taper efficiency and footprint, and (ii) wafer-scale uniformity of inter-layer transition loss. In this work, we introduce etch-back assisted chemical mechanical polishing (E-CMP) to achieve high wafer-scale uniformity of the spacer layer. Moreover, we break the efficiency-footprint trade-off by demonstrating a novel $κ$-engineered taper, achieving a reliability metric that is 75\% higher than the traditional linearly tapered structure. Building on these design and fabrication developments, we enable reliable 3D PICs with typical loss of 0.077 and 0.068 dB/cm on two silicon nitride (SiN) waveguide layers and typical 3D transition loss as low as 6 mdB. Furthermore, the low 3D transition loss enables the first class of 3D high-Q optical cavities occupying two distinct device layers, providing new design space for high-Q optical cavities. The scalable fabrication process and design methodology provide routes for wafer-scale reliable 3D PICs that are promising in a series of applications ranging from photonic interconnects and computing networks to high-density photonic sensors and nonlinear photonics.

title: Fidelity of Machine Learned Potentials: Quantitative Assessment for Protonated Oxalate
generated_summary:
This study quantitatively assesses the fidelity of two distinct machine-learned potential energy surfaces (ML-PESs) for the protonated oxalate anion (OxH): a permutationally invariant polynomial (PIP) PES using linear regression and a PhysNet neural network-based PES. Both are trained on the same reference datasets at the MP2 and CCSD(T)/aug-cc-pVTZ levels of theory, with transfer learning employed to elevate accuracy.

The authors conduct rigorous "stress tests" beyond standard fitting metrics by computing infrared spectra using VSCF/VCI calculations and ground-state tunneling splittings using ring polymer instanton theory, diffusion Monte Carlo simulations, and reduced-dimensional approaches. Each method samples approximately 10⁹ configurations, providing an extensive probe of PES quality.

The two ML-PESs yield nearly identical results across all tested properties. The computed IR spectra are visually indistinguishable, successfully reproducing the highly dispersed OH-stretch band observed experimentally between 2500–3200 cm⁻¹. Tunneling splittings consistently fall between 33–36 cm⁻¹ across methods and PESs for the CCSD(T)/aVTZ barrier of 1172 cm⁻¹, with a corrected CBS-limit barrier yielding approximately 28 cm⁻¹. The predicted ground-state tunneling splitting of ~30 cm⁻¹ represents a testable experimental prediction.

This work demonstrates that fundamentally different ML architectures, when trained on identical high-quality data, can achieve equivalent predictive accuracy for demanding spectroscopic and quantum dynamical properties, establishing confidence in ML-PES reliability for challenging chemical applications.
original_abstract: There has been a veritable explosion of methods and software to perform machine-learned regression on datasets of electronic energies and forces to develop high-dimensional machine learned potential energy surfaces (ML-PESs). A major, but not deeply-studied aspect is how well different ML-PESs represent the same dataset on which they are trained, beyond the standard fitting precision metrics. Here, this is examined in detail using several ''stress tests'', for two widely applied machine-learned potential approaches. One is based on permutationally invariant polynomial (PIP) linear least square regression and the other is the message-passing neural network PhysNet approach. These potentials and dipole moment surfaces are used in VSCF/VCI calculations of vibrational energies and wavefunctions. The energies from the two PESs are directly compared as are the IR spectra. In addition, tunneling splittings for the hydrogen transfer between two equivalent structures are reported from using three methods: ring polymer instanton theory, diffusion Monte Carlo simulations, and the $Q_{im}$ path method. These calculations require the evaluation of on the order of one billion energies that are widely dispersed in the 15-dimensional configurational space. The two PESs yield results for these quantities in excellent agreement with each other.

title: Precursors of extreme events and critical transitions
generated_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical framework based on fast-slow dynamical systems to predict extreme events and critical transitions by analyzing the behavior of covariant Lyapunov vectors (CLVs) in the tangent space. The authors identify three dynamical regimes preceding critical transitions: a slow regime, where fast CLVs align with fast eigenvectors and remain transversal to the slow subspace; a transition regime, where fast eigenvalues approach zero and fast CLVs detach from fast eigenvectors; and a critical regime, where a dominant positive eigenvalue attracts multiple CLVs, producing tangencies between fast and slow subspaces.

Based on this theoretical cascade, two precursors are proposed: monitoring principal angles between fast and slow CLV subspaces, and tracking the decoupling between instantaneous covariant Lyapunov exponents and Jacobian eigenvalues. The framework is validated numerically on systems of increasing complexity—a Van der Pol oscillator, a bistable Rössler system, coupled FitzHugh-Nagumo units, and a modified multiscale Lorenz-96 model. Across all test cases, the precursors achieve near-perfect precision and recall (F1 scores of 0.994–1.0), consistently forewarning critical transitions with meaningful lead times.

The significance of this work lies in providing theoretically grounded, geometrically interpretable precursors for extreme events, moving beyond purely statistical indicators. This tangent-space approach opens new avenues for prediction in multiscale dynamical systems relevant to climate science and other complex systems.
original_abstract: We propose a theory based on dynamical systems to explain and predict the occurrence of extreme events, of which critical transitions form a subset. In fast-slow nonlinear systems, we identify a cascade of events preceding extreme events: (i) a slow regime, in which the fast covariant Lyapunov vectors (CLVs) are both tangent to the fast eigenvectors and remain transversal to the slow subspace; (ii) a transition regime, in which the fast eigenvalues become neutrally stable while the fast CLVs are no longer tangent to the fast eigenvectors; and (iii) a critical regime, in which a strong spectral gap in the eigenvalues causes both fast and slow CLVs to become tangent along the dominant fast direction, breaking the transversality between fast and slow subspaces. Building on this cascade, we propose two precursors to forewarn the occurrence of extreme events. We numerically test the theory and precursors on low- and higher-dimensional systems. The proposed precursors predict extreme events and critical transitions with 100% precision and recall. This work opens opportunities for time-forecasting extreme events using theoretically grounded precursors.

title: Atomistic Modeling of Methane and Carbon Dioxide Structure I Gas Hydrates Under Pressure: Guest Effects and Properties
generated_summary:

original_abstract: Gas hydrates are potential candidates in future energy sources while simultaneously providing structures with extensive applications in carbon capture and storage, gas transport, and important separation processes. Prior research in the field considers the dynamics of the water molecule backbone in particular. We investigated the pressure-enthalpy landscape and mechanical stability envelope of sI methane and carbon dioxide hydrates simulated using DFT. We investigated the effect of the revPBE + DFT-D2 and the SCAN + rVV10 and their treatment of the exchange correlation interactions. We examined the zero pressure material properties, finding that revPBE comparatively underbinds the interactions, causing more flexible structures with large equilibrium volumes. Under pressure, the carbon dioxide molecule was found to align itself parallel to the hexagonal faces of the large cage despite the functional used. Additionally, the property differences are caused by the ability of the carbon dioxide molecule to rotate and disperse the changes in the energy landscape in ways that methane molecules cannot. This computational methodology describes the elastic stability of gas hydrate, marginal stability, and critical differences across important molecular interactions, confirming experimentally observed restrictions in guest molecule rotations and novel pressure behaviors under hydrostatic loads

title: Simultaneous PW-scale laser driven MeV X-ray and neutron beam characterization for dual radiography capability

The authors demonstrate through simulations that moderated MeV neutrons enable Neutron Resonance Transmission Analysis for elemental identification, complementing established MeV X-ray tomography capabilities. original_abstract: Laser-driven, high-brilliance secondary sources (electrons, ions, neutrons, X-rays) open new perspectives for compact material probing and imaging of high-speed events. A key advantage is their ability to perform multiplexed probing, as these sources are generated simultaneously in a single shot using a single laser beam. Here, we report the first quantitative measurements of photon spectra (0.1--100 MeV) and angular distributions in the petawatt interaction regime, using an ultra-intense ($>10^{21}\,\rm W/cm^2$), ultra-short (24~fs) laser pulse. These results are complemented by the characterization of simultaneously produced MeV neutrons. We demonstrate that these neutrons, once moderated, can enable in-depth material identification via resonance transmission analysis. This work highlights the potential of compact, ultrashort-pulse PW lasers for dual neutron and X-ray radiography of dense materials.

title: 2D quantum-path interference in high-harmonic generation driven by highly-bichromatic fields
generated_summary:

Experimentally, HHG spectra from argon atoms are recorded while scanning the two-colour relative phase between the field components. The key finding is that even and odd harmonics exhibit distinctly different intensity modulation patterns: odd harmonics display monomodal modulations while even harmonics show bimodal modulations as a function of the relative phase. The SFA quantum-orbit analysis reveals that this behavior originates from dynamical symmetries of the driving field imprinted onto the harmonic dipole. Specifically, electron trajectories in consecutive half-cycles are mirror-flipped along the fundamental polarization axis while retaining the same second-harmonic polarization component, causing even harmonics to be polarized along the second-harmonic direction with inherently more complex phase behavior.

These results establish the bichromatic phase delay as a new observable for quantum-path interference and provide a foundational understanding for controlling harmonic emission in the highly-bichromatic regime, paving the way toward multidimensional attosecond spectroscopy techniques for resolving ultrafast electronic dynamics and tomographic molecular information.
original_abstract: We experimentally observe a new type of quantum-path interference, in two-dimensions (2D-QPI), in high-harmonic generation (HHG) driven by an orthogonally-polarised highly-bichromatic field. This regime is marked by comparable intensities of the two orthogonal colours. In this highly-bichromatic regime, we demonstrate that 2D-QPI is encoded in the measured harmonic intensity modulations with respect to the relative phase of the two-colour field. The modulations of the odd-order harmonics show a monomodal behaviour, whereas the even harmonics are modulated in a bimodal structure. Our calculations using the strong-field approximation and saddle-point method disentangle contributions from multiple quantum orbits in this HHG regime, revealing that the dipole response for both odd and even harmonics inherits the dynamic symmetry of the orthogonally-polarised driving field. This new type of 2D-QPI offers a novel route to HHG spectroscopy of attosecond electron dynamics by lifting up the dimensionality of the quantum paths involved in the interference.

title: All optical ultrafast pure spin current in the altermagnet Cr$_2$SO
generated_summary:
This paper proposes an all-optical method for generating ultrafast pure spin currents in the two-dimensional altermagnet Cr₂SO, overcoming a fundamental symmetry obstacle that previously appeared to exclude d-wave altermagnets from such applications. Unlike transition metal dichalcogenides, altermagnets possess non-relativistic spin splitting, which prevents detrimental spin mixing but introduces highly anisotropic valley structures with a magnetic point group symmetry that seemingly precludes the charge current compensation necessary for pure spin currents.

The authors design a hybrid light pulse scheme combining a terahertz (THz) envelope with linearly polarized infrared valley excitation pulses. The key insight is that a THz field imparts momentum shifts to valley excitations proportional to the THz vector potential rather than the electric field. By temporally positioning two successive infrared pulses—one exciting the spin-up X valley and the other the spin-down Y valley—at specific points within the THz waveform, the resulting charge currents from opposite valleys cancel exactly while the spin currents add constructively.

The authors demonstrate this approach works for both idealized THz monocycles and realistic spintronic emission THz waveforms, achieving nearly 100% spin-polarized currents with complete macroscopic charge cancellation. The generated currents exhibit strong anisotropic dependence on THz polarization angle, reflecting the underlying d-wave symmetry. These findings establish altermagnets as a promising platform for dissipationless spintronics, combining the advantages of low spin-orbit coupling with controllable optical spin current generation.
original_abstract: All-optical generation of pure spin current -- the flow of spin in the absence of a corresponding charge flow -- relies on a symmetry based compensation of valley charge. The 2d $d$-wave altermagnets, ideal spintronics materials due to a very low spin-orbit coupling, possess a magnetic point group and highly anisotropic valley manifolds that would appear to preclude such current compensation, excluding them as materials for the ultrafast generation of pure spin current. Here we show that infra-red valley excitation combined with a THz pulse envelope allows the generation of large and nearly 100\% pure spin currents in the altermagnet Cr$_2$SO. Our approach is based on a valley selection rule coupling linearly polarized light to spin opposite valleys, along with the intrinsic momentum shift that a co-occurring THz pulse imbues a valley spin excitation with. These results thus provide a practical and all-optical route to the generation of pure spin current in $d$-wave 2d altermagnets, opening a route to lightwave control of spin in an environment with very low intrinsic spin mixing.

title: Low-confinement silicon nitride waveguides manufactured via direct glass bonding
generated_summary:
This paper presents an alternative fabrication technology for low-confinement silicon nitride (SiN_x) waveguides using direct thermal bonding of Borofloat 33 glass wafers. The main contribution is a novel process that creates symmetric dielectric cladding around ultra-thin waveguide cores, enabling low-loss optical coupling to standard single-mode fibers while offering manufacturing scalability.

The fabrication methodology involves etching nano-trenches into a glass substrate, filling them with SiN_x via inductively coupled plasma chemical vapor deposition, removing excess material, and thermally bonding a second glass wafer to encapsulate the waveguide. This approach produces waveguides with core thicknesses of approximately 50 nm and widths ranging from 1.3 to 3.5 μm, embedded within a symmetric glass cladding structure.

Test samples consisting of 1 cm long straight waveguides were characterized at 1550 nm using butt-coupling to SMF-28 fiber. Measured transmissions reached up to 60%, corresponding to input/output losses of approximately 1 dB per facet. Comparison with FDTD simulations confirmed that the transmission dependence on waveguide width is primarily governed by modal overlap between fiber and waveguide modes, with systematic deviations attributed to propagation losses and fabrication imperfections.

The proposed platform is significant for scalable production of low-loss photonic circuits with simplified passive fiber packaging, particularly suited for applications requiring long delay lines, high-Q resonators, and low phase noise, including coherent telecommunications and microwave photonics systems.
original_abstract: Reduction of the fabrication cost of the photonic integral circuits with low optical losses and technological simplicity are the key conditions for their widespread implementation. In conventional manufacturing methods, dielectric cladding thickness around waveguides usually limited to ~20 μm, which complicates suppression of radiative losses and parasitic scattering. In this paper, we propose and experimentally demonstrate an alternative technology for forming low-confinement waveguides based on Borofloat 33 glass, based on thermal fusion bonding of two glass wafers. The waveguide pattern is formed in the following manner: trenches on the order of tens of nanometers are etched into the glass, then filled with silicon nitride, followed by removal of the excess layer and bonding, which ensures high-quality contact surfaces and a thick, symmetric dielectric cladding. As a proof of concept, we fabricated straight waveguides with a core height of 50 nm and widths from 1.3 to 3.5 μm. With butt coupling to standard SMF-28 single-mode fiber at a wavelength of 1550 nm, transmission of up to 60% was obtained, corresponding to input/output coupling losses of 1 dB per facet and consistent with numerical estimates. The proposed approach provides a low-cost and scalable route to fabricate low-confinement integrated photonic devices, promising for chips with simplified passive packaging and for devices based on long delay lines and ring resonators.

title: Spectroscopy of analogue black holes using simulation-based inference
generated_summary:
This paper introduces simulation-based inference (SBI) as a novel framework for performing spectroscopy of analogue black holes, addressing the fundamental challenge that stochastic noise driving these systems is intrinsic rather than separable from the signal, rendering standard Bayesian likelihood-based methods impractical.

The authors apply neural posterior estimation (NPE), a machine-learning technique using normalizing flows, to two theoretical models relevant to analogue gravity experiments: a Pöschl-Teller potential barrier in a finite cavity and shallow-water waves on a vortex flow. Training data consists of power spectra generated by numerically solving stochastic wave equations with parameters drawn from uniform priors. The NPE learns to map noisy spectra directly to posterior distributions without requiring an explicit likelihood function.

Key results demonstrate successful recovery of all model parameters from single noisy spectral realizations, including boundary reflectivities that encode effective boundary conditions—quantities notoriously difficult to determine from first principles in fluid experiments. For the Pöschl-Teller case, the authors recover a 7-dimensional posterior and reconstruct the system's Green's function, enabling full characterization of the scattering problem. Calibration analyses confirm reliable posterior estimation for both models.

This work establishes SBI as a powerful tool for analogue gravity experiments where limited statistics, uncontrollable initial conditions, and intrinsic stochasticity preclude traditional analysis methods, with direct applicability to ongoing laboratory black hole simulations.
original_abstract: The emergence of precision gravity simulators in quantum and fluid systems is opening new avenues for probing curved-spacetime physics and black-hole phenomenology under controlled laboratory conditions. In parallel, advances in understanding how fundamental physics can be probed in the spectral signatures of black holes and exotic compact objects motivate the development of modern spectroscopic techniques within analogue-gravity experiments. In this work, we model the spectral properties of analogue black holes sourced by broadband stochastic noise, a crucial aspect in realistic experiments that poses substantial challenges for established data-analysis techniques. Using simulation-based inference, we demonstrate that the physical parameters encoded in noisy spectra can be reliably extracted, showing that these techniques provide a powerful tool for studying both spacetime properties and boundary effects in gravity simulators.

title: Stable Fine-Time-Step Long-Horizon Turbulence Prediction with a Multi-Stepsize Mixture-of-Experts Neural Operator
generated_summary:

The key insight is that learning a single fixed-stride time-advancement operator leads to error accumulation and instability under deep autoregressive rollout, particularly at fine time steps where successive snapshots are highly correlated.

The authors propose Multi-Stepsize Mixture-of-Experts IFactFormer (Ms-MoE-IFactFormer), which learns a family of stride-conditioned time-advancement operators within a single network. The architecture combines a shared expert capturing common dynamics with scale-specific routed experts activated through a Gaussian kernel-based time-step router operating on logarithmic stride coordinates. A lightweight stride-indexed corrector further refines predictions. This design enables multi-stride supervision during training without requiring expensive multi-step backpropagation through unrolled trajectories.

Experiments on turbulent channel flow (Re_τ ≈ 180) and forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (Re_λ ≈ 100) at two fine sampling intervals demonstrate that fixed-stride baselines (FNO and IFactFormer) become numerically unstable or exhibit significant statistical drift under long autoregressive rollouts of up to 4,000 steps. Ms-MoE-IFactFormer maintains stable predictions and produces energy spectra, velocity profiles, Reynolds stresses, and probability distributions that closely match filtered DNS references.

The work is significant because it demonstrates that conditioning neural operators on temporal stride through mixture-of-experts routing provides a practical path toward simultaneously achieving fine temporal resolution and stable long-horizon turbulence prediction—requirements critical for downstream applications like Lagrangian particle tracking and data assimilation.
original_abstract: Neural operators have been increasingly used as data-driven surrogates for time-marching predictions of turbulent flows. However, long-horizon autoregressive prediction is sensitive to error accumulation and the choice of prediction interval. Excessively small time increments may increase temporal redundancy and lengthen rollouts, which can degrade the stability of neural operators in turbulence forecasting. This work pursues a unified objective: stable long-horizon autoregressive prediction at fine temporal resolution for three-dimensional turbulence. We propose a multi-stepsize mixture-of-experts (Ms-MoE) neural operator built on an implicit factorized Transformer (IFactFormer) backbone. The model conditions on a requested relative stride and uses a time-step router to activate scale-specific routed experts together with a shared expert, yielding a single architecture that represents a family of stride-parameterized time-advancement operators. We evaluate the approach on forced homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) and turbulent channel flow using filtered direct numerical simulation datasets. Relative to sampling intervals used in previous studies, we construct training datasets with up to 20 times finer temporal resolution and report long-horizon autoregressive rollouts using qualitative time-slice comparisons and long-time-averaged statistics. Ms-MoE-IFactFormer yields more stable long-horizon rollouts and improved agreement with long-time-averaged statistics on both HIT and turbulent channel flow, suggesting potential for stable time-marching at fine temporal resolution in more complex turbulent flows.

title: Shape of an interface hit by an oblique jet
generated_summary:
This study investigates the deformation of a liquid interface when struck by an oblique plunging jet, addressing a gap in quantitative modeling of cavity formation that occurs when axisymmetry is broken. The main contribution is a predictive model for the cavity width that forms on the obtuse side of an inclined jet impacting a liquid bath.

The authors employ a multi-pronged methodology combining experiments, direct numerical simulations, and analytical modeling. They first study a simplified analog system where the jet is replaced by an inclined glass fiber in silicone oil, deriving an analytical expression for the maximum meniscus height difference as a function of fiber radius and inclination angle. They then perform numerical simulations of the full jet problem to characterize the velocity and pressure fields near the impact region.

Key results reveal that the oblique impact creates an asymmetric interface: a cavity forms on the obtuse side of the jet while a meniscus attaches to the acute side. Numerical simulations identify two critical features — a low-speed region in the outer interface justifying hydrostatic treatment, and streamline contraction due to asymmetric flow separation that generates a depression driving cavity formation. These insights enable a force balance model that successfully predicts how cavity width depends on jet speed, radius, and inclination angle.

The significance of this work lies in providing the first quantitative description of oblique jet cavity shapes, which is essential for understanding air entrainment and bubble creation in low-viscosity liquid systems relevant to both natural and industrial processes.
original_abstract: We report on the shape taken by the interface of a liquid bath when hit by a smooth oblique steady jet. When the angle between the jet and the bath decreases below $50^\circ$, a cavity is formed in front of the jet. In the inertial regime we explore, the jet boundary layer detaches in the impact region, thereby delimiting a core jet region outside of which the liquid is mainly in hydrostatic equilibrium. The shape of the outer meniscus is shown to be related to the one outside a tilted fiber piercing the fluid interface. In order to unravel the flow features and separation, we perform direct numerical simulations and show that the flow detachment displays an asymmetry, which results in the acceleration of the liquid below the surface, thereby creating a depression. With this observation, we propose a model balancing the suction force of this depression with the weight of the displaced water and the surface tension force to obtain a prediction for the typical width of the cavity.

title: Engineering strong coupling in ultra-compact photonic crystal/2D material platforms
generated_summary:
This theoretical study investigates strong light-matter coupling between excitons in WS₂ monolayers and guided-mode resonances (GMRs) of photonic crystal (PhC) grating slabs, providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the optical response of these ultra-compact hybrid platforms.

The authors employ rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) to solve Maxwell's equations with realistic material parameters, combined with coupled-mode theory (CMT) and an effective slab waveguide model. This multi-method approach enables them to link the optical spectra directly to the underlying electromagnetic mode profiles within the PhC unit cell.

A central finding is the explanation of the three-peak structure observed in absorption spectra of strongly coupled PhC/2D semiconductor systems. Beyond the conventional upper and lower polariton branches, a third peak arises from weakly coupled excitons located in regions of low electromagnetic field intensity within the unit cell. The authors demonstrate this explicitly by selectively patterning the WS₂ monolayer in high- and low-field regions, showing that removing material from low-field areas eliminates the third peak while preserving the Rabi splitting. They further show that coupling strength can be estimated from the electric field profile and mode volume, and that varying the PhC filling factor enables tuning between weak and strong coupling regimes.

These results provide essential design principles for engineering polariton-based optoelectronic devices that combine weakly and strongly coupled exciton physics on sub-micron scales at room temperature.
original_abstract: Sub-wavelength thick photonic crystal (PhC) slabs coupled to 2D excitonic materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), are a promising platform for highly tunable, room-temperature, on-chip optoelectronic devices. Unlike conventional Fabry-Perot microcavities, these compact open cavities exhibit non-trivial electric field profiles, leading to spatially distinct regions of weak and strong coupling with excitons within the PhC unit cell. Using coupled mode theory and rigorous solutions to Maxwell's equations, we investigate how the PhC geometry can be used to control these coexisting exciton/polariton contributions and tailor the resulting optical spectra. For large filling factors, i.e., small air gaps, we show that PhC polaritons can be modeled as dark waveguide modes brightened via the periodicity of the PhC slab. Furthermore, by spatially patterning the TMD monolayer based on the local field intensity, we reveal the simultaneous presence of excitons in both the weak and strong coupling regimes. Overall, this work provides fundamental insights into the strong light-matter coupling regime in structured photonic environments, offering a pathway to design and optimize metal-free, ultra-compact polaritonic devices.

title: DoseRAD2026 Challenge dataset: AI accelerated photon and proton dose calculation for radiotherapy
generated_summary:
The paper introduces DoseRAD2026, the first publicly available radiotherapy dose dataset providing paired CT and MRI scans alongside beam-level Monte Carlo (MC) dose distributions for both photon and proton therapy. Built upon the SynthRAD2025 paired imaging dataset, it addresses the lack of large-scale benchmarks for developing deep learning-based dose calculation methods, particularly for MRI-guided and adaptive radiotherapy workflows.

The dataset spans thoracic and abdominal anatomies and is organized around four tasks: photon segment dose calculation on CT, direct photon dose prediction on MRI, proton pencil beam dose calculation on CT, and direct proton dose prediction on MRI. Dose ground truth is generated using Geant4 MC simulations, while photon VMAT plans are created using the open-source matRad toolkit. CT-to-MRI alignment employs ConvexAdam deformable registration with manual quality control. Beam-level rather than plan-level dose labels substantially increase training samples per patient and enable flexible plan accumulation.

The authors acknowledge limitations including simplified non-clinical beam models, single-center MRI data from one MRI-linac system, and potential residual registration errors between CT and MRI. Despite these constraints, the dataset provides physically consistent MC ground truth suitable for benchmarking deep learning algorithms targeting sub-second dose computation. This work is significant for advancing real-time adaptive radiotherapy, offering a pathway from CT-dependent dose calculation toward direct MRI-based dose prediction while ensuring full reproducibility through open-source code release.
original_abstract: Purpose: Accurate dose calculation is essential in radiotherapy for precise tumor irradiation while sparing healthy tissue. With the growing adoption of MRI-guided and real-time adaptive radiotherapy, fast and accurate dose calculation on CT and MRI is increasingly needed. The DoseRAD2026 dataset and challenge provide a public benchmark of paired CT and MRI data with beam-level photon and proton Monte Carlo dose distributions for developing and evaluating advanced dose calculation methods. Acquisition and validation methods: The dataset comprises paired CT and MRI from 115 patients (75 training, 40 testing) treated on an MRI-linac for thoracic or abdominal lesions, derived from the SynthRAD2025 dataset. Pre-processing included deformable image registration, air-cavity correction, and resampling. Ground-truth photon (6 MV) and proton dose distributions were computed using open-source Monte Carlo algorithms, yielding 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Data format and usage notes: Data are organized into photon and proton subsets with paired CT-MRI images, beam-level dose distributions, and JSON beam configuration files. Files are provided in compressed MetaImage (.mha) format. The dataset is released under CC BY-NC 4.0, with training data available from April 2026 and the test set withheld until March 2030. Potential applications: The dataset supports benchmarking of fast dose calculation methods, including beam-level dose estimation for photon and proton therapy, MRI-based dose calculation in MRI-guided workflows, and real-time adaptive radiotherapy.

title: Exact demagnetisation field for periodic one-dimensional array of rectangular prisms
generated_summary:
This paper derives closed-form analytical expressions for the demagnetization field of an infinite one-dimensional periodic array of identical rectangular prisms aligned end-to-end along one axis, addressing a fundamental challenge in micromagnetic simulations involving periodic boundary conditions (PBCs). The authors first solve the analogous problem for a 1D array of point dipoles using polygamma functions, then extend the approach to rectangular prisms by Taylor expanding the demagnetization tensor under the assumption that transverse prism dimensions are small compared to the inter-copy distance. The resulting expressions, which become exact on the prism center axis in the limit of infinitesimally thin prisms, involve readily computable trigamma functions.

The key practical application is supplementing the macrogeometry approach commonly used in micromagnetic software, where a finite number of domain copies approximate the infinite periodic system. Convergence tests demonstrate that incorporating the analytical prism solution for distant copies dramatically reduces the number of explicit domain copies needed to achieve a given accuracy. The analytical prism approach shows superior convergence compared to both the standard macrogeometry method and the uniform magnetization approximation, particularly when the simulation domain is elongated along the periodic direction.

These results provide a computationally efficient and exact framework for implementing 1D periodic boundary conditions in micromagnetic simulations, potentially improving the accuracy and speed of modeling extended magnetic systems such as nanowire arrays and patterned magnetic structures.
original_abstract: The magnetic field from a uniformly magnetised, rectangular prism is known exactly, which is the basis for a large number of micromagnetic simulations. Here we derive an analytical solution for the field from a periodically repeating infinite array of prisms aligned end-to-end, which becomes exact on the center axis in the limit of infinitesimally thin prisms. Using the same method we derive the on-axis field for a one-dimensional array of point dipoles. We validate the obtained results numerically and furthermore compare with the common macrogeometry approach and more recent uniform magnetisation method, demonstrating an excellent convergence rate for the novel method.

title: Constraining Electron-Impact Ionization of O$_2$ Through UV Aurora Observations at Ganymede
generated_summary:
This study introduces a novel method to constrain electron-impact ionization rates of molecular oxygen (O₂) at Ganymede by exploiting the relationship between ionization and dissociative excitation cross sections of O₂. The key insight is that the ratio of ionization to OI 1356 Å excitation rate coefficients remains bounded between 10 and 60, regardless of the electron energy distribution. This allows direct estimation of ionization rates from observable ultraviolet auroral brightness without requiring independent knowledge of electron fluxes or neutral oxygen column densities.

The authors apply this method to Juno UVS observations of Ganymede's aurora during the PJ34 flyby, producing a global empirical map of electron-impact ionization rates. The auroral emissions are structured into two bright bands near the open-closed field line boundaries, with average brightnesses of approximately 120 Rayleighs, while polar and equatorial background regions average about 8 Rayleighs. Using a chemical equilibrium model combined with these ionization rates, the study finds that modeled ionospheric densities significantly exceed those measured by radio occultation experiments, indicating that transport processes—rather than purely local recombination—dominate ion loss. Approximately 90% of produced O₂⁺ ions are lost through transport, with 70–90% returning to the surface and 10–30% escaping as ionospheric outflow. The resulting surface ice erosion rate is estimated at 0.03–0.5 cm per million years, comparable to Europa's when accounting for Ganymede's larger surface area. These results provide important constraints for future ionospheric and atmospheric models.
original_abstract: While photoionization rates of Ganymede's O$_2$ dominated atmosphere are well constrained, the contribution of electron-impact ionization is rather uncertain. Previous quantitative estimates have relied on assumptions about densities and energy distributions of precipitating electrons, or on rare spacecraft measurements that cannot be unambiguously mapped to the regions of ionization. In this study, we present a novel approach to quantify electron-impact ionization rates directly through OI 1356 Å emission brightness observations. The analysis of measured cross sections reveals that the ionization-to-excitation ratio is limited to 10-60 over all electron energies, reducing the uncertainty of estimating ionization rates to a factor less than 6. We apply this method to Juno UVS observations of Ganymede's aurora. We find that the OI 1356 Å brightness of the auroral ovals is well described by 3-5° latitude wide Gaussian distributions centered on the open-closed field line boundary, with an average peak of 120 R. The average brightness outside the ovals in the polar and equatorial background regions is ~8 R. From these observations, we derive a global map of electron-impact ionization rates, which are at least an order of magnitude higher than photoionization rates. The estimated total global ionization rate is 1.3-7.6$\times$10$^{26}$ s$^{-1}$, with average column rates of ~5$\times$10$^{9}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ in the ovals and ~3$\times$10$^{8}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ in the background regions. Comparison of radio occultation measurements with predicted electron densities indicates that transport processes are the dominant loss mechanism in Ganymede's ionosphere. The rate of ionospheric outflow of O$_2^+$ is 0.1-2$\times$10$^{26}$ s$^{-1}$ or 0.5-11 kg s$^{-1}$, indicating 0.03-0.5 cm Myr$^{-1}$ erosion of Ganymede's surface ice.

title: Automated Design of Tubular Origami with Anisotropic Stiffness
generated_summary:
This paper presents an automated design framework for tubular origami structures that systematically explores both local vertex topology (vertex degree) and global tube topology (polygonal cross-section) to achieve programmable anisotropic stiffness. The framework introduces a mirror-symmetric parameterization of generalized degree-n vertices, enabling automated generation of tubular origami configurations that extend beyond the conventional degree-four designs predominant in existing literature.

The methodology employs a nonlinear bar-and-hinge model to evaluate translational and rotational stiffness under large deformations across axial, radial, and rotational directions. Two objective functions capturing translational and rotational stiffness anisotropy are formulated within a multi-objective optimization framework, producing Pareto fronts of optimal designs. Structures are fabricated from laser-cut cardboard sheets and experimentally validated.

Key results demonstrate that increasing the number of polygonal cross-section vertices improves stiffness anisotropy, with convergence occurring around eight vertices. Importantly, increasing vertex degree significantly enhances performance when cross-sectional vertices are few, revealing that higher local kinematic freedom can counterintuitively amplify structural stiffness through geometric coupling. Optimized designs achieve over 50 times higher constrained rotational stiffness compared to state-of-the-art benchmarks, with experimental measurements agreeing within 8% of numerical predictions. Monte Carlo analysis confirms robustness against geometric imperfections.

This work establishes polygonal cross-sectional topology and higher-degree vertices as effective design variables for engineering anisotropic mechanical behavior in tubular origami, with potential applications in robotics, biomedical devices, and deployable structures.
original_abstract: Thin sheets can be assembled into tubular origami structures that combine deployability with pronounced anisotropic stiffness, enabling applications ranging from robotics to deployable systems. However, most existing tubular origami designs remain limited to degree-four vertex topologies and are characterized primarily in axial and radial loading modes, without a full assessment of anisotropic stiffness. Here, we present an automated design framework for tubular origami that jointly explores local vertex topology through generalized degree-$n$ vertices and global tube topology through the polygonal cross-section, for the systematic design and optimization of anisotropic stiffness. Using a calibrated bar-and-hinge model together with experimental validation, we quantify large-deformation stiffness responses in axial translation, in-plane translation, torsion about the tube axis, and rotation about in-plane axes, thereby characterizing the anisotropic stiffness of the tube across its compliant and constrained deformation modes. The resulting design-space exploration showed that the polygonal cross-sectional topology is the primary factor governing the anisotropic stiffness. We further show that increasing the local vertex degree can improve global structural performance, particularly for tubes with a small number of cross-sectional vertices, demonstrating that higher local kinematic freedom does not necessarily compromise stiffness at the structural scale. Compared with a benchmark design, the optimized architectures achieve more than 50 times higher constrained rotational stiffness. Together, these results highlight higher-degree vertices and polygonal cross-sectional topology as powerful design variables for tailoring anisotropic stiffness in tubular origami.

title: Transferable excited-state dynamics enable screening of fluorescent protein chromophores
generated_summary:
This paper introduces X-MACE, a transferable machine learning framework for screening excited-state dynamics across large families of fluorescent protein chromophores, representing the first step toward a foundational model for photodynamics. The approach addresses the prohibitive computational cost of running non-adiabatic dynamics simulations for hundreds of molecular variants using conventional quantum chemical methods.

title: Hierarchical generative modeling for the design of multi-component systems

title: Kelvin waves over a differentially rotating spherical shell

title: Projection of purification performance for the RELICS experiment

title: Predicting success of cooperators across arbitrary heterogeneous environmental landscapes

original_abstract: Cooperation is central to the organization of complex biological and social systems. Most theoretical models assume homogeneous environments; in reality, populations inhabit spatially varying landscapes in which the payoffs of cooperation differ across space. Here, we introduce a general framework for the evolution of cooperation in complex, heterogeneous environments where the benefit of cooperation depends on local environmental quality. Cooperators in environmentally rich sites confer greater benefits than those on poor sites. We show that whether heterogeneity promotes or suppresses cooperation is determined primarily by the spatial organization of environmental states. Across arbitrary environmental landscapes, a single quantity, the spatial correlation index (SCI), predicts the fixation probability of cooperators. Under weak selection, segregated environments enhance cooperation, whereas highly intermixed, checkerboard-like landscapes suppress it. Beyond fixation probabilities, environmental organization also controls evolutionary timescales: segregated landscapes generate long-lived metastable coexistence, whereas intermixed landscapes lead to faster but less successful fixation of cooperators. Together, these results provide a unifying description of how spatial environmental heterogeneity shapes the evolution of cooperation and suggest measurable predictors of cooperative success in biological and social settings.

Key results demonstrate that the Ritz method performs reliably only when fluctuation data are approximately Gaussian with low kurtosis, as it approximates fourth-order moments using second-order statistics (Millionshchikov's approximation). For data with large kurtosis, the method produces erroneous transfer functions. In contrast, the Kim method, which retains fourth-order cumulants, yields consistent and physically meaningful energy transfer estimates regardless of statistical character. original_abstract: Energy transfer among various spectral components of fluctuating physical parameters in plasma occurs due to the nonlinear interactions, but these effects are typically not captured by the traditional linear spectral methods. Plasma density fluctuations measured in the Inverse Mirror Plasma Experimental Device (IMPED) have signatures of nonlinear mode interactions among various instability modes, i.e. Rayleigh-Taylor (RT) and Drift-Wave (DW) modes. In this paper, the energy transfer among these modes as a result of nonlinear wave interactions (through the quadratic coupling processes) have been investigated in detail. The existing computational methods for single field turbulence model such as Ritz method and Kim method have been explored to understand the turbulence dynamics. Both methods are applied and validated in simulation as well as experimental data from IMPED for developing plasma turbulence. We find that the validity and applicability of the methods depend on the statistical nature of the data, particularly higher-order moments such as kurtosis, and on spatial stationarity. Energy transfer analysis at different radial locations using these methods reveals the transfer of energy from RT modes to a comparatively low-frequency DW mode, demonstrating the capability of the method to quantify spectral energy transport in the plasma turbulence.

title: Acoustic instability at shock-wave precursors

To study this phenomenon, we use the PLUTO code to carry out 2D (and some 3D) magnetohydrodynamical simulations of the evolution of small density perturbations in the presence of an assigned cosmic-ray pressure gradient. Adopting more realistic values of Mach number and cosmic-ray acceleration efficiency than previously assumed in the literature, we show that the acoustic instability can transform small density perturbations into large nonlinear structures while the fluid crosses the precursor region of a cosmic-ray-modified shock. We study the power spectrum of turbulent magnetic fluctuations that may be important to scatter particles. In the latter case, it may be directed either with the flow or against the flow, creating backflow regions. In this parameter space and with the presence of vortex promoters at the inlet of the duct we identify $4$ types of flow. original_abstract: As one of the cornerstones of fluid mechanics, stability analyses provide essential physical insights into the growth of perturbations and eventual transition to turbulence. However, classical \enquote{frozen-time} stability analyses implicitly assume a time-independence of their base flow and thus fail for \enquote{rapidly} diffusing shear layers. Here, we propose a self-similar ansatz to naturally incorporate the \enquote{diffusive} base-state expansion into the stability operator. Our approach reveals two competing physical mechanisms: an \enquote{expansion wind} delays the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability whereas a diminishing effective viscosity sustains this instability far beyond classical predictions. Direct numerical simulations confirm that our framework accurately captures the instability's extended lifespan, growth rate, and spectral topology, eventually revising the timeline of shear-induced mixing fundamentally.

title: Experimental Determination of the $D1$ Magic Wavelength for $^{40}$K

original_abstract: Neutral-atom arrays offer a promising path for quantum simulation, yet the potential of fermionic $^{40}$K remains largely constrained by state-dependent light shifts that degrade cooling and detection fidelities. This problem can be resolved by working at a magic wavelength, where the differential light shift vanishes. We report the first experimental determination of the magic wavelength for the D1 transition in fermionic $^{40}$K at 1227.54(3) nm. Using in-trap loss spectroscopy in a wavelength-tunable optical tweezer, we map the differential AC Stark shift across a range of trapping powers and wavelengths. By converting these shifts to differential scalar polarizabilities, we find excellent agreement with relativistic all-order calculations. Benchmark measurements at 1064.49 nm further reveal the significant intensity-sampling systematics that plague standard trapping wavelengths, contrasting with the "mechanically clean" environment provided by the magic condition. Our results provide an important step toward high-fidelity in-trap D1 cooling, fluorescence imaging, and light-assisted loading, establishing a robust path toward scaling fermionic neutral-atom arrays for quantum information science.

title: Learning step-level dynamic soaring in shear flow

original_abstract: Dynamic soaring enables sustained flight by extracting energy from wind shear, yet it is commonly understood as a cycle-level maneuver that assumes stable flow conditions. In realistic unsteady environments, however, such assumptions are often violated, raising the question of whether explicit cycle-level planning is necessary. Here, we show that dynamic soaring can emerge from step-level, state-feedback control using only local sensing, without explicit trajectory planning. Using deep reinforcement learning as a tool, we obtain policies that achieve robust omnidirectional navigation across diverse shear-flow conditions. The learned behavior organizes into a structured control law that coordinates turning and vertical motion, giving rise to a two-phase strategy governed by a trade-off between energy extraction and directional progress. The resulting policy generalizes across varying conditions and reproduces key features observed in biological flight and optimal-control solutions. These findings identify a feedback-based control structure underlying dynamic soaring, demonstrating that efficient energy-harvesting flight can emerge from local interactions with the flow without explicit planning, and providing insights for biological flight and autonomous systems in complex, flow-coupled environments.

title: Permutationally symmetric molecular aggregates

original_abstract: Linear optical spectra of molecular aggregates are often approximated by classical optics methods such as the discrete-dipole approximation (DDA), coherent exciton scattering (CES), and coherent potential approximation (CPA), where the only quantum-mechanical input to the calculation is the linear susceptibility of the monomers. However, the limits of validity of these classical optics methods remain opaque. Here, starting from a quantum mechanical Hamiltonian for the aggregate, we identify a limit where DDA/CPA/CES is exact: all-to-all coupled permutationally symmetric aggregates of $N \to \infty$ monomers. The permutational symmetry of this molecular version of the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, which is closely related to that of the molecular polariton problem of many identical molecules coupled to a single-cavity mode, allows us to borrow recent techniques developed for the latter. In particular, we identify a $1/N$ expansion that corrects the classical optics limit with finite $N$ corrections to the linear response of the aggregate. These corrections feature as Raman-like transitions of a single monomer. We illustrate these findings with calculations on the very physically-relevant setup of a homodimer. Our findings clarify how quantum optical features that go beyond classical optics can already be present in simple arrays of quantum emitters such as molecular aggregates.

title: Velocity Formulations for Hyper-Rayleigh Scattering Optical Activity Spectroscopy: Addressing the Origin-dependence Problem

original_abstract: The theory of hyper-Rayleigh scattering optical activity (HRS-OA) spectroscopy has previously been described within the length formulation of the pure electric-dipole and mixed (electric-dipole/magnetic-dipole and electric-dipole/electric-quadrupole) first hyperpolarizabilities required for the description of this process. In this work, we provide an alternative formulation of these pure and mixed hyperpolarizabilities. This new formulation made use of the velocity form of the electric-dipole and electric-quadrupole moment operators that enter in the quadratic response functions. A one-to-one correspondence is found for the gauge-origin shifts obtained in the two formulations. These relations ensure the origin-independence of the theory also for the velocity formulation. Furthermore, even though the basis set dependence of the velocity formulation is more significant compared to the length one, the former is origin-independent by design. This property makes it particularly suitable for calculations of HRS-OA invariants using approximated (variational or not) wavefunctions.

title: A Periodic Orbit Trace Formula for Quantum Scrambling: The Role of the Normally Hyperbolic Invariant Manifold

original_abstract: Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) quantify quantum information scrambling, but their connection to localized phase-space structures, such as chemical transition states, requires formal development. We derive a leading-order semiclassical expansion for the local microcanonical OTOC in systems with an index-1 saddle point, expressing the scrambling rate as a coherent sum over unstable periodic orbits on the Normally Hyperbolic Invariant Manifold (NHIM). Valid in the semiclassical limit and the intermediate-time regime before the Ehrenfest time, our derivation utilizes the Normal Form theory of the transition state, which transforms the Hamiltonian near the saddle into an integrable (though generally non-separable) form dependent on conserved actions. We outline the derivation of the microcanonical trace, the semiclassical propagator for integrable systems, the factorization of the stability matrix, and the Schur complement reduction of the stationary phase approximation. Our result extends periodic-orbit trace methods to scrambling observables, yielding a local instability exponent Λ(J) governing the leading semiclassical growth window. As a special case, when the observation time coincides with the intrinsic periods of the contributing orbits, the trace sum reduces to an effective 1.5Λ scaling, resulting from the competition between local hyperbolic growth and wavepacket dilution. This simplified form is conditional; the full expansion retains a coherent sum over orbit periods. Finally, we discuss how the dependence of the instability on transverse actions establishes a theoretical mechanism for mode-selective control of scrambling, and outline a numerical evaluation strategy to test these predictions.

title: Cross-Domain Transfer with Particle Physics Foundation Models: From Jets to Neutrino Interactions

The authors interpret these results as evidence that pre-training instills useful geometric and kinematic priors applicable across particle physics domains. This finding suggests that foundation models could reduce labeled simulation requirements during detector commissioning and enable more rapid hypothesis testing, representing a step toward detector-agnostic inference in particle physics.
original_abstract: Future AI-based studies in particle physics will likely start from a foundation model to accelerate training and enhance sensitivity. As a step towards a general-purpose foundation model for particle physics, we investigate whether the OmniLearned foundation model pre-trained on diverse high-$Q^2$ simulated and real $pp$ and $ep$ collisions can be effectively transferred to a few-GeV fixed-target neutrino experiment. We process MINERvA neutrino--nucleus scattering events and evaluate pre-trained models on two types of tasks: regression of available energy and binary classification of charged-current pion final states ($\mathrm{CC1π^{\pm}}$, $\mathrm{CCNπ^{\pm}}$, and $\mathrm{CC1π^{0}}$). Pre-trained OmniLearned models consistently outperform similarly sized models trained from scratch, achieving better overall performance at the same compute budget, as well as achieving better performance at the same number of training steps. These results suggest that particle-level foundation models acquire inductive biases that generalize across large differences in energy scale, detector technology, and underlying physics processes, pointing toward a paradigm of detector-agnostic inference in particle physics.

title: Geometric phase-assisted simple phase compensation enabling quantum key distribution using phase-shifted Bell states

Using a polarization Sagnac interferometer with a periodically poled KTP crystal for spontaneous parametric down-conversion, the authors generate entangled photon pairs and implement the BBM92 QKD protocol. The QBER is measured as a function of this phase, revealing that secure key distribution requires relative phases within approximately ±0.31 radians of the ideal Bell state.

The key result demonstrates that phase distortions—whether deliberately introduced or arising from experimental imperfections such as crystal misalignment—can be effectively compensated by applying a counter-geometric phase at the detection stage. This compensation restores QBER to approximately 3% and achieves Bell state fidelities exceeding 98%, as confirmed by quantum state tomography. original_abstract: Entanglement-based quantum key distribution (QKD) relies on the distribution of high-fidelity maximally entangled Bell states, typically generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). In practical systems, unwanted relative phases arise from birefringence, pump-beam contributions, imperfect photon-pair generation, transmission through physical channels, and collection, transforming Bell states into phase-shifted states. This degrades interference visibility, increases the quantum bit error rate (QBER), and limits secure key generation. Conventional compensation techniques, such as birefringent crystals, interferometric stabilization, and spatial light modulators, are often impractical in real-world deployments. Here, we demonstrate a simple and versatile phase-compensation scheme that can be implemented at either the source or the receiver to eliminate arbitrary relative phases in Bell states. We theoretically and experimentally quantify the dependence of QBER in the BBM92 protocol on the relative phase and show that geometric-phase-based control can effectively restore entanglement quality. In a proof-of-concept experiment using a nondegenerate polarization Bell state, we achieve a fidelity exceeding 95% and reduce QBER below the 11% security threshold required for secure QKD. This robust approach enables practical phase control in entangled-photon systems and can be extended to time-bin QKD via time-polarization mapping, offering a promising route toward stable, low-QBER quantum communication.

title: Recurrent bifurcations of stability spectra for steep Stokes waves in a deep fluid

The four bifurcations occur in a fixed sequence: (a) figure-8 bands appearing at extremal points of wave speed, (b) degeneration of figure-8 bands to vertical slopes followed by splitting into instability bubbles, (c) new circular instability bands emerging at period-doubling bifurcations, and (d) reconnection of bands at extremal points of energy.

The authors employ a formulation based on pseudo-differential operators in conformal variables, deriving the modulational stability problem through Floquet-Bloch theory. For each bifurcation type, they derive normal forms through direct Puiseux expansions of eigenvalues and justify them rigorously using the Newton polytope method applied to characteristic polynomials. The analysis handles the non-analyticity of the original spectral problem at zero Floquet parameter through careful analytic extension.

Key results include explicit normal form equations for all four bifurcations, with numerically computed coefficients for the first two bifurcation cycles showing excellent agreement between analytical predictions and direct numerical computations of spectral bands. The bifurcation labeled (b), involving tangential intersection of double-degenerate spectral bands, is identified for the first time in this context. This work provides a comprehensive analytical framework explaining the recurrent spectral structure governing the transition from modulational instability of small-amplitude waves to the complex stability landscape of near-limiting Stokes waves.
original_abstract: We study the modulational stability problem for the traveling periodic waves (called Stokes waves) in an infinitely deep fluid by using pseudo-differential operators in conformal variables. We derive the criteria and the normal forms for four bifurcations which are repeated recurrently when the steepness of the Stokes wave is increased towards the highest wave with the peaked profile. The four bifurcations are observed in the following order: (a) new figure-8 bands appearing at each extremal point of speed, (b) degeneration of figure-8 bands resulting in vertical slopes, (c) new circular bands around the origin appearing at each period-doubling bifurcation, and (d) reconnection of figure-$\infty$ bands at each extremal point of energy. Our work uses the analytic theory of Stokes waves developed previously for Babenko's equation. The novelty of our work is the analytic extension of the modulational stability problem for singular pseudo-differential operators in terms of the Floquet parameter. The derivation of the normal form uses some structural assumptions which are known to be true for the Stokes waves. For the first and second bifurcation cycles, we compute numerically with a higher-order accuracy the actual values of wave steepness for which the structural assumptions are satisfied and the numerical coefficients of the normal forms to show the excellent agreement between the normal form theory and the numerical approximations of the spectral bands.

title: Polymer-free van der Waals assembly of 2D material heterostructures using muscovite crystals

original_abstract: The advent of van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures has enabled formation of bespoke materials with atomic precision, where numerous quantum and topological phenomena have already been discovered. This atomic-layer tunability, however, comes at a cost: individual 2D layers must be picked up, moved, and placed in a deterministic manner while keeping their interfaces atomically clean. Recent advances in machine learning and robotics place even stronger emphasis on the deterministic aspect of vdW assembly.
