To this end, solutions are needed where adhesion can be dynamically and deterministically controlled without leaving organic contamination. Here, we present a polymer free transfer technique employing thin muscovite (mica) crystals. Temperature control over mica adhesion enables deterministic pick-up, stacking, and release of 2D materials, while their crystalline, inorganic nature ensures pristine interfaces and suppresses strain. Fully compatible with existing fabrication workflows, this approach enables the assembly of demanding vdW heterostructures, including those with exposed conductive layers, moiré superlattices and suspended membranes. Our method represents a promising strategy for vdW heterostructure fabrication toward its automatization.

title: Improving Molecular Force Fields with Minimal Temporal Information
generated_summary:
This paper introduces FRAMES, a model-agnostic training strategy that distills temporal information from molecular dynamics (MD) trajectories into static energy and force predictors through an auxiliary loss function. The key insight is that minimal temporal information—pairs of just two consecutive frames—is sufficient and optimal for grounding models in physical dynamics, challenging the assumption that longer temporal histories yield better performance.

The methodology employs a shared equivariant GNN backbone (instantiated with Equiformer) that processes atomic configurations into latent representations, coupled with two prediction heads: a primary head for energy and force prediction, and an auxiliary head trained to predict atomic displacements to the next frame from concatenated temporal embeddings. Crucially, the auxiliary head is discarded at inference time, leaving a purely static predictor that requires only a single configuration as input.

Experiments on MD17 and ISO17 benchmarks demonstrate that FRAMES significantly improves the accuracy of the Equiformer baseline, achieving highly competitive results in both energy and force prediction. A systematic ablation varying the number of historical frames (T=1, 2, 3) provides strong empirical evidence for a "less is more" principle: using two frames (encoding velocity information) proves optimal, while three frames (encoding acceleration) degrades performance due to data redundancy—a finding corroborated by both molecular benchmarks and an illustrative spring-mass system.

This work offers a simple, computationally efficient strategy for creating more physically-grounded molecular predictors applicable to any equivariant architecture.
original_abstract: Accurate prediction of energy and forces for 3D molecular systems is one of fundamental challenges at the core of AI for Science applications. Many powerful and data-efficient neural networks predict molecular energies and forces from single atomic configurations. However, one crucial aspect of the data generation process is rarely considered while learning these models i.e. Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulation. MD simulations generate time-ordered trajectories of atomic positions that fluctuate in energy and explore regions of the potential energy surface (e.g., under standard NVE/NVT ensembles), rather than being constructed to steadily lower the potential energy toward a minimum as in geometry relaxations. This work explores a novel way to leverage MD data, when available, to improve the performance of such predictors. We introduce a novel training strategy called FRAMES, that use an auxiliary loss function for exploiting the temporal relationships within MD trajectories. Counter-intuitively, on two atomistic benchmarks and a synthetic system we observe that minimal temporal information, captured by pairs of just two consecutive frames, is often sufficient to obtain the best performance, while adding longer trajectory sequences can introduce redundancy and degrade performance. On the widely used MD17 and ISO17 benchmarks, FRAMES significantly outperforms its Equiformer baseline, achieving highly competitive results in both energy and force accuracy. Our work not only presents a novel training strategy which improves the accuracy of the model, but also provides evidence that for distilling physical priors of atomic systems, more temporal data is not always better.

title: Towards grounded autonomous research: an end-to-end LLM mini research loop on published computational physics

At scale, the agent processes 111 open-access computational physics papers, successfully reproducing approximately three-quarters of in-scope claims within 5% of published values. Notably, it raises substantive methodological critiques on 42% of papers, with 97.7% of these critiques requiring actual computation to surface—demonstrating that critical scientific scrutiny emerges from grounded execution rather than text-level pattern matching. In a depth study on a Nature Communications paper about 2D-material MOSFETs, a single unsupervised agent session produces a six-page publishable Comment with new HSE06 calculations and contact-resistance modeling that revise the paper's headline conclusion at the 5 nm gate-length scale. These findings do not appear in the original peer review.

The authors argue this paradigm is structurally resistant to hallucination because calculations either reproduce physical targets or fail verifiably. The work establishes that current limitations are engineering challenges in the orchestration harness rather than fundamental model deficiencies, paving the way toward fully autonomous physical science research.
original_abstract: Recent autonomous LLM agents have demonstrated end-to-end automation of machine-learning research. Real-world physical science is intrinsically harder, requiring deep reasoning bounded by physical truth and, because real systems are too complex to study in isolation, almost always built on existing literature. We focus on the smallest meaningful unit of such research, a mini research loop in which an agent reads a paper, reproduces it, critiques it, and extends it. We test this loop in two complementary regimes: scale and depth. At scale, across 111 open-access computational physics papers, an agent autonomously runs the read-plan-compute-compare loop and, without being asked to critique, raises substantive concerns on ~42% of papers - 97.7% of which require execution to surface. In depth, for one Nature Communications paper on multiscale simulation of a 2D-material MOSFET, the agent runs new calculations missing from the original and produces, unsupervised, a publishable Comment -- composed, figured, typeset, and PDF-iterated -- that revises the paper's headline conclusion.

title: Learning Parameterized Nonlinear Elasticity on Curved Surfaces
generated_summary:

The methodology employs a fully connected neural network conditioned on spheroidal curvature, defect charge, and Poisson ratio, trained by minimizing a loss function that enforces curvature-dependent equilibrium equations, boundary conditions, and a small subset of ground-truth data. The approach is validated on a symmetry-reduced benchmark of a centered disclination on a spheroidal surface, which retains geometrically nontrivial nonlinear structure despite dimensional reduction.

Key results show that the network accurately reproduces finite element solutions across a three-dimensional parameter space, including parameter combinations excluded from training, demonstrating genuine interpolation rather than memorization. The model remains stable under variations in collocation density and network architecture, though certain architectural configurations exhibit convergence failures.

The significance lies in establishing a scalable, geometry-aware learning framework for nonlinear mechanics on curved surfaces, providing a foundation for extending to fully two-dimensional, multi-defect configurations relevant to understanding viral capsid assembly and other curved elastic networks.
original_abstract: We learn parameterized nonlinear elasticity on curved surfaces using a physics-informed neural network that enforces governing equations and boundary conditions directly through the loss function, enabling a single trained model to represent a continuous family of elastic equilibria across geometric and material parameters. Nonlinear elasticity on curved manifolds underlies the mechanics of crystalline shells, elastic membranes, and viral capsids, where curvature and topological defects determine equilibrium structure and stability. Traditional exact and finite element solvers rely on symmetry reduction and must be reinitialized for each parameter choice, limiting scalability when symmetry is broken or parameters vary. We validate the proposed learning-based solver on a benchmark problem from curved elasticity, namely the one-dimensional single disclination on a spheroidal surface with known exact and numerical solutions. The network accurately reproduces these solutions, including parameter combinations excluded from training, demonstrating generalization across geometry and material regimes. This study establishes a scalable framework for learning nonlinear elastic systems on curved manifolds and lays the groundwork for extensions to fully two-dimensional and multi-defect configurations relevant to protein shells and other curved elastic networks.

title: XANE(3): An E(3)-Equivariant Graph Neural Network for Accurate Prediction of XANES Spectra from Atomic Structures

The architecture employs equivariant message passing with tensor-product interactions and spherical harmonic features to learn symmetry-aware atomic representations. A key design element is absorber-conditioned attention pooling, which identifies atoms most relevant to the absorbing site's spectrum. The spectral readout reconstructs spectra using multi-scale Gaussian basis functions with an optional sigmoidal background, rather than predicting discretized intensities directly. The training objective incorporates first- and second-derivative losses alongside pointwise mean squared error to enforce accurate line-shape reproduction, with a curriculum-based loss annealing strategy for stable optimization. Custom equivariant layer normalization and adaptive gated residual connections preserve geometric information in higher-order tensor features.

Trained on 5,941 FDMNES-simulated Fe K-edge spectra, XANE(3) achieves a test MSE of 1.0 × 10⁻³, accurately reproducing pre-edge features, main edge structure, and post-edge oscillations. Ablation studies confirm the importance of each architectural component. original_abstract: We present XANE(3), a physics-based E(3)-equivariant graph neural network for predicting X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra directly from atomic structures. The model combines tensor-product message passing with spherical harmonic edge features, absorber-query attention pooling, custom equivariant layer normalization, adaptive gated residual connections, and a spectral readout based on a multi-scale Gaussian basis with an optional sigmoidal background term. To improve line-shape fidelity, training is performed with a composite objective that includes pointwise spectral reconstruction together with first- and second-derivative matching terms. We evaluate the model on a dataset of 5,941 FDMNES simulations of iron oxide surface facets and obtain a spectrum mean squared error of $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ on the test set. The model accurately reproduces the main edge structure, relative peak intensities, pre-edge features, and post-edge oscillations. Ablation studies show that the derivative-aware objective, custom equivariant normalization, absorber-conditioned attention pooling, adaptive gated residual mixing, and global background term each improve performance. Interestingly, a capacity-matched scalar-only variant achieves comparable pointwise reconstruction error but reduced derivative-level fidelity, indicating that explicit tensorial channels are not strictly required for low intensity error on this dataset, although they remain beneficial for capturing finer spectral structure. These results establish XANE(3) as an accurate and efficient surrogate for XANES simulation and offer a promising route toward accelerated spectral prediction, ML-assisted spectroscopy, and data-driven materials discovery.

title: On the possibility of chemically driven convection in red giants. Implications for the He-core flash and mixing above the Red Giant Branch Bump
generated_summary:
This study revisits the instability criteria for chemically driven convection and thermohaline mixing in stellar interiors, demonstrating that the criterion commonly used in stellar evolution codes significantly underestimates the conditions under which fast, nearly adiabatic chemically driven convection can develop. The authors derive a new, simplified instability criterion by analyzing an extended mixing length theory (MLT) that incorporates the effects of chemical gradients on convective stability. They apply this framework to two important astrophysical contexts: mixing above the red giant branch bump (RGBB) and mixing below the off-center helium-core flash convective zone in low-mass stars.

For the RGBB, the results show that regions at the base of the convective envelope are only marginally unstable, and the pp-chain reactions cannot sustain sufficient molecular weight inversions once fast mixing develops, suggesting that chemically driven convection alone cannot explain observed extra mixing. Enhanced thermohaline mixing by magnetic fields appears more promising. In contrast, for the helium-core flash, even very small convective elements satisfy the new instability criterion, and the triple-alpha reaction can maintain molecular weight inversions sufficient for steady-state chemically driven convection. This could fundamentally alter understanding of helium-core flash evolution, potentially leading to central ignition and eliminating the helium sub-flashes predicted by standard models. The findings call for a broad reanalysis of inverse chemical gradients across stellar evolution computations.
original_abstract: Turbulent mixing remains one of the primary uncertainties in the modeling of stellar interiors. In stellar evolution simulations, regions where mixing occurs are typically identified using instability criteria. A particularly interesting situation arises when nuclear reactions produce inversions in the mean molecular weight within stellar interiors. Under these conditions, the material can become unstable to either thermohaline or a Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities. We demonstrate that the standard criterion adopted in stellar evolution calculations does not accurately distinguish between these two regimes. We derive an alternative criterion and show that chemically driven convection in stellar interiors might be viable under much smaller mean molecular weight inversions than it is normally assumed. We investigate whether inversions in the mean molecular weight can trigger chemically driven convection above the red giant branch bump (RGBB) or during the helium core flash. We find that the inversion at the base of the convective envelope above the RGBB is too weak and short-lived to sustain steady-state convection. In contrast, rapid carbon production at the base of the He-flash-driven convective zone can maintain a steady chemically driven convective region. This process could significantly alter our understanding of the He-core flash and warrants further study.

title: Quantum Geometry, Fractionalization, and Provability Hierarchy: A Unified Framework for Strongly Correlated Systems
generated_summary:

The methodology involves synthesizing recent experimental and theoretical advances—including the identification of distinct pseudogap phases in twisted WSe₂, realization of fractional Chern insulators in rhombohedral graphene moiré systems, and observation of quantum metric magnetoresistance in oxide interfaces—into a coherent framework. The authors employ analytical theory and density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) numerical verification.

Key results include establishing quantum geometry as an independent tuning knob for Mott transitions beyond conventional bandwidth control; predicting golden ratio scaling (~0.618) of quantum geometry fluctuations at the Mott critical point; identifying a correspondence between fractional charge denominators and quantum geometry subgroup indices following a Fibonacci sequence; classifying strange metal behavior as QMA-hard within a proposed Provability Hierarchy Theorem; and predicting interference oscillations in the nonlinear Hall effect within the pseudogap phase.

The significance lies in providing a unified language—quantum geometry—that explains material diversity among correlated systems, connects fractionalization to geometric structure, and offers concrete experimental predictions testable in moiré material platforms, potentially reshaping the theoretical foundations of condensed matter physics.
original_abstract: Mott physics - the interplay between itinerancy and localization of electrons - is undergoing a paradigm shift from the binary "bandwidth - filling" tuning framework to an intertwining of geometric, topological, and fractionalized degrees of freedom. Based on a series of breakthroughs in 2024 - 2025, this paper proposes five pioneering discoveries: (1) Prediction of the golden-ratio scaling of quantum metric fluctuations near the Mott critical point, supported by functional renormalization group arguments and DMRG numerical verification (phi = 0.618 +/- 0.005); (2) Establishment of a correspondence between the denominator q of fractional Chern insulator charge and the subgroup index of the quantum geometry group, predicting that allowed q values follow the Fibonacci sequence {2,3,5,8,13,...} with specific material realizations; (3) Proposal of the Provability Hierarchy Theorem, classifying critical states like strange metals as "true but unprovable" QMA hard problems, establishing a rigorous connection to the complexity of the Consistency of Local Density Matrices(CLDM) problem; (4) Prediction of interference oscillations in the nonlinear Hall conductance within the pseudo gap phase, induced by geometric phase differences, supported by tight-binding numerical simulations; (5) Unveiling the quantum geometric tensor as a unified descriptor of band geometry and topology. These findings provide an experimentally testable theoretical framework for understanding strongly correlated quantum materials.

title: Why does the wavefunction 'collapse' in relational approaches to quantum mechanics?
generated_summary:
This paper addresses a persistent criticism of relational approaches to quantum mechanics—namely, the difficulty of precisely defining when and how "quantum events" (analogous to wavefunction collapse) occur. The author argues that there is a natural explanation for why such events are inevitable in any relational framework: since a reference system cannot be represented in the description relative to itself, a discontinuity necessarily arises whenever the interaction between the observed system and the reference system becomes significant.

The paper employs conceptual and philosophical analysis of relational quantum mechanics (RQM) and its variants, examining the logical consequences of treating quantum descriptions as fundamentally relational. The author proposes that quantum events should not be understood as discrete, instantaneous occurrences but rather as periods during which the relational description breaks down because the system and reference are interacting too strongly. Since the relevant interactions are continuous, there is no sharp boundary demarcating when a quantum event occurs—it is inherently approximate.

A key implication is that quantum mechanics should be regarded as an approximation valid only when system-reference interactions are sufficiently weak, rather than a complete description of reality. This challenges the standard RQM commitment to the completeness of quantum mechanics and suggests that an underlying absolute reality may exist beyond the quantum formalism. The author thus reframes recent criticisms of relational approaches not as fatal objections but as productive clues pointing toward a richer theoretical framework where relational quantum descriptions approximate a more fundamental, possibly absolute, description of nature.
original_abstract: I argue that there is a straightforward way to understand the occurrence of wavefunction collapses or 'quantum events' in relational approaches to quantum mechanics: we necessarily encounter a discontinuity in our description when a system interacts with the reference relative to which we are describing it, since the reference system cannot be described relative to itself. This makes it clear how recent concerns around quantum events in relational quantum mechanics should be resolved. However, the solution requires accepting that quantum mechanics is not a complete description of all physical facts, and moreover I argue that this is most likely inevitable if we want to be able to give a precise description of quantum events.

title: E-biofuels reduce the cost of achieving emissions targets in hard-to-electrify sectors
generated_summary:
This study investigates the role of e-biofuels—renewable fuels produced by integrating green hydrogen into biomass conversion processes to enhance carbon utilization—in reducing the cost of decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors such as aviation and shipping in Europe.

Using PyPSA-Eur, an open-source sector-coupled European energy system optimization model, the authors introduce four e-biofuel pathways (e-biomass-to-liquid, e-biomethanol, e-bioSNG, and e-biogas-to-methanol) and evaluate their impact across scenarios varying carbon sequestration availability, biomass imports, electrolyzer capacity, and EU renewable fuel mandates. The model co-optimizes capacity expansion and operation across electricity, hydrogen, and gas networks at 39-node spatial resolution with 3-hourly temporal resolution.

Key results show that e-biofuels reduce total system costs across a wide range of carbon sequestration levels, with the greatest savings occurring under intermediate conditions—where biomass availability is moderate and sequestration capacity does not greatly exceed the EU's 2040 target of 250 Mt/year. Unlike conventional biofuels, e-fuels, or fossil fuels, which dominate only under extreme resource assumptions, e-biofuels emerge as the preferred option under more plausible real-world constraints by diversifying the resource base across biomass, renewable electricity, and carbon storage.

The findings highlight e-biofuels as a strategically resilient bridge technology, offering flexibility to adapt investment pathways as uncertainties around hydrogen availability and carbon sequestration resolve, while calling for clearer regulatory frameworks to unlock their deployment.
original_abstract: Renewable liquid fuels are essential for achieving emissions targets for hard-to-electrify sectors such as aviation and shipping. While biofuels and synthetic e-fuels have been well-studied, e-biofuels, produced by adding renewable hydrogen to biomass conversion to better utilise the biogenic carbon, remain understudied and lack a clear role in EU fuel regulations. In this paper, using a sector-coupled European energy system model, we find that e-biofuels are cost-effective to meet stringent emissions targets if biomass availability is limited and fossil fuels are ineligible, either due to limited carbon sequestration capacity or to high renewable fuel mandates. By directly increasing utilisation of biogenic carbon instead of synthesising fuels based on captured $CO_2$, there are savings from fuel production and carbon capture that reduce total system costs by up to 2.7% and liquid fuel costs by more than 10%. Our results highlight the role of e-biofuels as a potential hedge against uncertainty in biomass, hydrogen, and carbon storage availability, as well as evolving policy implementation.

title: A Fast Spectral Formulation of the Multiscale Proper Orthogonal Decomposition
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a fast spectral formulation of the multiscale Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (mPOD), addressing the computational bottlenecks of the classical filter-bank-based implementation. The classical mPOD uses FIR filters to partition the frequency axis into prescribed bands, but the resulting scale-specific correlation matrices are not strictly low-rank, requiring full-order eigenvalue problems at each scale that become prohibitively expensive for large datasets.

The proposed approach replaces FIR filters with spectral masks that enforce strictly disjoint frequency bands. This yields scale-specific correlation matrices that are exactly low-rank, enabling eigenvalue problems to be solved in reduced spectral subspaces whose dimensions correspond only to the non-zero spectral content within each band. Two algorithm variants are presented: a correlation-based version suited for tall, slender data matrices and a data-based version optimized for short, wide matrices.

Verification on synthetic data reveals a trade-off between spectral separation and Gibbs phenomenon mitigation—the fast mPOD exhibits slightly stronger oscillations than the FIR-based formulation but remains far superior to sharp spectral truncation. Application to experimental cylinder wake data at Re = 100 demonstrates that the fast mPOD accurately reproduces the spatial structures and spectral content of the classical formulation, with differences confined to low-energy regions. Computational benchmarks confirm speedups of up to two orders of magnitude, validating theoretical scaling predictions. This advancement enables efficient multiscale analysis of large-scale fluid dynamics datasets while preserving the interpretability and energy-optimality properties of the original mPOD framework.
original_abstract: Multiscale Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (mPOD) decomposes fluid flows into energy-optimal modes within prescribed frequency bands by combining Proper Orthogonal Decomposition with a multiresolution analysis (MRA). In its classical formulation, mPOD relies on a filter bank of finite impulse response (FIR) filters, enabling lossless reconstruction while mitigating Gibbs oscillations and temporal ringing. However, the smooth transition bands required for this purpose introduce partial spectral overlap between adjacent scales and require, for each band, the solution of an eigenvalue problem spanning the full temporal dimension. This work introduces a fast spectral formulation of the mPOD that substantially reduces the computational cost. The proposed approach replaces time-domain FIR filters with compact spectral masks enforcing strictly disjoint frequency supports, thereby exactly decoupling the problem across scales. This leads to a block-diagonal correlation operator in spectral space, so that each band can be treated independently. The resulting eigenvalue problems reduce to small systems whose size depends on the number of active frequencies per band rather than the full time dimension. The approach is validated on a synthetic dataset highlighting spectral windowing effects and on experimental particle image velocimetry (PIV) data of a cylinder wake at Reynolds number \(\mbox{Re} \approx 5000\). In both cases, the proposed formulation accurately recovers the modal structures and singular values of the classical mPOD while reducing the computational cost by orders of magnitude.

title: On the optimal period of spanwise wall forcing for turbulent drag reduction
generated_summary:
This study investigates the physical significance of the optimal oscillation period for spanwise wall forcing in turbulent drag reduction. The authors introduce an extended Stokes layer (ESL) concept that decouples the two key parameters—oscillation period *T* and Stokes layer thickness *δ*—which are inherently linked in conventional oscillating-wall configurations through the relation *δ* ∝ √(*T*).

Using 111 direct numerical simulations of turbulent channel flow at a friction Reynolds number of 400, the authors independently vary *T* and *δ* by supplementing the oscillating-wall boundary condition with a spanwise body force that imposes a prescribed spanwise velocity profile. The forcing amplitude is held constant at *A*⁺ = 12.

The key finding is that the conventionally reported optimal period *T*⁺ ≈ 100 does not reflect an intrinsic turbulence timescale but rather emerges from the constraint coupling *δ* and *T*. When these parameters are varied independently, greater drag reductions and net energy savings are achievable in regions of the (*T*, *δ*) parameter space inaccessible to standard wall oscillations. The optimal ESL configuration features a thinner Stokes layer and shorter period than the conventional optimum, demonstrating that conventional oscillating walls do not fully exploit the drag reduction potential of spanwise forcing.

These results provide new physical insight into the drag reduction mechanism and open pathways toward more effective spanwise forcing strategies that transcend the limitations of simple wall oscillations.
original_abstract: Turbulent channel flow controlled by spanwise wall oscillations is studied using direct numerical simulations to improve how spanwise forcing reduces skin-friction drag. Harmonic wall oscillations generate a periodic transverse Stokes layer whose thickness $δ$ is determined by the forcing period $T$. Although an optimal $T$ that maximizes drag reduction is known to exist, its physical significance remains unclear. To elucidate it, we extend the spanwise Stokes layer by augmenting wall oscillation with an additional spanwise body force. In this formulation, $δ$ and $T$ become decoupled and can be varied independently. The oscillating wall thus appears as a special and suboptimal case of spanwise forcing. Optimal performance is obtained for substantially smaller $T$ and larger $δ$ than those of the classical Stokes layer. For the conditions examined, with Reynolds number and forcing amplitude held fixed, the maximum drag reduction increases by approximately one third, while the maximum net energy saving improves markedly from $-35\%$ to $+16\%$. These findings suggest that drag-reduction strategies based on spanwise forcing deserve renewed scrutiny: wall oscillation represents only one possible actuation method, and not necessarily the most effective one.

title: A hydrodynamic origin of Korteweg stresses from shear-induced horizontal buoyancy
generated_summary:
This paper establishes a formal connection between shear-induced horizontal buoyancy forces in narrow-channel flows and Korteweg stress tensors, demonstrating that quadratic density-gradient stresses can arise from purely hydrodynamic mechanisms rather than molecular-scale interactions.

The authors analyze non-Boussinesq, depth-averaged flows in narrow channels where horizontal density gradients drive internal Ostroumov circulation. By examining the shear-induced buoyancy force that emerges when the Boussinesq approximation is abandoned during depth-averaging, they show that this force can be formally reinterpreted as the divergence of a Korteweg stress tensor. The analysis is restricted to a low-order asymptotic regime appropriate for narrow-channel geometries.

The key finding is that the emergent Korteweg stress tensor is fundamentally non-variational — it cannot be derived from standard Cahn-Hilliard or Ginzburg-Landau energy functionals. The stress coefficients violate the thermodynamic consistency relations identified by Dunn and Serrin, indicating that this represents a purely kinetic phenomenon arising from momentum flux rather than free-energy minimization. Additionally, the authors show that the resulting pressure jump across miscible interfaces exhibits accelerated power-law decay, contrasting with classical surface tension, because the same buoyancy-driven shear generating the stress simultaneously smooths the density gradient.

This work is significant because it identifies a new class of "kinetic" Korteweg stresses outside the classical potential-based framework, offering fresh perspectives on miscible interface mechanics and suggesting that complete descriptions of such stresses in variable-property fluids may require accounting for viscosity gradient dependence.
original_abstract: Recent study \cite{rajamanickam2025shear} of non-Boussinesq fluids in narrow channels identified a novel shear-induced horizontal buoyancy force that emerges upon depth-averaging the Navier--Stokes equations. This note demonstrates that this force is formally equivalent to the divergence of a Korteweg stress tensor. Unlike classical Korteweg stresses, which are typically attributed to molecular-scale cohesive potentials or implemented through assumed constitutive relations, we show that this emergent stress arises purely from self-coupled transport where the internal Ostroumov flow is "enslaved" to the local density gradient. We derive explicit expressions for the effective stress coefficients, revealing a fundamental dependence on the Prandtl number and Grashof number and identifying a transition in the effective internal pressure at $Pr=1/2$, which marks the crossover between the internal inertia of the shear flow and the hydrostatic tilting induced by the shear. This correspondence is contrasted with classical Taylor dispersion, where the absence of self-coupling yields only a uniaxial stress. Our results suggest that quadratic Korteweg-type stresses may be a universal manifestation of sub-scale transport in gradient-driven flows, providing a rigorous macro-scale origin for capillary-like stresses in miscible fluids.

title: And Yet Another FEM-Based Mode Solver for Dielectric Waveguides

This paper presents an open, reproducible finite element method (FEM) mode solver for dielectric optical waveguides, implemented in both MATLAB and Python environments, including cloud-based platforms such as Google Colab. The solver is validated through two case studies: a Si₃N₄ waveguide in SiO₂ cladding and a high-index-contrast rectangular dielectric waveguide. Results are benchmarked against COMSOL Multiphysics, demonstrating relative errors below 0.004% for the first case and below 0.05% for the high-contrast case across all computed modes. Convergence analysis shows systematic error reduction with increasing mesh resolution, with computation times comparable to COMSOL. The mixed element formulation inherently suppresses spurious modes while maintaining computational tractability.

The significance of this work lies in democratizing access to accurate full-vector waveguide mode solving by providing open implementations suitable for research and education, particularly for integrated photonics applications involving complex waveguide geometries where finite-difference methods prove insufficient. Future extensions include adaptive mesh refinement, anisotropic materials, and ring resonator modeling.
original_abstract: We present a full-vector finite element method (FEM) mode solver for dielectric waveguides based on a mixed Nedelec-Lagrange discretization of Maxwell's curl equations in the frequency domain. The formulation combines edge elements for transverse field components with nodal elements for the longitudinal component, enabling accurate modeling of hybrid modes while effectively suppressing spurious solutions. The solver is implemented in both MATLAB and Python with an emphasis on reproducibility, computational efficiency, and accessibility, including compatibility with cloud-based platforms. Numerical validation is performed on representative waveguide structures, demonstrating excellent agreement with COMSOL Multiphysics, with relative errors below 0.05%. Convergence studies confirm the expected accuracy trends with mesh refinement, while highlighting the trade-off between computational cost and precision. The proposed implementation provides a flexible and reliable open-source tool for integrated photonics research and education.

title: Surface Plasmons in the Continuum
generated_summary:
This study addresses the challenge of accurately calculating surface-plasmon resonances (SPRs) in aluminum clusters at energies above the ionization potential, where excited states are embedded in the ionization continuum. The authors demonstrate that standard real-time time-dependent density functional theory (RT-TDDFT) calculations produce unphysical spectral artifacts because electrons excited into continuum states reflect off finite simulation domain boundaries, creating spurious interference patterns that fail to converge with increasing domain size.

To resolve this, the authors implement absorbing boundary conditions via a complex absorbing potential within grid-based RT-TDDFT, effectively simulating the ionization process by preventing electron reflection. The approach is validated against an exact Green's function-based linear-response TDDFT reference using a spherical jellium model, showing excellent agreement. Further validation comes from comparison with an independent linear-response TDDFT method employing multicenter B-spline basis sets specifically designed for scattering problems, which also yields consistent results for the atomistic Al₁₃⁻ cluster.

Key findings include the identification of a broad SPR feature in the far UV with overlaid Fano-type asymmetric fine structures representing well-defined excited states in the continuum. The method successfully captures the evolution from molecular-like discrete excitations in Al₆ to a single broad plasmonic band in Al₃₀₉. This work resolves existing literature discrepancies regarding aluminum cluster spectra and establishes a scalable framework for studying UV-plasmonic materials at the ab initio level.
original_abstract: The interest to foster plasmonic applications at energies in the ultra-violet, has escalated research initiatives in clusters of unconventional plasmonic materials like aluminum and indium,for which the surface-plasmon resonance appears above the ionization potential. Naturally, the quantum mechanical description calls for the incorporation of the ionization process, thereby making the ab initio calculations challenging. We present a robust approach within the time-evolution formalism of the time-dependent density-functional theory to calculate surface plasmon resonance in the continuum of metal clusters. Using the much studied Al$_{13}^-$ as a system of reference, we show that accurate description of the continuum and of the ionization of the cluster allow to capture a broad surface-plasmon in the UV. Application of this approach in aluminum clusters has given the size-dependent evolution from discrete spectral features in Al$_{6}$ to the surface-plasmon in larger clusters in the deep ultra-violet.

title: Subsystem-Resolved Spectral Theory for Quantum Many-Body Hamiltonians

The methodology relies on standard operator norm estimates and spectral perturbation bounds within a tensor product Hilbert space setting. The authors define an interaction norm parameterized by a decay constant that quantifies how interaction terms grow with the size of their support, encoding the influence between distant regions.

The key results establish three main properties. First, subsystem Hamiltonians can be approximated by operators supported on finite neighborhoods, with errors decaying exponentially in neighborhood size. Second, the associated spectra are stable under such truncations. Third, for disjoint subsystems, the spectrum of their union is approximately equal to the sum of the individual spectra, with an error that decays exponentially in the distance between the subsystems. For finite-range interactions, this spectral additivity becomes exact.

The significance of this work lies in demonstrating that spectral properties inherently reflect interaction geometry, providing a principled framework that connects the spatial structure of many-body interactions directly to spectral behavior and enabling region-by-region spectral analysis of complex quantum systems.
original_abstract: We study spectral properties of quantum many-body Hamiltonians through a subsystem-based framework. Given a Hamiltonian of the form $H = \sum_{X \subseteq Λ} Φ(X)$ acting on a tensor product Hilbert space, we associate to each subset $S \subseteq Λ$ a subsystem Hamiltonian $H_S$ and its spectrum $\mathcal{S}(S) = σ(H_S)$. This produces a family of spectra indexed by subsystems, allowing spectral data to be organized according to interaction structure. We show that subsystem Hamiltonians admit local approximations: $H_S$ can be approximated by operators supported on finite neighborhoods with an error bounded by $\|H_S - H_{S,r}\| \le |S| e^{-μr} \|Φ\|_μ$. As a consequence, subsystem spectra are stable under truncation in the sense that $d_H(\mathcal{S}(S), σ(H_{S,r})) \le |S| e^{-μr} \|Φ\|_μ.$ We then prove that for disjoint subsets $S_1, S_2 \subseteq Λ$, the subsystem spectrum is approximately additive: $d_H\big(\mathcal{S}(S_1 \cup S_2), \mathcal{S}(S_1) + \mathcal{S}(S_2)\big) \le (|S_1| + |S_2|) e^{-μD} \|Φ\|_μ,$ where $D = d(S_1, S_2)$. In the finite-range case, this relation becomes exact. The results show that spectral properties reflect the locality of interactions not only at the level of operators, but also at the level of spectra. The framework provides a way to study many-body systems in which interaction geometry directly shapes spectral behavior.

title: Hodge theory for combinatorial projective bundles
generated_summary:

As applications, the authors derive Bloch-Gieseker type injectivity/surjectivity statements for multiplication by Chern classes, and verify new cases of Grothendieck's standard conjecture of Hodge type for projectivizations of globally generated toric vector bundles over fields of positive characteristic—a setting where classical Hodge-theoretic methods are unavailable. original_abstract: We prove the Hard Lefschetz theorem and Hodge-Riemann relations for certain rings which resemble the cohomology rings of projectivizations of globally generated vector bundles over toric varieties. This proves new cases of the standard conjecture of Hodge type and gives Bloch-Gieseker-type results for tautological classes of matroids.

title: A structure-preserving semi-implicit finite volume scheme on vertex-staggered unstructured meshes

The key innovation lies in combining compatible discrete differential operators on primal (triangular) and dual meshes that exactly satisfy the fundamental vector calculus identities—curl of gradient and divergence of curl equal zero—at the discrete level.

The methodology employs a semi-implicit time discretization that treats nonlinear convective terms explicitly while handling the pressure term implicitly, yielding a symmetric positive definite linear system solvable via conjugate gradient methods. Validation through benchmark problems—including the Taylor-Green vortex, Sod shock tube, Gresho vortex, MHD vortex, and solid rotor—confirms that divergence and curl constraints are maintained to machine precision. original_abstract: We present a novel structure-preserving semi-implicit finite volume method on vertex-based staggered meshes for the compatible discretization of first order systems of time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs). The method preserves divergence-free and curl-free vector fields exactly thanks to the compatible vertex-staggered discretization of the state variables on unstructured grids that are constituted by primal Delaunay triangles and their dual polygons. For the weakly compressible Euler equations, the scheme is asymptotic preserving, yielding a consistent discretization of the incompressible limit as the Mach number goes to zero. The new scheme applies to a broad spectrum of PDEs, including the weakly compressible and incompressible Euler and Navier-Stokes equations, the incompressible magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) system, and the incompressible version of the first-order hyperbolic Godunov-Peshkov-Romenski (GPR) model for continuum mechanics. The computational domain is covered by a primal triangular mesh and a dual tessellation made of so-called star polygons. Scalar quantities (pressure, density, viscous stress) are defined at nodes, with pressure updated implicitly in a continuous finite element fashion, yielding a symmetric and positive definite pressure system. Instead, vector fields (velocity, momentum, magnetic and distortion fields) are stored at triangle barycenters and evolved explicitly using a compatible finite volume scheme. Thanks to the semi-implicit discretization, the CFL condition is independent of the sound speed, allowing simulations at low Mach numbers. The fully compatible formulation ensures exactly divergence-free velocity field in the incompressible limit, exactly divergence-free magnetic field for MHD, and exactly curl-free inverse deformation gradient in solid mechanics. The method is validated through a wide set of test cases.

title: Kneser Graphs of Triangulations are Hamiltonian
generated_summary:

The proof employs a purely combinatorial strategy combining three ingredients. First, rotational symmetry of the polygon decomposes the Kneser graph into cycles corresponding to rotation orbits. Second, a sparse guide cycle is constructed from a Hamiltonian cycle of the flip graph on triangulations of a smaller polygon, extended by appending a fixed diagonal ("ear"). This guide cycle meets every rotation orbit while forming an independent set in the Kneser graph. Third, a geometric bridge lemma shows that if two triangulations differ by a single flip, rotating one by a single step makes them disjoint, converting flip-graph transitions into Kneser graph edges between distinct orbits. A greedy algorithm then splices all orbit-cycles into a single Hamiltonian cycle.

The authors also prove that the Kneser graph of the permutohedron contains the kth power of a Hamiltonian cycle for sufficiently large n, contrasting sharply with the associahedron case, which cannot even contain the square of a Hamiltonian cycle. The work suggests a general paradigm—symmetry-based decomposition, guide cycles, and local bridges—for establishing Hamiltonicity in Kneser graphs of combinatorial set systems, with natural extensions to graph associahedra.
original_abstract: For every $n \geq 5$, we show that the Kneser graph of triangulations of a convex $n$-gon contains a Hamiltonian cycle.

title: Guaranteed inf-sup bounds and existence verification for semilinear elliptic problems via nonconforming finite elements
generated_summary:

The methodology centers on a Newton-Kantorovich-type verification theorem adapted for nonconforming schemes. A key innovation is the use of a smoothing operator that maps nonconforming approximations to conforming surrogates, enabling the application of classical fixed-point arguments. The authors derive guaranteed lower bounds on continuous inf-sup constants from computable discrete data through a post-processing technique and a novel approximation estimate for elliptic problems with right-hand sides in negative Sobolev spaces. Additionally, a genericity result establishes that for a dense open set of source terms, all solutions are regular with finite multiplicity, confirming that bifurcations are rare phenomena.

The framework is applied to the stream-function formulation of the two-dimensional stationary Navier-Stokes equations using the Morley finite element method. Numerical experiments on unit square and L-shaped domain benchmarks demonstrate optimal convergence rates and successful certification of solution existence and local uniqueness, with a modified adaptive refinement strategy ensuring mesh size reduction proving essential for sharp inf-sup bounds.

This work significantly broadens the applicability of rigorous verification methods beyond conforming discretizations, enabling certified computations for important fourth-order problems.
original_abstract: A Newton--Kantorovich-type argument enables the a posteriori existence verification of a unique regular root near a computed approximation, purely from computable data. This framework allows for non-selfadjoint problems and extends the existing verification theory to nonconforming discretisations. A key ingredient is a guaranteed lower bound on the continuous inf-sup constant from a quasi-optimal nonconforming discretisation that enables a novel a priori error estimator. All quantities are obtained by post-processing a single discretisation; convergence rates are proved. The theory is applied to a fourth-order formulation of the stationary two-dimensional Navier--Stokes equations and illustrated by numerical experiments.

title: Geometric Decoupling and the Color--Speed Mechanism in Multispeed Stochastic Klein--Gordon Systems
generated_summary:
This paper identifies and rigorously analyzes a "color-speed separation mechanism" in coupled stochastic Klein-Gordon systems on three-dimensional space, where two field components propagate at distinct speeds and are driven by independent space-time white noises. The main contribution is demonstrating that the multispeed structure fundamentally alters the renormalization geometry compared to scalar quadratic stochastic wave equations, eliminating the most singular contraction channel that plagues the scalar theory.

The authors employ a paracontrolled approach to analyze the system's nonlinear interactions. The methodology exploits two key features: the independence of the noise sources (termed "color channels") and the non-resonance arising from differing propagation speeds. In the paracontrolled expansion, four mixed random operators emerge. Cross-color operators have zero contraction by noise independence, while same-color operators necessarily involve different propagation speeds in their Duhamel integrals. Consequently, the problematic "same color, same speed, low-high pure difference" channel—the critical obstruction in scalar theories—never appears.

The key result is an unconditional pathwise random-operator theorem establishing that the random-operator regularity threshold of three-quarters arises as a purely structural consequence of this geometric decoupling. The authors also construct baseline stochastic symbols at their natural distributional regularities, while stating the full local well-posedness theory conditionally on further cubic source smoothing.

The significance lies in revealing that features initially appearing to complicate coupled singular SPDEs—namely multispeed propagation—can instead be leveraged to simplify the renormalization structure, opening pathways for analyzing broader classes of dispersive stochastic systems.
original_abstract: We study a two-component fractional stochastic Klein--Gordon system on $\mathbb{T}^3$ driven by independent space-time white noises. Our main result is the identification of a new color-speed separation principle for the mixed paracontrolled random operators in the multispeed regime. This principle is created by the interaction between probabilistic cancellation, multispeed dispersive phase separation, and the nonlinear random-operator structure generated by the paracontrolled expansion. At the level of the nonlinear expansion, it reorganizes the singular contraction geometry of the mixed random operators: cross-color contraction channels vanish by independence, while the surviving same-color contractions are forced into speed-separated oscillatory interactions and therefore become finite Volterra-type deterministic multipliers. In this way, the multispeed structure does not merely alter the linear phase geometry; it changes the nonlinear singular interaction mechanism itself and regularizes the most singular contraction channels produced by the quadratic coupling. We prove the almost sure pathwise convergence of the centered fluctuation operators and the convergence of the same-color deterministic contractions, with no singular random-operator centering required in the limiting equation. Our analysis identifies $α= \frac{3}{4}$ as the intrinsic structural threshold of the mixed random-operator algebra. In addition, we construct the baseline stochastic lift and formulate a conditional deterministic closure for the full paracontrolled system. These results show that, in coupled singular dispersive SPDEs, multispeed propagation can act as a geometric regularizer precisely through its effect on the nonlinear random-operator structure.

title: One-dimensional non-Hausdorff manifolds and CW complexes
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the topological structure of one-dimensional non-Hausdorff manifolds, establishing a fundamental connection between such manifolds and one-dimensional CW complexes (topological graphs). The central concept involves branch points—pairs of points that cannot be separated by open neighborhoods—and the equivalence relation of chain inseparability, which is the transitive closure of the inseparability relation.

The main result demonstrates that for connected "graph-like" one-dimensional manifolds (those with locally finite branch point sets and countable base on each connected component of Hausdorff points), the quotient space obtained by collapsing chain inseparability classes is an open one-dimensional CW complex. The vertices of this CW complex correspond precisely to the images of branch points under the quotient map. Furthermore, this quotient space is shown to be the minimal Hausdorff factor of the manifold, meaning it satisfies a universal property: any continuous map from the manifold to a Hausdorff space factors uniquely through this quotient.

The authors develop their framework through careful analysis of quotient mappings, Hausdorff closures, and embeddings of open intervals into topological spaces. Several illustrative examples are provided, including the classical line with two origins, the non-Hausdorff letter Y, and more complex configurations, alongside counterexamples showing the necessity of the graph-like condition. This work contributes to the growing study of non-Hausdorff manifolds, which arise naturally as leaf spaces of foliations and have applications in parallel computing and theoretical physics.
original_abstract: This paper studies one-dimensional non-Hausdorff manifolds that are similar to "graphs with split vertices". It is shown that if $M$ is a connected one-dimensional non-Hausdorff manifold such that the set of its "non-Hausdorff" points is locally finite, and each component of its complement has a countable base, then there exists a quotient map $π\colon M \to Γ$ onto an open one-dimensional CW complex, which maps the non-Hausdorff points of $M$ to the vertices of $Γ$. Moreover, $Γ$ is the minimal Hausdorff quotient of $M$, that is, for every continuous map $f\colon M \to N$ into a Hausdorff space $N$, there exists a unique continuous map $\hat{f}\colon Γ\to N$ such that $f = \hat{f} \circ π$.

title: Nonparametric f-Modeling for Empirical Bayes Inference with Unequal and Unknown Variances
generated_summary:
This paper develops a nonparametric empirical Bayes framework for inference in heteroscedastic normal means models where variances are both unequal and unknown. The main contribution is twofold: first, the authors derive a generalized Tweedie-type formula expressing the Bayes estimator in terms of the joint marginal density of observed means and sample variances along with its partial derivatives; second, they introduce a moment generating function (MGF) representation to recover the full posterior distribution of the mean and variance parameters, overcoming a long-standing limitation of f-modeling approaches that were previously restricted to point estimation.

The methodology employs bivariate kernel density estimation of the joint marginal distribution of observed statistics, combined with the MGF-based posterior characterization, enabling unified inference for point estimation, confidence interval construction, and multiple hypothesis testing without specifying any parametric prior distribution.

Theoretical analysis establishes regret bounds for the empirical Bayes estimator and error bounds for posterior approximation. Numerical studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves stable performance across diverse settings, with competitive mean squared error and near-nominal coverage probabilities. Application to baseball batting data reveals that parametric competitors suffer from over-shrinkage for players with low batting averages, while the proposed nonparametric method maintains uniformly reliable inference across all signal strengths.

This framework significantly broadens the scope of f-modeling empirical Bayes methods, offering a theoretically grounded and practically robust foundation for large-scale inference in heterogeneous data environments.
original_abstract: Empirical Bayes methods are widely used for large-scale inference, yet most classical approaches assume homoscedastic observations and focus primarily on posterior mean estimation. We develop a nonparametric empirical Bayes framework for the heteroscedastic normal means problem with unequal and unknown variances. Our first contribution is a generalized Tweedie-type identity that expresses the Bayes estimator entirely in terms of the joint marginal density of the observed statistics and its partial derivatives, extending the classical Tweedie's formula to settings with heterogeneous and unknown variances. Our second contribution is to introduce a moment-generating-function representation that enables recovery of the full posterior distribution within the f-modeling paradigm without specifying or estimating the prior distribution. The resulting method provides a unified framework for point estimation, uncertainty quantification, and hypothesis testing while accommodating arbitrary dependence between means and variances. Simulation studies and real-data analysis demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves accurate shrinkage estimation and reliable posterior inference in heterogeneous data environments.

title: Counting sunflowers with restricted matching number
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the maximum number of sunflowers and the maximum ℓp-norm of codegrees in k-uniform hypergraphs with restricted matching numbers, extending the classical Erdős matching conjecture to counting substructures beyond edges.

The main contributions are two extremal results: for sufficiently large n, among all k-uniform families on n vertices with matching number at most s, the family H_{n,k,s} (consisting of all k-sets containing at least one of s fixed elements) uniquely maximizes both the number of sunflowers S_{k,l}^{k-1} (sunflowers with l petals and core size k−1) and the ℓp-norm of codegrees. Notably, when p = 1, the ℓp-norm result recovers the Erdős matching conjecture for large n.

The methodology centers on stability analysis. The authors first establish that if a k-uniform family with bounded matching number has a sufficiently large ℓp-norm, then its (k−1)-shadow must have large cardinality. Using a stability lemma for the Erdős matching conjecture, they show this shadow decomposes into s trivial intersecting families, which in turn forces the original family to share this structure. The sunflower counting result is then derived by reducing it to the ℓp-norm analysis through an algebraic relationship between sunflower counts and codegrees.

For the special case k = 3, the authors establish a linear threshold n ≥ 7s + 6, improving upon previous bounds. These results generalize earlier work on sunflowers with two petals and ℓ2-norms, providing a unified framework connecting matching number constraints to substructure counting in extremal combinatorics.
original_abstract: For a family $\mathcal{H} \subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}$, a subset $\{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_m\} \subseteq \mathcal{H}$ is called a \textit{matching} of size~$m$ if the sets $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_m$ are pairwise disjoint. The \textit{matching number} of $\mathcal{H}$, denoted by $ν(\mathcal{H})$, is the largest integer~$m$ for which such a matching exists. $\{A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_l\}\subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}$ is said to be a \textit{$k$-uniform sunflower} with $l$ \textit{petals}, if there exists a core set $C\subseteq[n]$ contained in every $A_i$ and $A_i\setminus C$ are pairwise disjoint, for $1\leq i\leq l$. Let $S_{k,l}^{k-1}$ denote the $k$-uniform sunflower with $l$ petals and the core set of size $k-1$. The \textit{codegree} of $E$ in $\mathcal{H}$, denoted by $d_{\mathcal{H}}(E)$, is defined as $d_{\mathcal{H}}(E) =|\{F\in \mathcal{H}:E\subseteq F\}|$. Let the \textit{$\ell_p$-norm} of $\mathcal{H}$ be $co_p(\mathcal{H})= \sum_{E\in \binom{[n]}{k-1}}(d_{\mathcal{H}}(E))^p$. For sufficiently large $n$, we determine the maximum $\ell_p$-norm and the maximum number of sunflowers $S_{k,l}^{k-1}$ for a family $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}$ with matching number $ν(\mathcal{F}) = s$. These results can be viewed as a Turán-type problem (specifically $\mathrm{ex}_k(n, S_{k,l}^{k-1}, M_s)$) and a generalization of the Erdős Matching Conjecture. Furthermore, for the case $k = 3$, we establish a linear threshold for $n$.

title: Betting on Bets: Anytime-Valid Tests for Stochastic Dominance
generated_summary:
This paper develops anytime-valid sequential testing procedures for stochastic dominance (SD) based on e-processes, enabling researchers to continuously monitor accumulating data and stop at any adaptively chosen time while maintaining rigorous type I error control. The main contribution is a comprehensive framework for testing first-order and higher-order SD that is nonparametric, robust to arbitrary dependence between compared random variables, and achieves asymptotic power one under any alternative.

The methodology constructs growth-rate optimal (GRO) e-variables for first-order SD testing and universal portfolio-based e-variables for higher-order SD, combined with adaptive weighting strategies borrowed from online learning. These strategies, particularly exponential weighting, allocate betting capital across thresholds where SD violations may occur, enabling the tests to adapt to unknown non-dominance regions in the data.

Simulation experiments demonstrate that all proposed e-processes maintain valid type I error control under continuous monitoring, including under maximal anti-monotonic dependence. Adaptive GRO e-processes with exponential weights consistently achieve the highest statistical power, particularly when non-dominance regions are small or misaligned with initial search intervals. Compared to classical resampling-based SD tests, which fail to control error under optional stopping, the proposed methods achieve competitive or superior rejection times while providing anytime-valid guarantees.

This work represents a significant advance for sequential decision-making applications—such as clinical trials, A/B testing, and economic policy evaluation—where practitioners need to compare uncertain prospects as data accumulates over time.
original_abstract: How can we monitor, in real time, whether one uncertain prospect has any upside over another? To answer this question, we develop a novel family of sequential, anytime-valid tests for stochastic dominance (SD; also known as stochastic ordering), a classical and popular notion for comparing entire distribution functions. The problem is distinct from the popular problem of testing for dominance in means, which would not capture distributional differences beyond the first moment. We first derive powerful, nonparametric e-processes that quantify evidence against the null hypothesis that one prospect is dominated by another. For first-order SD, these e-processes are constructed as a mixture of asymptotically growth-rate optimal e-variables and yield a test of power one. The approach further generalizes to sequential testing for SD beyond the first order, including any higher-order SD. Empirically, we demonstrate that the resulting sequential tests are competitive with existing non-sequential SD tests in terms of power, while achieving validity under continuous monitoring that existing methods do not. Finally, we sketch the complementary and challenging problem of testing the non-SD null hypothesis, which asks whether a prospect has a definite upside, and describe the conditions under which we can derive a nontrivial anytime-valid test.

title: Does PCA Work for Rough Functional Data?
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the reliability of functional principal component analysis (FPCA) when applied to rough functional data, where eigenvalues of the covariance operator decay slowly and the effective rank grows proportionally with sample size. The authors introduce a spiked covariance model that explicitly accounts for functional roughness, combining a small number of spiked eigenvalues with a continuum of bulk eigenvalues characterized by a decay function.

The key theoretical contribution is the identification of a critical phase transition in FPCA performance. When spiked eigenvalues fall below a critical threshold determined by the bulk eigenvalue structure (subcritical regime), empirical eigenvalues and eigenfunctions become asymptotically uninformative about their population counterparts—eigenfunctions are effectively orthogonal to the true ones. In the supercritical regime, empirical estimators remain informative but exhibit persistent bias. The authors derive explicit asymptotic formulas for estimation errors in both regimes and develop an eigengap ratio test statistic to distinguish informative from uninformative components in practice.

The methodology combines tools from functional data analysis, random matrix theory, and generic chaining techniques. Empirical validation uses temperature data from Hohenpeissenberg and streamflow data from the Ninnescah River, demonstrating severe FPCA instability consistent with theoretical predictions. Monte Carlo simulations confirm the phase transition phenomena. These findings have significant implications for FDA practice, as they reveal fundamental limitations of FPCA for rough data and caution that pre-smoothing does not straightforwardly resolve these issues.
original_abstract: Functional data analysis is concerned with the analysis of infinite-dimensional data functions. Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) is a key method to obtain finite-dimensional summaries. Consistency of FPCA has been theoretically established for sufficiently regular data functions. However, empirical evidence shows that FPCA can become severely inconsistent when the underlying functions are too rough. This paper provides the first theoretical explanation for this phenomenon. We propose a model that explicitly captures the roughness of functional data and allows us to quantify the resulting bias of FPCA, depending on the functional roughness. The model undergoes a phase transition marking the point at which FPCA becomes entirely uninformative. Based on these probabilistic results, we discuss diagnostic tests for informative principal components. As an additional contribution, we derive results on spectral statistics that may serve as a foundation for goodness-of-fit tests for rough functional data. Mathematically, our approach combines recent advances in random matrix theory and generic chaining with tools from FDA. We illustrate the effects of roughness on FPCA using simulations, as well as climate and environmental datasets.

title: Anti-Ramsey numbers for cancellative configurations in p-graphs
generated_summary:
This paper investigates anti-Ramsey numbers for cancellative configurations in p-uniform hypergraphs, determining the maximum number of colors in edge-colorings of complete hypergraphs that avoid rainbow copies of cancellative patterns. A p-graph is cancellative if it contains no distinct edges A, B, C satisfying the symmetric difference condition A△B = A△C.

The main contribution is a complete determination of the anti-Ramsey number for rainbow cancellative configurations for all uniformities p ≥ 3. The authors prove that ar(n, F^(p)) = ⌊n/p⌋ + 1 for n ≥ p + 1, establishing an exact linear answer and characterizing all extremal colorings. The methodology combines structural analysis of forbidden subhypergraph families with careful case arguments showing that rainbow cancellative colorings must avoid certain star-like configurations.

For the 3-uniform case, the authors decompose the cancellative family into two specific configurations, F₄ and F₅, and prove a surprising structural result: in complete 3-graphs, forbidding rainbow F₅ automatically forbids rainbow F₄, implying that ar(n, F₅) = ⌊n/3⌋ + 1. For the more challenging F₄ configuration, which exhibits quadratic behavior, the authors improve known bounds using design-theoretic constructions based on partial Steiner triple systems and projective geometry, achieving stronger lower bounds particularly when n = 2^s − 1.

These results significantly advance the understanding of anti-Ramsey phenomena in hypergraphs, an area where exact results remain scarce compared to the graph setting, and reveal interesting connections between extremal combinatorics and combinatorial design theory.
original_abstract: We study edge-colorings of the complete $p$-graph on $n$ vertices that contain no three edges $A,B,C$ of distinct colors such that the symmetric difference of $A$ and $B$ is contained in $C$. For $p\ge3$ and $n\ge p+1$, we show that every such coloring contains at most $1+\floor{n/p}$ colors and characterize the extremal colorings, generalizing a theorem of Erdős, Simonovits and Sós. %\cite{erdos1975}. When $p=3$, the condition $A\triangle B\subseteq C$ implies $|A\triangle B|=2$, and the three edges necessarily form a copy of $F_4\coloneqq\{abc,abd,bcd\}$ or $F_5\coloneqq\{abc,abd,cde\}$. For $n\ge5$, we show that every rainbow $F_5$-free edge-coloring is rainbow cancellative. For rainbow $F_4$-free colorings, we construct colorings with $m(n)+1$ colors for all $n\ge4$, where $m(n)$ is the size of a maximum partial Steiner triple system of order $n$ and satisfies $m(n)=n^2/6+O(n)$, improving the linear lower bound by Budden and Stiles. %\cite{budden}. Moreover, for $n=2^s-1$, we obtain $\ar(n,F_4)\ge m(n)+n^2/42+o(n^2)=4n^2/21+o(n^2)$ via a construction based on independent sets in the Grassmann graph. We also prove that $\ar(n,F_4)\le (5n^2-8n)/21$ for $n\ge4$, improving the quadratic coefficient in the upper bound of Budden and Stiles from $1/4$ to $5/21$.

title: Gauging the Categorical Connes' $\tildeχ(M)$
generated_summary:
This paper develops a gauging framework for the categorical Connes' invariant χ̃(M), a unitary braided tensor category constructed from bimodules over a II₁ factor M that generalizes Connes' classical group-theoretic invariant χ(M). The gauging procedure, realized through group equivariantization and deequivariantization, provides a categorical generalization of Connes' short exact sequence relating approximately inner and centrally trivial automorphisms.

The main technical results establish that for an outer action of a finite group G on a McDuff II₁ factor M, the representation category of a quotient group G/KL embeds as a unitary braided full subcategory of χ̃(M⋊G), and the deequivariantization of χ̃(M⋊G) decomposes as a G/K-crossed braided tensor category. The author proves that invertible liftable objects in this deequivariantization correspond precisely to the intersection of G-centrally trivial and G-approximately inner automorphisms modulo inner automorphisms, completing the categorical generalization.

As a key application, the author computes χ̃(M) for countable infinite spatial tensor products of non-Gamma II₁ factors with entry-wise group actions, showing χ̃(M⋊G) ≅ Rep(G). This demonstrates that any finite group's representation category can be realized as χ̃(M) for some McDuff II₁ factor, yielding examples where χ̃(M) is not modular. Notably, this provides a negative answer to the categorical generalization of Connes' conjecture relating McDuff and s-McDuff factors, showing that trivial χ̃(M) does not imply s-McDuff.
original_abstract: We prove that if a finite group $G$ acts outerly on a McDuff $\rm II_1$ factor $M$, then $\mathsf{Rep}(G/KL)$ is a braided monoidal full subcategory of the categorical Connes' $\tildeχ(M\rtimes G)$ defined in arXiv:2111.06378, where $K$ and $L$ are the centrally trivial and approximately inner parts in $G$ respectively. When $L$ is trivial, we give an explicit formula for the $G/K$-gauging procedure on $\tildeχ(M\rtimes G)$. This is the categorical generalization of Connes' short exact sequence on $χ(M\rtimes G)$. Using this machinery, for any finite group $G$, we construct a McDuff $\rm II_1$ factor $M$, whose $\tildeχ(M)$ is braided equivalent to $\mathsf{Rep}(G)$. This is the first example of a braided fusion category which is not modular as $\tildeχ$.

title: Direct Problem for Gas Diffusion in Polar Firn with Variable Coefficients
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the direct problem of gas diffusion in polar firn (the upper compacted snow layers of ice sheets), extending a previously studied model by allowing both the effective diffusion coefficient D(z) and the average volume fraction of open pores f(z) to be variable, positive functions that may degenerate at the firn's lower boundary. In this paper, we assume both the diffusion coefficient D(z) and the volume fraction f(z) are functions. The difficulty in this problem, both theoretically and computationally, arises from the fact that D(z) and f(z) may be zero at bottom of the firn. To handle such degeneracy, we defined appropriate weighted Sobolev spaces and used Lion's theorem to prove existence and uniqueness of the semi-variational formulation of the Firn PDE. A full discrete system is obtained through a P1 Finite element Galerkin procedure in space and an Euler-Implicit scheme in time. Sufficient conditions for the existence and uniqueness of the solution for the discrete system are obtained.

Our framework not only includes all recent results but also provides many new results. We consider two, slightly different, multigrid operators. The first one is the natural generalization of the error operator in the HPD case. The second operator is simpler to apply and has been studied before. However, an additional condition for the smoother $M^{-1}A$ is needed, which is in our terminology the $B$-normality. We explain the differences and similarities of both operators in detail and show, why the extra condition is needed. We consider arbitrary interpolation and restriction operators that result in $B$-orthogonal coarse-grid corrections and give sharp estimates for the norm of the error propagation matrices for the two-grid methods. We also show, that the norms are decreasing if we increase the size of the coarse space. Moreover, we are able to extend the landmark $V$-cycle bound by McCormick to the nonsymmetric case.

original_abstract: This paper investigates the $H_{2}/H_{\infty}$ control problem for linear stochastic differential systems under partial observation. Unlike existing studies that assume full state accessibility, we consider the scenario where the controller has access only to an observation process. The objective is to design a controller that balances the $H_2$ performance criterion with the $H_\infty$ robustness requirement under worst-case disturbances, formulated as a nonzero-sum differential game. Using the Kalman filtering method, we derive the corresponding optimal filtering equation. Furthermore, a Stochastic Bounded Real Lemma under the partial observation framework is established, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the $H_\infty$ robustness constraint. We also show the connection between the existence of a Nash equilibrium and the solvability of the cross-coupled Riccati equations, and illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach through a numerical example involving an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV).

title: Fast Algorithm For Solving Time-dependent Multiscale radiative transport Equation

original_abstract: When solving the time-dependent radiative transport equation (RTE), implicit time discretization is often employed for its robustness and stability. This results in a sequence of steady-state RTEs with identical cross-sections but varying source terms, whose repeated solution is computationally costly. To address this, we first apply the adaptive tailored finite point scheme (TFPS) for spatial discretization. This scheme exploits prior knowledge of the background media's optical properties to adaptively compress the angular domain, constructing a compressed linear system. A key feature is its ability to reconstruct the layer structure after compression, faithfully capturing the variance at the layer. We then use the Recursive Skeleton Method (RSM) to obtain an explicit multilevel decomposition of the inverse discrete operator, which is reused for all steady-state solutions. title: Maximum principle and local stability for a class of coupled nonlinear thermo--reaction--phase systems

original_abstract: We study a nonlinear coupled system of partial differential equations arising from thermo--reaction--phase models. The system combines a heat diffusion equation, temperature-dependent chemical reactions of Arrhenius type, and a phase variable, and is formulated as a strongly coupled parabolic problem with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. We first establish a maximum principle ensuring the positivity of the temperature on a suitable time interval, as well as the invariance of the physically admissible domain. In particular, we prove that the internal variables remain in the interval [0,1]. We then analyse the asymptotic behaviour of the system in the free regime, that is, in the absence of external forcing. By introducing a relative energy functional and exploiting the structure of the coupling terms, we obtain local asymptotic stability of a homogeneous stationary state. original_abstract: We develop an unconditionally energy-stable tensor-product space-time discretization framework for the solution of a linear kinetic transport equation in one space dimension. Our numerical discretization is based on the well-known technique of micro-macro decomposition which results in a system of balance laws for equilibrium and non-equilibrium quantities and facilitates preservation of the asymptotic limit for vanishing scaling parameters at the discrete level. We prove fully discrete stability and asymptotic preservation for general spatial and temporal discretizations having the summation-by-parts property. A new provably energy-stable Dirichlet boundary treatment for the micro-macro decomposed system is developed based on the introduction of simultaneous approximation terms. title: On the induction functor from group algebras to distribution algebras

original_abstract: Let $G$ be a reductive algebraic group scheme defined over ${\mathbb F}_{p}$ and $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p$. title: Modeling dependency between operational risk losses and macroeconomic variables using Hidden Markov Models

original_abstract: Predicting future operational risk losses gives rise to a significant challenge due to the heterogeneous and time-dependent structures present in real-world data.
