original_abstract: The quadratic assignment problem (QAP) is a fundamental NP-hard task that poses significant challenges for both traditional heuristics and modern learning-based solvers. Existing QAP solvers still struggle to achieve consistently competitive performance across structurally diverse real-world instances. To bridge this performance gap, we propose PLMA, an innovative permutation learning framework. PLMA features an efficient warm-started MCMC finetuning procedure to enhance deployment-time performance, leveraging short Markov chains to anchor the adaptation to the promising regions previously explored. For rapid exploration via MCMC over the permutation space, we design an additive energy-based model (EBM) that enables an $O(1)$-time 2-swap Metropolis-Hastings sampling step. Moreover, the neural network used to parameterize the EBM incorporates a scalable and flexible cross-graph attention mechanism to model interactions between facilities and locations in the QAP. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PLMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across various benchmarks. In particular, PLMA achieves a near-zero average optimality gap on QAPLIB, exhibits remarkably superior robustness on the notoriously difficult Taixxeyy instances, and also serves as an effective QAP solver in bandwidth minimization.

title: A Benchmark of 25 Nonlinear Functions with Domain-Induced Discontinuity for Global Optimization
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the CPC Benchmark, a suite of 25 challenging nonlinear functions featuring domain-induced discontinuities, designed to address the inadequacy of existing benchmark suites for evaluating global optimization algorithms. Unlike traditional discontinuous benchmarks that rely on piecewise definitions or step functions, the CPC functions contain discontinuities arising from intrinsic mathematical structures—such as logarithmic, fractional power, and reciprocal terms—that create fragmented feasible regions within the search space.

The authors establish a taxonomy classifying discontinuities into four categories: numerically induced pseudo-discontinuity, piecewise structural discontinuity, stepwise quantization discontinuity, and domain-induced discontinuity. Six representative optimization algorithms spanning deterministic, stochastic, gradient-based, and gradient-free paradigms—including Branch & Bound, Genetic Algorithm, Simulated Annealing, BFGS with multi-start, GPSO, and UGO—are evaluated across all 25 functions with independent solution verification using high-precision arithmetic.

Results demonstrate that traditional discontinuous benchmarks are easily solved by most algorithms, whereas the CPC functions produce substantial performance differentiation. Gradient-based methods perform particularly poorly, with BFGS achieving no global solutions. Key challenges include extremely low feasible ratios, precision sensitivity near feasibility boundaries, and implicit constraints that algorithms must infer autonomously. The benchmark reveals that domain-induced discontinuities pose fundamentally different challenges than conventional discontinuities, providing a more discriminative and realistic testbed for advancing global optimization algorithm development and evaluation.
original_abstract: A benchmark of 25 nonlinear optimization problems with domain-induced discontinuity is proposed to support the performance evaluation of global optimization algorithms under feasibility-scarce and structurally discontinuous landscapes. Referred to as the CPC Benchmark (Challenging Problems for Computation), the test suiteconsists of functions that are continuous on their natural domains, while infeasible regions and undefined evaluations are implicitly embedded in the objective, creating substantial challenges for global minimization. Six representative algorithms from diverse methodological paradigms are assessed to examine the structural complexity and discriminative capability of the benchmark. Numerical results show that many functions possess extremely small feasible regions and strong precision sensitivity near feasibility boundaries, complicating initialization, feasibility discovery, and reliable objective assessment. The findings demonstrate that the CPC benchmark provides clear discriminative power across algorithmic paradigms and offers a rigorous, software-oriented testbed for advancing research in global optimization.

title: Carathéodory Number in Cycle Convexity
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the Carathéodory number in cycle convexity, a graph convexity notion introduced by Araújo et al. in 2018 where a set is convex if no vertex outside it forms a cycle with vertices inside it. The Carathéodory number of a graph measures the maximum size of a Carathéodory independent set—a set where no vertex belongs to the convex hull of the remaining vertices.

The authors establish both computational hardness and structural results. Their primary complexity-theoretic contribution demonstrates that deciding whether the Carathéodory number of a graph is at least a given integer k is NP-complete, even when restricted to bipartite graphs. The reduction is constructed from the One-In-Three 3-SAT problem.

On the positive side, the paper derives constant upper bounds on the Carathéodory number for several graph classes, including forests (at most 2), cycles, complete graphs, complete multipartite graphs, split graphs, and P₄-sparse graphs, all yielding polynomial-time algorithms. The authors characterize graph families achieving Carathéodory number n−1, showing these comprise precisely the cycles Cₙ, and introduce a family achieving n−2. Additionally, they establish results for graph products, including strong, lexicographic, and Cartesian products.

The methodology combines structural analysis of Carathéodory independent sets—proving properties such as inducing forests and containing no leaves in their hulls—with classical complexity-theoretic reductions. These results advance understanding of cycle convexity parameters and contribute to the broader study of graph convexities and their algorithmic aspects.
original_abstract: Let $G$ be a graph and $S \subseteq V(G)$. In the cycle convexity, we say that $S$ is \textit{cycle convex} if for any $u\in V(G)\setminus S$, the induced subgraph of $S\cup\{u\}$ contains no cycle that includes $u$. The \textit{cycle convex hull} of $S$, denoted by $\hullc (S)$, is the smallest cycle convex set containing $S$. A set $S \subseteq V(G)$ is said to be \textit{Carathéodory independent} if there exists a vertex $u \in \hullc(S) $ such that $u \notin\displaystyle \bigcup_{a \in S} \hullc (S \setminus \{a\}) $, and the Carathéodory number $\car(G)$ is the maximum size of such a set. In this paper, we prove that given a graph $G$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, deciding whether $\car(G) \geq k$ is \NP-complete, even when $G$ is bipartite. On the other hand, we derive exact values and constant upper bounds for several graph classes, leading to polynomial-time algorithms. Some of them include forests, cycles, complete graphs, complete multipartite, split, and $P_4$-sparse graphs. In addition, we present a characterization of $n$-vertex graphs $G$ with extremal values near to $n$, including $\car(G) = n-1$ and $\car(G) = n-2$. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the Carathéodory number under graph products such as the strong, lexicographic, and Cartesian products.

title: Vertex misalignment and changepoint localization in network time series
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how vertex misalignment affects changepoint localization in time series of networks, representing the first systematic study of label error impacts in this context. The authors consider networks governed by latent position processes, where vertices have unobserved low-dimensional vectors determining connection probabilities, and examine how losing vertex correspondence across time degrades the ability to detect distributional changes.

The methodology centers on two tractable models representing extreme cases: the "London" model, where changepoint signal resides in marginal distributions of latent positions, and the "Atlanta" model, where signal depends on joint distributions across time. The authors employ Euclidean mirror methodology—constructing dissimilarity matrices between time-indexed networks and embedding them via classical multidimensional scaling—alongside Wasserstein distances, average degree statistics, and graph matching procedures to attempt changepoint recovery under varying degrees of vertex shuffling.

Key results demonstrate that in the London model, changepoint localization remains robust regardless of vertex misalignment, with marginal-based metrics (Wasserstein distance, average degree) performing comparably or better than alignment-dependent methods. In the Atlanta model, even modest shuffling (beyond approximately 15% of vertices) destroys changepoint signal irrecoverably, and graph matching or optimal transport fail to restore it.

These findings provide crucial practical guidance: practitioners should assess whether signals of interest reside in marginal or joint distributions, explore multiple dissimilarity measures, and exercise caution when applying graph matching to recover lost alignments, as recovered correspondences may capture only marginal information.
original_abstract: Inference for time series of networks often relies on accurate vertex correspondence between network realizations at different times. In practice, however, such vertex alignments can be misspecified or unknown. We study the impact of vertex alignment on changepoint localization for dynamic networks through two illustrative models, each with a similar changepoint, with the key distinction being whether changepoint information is contained in marginal or joint distributions of the time-varying latent positions. We compare localization techniques ranging from the simple network statistic of average degree to the modern procedure of Euclidean mirrors. In one model, vertex misalignment causes little error, and in the other, it impairs localization in ways that cannot be corrected through graph matching or optimal transport, which we show are closely related in this setting. Our results demonstrate that robust network inference necessitates reckoning with the subtle interplay of marginal and joint information in the observed network time series.

title: A critical note on back-and-forth Data Assimilation Nudging Algorithm
generated_summary:
This paper critically examines the Back-and-Forth Nudging (BFN) data assimilation algorithm, which attempts to recover initial conditions of dynamical systems by iteratively nudging forward-in-time and backward-in-time equations toward sparse spatial observational data. The authors adapt the Azouani-Olson-Titi continuous data assimilation framework to the BFN setting and systematically test it across multiple systems: the Lorenz 1963 model, heat equation, linear transport equations, Burgers equations, 2D Navier-Stokes equations, and Korteweg-de Vries equations.

The methodology combines analytical counterexamples with extensive numerical experiments. The authors construct cases where distinct initial conditions produce identical sparse observational data, proving that initial state recovery is mathematically impossible under low-mode observations. They also introduce a Voigt-regularized BFN variant to address the ill-posedness of backward-in-time evolution in dissipative systems.

Key results demonstrate that BFN succeeds only when the full solution is observed at every spatial point—a scenario rendering data assimilation redundant. Under realistic sparse observations, the algorithm fails to reconstruct unobserved components and high-frequency modes, reaching persistent error floors. While Voigt regularization stabilizes backward iterations and outperforms diffusive BFN by introducing less bias in observed scales, it cannot recover unobserved spectral content.

These findings expose a fundamental limitation of BFN for practical applications, where only incomplete spatial observations are available, suggesting the community should reconsider its applicability for initial state reconstruction from sparse data.
original_abstract: This work investigates the effectiveness of the Back-and-Forth Nudging (BFN) data assimilation algorithm, specifically its performance when employing the Azouani-Olson-Titi (AOT) continuous data assimilation downscaling nudging algorithm, for recovering initial conditions of dissipative dynamical systems. Contrary to previous reports in the literature, we show that, for several systems of interest, one can construct initial conditions that BFN cannot reliably recover. Our key finding is the construction of infinitely many distinct solutions for certain dissipative systems that share identical spatially sparse observational data. Since these observations are indistinguishable, no data assimilation method relying only on them can differentiate between these solutions or recover the correct initial condition. We illustrate these pathological initial conditions for the Lorenz 1963 model and several 1D partial differential equations: the heat equation, viscous linear transport, and viscous and inviscid Burgers equations. Our analytical results are supported by numerical simulations. To address the numerical ill-posedness of backward-in-time iterations, an essential step of BFN for dissipative models, we introduce a regularized backward step, the Voigt-regularized BFN (VBFN). We investigate its performance for the 2D Navier-Stokes equations and the viscous 1D KdV equation, comparing it with standard BFN and Diffusive BFN (dBFN). While VBFN improves numerical stability and reduces model bias relative to dBFN, it still cannot reconstruct the unobserved fine spatial scales of the reference solution. This reinforces our main conclusion: even with regularization, BFN-type algorithms are limited in recovering the full state, and in particular the initial data, from sparse spatial observations.

title: A posteriori error analysis, Pod-Deim reduced order geometrically parametrized models and unfitted FEMs
generated_summary:

The authors develop three complementary error estimators: DEIM approximation quality indicators measuring matrix and vector interpolation errors, dual-norm residual estimators (plain and Jacobi-preconditioned variants), and POD tail energy bounds. The methodology employs CutFEM with Nitsche boundary conditions on a fixed background mesh, enabling parameter-dependent domain geometries (elliptical domains) without remeshing. A key theoretical contribution is proving uniform coercivity of the CutFEM bilinear form with an explicit coercivity constant, and demonstrating that ghost-penalty degrees of freedom contribute zero residual for true solutions, necessitating restriction of estimators to active degrees of freedom.

The ROM achieves approximately 4× speedup over the full-order model with consistent results across independent random runs.

This work addresses a previously open problem in certified reduced order modeling for unfitted discretizations, providing essential tools for reliable ROM deployment in problems with parameter-dependent geometries.
original_abstract: We develop and analyze a posteriori error estimators for a proper orthogonal decomposition-discrete empirical interpolation method (Pod-Deim) reduced order model applied to a parametric Poisson equation posed on a parameter-dependent domain defined by a level-set function. The full-order discretisations employ a cut finite element method (Cutfem) with Nitsche boundary conditions and ghost-penalty stabilization. Three complementary estimators are proposed: (i) Deim approximation quality indicators for the stiffness matrix and force vector, which are constant in the number of Pod modes, (ii) dual-norm residual estimators in both plain and Jacobi-preconditioned form, and (iii) a Pod tail-energy indicator. A rigorous theoretical framework is established, comprising a uniform coercivity result for the Cutfem bilinear form, an active-dof residual bound that accounts for ghost-penalty degrees of freedom, a combined a posteriori bound, and sharp effectivity analysis for the residual estimators. The key theoretical finding is that the large observed effectivity indices are explained by ghost-penalty degree-of-freedom inflation, and that restricting the residual to active degrees of freedom is predicted to reduce effectivity. Numerical experiments on a parametric ellipse domain with semi-axes confirm the theoretical predictions, achieve significant online speedup, and demonstrate algebraic convergence of the true error alongside exponential decay of the residual estimators.

title: On Threshold Compatibility Graphs
generated_summary:
This paper introduces (k,t)-threshold-PCGs as a unifying framework for studying generalizations of Pairwise Compatibility Graphs (PCGs). In this model, vertices are declared adjacent when at least t out of k underlying PCG predicates accept the pair. This single definition subsumes ordinary PCGs (k=1, t=1), k-OR-PCGs (t=1), and k-AND-PCGs (t=k), connecting previously parallel lines of research.

The authors establish a sharp dichotomy in the model's expressive power. When the number of predicates grows with graph size, universality holds: every n-vertex graph is an (n,t)-threshold-PCG for all valid thresholds. Conversely, for any fixed k, the union of all threshold classes across all thresholds has asymptotic density zero among all graphs, demonstrating structural restrictiveness. The paper further shows that threshold combinations are substantially more expressive than multi-interval representations, proving that for sufficiently large k, k-OR-PCG strictly contains k-interval-PCG. Explicit obstruction families are constructed using set-system incidence graphs, yielding concrete lower bounds for threshold representations and infinite families outside low-level threshold classes. For the conjunction setting, the authors establish a strict hierarchy—k-AND-PCG is properly contained in (k+1)-AND-PCG—and demonstrate that k-AND-PCG classes are not closed under complementation.

These results demonstrate that threshold-PCGs provide a robust organizing framework that is simultaneously expressive enough to unify existing PCG variants and rigid enough to admit strong structural theorems, hierarchy results, and explicit obstructions, advancing the understanding of tree-distance graph representations.
original_abstract: Pairwise Compatibility Graphs (PCGs) form a tree-metric graph class that originated in phylogeny and has since attracted sustained interest in graph theory. Several natural generalizations have been proposed in order to overcome the expressive limitations of classical PCGs, including $k$-interval-PCGs, $k$-OR-PCGs, and $k$-AND-PCGs. In this paper, we introduce $(k,t)$-threshold-PCGs, a threshold-based framework that unifies these generalized notions: adjacency is determined by whether at least $t$ among $k$ underlying PCG predicates accept the vertex pair. We investigate the expressive power of this model from both constructive and asymptotic viewpoints. On the positive side, we show that every graph on $n$ vertices is a $(n,t)$-threshold-PCG for every $1 \le t \le n$. On the negative side, we prove that for every fixed pair $(k,t)$, the class of $(k,t)$-threshold-PCGs is asymptotically rare among all graphs. As a consequence, we obtain sharp separations from previously studied models, including a strict expressive gap relative to $k$-interval-PCGs. We also study explicit obstruction families through incidence graphs and derive additional structural consequences for the conjunction case, including the strictness of the $k$-AND-PCG hierarchy and the failure of closure under complement.

title: On Uniqueness of Mock Theta Functions
generated_summary:
This paper presents a new method for proving the uniqueness of mock theta functions when continued across their natural boundary on the unit circle in the complex plane. The work addresses a fundamental challenge in the theory of mock modular forms: how to uniquely extend these functions beyond the unit disk where their q-series converge.

The authors employ a framework based on resurgent asymptotics, where the key analytic objects are Mordell-Appell integrals rather than the q-series themselves. These integrals admit representations as Laplace transforms of resurgent kernels in the Borel plane, enabling analytic continuation through the natural boundary. Near Stokes lines, the continued integrals decompose canonically into q-series and q₁-series components, a splitting determined uniquely by the singularity structure of the resurgent kernel.

The central principle is a "resurgent permanence of relations": the modular equations satisfied by the analytically continued integrals are preserved by exactly one set of mock theta functions, establishing uniqueness. The authors provide independent proofs of uniqueness for order 3 and order 5 mock theta functions using elementary tools from analysis and number theory, overcoming limitations of previous approaches that relied on Hauptmoduls or special features of low-order cases.

The significance of this work is twofold: it establishes a rigorous uniqueness framework applicable to broader classes of mock theta functions, and it connects to physical applications in Chern-Simons theory, where crossing the natural boundary corresponds to orientation reversal of three-dimensional manifolds, linking topological invariants of orientation-reversed manifolds.
original_abstract: We develop a resurgent approach to the problem of unique continuation of mock theta functions across their natural boundary. The starting point is the representation of the associated Mordell-Appell integrals as Laplace transforms of resurgent functions, which serve as the primary analytic objects. By rotating the Laplace contour by $π$, i.e. onto the Stokes line, one obtains, in all known cases, the mock-modular relations between the Mordell-Appell integrals and the corresponding unary series in $\hat q=e^{-πi τ}$ and $\hat q_1=e^{-πi (-1/τ)}$. We then prove that these relations admit a unique solution on the $q$-side, expressed in terms of $q=e^{πi τ}$ and $q_1=e^{πi (-1/τ)}$, with coefficients determined by the corresponding Mordell-Appell integrals. This yields a canonical continuation across the natural boundary, given by a resurgent extension of the classical principle of permanence of relations, and singles out a distinguished family of mock theta functions in each group. We present a complete analysis for the order 3 and 5 cases (mf3 and mf5). The method extends naturally to higher orders; a general theory will appear in a separate paper.

title: Decision-Focused Federated Learning Under Heterogeneous Objectives and Constraints
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Decision-Focused Federated Learning (DFFL), bridging two previously separate fields: decision-focused learning (DFL), which trains predictive models to optimize downstream decision quality rather than prediction accuracy, and federated learning (FL), which enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data. The key challenge addressed is that federated clients may differ not only in their data distributions but also in their downstream optimization problems, including distinct objective functions and feasible regions.

The authors develop theoretical heterogeneity bounds for the SPO+ loss under objective and feasible-set shifts, leveraging support-function representations of downstream optimization problems. They introduce a client-mixture discrepancy measure that quantifies how a client's decision-focused risk deviates from the pooled risk, yielding a federation-gain condition: clients benefit from federation when the heterogeneity penalty is smaller than the statistical advantage of pooled data. Sharper bounds are derived for strongly convex feasible sets by exploiting optimizer stability.

Experiments on fractional knapsack (polyhedral) and entropy-constrained portfolio (strongly convex) problems, along with a real-world energy pricing case study using PJM Interconnection data, demonstrate that federation can improve downstream decision quality even under significant heterogeneity across objectives, constraints, and data availability. original_abstract: We consider what we refer to as {Decision-Focused Federated Learning (DFFL)} framework, i.e., a predict-then-optimize approach employed by a collection of agents, where each agent's predictive model is an input to a downstream linear optimization problem, and no direct exchange of raw data is allowed. Importantly, clients can differ both in objective functions and in feasibility constraints. We build on the well-known SPO+ approach and develop heterogeneity bounds for the SPO+ surrogate loss in this case. This is accomplished by employing a support function representation of the feasible region, separating (i) objective shift via norm distances between the cost vectors and (ii) feasible-set shift via shape distances between the constraint sets. In the case of strongly convex feasible regions, sharper bounds are derived due to the optimizer stability. Building on these results, we define a heuristic local-versus-federated excess risk decision rule which, under SPO+ risk, gives a condition for when federation can be expected to improve decision quality: the heterogeneity penalty must be smaller than the statistical advantage of pooling data. We implement a FedAvg-style DFFL set of experiments on both polyhedral and strongly convex problems and show that federation is broadly robust in the strongly convex setting, while performance in the polyhedral setting degrades primarily with constraint heterogeneity, especially for clients with many samples. In other words, especially for the strongly convex case, an approach following a direct implementation of FedAvg and SPO+ can still yield promising performance even when the downstream optimization problems are noticeably different.

title: Error estimates for the patch bubble method for convection-dominated channel flow problem

original_abstract: We present error estimates for the BMZ (Bubble Mesh Zoom) residual-free bubble method applied to a convection-diffusion equation in the convection-dominated regime. The method incorporates both element bubbles and residual-free bubbles supported on patches of two adjacent elements. We focus on the case of a parallel flow in a square domain and derive error estimates in an energy norm that remain valid as diffusion becomes small. The theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical experiments, which also exhibit a competitive performance of the method.

title: Pressure-Robust $H(\mathrm{div})$-Conforming HDG Methods for the Steady Stokes Equations with an Application to Tangential Boundary Control

original_abstract: We develop a family of $H(\mathrm{div})$-conforming hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin methods for the steady Stokes equations based on BDM and RT velocity spaces with either discontinuous or continuous hybrid traces. In contrast to our earlier pressure-robust HDG method for tangential boundary control, the present analysis does not require the pressure to belong to $H^1$; instead, the consistency argument only assumes low pressure regularity. The discrete velocities are exactly divergence-free, which yields pressure robustness. For the BDM variants we derive optimal energy-norm estimates and optimal $L^2$-velocity convergence, while for the RT variants we obtain optimal velocity convergence and weaker pressure estimates. We also analyze the hybridized linear system and prove a uniform spectral equivalence for the pressure Schur complement relevant to iterative solvers. As an application, we revisit the Stokes tangential boundary control problem and derive error estimates for the control, state, and adjoint variables using the BDM discontinuous-trace scheme. Two- and three-dimensional numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, the exact divergence-free property, and the robustness of the method with respect to the viscosity parameter.

title: Weighted Holm Procedures: Theory, Properties, and Recommendations

The key theoretical result establishes that WHP uniformly dominates WAP in power under arbitrary dependence structures. original_abstract: In many statistical applications, particularly in clinical studies, hypotheses may carry different levels of importance, motivating the use of weighted multiple testing procedures (wMTPs) to control the familywise error rate (FWER). Among these approaches, two weighted Holm procedures are commonly used: the weighted Holm procedure (WHP), which is based on ordered weighted $p$-values, and the weighted alternative Holm procedure (WAP), which relies on ordered raw $p$-values. This paper provides a systematic comparison of these two procedures, along with practical recommendations for their use. We first examine their corresponding closed testing procedures (CTPs) and show that WHP is uniformly more powerful than WAP. We further investigate their structural properties, demonstrating that WAP, while consonant, lacks monotonicity. To facilitate communication with non-statisticians, we introduce graphical representations of both procedures using a common initial graph and distinct updating strategies. In addition, we derive adjusted $p$-values and adjusted weighted $p$-values for both methods. Finally, we establish an optimality result: WHP cannot be improved by enlarging any of its critical values without violating FWER control, whereas WAP is optimal only under specific conditions. Simulation studies support these theoretical findings and highlight the superior FWER control and average power of WHP.

title: A hierarchy of edge-weight symmetries in perfect matchings
generated_summary:
This paper investigates a hierarchy of edge-weight symmetry properties in perfect matchings, motivated by the long-standing open problem of finding deterministic polynomial-time algorithms for exact weight perfect matching. The authors define five progressively weaker properties of edge-weight functions on graphs: node-induced weights, even walk symmetry, even cycle symmetry, perfect matching equality, and edge min-max. They establish that each property strictly implies the next in matching-covered graphs.

The main contributions include several precise characterizations of when these properties collapse. The authors prove that node-induced weights and even walk symmetry are always equivalent. Even cycle symmetry implies node-induced weights precisely when the graph's block decomposition contains at most one non-bipartite block. Perfect matching equality implies node-induced weights if and only if the tight cut decomposition contains at most one brick. These characterizations leverage structural graph theory tools including tight cut decompositions, ear decompositions, and the theory of bricks and braces.

A key negative result answers an open question: there exist matching-covered graphs where the edge min-max property holds but perfect matching equality fails, meaning no single forced edge can eliminate all minimum-weight or all maximum-weight perfect matchings. The authors further extend structural results about forcing sets to b-factors and arborescences. These findings deepen understanding of the combinatorial structure underlying weighted matching problems and clarify the boundary between tractable and challenging cases in exact weight optimization.
original_abstract: Motivated by the exact weight perfect matching problem and recent parameterized algorithms for finding an $\ell$-th smallest perfect matching, we study structural properties of edge-weight symmetries in graphs. Recent work by El Maalouly et al. (ESA 2025) showed that excluding all perfect matchings whose weight is at most the $(\ell - 1)$-th smallest possible value in the graph requires fixing at most $2(\ell-1)$ edges in non-bipartite graphs and at most $\ell-1$ edges in bipartite graphs. A natural open question is whether fixing a single edge is always sufficient to shift the extreme (minimum or maximum) weight of a perfect matching when the global minimum and maximum weights differ. To address this, we define and analyze a hierarchy of progressively weaker edge-weight properties: node-induced weights, even walk and cycle symmetries, perfect matching equality, and the edge min-max property. We derive a basic hierarchy among these conditions and show that they become equivalent in bipartite graphs. For general graphs, we provide tight structural characterizations, based on block and tight cut decompositions, under which even cycle symmetry and perfect matching equality force node-induced weights. Finally, we resolve the motivating open question in the negative by constructing a matching-covered non-bipartite graph that satisfies the edge min-max property (every edge is contained in a minimum-weight perfect matching and a maximum-weight one) but violates perfect matching equality (all perfect matchings have the same weight). This counterexample shows that a single edge is not always sufficient to eliminate all minimum-weight or maximum-weight perfect matchings, thereby proving the tightness of the $2(\ell-1)$ bound for $\ell=2$. We also discuss extensions of this framework to $b$-factors and arborescences.

title: $F$-finite schemes have a dualizing complex
generated_summary:

Specifically, for any finite type morphism f between F-finite schemes, the canonical dualizing complex satisfies a natural isomorphism with the upper shriek functor f!, making it a (−)!-crystal. For F-finite regular integral schemes, this dualizing complex is identified with the determinant of absolute Kähler differentials placed in appropriate degree.

The methodology centers on two approaches. The primary approach introduces a novel completed tensor product and constructs a symmetric monoidal "⊗-product" operation on the bounded-below derived category of coherent sheaves, showing that the canonical dualizing complex serves as its unit. The key technical ingredient is a refined version of Gabber's construction, which associates to each F-finite ring a regular ring surjecting onto it, along with new functoriality and uniqueness results for this construction. A secondary approach via classical Grothendieck duality is also sketched.

A notable consequence is Frobenius compatibility: the canonical dualizing complex is preserved under the Frobenius upper shriek functor, yielding a canonical F-module structure. The paper also constructs canonical modules for locally equidimensional F-finite schemes with explicit descriptions in the normal case. These results are significant because they provide a uniform, choice-independent framework for duality theory in positive characteristic without requiring a fixed base scheme.
original_abstract: In this paper we show that any Noetherian $F$-finite scheme has a dualizing complex $ω^{\bullet}_{X}$ with the property that for all finite type maps $f \colon X \to Y$ between $F$-finite Noetherian schemes there is a canonical isomorphism $ω^{\bullet}_{X} \xrightarrow{\cong} f^!ω^{\bullet}_{Y}$ in $D^b_{coh}(X)$. This, in particular, applies to the Frobenius morphism $F \colon X \to X$ so that we obtain a canonical isomorphism $ω^{\bullet}_{X} \xrightarrow{\cong} F^!ω^{\bullet}_{X}$. To prove this, we rely on a result of Gabber that every Noetherian $F$-finite ring is a quotient of a regular ring, from which it follows that every $F$-finite Noetherian scheme has a (potentially non-canonical) dualizing complex. To make this canonical, we identify the dualizing complex of any $F$-finite Noetherian scheme as a unit of an alternate symmetric monoidal structure on $D^b_{coh}(X)$ we call the $!$-tensor product. We also sketch an alternate approach to finding this canonical dualizing complex following the more classical approach to Grothendieck duality.

title: A continuum of Künneth theorems for persistence modules

The authors employ sheaf-theoretic techniques, defining analogues of Grothendieck's six operations for persistence modules. Specifically, for an order-preserving poset morphism, they construct tensor products, internal hom functors, and compute their derived functors explicitly for interval modules. The framework builds on inverse and direct image functors associated with poset morphisms, leveraging the equivalence between persistence modules and sheaves on posets with the Alexandrov topology.

The key results include a continuum of Künneth short exact sequences parameterized by p ∈ (0, ∞], where different ℓᵖ-norm combinations yield distinct tensor products. The authors also derive Universal Coefficient Theorems for persistence modules and demonstrate the first computation of Borel-Moore persistent homology in the persistent setting.

The practical significance is substantial: the framework enables approximation of Vietoris-Rips persistent homology on product metric spaces equipped with ℓᵖ metrics, potentially reducing computations on point clouds with millions of points to the complexity of processing roughly one thousand points. Applications to tori and other product spaces are demonstrated with several examples.
original_abstract: We develop new aspects of the homological algebra theory for persistence modules, in both the one-parameter and multi-parameter settings. For a poset $P$ and an order preserving map $\varphi:P\times P\to P$, we introduce a novel tensor product of persistence modules indexed by $P$, $\otimes_{\varphi}$. We prove that each $\otimes_{\varphi}$ has a right adjoint, $\mathbf{Hom}^{\varphi}$, the internal hom of persistence modules that also depends on $\varphi$. We prove that every $\otimes_{\varphi}$ yields a Künneth short exact sequence of chain complexes of persistence modules. Dually, the $\mathbf{Hom}^{\varphi}$ also has an associated Künneth short exact sequence in cohomology. As special cases both of these short exact sequences yield Universal Coefficient Theorems. We show how to apply these to chain complexes of persistence modules arising from filtered CW complexes. For the special case of $P=\mathbb{R}_+$, the $p$-quasinorms for each $p\in (0,\infty]$ yield a distinct $\otimes_{\ell^p_c}$ and its adjoint $\mathbf{Hom}^{\ell^p_c}$. We compute their derived functors, $\mathbf{Tor}^{\ell^p_c}$ and $\mathbf{Ext}_{\ell^p_c}$ explicitly for interval modules. We show that the Universal Coefficient Theorem developed can be used to compute persistent Borel-Moore homology of a filtration of non-compact spaces. Finally, we show that for every $p\in [1,\infty]$ the associated Künneth short exact sequence can be used to significantly speed up and approximate persistent homology computations in a product metric space $(X\times Y,d^p)$ with the distance $d^p((x,y),(x',y'))=||d_X(x,x'),d_Y(y,y')||_p$.

title: Covariance Steering of Discrete-Time Markov Jump Linear Systems with Multiplicative Noise
generated_summary:

Instead, the authors prove that optimal control laws require mode-dependent linear feedback, feedforward terms, and an additional independent random component.

The authors show this lifted moment-steering problem is exactly equivalent to the original covariance steering problem and derive an exact semidefinite programming (SDP) reformulation. Key results include numerical demonstrations on chance-constrained MJLS problems showing monotonic cost improvement across iterations, and a dynamic hedging application where the framework successfully manages regime-switching Delta/Vega exposures under volatility-scaled uncertainty and execution risk while enforcing probabilistic bounds. The framework is significant for applications spanning finance, robotics, aerospace, and fault-tolerant control, where regime-dependent dynamics and multiplicative uncertainties must be jointly addressed with terminal distributional specifications.
original_abstract: We study a finite-horizon covariance steering problem for discrete-time Markov jump linear systems (MJLS) with both state- and control-dependent multiplicative noise. The objective is to minimize a quadratic running cost while steering the system from given mode-conditioned initial means and covariances to a prescribed terminal mean and covariance. We first show that, without loss of generality, feasible controls may be represented by mode-dependent linear feedback together with feedforward and independent random components, and we highlight that, in contrast to the case without multiplicative noise, a purely affine state-feedback law does not in general suffice. To this end, we introduce a lifted-state formulation that embeds the mean and covariance information into a unified second-moment description, and we prove that the resulting lifted problem is equivalent to the original covariance steering problem formulation. This leads to a lossless relaxation in moment variables and an SDP reformulation for the unconstrained case. We further study chance-constrained covariance steering with ball and half-space constraints on the state and control, derive tractable sufficient convex surrogates, and establish an iterative reference-update scheme to reduce conservatism. Numerical experiments on a finance application illustrate our results.

title: Achieving the Kesten-Stigum bound in the non-uniform hypergraph stochastic block model
generated_summary:

Their methodology includes deriving a new Ihara-Bass formula for weighted non-uniform hypergraphs, which yields a reduced non-backtracking matrix of dimension 2Kn × 2Kn (where K is the number of layers and n is the number of vertices). The analysis covers both assortative and disassortative settings without requiring shared eigenbases across layers.

Key results include precise characterization of bulk and outlier eigenvalues, eigenvector overlap guarantees, and a polynomial-time spectral algorithm achieving weak recovery whenever the combined signal-to-noise ratio across all layers exceeds the KS threshold. The optimal hyperedge reweighting scheme is derived via a Cauchy-Schwarz argument. For the unweighted case, the authors also confirm a separate conjectured algorithmic threshold that does not require knowledge of model parameters. These results establish fundamental computational limits for community detection in multi-layer hypergraph models and connect to broader problems in multi-view clustering and spiked tensor models.
original_abstract: We study the community detection problem in the non-uniform hypergraph stochastic block model (HSBM), where hyperedges of varying sizes coexist. This setting captures higher-order and multi-view interactions and raises a fundamental question: can multiple uniform hypergraph layers below the detection threshold be combined to enable weak recovery? We answer this question by establishing a Kesten--Stigum-type bound for weak recovery in a general class of non-uniform HSBMs with $r$ blocks, generated according to multiple symmetric probability tensors. In the case $r=2$, we show that weak recovery is possible whenever the sum of the signal-to-noise ratios across all uniform hypergraph layers exceeds one, thereby confirming the positive part of a conjecture in (Chodrow et al., 2023). Moreover, we provide a polynomial-time spectral algorithm that achieves this threshold via an optimally weighted non-backtracking operator. For the unweighted non-backtracking matrix, our spectral method attains a different algorithmic threshold, also conjectured in (Chodrow et al., 2023). Our approach develops a spectral theory for weighted non-backtracking operators on non-uniform hypergraphs, including a precise characterization of outlier eigenvalues and eigenvector overlaps. We introduce a novel Ihara--Bass formula tailored to weighted non-uniform hypergraphs, which yields an efficient low-dimensional representation and leads to a provable spectral reconstruction algorithm. Taken together, these results provide a principled and computationally efficient approach to clustering in non-uniform hypergraphs, and highlight the role of optimal weighting in aggregating heterogeneous higher-order interactions.

title: Tonnetz Theory, Classical Harmony, and the Combinatorial Geometry of Abstract Musical Resources
generated_summary:

The key results include several constructions. For diatonic harmony, triadic degrees and pitch classes form a bipartite graph of type 7₃ with girth four, while seventh chords yield a distinct 7₃ structure corresponding to the Fano configuration, representable via the Heawood graph. For pentatonic music, two-element and three-element subsets of a five-tone set produce the Desargues configuration 10₃. For twelve-tone music, the duads and synthemes derived from a hexachord generate the Cremona-Richmond configuration 15₃. The significance of this work lies in revealing that diverse musical systems share a common emergent structure—biregular graphs—whose associated configurations and tessellations provide multiple complementary geometric perspectives on harmonic relationships, enriching both mathematical music theory and the practical understanding of compositional resources.
original_abstract: In a previous submission, we established a fundamental relation between tone networks and configurations. It was shown that the Eulerian tonnetz can be represented by a $\{12_3\}$ of Daublebsky von Sterneck type D222. We also constructed a tonnetz for Tristan-genus chords (dominant sevenths and half-diminished sevenths) and we showed that this tonnetz can be represented by a $\{12_3\}$ of type D228. In both of these constructions the associated Levi graphs play an important role. Here we look at the tonnetze associated with some other musical systems, thereby offering several concrete examples of an abstract view of music as combinatorial geometry. First, we look at the tonal harmonies typical of the classical period. In the case of diatonic triads, we show the existence of a bipartite graph of type $\{7_3\}$ and girth four that represents the well-known relations between the seven diatonic degrees and their pitch classes. In the case of diatonic seventh chords, we obtain a Fano configuration $\{7_3\}$ which gives a complete characterization of the voice-leading relations that hold between such chords. Next, we construct a tonnetz for pentatonic music based on the Desargues configuration $\{10_3\}$ and we construct a tonnetz for the 12-tone system based on the Cremona-Richmond configuration $\{15_3\}$. Both can be used as a resource for musical compositions. Finally, we show that the relation between the chromatic pitch class set and the major triad set is also represented by a D222. The minor triads are in one-to-one correspondence with the members of a certain class of hexacycles in the Levi graph of this configuration. In this way, the characteristic duality between major and minor triads in the tonnetz can be broken.

title: Sharp global and almost everywhere convergence rates for periodic homogenization of viscous quadratic Hamilton-Jacobi equations
generated_summary:
This paper establishes sharp convergence rates for the periodic homogenization of viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations with quadratic (mechanical) Hamiltonians of the form H(y,p) = ½|p|² + V(y). While prior work showed an O(ε^(1/2)) convergence rate for general Hamiltonians—proven to be optimal in the non-strictly-convex case—numerical evidence suggested faster convergence for quadratic Hamiltonians. The authors confirm this by proving an optimal O(ε|ln ε|) rate in the sup-norm, matching known lower bounds.

The methodology connects three complementary perspectives: quantitative homogenization theory, probabilistic semigroup methods with Feynman-Kac representations, and spectral theory for periodic operators. The key innovation employs the Hopf-Cole transform to convert the viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation into a linear parabolic equation, then uses Doob's h-transform to analyze a conservative diffusion process. A central ingredient is a "ballistic estimate" for the transformed diffusion kernel, derived through large-time Gaussian asymptotics in periodic media. This approach separates the analysis into exponential-scale behavior governed by tilted principal eigenvalues and pre-exponential corrections controlled by long-time kernel asymptotics.

The authors additionally prove an almost-everywhere pointwise convergence rate of O(ε) at points where the homogenized solution is twice differentiable. The results raise open questions about whether similar sharp rates hold for other strictly convex Hamiltonians and more general diffusion operators, with potential applications to flame propagation models involving curvature effects.
original_abstract: We study the periodic homogenization of the viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation \[ u_t^\varepsilon + \frac{1}{2}|Du^\varepsilon|^2 + V\!\left(\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right) = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}Δu^\varepsilon \qquad \text{in } \mathbb{R}^n \times (0,\infty), \] with initial datum $g \in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, where $V$ is Lipschitz continuous and $\mathbb{Z}^n$-periodic. We prove the sharp global estimate \[ |u^\varepsilon(x,t)-u(x,t)| \leq \varepsilon\!\left(C+\frac{n}{2}\log\!\left(\frac{\max\{t,\varepsilon\}}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) \qquad \text{for all } (x,t)\in \mathbb{R}^n \times [0,\infty), \] where $\varepsilon \in (0,1]$, $u$ solves the limiting (homogenized) equation and $C>0$ is a constant depending only on $\|Dg\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)}$, $\|DV\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)}$, and $n$. We further show that if $g$ is locally semiconcave, then \[|u^\varepsilon(x,t)-u(x,t)| \leq C_{x,t}\varepsilon \qquad \text{for a.e. } (x,t)\in \mathbb{R}^n \times (0,\infty),\] where $C_{x,t}$ depends on $(x,t)$, $\|Dg\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)}$, and $\|DV\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)}$. More precisely, the above improved rate holds at every point $(x,t)$ where $u(\cdot,t)$ is twice differentiable at $x$. In particular, this occurs for a.e. $x\in \mathbb{R}^n$, since $u(\cdot,t)$ is locally semiconcave. We conclude by raising the open problem of whether the same $O(\varepsilon |\log \varepsilon|)$ rate remains valid for general strictly convex Hamiltonians or general periodic diffusions.

title: SAT + NAUTY: Orderly Generation of Small Kochen-Specker Sets Containing the Smallest State-independent Contextuality Set

This overcomes a fundamental limitation: standard lexicographical canonicity checks used in SAT-based orderly generation fail to scale for highly structured graphs, while nauty's canonical labeling alone is not hereditary and thus cannot be directly embedded in SAT-based search. The RCL approach achieves nearly four orders of magnitude speedup over lexicographical methods on structured instances.

The authors exhaustively enumerate all KS sets up to 33 rays that extend the 25-ray complete SI-C closure obtained from the Yu-Oh 13-ray set. The key finding confirms that the 33-ray Schütte set is the unique KS set containing this 25-ray core, up to order 33. The results are accompanied by independently verifiable proofs using an extended DRAT format supporting canonicity and orthogonality clauses.

This work is significant for quantum foundations, as it rigorously maps the geometric boundaries of contextual structures arising from the minimal SI-C witness in dimension 3, and the framework generalizes to other combinatorial generation problems where symmetry handling is the primary computational bottleneck.
original_abstract: We present a search for small Kochen-Specker (KS) sets in dimension 3, specifically targeting extensions of the 13-ray Yu-Oh set, which has been proven to be the minimal witness to state-independent contextuality. To enable this search, we introduce a novel SAT-based orderly generation framework integrating recursive canonical labeling (RCL) with the graph isomorphism tool NAUTY. We demonstrate that previous SAT approaches relying on lexicographical canonicity suffer from exponential scaling on canonical graphs. This limitation renders them intractable on the large instances (25 to 33 vertices) encountered in our search, whereas our RCL check maintains consistent millisecond-level performance, effectively eliminating the bottleneck. Overcoming this bottleneck allows us to perform the first exhaustive enumeration of all KS sets with up to 33 rays containing the complete 25-ray state-independent contextuality (SI-C) set obtained by rigid extensions of the Yu-Oh set in 1,641 CPU hours. We found and verified that the 33-ray set discovered by Schütte is the smallest three-dimensional KS set containing the complete 25-ray SI-C set. All non-existence results are backed by independently verifiable proof certificates via an extension of the DRAT proof format.

title: The Evans function as a lower bound on the spectral distance function

Conventionally, only the zeros of the Evans function matter, as they correspond to eigenvalues, while the function's magnitude carries no significance. The authors demonstrate that for many eigenvalue problems arising on compact intervals with separated or periodic boundary conditions—common in applications—there exists a natural and computationally accessible normalization that gives geometric meaning to the function's magnitude.

The key result establishes that, under this normalization, the magnitude of the Evans function at a point λ in the resolvent set provides a lower bound for the spectral distance function: if |E(λ)| is nonzero, then a disk of radius |E(λ)| centered at λ is guaranteed to be free of eigenvalues. The methodology relies on careful choice of bases for the boundary condition subspaces, assuming a traceless coefficient matrix (achievable through standard transformations), and extends naturally to parameter-dependent problems.

The authors validate their results through numerical experiments and highlight significant practical implications. The normalized Evans function enables more efficient root-finding algorithms by eliminating open regions from consideration with single computations. Perhaps most importantly, it offers a substantially simpler approach to rigorous numerics, where proving eigenvalue-free intervals traditionally requires involved Chebyshev interpolation procedures with error bounds.
original_abstract: The Evans function is an analytic function that encodes information about the intersection of certain subspaces in ODE boundary value problems. As such it is a useful tool for computing the spectrum of boundary value problems arising in the stability of coherent structures. In typical applications one is interested in the roots of the Evans function, but the overall normalization is somewhat arbitrary. We present a natural normalization of the Evans function on compact domains such that the magnitude of the Evans function provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest point in the spectrum. In other words the magnitude of the Evans function at a point in the resolvent set implies that a ball about the point in question lies in the resolvent set. Thus, when appropriately normalized, not only does the Evans function $E(λ)$ vanish if and only if $λ$ lies in the spectrum of the operator in question, but a non-zero value for the Evans function guarantees that a disk of radius $|E(λ^*)|$ about the point $λ^*$ lies in the resolvent set. We present some calculations for some common sets of boundary conditions on a compact interval, and present some numerical experiments for 2nd and 4th order self-adjoint operators and for a linearized modified Korteweg-De Vries equation.

title: Designing for the Development of Probabilistic Thinking: A Design-Based Research Study in Lower Secondary Education

title: Fluctuation theory for spectrally negative Lévy processes killed by additive functionals

The methodology proceeds in two stages: first, the case of finite atomic Revuz measures (corresponding to finite mixtures of local times) is analyzed, extending prior results to cover both bounded and unbounded variation processes. The key results demonstrate that classical fluctuation identities—including two-sided and one-sided exit problems and resolvent measures—retain their canonical form in this general setting. These identities are expressed through generalized scale functions characterized as unique solutions to Volterra-type integral equations driven by Radon measures. Existence and uniqueness of solutions to these equations are rigorously established.

The significance of this work lies in providing a robust analytical framework that unifies and extends the fluctuation theory for killed Lévy processes, with potential applications to self-similar Markov processes and time-changed Lévy processes through Lamperti-type transformations.
original_abstract: In this paper, we study fluctuation identities for spectrally negative Lévy processes killed by a general class of additive functionals. We consider positive co-natural additive functionals (PcNAFs), which include as special cases both absolutely continuous functionals and finite mixtures of local times. Our main result shows that the associated fluctuation identities, such as two-sided exit problems and resolvent measures, retain the same structure as in the classical case and can be expressed in terms of generalized scale functions. These scale functions are characterized as the unique solutions to Volterra-type integral equations driven by Radon measures, thereby extending the results of Li and Palmowski and Li and Zhou. Our approach is based on representing the additive functional as a mixture of local times with respect to its Revuz measure, combined with classical fluctuation identities and an approximation scheme for general Radon measures using Poisson random measures.

title: A Proximal Primal-Dual Approach to Generalized JKO Schemes for Doubly Nonlinear Parabolic Equations
generated_summary:

The methodology builds on a generalized Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme, where the Wasserstein-2 distance is replaced by a generalized transport distance. Following a discretize-then-optimize approach, each JKO iteration is formulated as a large-scale convex optimization problem solved via a Chambolle-Pock proximal primal-dual splitting method. The proximal operator computations reduce to scalar root-finding problems solvable by Newton-Raphson iteration at each grid point. Two formulations—separate and joint proximal operators—are presented and shown to produce essentially identical results.

Numerical experiments in one dimension validate the scheme against analytical Barenblatt-type solutions for the p-Laplacian across different diffusion regimes and against known limiting behaviors of the relativistic heat equation. The scheme achieves first-order accuracy in time, reproduces finite and infinite speed of propagation phenomena, and maintains monotone entropy decay. This work is significant as it provides a unified, regularization-free computational framework for gradient flows with general costs, avoiding error accumulation inherent in entropic regularization approaches over long-time evolution.
original_abstract: Variational methods based on optimization strategies are proposed to numerically solve a large family of nonlinear partial differential equations. They are all particular instances of gradient flows with general costs, including the $p$-Laplace equation and flux-limited equations such as the relativistic heat equation. This is achieved by computing explicit formulas for proximal operators with general costs amenable to efficient numerical approximation. We showcase our numerical approach via validation of the results by recovering the qualitative behavior of particular known cases of this large family of steepest descent evolutions.

title: A Space-time Approach to Entropy-Stable Discontinuous Galerkin and Flux Reconstruction
generated_summary:

The methodology builds on skew-symmetric formulations, extending previous entropy-stable DG spectral element space-time methods by incorporating flux reconstruction and supporting uncollocated node distributions. The authors prove discrete conservation, entropy preservation, and entropy stability for the DG case and identify a range of the FR correction parameter *c* for which a broken Sobolev inner product remains non-negative, implying entropy stability for small *c* values.

Numerical experiments on linear advection, Burgers' equation, and the Euler equations confirm optimal *p*+1 convergence rates, entropy preservation, and entropy stability across multiple node configurations. Importantly, FR consistently reduces the computational cost of solving the implicit space-time system compared to pure DG, with cost reductions observed across all test cases, including for Huynh's FR scheme.

The significance of this work lies in achieving fully-discrete entropy stability without relaxation Runge-Kutta methods while simultaneously leveraging FR's favorable properties for reducing implicit solve costs, offering a promising framework for robust high-order simulations of nonlinear conservation laws.
original_abstract: We present a high-order space-time discretization equipped with fully-discrete entropy stability properties for general choices of volume and surface quadrature rules. The formulation uses flux reconstruction (FR) in the spatial dimension paired with a discontinuous Galerkin (DG) method in the temporal dimension. The result is a fully-implicit system using polynomial bases in space and time. An energy-stable discretization is applied to the linear advection equation, yielding optimal $p+1$ convergence for small FR correction parameters and $p$ convergence at the same filter strength as method-of-lines implementations. We can thus recover the space-time equivalent to schemes such as DG, Huynh's FR, or spectral difference through a single parameter $c$. We follow with a similar space-time nonlinearly-stable flux reconstruction (ST-NSFR) scheme, which uses skew-symmetric stiffness operators in both space and time. The ST-NSFR scheme is fully-discretely entropy preserving using the $c_{DG}$ parameter or entropy-stable for small $c$. Numerical experiments using the linear advection and Euler equations confirm convergence orders and stability properties. The advantage of FR in a space-time context is demonstrated by a reduction in computational cost up to about $70\%$ as $c$ is increased.

title: Stable Mesh-Free Variational Radial Basis Function Approximation for Elliptic PDEs and Obstacle Problems
generated_summary:
This paper presents a mesh-free variational framework for solving elliptic partial differential equations and obstacle-type free boundary value problems using Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) approximations. The main contribution is combining stabilized RBF networks with truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD) for regularization and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) for handling non-smooth ℓ¹-penalty constraints arising in obstacle problems.

The methodology formulates elliptic boundary value problems as energy minimization problems, with Dirichlet boundary conditions enforced through penalty terms. Solutions are approximated as linear combinations of Gaussian RBFs with centers distributed on an expanded domain beyond the physical boundary, which reduces boundary effects and improves stability. For obstacle problems, inequality constraints are imposed via ℓ¹-penalty terms, and the resulting non-smooth optimization is solved using ADMM. TSVD addresses the severe ill-conditioning inherent in Gaussian RBF matrices.

Numerical experiments on one-dimensional Poisson equations, one- and two-dimensional obstacle problems demonstrate that the proposed method achieves rapid convergence and high accuracy, significantly outperforming finite-difference, physics-informed neural network, and Galerkin methods. The RBF method attains approximately 2.7-order convergence for the Poisson problem and reaches near machine-precision errors for obstacle problems. Sensitivity analyses validate parameter choices for the domain expansion factor, kernel shape parameter, and truncation threshold.

The framework offers a flexible, high-accuracy mesh-free alternative for variational PDEs, with practical guidance for parameter selection balancing accuracy, conditioning, and stability.
original_abstract: We present a comprehensive study of radial basis function (RBF) approximations for elliptic and obstacle-type boundary value problems under a variational formulation. Our focus is on practical accuracy, robustness and efficiency. To address ill-conditioning in dense systems, we apply truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD) and investigate its effect on stability and accuracy trade-offs. Numerical experiments report benchmarks on accuracy and show fast error decay. We investigate the trade-off between approximation and truncation errors for practical settings for the number of basis functions, the oversampling ratio and the truncation threshold. In comparison with other methods, RBF variational solvers deliver high accuracy at similar or lower cost for boundary value problems.

title: Excitability in quantum field theory
generated_summary:
This paper revisits the foundational question of when one quantum field theory state can be "excited" out of another — that is, when a state's correlation functions can be reproduced by a density matrix within the GNS Hilbert space of a different state. The authors reframe the classical mathematical problem of quasiequivalence of GNS representations in terms of physically motivated excitability relations, providing what they argue is a substantial conceptual and technical simplification over prior approaches, particularly the Araki-Yamagami theorem.

The methodology combines algebraic quantum field theory with information-theoretic tools, notably canonical purifications of algebraic states. The authors decompose the excitability problem for general Gaussian states into components involving pure and abelian pieces, employing techniques such as Hilbert-Schmidt conditions on operators constructed from two-point functions rather than relying on symplectic transformations or results from constructive quantum field theory.

The key results establish concrete necessary and sufficient conditions for excitability between zero-mean Gaussian states in free field theories, expressed through absolute continuity of phase-space inner products, Hilbert-Schmidt conditions on differences of certain operators, and triviality of a kernel condition. A particularly striking finding is that one-way excitability always implies mutual excitability (quasiequivalence) for zero-mean Gaussian states, despite this not holding for general algebraic states.

These results have significant implications for geometric modular flow conjectures, sector equivalence in holographic AdS/CFT at large N, and understanding the role of higher-form symmetries in local algebras.
original_abstract: In quantum field theory, it is not always possible to excite one state out of another using only local operators. This paper establishes abstract algebraic criteria for (local) excitability in general quantum theories, and computes these criteria explicitly for zero-mean Gaussian states in (generalized) free field theories. We find that in this context, due to the special nature of Gaussian states, one-way excitability always implies two-way excitability, and our results generalize the "quasiequivalence theorems" of Powers, Stormer, van Daele, Araki, and Yamagami. A key role in our proof is played by the information-theoretic tool of canonical purification. In appendices, we provide a pedagogical introduction to the algebraic formulation of (generalized) free field theory.

title: Phase Transitions in the Fluctuations of Functionals of Random Neural Networks
generated_summary:

The methodology combines Hermite (Wiener chaos) expansions, fixed-point analysis of the covariance kernel, tools from holomorphic dynamics, and Malliavin-Stein techniques for quantitative bounds. The authors analyze how the renormalized covariance iterates converge and how singularities in the limiting function determine which chaotic components dominate.

Three regimes emerge based on the derivative of the covariance kernel at its fixed point. In the low-disorder regime, functionals converge to a generally non-Gaussian distribution evaluated at a well-defined limiting Gaussian field. In the high-disorder and sparse regimes, a sharp phase transition occurs at the critical threshold determined by the Hermite rank and a singularity exponent: below this threshold, limits are non-Gaussian (belonging to a novel family of distributions introduced here); at criticality, Gaussian limits arise with logarithmic corrections; above it, Gaussian limits follow from contributions of infinitely many chaotic components.

These results establish a surprising parallel with classical Breuer-Major theory for stationary fields, revealing that singularity structure in the limiting covariance plays an analogous role to correlation decay in large-domain asymptotics.
original_abstract: We establish central and non-central limit theorems for sequences of functionals of the Gaussian output of an infinitely-wide random neural network on the d-dimensional sphere . We show that the asymptotic behaviour of these functionals as the depth of the network increases depends crucially on the fixed points of the covariance function, resulting in three distinct limiting regimes: convergence to the same functional of a limiting Gaussian field, convergence to a Gaussian distribution, convergence to a distribution in the Qth Wiener chaos. Our proofs exploit tools that are now classical (Hermite expansions, Diagram Formula, Stein-Malliavin techniques), but also ideas which have never been used in similar contexts: in particular, the asymptotic behaviour is determined by the fixed-point structure of the iterative operator associated with the covariance, whose nature and stability governs the different limiting regimes.

title: Greedy Routing in a Sequentially Grown One-Dimensional Random Graph
generated_summary:
This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis of greedy routing in a one-dimensional random graph model where vertices are inserted sequentially in uniformly random order, with each new vertex connecting to its nearest already-inserted neighbors on the left and right. The work resolves a long-standing empirical conjecture that greedy routing in sequentially grown nearest-neighbor graphs operates in polylogarithmic time.

The key methodological insight is a combinatorial characterization: the greedy path from vertex 1 to vertex n traverses exactly the left-to-right minima of the insertion-time permutation until reaching the global minimum, then follows the right-to-left minima to the target. This reduces the routing problem to classical permutation statistics, yielding the exact identity S_n = L_n + R_n − 2, where L_n and R_n count left-to-right and right-to-left minima, respectively.

From this characterization, the authors establish that the expected number of routing steps is 2H_n − 2 (where H_n is the harmonic number), with variance 2H_n − 2π²/3, and prove sharp concentration showing S_n = Θ(log n) with high probability. The routing complexity follows an asymptotically normal distribution.

The significance is twofold: the result demonstrates that navigability emerges naturally from sequential geometric growth without engineered long-range connections or degree-biased attachment, and it establishes a foundational bridge between empirical observations and rigorous theory. The connection to Cartesian trees and permutation records links geometric routing theory with classical combinatorics, providing a stepping stone toward analyzing higher-dimensional settings.
original_abstract: We analyze greedy routing in a random graph G_n constructed on the vertex set V = {1, 2, ..., n} embedded in Z. Vertices are inserted according to a uniform random permutation pi, and each newly inserted vertex connects to its nearest already-inserted neighbors on the left and right (if they exist). This work addresses a conjecture originating from empirical studies (Ponomarenko et al., 2011; Malkov et al., 2012), which observed through simulations that greedy search in sequentially grown graphs exhibits logarithmic routing complexity across various dimensions. While the original claim was based on experiments and geometric intuition, a rigorous mathematical foundation remained open. Here, we formalize and resolve this conjecture for the one-dimensional case. For a greedy walk GW starting at vertex 1 targeting vertex n -- which at each step moves to the neighbor closest to n -- we prove that the number of steps S_n required to reach n satisfies S_n = Theta(log n) with high probability. Precisely, S_n = L_n + R_n - 2, where L_n and R_n are the numbers of left-to-right and right-to-left minima in the insertion-time permutation. Consequently, E[S_n] = 2H_n - 2 ~ 2 log n and P(S_n >= (2+c) log n) <= n^(-h(c/2) + o(1)) for any constant c > 0, with an analogous lower tail bound for 0 < c < 2, where h(u) = (1+u) ln(1+u) - u is the Bennett rate function. Furthermore, we establish that this logarithmic scaling is robust: for arbitrary or uniformly random start-target pairs, the expected routing complexity remains E[S_{s,t}] = 2 log n + O(1), closely mirroring decentralized routing scenarios in real-world networks where endpoints are chosen dynamically rather than fixed a priori.

title: The non-perturbative topological string: from resurgence to wall-crossing of DT invariants
generated_summary:
