original_abstract: This paper develops structural consequences of the thermodynamic formalism for Axiom A diffeomorphisms, with four main results. The Pesin Entropy Formula equates the metric entropy of the SRB measure to the sum of positive Lyapunov exponents, with complete proofs of absolute continuity of conditional measures along unstable manifolds. title: Statistical Limit Theorems for Axiom A Diffeomorphisms: Mixing, Central Limit Theorem, and Large Deviations

original_abstract: We establish statistical limit theorems for equilibrium states of Axiom A diffeomorphisms, derived from the spectral gap of the Ruelle transfer operator. This paper contains five main results. The first proves the Volume Lemma with explicit two-sided bounds on the Riemannian volume of dynamical Bowen balls. The second establishes exponential decay of correlations with explicit mixing rates. The third proves the Central Limit Theorem with Berry-Esseen bounds at the optimal rate, with an explicit spectral formula for the asymptotic variance and a characterization of its degeneracy through the Livshits coboundary condition. The fourth establishes the Almost Sure Invariance Principle, providing pathwise Brownian approximation with polynomial error. The fifth proves a large deviations principle with rate function given by the Legendre transform of the pressure. The individual results are due to Sinai, Ruelle, Ratner, Denker-Philipp, Gouezel, Kifer, Melbourne-Nicol, and Young; the contribution is their derivation from a single spectral mechanism with explicit dependence on hyperbolicity data. title: Gibbs Equivalence and SRB Measures for Axiom A Diffeomorphisms: Transfer Operators, Structural Stability, and Physical Measures

original_abstract: We develop the Ruelle transfer operator theory for Axiom A diffeomorphisms and construct Sinai-Ruelle-Bowen measures, carrying the symbolic spectral results of Part I over to smooth dynamics through the Markov partition coding established in Part III. This paper contains four Main Theorems. The first proves structural stability of Axiom A diffeomorphisms satisfying the strong transversality condition, with an explicit Hölder exponent for the conjugating homeomorphism computed in terms of the hyperbolicity data, refining the classical results of Robbin and Robinson. The second establishes quasi-compactness of the transfer operator on Hölder spaces, with a quantitative spectral gap bound; as consequences we obtain exponential decay of correlations with explicit rate, the central limit theorem for Hölder observables via the Nagaev-Guivarc'h spectral perturbation method, real-analyticity of the pressure in the potential direction, and meromorphic continuation of the Ruelle dynamical zeta function. The third constructs SRB measures on mixing basic sets as the unique equilibrium states for the geometric potential given by minus the logarithm of the unstable Jacobian, proves absolute continuity of the unstable foliation, and derives an explicit product-formula for the conditional densities along unstable manifolds. The Gibbs Equivalence Theorem, assembling the symbolic, variational, spectral, and geometric characterizations of the equilibrium state on a mixing basic set into a single quantitative statement, follows from these four Main Theorems together with the imported results of Parts I and III. title: Capacity Expansion Planning for Puerto Rico's Electric Power System
generated_summary:
This study develops a high-fidelity capacity expansion planning (CEP) model for Puerto Rico's electric power system, which faces severe reliability challenges including frequent outages averaging 30 hours annually per customer. The work differs from previous studies, notably the PR100 study, by incorporating detailed operational modeling of thermal generators, stochastic outage scenarios, nodal network resolution, explicit fuel supply constraints, and hourly temporal resolution within the optimization framework.

The model is formulated as a stochastic optimization problem solved using Progressive Hedging decomposition on high-performance computing resources. Multiple planning scenarios are examined, varying load projections, fuel supply assumptions, baseline fleet configurations, and allowable generation technologies for the year 2030 and near-term horizons.

Key findings indicate that an optimal investment portfolio includes at least 1.5 GW of new H-class combined cycle units to replace unreliable existing thermal generators, effectively reducing load shedding to near zero. Restricting investments to renewables only increases costs by approximately 20%, while a fully renewable system without any thermal generation raises costs by 71% and results in significant load shedding. Results also suggest that the currently planned 2.1 GW of battery storage deployment may exceed what is necessary for optimal operation when thermal investment is unconstrained, though batteries may provide additional stability value not captured in the model.

The study provides decision-makers with an exploratory tool for evaluating infrastructure investment pathways while highlighting the critical tradeoff between reliability improvement and renewable energy goals.
original_abstract: This study presents a mathematical optimization framework and preliminary analysis for long-term investment planning in Puerto Rico's electric power system. We develop a high-resolution capacity expansion model to identify least-cost generation and storage investments that improve system reliability. The model co-optimizes new investments and thermal generator retirements while representing generator dispatch, unit commitment, fuel selection, and storage operations under constraints of equipment engineering limits, fuel supply limitations, and load satisfaction. Key methodological advances relative to prior long-term planning studies for Puerto Rico include: (i) nodal transmission modeling at 38 kV and above, (ii) hourly chronological operations for representative days, (iii) explicit unit commitment for existing and new thermal units with realistic ramping, minimum up and down times, and startup costs, (iv) system-wide fuel supply constraints, and (v) stochastic operating scenarios reflecting load variation, renewable availability, and the high forced outage rates of legacy units. Using data from LUMA, PREPA, DOE, and public sources, we build present-day (2024) and future (2030) test systems, with the latter including planned generation and storage projects. We evaluate planning scenarios that vary future load, fuel supply assumptions, realization of planned expansion, and allowable new technologies. Results show that, given the recent relaxation of interim renewable goals for the near future in Puerto Rico, an optimal portfolio includes at least 1.5 GW of new H-class combined cycle capacity beyond planned projects. These additions are needed mainly to replace unreliable legacy thermal units rather than to serve new load. The new combined cycle units eliminate modeled bulk-system load shedding and restore a strong reserve margin, even under stressed load and outage conditions.

title: Lindbladian Homotopy Analysis Method to Solve Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Lindbladian Homotopy Analysis Method (LHAM), a quantum computing approach for solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). The method combines two key techniques: homotopy analysis for linearization and Lindbladian dynamics simulation for handling nonunitary evolution. The homotopy analysis method converts a nonlinear PDE into a series of linear PDEs through an embedding parameter, avoiding the exponential state space expansion seen in approaches like Carleman linearization and Koopman-von Neumann methods. The Lindbladian simulation encodes dissipative dynamics in quantum channels using the Lindblad master equation, requiring only two ancilla qubits—significantly fewer than alternative methods such as Schrödinger­ization or linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation, which need logarithmically increasing ancilla qubits.

The authors demonstrate that LHAM's Hilbert space dimension scales logarithmically with the inverse truncation error, compared to polynomial scaling in Carleman linearization and Koopman-von Neumann approaches, yielding an exponentially smaller state space. The method is validated on two benchmark problems: Burgers' equation, achieving RMS and relative L² norm errors of approximately 1.015% and 1.475% at fourth homotopy order, and two-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics equations, producing results matching classical pseudo-spectral method solutions. These results demonstrate LHAM's potential to significantly improve the scalability of quantum nonlinear differential equation solvers, addressing fundamental challenges in quantum scientific computing for complex physical simulations.
original_abstract: Quantum scientific computing is to solve engineering and science problems such as simulation and optimization on quantum computerss. Solving ordinary and partial differential equations (PDEs) is essential in simulations. However, existing quantum approaches to solve nonlinear PDEs suffer from the issues of curse of dimensionality and convergence during the linearization process. In this paper, a Lindbladian homotopy analysis method (LHAM) is proposed as a quantum differential equation solver to simulate nonunitary and nonlinear dynamics. The original nonlinear problem is first converted to a recursive sequence of linear PDEs with the homotopy analysis and reformulated as a higher-dimensional lower block triangular linear homogeneous system. The solution is then embedded in the density matrix and obtained through the Lindbladian dynamics simulation. original_abstract: This paper is concerned with a fluid-particle system given by the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations coupled with the Vlasov(-Fokker-Planck) equation through a drag force. original_abstract: In this work we develop and analyze a semi-smooth Newton method for the general nonlinear conic programming problem. In particular, we study the problem with a generalized simplicial cone, i.e., the image of a symmetric cone under a linear mapping. The resulting system is equivalent to the KKT conditions associated with the nonlinear conic programming problem. We study properties of generalized simplicial cones and prove strong semi-smoothness of the projection operator onto them. original_abstract: It is well known that mirror descent may diverge or cycle on merely monotone variational inequalities. In this paper, we propose \emph{Target Mirror Descent} (TMD), a unified framework that stabilizes monotone flows via a target point correction mechanism in the dual update. By appropriate design choices, TMD recovers the proximal point algorithm, extragradient methods, splitting methods, Brown-von Neumann-Nash dynamics, forward-backward-forward dynamics, and discounted mirror descent as special cases. Thus, we establish a unified perspective on these landmark algorithms and their convergence. Beyond unification, we leverage the TMD framework to correct an equilibrium misalignment in discounted mirror descent and to generalize its higher-order extension beyond interior solutions. Moreover, a key structural feature of TMD is the explicit decoupling of the mirror map from the target determination, which enables \emph{geometric ensembles}: multiple algorithms solve the same problem in parallel using distinct mirror maps, while sharing a common dual update. We show that such an ensemble rigorously reduces to a single TMD with a synthesized mirror map, and thus inherits these convergence guarantees.

title: Analysis of persistence thresholds for a nonlocal PDE--ODE model of bacterial persister cells

title: Tropical low-rank approximation and application to optimal control of N-body systems
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a trajectory-based tropical (max-plus) tensor low-rank approximation method for solving high-dimensional deterministic optimal control problems, particularly for N-body systems. The key contribution lies in combining tropical algebra's max-plus linearity with structured low-rank representations and trajectory-based propagation to overcome both the curse of dimensionality and the curse of complexity that plague existing approaches.

The methodology exploits the fact that, for N-body systems with pairwise interactions admitting tropical tensor low-rank structure, the value function can be approximated as a supremum of additively separable quadratic basis functions. The authors propose an iterative backward-forward algorithm that enriches a lower approximation of the value function by adding one supporting quadratic function per time step per iteration, propagated along relevant trajectories rather than over the entire state space. Semiconvexity of the value function is shown to be preserved by the discrete Bellman equation, ensuring the approximation scheme is well-founded.

Numerical experiments on planar swarms with softened Coulomb interactions demonstrate the method's effectiveness up to 100 agents (dimension 200) within approximately 30 minutes on a standard laptop. The results reveal physically meaningful behavior including turnpike phenomena, where optimal trajectories concentrate near steady-state annular configurations. The approximations produce monotonically improving computable lower bounds with tropical tensor rank growing only linearly in the number of iterations, representing a significant advance in tractable optimal control for coupled multi-agent systems.
original_abstract: We study the approximation of the value function of deterministic optimal control problems with fixed initial state, motivated by \(N\)-body systems. In this setting, the action functional consists of local kinetic and potential terms, along with an interaction potential. We exploit this structure to approximate the value function using a tropical tensor of small rank, i.e.\ a supremum of a small number of additively separable functions. We propose a trajectory-based tropical low-rank approximation method. Rather than propagating basis functions globally, as in usual tropical numerical methods, the approximation of the value function is improved only along a sequence of relevant trajectories. The resulting approximations form a monotone family of computable lower bounds for the exact value function, with the tropical tensor rank increasing at most linearly with the number of outer iterations. Under suitable regularity assumptions, we show that at the initial state, and also at the optimal trajectory starting from this state, the lower bounds converge to the exact value. In the $N$-body setting, the generated basis functions remain additively separable across subsystems, thereby yielding a structured tropical low-rank approximation. Numerical experiments on $N$-body systems with Coulomb-type repulsion illustrate the effectiveness of the approach up to state dimension \(200\), within a half hour time budget.

title: A Dynamic Mode Decomposition Approach to Parameter Identification
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Discrete Control Liouville Dynamic Mode Decomposition with Parameter Identification (DCLDMDPID) algorithm, a fully data-driven operator-theoretic method for simultaneous system and parameter identification in control-affine nonlinear systems. Unlike traditional parameter estimation approaches that require prior knowledge of how unknown parameters enter the system dynamics, DCLDMDPID makes no assumptions about the parameter-dynamics coupling beyond continuity.

The methodology extends the existing DCLDMD framework by augmenting the system state with unknown physical parameters and embedding the resulting augmented dynamics into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) structure. A finite-rank approximation of the control Liouville operator is constructed from open-loop trajectory data. Once a predictive model is obtained, parameter identification proceeds by comparing model predictions across a mesh of candidate parameter values with observed trajectories, selecting the parameter combination that minimizes mean squared error.

Numerical experiments on a controlled Duffing oscillator demonstrate that the algorithm accurately recovers both state trajectories and three unknown parameters, with trajectory errors on the order of 10⁻³ over five seconds. When the parameter mesh contains the true values, exact recovery is achieved with clear error separation. When the mesh excludes true values, the algorithm still identifies a low-error cluster of nearby parameters.

The approach is significant as it bridges operator-theoretic dynamical systems methods with parameter identification, though current limitations include dependence on mesh resolution and the lack of gradient-based refinement, which are identified as directions for future work.
original_abstract: This paper presents a data-driven algorithm for simultaneous system identification and parameter estimation in control-affine nonlinear systems. Parameter estimation is achieved by training a data-driven predictive model using state-action measurements and various known values at the parameters of interest. The predictive model is then used in conjunction with state-action data corresponding to unknown values of the parameters to estimate the said unknown value. Numerical experiments on the controlled Duffing oscillator with unknown damping, stiffness, and nonlinearity coefficients demonstrate accurate recovery of both the system trajectories and the unknown parameter values from data collected under open-loop excitation.

title: The Isoperimetric Problem in Regular Trees
generated_summary:
This paper provides a complete solution to the inner vertex-isoperimetric problem on the infinite d-regular tree T_d, determining the exact isoperimetric profile and characterizing all optimal domains. The inner vertex boundary measures the number of vertices within a domain that have at least one neighbor outside it—a natural boundary notion for vertex-based models such as epidemic spreading and information flow in networks.

The authors establish the exact inner isoperimetric profile of T_d through an explicit formula and introduce key structural concepts to analyze optimal domains. Central to their approach is the decomposition of a domain's boundary into leaves (degree-one vertices) and residual boundary vertices, leading to the notion of a "full domain"—one whose entire boundary consists of leaves. They introduce a fundamental combinatorial invariant called the boundary branching excess β(D) and prove that a domain is isoperimetrically optimal if and only if β(D) ≤ d−2. Full domains, satisfying β(D) = 0, are always optimal, but the class of optimal domains is considerably richer than just metric balls.

A major contribution is the introduction of the "stem" of a domain—a finite tree encoding how full components are assembled along the residual boundary. The authors demonstrate that any domain can be reconstructed from its stem together with full domains and gluing data, yielding the first complete constructive classification of all inner vertex-isoperimetric minimizers in the regular tree.
original_abstract: We investigate the inner vertex-isoperimetric problem on the $d$-regular tree $T_d$. We first determine the exact value of the inner vertex-isoperimetric profile $I_d(k) = \min\{ |\partial D| \mid D\subset T_d \text{ finite and connected},\ |D|=k \}$, and we then introduce a boundary invariant, called the boundary branching excess $τ(D)$, and show that it provides a simple criterion for optimality. A domain $D\subset T_d$ is shown to be isoperimetrically optimal if and only if $τ(D)\le d-2$. Finally, we show that every domain in $T_d$ admits a canonical decomposition as an iterated gluing of full domains, namely domains whose entire boundary consists of leaves. This yields a complete description of all inner vertex-isoperimetric minimizers in $T_d$.

title: CCOpt: an Open-Source Solver for Large-Scale Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CCOpt, an open-source solver suite designed for Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints (MPCCs), a class of optimization problems that arise in robotics, power systems, optimal control, and bi-level optimization. Complementarity constraints violate standard constraint qualifications, making these problems particularly challenging for conventional nonlinear programming solvers.

The solver implements two interior-point methods: one based on Scholtes' global relaxation approach and another using a penalty-based reformulation, both built on the MadNLP interior-point framework. The authors introduce several algorithmic innovations, including a Hessian regularization scheme that exploits complementarity structure to address indefiniteness in the KKT system, an "endgame" bound relaxation strategy that selectively adjusts lower bounds on complementarity variables to improve conditioning as the relaxation parameter approaches zero, and MPCC-tailored adaptive parameter update rules that simultaneously manage barrier and relaxation parameters. Additionally, a crossover method to an active-set algorithm enables verification of B-stationarity.

Extensive benchmarking across large-scale problems from optimal control, security-constrained optimal power flow, and quadratic programs with complementarity constraints demonstrates that CCOpt achieves often order-of-magnitude performance improvements over existing methods, including commercial solvers with specialized MPCC algorithms. The solver is released under the MIT license with interfaces to Julia, Python, MATLAB, and C++ through CasADi integration, making high-performance MPCC solving accessible to the broader scientific and engineering community.
original_abstract: This paper presents the Julia package CCOpt, built on top of the interior-point solver MadNLP. CCOpt implements a suite of algorithms for Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints (MPCCs). The solver additionally comes with interfaces for use in Matlab, Python, and C++. MPCCs have recently gained renewed attention in engineering optimization, as complementarity provides a powerful modeling tool for nonsmooth functions and logical conditions. These problems are inherently challenging since their nonlinear programming reformulations violate classical regularity conditions at all feasible points, complicating both theoretical analysis and numerical treatment. Consequently, specialized algorithms are required to handle this degeneracy, and several approaches have been proposed. We implement a toolbox of methods, including relaxation and penalty approaches, as well as a crossover to recently proposed active-set methods. Our solver is based on nonlinear interior-point algorithms that couple the relaxation or penalty parameter with the barrier parameter, yielding substantial speedups compared to standard implementations. Both monotone and nonmonotone strategies for updating this joint parameter update are proposed and investigated. In addition, we propose regularization techniques that improve the conditioning of the KKT system for small relaxation parameters, enhancing robustness and computational efficiency. The implementation is validated on the classical MacMPEC benchmark, large-scale problems in security-constrained optimal power flow, optimal control of nonsmooth systems, as well as on quadratic programs with complementarity constraints arising in model predictive control. This benchmarking reveals an algorithmically driven improvement of often an entire order of magnitude over other methods, including commercial solvers.

title: Transfer Operators for Stochastic Hybrid Systems on Manifolds with Guard-Induced Resets
generated_summary:
This paper develops a transfer operator framework for stochastic hybrid systems where discrete transitions are deterministically triggered by guard conditions and reset maps, rather than by spontaneous stochastic jumps. The main contribution is a Frobenius-Perron formulation that couples within-mode Fokker-Planck dynamics with explicit inter-mode transfer terms induced by reset maps, providing a unified density evolution equation that ensures conservation of total probability mass across hybrid modes.

The methodology builds on the duality between Koopman and Frobenius-Perron operators. The authors represent reset-induced probability transfer as the image of probability flux across guard sets under the reset map, linking the backward Kolmogorov equation for observables with the forward Kolmogorov equation for densities. The entire framework is formulated intrinsically on differentiable manifolds, yielding a coordinate-free treatment consistent with the geometric structure of the state space. A finite volume computational scheme is developed that preserves conservation properties while accurately capturing fluxes across guards and reset-induced transfers.

Key results include demonstrations on one-dimensional examples illustrating reflecting, absorbing, and resetting boundary conditions, as well as a multi-mode hybrid system on a torus. Numerical simulations verify the computed densities against Monte Carlo methods and confirm probability mass conservation. The framework's significance lies in providing a systematic, geometrically consistent approach to uncertainty propagation in hybrid systems encountered in robotics, biomechanics, and networked systems, where stochastic continuous dynamics interact with deterministic event-triggered transitions.
original_abstract: This paper develops a transfer operator framework for stochastic hybrid systems with guard-induced resets, encompassing both the Koopman and Frobenius--Perron operators. Exploiting their duality, we derive a unified formulation in which observables and probability densities evolve under adjoint generators corresponding to the backward and forward Kolmogorov equations. The formulation is developed in a global and intrinsic manner on differentiable manifolds, ensuring consistency with the underlying geometric structure of the state space. In addition, we propose a finite volume computational scheme on manifolds that preserves total probability mass while accurately capturing fluxes across guards and reset-induced transfers. The proposed framework provides a unified and geometrically consistent approach to uncertainty propagation in stochastic hybrid systems, bridging continuous stochastic dynamics and hybrid transitions within a transfer operator perspective.

title: The strong unique continuation principle for the fractional $p$-Laplacian
generated_summary:
This paper establishes the strong unique continuation principle (SUCP) for the fractional p-Laplacian, a nonlinear nonlocal operator that arises in non-Newtonian fluid mechanics, game theory, and anomalous diffusion. While unique continuation properties for linear fractional operators have been extensively studied, the nonlinear setting has remained open due to the incompatibility between traditional UCP techniques and the nonlinear structure of the operator.

The authors extend a recent approach for the weak UCP to obtain the strong version. The key methodology involves setting up finite difference quotients centered at the origin rather than directly differentiating the equation, since differentiation is not possible near the point of vanishing. The authors prove convergence of these difference quotients by hand, leveraging the assumption that solutions are strong solutions. Combined with a density argument using the Stone-Weierstraß theorem, this yields the desired result.

The main result shows that if a strong solution to the fractional p-Laplacian Schrödinger equation vanishes to infinite order at a point (under appropriate regularity conditions on the solution, potential, and inhomogeneity), then the solution must be identically zero on the entire space. This global vanishing—stronger than in the local case—is a consequence of the nonlocal nature of the operator. As a corollary, the strong UCP extends to weak solutions under suitable parameter restrictions via known interior regularity results. The authors note that this purely nonlocal phenomenon cannot be used asymptotically to resolve the still-open UCP for the classical p-Laplacian.
original_abstract: We provide a simple and direct proof of the strong unique continuation principle for the fractional $p$-Laplacian $(-Δ_p)^s$ for a range of $s$ and $p$. The result extends to strong solutions of the fractional nonlinear Schrödinger equation. We adapt the recent proofs of the weak UCP by Berger, Schilling and Prasad.

title: Non-linear Lie Conformal Algebras and One-Loop Corrections of self-dual Yang-Mills amplitudes
generated_summary:
This paper reformulates constructions from celestial holography in the mathematical framework of non-linear Lie conformal algebras. The authors study the vertex algebra Ŝ(g), where g is a finite-dimensional simple complex Lie algebra, which arises in the context of self-dual Yang-Mills amplitudes and the celestial holography program connecting twistor theory to scattering amplitudes.

The methodology centers on translating physically motivated deformations of the vertex algebra Ŝ(g)—originally introduced in connection with collinear limits in one-loop QCD scattering amplitudes—into the rigorous language of non-linear Lie conformal algebras. The authors work with the formal theory of Lie conformal algebras, non-linear conformal algebras, and their associated tensor algebra constructions, systematically verifying the required axioms including sesquilinearity, skew-symmetry, and Jacobi identities.

The key result establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for the Jacobi identity to hold in the deformed algebra: the deformation parameters must either all vanish (D = C = ε = 0) or satisfy specific non-trivial constraints relating the parameters to the dual Coxeter number of the Lie algebra. The authors verify all cases of the Jacobi identity through explicit computation across different generator combinations.

The significance of this work lies in providing a rigorous mathematical foundation for algebraic structures emerging from celestial holography and one-loop amplitude calculations, bridging physical constructions with the established mathematical theory of vertex algebras and non-linear Lie conformal algebras. The authors indicate future directions connecting to logarithmic vertex algebras.
original_abstract: This work is motivated by recent developments in celestial holography. In \cite{CP}, the authors interpreted QCD collinear singularities in terms of operator product expansions in a two-dimensional CFT. We reformulate the algebraic structures arising in their work using the formalism of non-linear Lie conformal algebras developed in \cite{SK}.

title: Minimax optimal dual control -- The single input case
generated_summary:
This paper presents an explicit solution to the minimax optimal dual control problem for single-input linear systems with unknown input matrix (B-matrix), extending previous work beyond sign uncertainty to norm-bounded sets of stabilizable systems. The dual control framework addresses the fundamental tradeoff between exploiting current knowledge for control performance and exploring to learn uncertain system parameters.

The methodology centers on solving a Bellman inequality for worst-case disturbances and parametric uncertainty. The authors assume a known A-matrix and characterize the uncertain B-matrix as belonging to the union of two convex second-order cones. The proof leverages von Neumann's minimax theorem, exploiting the linear-convex structure of the problem, and distinguishes between two operating regimes: an "exploitation" mode where the controller uses current estimates and an "exploration" mode where input actions are designed to reduce parameter uncertainty. The resulting feedback law is a randomized nonlinear controller that simultaneously estimates B and controls the system.

The key result establishes a guaranteed upper bound on the nonlinear gain from disturbance energy to the expected weighted sum of state and input energy, valid for all admissible B-matrices. Notably, the controller can stabilize systems even under sign uncertainty in B, where linear time-invariant controllers fundamentally fail. This work is significant because it provides a constructive, explicitly computable dual control solution with rigorous worst-case performance guarantees, contributing to the growing intersection of robust control theory and adaptive learning.
original_abstract: An explicit solution is derived for the Bellman inequality corresponding to minimax optimal dual control. The minimizing player determines control action as a function of past state measurements and inputs. The maximizing player selects disturbances and model parameters for the underlying linear time-invariant dynamics. The optimal minimizing policy is a dual controller that optimizes the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation. Once sufficient data has been collected, the policy becomes a deterministic certainty equivalence controller. However, when data is insufficient, the policy introduces a randomized term to improve excitation.

title: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Risk-Sensitive Estimation via Conditional Value-at-Risk
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a framework for distributionally robust risk-sensitive estimation that minimizes the worst-case conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of squared estimation error over a type-2 Wasserstein ambiguity set centered at a nominal distribution. The approach addresses a key limitation of standard risk-sensitive estimators: their effectiveness depends on how accurately the assumed distribution captures tail events, which are inherently difficult to estimate from limited data.

The authors restrict attention to affine estimators and formulate the problem as minimizing the worst-case CVaR of squared error over all distributions within a Wasserstein ball. By exploiting strong duality in Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, they derive an equivalent convex reformulation applicable to generic quadratic loss functions. When the nominal distribution is finitely supported, the estimation problem reduces to a tractable semidefinite program. The framework subsumes several existing estimation paradigms as special cases, including distributionally robust mean squared error minimization (when the CVaR level equals one) and robust minimax estimation (as the CVaR level approaches zero).

Numerical experiments on an electricity price forecasting task demonstrate that the proposed estimators achieve improved out-of-sample CVaR of estimation error compared to existing methods, producing more accurate predictions during periods with pronounced price spikes while incurring only modest accuracy loss on typical days. This work is the first to combine Wasserstein distributional robustness with CVaR-based squared error criteria for estimation problems.
original_abstract: We propose a distributionally robust approach to risk-sensitive estimation of an unknown signal x from an observed signal y. The unknown signal and observation are modeled as random vectors whose joint probability distribution is unknown, but assumed to belong to a given type-2 Wasserstein ball of distributions, termed the ambiguity set. The performance of an estimator is measured according to the conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of the squared estimation error. Within this framework, we study the problem of computing affine estimators that minimize the worst-case CVaR over all distributions in the given ambiguity set. As our main result, we show that, when the nominal distribution at the center of the Wasserstein ball is finitely supported, such estimators can be exactly computed by solving a tractable semidefinite program. We evaluate the proposed estimators on a wholesale electricity price forecasting task using real market data and show that they deliver lower out-of-sample CVaR of squared error compared to existing methods.

title: Soft tilings
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of "softening" three-dimensional tilings—transforming space-filling arrangements of cells so that all cells become smooth (free of sharp corners or "spikes"). While previous work established that planar tilings require cells with at least two spikes on average, the three-dimensional setting is fundamentally different, permitting tilings composed entirely of soft cells.

The main contribution is a proof that every locally polyhedral tiling of three-dimensional space can be completely softened, confirming and extending a conjecture by Domokos, Goriely, Horváth, and Régős. A locally polyhedral tiling is one where each node has a neighborhood homeomorphic to that of a node in a standard polyhedral tiling, though the global tiling need not be homeomorphic to any polyhedral tiling.

The authors achieve this through a novel edge-bending algorithm that applies local homeomorphisms to eliminate all spikes from cells. A key advance over previous methods is that the new algorithm does not require a restrictive combinatorial condition on vertex colorings—specifically, it works even when the color classes of vertex polyhedra are disconnected, a scenario that prior approaches could not handle.

The paper illustrates the softening procedure on several examples, including the classical cube tiling, where the softened cube serves as a monotile. The authors also identify limitations of the edge-bending approach for general polyhedric tilings that are not locally polyhedral. These results significantly advance understanding of smooth space-filling shapes in three dimensions.
original_abstract: By means of constructing a new edge-bending algorithm, we prove that every locally polyhedral tiling of $\mathbb{R}^3$ can be completely softened. A weaker form of this statement, for polyhedral space tilings, was conjectured by Domokos, Goriely, G. Horváth and Regős in 2024. We also provide a short proof for a result of Domokos, G. Horváth, and Regős, stating that in a balanced polygonic tiling of the plane, the average number of spikes is at least 2 per cell.

title: Duality for the Adversarial Total Variation
generated_summary:
This paper derives dualization formulas for the nonlocal adversarial total variation functional, a key component in the mathematical formulation of adversarial training for machine learning classifiers. The adversarial total variation arises from reformulating the adversarial training problem as a regularization problem, where it serves as a nonlocal measure of the decision boundary length.

The authors develop duality results in two complementary settings. In the first, the base space is the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on a proper metric space, where the subdifferential lies in the space of finite signed Radon measures. Here, the dual formulation involves maximization over "random walks"—families of probability measures supported on closed balls around data points—and subgradients are characterized as nonlocal divergences of these random walks via the measurable maximum theorem. In the second setting, the base space is the space of essentially bounded functions on an open subset of Euclidean space, where test functions are more regular (L¹ functions) but compactness is lost, requiring a generalized measurable maximum theorem and yielding only a limit characterization of subgradients.

The key results establish that both formulations are consistent with each other and recover classical local differential operators as the adversarial budget tends to zero. These dualization formulas are significant because they provide the theoretical foundation for developing provably convergent primal-dual optimization algorithms for adversarial training, analogous to successful methods used for classical total variation minimization in image processing.
original_abstract: Adversarial training of binary classifiers can be reformulated as regularized risk minimization involving a nonlocal total variation. Building on this perspective, we establish a characterization of the subdifferential of this total variation using duality techniques. To achieve this, we derive a dual representation of the nonlocal total variation and a related integration of parts formula, involving a nonlocal gradient and divergence. We provide such duality statements both in the space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity on proper metric spaces and for the space of essentially bounded functions on Euclidean domains. Furthermore, under some additional conditions we provide characterizations of the subdifferential in these settings.

title: Positive, Negative, and Reliable Information in a First-Order Logic of Evidence and Truth
generated_summary:
This paper introduces **QletF**, a first-order extension of the logic of evidence and truth **letF**, designed as an information-based logic capable of representing three primitive and mutually independent notions: positive information, negative information, and reliable information. The logic extends Belnap-Dunn's four-valued logic by incorporating a classicality operator ○, where ○A expresses that information about A is reliable, subject to the constraint that reliability cannot hold when information is both inconsistent and lacking.

The authors develop the concept of *extended literals*—formulas A, ¬A, and ○A for atomic A—which serve as the semantic building blocks. Once semantic values are assigned to extended literals, all other formulas receive values deterministically, distinguishing this approach from typical logics with recovery operators that exhibit non-deterministic semantics. The first-order semantics employs twist structures based on six values corresponding to six informational scenarios, with predicates interpreted through extensions, anti-extensions, and novel ○-extensions.

Key results include a sound and complete six-valued semantics for QletF, the replacement property (allowing substitution of equivalent formulas in any context), conjunctive and disjunctive normal forms, and a prenex normal form theorem—metatheoretical properties rarely achieved together in paraconsistent logics with recovery operators.

The significance lies in providing a well-behaved, deterministic first-order framework for reasoning about information that may be incomplete, inconsistent, or unreliable, with potential applications to contexts involving informational disorder and database management.
original_abstract: In this paper we present the first-order logic QLETF+, a quantified version of the logic LETF+, introduced in Coniglio and Rodrigues (Studia Logica 112:561-606, 2024). QLETF+ exhibits several properties that are not always enjoyed by logics equipped with classicality operators. We show that it satisfies the replacement property and admits conjunctive, disjunctive, and prenex normal forms. Alongside extensions and anti-extensions, as in the previously studied first-order semantics for LETs, we make use here of what we call o-extensions: given an n-ary predicate symbol P, the o-extension of P is the set of n-tuples of individuals that satisfy the predicate oP. We prove the soundness and completeness of the deductive system of QLETF+ with respect to the six-valued first-order semantics.

title: BBP transition and the leading eigenvector of the spiked Wigner model with inhomogeneous noise
generated_summary:
This paper investigates an inhomogeneous spiked Wigner model in which the noise matrix entries have random, non-identically distributed variances, defined through a factorized variance profile where individual variance parameters are drawn from an arbitrary distribution. This extension naturally arises as the high-connectivity limit of adjacency matrices of random graphs with heterogeneous degree distributions.

Using the cavity method for dense random matrices combined with resolvent-based techniques, the authors derive exact equations in the high-dimensional limit for the empirical spectral density, spectral edges, outlier eigenvalue, and the Baik–Ben Arous–Péché (BBP) transition line as functions of the variance profile and spike prior. A central contribution is an analytic expression for the full distribution of the outlier eigenvector components, shown to be a weighted superposition of Gaussians whose parameters depend on both the signal prior and variance profile—going beyond previous results that characterized leading eigenvectors only through their projection onto the spike.

Applying these results to a truncated power-law variance profile, the authors reveal a rich, non-monotonic dependence of the BBP critical line on the noise-inhomogeneity parameters. Notably, when the variance distribution concentrates weight near small values, noise inhomogeneity can enhance signal detectability by lowering the critical signal-to-noise ratio. Conversely, broadly distributed variances with large modes suppress detection. All theoretical predictions show excellent agreement with finite-dimensional numerical diagonalizations, demonstrating that noise structure plays a crucial and sometimes beneficial role in high-dimensional spectral inference.
original_abstract: The spiked Wigner ensemble is a prototypical model for high-dimensional inference. We study the spectral properties of an inhomogeneous rank-one spiked Wigner model in which the variance of each entry of the noise matrix is itself a random variable. In the high-dimensional limit, we derive exact equations for the spectral edges, the outlier eigenvalue, and the distribution of the components of the outlier eigenvector. These equations determine the BBP transition line that separates the gapped phase, where the signal is detectable, from the gapless phase. In the gapped regime, the distribution of the outlier eigenvector provides a natural estimator of the spike. We solve the equations for a noise matrix whose variances are generated from a truncated power-law distribution. In this case, the BBP transition line is non-monotonic, showing that an inhomogeneous noise can enhance signal detectability.

title: Learning the Riccati solution operator for time-varying LQR via Deep Operator Networks
generated_summary:
This paper introduces an operator learning framework using Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets) to approximate the solution operator of the Riccati equation arising in Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problems, replacing the need to repeatedly solve computationally expensive differential Riccati equations for varying system parameters. The approach recasts the Riccati equation as a nonlinear mapping between function spaces, where a DeepONet learns to map time-dependent system matrices to the corresponding matrix-valued Riccati solutions in an offline training phase, enabling near-instantaneous evaluation for new parameter configurations.

The authors establish rigorous theoretical guarantees linking operator approximation error to control performance, demonstrating that feedback gain accuracy, trajectory deviation, cost suboptimality, and closed-loop stability are preserved when approximation errors remain below identified thresholds. A progressive learning strategy is also proposed to transfer knowledge from lower to higher dimensions, reducing trainable parameters by approximately 95% with minimal accuracy loss.

Numerical experiments on systems of dimensions 3, 4, and 10, for both time-invariant and time-varying settings, demonstrate stability preservation rates exceeding 97.5% and inference speedups of up to several hundred times compared to classical solvers. Rare failure cases align precisely with theoretical predictions. The framework represents a promising paradigm for amortized optimal control, offering significant computational advantages in parametric, real-time, and high-dimensional control applications where repeated Riccati equation solutions are required.
original_abstract: We propose a computational framework for replacing the repeated numerical solution of differential Riccati equations in finite-horizon Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problems by a learned operator surrogate. Instead of solving a nonlinear matrix-valued differential equation for each new system instance, we construct offline an approximation of the associated solution operator mapping time-dependent system parameters to the Riccati trajectory. The resulting model enables fast online evaluation of approximate optimal feedbacks across a wide class of systems, thereby shifting the computational burden from repeated numerical integration to a one-time learning stage. From a theoretical perspective, we establish control-theoretic guarantees for this operator-based approximation. In particular, we derive bounds quantifying how operator approximation errors propagate to feedback performance, trajectory accuracy, and cost suboptimality, and we prove that exponential stability of the closed-loop system is preserved under sufficiently accurate operator approximation. These results provide a framework to assess the reliability of data-driven approximations in optimal control. On the computational side, we design tailored DeepONet architectures for matrix-valued, time-dependent problems and introduce a progressive learning strategy to address scalability with respect to the system dimension. Numerical experiments on both time-invariant and time-varying LQR problems demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high accuracy and strong generalization across a wide range of system configurations, while delivering substantial computational speedups compared to classical solvers. The method offers an effective and scalable alternative for parametric and real-time optimal control applications.

title: A primality test for $Kp^\ell - 1$ numbers
generated_summary:
This paper presents a deterministic primality test for integers of the form $N = c_D k p^\ell - 1$, where $p$ is an odd prime, by leveraging the algebraic structure of unitary groups over arbitrary quadratic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$. The work significantly generalizes previous primality tests that were restricted to specific quadratic extensions such as the Gaussian integers or particular small primes.

The methodology centers on determining the order of the group $G_p(D)$ over finite fields, proving it equals $p - \left(\frac{D}{p}\right)$ and is cyclic. Using the norm map on quadratic extensions and the Chinese Remainder Theorem, the authors establish a natural analogue of Euler's totient function in this setting. They then exploit the cyclic structure to formulate conditions involving modular exponentiation and cyclotomic polynomials within the associated quotient ring.

The key results include a necessary and sufficient primality criterion (Theorem 1), a generalized Lucasian certificate providing a sufficient condition requiring verification of two modular conditions (Theorem 2), and a generalized Miller-Rabin test adapted to numbers of the form $N+1 = 2^s u$ (Theorems 3 and 4). The authors also introduce generalized notions of pseudoprimes and Carmichael numbers with an analogue of Korselt's criterion.

The test requires only a single modular exponentiation with computational complexity $\tilde{O}(\ell \log^2 p)$, making it efficient for practical applications. The framework unifies and extends numerous earlier results for specific forms such as $A \cdot 3^n - 1$, $A \cdot 5^n - 1$, and $A \cdot 7^n - 1$ into a single coherent theory.
original_abstract: We develop an algebraic framework over arbitrary quadratic fields $L = \mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{D})$ to generalize the Miller-Rabin primality test. Consequently, we present a deterministic primality test for integers of the form $N = c_D k p^{\ell} - 1$ that requires only a single modular exponentiation and achieves a computational complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log^2 N)$. Furthermore, we also establish an analogue of Korselt's criterion within this setting. Finally, computational data generated using SageMath confirm its efficiency, successfully establishing the primality of numbers in the associated quadratic field within milliseconds.

title: An elementary proof of Sierksma's conjecture for seven points in the plane
generated_summary:
This paper presents a new elementary proof of a special case of Sierksma's conjecture, a long-standing open problem in combinatorial geometry. Sierksma's conjecture (1979) asserts that every set of (r−1)(d+1)+1 points in ℝᵈ admits at least ((r−1)!)ᵈ Tverberg partitions into r parts whose convex hulls intersect. The authors specifically prove that every set of seven points in the plane has at least four Tverberg partitions into three parts, confirming the case r=3, d=2.

The key contribution is methodological: while the only previous proof of this result, by Hell (2008), relied on advanced topological machinery, the authors employ purely elementary geometric arguments inspired by Birch's original 1959 proof of Tverberg's theorem. The approach involves analyzing the structure of the "3-core" of the point set—the region covered by at least three of the triangles formed by the points—and systematically considering cases based on its dimension. Through careful geometric reasoning about half-spaces, sectors, and convex hulls, they establish the required lower bound on Tverberg partitions in each case.

In 1956 Amitsur famously proved that, when k is uncountable, D cannot be k-affine unless D is algebraic over k. The primary applications are to division algebras of fractions of suitably conditioned iterated skew polynomial rings over k, including many examples naturally arising in Lie theoretic and quantum group settings. title: On the Independence Number of the Prime-Coprime Graph of a Finite Group

original_abstract: The prime-coprime graph $Θ(G)$ of a finite group $G$ is the simple graph with vertex set $G$, where two distinct elements are adjacent whenever the greatest common divisor of their orders is either $1$ or a prime. We characterize all finite groups $G$ for which $Θ(G)$ is a split graph. We establish a general lower bound for the independence number of $Θ(G)$ of an arbitrary finite group $G$. Moreover, we explicitly compute the independence number of $Θ(G)$ for several distinguished families of finite groups, including cyclic, dihedral, dicyclic, and semidihedral groups.

title: High-fidelity and Network-based Spatio-temporal Mathematical Models of Alzheimer's Disease Progression and their Validation Against PET-SUVR Imaging Data

original_abstract: Alzheimer's disease is the most common neurodegenerative disorder. Its pathological development is connected with the misfolding and accumulation of two toxic proteins: amyloid-beta and tau proteins. Mathematical models provide a valuable quantitative tool for monitoring disease progression. In this work, we proposed and compare a novel framework where the spatio-temporal dynamics of amyloid-beta and tau proteins is modeled based on employing either three-dimensional patient-specific geometries or through reduced network-based models defined on the brain connectome. More specifically, a high-fidelity biophysical model is proposed on three-dimensional brain geometries reconstructed from magnetic resonance imaging, whereas a network-based reduced formulation is defined on the brain connectome. For both approaches, a suitable numerical discretisation is proposed. A sensitivity analysis is presented to quantify the influence of model parameters on protein concentration patterns as well as compare the quality of the predictions. For both approaches, the results are validated against PET-SUVR clinical data using 18FAZD4694 for amyloid-beta and 18FMK6240 for tau protein. The results indicate that the three-dimensional model provides the most accurate and biologically consistent description of the disease progression, but remains computationally demanding. On the other hand, the reduced graph-based model is cheaper, but it is not always able to achieve reliable results.

title: On the quasi-monomiality of the $α$-and $δ$-invariants

title: Spectral theory of plasmonic resonances in the nonlocal regime

original_abstract: We present a rigorous spectral analysis of plasmonic resonances in the nonlocal regime of spatially dispersive media. We adopt the quasi-static approximation of the hydrodynamic Drude model, which provides an analytically tractable setting to account for nonlocal effects. By reformulating the governing equations as a boundary integral system, we obtain an analytic Fredholm operator pencil that characterizes resonant behaviour. This framework enables the study of nonlocal plasmonic eigenvalues in general bounded Lipschitz domains, together with a corresponding resonant expansion of the scattered field. Our main result reveals a fundamental change in spectral structure: in contrast to the local theory -- which exhibits infinitely many surface plasmon modes and field singularities in domains with corners -- the nonlocal model admits a discrete real spectrum with a single accumulation point at a strictly positive value. Consequently, only finitely many surface plasmon modes exist, and the singular behaviour associated with sharp geometries is regularized. As such, our results show that nonlocality does not merely shift plasmonic resonances but completely reshapes the spectral landscape in a way that provides a mathematically transparent explanation for several nonlocal phenomena previously observed in numerical studies.

original_abstract: We introduce the notion of confined subalgebras in the context of the group von Neumann algebra. We also define Uniformly Recurrent States -- an operator-algebraic analog of Uniformly Recurrent Subgroups. Using this framework, we show that a countable discrete group is $C^*$-simple if and only if it admits no non-trivial amenable confined subalgebras. This generalizes the well-known result of Kennedy that characterizes $C^*$-simplicity in terms of trivial amenable uniformly recurrent subgroups.

title: Geometric Trajectory Optimization for TRACON Arrivals: An NLP Approach with ATC Vectoring Maneuver Modeling

original_abstract: Terminal airspace congestion remains a major bottleneck in the global air traffic network. Although the Aircraft Sequencing and Scheduling Problem (ASSP) has been widely studied, many methods rely on simplified node-link abstractions that ignore the practical flight path, producing schedules that can be hard to execute under real airspace geometric constraints. We formulate a single-stage nonlinear programming (NLP) model with a weighted objective function that optimizes Baseleg path extension and segment-wise speed profiles for arriving aircraft. The model enforces nonlinear geometric coupling between Baseleg extensions and the required Radius-to-Fix (RF) turn for Final Approach Fix (FAF) intercept through closed-form expressions. Under the First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) rule, it generates separated, operationally feasible trajectories aligned with controller practice. Monte Carlo simulations with ample runs on the A80 TRACON in Atlanta demonstrate minimal separation violations below the runway capacity threshold through tactical path stretching, with violations occurring only when arrival rates exceed the maximum tolerable rate.

title: On the Effect of Quadratic Regularization in Direct Data-Driven LQR

original_abstract: This paper proposes an explainability concept for direct data-driven linear quadratic regulation (LQR) with quadratic regularization. Our perspective follows the parametric effect of regularization, an analysis approach that translates regularization costs from auxiliary variables to system quantities, enabling intuitive interpretations. The framework further enables the elimination of auxiliary variables, thereby reducing computational complexity. title: Kernel-Preserving Dynamics and Symmetry Classification for Synchronization Subspaces

original_abstract: We study the preservation and stability of synchronization subspaces in tensor products of finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Given self-adjoint operators $T_A$ and $T_B$ on local subsystems, the synchronization subspace is defined as the kernel of the difference operator $K = T_A \otimes I - I \otimes T_B$. We establish two main results: First for $ε$-compatible dynamics satisfying $||[H,K]|| \leq ε$, we prove a sharp drift bound where any initially synchronized state deviates from the kernel at a rate at most linear in time with slope $ε$. We show by explicit construction that this estimate is optimal to leading order. Second in the presence of finite group symmetry, we show that the synchronization subspace coincides with the diagonal isotypic component in the tensor product decomposition and we characterize the algebra of synchronization-preserving dynamics as the intersection of the commutants of the group action and synchronization operator.

title: Real-Time Algorithms for Model Predictive Control of Hybrid Dynamical Systems

original_abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of hybrid dynamical systems is challenging because the associated optimization problem is nonsmooth and the resulting feedback law is discontinuous. This paper develops real-time MPC algorithms for nonlinear hybrid systems modeled as dynamical complementarity systems. The resulting optimal control problems are formulated as mathematical programs with complementarity constraints (MPCCs). To address this, we introduce three real-time hybrid MPC schemes whose feedback phase solves a quadratic program with complementarity constraints per sample, yielding local discontinuous piecewise affine approximations of the MPC feedback law. Moreover, we derive continuity and differentiability results for parametric MPCCs, and establish conditions under which the approximation error of our new hybrid MPC algorithms remains uniformly bounded despite solution discontinuities. The algorithms are demonstrated on a robotic manipulation example, where contact sequences are discovered online.

title: Balance-Guided Sparse Identification of Multiscale Nonlinear PDEs with Small-coefficient Terms

original_abstract: Data-driven discovery of governing equations has advanced significantly in recent years; however, existing methods often struggle in multiscale systems where dynamically significant terms may have small coefficients. Therefore, we propose Balance-Guided SINDy (BG-SINDy) inspired by the principle of dominant balance, which reformulates $\ell_0$-constrained sparse regression as a term-level $\ell_{2,0}$-regularized problem and solves it using a progressive pruning strategy. Terms are ranked according to their relative contributions to the governing equation balance rather than their absolute coefficient magnitudes. Based on this criterion, BG-SINDy alternates between least-squares regression and elimination of negligible terms, thereby preserving dynamically significant terms even when their coefficients are small. Numerical experiments on the Korteweg--de Vries equation with a small dispersion coefficient, a modified Burgers equation with vanishing hyperviscosity, a modified Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equation with multiple small-coefficient terms, and a two-dimensional reaction--diffusion system demonstrate the validity of BG-SINDy in discovering small-coefficient terms. title: Crossed product C*-algebras associated with non-minimal actions on the circle

For non-minimal actions, the algebra has a unique maximal ideal that is a continuous-trace C*-algebra of topological dimension one. For actions of ℤᵈ, the authors compute the ordered K-theory and trace pairing, extending classical results for irrational rotation algebras and noncommutative tori.

original_abstract: We examine crossed product C*-algebras associated with non-minimal free actions of countably infinite discrete abelian groups on the circle, extending the work of Putnam, Schmidt, and Skau. We obtain a large class of unital separable nuclear and non-simple C*-algebras that are quasidiagonal, have stable rank one, and admit a unique tracial state. We determine their ideal structure and establish an improved uniform upper bound for their nuclear dimension. Finally, in the case $G = \mathbb{Z}^d$, we compute the ordered K-theory and its trace pairing.

title: Function spaces and potential theory in the Orlicz setting

original_abstract: In this article, we study certain transcendental function spaces arising in potential theory within the framework of Orlicz spaces. Specifically, we generalize Bessel and Lizorkin-Triebel spaces to the nonstandard setting of Orlicz spaces. We recover classical results from potential theory, such as the fact that Bessel-Orlicz spaces of integer order coincide with Orlicz-Sobolev spaces (Calderón type theorem), and we establish inclusion results for fractional orders. Moreover, we prove a Strauss-type lemma for potential spaces. In the last sections, we show that certain Orlicz-Lizorkin-Triebel spaces coincide with Bessel-Orlicz spaces, and we provide a useful atomic decomposition for these spaces.

title: Virtual element methods for a quad-curl problem on general planar domains

The methods achieve optimal convergence rates consistent with solution regularity: O(h^k) for smooth solutions on convex domains and reduced rates (e.g., O(h^{2/3})) on non-convex domains where singular solutions arise. The quadratic VEM consistently outperforms the linear VEM for comparable degrees of freedom.

The significance of this work lies in providing the simplest polytopal method to date for the two-dimensional quad-curl problem, with natural extensions possible to three dimensions and other electromagnetics problems through combination with existing virtual element frameworks.
original_abstract: We design and analyze virtual element methods for a quad-curl problem on general polygonal domains that are based on the Hodge decomposition of divergence-free vector fields. Numerical results that corroborate the theoretical analysis are also presented.

title: Nested Sequents for Horn-Characterizable Quantified Modal Logics with Equality via Reachability Rules
generated_summary:
This paper presents a unified nested sequent framework for a broad class of quantified modal logics (QMLs) with equality, characterized by Horn-definable frame and domain conditions. The logics considered extend a base system with seriality, generalized path conditions, and various domain conditions (increasing, decreasing, constant, classical, non-empty, or varying inner domains), following the semantic framework of Corsi's normal models with inner and outer domains.

The methodology centers on two key innovations: incorporating signatures (multisets of terms) into nested sequents to handle quantificational reasoning across different domain conditions, and introducing reachability rules parameterized by formal grammar systems (Σ-systems). These reachability rules propagate or consume formulae and terms along paths in nested sequents, enabling modular toggling between different QMLs by simply changing the parameterizing grammar. The authors work with one-sided nested sequents in negation normal form.

The key results include sound and cut-free complete nested sequent calculi for all QMLs in the considered class, height-preserving admissibility and invertibility results for structural rules, and a uniform syntactic cut-elimination theorem. Notably, the authors observe that the Extended Barcan Rule is naturally entailed by the standard universal quantifier rule in the nested setting, confirming that nested sequents inherently capture QMLs with constant outer domains.
