original_abstract: We develop a qualitative-dynamics framework for general Iterated Function Systems (IFSs) on locally compact spaces. Our approach extends to IFSs a framework recently developed in the semiflows setting by James Yorke and the present author based on binary relations (streams) that encode which point can be regarded as "downstream" from which. This leads to a graph representation of the global qualitative dynamics that separates recurrent behavior from gradient-like behavior.

title: Recovery Guarantees for Continual Learning of Dependent Tasks: Memory, Data-Dependent Regularization, and Data-Dependent Weights
generated_summary:
This paper develops theoretical recovery guarantees for continual learning (CL) methods applied to nonlinear regression tasks with explicitly modeled task dependencies. The authors propose an autoregressive task dependency model where data from each task is generated through deterministic nonlinear transformations of previous tasks' data, inspired by dynamical systems, rotated/permuted MNIST benchmarks, and geometric vision applications. This structured dependency—rather than arbitrary cross-task dependence—enables tractable analysis while remaining practically relevant. The framework considers learning a shared true predictor from partial observations stored in memory buffers.

Key results include estimation error bounds that exhibit only logarithmic dependence on transformation Lipschitz constants, significantly improving over prior work's linear dependence. The bounds eliminate the logarithmic degradation with the number of tasks seen in previous analyses. For weighted experience replay, optimal bounds inversely proportional to total available data are achieved. For knowledge distillation regularization, bounds are derived through a recursive argument. For data-dependent weights, the analysis extends to handle weights as random variables.

The significance lies in bridging the gap between analyses of simple linear models and overly general frameworks, providing the first unified theoretical treatment demonstrating how structured task dependency benefits continual learning across multiple paradigms.
original_abstract: Continual learning (CL) is concerned with learning multiple tasks sequentially without forgetting previously learned tasks. Despite substantial empirical advances over recent years, the theoretical development of CL remains in its infancy. At the heart of developing CL theory lies the challenge that the data distribution varies across tasks, and we argue that properly addressing this challenge requires understanding this variation--dependency among tasks. To explicitly model task dependency, we consider nonlinear regression tasks and propose the assumption that these tasks are dependent in such a way that the data of the current task is a nonlinear transformation of previous data. With this model and under natural assumptions, we prove statistical recovery guarantees (more specifically, bounds on estimation errors) for several CL paradigms in practical use, including experience replay with data-independent regularization and data-independent weights that balance the losses of tasks, replay with data-dependent weights, and continual learning with data-dependent regularization (e.g., knowledge distillation). To the best of our knowledge, our bounds are informative in cases where prior work gives vacuous bounds.

title: Diverse Dictionary Learning
generated_summary:
## Summary

This paper introduces **diverse dictionary learning**, a framework for recovering latent variables from observations under minimal assumptions, without requiring parametric constraints, auxiliary supervision, or interventional data. The main contribution is a novel notion of **generalized identifiability** based on set-theoretic operations: even when full recovery of all latent variables is impossible, structured subsets defined by intersections, complements, and symmetric differences of latent supports associated with observed variables remain identifiable. This provides meaningful partial recovery guarantees in general nonparametric settings.

The methodology formalizes set-theoretic indeterminacy and proves that the dependency structure between latent and observed variables is identifiable up to permutation. When the dependency structure exhibits **sufficient diversity**—a condition strictly weaker than existing structural sparsity requirements—full element-wise identifiability is achieved. Crucially, the only required inductive bias is dependency sparsity regularization on the Jacobian, applicable to any differentiable generative model.

Experiments on synthetic data confirm that set-theoretic disentanglement holds as predicted, and element-wise recovery succeeds when diversity conditions are met. On benchmark disentanglement datasets (Cars3D, Shapes3D, MPI3D), dependency sparsity consistently improves performance across VAE, GAN, and diffusion model backbones, often outperforming latent sparsity regularization.

The significance lies in providing a universal, assumption-light regularization principle with formal guarantees, bridging the gap between theoretical identifiability and practical applicability across diverse latent variable modeling scenarios.
original_abstract: Given only observational data $X = g(Z)$, where both the latent variables $Z$ and the generating process $g$ are unknown, recovering $Z$ is ill-posed without additional assumptions. Existing methods often assume linearity or rely on auxiliary supervision and functional constraints. However, such assumptions are rarely verifiable in practice, and most theoretical guarantees break down under even mild violations, leaving uncertainty about how to reliably understand the hidden world. To make identifiability actionable in the real-world scenarios, we take a complementary view: in the general settings where full identifiability is unattainable, what can still be recovered with guarantees, and what biases could be universally adopted? We introduce the problem of diverse dictionary learning to formalize this view. Specifically, we show that intersections, complements, and symmetric differences of latent variables linked to arbitrary observations, along with the latent-to-observed dependency structure, are still identifiable up to appropriate indeterminacies even without strong assumptions. These set-theoretic results can be composed using set algebra to construct structured and essential views of the hidden world, such as genus-differentia definitions. When sufficient structural diversity is present, they further imply full identifiability of all latent variables. Notably, all identifiability benefits follow from a simple inductive bias during estimation that can be readily integrated into most models. We validate the theory and demonstrate the benefits of the bias on both synthetic and real-world data.

title: Composition and tensor train structure in polynomial optimization
generated_summary:

The key insight is that even fully dense polynomials can sometimes be decomposed into sequential compositions of local maps operating on low-dimensional intermediate states, and this structure can be leveraged for scalable optimization.

The authors propose two methods to exploit this structure within the moment-SOS hierarchy: one based on **correlative sparsity** (chordal approach) and another using **push-forward operators** from measure theory. Both methods introduce auxiliary lifting variables that reveal sparse structure in the reformulated problem. The chordal approach handles higher-rank problems more efficiently, while the push-forward approach yields smaller variable groups but at the cost of higher polynomial degrees. The paper proves convergence for both hierarchies and provides detailed complexity analyses.

**Tensor train polynomials** emerge as an important special case where composition maps are linear in their first coordinate. The framework is demonstrated on diverse applications including Markov chain control, quantum optimal control of single qubits, and reachability analysis of feedforward neural networks with polynomial activations, successfully handling problems with dozens of variables where dense approaches would be intractable.

This work bridges tensor decomposition methods and moment-SOS certification, opening pathways toward scalable, globally certified polynomial optimization for structured high-dimensional problems, with natural extensions to more general tensor network topologies.
original_abstract: We study polynomial optimization problems whose objective has a composition or tensor train structure. These polynomials can be evaluated as a sequence of maps, giving rise to intermediate variables (``states'') of dimension lower than the ambient dimension. Structures like these arise naturally in dynamical systems, Markov chains, and neural networks. We develop two moment-SOS (sums of squares) hierarchies that exploit this composition structure in different ways. The first one, termed state-lifting chordal, is based on the correlative sparsity graph of the problem. The second one, termed state-lifting push-forward, encodes the structure at the level of the measures directly. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed methods can compute certified bounds for problems with hundreds or even a thousand variables. To illustrate the versatility of the hierarchies we apply them to Markov chain optimization, quantum optimal control, and neural networks.

title: The Multi-Block DC Function Class: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications
generated_summary:

original_abstract: Persistent homology (PH) encodes global information, such as cycles, and is thus increasingly integrated into graph neural networks (GNNs). PH methods in GNNs typically traverse an increasing sequence of subgraphs. In this work, we first expose limitations of this inclusion procedure. To remedy these shortcomings, we analyze contractions as a principled topological operation, in particular, for graph representation learning. We study the persistence of contraction sequences, which we call Contraction Homology (CH). We establish that forward PH and CH differ in expressivity. We then introduce Hourglass Persistence, a class of topological descriptors that interleave a sequence of inclusions and contractions to boost expressivity, learnability, and stability. We also study related families parametrized by two paradigms. We also discuss how our framework extends to simplicial and cellular networks. title: Joint Exclusivity

original_abstract: We introduce joint exclusivity (JE), a form of extremal negative dependence that extends the classical notion of mutual exclusivity. title: Complete Isocategorical Classification of Groups of Order 64 via GAP

title: Beyond the Bellman Fixed Point: Geometry and Fast Policy Identification in Value Iteration

original_abstract: Dynamic programming is one of the most fundamental methodologies for solving Markov decision problems. Among its many variants, Q-value iteration (Q-VI) is particularly important due to its conceptual simplicity and its classical contraction-based convergence guarantee. Despite the central role of this contraction property, it does not fully reveal the geometric structure of the Q-VI trajectory. In particular, when one is interested not only in the final limit $Q^*$ but also in when the induced greedy policy becomes effectively optimal, the standard contraction argument provides only a coarse characterization. To formalize this notion, we denote by $\mathcal X^*$ the set of $Q$-functions whose corresponding tie-broken greedy policies are optimal, referred to as the practically optimal solution set (POS). In this paper, we revisit discounted Q-VI through the lens of switching system theory and derive new geometric insights into its behavior. In particular, we show that although Q-VI does not reach $Q^*$ in finite time in general, it identifies the optimal action class in finite time. Furthermore, we prove that the distance from the iterate to a particular subset of $\mathcal X^*$ decays exponentially at a rate governed by the joint spectral radius (JSR) of a restricted switching family. This rate can be strictly faster than the standard $γ$ rate when the restricted JSR is strictly smaller than $γ$, while the convergence of the entire $Q$-function to $Q^*$ can still be dominated by the slower $γ$ mode, where $γ$ denotes the discount factor. These results reveal a two-stage geometric behavior of Q-VI: a fast convergence toward $\mathcal X_1$, followed by a slower convergence toward $Q^*$ in general.

title: Refined 3D index

The authors formulate a precise mathematical expression for the refined 3D index and establish a main conjecture relating refined indices computed from different Dehn surgery representations of the same 3-manifold via injective linear maps between refinement parameter spaces. Key results demonstrate that the refined index provides a strictly stronger invariant than the unrefined version, distinguishing 3-manifolds (such as certain Seifert-fibered spaces) that are indistinguishable by the original index. The refinement also regularizes divergences appearing in the unrefined index for non-hyperbolic manifolds containing incompressible tori, and discriminates between distinct IR phases of the associated gauge theories, including mass-gapped TQFTs versus N=4 superconformal theories. original_abstract: We introduce a refined version of the 3D index for 3-manifolds, building on the construction of the 3D $\mathcal{N}=2$ gauge theory $T[M]$ by Dimofte-Gaiotto-Gukov and Gang-Yonekura. The refined index is a superconformal index of $T[M]$ equipped with additional gradings that capture enhanced flavor symmetries of the effective theory. Our construction is based on a Dehn surgery presentation of $M$ in terms of an ideally triangulated link complement $N$. We derive an explicit infinite-sum formula for the refined index and provide nontrivial checks in representative examples, supporting its invariance under changes of triangulation, Dehn surgery presentation, and other auxiliary data. As a strictly stronger invariant, the refined index enables finer distinctions among 3-manifolds and among distinct IR phases of the associated gauge theories. We also introduce a computational tool, \textsc{Refined Index Calculator}, for its explicit evaluation.

title: Orderings of Generalized k-Markov Numbers

The methodology centers on a combinatorial approach using fence posets and snake graphs from generalized cluster algebras. The authors associate a fence poset to each pair of integer lattice points via intersections of line segments with a lattice of lines, then define the k-Markov distance between points as the number of order ideals of the corresponding poset. A key technical tool is an expanded generalized Ptolemy relation that accommodates collinear points, along with detailed analysis of k-analogues of Fibonacci and Pell number sequences.

The main result precisely characterizes monotonicity behavior along lines with rational slope: for slopes above a critical threshold depending on k, generalized k-Markov numbers strictly increase; below another threshold, they strictly decrease; between these thresholds, they first decrease then increase. Notably, the gap between these thresholds shrinks as k grows, implying that a k-version of the famous Uniqueness Conjecture holds in the limit. This work unifies and extends several recent results on Aigner's conjectures to the broader k-Markov setting.
original_abstract: A $k$-Markov number is a positive integer that appears in a positive integral solution to the Diophantine equation $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + k(xy + xz + yz) = (3+3k)xyz$. This equation was introduced by Gyoda and Matsushita. When $k =0$, this definition recovers that of ordinary Markov numbers. The set of $k$-Markov numbers can be indexed by pairs of coprime positive integers. There is a consistent way to label non-coprime pairs with positive integers as well, yielding a larger set of ``generalized $k$-Markov numbers.'' In this paper, we classify lines along which the generalized $k$-Markov numbers grow monotonically, extending work in the ordinary case by Lee-Li-Rabideau-Schiffler and by the second author. We find that, as $k$ grows, the $k$-Markov numbers are more likely to be monotonic along a random line. This gives evidence that a $k$-version of Frobenius' uniqueness conjecture, which has been proposed by Gyoda and Maruyama, could be true.

title: Elementary symmetric polynomials and a potentially injective family of maps on partitions
generated_summary:

The main contributions are fourfold. First, the authors disprove Conjecture 2, which claimed pre_k is injective on partitions of n with at least k parts for k ≥ 3, by constructing an infinite family of counterexamples showing pre_k fails to be injective on partitions with exactly k parts. They then propose a refined conjecture restricting attention to partitions with at least k+1 parts. Second, they establish a transfer theorem showing that if pre_k is injective on partitions with ℓ parts, then pre_{ℓ-k} is also injective on the same set, enabling results about one map to yield results about others. Third, they prove the injectivity of pre_2 on partitions with four, five, and six parts using lattice-theoretic analysis of the partial order on parts, extending earlier work that handled at most three parts. Fourth, they initiate the study of the image of pre_2, proving that the number of partitions of n in this image satisfies a lower bound involving the divisor function τ(n+1).

The work demonstrates that treating the family of pre_k maps collectively, rather than individually, provides a more productive framework for understanding their injectivity properties.
original_abstract: In this article, we provide an infinite family of examples to disprove a recent conjecture due to Ballantine and her collaborators on the injectivity of a class of maps, namely pre_k, defined on integer partitions. These maps arise from applying the sequence of elementary symmetric polynomials to integer partitions, where pre_k is associated with the kth polynomial. Subsequently, we state a modified version of their conjecture. Throwing fresh light on these class of maps, we study the inter-relationships between them, deviating from the approaches so far, which study these maps one at a time. Though one case of the conjecture (k=2) has now been settled independently by the work of Ballantine and collaborators, and Li, we provide alternate proofs of three subcases corresponding to this settled case. We also discuss lower bounds for the number of partitions of n which are in the image of the map pre_2.

title: Algorithmic Contiguity from Low-Degree Heuristic II: Predicting Detection-Recovery Gaps

The key insight is that recovery is fundamentally harder than detection, requiring exponentially larger statistical divergence, and the authors develop an algorithmic analogue of this principle within the low-degree polynomial framework.

The methodology proceeds in three steps: reducing recovery to a detection problem with highly imbalanced error probabilities (high type-I accuracy but exponentially small type-II error), establishing mild upper bounds on the low-degree testing advantage, and deriving contradictions via an refined algorithmic contiguity argument. This approach is notably simpler and more modular than prior methods that directly bound the low-degree minimum mean squared error.

The authors apply this framework to six canonical models: planted submatrix, planted dense subgraph, stochastic block model, multi-frequency angular synchronization, orthogonal group synchronization, and multi-layer stochastic block models. Key results include evidence that the Kesten–Stigum threshold governs computational recovery in stochastic block models for up to polynomially many communities, and that the Baik–Ben Arous–Péché spectral threshold remains the computational barrier for synchronization problems even with growing frequency or dimension parameters—resolving open questions from prior work.

The significance lies in providing a unified, relatively simple methodology that predicts sharp detection-recovery gaps across diverse models, conditional on the low-degree conjecture for related testing problems.
original_abstract: The low-degree polynomial framework has emerged as a powerful tool for providing evidence of statistical-computational gaps in high-dimensional inference. For detection problems, the standard approach bounds the low-degree advantage through an explicit orthonormal basis. However, this method does not extend naturally to estimation tasks, and thus fails to capture the \emph{detection-recovery gap phenomenon} that arises in many high-dimensional problems. Although several important advances have been made to overcome this limitation \cite{SW22, SW25, CGGV25+}, the existing approaches often rely on delicate, model-specific combinatorial arguments. In this work, we develop a general approach for obtaining \emph{conditional computational lower bounds} for recovery problems from mild bounds on low-degree testing advantage. Our method combines the notion of algorithmic contiguity in \cite{Li25} with a cross-validation reduction in \cite{DHSS25} that converts successful recovery into a hypothesis test with lopsided success probabilities. In contrast to prior unconditional lower bounds, our argument is conceptually simple, flexible, and largely model-independent. We apply this framework to several canonical inference problems, including planted submatrix, planted dense subgraph, stochastic block model, multi-frequency angular synchronization, orthogonal group synchronization, and multi-layer stochastic block model. In the first three settings, our method recovers existing low-degree lower bounds for recovery in \cite{SW22, SW25} via a substantially simpler argument. In the latter three, it gives new evidence for conjectured computational thresholds including the persistence of detection-recovery gaps. Together, these results suggest that mild control of low-degree advantage is often sufficient to explain computational barriers for recovery in high-dimensional statistical models.

title: Phase-Scheduled Multi-Agent Systems for Token-Efficient Coordination
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Phase-Scheduled Multi-Agent Systems (PSMAS), a continuous control framework for coordinating LLM-based multi-agent systems to reduce token consumption while preserving task performance. Unlike static pruning, hierarchical decomposition, or discrete routing approaches, PSMAS treats agent coordination as a continuous control problem over shared attention space. Agents are mapped onto a circular manifold with topologically assigned phases, and a sweep signal continuously controls which agents are active at any given time. Active agents receive full context while idle agents receive compressed summaries, with scheduling and compression gains formally proven to be independent.

The methodology involves assigning agent phases based on dependency DAG topology, where the circular manifold is shown to be the necessary—not merely convenient—topology for periodic coordination. The framework provides formal guarantees including ordering correctness, stability under latency noise, and convergence to a full-activation fixed point.

Evaluated across four benchmarks (HotPotQA, HumanEval, ALFWorld, and WebArena), PSMAS with weighted phase assignment achieves 34.8% token reduction with only 2.1 percentage points of performance degradation, outperforming the strongest adaptive baseline (RouterLLM) by 5.6 percentage points in token savings with 2.0 percentage points less quality loss. Benefits are largest for deep sequential dependency chains and diminish for embarrassingly parallel tasks.

The work's significance lies in reframing multi-agent coordination from discrete scheduling to principled continuous control, enabling formal stability and optimality guarantees unavailable to existing approaches.
original_abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) powered by large language models suffer from severe token inefficiency arising from two compounding sources: (i) unstructured parallel execution, where all agents activate simultaneously irrespective of input readiness; and (ii) unrestricted context sharing, where every agent receives the full accumulated context regardless of relevance. Existing mitigation strategies - static pruning, hierarchical decomposition, and learned routing - treat coordination as a structural allocation problem and fundamentally ignore its temporal dimension. We propose Phase-Scheduled Multi-Agent Systems (PSMAS), a framework that reconceptualizes agent activation as continuous control over a shared attention space modeled on a circular manifold. Each agent i is assigned a fixed angular phase theta_i in the range [0, 2*pi], derived from the task dependency topology; a global sweep signal phi(t) rotates at velocity omega, activating only agents within an angular window epsilon. Idle agents receive compressed context summaries, reducing per-step token consumption. We implement PSMAS on LangGraph, evaluate on four structured benchmarks (HotPotQA-MAS, HumanEval-MAS, ALFWorld-Multi, WebArena-Coord) and two unstructured conversational settings, and prove stability, convergence, and optimality results for the sweep dynamics. PSMAS achieves a mean token reduction of 27.3 percent (range 21.4-34.8 percent) while maintaining task performance within 2.1 percentage points of a fully activated baseline (p < 0.01, n = 500 per configuration), and outperforms the strongest learned routing baseline by 5.6 percentage points in token reduction with 2.0 percentage points less performance drop. Crucially, we show that scheduling and compression are independent sources of gain: scheduling alone accounts for 18-20 percentage points of reduction, robust to compression degradation up to alpha = 0.40.

title: A Null Model for Mapper Subtype Claims
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a covariance-preserving Gaussian null model for evaluating subtype claims made using the Mapper algorithm from topological data analysis. The key insight is that existing null models either use independent Gaussians that fail to preserve correlation structure or rely on label permutation, both of which produce misleading significance assessments. The authors prove theoretically that covariance geometry alone drives positive community dissociation in Mapper graphs, meaning filter-based partitions inevitably produce communities with detectably different feature profiles even absent genuine subtypes, while permutation-based baselines always reject as sample size grows.

The methodology generates synthetic data matching the observed covariance structure, applies the identical Mapper pipeline, and compares community differentiation using a dissociation metric. The authors apply this framework to four case studies: breast cancer genomics, Congressional voting records, NBA player performance, and lower-grade glioma gene expression data. In every case, community differentiation does not exceed the covariance-preserving null at the 0.05 significance level once singleton communities are accounted for, despite all analyses being highly significant under label-permutation or independence-based null models.

The framework has notable limitations: it can overreject under heavy-tailed or skewed distributions, and the dissociation metric is insensitive to certain mixture alternatives already captured by the covariance matrix. Nevertheless, the work establishes that Mapper's exploratory output should not be treated as confirmatory evidence for subtypes without covariance-aware statistical testing, providing practitioners with concrete recommendations for more rigorous Mapper-based analyses.
original_abstract: The Mapper algorithm from topological data analysis constructs a graph summarizing the shape of a high-dimensional dataset, and groups of data points identified within this graph are widely interpreted as evidence of distinct subtypes. However, the covariance structure of the data alone can make such groups appear differentiated, even when no subtypes are present. Existing validation approaches do not account for this effect and thus cannot distinguish covariance artifacts from genuine subtypes. We propose a Gaussian null model that generates reference data matching the sample covariance matrix. We pair it with a test statistic that measures mean-level differentiation between communities. In an idealized setting, we prove that covariance geometry alone causes Mapper communities to differ in their average feature profiles, and we show that a simpler label-permutation baseline cannot detect this effect. Simulations confirm well-controlled Type I error under Gaussian data. We apply the framework to four published Mapper analyses spanning breast cancer gene expression, Congressional voting, NBA player performance, and lower-grade glioma genomics. In every case, once outlier singleton communities are accounted for, the observed differentiation does not exceed what the null produces at the α = 0.05 level. This result does not rule out subtypes in these datasets, but it does indicate that the observed structure is consistent with what covariance geometry alone can produce. Stronger evidence would be needed to support a subtype claim.

title: The inversion number statistic for inversion sequences
generated_summary:
This paper introduces and studies the inversion number statistic for inversion sequences, extending a classical permutation statistic to this broader combinatorial setting. The authors define a five-variable polynomial F_n(x; y, z, p, q) that tracks the joint distribution of five statistics on inversion sequences: inversions, entry sum, zero count, empty lines, and upper empty lines.

The methodology centers on establishing a recurrence relation for F_n using the q-derivative operator and q-exponential operator, which enables systematic analysis of specializations. The authors demonstrate that F_n serves as a master polynomial unifying diverse combinatorial structures through parameter specializations. When q=1, the polynomial recovers symmetric group statistics, yielding generating functions for unsigned Stirling numbers of the first kind, Mahonian distributions, and Eulerian numbers. When q=0, inversion sequences reduce to weakly increasing sequences counted by Catalan numbers, and refined specializations produce Narayana numbers and Dyck path statistics. A surprising result emerges at q=−1, where a sign-reversing involution on inversion sequences shows that the surviving terms count involutions in the symmetric group.

Additionally, the paper provides a combinatorial interpretation for q-Stirling numbers of the second kind through a special family of inversion sequences and derives a q-analog of Comtet's expansion formula for differential operators. The work demonstrates that inversion sequences provide a natural combinatorial framework connecting permutation statistics, lattice path enumeration, and operator calculus, offering new proofs and interpretations of classical identities.
original_abstract: Inversion sequences, also known as subexcedant sequences, form a fundamental class of objects in enumerative combinatorics. In this paper, we study the joint distribution of five statistics on inversion sequences. While several statistics on inversion sequences have been extensively investigated, our contribution is to introduce the inversion number statistic, originally defined for permutations, into the context of inversion sequences. As special cases, we recover classical permutation statistics, including the Stirling, Mahonian and Eulerian distributions, as well as the Catalan and Narayana numbers. Somewhat unexpectedly, our specializations also include the number of involutions in the symmetric group. Our study arises from a $q$-analog of Comtet's expansion formula obtained by substituting the classical derivative operator $D$ with the $q$-derivative operator $D_q$.

title: Projection, Measure, and Idempotent Relations: Independent Axioms and a Fixed-Point Coupling Law
generated_summary:

The authors demonstrate consistency by constructing explicit finite and countable models and prove mutual independence of all three axioms and the three subclauses of Axiom III through separating models. A central result reformulates the coupling law as a Banach-contraction fixed-point equation, yielding a closed-form solution with a Neumann-series expansion. A quotient-factorization theorem reduces the general admissibility problem to an identity-retraction case under fiber measurability conditions, where each equivalence class carries mass either zero or a specific value determined by the coupling parameter. The authors also show that under σ-additive probability normalization, the coupling parameter is forced to zero, meaning nontrivial coupling requires finite additivity or non-probability measures.

original_abstract: We introduce a minimal ZFC-internal axiom system for pre-structural data (X, A, mu, mu^{otimes 2}, R, I, Pi_R, G, E_0, eta), where Pi_R : X -> R is a designated map and G subset X x X is a measurable relation; admissible structural models are those pre-structural data satisfying Axioms I-III, which couple a finitely additive measure, an idempotent retraction, and an idempotent symmetric relation through a single coupling law (Axiom III). The axiom system is satisfiable in ZFC via explicit finite and countable models, including finite families with eta neq 0. The three axioms, and the three subclauses of Axiom III, are mutually independent, witnessed by explicit separating models. The coupling law admits a fixed-point reformulation: it is the unique bounded finitely additive solution of a Banach-contraction equation f = T_eta f determined by (mu, Pi_R, eta), with closed form f_*(B) = mu(B) + (eta/(1-eta)) mu(Pi_R^{-1}(B)) and a Neumann-series expansion. Admissible structural models with a common eta form a category Struct_eta in which Pi_R and G appear as idempotents analogous to the two sides of a monad-comonad pair. Under fiber measurability together with either a finiteness hypothesis (R-fin) or countability plus sigma-additivity (R-ctbl), a quotient-factorization theorem reduces the general admissibility problem to the identity-retraction case Pi_R = id_X; in that case, under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.6 (pi-id-classification), each G-equivalence class C_k satisfies mu(C_k) in {0, (1-eta)^{-1}}.

title: Entropy-Driven Drift as a Source of Optimization Difficulty in Combinatorial Spaces
generated_summary:
This paper identifies a structural mechanism called "entropy-driven drift" that constitutes a fundamental source of optimization difficulty in high-dimensional combinatorial spaces. Unlike traditional perspectives that attribute search difficulty to properties of individual states (such as local optima or ruggedness), this work adopts a trajectory-based perspective, arguing that optimization difficulty is inherently a trajectory-level phenomenon.

The authors analyze random walks on the Johnson graph, which models k-of-n subset selection problems under local swap-based operators. By considering a flat objective landscape, they isolate entropy-driven drift from objective-driven drift. The combinatorial variation in the number of states at different distances from a target configuration creates an asymmetry in local transitions, systematically biasing trajectories toward high-entropy regions and away from the target.

Key results demonstrate that this drift causes target-reaching trajectories to become atypical under the induced dynamics, even when the search process mixes rapidly. The authors further reveal an intrinsic information limitation: the coordinate governing the drift depends on the unknown target configuration and is not directly observable, preventing the search process from compensating for the bias. Even moderate objective-based guidance (e.g., Metropolis dynamics) cannot fully counteract entropy-driven drift near the target.

The significance of this work lies in providing a mechanistic explanation for optimization difficulty that extends beyond the Johnson graph to any combinatorial search space exhibiting non-uniform distance shell structure and local transitions, offering new insights for algorithm design in high-dimensional combinatorial optimization.
original_abstract: Understanding the origin of optimization difficulty in high-dimensional combinatorial spaces remains a fundamental problem. Existing perspectives typically characterize difficulty in terms of properties of states, their connectivity, or distributions over states. However, search algorithms operate as stochastic processes evolving over time, and optimization is inherently a trajectory-level phenomenon. This motivates a shift from state-based to trajectory-based analysis. In this work, we adopt a trajectory-based perspective and analyze search dynamics through the evolution of a distance process. We identify a structural mechanism, which we term entropy-driven drift. This mechanism systematically biases trajectories toward high-entropy regions. This drift arises from asymmetry in local transitions induced by the underlying graph structure, independent of objective variation. In the absence of objective variation, trajectories that reach the target are atypical under the induced dynamics, leading to a discrepancy between rapid mixing and slow hitting. We formalize this mechanism in a canonical combinatorial setting with a highly symmetric underlying graph, where the symmetry allows explicit characterization of the induced drift. The mechanism highlights entropy-driven drift as a source of optimization difficulty and provides a trajectory-level framework for understanding search dynamics in combinatorial spaces.

title: Evaluation of Gauss-Legendre curves
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of efficiently evaluating Gauss-Legendre (GL) curves, a recently introduced class of polynomial parametric curves that offer superior shape control properties compared to Bézier curves, as they closely follow their control polygon even at high degrees. The authors note that while GL curves have promising applications in computer-aided geometric design, numerical analysis, and computer graphics, their evaluation is nontrivial due to the complicated definition of the underlying GL polynomials.

The authors derive new representations of GL polynomials and their derivatives in two frameworks: the shifted power basis and orthogonal bases related to symmetric Jacobi polynomials. Based on these representations, they propose two fast and numerically stable evaluation algorithms. Both approaches achieve O(n² + dn) computational complexity for computing a single point on a GL curve of degree n in d-dimensional space. For the practically important problem of multipoint evaluation—essential for rendering—the authors develop algorithms running in O(Mdn + dn²) time, where M is the number of evaluation points. Since typically M >> n and d is small, the effective complexity reduces to O(Mdn).

Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithms are stable and computationally efficient, though the shifted power basis approach exhibits instability at higher degrees, while the orthogonal basis expansions remain robust. These results represent a significant step toward making GL curves practical for applications, providing the computational tools necessary for their adoption in geometric modeling and related fields.
original_abstract: We present new representations of Gauss--Legendre polynomials and their derivatives in the shifted power basis and in bases related to symmetric orthogonal Jacobi polynomials. Using these representations and certain recurrence relations, we propose efficient $O(n^2+dn)$ methods for evaluating a Gauss--Legendre curve of degree $n$ in $\mathbb E^d$. We also propose algorithms for multipoint evaluation with computational complexity $O(Mdn+dn^2)$, where $M$ is the number of evaluation points.

title: On Fixed Points of Nonlinear Monotone and Strongly Concave Operators Acting in Normal Cones
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the notion of strong concavity for nonlinear monotone operators acting in normal cones of real Banach spaces and develops a comprehensive theory for the existence, uniqueness, and constructive approximation of nontrivial fixed points of such operators. A monotone operator is defined as strongly concave if it satisfies a specific inequality involving a continuous, monotonically increasing, concave mapping with prescribed boundary behavior.

The methodology builds upon classical fixed point theory for monotone operators in ordered Banach spaces, extending results by Bakhtin, Krasnosel'skii, Birkhoff, and Tarski. The authors prove constructive existence theorems for nonzero fixed points in normal cones, demonstrating that iterative successive approximations converge in norm at a rate governed by a decreasing geometric progression determined by the concave mapping. Notably, some results do not require operator continuity. Uniqueness of the constructed fixed point is established within sufficiently wide conical segments, without necessarily assuming cone normality or operator continuity.

The theory is applied to three significant problems: nonlinear integral equations arising in the dynamic theory of p-adic strings, where bounded sign-changing solutions are constructed; Urysohn-type integral equations relevant to nonlinear radiation transfer and kinetic gas theory; and Cauchy problems for semilinear heat equations, where mild global positive solutions are obtained. These applications demonstrate the broad applicability of the strong concavity framework to problems in mathematical physics and mathematical biology where nontrivial fixed points of critical operators must be constructed.
original_abstract: We introduce and study a new class of nonlinear monotone operators acting in normal cones of real Banach spaces and possessing the property of strong concavity. We establish new constructive principles for the existence of nonzero fixed points for this class of operators. Further, we prove that the corresponding iterative process converges to the fixed point at geometric rate. We also establish the uniqueness of the fixed point in a sufficiently wide conical segment. These results are applied to Hammerstein-type and Urysohn-type nonlinear integral operators acting in non-reflexive Banach spaces, as well as to the Cauchy problem for a nonlinear heat equation.

title: Flat Lorentzian Lie groups: A complete description
generated_summary:
This paper provides a complete structural classification of flat Lorentzian Lie groups, resolving a longstanding open problem in pseudo-Riemannian geometry. Prior work had identified two main classes of flat Lorentzian Lie algebras—those arising from the double extension process applied to flat Euclidean Lie algebras and those whose Levi-Civita product is of Novikov type—but whether these classes exhausted all possibilities remained unknown.

The authors establish that every flat Lorentzian Lie algebra admits either a timelike parallel left-invariant vector field or is of Kundt type. Starting from this dichotomy, they systematically analyze the Levi-Civita product structure using refined versions of Milnor's theorem for flat Euclidean Lie algebras, the double extension construction, and three key technical lemmas concerning skew-symmetric endomorphisms and their interactions with algebraic structures. The methodology involves reducing the classification to solving systems of equations governing the double extension process, which the authors accomplish through careful algebraic analysis.

The main result shows that flat Lorentzian Lie algebras fall into exactly six distinct classes: three of Novikov type and three arising from double extensions. The authors provide explicit models for each class and verify the classification in low dimensions. This result definitively answers the question of whether the two previously known classes suffice, providing a negative answer while completing the full picture. The work connects to general relativity through Kundt spacetimes and to mathematical physics through Novikov algebras arising in hydrodynamical Poisson brackets.
original_abstract: We prove that a Lie group $(G,h)$ endowed with a left-invariant flat Lorentzian metric either admits a left-invariant parallel timelike vector field or is of Kundt type. As a consequence, we provide a complete structural description of such Lie algebras. In particular, we obtain a classification in dimensions three and four. This completely resolves a previously open problem concerning the determination of Lie groups endowed with left-invariant flat Lorentzian metrics.

title: Fučik spectrum for the operator with rapidly increasing weight and applications
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the Fučík spectrum of the operator L, which arises naturally in the study of self-similar solutions of the heat equation and possesses a variational structure through its divergence form with a rapidly increasing weight. The Fučík spectrum generalizes the classical eigenvalue problem by treating the positive and negative parts of solutions asymmetrically, a concept introduced by Fučík and Dancer in the 1970s.

The authors employ a minimax variational approach to construct three curves within the Fučík spectrum of the operator L. Specifically, they obtain curves expressed through critical values of an associated functional, and they establish important qualitative properties of these curves, including Lipschitz continuity, strict monotonicity (decreasing behavior), and asymptotic behavior. The analysis is carried out in a weighted Sobolev space equipped with embedding theorems previously developed for this operator.

As an application, the authors study the solvability of a related nonlinear equation. Using the mountain pass theorem combined with Ekeland's variational principle, they establish the existence of at least two positive nontrivial solutions under appropriate conditions on the nonlinearity. The proof relies on verifying the Cerami compactness condition and demonstrating the mountain pass geometry of the associated energy functional.

This work extends Fučík spectrum theory to operators with rapidly growing weights on unbounded domains, bridging the gap between classical Fučík spectrum results for the Laplacian on bounded domains and more general differential operators arising in parabolic equations and self-similar solution theory.
original_abstract: In this paper, we study the Fučik spectrum for the operator with rapidly increasing weight, which is defined as a set $Σ$ comprising those $(α, β) \in \mathbb{R}^2$ such that \begin{equation*} \left\{\begin{array}{l} L u:=-Δu-\frac{1}{2}(x \cdot \nabla u)=αu^{+}-βu^{-}, \text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^N,\\ u\in X, \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} has a non-trivial solution $u$, where, $N\geq1$, $u^{ \pm}=\max ( \pm u, 0)$, $u=u^{+}-u^{-}$. The existence of a first nontrivial curve $\mathcal{C}$ of this spectrum, along with some of its properties (e.g., Lipschitz continuity, strict decrease and asymptotic behavior) is investigated in this paper. Our difficulty is that the problem is defined on the whole space $\mathbb{R}^N$, and therefore certain estimates do not carry over from the Fučik problem on bounded domains. As an application, we establish the multiplicity of solutions to the following problem \begin{equation*} \left\{\begin{array}{l} -Δu-\frac{1}{2}(x \cdot \nabla u)=f(x,u), \text{in}\ \mathbb{R}^N,\\ u\in X, \end{array}\right. \end{equation*} where, $N\geq1$ and the nonlinearity $f$ is asymptotically linear at zero and at infinity.

title: Generalized Composed Alternating Relaxed Projection Algorithm for Two-Set Feasibility Problem

original_abstract: We study the two-set feasibility problem of finding a point in the intersection $X\cap Y$ of closed convex sets in a Hilbert space. We propose a generalized composed alternating relaxed projection algorithm (gCARPA) that blends Douglas-Rachford-type and projection-reflection-type dynamics via an outer averaging step $μ$ and an internal relaxation $(γ,θ,η)$. The algorithm contains several classical projection methods as special cases. We also introduce its non-stationary variant, in which $(γ_k,θ_k,η_k)$ vary over iterations, and establish its convergence. For the subspace feasibility model, we derive an explicit spectral characterization via principal-angle block decompositions, yielding computable subdominant-eigenvalue factors and a minimax parameter-selection recipe in a symmetric regime that targets critical damping on principal-angle planes. Numerical experiments illustrate that the generalized relaxation and its non-stationary tuning can improve or match baseline methods in problem-dependent regimes.

title: Solving Stochastic Constraints by Oracle-based Gradient Descent and Interval Arithmetic

original_abstract: Stochastic constraints, which incorporate both deterministic parameters and random variables, extend classical deterministic constraints by explicitly accounting for uncertainty. These constraints are increasingly prevalent in data science, artificial intelligence, and bioinformatics; however, solving them requires addressing quantitative satisfaction problems that remain a significant challenge in computer science. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for deciding deterministic parameters that maximize the satisfaction probability. Our approach features a unique synergy between stochastic optimization and symbolic techniques: at the high level, it employs \emph{oracle-based stochastic gradient descent} to identify high-quality parameter candidates, while at the low level, it utilizes \emph{interval arithmetic} to compute rigorously certified lower bounds. This framework produces a sequence of sound and increasingly tight lower bounds for the true maximum satisfaction probability, supported by a high-probability convergence guarantee. We demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach through its application to Stochastic Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SSMT) problems and a stochastic trajectory planning task.

title: Generalized spectral Turán problems for disjoint cliques

This provides a unified spectral generalization of several classical results, including the spectral Turán theorem for disjoint cliques by Ni, Wang, and Kang (recovered when t = 2) and the generalized Turán result of Gerbner for counting t-cliques in kK_{r+1}-free graphs.

The methodology employs a hypergraph tensor framework, specifically the t-clique tensor introduced by Liu and Bu, which encodes the structure of t-cliques in a graph as a symmetric nonnegative tensor. The proof strategy combines a spectral stability lemma (analogous to the Erdős–Simonovits stability theorem) with detailed structural analysis of near-extremal graphs, including partition properties inherited from proximity to the Turán graph, t-clique connectivity arguments establishing tensor irreducibility, and careful eigenvector analysis.

The significance of this work lies in demonstrating how spectral methods via higher-order tensors can simultaneously capture both classical edge-extremal and generalized subgraph-counting extremal results, strengthening the connection between spectral graph theory and extremal combinatorics.
original_abstract: The generalized Turán number $\text{ex}(n, H, F)$ denotes the maximum number of copies of $H$ in an $n$-vertex $F$-free graph. Let $kK_{r+1}$ be the disjoint union of $k$ copies of the complete graph $K_{r+1}$. Recently, Gerbner determined $\text{ex}(n, K_{t},kK_{r+1})$ for all sufficiently large $n$. In this paper, we study a spectral analogue of this problem via the $t$-clique tensor of a graph. We prove that if an $n$-vertex $kK_{r+1}$-free graph $G$ maximizes the $t$-clique spectral radius, then for sufficiently large $n$, $G$ is the join of a complete graph $K_{k-1}$ and the $r$-partite Turán graph $T_{r}(n-k+1)$. This establishes a spectral counterpart of Gerbner's Theorem. Moreover, in the case $t=2$, our result recovers a theorem of Ni, Wang, and Kang on the maximum spectral radius of $kK_{r+1}$-free graphs.

title: Bootstrap consistency for general double/debiased machine learning estimators
generated_summary:

While DML estimators are known to be root-n consistent and asymptotically normal, these properties alone do not guarantee bootstrap consistency, as demonstrated by counterexamples involving other estimators such as nearest-neighbor matching estimators and Chatterjee's rank correlation.

The authors study the exchangeably weighted bootstrap framework, which encompasses Efron's bootstrap, the Bayesian bootstrap, multiplier bootstrap, and other common resampling schemes. The bootstrap procedure resamples from the full dataset without refitting the nuisance parameter estimators, preserving the cross-fitting structure central to DML. The analysis focuses on this single-round resampling approach, which is both practically common and technically more challenging than within-fold resampling alternatives.

The central result establishes a bootstrap linear representation and proves conditional weak convergence of the bootstrap law to the sampling distribution of the original DML estimator. Crucially, this is achieved under exactly the same conditions required for the validity of the original DML estimators—specifically, Neyman orthogonality and cross-fitting—without imposing the classical Donsker-type empirical process conditions typically invoked in related bootstrap studies for semiparametric estimation.

original_abstract: Double/debiased machine learning (DML) provides a general framework for inference with high-dimensional or otherwise complex nuisance parameters by combining Neyman-orthogonal scores with cross-fitting, thereby circumventing classical Donsker-type conditions in many modern machine-learning settings. Despite its strong empirical performance, bootstrap inference for DML estimators has received little theoretical justification. This is particularly noteworthy since bootstrap methods are suggested ad used for inference on DML estimators, even though bootstrap procedures can fail for estimators that are root-$n$ consistent and asymptotically normal. This paper fills this gap by establishing bootstrap validity for DML estimators under general exchangeably weighted resampling schemes, with Efron's bootstrap as a special case. Under exactly the same conditions required for the validity of DML itself, we prove that the bootstrap law converges conditionally weakly to the sampling law of the original estimator.

title: Learning Mixtures of Nonparametric and Convolutional Measures on Effectively Low-dimensional Affine Spaces
generated_summary:

Unlike prior work on nonparametric mixtures that requires strong separation between component supports, the low-dimensional constraint enables identifiability even when supports intersect, under mild geometric conditions. Second, for a specific parametrization where each component's latent measure is supported on a convex polytope (modeling observations as noisy convex combinations of end-members), they derive posterior contraction rates for parameter estimation in a Bayesian framework. The key technical tool is a novel inverse bound that translates density-level convergence to parameter-level convergence by leveraging the geometry of convex polytopes, yielding parametric estimation rates.

The significance of this work lies in extending theoretical understanding of latent variable models beyond Gaussian mixtures to semi-parametric settings with both discrete and continuous latent variables. The authors also develop MCMC algorithms and validate their theoretical findings through simulations, demonstrating practical applicability of the framework.
original_abstract: In this paper, we develop a finite mixture of convolutional distributions, a statistical model to analyze continuous data distributed approximately on a mixture of low-dimensional affine subspaces. The observations are assumed independent and identically distributed from the mixture of distributions, where each component arises from a convolution of a distribution supported on a low-dimensional subspace with a suitable noise kernel. We discuss theoretical properties of such class of models, including identifiability under very general conditions - in particular, showing that the minimal representation for such mixtures is uniquely identifiable in a semi-parametric setting. We further study the posterior contraction rates for the parameters for a parametrized class of such models where the supports of the component mixing measures are assumed to be convex polytopes under a suitable well-specified Bayesian regime. This still requires developing novel inverse bounds for problems involving a nested mixture structure, where the mixture kernel is itself another continuous mixture. Our approach for both the identifiability theory and posterior contraction rates is to exploit the geometric structure of the underlying support of the latent measures. Apart from applications in end-member analysis, spectral unmixing and topic models, this study provides a grounded framework for subspace clustering with the goal of exploring conditions for learning multiple latent low-dimensional structures. We illustrate our findings through careful simulation study, which also includes developing new algorithms for such class of models

title: Alternating and Symmetric Separability of Free Products
generated_summary:

The main contribution establishes conditions under which finitely generated subgroups of a free product F_r * G (where F_r is a free group of rank greater than one and G is a LERF group) are separable with respect to the class of alternating and symmetric groups.

The methodology combines several techniques: Wilton's construction for alternating separability in free groups, Markus-Epstein's algorithm for analyzing subgroup structure via labeled graphs, the theory of precovers for free products developed by Gitik, and Jordan's theorem on primitive permutation groups. The proof proceeds by embedding monochromatic components of a relative Cayley graph into finite covers, constructing a precover through pushout operations, and modifying components to achieve the desired prime-index cover with appropriate permutation properties.

The key result shows that a finitely generated subgroup H of F_r * G is alternating-symmetric separable if either H intersects trivially with every conjugate of F_r, or H intersects some conjugate of F_r in an infinite-index subgroup. As an immediate corollary, any finitely generated infinite-index subgroup of F_r is alternating-symmetric separable in F_r * G, generalizing Wilton's earlier theorem on free groups. The paper also demonstrates that the infinite-index condition is essential by exhibiting a finite-index normal subgroup that fails to be alternating separable.
original_abstract: Let $F \ast G$ be a free product of a free group $F$ and a LERF group $G$. In this note, we provide sufficient conditions for a subgroup $H$ of $F \ast G$ to be $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{S}$-separable, that is, for any finite set $\{γ_1, \ldots, γ_n\} \subset (F \ast G) \setminus H$, there is a surjection $f$ from $F \ast G$ to an alternating or symmetric group such that $f(γ_i) \notin f(H)$ for all $i$. As a corollary, any finitely generated infinite-index subgroup of a free group is $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{S}$-separable in the free product of the free group and an arbitrary LERF group, generalizing a result of Wilton.

title: Bilinear Input Modulation for Mamba: Koopman Bilinear Forms for Memory Retention and Multiplicative Computation

The authors propose two variants: Coupled-BIM, which introduces full state-input products within the recurrence but requires sequential computation, and Coupled-GM (Gate Modulation), which freezes the state at a learned prior to preserve parallelizability.

The methodology builds on the Integrated State Prediction Model (ISPM) framework, modifying only the Mamba block. Two benchmarks are designed to dissociate memory retention from nonlinear computation: a multiple input-delay pendulum (linear memory task) and NARMA-10 (requiring bilinear computation over memory).

Results reveal a clear functional dissociation: Coupled-GM improves memory retention on the input-delay task with no additional training cost, while only Coupled-BIM enables the bilinear computation necessary for NARMA-10, achieving 96% improvement over standard Mamba at larger state dimensions. Crucially, parameter-matched ablations confirm the gains stem from the bilinear mechanism rather than increased parameter count, and performance scales when state dimension and sequence length increase together.

This work demonstrates that Koopman-inspired bilinear terms can meaningfully extend the computational expressiveness of state space models for dynamical systems prediction.
original_abstract: Selective State Space Models (SSMs), notably Mamba, employ diagonal state transitions that limit both memory retention and bilinear computational capacity. We propose a factorized bilinear input modulation that augments the SSM with a state-input product, interpretable as a finite-dimensional Koopman bilinear form. After introducing a shared state across channels (Coupled SSM), the modulation admits two implementations. Coupled Bilinear Input Modulation (Coupled-BIM) retains the full bilinear product at the cost of sequential computation, while Coupled Gated Modulation (Coupled-GM) linearizes it into a gate modulation that is compatible with the parallel scan. Experiments on a multiple input-delay pendulum (memory retention) and NARMA-10 (bilinear computation) reveal a clear dissociation. Coupled-GM substantially improves memory retention but not bilinear computation, while Coupled-BIM improves both. A pathway ablation confirms that the two downstream routes of the bilinear signal serve complementary roles. The improvement is statistically robust, with Coupled-BIM consistently outperforming all other variants on bilinear computation. Furthermore, only Coupled-BIM benefits from increasing the SSM state dimension, while coupling or gate modulation alone show no improvement, establishing the bilin-ear mechanism as uniquely capable of exploiting larger state spaces.

title: Symplectic Inductive Bias for Data-Driven Target Reachability in Hamiltonian Systems
generated_summary:

The framework combines controlled energy reduction with this natural recurrence to achieve target reachability, with data requirements depending on geometric and recurrence properties of the Hamiltonian rather than the ambient state dimension.

Numerical experiments on spring-mass and pendulum systems demonstrate that the chain policy achieves perfect success rates with as few as one to three expert trajectories, dramatically outperforming a behavior cloning baseline trained on the same data. For example, in the spring-mass system, the chain policy achieves 100% success with a single demonstration, while behavior cloning achieves only 6.2%.

The work highlights the potential of physics-informed inductive biases to fundamentally improve data efficiency in nonlinear data-driven control, offering a promising alternative to dimension-dependent sample complexity bounds.
original_abstract: Inductive bias refers to restrictions on the hypothesis class that enable a learning method to generalize effectively from limited data. A canonical example in control is linearity, which underpins low sample-complexity guarantees for stabilization and optimal control. For general nonlinear dynamics, by contrast, guarantees often rely on smoothness assumptions (e.g., Lipschitz continuity) which, when combined with covering arguments, can lead to data requirements that grow exponentially with the ambient dimension. In this paper we argue that data-efficient nonlinear control demands exploiting inductive bias embedded in nature itself, namely, structure imposed by physical laws. Focusing on Hamiltonian systems, we leverage symplectic geometry and intrinsic recurrence on energy level sets to solve target reachability problems. Our approach combines the recurrence property with a recently proposed class of policies, called chain policies, which composes locally certified trajectory segments extracted from demonstrations to achieve target reachability. We provide sufficient conditions for reachability under this construction and show that the resulting data requirements depend on explicit geometric and recurrence properties of the Hamiltonian rather than the state dimension.

title: Functional correlation bound for random Lasota--Yorke maps with holes and its applications to conditional normal approximations
generated_summary:

The methodology combines the FCB framework for Stein's method with Lasota–Yorke type inequalities specifically tailored for open transfer operators. The authors adapt the abstract FCB mechanism to account for decreasing mass by developing new spectral estimates for open transfer operators. For the Kolmogorov distance bound, they introduce a new abstract theorem based on Tikhomirov's method.

The key results include two main theorems. The first establishes an exponentially decaying functional correlation bound that holds uniformly across environment realizations and time horizons. The second derives quantitative conditional normal approximation results: a conditional Central Limit Theorem with explicit convergence rates in both Wasserstein and Kolmogorov distances, and a conditional functional CLT with explicit rates measured via an integral distance over Barbour's class of smooth test functions.

These results are entirely new even in the deterministic setting of a single Lasota–Yorke map with a hole. The work bridges two active research areas—open dynamical systems and quantitative limit theorems via Stein's method—providing a unified framework for obtaining precise convergence rates for conditioned stochastic processes in systems with escape.
original_abstract: This paper investigates the statistical properties of random open dynamical systems generated by families of Lasota--Yorke maps. Open systems, in which trajectories may escape through `holes', model transient phenomena and present additional difficulties for statistical analysis because the underlying ensemble loses mass over time. We show that the framework of functional correlation bounds (FCB), originally developed for closed systems, can also be adapted to this random open setting. The extension requires new ingredients based on Lasota--Yorke type inequalities in order to control the effect of escaping trajectories. We establish an FCB with exponential decay and combine it with the abstract normal-approximation results of \cite{LNN25,LS20} to obtain a conditional CLT with rates in Wasserstein distance and a conditional functional CLT with a rate in an integral distance over Barbour's class of smooth test functions. Additionally, we adapt Tikhomirov's method to obtain a bound in Kolmogorov distance for the conditional CLT.

title: Intent-aligned Autonomous Spacecraft Guidance via Reasoning Models
generated_summary:

Key results in close-proximity inspection scenarios demonstrate that the trained waypoint generator achieves approximately 90% SCP convergence compared to 72% for heuristic baselines. The fully trained pipeline achieves 100% feasibility in behavior-sequence generation, with over 50% of reasoning traces matching both top-priority intent metrics. The neural reasoning module yields roughly 1.5× improvement in dual-metric win rates over heuristic reasoning.

original_abstract: Future spacecraft operations require autonomy that can interpret high-level mission intent while preserving safety. However, existing trajectory optimization still relies heavily on expert-crafted formulations and does not support intent-conditioned decision-making. This paper proposes an intent-aligned spacecraft guidance framework that links high-level reasoning and safe trajectory optimization through explicit intermediate abstractions, based on behavior sequences and waypoint constraints. A foundation model first predicts an intent-aligned behavior plan, a waypoint generation model then converts it into waypoint constraints, and the safe trajectory is computed via optimization. This decomposition enables scalable supervision without sacrificing safety. Numerical experiments in close-proximity operation scenarios demonstrate that the proposed pipeline achieves over 90\% SCP convergence and yields a $1.5\times$ higher rate of generating trajectories that satisfy the top intent-prioritized performance criteria than heuristic decision-making. These results support the use of intermediate behavior abstraction as a practical interface between foundation-model reasoning and safety-critical onboard spacecraft autonomy.

title: On the Unification of Optimal Current Reference Theory for Wound Rotor Synchronous Machines
generated_summary:

The authors approximate the nonlinear flux map from finite-element data using a piecewise-affine (PWA) representation, which preserves the quadratic structure of the underlying physics. This enables formulation of the current reference problem as a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) within each PWA region. The solution structure is then characterized by identifying five distinct constraint regimes across the torque-speed envelope—cruise, launch-control, fast-driving, forceful-fast-driving, and rotor-constrained. For four regimes, closed-form or low-dimensional polynomial solutions are derived via KKT conditions, while the voltage-constrained regime is handled through a small semidefinite programming relaxation that is empirically verified to be exact throughout the tested operating range.

Validation on a prototype WRSM demonstrates that the framework matches or slightly improves upon solutions from the commercial nonlinear solver Gurobi (by up to 1 W) while reducing median solve time by approximately 95%, achieving sub-millisecond computation. These results make the approach suitable for real-time embedded implementation in electric vehicle traction drives, where efficient operation across wide speed-torque ranges is essential.
original_abstract: Controllers for motor drives typically require a current reference which will satisfy the requested torque subject to system constraints. This work generalizes existing current reference theory to the case of the Wound Rotor Synchronous Machine (WRSM). By incorporating the additional rotor-current degree-of-freedom, along with magnetic saturation, cross-coupling, and speed-dependent core losses, the problem of finding an optimal current reference is formulated within affine flux regions as a quadratically constrained quadratic program using a piecewise-affine approximation derived from finite-element data. The solution is characterized according to the active constraint regime, yielding closed-form or low-dimensional polynomial solutions in several cases, and a small semidefinite program in the voltage constrained regime. The proposed framework extends unified optimal current reference theory beyond the permanent-magnet setting to three degree-of-freedom WRSMs while remaining computationally tractable. Results on a physical WRSM prototype illustrate the effectiveness of the approach across the torque-speed operating envelope.

title: On the isotropy of differential Ore extensions
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the isotropy subgroups of differential Ore extensions A_h, algebras generated by elements x and t satisfying the relation tx - xt = h(x) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. The isotropy subgroup of a derivation consists of all automorphisms that fix that derivation under conjugation. This work completes the isotropy analysis for Ore extensions over polynomial algebras, as quantum planes and quantum Weyl algebras were previously studied.

The authors first provide explicit descriptions of the automorphism groups of A_h for polynomials h of degree at least one, using changes of variables to reduce to canonical forms. They then employ Nowicki's decomposition theorem, which expresses derivations as sums of inner derivations and differential derivations, to analyze how conjugation by automorphisms acts on each component. In the square-free case (where gcd(h, h') = 1), the authors demonstrate that inner derivations and differential derivations form independent submodules under the automorphism group action, enabling computation of isotropy groups as intersections of isotropy groups of individual components.

For the singular case (gcd(h, h') ≠ 1), an additional special component appears in the derivation decomposition, which is not stable under conjugation. The authors address this by passing to an Ore localization, combining inner and special parts into a localized element, and establishing a general criterion for isotropy. The work reveals fundamentally different structural phenomena between the square-free and singular cases, contributing to the broader understanding of symmetries in noncommutative algebra and their connections to foliations and Hochschild cohomology.
original_abstract: Let Ah = k[x][t; d] be the differential Ore extension. We study the action of the automorphism group of Ah on the derivations of Ah and explicitly describe, using Nowicki's decomposition of the derivations of Ah, the isotropy groups of this action. More precisely, we first obtain an explicit description of the automorphism group of Ah for deg(h) >= 1. Then we determine the isotropy groups of derivations of the form D = ad_w + Delta_s(x), which exhaust all derivations in the square-free case, that is, when gcd(h,h') = 1. In the singular case, where gcd(h,h') is not equal to 1 and special derivations of type EH appear, we show that the isotropy problem is governed by a suitable localization and by the element w* = w + psi^(-1)H, where psi = gcd(h,h'). This yields a general criterion for the isotropy of a derivation of the form D = ad_w + EH + Delta_s(x). Finally, we provide explicit examples illustrating the new phenomena that arise in this setting.

title: Partial degenerate Stirling numbers

The authors introduce the concept of weighted mixed partitions, where sets and partition blocks carry algebraic weights determined by parameters α, β, and γ. This framework provides a unified combinatorial interpretation of generalized Stirling numbers, enabling elegant recovery of known identities such as recursion formulas, boundary conditions, and scaling properties. The paper also employs the notion of (α, β, γ)-partitions involving cells with compartments and closing properties to give concrete combinatorial meaning to the numbers.

Key results include the demonstration that fundamental properties of both incomplete and degenerate Stirling numbers—including recursive relations, generating functions via incomplete exponential functions, and combinatorial identities—extend naturally to the combined setting. The significance of this work lies in deepening the understanding of partition-based combinatorial structures by systematically exploring how different generalizing conditions interact, contributing to the broader program of unifying the extensive literature on Stirling number variants.
original_abstract: In this paper, we study some combinations of the degenerate and incomplete Stirling numbers of the second kind. We use a combinatorial approach and provide some asymptotic results.

title: On the normality of the concatenated Fibonacci constant
generated_summary:
This paper investigates whether the concatenated Fibonacci constant ξ = 0.11235813213455... (formed by concatenating successive Fibonacci numbers) is normal in base 10 and base 2. The main theoretical contribution identifies a precise sufficient condition for normality: that almost all individual Fibonacci numbers are (ε,k)-normal—meaning their internal digit distributions are approximately uniform—for every block length k. The authors demonstrate that this condition lies beyond current equidistribution techniques due to the exponential growth of Fibonacci numbers, which places ξ outside the reach of classical Davenport-Erdős machinery designed for polynomial-growth sequences.

The methodology combines theoretical analysis with large-scale computation on the first 500,000 Fibonacci numbers, producing approximately 26.1 billion decimal digits and 86.8 billion binary digits. The authors perform single-digit frequency tests, block-frequency analyses for blocks of length 2–4 using Good's serial statistic, individual normality assessments, and a novel positional decomposition separating interior blocks from boundary blocks.

Key results show that digit frequencies are consistent with uniformity (χ² = 7.48, p = 0.587 in base 10), with deviations decaying at the D^{-1/2} rate expected of random sequences. The positional decomposition reveals that structured deviations concentrate entirely at junctions between consecutive Fibonacci numbers—driven by Benford-biased leading digits and Pisano-periodic trailing digits—while interior blocks comprising over 99.99% of all blocks show no significant departure from uniformity. These findings provide strong heuristic evidence for normality without constituting a proof, highlighting an important open problem at the intersection of number theory and digit distribution.
original_abstract: We study the concatenated Fibonacci constant $\mathcal{F} := 0.F_{1}F_{2}F_{3}\cdots = 0.11235813\cdots$, obtained by concatenating the Fibonacci numbers in the fractional part, and ask whether it is normal. We show that several classical sufficient conditions for normality by concatenation do not apply to the Fibonacci sequence because of its exponential growth, while a criterion of Pollack and Vandehey implies that the normality of $\mathcal{F}$ in base $10$ would follow if almost all Fibonacci numbers were $(\varepsilon,k)$-normal in base $10$. Their study in operations research was initiated by the foundational work of Bartholdi and Eisenstein ({\em Operations Research}, 1996), where a simplified version of the model is considered. Their main result shows that when workers are ordered from the slowest to the fastest, the system is stable and converges to a ``fixed point,'' where each worker oscillates between two limiting positions. They also observe that the dynamics can become highly complex when this ordering condition is not satisfied. The {\em no-station} setting, in which work is distributed continuously and uniformly along the production line, is given special attention in their work. In a subsequent paper with Bunimovich ({\em Operations Research}, 1999), they characterize all stable behaviors of this setting for up to three workers. In this work, we extend their analysis for three workers beyond the stable regime, providing a complete description when workers are ordered from the fastest to the slowest. We also show that, due to their restrictive notion of stability, some of their conclusions must be revisited. Finally, for an arbitrary number of workers, we prove that the fixed point is always unique in the no-station setting.

title: A model of anisotropic branched optimal transport
